AAA: An actively managed fund holding the safest, top-rated slices of CLOs, which are bundles of loans to US companies, and the loans pay interest that moves with short-term rates. It is spread over many CLOs, with each of the largest around 4% or 5%.
AAAA: A mix of about 80 percent stocks, with technology leading, and about a sixth bonds, plus some funds that guard against big drops. It's an all-in-one portfolio that leans toward growth, and its protection can cost it gains in rallies.
AAAB: Highly rated corporate bonds: loans to companies rated Aaa down to A, the strongest borrowers, with under ten years until they come due. It is a cautious core bond holding, paying a little more than Treasuries of similar length while keeping credit risk low.
AAAC: Only the highest-rated layer of CLOs, the AAA slice of bundles of business loans, which gets paid first and is last to absorb losses. It aims for income a step above Treasuries with top credit ratings, so the trade-off is complexity rather than obvious credit risk.
AAAD: The safest slice of the CLO market: AAA-rated tranches of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of company loans, priced in dollars. These top tranches pay floating interest and sit first in line for repayment, making this a cautious income holding within a risky-sounding asset class.
AAAP: Bundles of business loans packaged into securities called CLOs, which pay interest from the loan payments and are sliced into layers of risk. It is built for income with yields above ordinary bonds, and the managers can trade actively, though loan defaults are the central risk.
AAAU: Physical gold bars stored in a vault, so you own gold itself rather than mining companies. It's used as a hedge against inflation and market scares, but gold pays no income, and its price can be volatile and stay flat for years.
AADR: Foreign companies traded in the US as ADRs, chosen by Dorsey Wright's momentum method, which favors stocks already rising. The lineup spans banks, drug makers, miners and tech from many countries, and it shifts toward whichever overseas markets are strongest.
AAEQ: A broad mix of US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It's a core stock holding, and the managers tilt toward companies with strong financial quality and value traits, so it won't move exactly like the overall market.
AAPR: Gives exposure to the S&P 500 using options, aiming to protect against a set amount of losses over a two-year period ending April 2028. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only fully applies if you hold for the whole period.
AAPW: Built around one stock, Apple, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying income out every week. With leverage that resets weekly and a single company driving everything, it is meant for short-term trading rather than long-term holding.
AAPY: Aims for income by using options tied to Apple stock, while keeping some exposure to Apple's price moves. It limits how much gain it can capture, and the Treasury bills it holds mostly back those options rather than being the fund's focus.
AAUA: Large US companies, with technology at about 40 percent, chosen by a rules-based approach aiming for broad market exposure with a tilt toward better value. It's a core-style stock holding that moves broadly with the US market, with technology's weight adding some extra swings.
AAUB: US companies chosen by a rules-based formula, with technology about 45 percent and health care, financials and communication companies each around a tenth. It's a core stock holding that leans heavily toward tech, so it can swing more than the broad market.
AAUS: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes and styles, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care next. It's a core stock holding, and the managers lean toward companies with strong financial quality, so it can move a little differently from the overall market.
AAVM: A fund of other ETFs that together apply value and momentum factor investing to smaller companies around the world. It is a systematic, research-driven holding from Alpha Architect that hunts for the long-run factor premiums in global small and mid caps rather than picking individual stocks.
AAXJ: Stocks from Asia's growth economies outside Japan, such as China, Taiwan, India and South Korea, with technology about half and financials under a fifth. It's a way to add emerging Asian growth to a portfolio, but it leaves out Japan and swings more than US stocks.
ABCS: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US stocks, built mostly by holding Vanguard small-cap and mid-cap ETFs. The managers shift the mix with market conditions, so it is not a fixed index fund, and financials and health care are the biggest sectors.
ABEQ: Mostly US stocks that a manager thinks are priced cheaply, led by financials, materials, industrials and energy, plus some bonds and cash. It's a value-focused core holding, and the manager's choices mean it can lag a broad index when growth stocks are leading.
ABFL: An actively managed group of US companies chosen for strong free cash flow, the cash left after paying business expenses. Technology is about a third and health care a fifth, so it's a growth-leaning core holding with a more concentrated mix than the broad market.
ABI: Bonds backed by pools of assets such as loans, leases and other receivables, with a cash portion, actively managed for income. It aims for higher yield than regular bonds, but it carries more credit risk and can fall when borrowers have trouble.
ABIG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the manager sees as high quality, enduring businesses. It is concentrated: Amazon, Alphabet and NVIDIA are each about 10% of the fund.
ABLD: Real asset companies, energy producers and pipelines alongside property owners, chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital in the business. It is an income-leaning bet on physical assets, so it moves with energy prices and property markets more than with the broad stock market.
ABLG: Leading companies outside the US, chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital in the business, currently heavy in Asian and European chipmakers and chip equipment firms. It is a quality-screened foreign holding, so currency moves and the global chip cycle both shape its returns.
ABLS: Small US companies chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital invested in the business, spread across health care, finance, technology and industry. It is a quality-focused way to own small caps, which swing more than big-company stocks, with a screen meant to skip the weakest balance sheets.
ABND: A mix of bonds including corporate bonds, government securities, bonds backed by pools of loans and emerging market debt, run by active managers. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion for stocks, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
ABOT: Innovative large companies chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital invested in the business, currently led by chipmakers, device makers and drug companies. It pairs an innovation theme with a cash-flow quality screen, so it behaves like a growth holding with a financial filter on top.
ABUF: A fund made up of four buffer funds that reset in different quarters, each following SPY up to a cap while shielding against the first 15% of losses. Staggering the start dates smooths out when protection renews, but each piece still limits gains.
ABXB: A flexible bond fund built from Treasury funds of different lengths, shifted around as the managers judge where the value sits along the maturity range. Owning only government debt keeps credit risk near zero, so its results hinge almost entirely on interest rate calls.
ACBE: Swaps following an index of autocallable notes, structured products that pay regular income from stock market exposure and can end early when markets cooperate. This version aims for core portfolio income with a steadier profile than the high income variant, at the cost of lower payouts.
ACBH: Swaps that follow an index of autocallable notes, structured products on stock markets that pay high income and can end early in calm markets. It is built for maximum payouts from that note design, which means capped gains and losses if markets fall hard.
ACEI: Exposure to autocallable notes built on a basket of the largest US stocks, notes that pay income while stocks behave and can return principal early when they rise. The catch is equity like losses if the basket falls past its barrier, an income trade with a cliff edge.
ACEP: US companies picked by active managers as a core portfolio, with technology about a third but unusually large slices of energy, miners and banks alongside. It is a stock picker's blend fund, so its sector mix and results can wander well away from a standard index fund.
ACES: Clean energy companies in the US and Canada: solar panel and inverter makers, wind and geothermal power producers, hydrogen firms and electric vehicle names. It is a focused bet on the energy transition, so it swings with policy support and green energy sentiment.
ACGO: Large US growth companies picked by professional researchers, with technology well over half the fund and a concentrated lineup led by chip and internet giants. It is an active bet on fast-growing businesses, so it swings more than a broad index fund and lives or dies by its stock picks.
ACGR: Large US growth companies, actively picked by American Century's managers, currently led by the giant chip, software and internet names. It is a growth holding whose results depend on stock selection, so it rises and falls harder than the broad market when big growth names swing.
ACHP: Asian semiconductor companies: the chipmakers, foundries and equipment firms of Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and their neighbors, the heartland of world chip production. It is a regional, single-industry bet, so it combines the chip cycle's swings with the political and currency risks of Asia.
ACIG: Growth companies outside the US, picked by Hartford's managers to beat the standard international growth yardstick. The hand-picked approach concentrates on firms seen as the strongest growers abroad, accepting the extra swing that comes with growth styles and foreign markets.
ACII: Mostly cash and short-term holdings paired with options tied to the S&P 500, Russell 2000 and Nasdaq-100. It aims to pay regular income that pays more if stocks hold up, and it can lose money if those indexes fall past a set level.
ACIO: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, protected by an options collar, which is a pair of options that limits both losses and gains. It's built for a smoother ride in stock markets, so it should fall less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
ACIV: Value stocks outside the US, picked by an active process hunting underpriced companies across developed and emerging markets, with industrials the biggest slice. It aims to catch value abroad that plain indexes miss, accepting currency swings and a mix that can look quite different from foreign benchmarks.
ACKY: About twenty US stocks copied from the publicly disclosed holdings of a prominent activist investor, plus an options program targeting a 15 percent yearly distribution rate. It lets anyone shadow a famous activist portfolio, with the options adding income and some drag on gains.
ACLC: Large US companies across industries, actively picked by American Century's managers, with the giant technology and internet companies prominent at the top. It is a core-style stock holding whose results depend on the managers' research rather than index weights, so it will not move exactly with the market.
ACLO: The safest top-rated slices of loan bundles called CLOs, which are pools of loans to lower-rated companies. It's meant for steady income above cash with small price swings, and its interest adjusts with rates, but it can still dip in market panics.
ACMG: Midsize US growth companies, chosen with American Century's insights models that look for firms whose earnings growth is strengthening. Midsize growers can become tomorrow's large companies, so the fund aims for that runway, accepting bigger swings than a large-company fund along the way.
ACOM: Raw materials of all kinds: energy, metals and farm goods, reached through futures contracts rather than owning the goods themselves. Managers actively shift the mix, so it can act as a diversifier beside stocks and bonds, though commodity prices are famously jumpy.
ACQQ: Exposure to a laddered set of autocallable notes on the Nasdaq-100, structured products that pay income while the index behaves and can end early. Laddering spreads the notes across many start dates, and the tech-heavy index underneath makes this income stream livelier than broad market versions.
ACRT: Autocallable notes tied to the Russell 2000 small-cap index, replicated through an index of staggered weekly notes that pay income and can end early. It is structured income on small-caps: payouts depend on the index staying above set levels, and sharp small-cap drops can cut the notes' value.
ACSG: Small US growth companies picked with a mix of hands on research and systematic, risk aware portfolio building, led by health care and technology. It hunts future mid sized winners early, so it carries the bigger swings and occasional wipeouts that come with small company investing.
ACSI: Large US companies that score well in customer satisfaction surveys, with communication, consumer and financial companies the biggest groups. It's a core-style stock holding built on a quality idea, so it can differ from the broad market.
ACSM: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen by Hartford's alpha capture process, which gathers ideas from across its investment teams into one portfolio. It aims to beat the Russell 2500 group of smaller companies through breadth of ideas rather than a few big bets.
ACSP: Exposure to an index that recreates autocallable notes on the big US stock index: structured payoffs that produce income while markets cooperate. It packages a strategy usually sold as bank notes into a tradable fund, with the same quirk that sharp market falls can turn income into losses.
ACSV: Small US companies bought at value prices, chosen by American Century managers combining hands-on fundamental research with systematic, risk-aware construction. Banks lead at about 29 percent, and the design aims for a steadier small value holding than the rough-and-tumble small-cap indexes usually deliver.
ACTS: An actively managed fund of stocks from the US and abroad, including emerging markets, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Bloom Energy and Amkor Technology each around 6% and a tilt toward technology and industrials.
ACVF: Large US companies chosen for passing a politically conservative screen, with technology the biggest slice at over 40 percent. It lets investors line up holdings with their values, and it looks fairly similar to the broad market, though the screen leaves some companies out.
ACVT: Convertible securities, the hybrid bonds that pay interest but can turn into stock when the issuer's shares rise, mostly from US companies. They offer a middle path: bond like income with a built in share of stock upside, and less downside cushion than their fans sometimes expect.
ACVU: US companies picked for value with a systematic twist: Hartford's process hunts for stocks whose prices lag the strength of their businesses. It is a core-style holding tilted toward cheaper companies, so it tends to trail when expensive growth stocks are leading the market.
ACWI: Stocks from around the world, from the US to developed and emerging markets, with technology the largest slice at about a third. It's a one-fund core holding for global stock exposure, though the US still makes up the biggest share.
ACWV: Stocks from developed and emerging countries picked to be less jumpy than the global market, led by technology, financials and health care. It's meant to give worldwide stock exposure with a smoother ride, though it usually trails when risky stocks surge higher.
ACWX: Stocks from developed and emerging countries around the world, everywhere except the US, with financials about a quarter and technology about a fifth. It's meant to round out a US-heavy portfolio with global exposure, and it moves with foreign economies and currencies rather than the American market.
ACYB: A ladder of autocallable contracts, rolled at staggered times, that pay income while the market behaves and build in a buffer against moderate drops. Autocallables can be called away early and cap gains, so it is a structured, income-first product rather than a simple stock or bond holding.
ACYN: Notes that pay income and end early if a stock index holds above a set level, backed mostly by cash and bonds. It's meant for high monthly income, but gains are capped and it can lose money if the market falls too far.
ACYQ: A fund that uses swaps and options to mimic autocallable yield notes, which pay high income but can end early or lose value if the market falls past a set barrier. The Treasury holdings are collateral, and the strategy is complex and tied to market moves.
ACYS: A fund using swap contracts to deliver income tied to a laddered set of structured notes that pay out unless markets fall past a set level. It's built for high income, and the catch is that a sharp stock market drop can cut or wipe out those payments.
ADIV: Dividend paying companies across the Asia Pacific region, led by banks with technology and consumer firms behind, all picked for sustainable payouts. It targets income from Asia's growing economies, so it mixes yield with exposure to currencies and markets that swing more than US stocks.
ADME: Large US stocks with technology the biggest piece at about forty percent, plus protective put options that pay off when markets fall. It's built for investors who want stock growth with a softer landing, but the cost of that protection means it trails in strong rallies.
ADPV: Large US companies, with health care near a third, then technology, financials and energy. The managers aim to own stocks when the market trends upward and can move to safer assets in downturns, so it's built for growth with some protection, but it may miss part of rebounds.
ADVE: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying companies in Asia. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 22% of it, and technology and financials each make up about 30%, so it leans on a few big Asian companies.
AEMC: Mid-sized US companies across technology, industrials, financials and health care, picked as a core middle-tier holding. It is actively managed exposure to the market's middle: mid-caps offer more growth room than giants, and the near-even spread across sectors keeps any one industry from dominating.
AEMG: Mid-sized growth companies, led by technology at about 40%, with industrials, health care and consumer stocks behind it. It is an actively managed growth holding in the market's middle tier: mid-cap growers can compound faster than giants, but they also swing more.
AEMV: Mid-sized companies trading at value prices, spread fairly evenly across financials, health care, industrials and technology. It is an actively managed value holding in the market's middle tier: the even sector spread keeps it balanced, and it tends to lag when growth stocks lead.
AESB: Small companies across financials, health care, technology and industrials, picked as a core small-cap holding. It is actively managed exposure to the market's smallest tier: small companies offer the most growth room and diversification across sectors, with bigger swings than large stocks.
AESG: Small growth companies, with health care the biggest slice at about a quarter, followed by technology, financials and industrials. It is an actively managed growth bet on smaller firms: they have the most room to grow, and the widest swings to go with it.
AESL: Small companies trading at value prices, led by financials at over a quarter, with real estate, industrials and health care behind it. It is an actively managed bargain hunt in the market's smallest tier: value small-caps can be overlooked gems, but they can also stay cheap for years.
AESR: US stocks that managers shift among industries, currently led by technology at over a third, with financials, industrials and health care next. It's a hands-on stock fund that aims to lean into whichever sectors look strongest, so it can differ a lot from the broad market.
AFDM: Stocks of companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, picked actively using several measures like value and momentum. It adds international diversification to a portfolio, but results can drift from a plain foreign index since it is not just market weighted.
AFEM: Emerging market companies chosen with an active factor approach, tilting toward technology at over two-fifths of the fund, mostly Asian chipmakers and internet firms. It aims to beat plain developing-market index funds by emphasizing the traits its managers believe drive returns there.
AFGR: Large US growth companies picked by several specialist management teams working side by side, with technology over half the fund. Using multiple managers is the point: it blends different stock-picking styles into one growth fund, softening the risk of any single team being wrong.
AFIF: A flexible mix of corporate bonds, government debt and preferred shares, which are stock-like securities that pay set dividends. It aims for broad income from many parts of the bond market, though its prices fall when interest rates rise and riskier holdings can slip in a downturn.
AFIX: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds, including corporate, mortgage-backed and government-related debt, with a small slice of foreign issuers paid in dollars. It's meant as a steady income core and a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
AFK: Companies across Africa, from South African and Moroccan banks to gold and copper miners and telecom firms, with materials and financials each about a third. It is one of the few single-continent bets available, tied to African growth, commodity prices and often fragile currencies.
AFLG: Large US companies picked by a manager's rules that look for strong momentum, quality and good value, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's a core stock holding that tilts toward appealing stocks, so it can differ from the broad market.
AFMC: Mid-sized US companies picked by a rules-based screen, with industrials and technology each about a fifth, plus consumer and financial firms. It's a core-style holding for the middle of the market, tilted toward stocks with strong recent momentum and quality traits.
AFOS: US stocks the manager considers high quality, with strong balance sheets and reasonable earnings growth, led by technology and industrials with energy and materials behind. It's an actively managed core stock holding with a focused list, so it can behave differently from the broad market.
AFSC: An actively managed fund holding a limited number of US small-cap stocks that the manager has strong conviction in. The biggest holdings are each about 3%, and health care, financials and industrials lead.
AFSM: Small US companies spread across health care, technology, financials and industrials, picked by managers using factors like value, quality and momentum. It's built for long-term growth from smaller firms, and it tends to swing more than large company funds, especially in downturns.
AGEM: Emerging market companies that pay dividends, led by technology and financials, with communication and industrials behind them. It's meant for income plus growth from developing economies, and it swings more than US stocks, partly due to local currencies.
AGG: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It is meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
AGGA: An actively allocated bundle of bond funds covering corporate debt, Treasuries of different maturities, high yield bonds and top-rated loan bundles. Managers move the mix as rates and credit shift, making it a flexible core bond holding rather than a fixed slice of the bond market.
AGGB: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds issued in the US. It is the classic core bond holding, meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
AGGH: Investment-grade US bonds held mainly through other bond funds, plus options and other tools meant to manage risk or boost income. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, and the extra strategies mean it can behave differently from a plain bond index.
AGGM: A broad mix of US bonds with one to ten years left: Treasuries, agency debt, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds. It's a core bond holding for income and stability, and because it skips the longest bonds, it swings less when interest rates change than a full bond market fund.
AGGS: A disciplined core bond portfolio of US dollar debt: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and company bonds, chosen within strict risk limits. It aims to be a portfolio's steady anchor, with the managers adjusting the mix as rates and credit conditions change.
AGGY: The broad US investment-grade bond market, meaning Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, adjusted to lean toward bonds that pay a bit more income. It works as a core bond holding and cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
AGIQ: A fund of US-listed companies working on agentic AI, meaning software that can carry out tasks on its own. It tracks a rules-based index and is mostly technology, with Alphabet, Qualcomm, NVIDIA and Palo Alto Networks each at about 7%.
AGIX: Technology-focused companies riding the artificial intelligence boom, with technology about 70% and communication, consumer and financial companies adding the rest. It can include some private companies, and it's a concentrated growth bet that swings more than the broad market.
AGMI: A fund of silver mining companies around the world, following an index of firms with major exposure to silver. Newmont, Fresnillo and Penoles are about 29% of it, so it tends to rise and fall with the silver business.
AGNG: Companies serving the world's aging population: drugmakers, medical device firms, health insurers and the owners of senior housing and care facilities, mostly in health care. It is a demographic bet on longer lives needing more medicine and care, steadier than most theme funds.
AGOX: A flexible mix of stock funds from around the world, led by technology and industrials, with a large cash position that changes with the manager's view. It aims for growth while stepping back from risk at times, so how much it swings depends on how much is in cash.
AGQI: Dividend paying companies around the world, chosen for quality and income across technology, banks, industrials and everyday consumer brands. It aims for a global income stream from stocks rather than bonds, so it still moves like a stock fund, just with a steadier, payer focused tilt.
AGRW: Large US growth companies, with technology over half and communication companies next. It's built for long-term growth, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market, and it has little exposure to slower, older industries.
AGZ: Short-to-medium term bonds issued by US government agencies, such as the mortgage-finance and farm-credit lenders. It's a low-risk place for steady income, and it moves little when stocks fall, but it pays less than corporate bonds.
AGZD: The broad US investment-grade bond market, with short positions in Treasuries added to offset the damage when interest rates rise. It's meant for bond income with less rate sensitivity, though it can lag when rates fall and bonds rally.
AHBM: Holds about ten Asian companies that make memory chips and related equipment, following an index of the sector. It is very concentrated, with SK hynix alone about a quarter of the fund, so it rides on one corner of the chip industry.
AHD: A portfolio of autocallable notes tied to Robinhood stock, structured products that pay high income while the stock behaves and can end early. If Robinhood falls hard and stays down, the notes can lose sharply, so the income carries real risk.
AHIC: Short-term corporate bonds with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, paying higher interest because the issuers are riskier. It's meant for extra income with less rate sensitivity than longer high-yield funds, but it can still fall along with stocks in downturns.
AHLT: A computer-driven strategy that bets on price trends, up or down, across stocks, bonds and currencies in over 20 markets using futures. It's meant as a diversifier that can do well when stocks fall, but it can lose money when markets reverse quickly.
AHYB: An actively managed fund of US junk bonds, meaning corporate bonds from lower-rated companies that pay higher interest for higher risk. It does not follow an index, and spreads its money across many bonds, none above about 1%.
AHYM: Bonds from state and local governments and their projects, with a focus on lower-rated, higher-paying ones whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It's built for tax-advantaged income, but the lower credit quality means it can fall harder than safer municipal bonds when markets get nervous.
AIA: Large companies across Asia outside Japan, with technology well over half, financials about a fifth, and the rest in consumer and communication firms. It's a way to add Asian growth to a portfolio, but it leans heavily on tech and swings more than the broad world market.
AIBF: US companies expected to profit from artificial intelligence by using it, not building it, led by health care, then consumer staples, industrials and consumer discretionary. It's a growth idea that avoids the usual chip makers, so it looks very different from typical AI funds.
AIBN: Corporate bonds issued by the companies building AI infrastructure, such as data center operators and the power and technology firms behind them. It is a way to lend to the AI buildout instead of owning its stocks, trading stock market upside for steadier interest payments.
AICH: Chinese companies building artificial intelligence, from chip and software firms to the platforms applying AI, mostly technology with some industrials. It is a single-country AI bet: it concentrates on China's tech race, so trade tensions and Chinese regulation hit it directly.
AIED: Large US stocks chosen by a momentum model driven by a large language model that scans for catalysts like earnings news and analyst shifts. Technology dominates at about 72 percent, and the AI-run selection makes it a fast-moving growth holding that can change its lineup as the news flow changes.
AIEQ: US stocks chosen by an artificial intelligence model that scans company data for promising picks, spread across technology, media, finance and industry, with technology the biggest slice at about a third. It is a bet on machine stock picking rather than human managers, so its lineup can change sharply as the model shifts.
AIFD: Companies the manager says are building or benefiting from artificial intelligence, with technology about three quarters and some communication and industrial firms. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
AIFR: Semiconductor foundries: the contract factories in Taiwan, the US and elsewhere that manufacture chips designed by other companies. It is a focused bet on chipmaking capacity rather than chip design, so it depends on global demand for outsourced manufacturing and on heavy spending for new plants.
AIHY: An actively managed fund focused on US-listed companies building the huge data centers behind artificial intelligence. It is very concentrated: Microsoft and Meta are each over 20% of it, and a large chunk sits in a government money market fund.
AIMG: Ten publicly traded companies at the center of the artificial intelligence value chain, from chips and cloud platforms to the software built on them. It is a concentrated AI bet: only ten names carry the whole fund, so it swings hard with the AI trade.
AIMS: Small US companies picked by active managers, spread across industrial, technology, health care and financial firms with no single holding dominating. Small caps offer more room to grow and more risk, and this fund's stock selection aims to find the durable growers among thousands of small names.
AINF: Companies making the chips that run artificial intelligence models after they are trained, the inference stage where AI answers questions in data centers and devices. It is a narrow bet on one stage of the AI buildout, separate from the firms that design the biggest training processors.
AINP: A mix of bonds from companies and governments, including some from emerging markets and lower-rated issuers. It's meant for higher income than a plain bond fund, and the extra yield comes with more risk, so it can fall in credit scares.
AINT: An actively managed fund that uses artificial intelligence to pick US large company stocks to buy and others to bet against, keeping the two sides about equal in size. It aims to earn returns that do not depend on the market going up.
AIOO: Options on the S&P 500 in a maximum protection design set for one year outcome periods: the fund is built to shield against losses on large US stocks in exchange for capped gains. It aims for peace of mind over performance, so strong bull markets will leave it far behind.
AIPI: Artificial intelligence related companies, almost entirely technology, paired with an options strategy that trades away some upside for monthly income. It's for income from a focused tech theme, and it trails in strong rallies while still dropping when AI stocks fall.
AIPO: Companies that build the power and computing backbone for artificial intelligence: industrial firms making grid equipment and data center components make up over half, with chip and computing hardware, utilities and energy filling out the rest. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
AIQ: Companies building or using artificial intelligence and big data, with technology about 70% of the fund and the rest in communication, consumer and industrial firms. It's a focused growth bet on the AI theme, so it can swing more than the broad market when tech sentiment shifts.
AIQD: An inverse leveraged bet against artificial intelligence stocks: an exchange-traded note designed to deliver three times the opposite of an AI index's daily move. It resets daily and is built for very short trades, so holding it in a rising or choppy market can grind its value down fast.
AIQU: A leveraged bet on artificial intelligence stocks: an exchange-traded note designed to deliver three times the daily move of an AI index. The leverage resets daily, so it is built for short-term trades, and in choppy markets the daily reset can grind its value down even when the index ends flat.
AIRR: Small and mid-sized US companies that make and build things, with industrials nearly 90%, including machinery, construction and engineering firms. It's a focused bet on the American industrial comeback, and because these firms are smaller, it swings more than the broad market.
AIS: Global companies at the heart of the artificial intelligence build-out, with technology over 90%, such as chip, software and hardware makers. It's a concentrated growth bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
AIUP: Large US companies chosen and managed with the help of artificial intelligence models, heavily weighted to technology at about 70 percent. The AI-driven stock picking sets it apart from human-managed funds, aiming to spot patterns in data that people might miss.
AIVC: Technology companies tied to artificial intelligence, such as chips, software and cloud computing, with each company given the same weight. It's a focused bet on the AI theme, and equal weighting means smaller names count as much as giants, so it swings more than the broad market.
AIVI: Value-priced stocks from developed markets outside the US and Canada, with computer models using AI to help pick and weight them. It leans toward banks, with Financials about 38% of it, plus energy and tobacco names.
AIVL: US mid-sized companies that look cheap compared to their worth, with technology and financials at about a fifth each. It uses a computer model to choose stocks, so it works as a value holding that can lag when growth stocks lead.
AIX: One hundred US companies picked for having an AI moat, meaning a position in artificial intelligence that rivals would find hard to copy. Technology is about seven-tenths of the fund, so it is a growth bet on AI winners that swings more than the broad market.
AIYY: An options income strategy tied to a small artificial intelligence software company, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting premiums for payouts. It is an income play on one speculative, fast moving stock, with gains capped and losses largely open.
AJAN: Options giving exposure to the S&P 500 over a fixed two year window ending in January 2028, built to shield the value from market losses over that span. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and it only works as designed if held for the whole period.
AJUL: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a two-year outcome period that ends in July. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, and the longer two-year window sets it apart from yearly versions.
AKAF: Stocks from countries on the world's economic frontier, meaning smaller emerging markets that are earlier in their development, spread across many industries. It is a high-risk growth holding: these markets can grow fast but tend to swing hard and can be harder to trade.
AKRE: A concentrated group of US stocks, with financials and technology each about 43%, chosen by an active manager looking for businesses that can grow for many years. Because it holds so few names, it can look very different from the market and swing both ways.
ALAI: Companies expected to benefit from artificial intelligence, with technology just under sixty percent, then communication, consumer and industrial firms. It's a growth bet on one theme, actively managed, and it swings more than the broad market.
ALDB: A fund made up of four other deep buffer funds, each starting in a different quarter, all tied to the S&P 500. Each aims to absorb a set amount of losses over a year, in exchange for capped gains, and the four are held in equal parts.
ALIL: A focused portfolio of small US companies Argent managers judge to be high quality with durable competitive advantages, spread across technology, industry and finance. It is a selective small-cap holding that favors proven, well-run businesses over the speculative end of the small company universe.
ALLW: A mix of bonds, stocks and other assets, with bonds the largest part, balanced to hold up across booming, slow, inflationary and falling price conditions. It's meant as a steadier, all-weather core holding, using borrowing that can magnify moves in the bond portion.
ALRG: An actively managed fund of large US companies, picked with a focus on quality businesses held for the long term. It is tilted to technology, and Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet together make up about 20% of the fund.
ALTL: Large US stocks that alternate between two ready-made lineups, a defensive low-volatility portfolio and a more aggressive one, switching with a rules-based risk signal. It is currently in its defensive stance, leaning on utilities and property firms, and the alternating design sets it apart.
ALTY: Five flavors of alternative income in one fund: real estate trusts, energy partnerships, preferred shares, option strategies and other high payout assets from around the world. It collects income from corners a normal stock and bond mix misses, though its holdings can be volatile and complex.
AMAX: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other ETFs across stocks, bonds and other assets, with hedging to soften swings and aim for income. About a fifth of it is a long-term Treasury bond ETF.
AMDW: A short-term trade on AMD, one company's shares, aiming for about 1.2 times the weekly move in the stock, with weekly payouts. It resets each week and uses leverage, so it's for short holding periods, and it can lose a lot quickly if AMD falls.
AMDY: An options strategy built around AMD, a single chip company, designed to pay out regular income instead of simply holding the stock. It earns monthly income from selling options, but it gives up much of AMD's upside and can still lose heavily if the stock falls.
AMEI: Dividend-paying companies chosen under Islamic investing principles, spread across technology, industrials and health care. The faith-based rules exclude banks and interest-heavy businesses, so it aims for equity income and steady payouts in a way that follows Sharia guidelines.
AMEM: Companies in developing countries, picked under Islamic investing principles, with technology close to half the fund and materials and health care behind. The faith-based screen leaves out banks and other interest-based businesses, giving emerging-market growth exposure that follows Sharia rules.
AMGR: Growth stocks chosen under Islamic investing principles, led by technology at about half the fund, with industrial and health care companies behind it. The faith-based screen rules out banks and other interest-driven businesses, so it offers growth exposure that follows Sharia guidelines.
AMHI: High income municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt from riskier local projects and authorities, industrial development deals, gas agencies and health and education facilities. The interest is generally free of federal tax, and the higher yield comes from borrowers a cautious muni fund would avoid.
AMID: Mid-sized US companies a manager believes are going through positive change, led by industrials, technology and financials. It's for adding mid-cap growth to a portfolio, and because it's actively picked, it can differ from a standard mid-cap index.
AMJB: Pipeline and energy storage partnerships in North America, packaged as a bank-issued note rather than a regular fund. It's for income from the energy infrastructure industry, and because it's a note, it also depends on the issuing bank's ability to pay, on top of swings in energy markets.
AMLP: Pipeline and energy infrastructure partnerships that move and store oil and gas, earning fees on volume rather than prices alone. It's built for high income, but it's structured as a corporation, so it pays tax itself and is a narrow bet on one industry.
AMMO: Companies in the defense supply chain, from weapons and vehicle makers to the parts and electronics suppliers behind them, mostly industrials with some technology. It is a focused bet on military spending: it rises and falls with defense budgets rather than the broad economy.
AMYY: An options income fund built around AMD, using derivatives on an AMD ETF rather than owning the shares directly. It aims to pay high income by selling options, which limits how much it gains if AMD rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing.
AMZA: Pipeline and energy infrastructure partnerships called MLPs, which move oil and gas and often pay large income. The fund borrows to boost its income, so it swings more than the broad market and is closely tied to energy demand and prices.
AMZP: An options income strategy on a single stock, Amazon, using contracts tied to its shares while most assets sit in Treasury bills. It pays regular distributions from selling options, but gains are capped and it rides entirely on Amazon's stock.
AMZW: Built around one stock, Amazon, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying income weekly. It is a trading tool on a single giant company, with leverage resetting every week and swings to match.
AMZY: A fund centered on Amazon's stock, built with options and Treasuries rather than owning the shares directly. It aims for high monthly income, but it gives up much of Amazon's upside and still falls when the stock drops.
ANG: Fallen angels: corporate bonds that were once rated investment grade and have since been downgraded to high yield, from US and Canadian issuers. The idea is that downgraded companies often work hard to win their good ratings back, so the fund buys their debt at the cheaper, riskier price.
ANGL: Bonds from companies that once had investment-grade ratings but were later cut to junk, which often leaves them priced cheaply. It's built for higher income than safe bonds, though it tends to fall with stocks when the economy weakens.
ANGU: Large US companies chosen by a research based screen, with technology around 40% and communication, financials and health care each near a tenth. It's a core US stock holding with a tilt toward companies the model rates well, so it can differ from the plain market.
ANTW: Companies in the ecosystem of Anthropic, the AI lab: its cloud partners, backers, suppliers and customers most exposed to its technology. Technology and finance names lead, and it is an unusually narrow theme, a bet on one AI company's orbit rather than the whole artificial intelligence field.
ANV: A note-like bet on NVIDIA stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or rises. If NVIDIA falls hard, the fund can drop sharply too, and its steady payouts come with a ceiling on gains.
AOA: A ready-made mix of about 80 percent stocks and 20 percent bonds, built from other funds that cover US and international companies. It's meant as a one-fund growth portfolio with a small bond cushion, and it still falls meaningfully in stock market declines.
AOCT: Options on the S&P 500 set for a two year outcome period ending in October 2028, designed to protect against losses on large US stocks over that whole stretch in exchange for capped gains. The longer term suits investors who want protection planned years ahead, not reset annually.
AOHY: Mostly bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay higher interest because they carry more risk of default. It's for investors seeking extra income, but it can fall in recessions when weaker companies struggle, and it's actively managed.
AOK: A ready-made mix of roughly two thirds bonds and one third stocks, spread across many countries. It's a conservative, all-in-one holding for people who want modest growth with a cushion, and it will fall less than an all-stock fund in a sell-off but also rise less.
AOM: A ready-made mix of about 60 percent bonds and 40 percent stocks, built from other index funds. It's meant as a one-fund, cautious portfolio, and the bond share means it should swing less than an all-stock fund but also grow more slowly in strong rallies.
AOR: A ready-made mix of about 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, built from other funds. It's meant as a one-fund core holding with a moderate amount of risk, so it should fall less than an all-stock fund in a downturn and also rise less in a rally.
AOTG: Actively picked growth companies built on business models where serving one more customer costs very little, mostly software and chip firms, with technology about seven-tenths of the fund. It is a concentrated growth bet, so a handful of big positions drives results and swings can be sharp.
APCB: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, mostly government and corporate, managed with a blend of active picks and index tracking. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income that cushions a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
APDB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each April to absorb a large share of a market fall over the following year. In exchange the upside is limited, so it is built for cautious investors who fear a big drop.
APIE: Large international companies, mostly foreign firms traded in the US as ADRs, spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a core way to own stocks outside the US, blending a hands-off index approach with some manager choices to try to beat its benchmark.
APLU: A broad mix of mostly US bonds, with room for some lower-quality and foreign bonds that earn extra interest. It's meant as a core bond holding with a bit more income than a standard bond fund, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
APLY: Exposure to Apple stock combined with an options strategy that sells some upside for monthly income, with most assets held in Treasuries and cash. It's for income from a single company, so it falls when Apple drops and trails when Apple rallies strongly.
APMU: Municipal bonds from US states and cities with short to medium maturities, mixing active and passive management. It's meant for steady income that is typically free from federal income tax, which suits higher earners, and its price can dip when interest rates rise.
APOC: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over each six-month period, April to October. In exchange, gains are capped, so protection resets every period and depends on timing.
APRB: Options on a fund of the largest US companies create a defined outcome over the year from April, under Aptus managers' buffer design. It aims to soften losses with a built-in buffer while keeping a share of gains up to a cap, and the terms reset each April.
APRH: Treasury bills paired with options on the big US stock index that pay a defined income stream unless the index falls through a 20 percent barrier during the year from April. It is built for income with a deep cushion, though crossing the barrier puts principal at risk.
APRJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the big US stock index that pay a defined income stream unless the index falls through a 30 percent barrier during the year from April. It is built for income with a deep cushion, though crossing the barrier puts principal at risk.
APRP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every April.
APRT: Options on the S&P 500 set each April for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. Like other buffer funds it trades strong rally potential for a known cushion, and the terms reset every April.
APRW: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that start a new one-year period each April. It's built as a cushion against drops, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses, but gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if you hold through the whole period.
APRZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb part of a decline over an outcome period that restarts each April, while surrendering a slice of gains. The actively managed structure tries to keep that protection intact as markets move during the period.
APUE: A broad slice of the whole US stock market, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and consumer companies making up much of the rest. It's built as a core stock holding, and managers blend index-style holdings with active picks to try to edge past the market.
APXM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each April. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
AQEC: High-quality US companies expected to grow over time, with technology about a third, followed by communication and health care. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and the manager's picks mean it can differ from the broad market.
AQLG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, meaning firms expected to grow faster than average, picked by HCM. The facts on its exact holdings are limited, so it is best read as a stock picker's large-cap growth fund.
AQLT: Large companies around the world with strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, with technology over 40% and health care next. It's a core holding favoring financially healthy firms, so it can trail in rallies led by riskier, lower-quality stocks.
AQWA: Companies that supply clean water: utilities that treat and deliver it, plus makers of pipes, pumps, meters and treatment equipment. Industrials and utilities split the fund, making it a steadier infrastructure-style theme than most single-industry bets.
ARB: Companies in the middle of being bought out, bought at a small discount to the price the acquirer has agreed to pay. It profits when deals close as planned, a strategy meant to earn steady gains unrelated to the stock market's direction, though a collapsed deal can sting.
ARCM: Very short term bonds, mostly maturing within two years, all investment grade, including mortgage and asset backed securities. It is a cash like holding with a bit more yield, managed carefully to keep price swings tiny for money that cannot afford surprises.
ARCP: A core bond holding with room to reach beyond plain vanilla: corporate bonds, government debt, mortgage and asset backed securities, mostly high quality. The plus is flexibility to hunt for extra yield around the edges, which adds a little more risk than a strict core fund.
ARGT: Argentine companies, led by consumer businesses at about 28%, then energy, financials and materials. It's a concentrated bet on one emerging country, so it swings widely with local politics, inflation and currency moves.
ARIA: A concentrated, actively managed fund holding only about 20 to 35 stocks from the US and abroad. Dell Technologies alone is roughly 27% of it, and technology is over half the fund, so a few companies drive most of the results.
ARKB: Holds actual bitcoin rather than company shares or bonds, so its price follows the price of bitcoin. It's a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and it swings sharply, with no income and no cushion from other assets.
ARKD: Exposure to an actively managed innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the first quarter, softening part of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on an already volatile growth fund, so the cushion matters more than the cap.
ARKE: Exposure to a flagship innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the third quarter, designed to take part in only half of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on a volatile growth fund, softening its famous swings.
ARKF: Companies reshaping money and payments, such as online payment, digital banking and crypto-related firms, split between technology and financials. It's a bet on financial technology, so it swings much more than the broad market, and a manager actively picks the stocks.
ARKG: Companies tied to genetics and biotech, such as gene editing, diagnostics and drug discovery, all in health care. It's a high risk bet on a single industry that is actively managed, so it swings far more than the broad market and can drop sharply.
ARKI: Exposure to an actively managed innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the second quarter, softening part of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on an already volatile growth fund, so the cushion matters more than the cap.
ARKK: Companies a manager believes are being reshaped by new technology, spread across health care, technology, financials and consumer firms. It's a high-risk growth bet on disruptive ideas, so it swings far more than the broad market, rising sharply in good times and falling hard in bad ones.
ARKQ: Companies working on self-driving vehicles, robots, drones and automation, mostly industrials and technology with some consumer companies. It's a focused growth bet on emerging technology, managed actively, so it swings much more than the broad market.
ARKT: Exposure to an actively managed innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the fourth quarter, softening part of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on an already volatile growth fund, so the cushion matters more than the cap.
ARKW: Companies tied to the internet, cloud computing, digital payments and crypto, with technology about half and financials, consumer and communication firms making up most of the rest. It's an actively managed growth bet that swings far more than the broad market.
ARKX: Companies tied to space and defense, mostly industrials such as aerospace, with technology about a quarter. It's an actively managed bet on a narrow theme, so it swings more than the broad market and owns well-known stocks and small risky ones.
ARKY: It builds income by mimicking autocallable notes, a kind of structured bet on individual stocks that pays regular income unless the stocks fall hard. This is a complex, engineered product: returns come from selling downside risk, so losses can arrive suddenly in a sell-off.
ARLI: Tracks international developed-markets stocks through options on an EFA ETF, with a buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set period ending in March 2027. Unlike capped versions, this one has no cap on gains.
ARLU: Options on the S&P 500 set each April for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual cap for a slow start on gains, a different shape of downside protection.
ARMH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of Arm, the British company whose chip designs sit inside nearly every smartphone. A built-in currency hedge softens moves between the pound and the dollar, so the fund follows Arm itself more purely.
ARMS: Income bonds from many corners of the market: company bonds of all credit grades, mortgage and asset backed bonds, and government debt, picked actively by the manager. Spreading across sectors aims for a higher yield than plain core bond funds, with more credit risk riding along.
ARMW: Built around one stock, Arm Holdings, the chip designer, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move plus weekly income payments. Everything depends on a single, richly priced chip stock, so it is a short-term trading tool with big swings.
ARMY: An actively managed fund of defense and aerospace companies from outside the US, such as Rocket Lab, Elbit Systems, Kongsberg and Hensoldt. It is a concentrated bet on one industry, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 7%.
ARP: A risk parity approach that balances stocks, bonds, commodities and gold so each contributes similar risk, then adapts the mix to broad economic trends. Right now commodities carry the largest weight, and the balancing act aims for steadier results across booms and busts alike.
ARTY: Companies expected to benefit from artificial intelligence, such as chip designers, software and cloud firms, with technology about 85%. It's a focused growth bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop hard if AI enthusiasm fades.
ARVR: Companies supporting the metaverse, meaning virtual and augmented reality, such as chipmakers and tech platforms, tracked by the Indxx Metaverse Index. Micron, AMD, Intel and STMicroelectronics are all in the top holdings, and the fund is mostly technology and communication stocks.
ARWG: US growth companies of many sizes, led by technology, with industry, health care and consumer names behind, including special situations the managers expect to be revalued. It is a broad growth hunt that depends on stock picking more than sector calls.
ASCE: US small and mid-sized companies, led by technology, health care, financials and consumer businesses at about a fifth or less each. It's an actively managed core holding for growth from smaller companies, which tend to swing more than large ones, with a small slice allowed abroad.
ASCI: An actively managed fund of small companies outside the US, picked by abrdn's managers. It is widely spread, with the top names like Diploma, ASICS and Hill & Smith each at about 4%, and it leans toward industrials.
ASD: Companies supporting the autism community worldwide: therapy and education providers, diagnostic and treatment developers, and researchers serving neurodivergent people. It is an impact-themed health care bet: most of the fund is health care stocks, chosen for their role in one cause rather than broad returns.
ASEA: The 40 largest companies in Southeast Asia across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, with banks taking nearly two-thirds of the fund. It is a regional bet dominated by Singapore's big banks, so it behaves more like a financial fund than its name suggests.
ASEC: Securitized bonds backed by less common loan types: aircraft and equipment leases, consumer loans, cell tower leases and data infrastructure. It looks for investment grade income away from plain mortgages and corporate bonds, so the holdings take effort to evaluate.
ASGM: An actively managed fund that tries to profit from big economic trends across global markets, using stock, bond and other positions. It aims to limit losses in rough markets, and a large part of it is held in broad index funds like the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF.
ASHR: Large mainland Chinese companies listed on China's domestic exchanges, with technology and financials leading and industrials and materials next. It's a focused bet on China's domestic market, which can swing more than global stocks and is heavily affected by Chinese policy.
ASHS: Five hundred smaller companies listed on mainland China's own exchanges, spread across technology, industry and materials. These A-shares are the domestic Chinese market foreigners rarely reach directly, with all the volatility and government influence that comes with it.
ASIA: Companies across Asia with Japan left out, picked actively, with chipmakers and other technology firms about half the fund and banks next. It is a growth bet on Asia's biggest economies, including China, Taiwan, Korea and India, run by a specialist in the region.
ASLV: Large US companies the managers think are undervalued, spread over technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's a value-minded core holding, and it can trail in growth-led rallies since it avoids expensive stocks.
ASMF: A managed futures program trading trends across stock, bond, currency and commodity markets worldwide, using futures and forwards. AlphaSimplex's models ride sustained moves in either direction, aiming to profit in crises when ordinary portfolios usually suffer together.
ASMH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of ASML, the Dutch company that makes the machines used to print advanced computer chips. A built-in currency hedge dampens euro and dollar swings, leaving the fund riding on one vital company in the chip supply chain.
ASTM: Municipal bonds from state and local governments whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, mostly in the short term. It's meant for tax-friendly income, though a portion is in lower-rated bonds, which adds more risk than top-quality muni funds.
AT: The muscles of robots: makers of actuators, motors and precision motion parts, mostly Japanese and US industrial companies, that let machines move. It is a narrow slice of the robotics industry rather than the whole field, so it lives or dies on factory automation spending.
ATC: Autocallable notes tied to a single stock, Coinbase, the crypto exchange, structured to pay income and potentially end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with fine print: everything rides on one crypto-linked stock whose price already swings with the whole crypto market.
ATCL: Exposure to synthetic autocallable notes through an index of them, notes that pay income while the underlying stocks cooperate and can be called away early when they rise. The income is the draw; the hidden risk is steep losses if stocks fall past the notes' barriers.
ATFV: Around 35 companies of any size, with technology half of the fund and communication about a quarter. It's a concentrated growth bet on firms the managers think are changing for the better, so it swings far more than the broad market.
ATTR: Options on large US stock indexes used to guard against rare, severe market crashes, alongside some stock exposure. It's a hedge meant to cushion deep sell-offs, but the protection costs money and it can drag on results in calm or rising markets.
AUAU: Gold mining companies from around the world, the whole fund in materials stocks that dig and process the metal. Miners usually move more sharply than gold itself, so this swings harder than simply owning gold.
AUGC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. The August start fixes the terms: this edition's shallower buffer leaves a higher cap than deeper-protection versions.
AUGM: Uses options linked to the S&P 500 to absorb as much of a set amount of losses as possible over a one year period that starts in August. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it is designed to be held for the full period.
AUGP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each August, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every August.
AUGT: Options on large US stocks that take the first 10% of a market loss over a year starting in August, the Buffer10 promise in its name. A moderate shield like this keeps more upside than deep buffers, though gains are still capped.
AUGU: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period starting in August, with a 15% buffer built into the design. Upside is uncapped past a starting spread, which is the twist versus ordinary capped buffers.
AUGW: Options tied to a large-company US stock fund, set up to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over a year starting each August, with gains capped. It's meant as a cushion for stock exposure, and it trails in strong rallies, so it works best held the full year.
AUGZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to soften part of a market drop over an outcome period that resets each August, while giving up some gains in strong rallies. What you get depends heavily on when during the period you buy, so timing matters more here.
AUMI: Gold mining companies worldwide, from the big producers to smaller explorers, in a single industry fund. Miners usually swing harder than gold itself because their profits are leveraged to the metal's price, so this is an amplified way to bet on gold rather than a calm store of value.
AUSF: US stocks spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care, with the mix shifting between value, quality and momentum styles as markets change. It's a core stock holding that tries to adapt on its own, so it may not move exactly in step with the broad market.
AV: Aerospace and aviation companies: aircraft and engine makers, defense contractors and the suppliers behind commercial flight, all in the industrial sector. It is a focused bet on air travel and military spending, so it moves with airline orders and defense budgets rather than the broad economy.
AVDE: Companies of all sizes from developed countries outside the US, with financials the biggest slice, then industrials and materials. It's a core international holding that tilts toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and foreign currency swings affect it.
AVDS: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, led by industrials, materials, consumer companies and financials, tilted toward cheaper, more profitable firms. It adds international small company diversification, and it swings more than large company funds and moves with foreign currencies.
AVDV: Small companies from developed countries outside the US that look cheap, spread across materials, industrials, consumer companies and financials. It's a way to add international small-company value stocks, and it swings more than large company funds, plus foreign currency moves affect it.
AVEE: Small companies in emerging markets, spread across technology, industrials, consumer businesses and materials, with extra weight on cheaper, more profitable names. It's a growth-minded add-on for a global portfolio, and small developing-country stocks tend to swing more than larger ones.
AVEM: Companies from emerging countries like China, India and Taiwan, with technology about 39 percent and financials about a fifth. It's an actively managed way to add developing economies, tilting toward cheaper, more profitable firms, and it swings more than developed-market funds.
AVES: Emerging-market companies that look cheaper and more profitable, with financials at about a quarter and technology near a fifth. It's a value-leaning way to add developing-country stocks, and it swings more than developed-market funds.
AVGB: An actively managed fund of investment grade bonds from US and foreign companies, with the currency risk hedged back to US dollars. It is widely spread across many issuers, and each is only about 1% of it.
AVGE: A fund of funds that spreads money across stocks in the US, other developed countries and emerging markets. It tilts toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and works as a one-fund global stock portfolio, though it can trail when growth stocks lead.
AVGV: A basket of other funds holding value stocks around the world, large and small, with financials at a quarter and industrials, consumer companies and energy filling out much of the rest. It's a one fund global value tilt that can lag when growth stocks lead.
AVGW: A single stock strategy built on Broadcom, the chip and software giant, using swaps for extra exposure plus an options program aiming to pay distributions weekly. It amplifies one popular semiconductor stock's moves and converts some of them into income, a concentrated and volatile ride.
AVIE: A fund of US companies the managers expect to hold up or gain when inflation rises, such as energy, health care and consumer staples firms. Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil, Procter & Gamble and Eli Lilly are among the largest holdings, each around 4% to 5%.
AVIG: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds from US and foreign issuers, including government, corporate and mortgage debt. It's a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and managers tilt toward bonds that pay more for the risk, though prices drop when rates rise.
AVIV: Large companies outside the US that look cheaply priced, with financials about a third, then industrials, energy and materials. It's a value-focused holding for international stocks, so it leans away from tech and can trail in growth-led rallies.
AVLC: Large US companies across many industries, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and consumer companies filling out the rest. It leans toward more profitable, cheaper stocks and skips some weaker ones, so it works as a core holding with a value tilt.
AVLV: Large US companies that look cheap and profitable, with financials the biggest slice, then consumer companies, energy and technology. It's a core value holding that's actively screened for quality, and it can trail when fast-growing stocks lead the market.
AVMA: A balanced mix of other Avantis funds, roughly two-thirds stocks from around the world and one-third bonds, all tilted toward cheaper and more profitable companies. It is a one-fund moderate portfolio for hands-off investors, with the factor tilts setting it apart from plain balanced funds.
AVMC: Mid-sized US companies across industrials, financials, technology and health care. It's a core mid-cap holding that tilts toward cheaper, more profitable and smaller firms, so it can behave differently from a plain mid-cap index, especially when value stocks fall out of favor.
AVMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds, loans to US states and cities, with medium-length maturities. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, so it's meant for tax-aware income, and its price can drop when interest rates rise.
AVMV: Mid-sized US companies, led by financials, consumer companies, industrials and energy, picked because they look cheap and profitable. It's a value-tilted way to add mid-sized stocks to a portfolio, and it can trail growth-focused funds when tech-heavy markets lead.
AVNC: Companies across developed and emerging markets outside the US, mixing direct stock holdings with broad international funds, tilted toward cheaper and more profitable firms. Avantis builds it as a core international holding, so the value tilt and wide diversification set it apart from plain index funds.
AVNM: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials, technology and materials. It's a one-fund way to add international stocks, and it leans toward cheaper, more profitable companies, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
AVNV: A fund of funds that holds three Avantis ETFs, giving value-tilted exposure to large and small companies in developed markets plus emerging markets outside the US. Value means it favors cheaper-looking stocks, and financials are the biggest sector.
AVOS: Stocks from around the whole world, combining direct holdings in big US companies with funds covering developed and emerging markets abroad. It is built as a single global core holding, and its active mix of individual stocks and index funds sets it apart from plain world index funds.
AVRE: Real estate companies around the world, mostly property owners that pass rental income to shareholders, spread across many kinds of buildings. It adds property exposure and income to a stock portfolio, and it can fall when interest rates rise because borrowing gets costlier for landlords.
AVRY: An actively managed fund that picks a small group of US stocks, mostly technology and internet companies. It is fairly concentrated, with Block, Zoom, Okta and Clear Secure each making up around 6% to 8% of it.
AVSC: Small US companies tilted toward cheaper, more profitable ones, spread over financials, consumer companies, industrials and health care. It's an actively managed small-company holding for growth over long periods, and it swings more than large company funds.
AVSD: Stocks of companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, with industrials, consumer companies and technology next, screened to avoid certain businesses on responsibility grounds. It's a way to diversify internationally, and its returns also move with foreign currencies.
AVSE: Stocks of companies in emerging markets, led by technology and financials, with firms screened out for concerns over their social or environmental practices. It's a way to add developing-world growth to a portfolio, and it swings more than funds that stick to developed markets.
AVSF: Short-term, investment-grade bonds, largely US Treasuries plus some corporate bonds. It's meant for steady income and a cushion for a stock portfolio, with less rate risk than longer bonds, though its price still falls a bit when rates rise.
AVSU: Large and mid-sized US companies, with technology about 37 percent, then financials, consumer companies and health care. It's a core stock holding that screens out companies with poor environmental and social records and leans toward cheaper, more profitable firms.
AVTM: Stocks from companies worldwide, with technology about a third, then financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's an all-in-one global stock holding that leans toward cheaper, more profitable companies, and a manager adjusts the mix between the US and other countries.
AVUC: US companies of every size, tilted toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms, which Avantis expects to deliver higher returns over time. It works as a core stock holding with a deliberate slant away from the biggest growth names, so it will not hug the index.
AVUQ: Large US growth companies with strong profits, with technology about half and communication and consumer businesses next. It's a growth holding that screens for high-quality, profitable firms, so it can lag the market when lower-quality stocks lead.
AVUS: US companies of all sizes across many industries, with technology about 30%, tilted toward cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market-weighted fund. It's a core US stock holding aiming for a slight edge, though it still moves closely with the market.
AVUV: Small US companies that look cheap and are profitable, led by financials, consumer firms and energy. It's an actively managed bet on small value stocks, so it can swing more than the broad market, and it can lag when big tech leads.
AVXC: Emerging market companies outside China, with technology around 40% and financials about a fifth. It's a way to add developing economies without China exposure, tilting toward smaller and cheaper companies, so it swings more than a fund holding developed markets.
AWAY: Travel technology companies worldwide: online booking platforms, reservation software and the digital plumbing behind trips. It is a growth bet on how travel is bought and managed rather than on airlines or hotels themselves, so it rides global travel demand with a technology twist.
AZTD: Small and mid-sized companies from developed markets across North America, Europe and the Pacific, picked by stock selection models. Smaller foreign firms get less attention from big investors, which is the opportunity, and currency moves add another layer of ups and downs.
AZYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged Amazon fund, which doubles the stock's daily moves before the options even come into play. It is an aggressive income trade: leverage plus options means fast swings, and it is built for short holding periods, not steady saving.
BAB: Taxable bonds issued by US states, cities and other local governments to pay for projects like schools, roads and transit. It offers interest income from high quality borrowers, and unlike most municipal bonds the interest is taxable, but its price falls when interest rates rise.
BABO: An options income strategy on a single stock, Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce and cloud giant, using contracts tied to its US-listed shares. It pays high distributions from Alibaba's volatility, with gains capped and China-related risks fully in play.
BABW: Leveraged exposure to Alibaba through swaps on its shares, structured to pay distributions every week. It is a short-term trading tool on one Chinese tech giant: leverage magnifies Alibaba's moves, and weekly payouts come from the swap structure, not from dividends.
