BAFE: Large US companies picked by active managers, led by technology and financials, followed by communication and health care. It's a core growth holding that can include smaller companies, so it may differ from the broad market, and it can trail or lead it.
BAGX: US companies of any size, with technology about two fifths and financials, consumer and health care making up much of the rest. It's an actively managed, growth-focused fund that can put a big share in a single company, so it takes more risk than a broad market fund.
BAGY: Gets exposure to Bitcoin's price and sells call options on it to produce high monthly income. The options limit how much of Bitcoin's gains it can capture, and Treasury bills in the portfolio mostly serve as backing.
BAI: Companies tied to artificial intelligence, chosen by managers, with nearly all in technology. It's a focused growth bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market, and managers can pick stocks across the US and abroad.
BAIV: Companies outside the US, in developed and emerging markets, that the manager thinks are priced below their worth, led by financials, consumer businesses and health care. It's a value-focused way to add international stocks, and it can lag when growth stocks lead and the dollar strengthens.
BALI: Large US companies, led by technology, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside in exchange for regular income. It aims to pay income and smooth the ride, so it usually holds up better when markets fall but trails in strong rallies.
BALQ: Nasdaq-listed companies, dominated by big technology names, with an options program designed to turn their price moves into premium income. It aims to keep much of the growth of the Nasdaq while paying income along the way, accepting less upside in the strongest rallies.
BALT: Holds options tied to the S&P 500 that are designed to cushion the first part of any drop over a one-year period. In exchange, there is a cap on the gains, so it trails in strong rallies and is meant for a smoother ride.
BAMA: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across US and foreign stocks, bonds and cash, shifted actively to wherever the manager sees opportunity. It works as a moderate, one stop allocation, and its results ride on the manager's asset picking rather than any fixed recipe.
BAMB: US Treasury bonds and high quality corporate bonds maturing within about ten years, managed actively for interest income. It is a middle of the road bond holding: steadier than long term bonds, with a bit more yield and movement than short term ones.
BAMD: Dividend-paying US stocks picked by active managers, led by banks and financial firms at about a quarter, with energy, technology and household brands behind. It is built for income from established payers rather than growth names, so the payout stream matters more than price fireworks.
BAMG: US companies a manager expects to grow earnings quickly, with technology about 45 percent and financials next. It's built for growth, and because it holds relatively few stocks and leans on tech, it tends to swing more than the broad market.
BAMO: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across stocks, bonds and cash worldwide, with the freedom to use leverage when the manager sees opportunity. It aims higher than a cautious balanced fund, and the borrowed exposure can magnify both gains and losses.
BAMV: US stocks a manager picks as good values, led by financials and technology with health care and industrials behind. It's for investors wanting a core stock holding with a value tilt, and since it's hand-picked, it can differ noticeably from the broad market.
BAMY: An income-focused fund of funds that gathers high yield bond funds and other paying investments like dividend stocks and preferred shares. The junk bond core reaches for higher income, which brings credit risk: payments look generous because the borrowers are shakier.
BAPR: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb some stock market losses over a one-year period starting each April. In return it limits how much you gain, and the protection only fully works if you hold from start to end of that period.
BASG: Large US growth companies that meet the manager's sustainability criteria, with technology at half the portfolio and financials next. It's a growth-oriented core holding that screens by sustainability, and it swings more than the broad market.
BASV: Large US companies that look cheap and meet sustainability standards, led by health care at about a quarter, then technology, financials and industrials. It's a value-style core holding, so it can trail when fast-growing tech stocks lead the market.
BATT: Companies across the lithium battery chain worldwide: miners that dig up lithium and copper, battery makers, and the carmakers that use the cells, with raw materials about half the fund. It is a focused bet on electric vehicle and battery demand, so it swings with commodity prices and EV sentiment.
BAUG: A basket of options on the S&P 500 that cushions a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in August, while capping how much gain you can capture. It's for investors wanting a smoother ride in stocks, and it works best if held for the full period.
BAVA: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Avalanche, the token known as AVAX, with part of the holdings staked to earn additional tokens as rewards. It gives brokerage-account access to that one digital asset, and its value swings as sharply as the crypto market itself.
BAY: Companies based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the region's big technology names plus its banks, health care and consumer firms. It is a hometown concentration bet: one metro area's economy drives it, so a tech downturn or regional shock hits harder than in a national fund.
BBAG: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant as a steady core holding that pays interest and cushions a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BBAX: Companies in developed Asia Pacific markets outside Japan, such as Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and South Korea, with financials the biggest slice at nearly half. It's a low-cost way to add the region to a portfolio, and it leans heavily on banks and miners.
BBB: About 75% in the S&P 500 and 25% in bitcoin, through bitcoin futures tied to the S&P CME Bitcoin Futures Index. The bitcoin share can swing sharply, and it is rebalanced to those weights, so it blends regular stocks with crypto.
BBBB: BBB-rated corporate bonds: loans to companies on the lowest rung of investment grade, one step above junk status. They pay more interest than higher-rated bonds to make up for the extra risk, so this is the yield-tilted end of a cautious bond portfolio.
BBBI: US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade, maturing in about five to ten years. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but it takes more credit risk, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
BBBL: Long-term corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade, from industrial, utility and financial companies. They pay more interest than safer bonds because the companies are closer to a downgrade, and long maturities make the price sensitive to interest rate moves.
BBBS: Short-term corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier of investment grade, maturing in about one to five years. It's meant for income that is higher than Treasuries with less price swing than longer bonds, though BBB companies carry a bit more risk of trouble in a downturn.
BBC: Small biotech companies whose main drug is still in clinical trials, spread widely so no single company dominates. It is a speculation on trial results: a successful drug can send a stock soaring, while failed trials can wipe out much of its value.
BBCA: Canadian companies, with financials about 40 percent and energy, materials and industrials behind. It's a focused bet on one country whose market leans on banks and natural resources, so it moves with commodity prices and has little technology.
BBCB: Investment grade corporate bonds from across the US market, weighted by size, spanning banks, technology firms, health care companies and other large issuers. It is a plain, broad company bond holding for steady interest, sitting between Treasuries and riskier high yield debt.
BBEM: Large and mid-sized companies from emerging markets, led by technology at about 42 percent and financials near a fifth. It's a low-cost, broad way to add developing economies to a portfolio for growth, and it swings more than US funds because of political and currency risks.
BBEU: Companies from developed European countries, mostly large, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and health care behind. It's a low-cost way to add Europe to a portfolio, and its returns also depend on the euro and pound against the dollar.
BBH: Around 25 US-listed biotechnology companies, all in health care. It's a focused bet on drug development, so it swings far more than the broad market, with big jumps or drops depending on trial results and approvals.
BBHL: A concentrated, actively managed group of large US companies chosen for quality, with technology at about 40% and financials next. It's a growth-leaning core holding, and holding fewer stocks than most funds means its results can differ noticeably from the market.
BBHM: A concentrated group of mid-sized companies chosen by a manager, led by industrials at about a third and technology at a quarter. It's a growth holding aimed at quality businesses, and holding fewer stocks means it can swing more than a broad mid-cap fund.
BBHY: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, so-called junk bonds, spread widely across the market. It's for higher income than safer bonds at a low cost, and it tends to fall with stocks when the economy weakens.
BBIB: US Treasury bonds with three to ten years left until they mature, the middle of the government bond curve. It pays steady interest with moderate price swings, moving down when interest rates rise, and serves as a classic core holding for the safer side of a portfolio.
BBIN: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US and Canada, led by financials and industrials, with technology and health care behind. It's a broad, low-cost core holding for international stock exposure, with a bigger weight in banks than US funds.
BBJP: Large Japanese companies, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses. It's a way to add a major developed economy to a portfolio, and because it's priced in yen, its value also moves with the Japanese currency against the dollar.
BBLB: US Treasury bonds with more than twenty years left until they mature, and nothing else. It is a pure bet on long-term interest rates: prices jump when rates fall and drop hard when rates rise, and it can act as a cushion when stocks sell off sharply.
BBLS: A fund focused on a small group of large energy companies it calls the Munificent Seven, with Chevron among its holdings. A large part of the fund is currently in short-term Treasury cash funds, so it is a narrow bet on the oil and gas business.
BBLU: Large, established US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about 30% and financials, communication and health care each around 15%. A manager picks the stocks rather than following an index, so it works as a core stock holding that can differ from the broad market.
BBMC: Mid-sized US companies, bigger than small caps but smaller than the giants, led by industrials, technology, health care and financials. It's a core holding for the middle of the market, with far less tech than the broad market.
BBP: US biotechnology companies that already have at least one drug approved by the FDA. It's a focused bet on medicine makers, so it swings more than the broad market, but approved drugs make it a bit steadier than companies still testing.
BBRE: Real estate investment trusts, which are companies that own buildings and collect rent: health care properties, warehouses, malls, data centers and storage. It's meant for income and for diversifying away from stocks, though it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
BBSB: US Treasury bonds maturing in one to three years, the short end of government debt. It pays modest interest with very small price swings, serving as a low risk parking place that still earns more than cash, and it barely reacts when interest rates move.
BBSC: Small US companies across technology, health care, financials and industrials, held in a low-cost, rules-based way. It's a growth-leaning part of a diversified portfolio, and small companies swing more than big ones.
BBUS: Most of the US stock market by value, led by large companies, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care following. It's built to be a low-cost core holding that moves with the overall US economy.
BBYY: An income fund built on options tied to a fund holding Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant, rather than owning those shares directly. It aims to pay frequent distributions, and what sets it apart is the China link: Alibaba's price swings with Chinese consumer spending and Beijing's rules for tech companies.
BCCC: A fund that aims to pay income and track Bitcoin through ETFs, using a synthetic covered call strategy, which sells options on Bitcoin funds for income. That income comes in exchange for capping some gains if Bitcoin jumps.
BCD: Futures contracts on a broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, backed by bonds and cash. It's a hedge against inflation and a way to diversify away from stocks, and it favors contracts further out in time, which can soften the cost of rolling futures forward.
BCDF: Companies developing blockchain technology and digital asset businesses, from crypto exchanges and financial firms to miners and tech suppliers, actively picked worldwide. It is Horizon Kinetics' stock-based route into crypto's growth, volatile like the industry but holding businesses rather than coins themselves.
BCEM: Growth companies in emerging markets, hand picked with a long term owner's mindset, led by Asian technology with banks and industrials behind. The managers hold relatively few names for years at a time, so it behaves like a concentrated bet on developing world businesses.
BCFN: Financial companies built on new technology: banking, lending, payments, insurance, market data and wealth platforms that develop or heavily use innovative tech. It skips the stodgiest corners of finance for its disruptors, making it a growth leaning take on the money business.
BCGD: An actively managed fund of global stocks from companies Baron believes have lasting competitive strengths, in the size range of the MSCI ACWI index. Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA and Amazon are about 21% of the fund.
BCGS: A select, actively managed set of large companies from around the world, led by industrial and technology firms. With only a few dozen holdings, it is a conviction portfolio: each pick counts, so results depend heavily on the managers' judgment.
BCHP: A concentrated collection of big, established US companies, led by technology, financials and communication. It's built for growth with a focus on well-known leaders, but a smaller number of holdings means it can swing more than the broad market.
BCI: A broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, gained through futures contracts, with the rest held in cash and short-term securities as collateral. It's a hedge against rising prices, not a source of income, and it drops when commodity prices fall.
BCIL: Large companies outside the US chosen one by one by active managers, an eclectic mix from Polish gym chains to Australian electronics retailers and Korean chipmakers. With no index to hug, results rest entirely on the managers' picks, making it a conviction-driven international growth fund.
BCKT: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income ending in 2030, with the schedule set in advance. It is an income planning tool for a known horizon: the fixed end date makes it act more like a maturing bond than an open-ended fund.
BCLO: The middle and lower layers of CLOs, bundles of business loans rated from BBB down to B, actively picked for their higher interest payments. Those layers pay more than top-rated CLOs because they absorb loan losses sooner, making this an income fund with real credit risk.
BCOM: A broad basket of commodities, energy, metals and farm goods, held through futures contracts that together mirror the overall commodity market. It is a one-fund way to own raw materials, which tend to move differently from stocks and can shine when inflation surprises, though futures add their own quirks.
BCOR: Companies worldwide that hold bitcoin on their balance sheets, spread across technology, consumer, financial and media stocks. It offers stock-market exposure to bitcoin adoption without holding crypto directly, but its price still swings with both the stock market and bitcoin sentiment.
BCPL: Mostly investment-grade corporate bonds, plus a smaller allowance for riskier bonds to earn extra interest. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BCSM: Small and mid-sized companies picked by Baron for long-term growth, led by technology, industrial and health care names. Baron's patient style holds growers for years, so the fund rides these younger companies through their ups and downs rather than trading around them.
BCTK: Technology companies from the US and abroad of all sizes, with industrial, communication and consumer firms making up the rest. It's an actively run growth bet on innovation, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on the managers' stock picks.
BCUS: Large US companies chosen by a manager, with industrials, technology, consumer and communication firms making up most of it. It's built as a core stock holding, and industrials get a bigger share than in most large-company funds, so it can behave differently from the broad market.
BD: A core plus bond portfolio built mainly on US government debt and agency mortgage securities, with corporate and other bonds added to lift income. It is meant to anchor a portfolio with steady interest, while the plus side flexibility reaches for a bit more yield than a plain core fund.
BDBT: A mix of bond funds held together, covering government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, and the managers choose the underlying funds actively, so it can differ from a standard bond index when interest rates move.
BDEC: US large company stocks, through options that absorb a set amount of losses over a year, resetting each December. In return it caps your gains, so it's for people who want market exposure with a cushion, as long as they hold the full year.
BDGS: A tactical blend of large US stocks and broad index funds, adjusted by the manager as conditions change, sometimes holding big defensive positions. With only a handful of holdings at a time, its results hinge on the manager's calls about when to be bold or cautious.
BDIV: Dividend-paying US companies picked for the ability to keep raising their payouts, spread across technology, banks, industrials and health care. It is built for income that grows over time, and because the managers choose the stocks, it leans on dividend growers rather than the highest yielders.
BDRY: Not a stock fund at all: it holds futures on shipping rates for bulk carriers, the giant ships that move coal, grain and iron ore. Its value jumps with global freight costs, making it a volatile bet tied to world trade rather than to company profits.
BDVG: US companies that pay and grow dividends, selected with a Berkshire-inspired discipline emphasizing durable businesses and shareholder returns. It is a value-leaning income and growth holding: dividends are central, but the managers look for payers whose dividends should keep rising rather than the highest yields today.
BDVL: Stocks from around the world picked to swing less than the market, led by technology, industrials and financials. It's meant as a core holding with a smoother ride, though it can trail in strong rallies.
BDYN: A mix mostly of stocks from around the world, led by technology, financials and industrials, which the managers can shift and balance with bonds or cash. It's meant as a flexible core holding, and the active approach means results depend on their calls.
BEDY: Mostly US dividend-paying stocks across financials, technology, health care and energy, with a small amount of bonds and preferred shares. It aims for income, and the managers also sell options to boost payouts, which can cap gains in strong rallies.
BEEX: Large and mid-sized US companies, with technology the biggest slice at nearly a third, followed by health care, industrials and consumer companies. It's a growth-leaning stock holding for the core of a portfolio, and the manager picks stocks actively, so it can differ from the broad market.
BEEZ: US companies of all sizes, led by industrials at about a third, with technology, health care and banks behind them. Managers pick the stocks actively, so it works as a broad core holding whose results rest on their choices rather than an index.
BEMB: A broad basket of emerging market bonds all borrowed in US dollars, from governments and companies across dozens of countries. Dollar borrowing removes direct currency risk, but the income comes with the credit risk of less settled economies and governments.
BEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, in a BNY Mellon portfolio spanning the developing world's debt. It pays higher interest than developed market bonds, and returns hinge on those countries' finances and currencies, so it belongs on the riskier side of a bond allocation.
BENJ: Mostly very short-term US Treasury bills, paired with stock options linked to large US companies, which are heavy in technology. It aims to earn steady interest while adding a bit of stock market upside, so it moves less than stocks but won't match a rally.
BESF: Actively managed US energy stocks: oil and gas producers, pipeline operators and energy service companies make up nearly the whole fund. It is a focused bet on the energy industry, used for its income and its link to fuel prices, and it swings with the price of oil and gas.
BESO: A fund holding three major cryptocurrencies, bitcoin, ether and solana, through other crypto ETFs. About half is bitcoin, with the rest split between solana and ether, and the ether and solana funds earn extra rewards by staking.
BETE: A fund that holds bitcoin and ether futures contracts in roughly equal amounts, giving exposure to both cryptocurrencies without owning the coins directly. Prices can swing sharply, and futures can behave a little differently from the coins themselves.
BETH: A fund that tracks bitcoin and ether together using futures contracts, weighted by the size of each coin's market value. It holds no actual coins, and since it is just two cryptocurrencies, its price can swing a lot.
BETZ: Sports betting and online gaming companies from around the world: bookmakers, casino apps and the data and platform firms behind them. It is a narrow wager on gambling going digital and legal in more places, and it swings with regulation and betting volumes.
BFAP: Options-based exposure to bitcoin with a floor built in, designed so losses over its outcome period stop at a set level, the Floor15 in its name. This April series gives up some gains in exchange for that protection, so it is a cautious way to hold bitcoin rather than chasing its whole rise.
BFEB: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in February. It's meant for people who want market exposure with a safety net, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BFEW: A ladder of four buffer funds on equal-weighted large US stocks, each with its own one-year protection period staggered through the year. The laddering smooths the timing risk of buying a buffer on the wrong day, in exchange for capped gains throughout.
BFIX: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment-grade US dollar bonds, with a lot of US Treasuries. Holdings are spread across a few Treasuries at about 5% each, and short maturities mean it should move less than longer bond funds.
BFJA: Bitcoin exposure with a built-in floor, using options to limit losses over an outcome period that started in January while keeping some upside. It is a cautious way to hold a volatile asset: the floor softens drops, gains are capped, and the terms reset each period.
BFJL: Bitcoin with a floor under it: over the period starting in July, it is designed to stop losses at about 15 percent while capping how much of bitcoin's gains it keeps. It suits investors who want bitcoin exposure with a hard limit on the downside.
BFLB: An actively managed fund that uses stock market options tied to the S&P 500 to soften a set amount of losses over a one year period. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
BFLX: Mostly large US stocks, with technology about a third, then financials and industrials. The managers use derivatives to adjust how much the fund moves with the market, aiming for stock-like growth with a smoother ride, though it can trail a plain stock fund in strong rallies.
BFOC: Bitcoin exposure with a built-in floor, using options to limit losses over an outcome period that started in October while keeping some upside. It is a cautious way to hold a volatile asset: the floor softens drops, gains are capped, and terms reset each period.
BFOR: Mid-sized US companies picked for strong growth and financial performance, spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a blend-style stock holding built on a rules-based screen, and it can trail the market if the chosen stocks stumble.
BFRZ: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that cushion losses over a set one-year period. It aims to cut downside while still joining in some gains, but upside is capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BFXU: US large-cap stocks through a ladder of four accelerator funds with staggered outcome periods, designed to multiply moderate market gains up to a cap. The ladder spreads out start dates, but acceleration cuts both ways in timing: strong rallies are capped, and losses are not cushioned.
BGCG: A concentrated portfolio of fast-growing companies outside the US, from Asian chipmakers to Latin American online marketplaces and European luxury and payment firms, with technology about two-fifths. Baillie Gifford picks for long-term growth and holds through ups and downs, so patience is part of the design.
BGDV: Large US companies that pay dividends, with technology the biggest slice at over a quarter, followed by financials, industrials and health care. It's built for income plus some growth in a core stock holding, and a manager picks the stocks rather than following an index.
BGEG: An actively managed fund of companies in emerging markets, chosen by Baillie Gifford for long-term growth potential. It leans heavily on technology, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung Electronics together are about a quarter of it.
BGFI: A mix of bonds from governments and companies around the world, with currency moves hedged back to the US dollar. It's meant for steady income and diversification beyond US bonds, and the hedging means swings in foreign currencies matter far less than in unhedged global bonds.
BGGG: Fast-growing companies from around the world held for the long haul, with technology about two fifths and consumer, communication and industrial companies behind it. It's a growth bet on a small number of stocks, so it swings much more than the broad market.
BGIA: An actively managed group of growth companies outside the US, from developed and emerging countries, led by technology and financials. It's for long-term growth abroad, and because the manager picks a limited number of stocks, it can differ a lot from broad international indexes.
BGIG: Large US companies that pay dividends and are expected to raise them, with technology, health care and financials leading. It's a stock fund for steady income and growth, and its focus on dividend payers means it may lag in fast, tech-led rallies.
BGLD: Options on a gold fund in a quarterly buffer design: gains on gold are capped each quarter in exchange for a cushion against drops over the same stretch. It suits gold holders who want a smoother ride, trading away part of a big gold rally for downside softness.
BGRN: Investment-grade bonds issued to pay for projects with environmental benefits, such as clean energy, from governments and companies worldwide. It's meant for steady income from a core bond holding with a climate angle, and it hedges the currency back to dollars while dropping in price when interest rates rise.
BGRO: An actively managed fund of large US companies expected to grow faster than average, with the managers choosing the stocks. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA is about 13% of the fund, and technology is over half of it.
BGUS: An actively managed fund of US growth companies picked by Baillie Gifford, aiming for businesses it expects to grow fast. It leans on one name: NVIDIA is about 16% of the fund, and technology is around 40% overall.
BHDG: A bitcoin tail-risk strategy: protective put options on bitcoin funds, paid for by selling call options, with most assets in bonds and cash. It is built to cushion a crypto crash, and in calm or rising markets the insurance cost drags on returns.
BHYB: Higher-yield corporate bonds in the middle of the junk range, with the weakest-rated bonds and banks left out. It's built for income above safe bonds with slightly less risk than the full junk bond market, but it still falls with stocks in downturns.
BHYP: A single digital coin, Hyperliquid, held directly, with nothing else in the fund. It's a speculative bet on that one cryptocurrency, so its price can rise or fall sharply in a day, and it behaves very differently from stocks and bonds.
BIBL: Large US companies screened for alignment with Biblical values, such as excluding businesses tied to certain products. Technology leads at about a third, then industrials and real estate, so it works as a values-based core stock holding.
BIDD: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, led by financials and technology at about a quarter each, then industrials and communication. It's built for income from foreign stocks, and an active manager picks them, so it can trail the market when growth stocks lead.
BIGY: Fifty of America's biggest companies, technology giants at the front, with covered call options sold against them to generate income. The Target 12 name points to the high payout it aims for, reached by giving up part of the stocks' gains.
BIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills that mature in one to three months, which is nearly the same as holding cash. It's a place to park money with almost no price swings, and its income rises and falls quickly with short-term interest rates.
BILD: Listed infrastructure companies around the world, such as utilities, pipelines, toll roads and airports, picked by an active manager. Utilities make up about half the fund, and the top holdings like Enbridge and United Utilities are each around 5%.
BILS: Short-term US Treasury bills that mature in three to twelve months, mostly government debt with a bit of cash. It's a place to park money safely and earn interest, and because the bills mature so soon, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
BILT: Infrastructure companies around the world, actively picked: electric utilities are about half, with railroads, toll roads, airports and pipelines making up most of the rest. These are steady, hard-to-replace businesses, so the fund is built as a defensive stock holding that can still pay dividends.
BINC: A mix of bonds actively picked by managers, including higher-yielding corporate bonds, government-backed mortgage bonds and debt from other countries. It's built for income, with managers free to shift between bond types, and the higher-yield portion means it can fall when the economy weakens.
BINT: Stocks from around the world, with technology near 30 percent, financials about a fifth and industrials next. It's an actively managed, all-in-one global stock holding, and because the manager chooses the mix, it can differ noticeably from a plain global index.
BINV: Large foreign companies picked by a manager who hunts for stocks that look cheap compared with their underlying worth. Consumer staples lead at about a quarter, followed by health care and consumer discretionary, making it a value-focused way to diversify beyond the US.
BIOY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged biotechnology fund that triples its index's daily moves. It stacks an income strategy on the market's most headline-driven sector: biotech already swings on trial results, and triple leverage multiplies every jump and drop.
BITA: Bitcoin exposure paired with covered call options sold against it each month, turning the cryptocurrency's price swings into premium income. The calls cap gains when bitcoin jumps, so it is an income-first way to hold crypto, with payouts that vary as volatility changes.
BITB: Holds actual bitcoin rather than company shares or bonds, so its price follows the price of bitcoin. It's a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and it swings sharply, with no income and no cushion from other assets.
BITC: A rotation strategy that moves between bitcoin futures and US Treasury securities following a trend signal based on bitcoin's price momentum. When bitcoin's trend is up it holds bitcoin futures, and when the trend turns down it shelters in Treasuries.
BITI: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of bitcoin's daily move, using bitcoin futures contracts. It resets every day, so over longer periods its results can drift away from the opposite of bitcoin's total move, and it is built for short-term use, not as a long hold.
BITO: Bitcoin futures contracts, which bet on bitcoin's price without holding any actual bitcoin, backed by cash and short-term holdings. It's a way to trade bitcoin in a regular account, though costs of rolling the futures can make it trail bitcoin and it swings wildly.
BITQ: Companies that serve the cryptocurrency world, such as miners, mining equipment makers and crypto finance firms, so financials are about 70 percent and technology about a quarter. It's a focused bet on the crypto industry without holding coins directly, and it swings sharply with crypto prices.
BITS: Two crypto exposures in one actively managed fund: shares of blockchain companies plus long positions in bitcoin futures traded in the US. It aims to capture the crypto economy from both the business and the coin side, and both parts are volatile, so swings are large.
BITW: A basket of several cryptocurrencies, not just bitcoin, held directly and rebalanced monthly to follow a crypto market index. It's a high-risk bet on digital assets that can swing wildly, and it pays no income.
BITY: Bitcoin exposure through a spot bitcoin fund and futures, paired with options meant to add about two percent in extra monthly income. The options target steadier payouts than bitcoin alone, though bitcoin's price still dominates the result.
BIV: Government and investment-grade corporate bonds that come due in five to ten years, a middle point between safe short bonds and bumpy long ones. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BIZD: Business development companies, firms that lend to small and mid-sized private businesses, along with some bonds and cash. It's meant for high income because these companies pay out most of their earnings, though it falls hard when the economy weakens and loans go bad.
BJAN: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500, whose stocks are about 40% technology, with financials, communication and health care behind it. It's built to absorb the first slice of market losses over a year starting in January, with gains capped in return.
BJUL: Large US companies, with technology around 40 percent, held through options that absorb the first slice of losses over a one-year period starting each July. It's meant to soften stock market drops, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BJUN: US large company stocks tied to the S&P 500, with technology about 40%, wrapped in options that cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each June. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the protection works best if you hold the whole year.
BKAG: The broad US investment-grade bond market, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BKCG: A concentrated group of large US growth companies, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths, followed by financials, communication and industrials. It's built for long-term growth through a small set of stocks, so it swings more than the broad market.
BKCH: Companies tied to blockchain and crypto, such as bitcoin miners, exchanges and crypto-related financial firms, with technology making up the rest. It's a focused bet on the digital asset industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and moves with crypto prices.
BKCI: A small group of companies from developed countries outside the US, led by technology, industrials, health care and consumer businesses. It's meant to add international growth to a portfolio, and because it holds relatively few stocks, it can differ a lot from broad international funds.
BKDV: Large US companies that managers think are cheap compared with what they're worth, spread across technology, financials, health care and consumer firms. It's a value-focused stock holding, so it may lag when growth stocks lead.
BKEM: Large and mid-sized companies across developing economies, from Asian chipmakers and internet firms to banks and miners, with technology over two-fifths of the fund. It is broad emerging market exposure in one holding, which means faster growth potential paired with bigger price swings and currency risk.
BKF: Large companies in Brazil, Russia, India and China, tracking the MSCI BIC index, though in practice the holdings today are mostly Chinese and Indian. Tencent and Alibaba together are around 13% of it, and banks and other financials are the biggest sector.
BKFI: A broad mix of US bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage debt, with active managers adjusting maturity and credit quality. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BKGI: Dividend-paying infrastructure companies around the world, led by utilities, with energy, industrials and real estate making up most of the rest. It's meant for income and steady cash flows, though it can fall when interest rates rise.
BKHY: Bonds issued by US companies with weaker credit ratings, which pay higher interest to make up for the added risk. It's meant for extra income beyond safer bonds, but it can fall alongside stocks in a downturn because these companies are likelier to struggle repaying.
BKIE: Large and mid-size companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials, then industrials, technology and health care. It's a broad, simple way to diversify away from the US, and it leaves out emerging markets.
BKLC: Large US companies in proportion to their size, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care behind it. It's a core holding that follows the big-company US market, so it moves with the overall economy and is heavily influenced by tech.
BKLG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers expect to grow faster than average. It aims to beat the market by picking stocks rather than copying an index, so its holdings can differ a lot from a plain large-growth index fund.
BKLN: Loans that banks made to companies with weaker credit, whose interest rates float with short-term rates. It's for income that rises when rates rise, so its price holds up better than ordinary bonds, though it can fall when companies default.
BKMC: Medium-sized US companies spread across industrials, technology, health care and financials. It's a core way to own the middle of the US market, a step between giants and small caps, and it tends to swing more than large company funds.
BKMI: Municipal bonds from US states and cities with medium maturities, paying interest that is free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-advantaged income and a steadier ride than stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BKMS: Municipal bonds with short maturities, mostly the US kind whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It's built for steady tax-free income with a small risk of price swings, which suits cautious savers in taxable accounts, though it earns less than longer municipal bonds.
BKSE: Six hundred small US companies spread across every industry, technology, finance, industry and consumer firms in small slices each. It is a core small cap holding that owns the whole small-company market rather than picking winners, accepting the group's bigger swings in exchange for its growth potential.
BLCK: The plumbing of crypto: exchanges, miners, custodians and trading platforms that make money from digital assets without the fund holding coins itself. Financial companies are more than four-fifths of the fund, and because their fortunes follow crypto prices, it swings nearly as hard as the coins do.
BLCR: Large US companies picked by a manager, with technology almost 40% and industrials, communication and consumer firms behind. It's a core stock holding that mixes computer-driven and human stock picking, so it can differ from the broad market in either direction.
BLCV: Large US value companies, which look inexpensive compared with their size, spread over technology, financials, consumer businesses and health care. It's a core value holding where managers pick the stocks, so results can differ from broad value benchmarks.
BLDG: Real estate companies around the world, property owners and REITs from developed and emerging markets alike, picked actively. It spreads rent driven income across countries and property types, so it moves with global property markets and local currencies as well as US rates.
BLDX: Infrastructure companies worldwide chosen with a sustainability lens: clean power utilities, water systems, railroads, data centers and materials for building. It is a defensive stock holding with a green filter, favoring businesses that conserve resources or widen access to essentials like water, energy and data.
BLES: Large companies from around the world, including emerging markets, spread across industrials, technology, financials and materials. It screens for companies that score well on a faith-based impact measure, so the mix can differ from the global market while still serving as a core holding.
BLGR: Large US growth companies, with technology a bit over half, followed by communication and consumer businesses. It's a growth holding chosen by a manager rather than an index, and it leans more on tech than the broad market, so it can fall harder in a sell-off.
BLOK: Companies building or using blockchain technology, including financial firms, crypto exchanges and tech companies, with some direct crypto holdings. It's a high-risk growth bet on an emerging industry, and it swings far more than the broad market, often moving with crypto prices.
BLOX: A mix of crypto-related company stocks, crypto-linked investments and an options strategy that generates income. It's for investors seeking income from the crypto world, but it swings with crypto prices, and the options give up some upside when prices surge.
BLST: A mix of short-term bonds from governments and companies, held mostly through other bond funds. It's built for modest interest income with a steadier price, since short maturities mean its value drops less than longer bonds when interest rates rise, though it earns less.
BLTD: Mostly long-term bonds, held directly and through other bond funds, which pay more interest than short-term ones. It's meant for income and as a cushion for stocks, but because the bonds last so long, its price falls sharply when interest rates rise.
BLUC: Large US companies chosen by a manager, with technology close to half, plus communication, consumer and financial firms. It's meant as a core stock holding, but the heavy tech weighting means it can swing harder than a typical broad market fund.
BLUI: A mix of income-producing funds, mostly bonds, plus stock funds focused on real estate and energy. It's built for income, but it's actively managed and leans on a few industries, so it can swing more than a plain bond fund.
BLUX: A fund of other funds that holds mostly US stocks of all sizes, with technology around a quarter, followed by financials and health care. A manager shifts the mix over time, so it works as a one-fund core stock holding, but it won't match the market exactly.
BLV: US government and investment-grade corporate bonds that mature in more than 10 years. It's meant for higher interest income than short-term bonds, but its price drops sharply when interest rates rise, so it swings more than most bond funds.
BMAR: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in March. It's meant for people who want market exposure with a safety net, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BMAY: Large US companies, led by technology at about forty percent, held through options that absorb some of the stock market's first losses. It's meant for people who want stock exposure with a cushion, but the protection resets yearly from May, and upside is capped.
BMED: Health innovation companies: drug developers, gene and cell therapy firms, diagnostics and life-science toolmakers, picked actively worldwide. It is a growth bet on medical breakthroughs, so trial results and regulators' decisions can swing it sharply.
BMOP: Municipal bonds from US states and cities, mostly with medium maturities, that pay interest free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-advantaged income, mainly for people in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
BMSI: A multisector bond portfolio from BNY Mellon, free to spread across government, corporate, mortgage and other debt sectors as its managers see fit. It plays the flexible core income role, shifting its mix with conditions rather than following any single bond index, though that freedom makes positioning vary over time.
BMVP: Fifty US stocks chosen by a combined score for momentum, low volatility, cheap valuation and profitability, picked sector by sector so no industry dominates. It is a balanced multifactor approach: instead of betting on one investing style, it blends four in roughly equal measure.
BNAV: Bitcoin exposure run tactically: the fund leans in when price trends look healthy and pulls back toward safety when they break down. The signal-driven approach aims for fewer deep crashes than plain bitcoin, accepting it can be caught out by sudden reversals.
BND: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BNDC: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including government, mortgage-backed and corporate debt. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and like most bonds its price falls when interest rates rise.
BNDD: A mostly long-term US Treasury fund, held largely through a Vanguard long-term Treasury ETF, with a small side layer of options tied to the shape of the interest rate curve. The options are meant to limit losses and help when inflation and rates fall, so it behaves differently from a plain Treasury fund.
BNDI: A core mix of US investment-grade bonds, with an options overlay on bond markets meant to boost income. It aims to pay more than a plain bond fund and serve as a cushion for stocks, but the options can limit gains and its price still drops when interest rates rise.
BNDP: A broad mix of US bonds, including government and corporate issues, with an added tilt toward higher-yielding bonds. It's meant for steady interest income as a core bond holding, and it pays a little more than a plain bond fund for taking a bit more risk.
BNDS: A high income mix that is half bonds and half preferred shares, leaning on energy and financial issuers that pay generous distributions. Preferred shares sit between stocks and bonds in risk, so the fund chases yield well beyond a core bond fund, with bigger price swings to match.
BNDW: A mix of investment-grade bonds from the US and the rest of the world, mostly government and corporate debt. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, and it hedges foreign currencies back to dollars so exchange rates matter less.
BNDX: Investment-grade bonds from governments and companies outside the US, spread across many countries and currencies. It diversifies bond holdings beyond America, and it hedges currency swings back to the dollar, so exchange rates matter less, though its price still drops when interest rates rise.
BNDY: Investment-grade US bonds, meaning loans to the government and solid companies, picked using a model that weighs past return and risk. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BNGE: Streaming and gaming companies: the services that beam shows and games to screens, plus game makers and betting platforms, mostly communication firms. It is a focused bet on entertainment moving online, so it rides hits, subscribers and screen time.
BNO: A fund that follows the price of Brent crude oil by holding oil futures contracts rather than actual barrels. It's a short-term bet on oil prices, so it swings widely, and the cost of rolling contracts forward can make it lag oil itself.
BNOV: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in November. It's meant for people who want market exposure with a safety net, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BOAT: Global shipping companies, mostly industrials such as container and cargo ship operators, plus about a quarter in energy shippers like oil tankers. It's a focused bet on world trade, and shipping profits rise and fall sharply with freight rates.
BOBP: Large US companies chosen by a rules-based system, tilted toward technology at about a third and industrial companies at close to another third. What sets it apart is flexibility: the strategy can move part of the fund into cash when conditions look risky, trading some upside for smaller drops.
BOCT: US large company stocks through the S&P 500, with an outcome window that starts each October and cushions part of the losses over the year. It's for investors who want some protection, but it caps the gains and only works as designed if held through the full period.
BOND: A broad mix of bonds, mostly US investment-grade, from government, mortgage-backed and corporate issuers, with a manager adjusting the mix. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, and it uses derivatives to tweak risk, though its price still drops when rates rise.
BOTT: Companies that earn a big share of their revenue from designing and building humanoid and service robots, following a Themes index. The holdings come from around the world, including Chinese robotics makers, Teradyne and Tesla, and each of the top few is about 5% to 9% of the fund.
BOTZ: Companies building robots, factory automation and artificial intelligence, mostly industrial firms with technology next and some health care. It's a focused bet on automation as a theme, so it swings more than the broad market and holds companies from around the developed world.
BOUT: Stocks picked as they break out above their recent trading ranges, using Investor's Business Daily methods to spot the start of sustained runs. The current mix leans into health care, and breakout strategies can suffer strings of false starts in choppy markets.
BOXA: US aggregate bond exposure built entirely from options contracts rather than by owning bonds, using option spreads engineered to mimic a broad bond index. The options-based design is unusual and can cut some of the costs and risks of holding thousands of bonds.
BOXX: Short-term box spreads, a pair of options trades that works like a loan, maturing in under three months and paying a return similar to short-term Treasury bills. It's a place to park cash with very little price swing, and it behaves differently from bond funds because it holds no actual bonds.
BPAY: An actively managed fund of companies in financial technology, such as payments, online brokerage and digital banking firms. Holdings like Global Payments, Robinhood, Chime and Capital One are each around 4% to 5%, and it keeps a notable share in cash.
BPH: One company, BP, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge that removes most of the pound-to-dollar exchange rate effect. It is a single-stock energy bet with the currency risk stripped out, so the result follows BP's business alone.
BPI: Bitcoin exposure built from options on bitcoin funds, structured to collect premium income while following bitcoin's price with a cap on gains. It is an income twist on a volatile asset: payouts come from option premiums, but the fund still falls when bitcoin drops.
BPRO: Assets meant to gain when paper money loses value: mostly physical gold, with silver, gold mining shares and bitcoin alongside. It is a hedge against currency debasement, the slow erosion of purchasing power, so it is built for fear of inflation and money printing rather than for growth.
BRAZ: An actively managed fund of Brazilian companies, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It leans toward banks, energy and mining, with Petrobras, Itau Unibanco and Nu Holdings together about a third of it.
BRCE: Large US companies across every industry, chosen by blending old-fashioned analyst research with computer models, MFS's signature approach. It is built as a core stock holding, technology-heavy like today's market, with stock picking meant to add an edge over a plain index.
BREE: Emerging market stocks picked with MFS's blended research process, combining analyst work with quantitative models, and heavily weighted to Asian technology at about 46 percent. It is a growth-leaning developing markets holding that accepts chip and internet concentration in exchange for those markets' biggest success stories.
BREM: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, mostly borrowed in hard currencies like dollars and euros, picked actively by BlackRock. Active management tries to dodge the weakest countries, a real risk in emerging market debt, while collecting its higher income.
BRES: A manager's picks of US stocks of any size, led by technology at about a third, then financials and consumer businesses. It's a growth-leaning stock fund, and with a small set of choices it can differ a lot from the broad market.
BREW: Coffee and energy drink companies from across the business: growers, roasters, bottlers and cafe chains, with consumer staples at about three-fifths of the fund. It is a focused bet on caffeine habits, so it depends on drinks staying in daily routines rather than on the wider food industry.
BRF: Small Brazilian companies across consumer, materials, industrial and property sectors, in a single-country fund. Small caps in Brazil swing hard with the real, local politics and commodity cycles, making this one of the most volatile ways to bet on Latin America's biggest economy.
BRHY: Lower-rated corporate bonds that mature within ten years, managed actively, with energy and materials leading the mix. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but it carries more default risk and tends to fall in sell-offs.
BRIB: An intermediate-term ladder of high-quality corporate bonds from companies that score well on the manager's Bright Score, a measure of benefit to the common good. It aims for steady income and keeping capital safe, and it is spread across many issuers at about 1% each.
BRIE: Large companies outside the US, led by technology and financials, with industrials and consumer staples next. It's an actively managed way to add developed overseas stocks, using research-driven picks, so it can differ somewhat from the broad international market.
BRIF: A concentrated group of large US companies chosen when their profits look to be strengthening, with technology about a third and health care, industrials and materials behind. It's a stock-picking approach for core growth exposure, but with fewer holdings it can swing more than the broad market.
BRKC: An options income fund tied to Berkshire Hathaway's B shares, aiming to pay regular distributions by selling call options rather than owning much of the stock. The Treasury bills shown are mostly collateral, and the options approach limits gains if Berkshire shares rise sharply.
BRKW: Leveraged weekly exposure to Berkshire Hathaway's class B shares through swaps and stock, plus weekly cash distributions. It turns a famously steady conglomerate into something far jumpier with leverage, and the payouts come from the structure rather than from dividends.
BRLN: Floating rate bank loans, debt owed by companies to banks whose interest payments reset as rates change, bought actively rather than by index. Rising rates lift its income instead of hurting it, the mirror image of most bond funds, though the loans carry real credit risk.
BRNY: Mid-sized US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths, followed by financials and consumer firms. It's an actively managed growth fund that rotates between investing styles, so what it owns shifts as the manager changes course.
BROL: Large US growth companies, led by technology at a bit over a third, chosen by Baron with an eye on limiting big drawdowns. It aims to keep growth investing's upside while softening its worst falls, a balance most growth funds do not attempt.
BRRR: Bitcoin itself, held directly with no stocks or bonds. It's a high-risk bet on a single digital asset, offering a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and its price can swing wildly, far more than the stock market.
BRSM: Small and midsize US companies selected with MFS's blended research, mixing analyst judgment with quantitative models across industry, technology, finance and health care. It is a diversified mid-market growth and value holding, positioned between volatile small caps and the steadier large company funds.
BRSV: Small US companies the manager sees as priced cheaply, with financials the largest group at about a third. It's a value-focused way to add small companies, which swing more than large ones and can lag when growth stocks lead.
BRTR: A mix of bonds, including corporate bonds, mortgage bonds, government bonds and other loans, picked by a manager. It aims for more total return than a plain bond fund, and its price will drop when interest rates rise.
BSCA: Investment grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2036, bought and held until the fund itself winds down that year. It behaves much like owning a single long-term bond: steady interest, a known end date, and plenty of price movement when rates change.
BSCQ: Investment-grade corporate bonds that all come due in 2026, so the fund is mostly holding cash as they mature. It's a short-term parking spot for money with a known end date, and it pays interest until the fund winds down.
BSCR: Investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2027, when the fund is set to wind down and return its money. It's meant for steady interest income with a known end date, and its price becomes less sensitive to interest rate moves as maturity nears.
BSCS: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all come due in 2028, paying regular interest. It's for steady income with a known end date, and the fund closes at the end of 2028 and returns the money rather than running forever.
BSCT: Investment-grade corporate bonds that all come due in 2029. It's built to pay interest and then return your principal near that date, so it works for a known timeline, though prices dip along the way if interest rates rise.
BSCU: A basket of investment-grade US company bonds that all mature in 2030. It's built for investors who want income and a known end date, since the bonds mature and the fund winds down, and the fund's price tends to drift back toward face value as that date nears.
BSCV: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2031. The fund winds down in that year and returns the money, so it suits someone who wants predictable income for a set time horizon rather than an ongoing fund.
BSCW: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2032. As the bonds age, the fund winds down and returns cash around that year, so it works for locking in income toward a set date, though its price moves with interest rates until then.
BSCX: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that all come due in 2033, so the fund ends on that date and returns the money. It's meant for predictable income with a known end, though prices dip when interest rates rise before then.
BSCY: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2034, so the fund is designed to wind down then, like a bond that pays interest along the way. It suits planning for a known date, though prices fall if rates rise before then.
BSCZ: US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2035, so the fund is built to wind down that year. It's meant for locking in income toward a known date, and its price drops when interest rates rise, though holding to the end reduces that worry.
BSEP: A set of options tied to the S&P 500, so it follows large US stocks, with technology around 40%. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in September, but it caps how much you can gain, and the protection works best if held for that full period.
BSGR: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2027, so the fund acts like one government bond with a set end date. It suits savers targeting a goal around then, paying government-backed interest with none of the credit risk of company bonds.
BSGT: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2029, so the fund behaves like a single government bond with a known end date. It suits savers aiming at a late-decade goal, paying government-backed interest without company credit risk.
BSJQ: Lower-rated US company bonds, often called junk bonds, that all come due in 2026. It pays out its money when the bonds mature, so it acts like a short-term holding, and it's for income with more credit risk than safer bonds.
BSJR: A basket of US junk bonds, meaning bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, that all mature in 2027. Because the bonds expire together, the fund ends in 2027 and returns the money, giving a more predictable income stream than an ordinary bond fund, though credit problems can still hurt.
BSJS: Lower-rated US company bonds, often called junk bonds, that all come due in 2028. It pays out its money when the bonds mature, so it acts like a medium-term holding, and it's for income with more credit risk than safer bonds.
BSJT: High-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, from US companies with weaker credit, all maturing in 2029. It's for investors seeking higher income than safer bonds pay, and it is designed to wind down at its maturity date, though defaults can hurt in a weak economy.
BSJU: Junk bonds, which are corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit, that all mature in 2030. It's built for high income, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down and returns cash, though it can lose value if some companies fail to repay.
BSJV: High-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, from US companies with lower credit ratings, all maturing in 2031. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, and since the bonds mature, the fund winds down in 2031, though prices drop if companies struggle or rates rise.
BSJW: High yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, packaged like a single junk bond with a known end date. It pays junk level interest until then, with more credit risk than investment grade target date funds, and its price swings shrink as 2032 approaches.
BSJX: High yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, in an Invesco BulletShares fund with a set end date. It works like a ladder rung for a 2033 goal, paying junk bond interest while defaults remain the key risk, and its price swings fade as the end approaches.
BSJY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk kind, that all mature in 2034, so the fund ends like a single bond. It pays higher interest than safer bond funds in exchange for more default risk, aimed at a goal in the mid 2030s.
BSMA: Municipal bonds that all mature around 2036, when the fund itself winds up and returns investors' money, much like holding one bond to maturity. The income is generally free of federal tax, and holding to the end date softens the effect of interest rate swings along the way.
BSMC: Small and mid-sized US companies that a manager thinks are priced below their worth, spread across health care, technology, consumer staples and industrials. It's a value-style holding for broadening beyond big companies, and it can lag for long stretches when growth stocks lead the market.
BSMQ: Investment-grade municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments, that mature in 2026, along with some cash as bonds come due. It pays interest free from federal income tax, and with the end date so near it behaves like a short-term holding with little price swing.
BSMR: Investment-grade municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments, that all mature in 2027. It's for tax-free income and getting your money back around a set date, and its price matters less if you hold the bonds until the end year.
BSMS: Investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments, that all mature in 2028. It's built for income that's generally free of federal income tax, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down and returns cash, so it behaves like a bond with a set end date.
BSMT: Investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2029, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income and returns the bond's face value around its end date, though the price still moves when rates change in the meantime.
BSMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments, that mature in 2030. It pays interest free from federal income tax, and because the bonds end in a set year, it works like a bond ladder rung for investors who want money back around then.
BSMV: Investment-grade municipal bonds from US states and cities that all mature in 2031. It's meant for income that is generally free of federal tax, and as bonds mature, the fund winds down on a set date, so it acts like a laddered bond with a known end.
BSMW: Investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2032, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down and returns your money, though prices drop when rates rise.
BSMY: Investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2034, so the fund winds down that year. It's built for tax-free income with a known end date, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
BSMZ: A basket of US municipal bonds, issued by cities and states, that all mature in 2035, tracking an Invesco index. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down at the end date.
BSOL: Holds Solana, a cryptocurrency, directly, and may earn extra by staking it, which means helping run the network for rewards. It's a high-risk bet on one digital asset, so its price can swing wildly, and it has no earnings or company behind it.
BSR: A fund of funds built mainly from big US index funds and sector funds, adjusted under Beacon's unified catalyst approach. Its top layer is plain large-company exposure, with tactical tilts around the edges that try to catch turning points in the market.
BSSX: Investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2033, so the fund winds down that year. It's built for tax-free income with a known end date, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
BSTP: Options on a large US stock fund, set for one year at a time, that can step its loss protection up to a higher level if stocks climb during the year. It is built for investors who want a cushion against drops that improves after gains, in exchange for capped upside.
BSTS: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2028, following an Invesco BulletShares index. The fund is set to close around that year, so it behaves more like a single bond that returns your money at the end.
BSTU: US Treasury bonds that all mature around 2030, held in a single fund that winds down as that year arrives. It is a goal-based income holding: the shared maturity date makes its interest-rate sensitivity predictable, and prices fall if rates rise before 2030.
BSTV: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2031, bundled so the fund ends like a single government bond. It is built for a goal in the early 2030s, paying government-backed interest with a known finish line and no company credit risk.
BSV: Short-term bonds that mature in one to five years, a mix of US government and investment-grade corporate bonds. It is meant for modest steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, and it drops far less than longer bond funds when interest rates rise.
BSVO: Small US companies that look cheap compared with their size, with financials about a third and consumer, energy and industrial companies making up much of the rest. It's meant for adding small value stocks to a portfolio, and these can lag in growth rallies while swinging more than large companies.
BTA: A tactical basket of alternative investments held through other ETFs: currencies, commodities, gold and futures-based strategies among them. It is a diversifier built to behave differently from stocks and bonds, shifting its mix as conditions change, and it can sit in cash-like holdings when signals are poor.
BTAL: Bets on calmer US stocks while betting against the most volatile ones in the same industries, in equal dollar amounts. It's meant as a hedge that tends to hold up when the market drops, but it usually lags badly when the market rallies.
BTC: Bitcoin itself, held through a trust so you can buy it like a stock instead of managing a crypto wallet. It's a speculative bet on a digital currency, with no earnings or dividends behind it, so its price swings far more than stocks or bonds.
BTCC: Options on a bitcoin fund, sold to generate income while the cash sits in Treasury bills. It turns bitcoin's volatility into regular payouts, with gains limited by the options and losses cushioned only by the income collected.
BTCI: Income built on bitcoin: the fund holds bitcoin funds and sells options on them, turning part of bitcoin's wild price movement into regular payouts. The options cap some of the upside, and the downside is still bitcoin's, so payouts come with big swings in the fund's price.
BTCK: A fixed mix of 80% bitcoin and 20% carbon credit futures, blending a crypto asset with contracts tied to the price of pollution permits. It is an unusual diversifier: the carbon slice is meant to move differently from bitcoin, though both parts can be volatile.
BTCO: Bitcoin itself, held directly by the fund rather than through companies that use it. It's a focused bet on one digital currency, not a diversified investment, so its price swings far more than stocks and can move sharply in either direction.
BTCW: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its daily price. It's a way to own the largest cryptocurrency in a regular brokerage account, with no income, and the price can swing wildly, far more than stocks or bonds.
BTGD: Full exposure to bitcoin and full exposure to gold at the same time, stacked through futures so each dollar carries both bets at once. The pairing mixes a wild digital asset with a classic haven, and the built in leverage means both can hit the fund together.
BTOT: Nearly the entire US dollar bond market in one fund: Treasuries, mortgage bonds, corporate and other investment-grade debt across maturities. It is a broad core bond holding designed for income and ballast, somewhat wider than funds limited to the standard aggregate index constituents.
BUCK: Short-term US Treasuries and cash-like holdings, plus an options strategy that adds extra income. It's built as a step up from cash for income, but the options can limit gains and lose money, so it's not as safe as plain Treasury bills.
BUFB: A set of buffered funds tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40% technology, that reset at different times of the year. It aims to cushion stock losses while limiting gains, and the staggered dates reduce the risk of buying at a bad moment.
BUFC: Options layered on an S&P 500 fund, built to cushion part of the market's losses over a set period in exchange for capping gains. It's a conservative choice for investors who want stock exposure with a smaller downside, so it gives up some upside in strong rallies.
BUFD: A ladder of twelve funds that each hold large US stocks with built-in downside protection, so the mix is about two fifths technology. It's meant as a cushion for stock investors who want smaller losses, but the protection limits how much of the gains you keep.
BUFE: A set of emerging-markets buffer funds from First Trust, each with a different start date, so the fund always holds options with staggered one-year periods. Each layer is meant to absorb part of the losses, while capping gains.
BUFF: A ladder of twelve funds that each use options to shield against S&P 500 losses beyond a small initial drop, in exchange for capped gains. It's built for stock exposure with a cushion, and it gives up some upside in strong rallies.
BUFG: A mix of funds that follow the S&P 500, heavy in technology at about 40%, each wrapped in options that cushion part of any drop. The protection has a cost: gains are limited by a cap, and the cushion only applies if you hold through the full outcome period.
BUFH: A fund of funds holding twelve FT Vest buffer ETFs, each starting at a different month, so the protection periods are staggered across the year. Each one cushions a set amount of S&P 500 losses while capping gains, with each about 8% of the fund.
BUFI: Developed-market stocks from Europe, Japan and Australia, held through options, with financials, industrials and technology the biggest slices. It's a cushion against moderate drops over a set one-year period, but it caps how much you gain in return, so it trails in strong rallies.
BUFM: A fund using options on an S&P 500 fund, so it follows large US companies, led by technology at about 40 percent. It aims to cushion a portion of losses over a set one-year period in exchange for capped gains, so it gives up some upside for protection.
BUFP: A ladder of twelve S&P 500 buffer funds, each cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period with a limit on gains, with start dates spread across the year. It's for stock exposure with some protection from drops, in exchange for giving up part of big rallies.
BUFQ: Large US stocks tied to the Nasdaq-100, heavy in technology at over two fifths, through a stack of four staggered buffer funds that cushion part of the losses. It's built for growth with a smoother ride in drops, but it caps how much you gain in strong rallies.
BUFR: US large-company stocks held through options that limit losses over a set one-year period, in exchange for capping the gains. It's a hedge for people who want some protection, so it trails in strong rallies and the protection only fully applies if held through the period.
BUFS: Small US company stocks held through a ladder of four staggered buffer funds that start at different times. It's built to cushion moderate losses in small companies while still joining in gains, but the protection is limited and gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
BUFT: A mix of buffer funds tied to the S&P 500, which is led by technology, set up to absorb some losses while capping gains. It leans defensive, so it aims for a smoother ride than stocks, but it trails in strong rallies.
BUFX: A ladder of twelve monthly buffer funds on the S&P 500, each aiming for roughly double the index's gains up to a cap with a buffer against the first 15 percent of losses. Staggering the start dates smooths the timing risk of buying protection all at once.
BUFY: International developed-market stocks, heavy in financials with industrials and technology behind, wrapped in a staggered set of buffer funds that each reset at different times. It aims to soften losses in exchange for capped gains, so it trails in strong rallies but cushions modest drops.
BUFZ: A ladder of twelve funds that each use options to cushion part of the S&P 500's losses, in exchange for capped gains over staggered one-year periods. It's built for stock exposure with a moderate downside shield, and it will lag when the market surges.
BUG: Companies that protect computers, networks and data from hackers, almost all of it in technology. It's a focused bet on the cybersecurity theme, so it can swing more than the broad market, and it holds software firms rather than general tech hardware.
BUIL: Companies rebuilding America's infrastructure: the builders, equipment makers, solar and materials firms behind new roads, grids and factories. It is a theme bet on the domestic building boom, led by industrial and technology suppliers rather than the utilities most infrastructure funds favor.
BUL: Mid-size and large US companies with strong cash left over after expenses, spread over consumer, health care and technology businesses. It's a growth-leaning stock holding that screens for financial strength, and it tends to trail the market when fast-growing, cash-hungry companies lead.
BULD: Companies engineering the future: robotics, 3D printing, design software and the chip equipment behind them, from around the world. Technology is about four fifths of the fund, making it a growth bet on how things get designed and made.
BUSA: US companies the manager thinks are priced below their true worth, led by health care and financials with industrials and technology behind them. It's a value-style core holding that leans away from the tech giants, so it can lag when growth stocks lead the market.
