BUXX: Short-term, mostly investment-grade bonds with a small cash portion, actively managed to earn more than plain cash. It's meant as a place to park money with a bit more income than cash, but it can dip a little in rough markets.
BUYB: Big US companies that have shrunk their share count for at least ten straight years through buybacks, spread across industry, finance and consumer sectors. Persistent buybacks signal cash-rich, disciplined firms, so this is a quality-tilted core holding built on a decade-long record rather than a single year's news.
BUYO: Small and mid-sized stocks chosen to resemble the companies private equity firms buy, with similar size, cash flow and industry traits. It offers a stock-market stand-in for buyout investing, without the lockups, but also without private equity's control over its companies.
BUYW: Stock funds covering US and foreign markets, with technology the biggest slice and financials, health care and energy next. It sells call options on its holdings for extra income, which can soften small drops but means it trails in strong rallies.
BUYZ: Companies changing how people shop, pay and order: online retail and consumer brands are the biggest part, with technology and media firms behind. It is a growth bet on the shift to digital commerce around the world, favoring disruptors over traditional stores.
BUZZ: US companies generating the most positive chatter online, chosen by scanning social media, news and blogs rather than financial statements. Technology is about half the fund, and the lineup rotates with the conversation, making it a bet on crowd enthusiasm that can turn quickly when sentiment flips.
BVAL: Large US companies that look cheaply priced compared with their size, led by technology, financials and health care. It's a value-focused core holding for stocks, and it may lag when fast-growing companies lead the market.
BWET: Futures contracts that bet on the cost of shipping crude oil on tankers, rather than on any company or on oil itself. It's a short-term trade on freight rates, which swing wildly, so it's risky and not meant for long holding periods.
BWQG: Companies the managers believe can grow faster than average for a long time, led by technology and internet names. It is a concentrated growth portfolio, mostly direct stocks with some index fund ballast, and growth stocks swing harder than the broad market.
BWTG: Large and mid-sized growth companies chosen from a model portfolio of the stocks that professional investors rate most highly for shareholder value. The mix roams across technology, energy, real estate and industry, so it looks quite different from a standard growth fund.
BWX: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US, priced in local currencies instead of dollars. It's a way to diversify away from US bonds, but currency swings can add gains or losses, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
BWZ: Short-term government bonds from countries outside the US, with maturities of one to three years. It's meant to diversify into foreign interest rates and keep price swings small, though changes in the dollar against foreign currencies can still move its value.
BYLD: A mix of bonds from governments and companies, chosen to squeeze out more yield than a standard bond fund. It aims for higher monthly income and a bond cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
BYRE: Real estate companies in the US and abroad, actively chosen by Principal managers across property types like housing, warehouses, retail and data centers. It is an opportunistic property holding that can hunt where managers see value rather than mirror the big real estate indexes, so its mix shifts over time.
BZZ: Drone makers and the young air taxi industry: companies building unmanned aircraft and the services around them, mostly industrial firms. It is a speculative bet on skies filling with delivery drones and flying taxis, so expect sharp swings.
CAAA: The top-rated slices of commercial mortgage securities: loans on malls, offices, hotels and other business properties, all carrying AAA ratings at purchase. It aims for bond income a notch above Treasuries with the highest-rated protection in commercial property debt.
CABZ: Self-driving car and robotaxi companies: the firms building driverless vehicles, their sensors and software, split between technology and consumer names. It is a bet on rides without drivers becoming normal, a futuristic theme that swings on regulation and testing news.
CAFG: Small US companies screened for unusually strong free cash flow margins, with technology and health care the biggest groups. It looks for small firms already generating real cash, a quality filter meant to weed out the most fragile small caps.
CAFX: Investment-grade bonds issued in US dollars, meaning borrowers rated in the top four credit tiers, with an average life of up to ten years. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
CAGE: US stocks held through a structure that aims to capture growth tied to an autocallable, a contract that pays out at set dates when the market is above a target level. It's a growth-oriented strategy with built-in complexity, so returns can differ noticeably from simply owning stocks.
CAIE: Income-focused fund that uses options-style contracts tied to big US companies, backed by Treasuries and cash. It aims to pay regular income rather than growth, but the payouts depend on how the market behaves, and the complex setup can limit gains when stocks surge.
CAIQ: Exposure to the Nasdaq-100 through swaps and Treasuries, with a structure that pays regular income when the index stays above set levels. It's meant for income with some stock exposure, but it can end early or lose out in a big market drop or surge.
CALF: Smaller US companies that generate lots of cash relative to their price, spread over consumer, technology, energy and industrial firms. It's a value tilted pick for small company exposure, and it can swing more than large company funds, especially in a slowing economy.
CALI: Short-term California municipal bonds, mostly investment grade, with interest generally free from federal and California income tax. It's for California savers who want tax-free income with little price swing, and short maturities mean lower income than longer muni funds.
CAM: Municipal bonds from California and its cities and agencies, with medium-term maturities. It's for residents who want income that is generally free of federal and California income tax, and it is concentrated in one state's finances.
CAML: Large US growth companies chosen by a manager, with technology about half the fund and industrials around a tenth. It's built for growth, so it can rise faster than the broad market, but it also drops harder when tech stocks fall.
CAMX: An actively managed fund that holds just 20 to 30 stocks, mostly in the US but with some elsewhere, which Cambiar considers undervalued. Each of the top few is about 4% to 5%, so it is fairly concentrated, with health care and industrials the biggest areas.
CANC: Companies earning at least half their revenue from cancer care, such as drug makers, diagnostics and treatment firms, all in health care. It's a focused bet on one medical area, so it swings more than the broad market.
CANE: Sugar futures contracts, rolled as they expire, giving direct exposure to the world sugar price without owning any physical sugar. It is a single commodity trading tool that swings with harvests, weather and energy markets, and futures rolling costs can eat into returns over time.
CANQ: Mostly bond funds holding mortgage bonds, high yield debt, government bonds and collateralized loans, combined with Nasdaq-100 equity exposure and options. The blend is shaped to behave like convertible bonds, offering stock-linked upside with bond-like income, though it owns few convertibles directly.
CAOS: A portfolio of options on large US stocks, used to protect against big market crashes. It's a hedge, not a growth fund, so the options can lose value in calm or rising markets, which makes it a drag when stocks do well.
CAPA: Makers of capacitors, the tiny parts that store and smooth electric charge inside every AI server and data center. It is a narrow bet on an unglamorous but essential corner of the AI build-out, so it rises and falls with chip spending.
CAPE: US stocks chosen for being cheap compared to their long-run earnings, tilted toward consumer, real estate and materials companies and away from the usual tech-heavy mix. It's a value-minded core holding that looks very different from the S&P 500, so it can lag when tech leads.
CARK: Large US growth companies picked by managers, with technology over half and communication, financials and health care behind it. It's built for growth rather than income, and it's heavy in tech, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
CARY: Bonds backed by pools of loans, such as home mortgages, commercial property, credit cards, auto loans and student loans. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, but those loan pools carry more risk, and it can drop if borrowers fall behind or rates rise.
CARZ: Companies building the future of vehicles: electric car makers, self driving technology, battery and parts suppliers, with technology about two thirds of the fund. It is a focused bet on the car industry's reinvention, swinging with auto cycles and tech sentiment alike.
CAS: A fund that holds Chinese stocks listed on mainland exchanges (China A shares), and adds income from options. Much of the fund is currently in a Simplify government money fund, so it is a mix of mainland China exposure and an income strategy.
CATF: Intermediate-term bonds issued by California cities, counties and agencies, with a small cash cushion. It's built for tax-free income for California residents, since the interest is exempt from federal and state income tax, but it's concentrated in one state's finances.
CATH: The S&P 500 with companies screened out for conflicts with Catholic values, leaving technology at about 40 percent, then financials, communication and health care. It's a core US stock holding for people who want their values reflected, and it moves much like the broad market.
CAUG: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. The late-summer start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CBIL: US Treasury bills with maturities of roughly three to twelve months, tracking an index of them. Because the bills are so short, the price moves very little and the income follows short-term interest rates.
CBLS: Stocks picked for strong finances and low prices, paired with short positions that bet against other stocks, so the fund is hedged rather than fully exposed to the market. The long short mix aims for steadier, stock picking driven returns, and it holds a large cash cushion from its short sales.
CBOA: Bitcoin with a built-in shock absorber: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while keeping gains only up to a cap. The trade is steadier bitcoin exposure in exchange for giving up the biggest rallies.
CBOJ: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin over a one-year period ending each January, joining bitcoin's gains up to a cap while adding protection against declines beyond a set point. It is bitcoin exposure with the edges trimmed, for investors wary of the full plunge.
CBOL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of four structured protection funds with staggered outcome periods, built to limit downside while keeping capped upside. It is the laddered sibling in its family: staggering smooths timing risk, though gains still stop at each underlying fund's cap.
CBON: Bonds issued inside China and priced in renminbi, mostly from the Chinese government and its policy banks. It gives direct access to China's onshore bond market, so returns for US investors depend on Chinese interest rates and on the currency, which can add or subtract a lot.
CBOO: Bitcoin with the roughest edges filed down: over each roughly one-year period starting in October, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while following its gains only up to a cap. It is built for investors who want bitcoin exposure without the full stomach-churning ride.
CBOT: Companies building robots and humanoid machines for factories, warehouses, hospitals, homes and farms, spread across technology, industrials and consumer names. It is an actively managed bet on embodied AI: the theme is exciting and early, so prices swing on prototypes and promises as much as sales.
CBOX: A set of stock options positions rather than ordinary shares, built to earn returns from options trading while managing taxes. It's an unusual strategy meant to behave differently from the stock market, and its results depend on option pricing and not simply on stocks rising.
CBOY: Bitcoin exposure with the roughest swings softened: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while following gains only up to a cap. It suits investors who want bitcoin in a portfolio without its full plunge risk.
CBSE: Small and mid sized companies from around the world picked for strong finances, low prices or growth potential, currently heavy in technology and energy. Active stock picking drives everything here, so it can look very different from global indexes and swing with its concentrated bets.
CBTA: Bitcoin exposure that trades some safety for more upside room: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 20 percent while capping gains. It softens deep crashes but leaves investors carrying ordinary dips themselves.
CBTJ: Bitcoin exposure wrapped in a structured protection design: Treasury bills and options aim to guard most of the downside, the 80 in its name, over the year starting each January. In exchange, bitcoin's gains are capped, so it suits investors who want some crypto exposure without the full plunge risk.
CBTL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of structured protection funds with staggered one-year outcome periods, aiming to shield against losses while capping gains. Staggering the periods means some protection is always partway through its term, though the fund still moves with bitcoin between resets.
CBTO: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin for a one-year period ending each October, taking part in bitcoin's gains up to a cap while adding protection against steep declines. It suits bitcoin-curious investors who want a defined payoff instead of the coin's full swings.
CBTY: Bitcoin with a partial safety net: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 20 percent while capping gains. It trades away crash protection on smaller dips for more room to rise than tighter shielded versions.
CBXA: Bitcoin with a partial shield: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent while following gains only up to a cap. It softens deep falls while leaving smaller dips with the investor.
CBXJ: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin built from short-term Treasury securities and over-the-counter options, over a one-year period ending each January. It aims to join bitcoin's gains up to a cap while cushioning deep falls, so it moves far less than bitcoin itself.
CBXL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of four structured protection funds with staggered outcome periods, built to limit downside while keeping capped upside. The ladder smooths the timing risk of a single outcome period, but it still falls with bitcoin and gains stop at each fund's cap.
CBXO: Bitcoin exposure with a safety net: over each roughly one-year period starting in October, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent while capping how much of bitcoin's rise it keeps. It suits people who want some bitcoin upside with a softer landing.
CBXY: Bitcoin paired with a partial shield: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent and follows gains only up to a cap. It offers a middle path between holding bitcoin outright and sitting out entirely.
CCEF: Closed-end income funds bought when they trade below the value of what they own, so the fund collects their payouts plus any discount that closes. Calamos hunts this arbitrage across dozens of CEFs, making income with a value twist rather than from bonds directly.
CCFE: A concentrated, actively managed set of small US companies the managers judge cheap relative to their worth, leaning heavily on industrial and consumer businesses. It is a focused value bet, so it can trail badly when small, out-of-favor stocks lag, and it holds some cash while hunting for ideas.
CCML: Companies that make multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) and other electronic components, the tiny parts found inside phones, cars and computers. It is concentrated: Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics together are about 40% of the fund.
CCNR: Companies that produce natural resources, with materials such as miners and chemical makers at about 40 percent and energy firms about a third, plus some farming-related names. It's a way to bet on commodity-driven businesses and hedge against inflation, but it swings with commodity prices.
CCOM: Commodity exposure linked to China, built from futures on raw materials traded in Chinese markets, in a structure designed to avoid K-1 tax forms. It is a niche diversifier for investors who want Chinese commodity prices in a brokerage account, and futures markets can behave differently from the goods themselves.
CCOR: High-quality US companies with growing dividends, paired with options positions intended to hedge against market falls and add return. It is an equity hedged design aiming for a steadier path than plain stocks: the dividend growers provide the base, and the options overlay works as the shock absorber.
CCRP: Corporate bonds picked actively across industries and maturities, company debt from banks, manufacturers, drug makers and others. It works as an income holding that takes company credit risk in exchange for higher interest than government bonds, with managers choosing where the pay is worth the risk.
CCSB: Short-term bonds carrying green or sustainability labels, meaning the money funds projects like clean energy or efficient buildings, with average maturity under five years. It is a cautious income holding for investors who want their bond money aimed at environmental projects without long-term rate risk.
CCSO: US-listed companies selling solutions to climate change, led by industrial firms like waste handlers and building efficiency makers, plus metal producers. It is an actively managed way to back the clean transition, so it skips most of the market and swings with green industries.
CDC: High dividend US large companies, led by utilities, then financials and consumer staples. It's aimed at income and a steadier ride, and it shifts toward cash when markets get shaky, so it can trail in strong rallies.
CDEI: Large US companies that score well on diversity, equity and inclusion under Calvert's responsible investment principles, spanning technology, finance and health care. It offers a core stock holding screened for workplace and governance practices, not just size and price.
CDIG: Stocks from around the world picked freely by the managers across industries and company sizes, currently leaning toward consumer, energy and utility companies. With no index to follow, results depend on the managers' calls, making it a go anywhere equity holding.
CDL: Large US companies with high dividends, led by utilities, financials and consumer staples, with calmer stocks given more weight. It's built for steady income and a smoother ride, though it will trail in strong tech-driven rallies since it holds little technology.
CDPI: Dividend-paying stocks across banks, health care, technology and everyday consumer brands, paired with an options strategy meant to add extra income on top of the dividends. It is built for high payouts now, accepting that option selling gives up some stock gains.
CDX: Junk bonds, which are corporate bonds from riskier companies, held mostly through other funds and cash, with derivatives that help protect against defaults. It's aimed at high yield income with a smoother ride, though the hedge can drag on returns when credit markets are calm.
CEF: Physical gold and silver bullion held together in one trust, so the shares follow the prices of both precious metals at once. Gold is the steadier store of value and silver the swingier industrial metal, and the blend sits between Sprott's single-metal trusts in how hard it moves.
CEFA: Large companies from developed markets outside the US, tracking an S&P index that screens out companies that conflict with Catholic values. It is widely spread across many holdings, with ASML the largest at only about 3%.
CEFS: Mainly closed-end funds, a type of fund that often trades at a discount to its holdings, with financials about half, plus some short positions to hedge. It's built for income and a smoother ride, though the use of discounts and hedges means results depend on the manager's calls.
CEFZ: An actively managed collection of closed-end funds and other income funds, spanning stocks and bonds around the world. RiverNorth hunts for income funds trading at discounts to their value, so the mix and the risk level shift as bargains appear and disappear.
CEMB: Bonds issued by companies in emerging markets, such as parts of Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. It's for extra income in exchange for more risk than US bonds, and it can fall sharply during global stress or when interest rates rise.
CEPI: Twenty-five companies in crypto and digital payments, about half financials and nearly half technology, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for income. It's for income tied to the crypto industry, but gains are capped and it still swings with crypto sentiment.
CERY: A broad basket of commodity futures, such as energy, metals and farm goods, with most of the money parked in cash and short-term holdings as backing. It's a hedge against rising prices, and it picks futures contracts to reduce the cost of rolling them forward, with no K-1 tax form.
CEW: A bet on emerging market currencies against the US dollar, built with currency contracts while the cash sits in Treasury bills. It gains when currencies from Latin America, Asia and other emerging markets strengthen, and it can fall quickly when investors flee to the dollar.
CFA: Large US companies spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care. It's a core stock holding with a twist: calmer, less jumpy stocks get bigger weights than wilder ones, so it tends to fall less than the broad market in sell-offs but may trail in sharp rallies.
CFIT: Bond funds of many kinds, from Treasury bills to high yield and emerging market debt, selected by a trend-following model. The model shifts toward whatever bond types are rising and steps back from falling ones, so the mix can change a lot over time.
CFO: 500 large US companies, similar to the S&P 500, but weighted so that steadier stocks count for more, with financials, industrials, technology and health care leading. It's a core holding built for a smoother ride, and it can trail the market in strong rallies.
CGBL: A balanced mix of roughly 60% stocks, led by technology, and about 36% bonds, all in one fund. It's built as a one-stop core holding that cushions stock drops with bonds, and the managers actively shift the mix, so it won't mirror a fixed index.
CGCB: A broad mix of US bonds, mostly investment grade, such as Treasuries and corporate debt, run by an active manager. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion against stock drops, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
CGCP: A mix of US investment-grade corporate bonds, government bonds and mortgage bonds, plus some lower-rated higher-yield debt, chosen by a manager. It's meant for steady interest income with a bit more yield than a basic bond fund, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
CGCV: Large US companies with dividends that look sustainable, led by technology, health care, financials and consumer staples. It aims for steadier growth with less swing than the broad market, so it may trail in strong rallies.
CGDG: Dividend-paying stocks from around the world, led by financials, technology, industrials and health care, chosen for the potential to grow their payouts over time. It's meant as a global core holding that combines income with growth, and it holds companies the manager picks rather than a whole index.
CGDV: Large, established companies that pay dividends, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40 percent, plus industrials, communication and consumer firms. It's an actively managed fund aiming for dividend income and growth, and it can hold up to a tenth in foreign companies.
CGFS: A single fund built from other funds: a hand-picked mix of stock ETFs covering large and mid-sized US companies plus focused themes like defense and cybersecurity. Technology ends up about a third of the whole, and the fund-of-funds design sets it apart from funds that pick individual stocks.
CGGE: A concentrated mix of growth-minded companies from around the world, led by technology, industrials and financials. It's actively managed as a core global stock holding, and because it owns fewer companies than most funds, it can move differently from the world market.
CGGG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, picked by Capital Group's team of portfolio managers. It is concentrated at the top, as NVIDIA, Broadcom, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta make up roughly 45% of the fund.
CGGO: Growth-oriented companies from around the world, with technology the biggest slice at over 40 percent, followed by industrials, health care and financials. It's an actively managed growth fund, so managers choose the stocks and it tends to swing more than a broad global fund.
CGGR: US-focused growth companies chosen by a team of managers, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, then communication, health care and consumer companies. It aims for growth and is actively managed, so it can differ from the market, and it can fall hard in downturns.
CGHM: Municipal bonds from state and local governments that pay interest free of regular federal income tax, with a large share rated below top quality. It's built for tax-advantaged income, and the lower-rated bonds mean it carries more risk of losses than safer municipal funds.
CGHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, including some corporate loans, with a small cash cushion. It aims for higher income than safer bonds, though it tends to fall when stocks do because these borrowers are likelier to default.
CGIB: Bonds from the US and other countries, held with currency risk hedged back to dollars, mixing government and corporate issuers. It's meant for income and diversification away from US-only bonds, and the hedge keeps foreign currency swings from affecting returns much.
CGIC: Stocks of companies based outside the US, including some in emerging markets, led by financials and technology, followed by industrials. It's a way to add international growth and dividend payers to a portfolio, and a manager picks the stocks, so it won't simply mirror an index.
CGIE: Growth-minded companies based outside the US, with industrials about a quarter, financials a bit under a quarter and technology about a fifth. It's meant as a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and its holdings are picked by managers rather than following an index.
CGMM: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen by active managers, with technology, industrials, financials and health care the largest groups. It's a growth-minded way to add smaller companies to a portfolio, and it swings more than a large company fund, with results depending on the managers' picks.
CGMS: A mix of US bonds across several areas, including corporate bonds, mortgage-backed bonds and lower-rated higher-yielding debt, with a little cash. It's built for steady income above regular bonds, and the lower-rated holdings mean it can fall more than safe bonds when the economy weakens.
CGMU: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, most of whose interest is exempt from regular federal income tax. It's for investors in taxable accounts who want tax-friendly income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
CGNG: Companies of all sizes that earn much of their money in developing countries, led by technology, financials and industrials. It's a growth holding that adds emerging market exposure, so it swings more than US stocks and owns a limited number of companies.
CGOV: Treasury bills maturing within three months, the shortest and safest US government debt. It is a cash alternative for parking money, earning a small interest trickle while keeping the value about as steady as a bank account.
CGPT: Companies that run AI inference, the behind-the-scenes computing that answers prompts and powers AI features in real time, all in the technology sector. It is a focused bet on the usage phase of AI rather than the training phase, riding data-center demand.
CGRO: Growth companies across Greater China: mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, led by consumer firms with industrials and technology behind them. It is an actively managed single-region growth bet: the manager picks high-growth sectors, and Chinese policy swings hit the whole fund at once.
CGSD: Mostly short-term, high-quality bonds with some cash, from companies, governments and mortgage-backed sources. It's meant for steady income with little price swing, as a cushion for a stock portfolio, and its short maturities mean it's less hurt when interest rates rise.
CGSM: Short-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, paying interest that is free of regular federal income tax. It's meant for tax-advantaged income with less ups and downs than longer bonds, because short maturities make its price less sensitive to interest rate changes.
CGUS: Large US companies picked by managers for growth and dividend potential, with technology over 40 percent and communication, consumer and financial companies behind it. It can be a core stock holding, but because managers pick stocks, it can differ noticeably from the market.
CGV: Companies from around the world that a manager thinks are cheap, spread across industrials, materials, energy and consumer staples. It's a value-style way to hold global stocks, and it leans away from the technology giants that dominate most global funds.
CGVV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings or assets, spread across technology, consumer, financials and industrials. It's a core-style stock holding with a value tilt, so it may lag when fast-growing stocks lead the market.
CGW: Companies tied to water, about half utilities that deliver it and over 40% industrials that make pipes, pumps and treatment equipment, from around the world. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it moves differently from the broad market and can swing with global growth.
CGXU: Growth-oriented companies outside the US, including emerging markets, led by technology with industrials, materials and financials behind. It's an actively managed way to diversify beyond US stocks, and the managers pick stocks rather than mirror an index.
CHAT: Global companies tied to generative AI, with technology about three quarters of the portfolio and communication companies making up most of the rest. It's a focused bet on one theme run by active managers, so it can swing far more than the broad market.
CHDG: Shares of S&P 500 funds paired with options hedges the manager adjusts to soften market drops. It is a defensive core holding: the goal is to keep most of the market's upside while falling less in sell-offs, accepting that the hedging costs something in calm markets.
CHGX: About 100 large and mid-sized US companies, equally weighted, with technology about 40% and financials, health care and consumer companies behind. It screens for sustainability, so it's a core style holding for investors wanting a values tilt, but it will differ from the broad market.
CHIP: Chipmaking companies from across the supply chain, including the firms that design AI processors and the ones that build the equipment used to manufacture them. It is a focused bet on artificial intelligence hardware, so it swings more than the broad tech sector and depends on chip spending staying strong.
CHIQ: Chinese consumer companies: online marketplaces, electric car makers, food delivery, travel booking and restaurant chains, nearly all in consumer discretionary. It is a focused bet on China's shoppers, so it moves with Chinese consumer confidence, regulation and the wider China market mood.
CHNL: Exposure to Chainlink, the network that feeds real-world data like prices into blockchains, gained through futures contracts rather than holding the token itself. Prices are set by speculators in the futures market, so the fund can drift from the token's spot price and swings hard either way.
CHPS: Semiconductor companies, the makers and designers of computer chips, screened for sustainability. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market and rises and falls with chip demand.
CHPX: Almost entirely technology: chip makers and related companies tied to artificial intelligence and quantum computing. It's a focused bet on one fast-moving industry, so it swings far more than the broad market.
CHPY: Semiconductor companies, all within technology, paired with an options strategy that aims to pay regular income. The income comes at a price: gains are capped in strong chip rallies, and since the fund is focused on one industry, it still swings sharply.
CHRI: The S&P 500 with companies screened out if they conflict with Christian values, such as those tied to things like abortion, adult entertainment or gambling. What is left looks a lot like the regular index: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
CHYG: High yield corporate bonds with five years or less to maturity, the shorter end of the junk bond market. Shorter maturities mean less damage when interest rates rise, though the below-investment-grade credit risk remains fully in place.
CIBR: Companies that sell cybersecurity tools and services, nearly all in the technology sector. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market, and it holds a limited number of companies rather than the whole tech industry.
CIEI: US Treasury bonds with three to seven years left until they mature, the middle ground of government debt. It pays steady interest with moderate price swings when rates move, steadier than long bonds but more rewarding than cash-like funds.
CIVG: Corporate bonds from solid, investment-grade companies with one to five years until they mature. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it works as a steadier income holding that pays a bit more than government bonds of similar length.
CJUL: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange. The July start fixes the terms: this edition's protection clock runs from mid-year, and later buyers get what remains.
CJUN: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. The mid-year start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CLCG: Large US growth companies, with technology over half the fund, picked by managers at a faith-based firm known for values screens. It plays the growth role in a portfolio, leaning on big tech and media names, and it can trail when investors rotate toward cheaper, slower stocks.
CLCV: Large US companies trading at value prices, drawn from the Russell 1000 Value universe across technology, finance, health care and industry. It owns some big tech names when they trade cheaply, so it is a value fund comfortable crossing style lines.
CLIM: Real estate investment trusts around the world screened for climate resilience: property owners judged better prepared for floods, heat and other weather risks. It is a property income holding with an environmental filter, so the usual REIT risks come with a climate scorecard attached.
CLIP: Very short US Treasury bills that come due in one to three months, essentially cash. It's a parking spot for money you want to keep safe while still earning interest, and since it barely reacts to interest rate changes its price stays very steady, though its income moves with short-term rates.
CLNK: Holds Chainlink, a cryptocurrency that supplies real world data to blockchain applications, directly rather than through futures. Its price follows the price of Chainlink, which can swing a lot, and it owns no stocks or bonds.
CLOA: Bundles of corporate loans, called collateralized loan obligations, from only the top AAA rated slices that get paid first. It's meant for income with low credit risk, and because the payments float with short-term rates, it holds its price better than most bonds when rates rise.
CLOB: Mostly collateralized loan obligations, bundles of loans to companies, rated in the middle to upper tiers from AA down to BB, with a bit of cash. It's meant for extra income over regular bonds, and because the interest payments float with rates, it holds up when rates rise.
CLOC: An actively managed fund of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans to companies sliced into bonds that pay interest. It spreads its money across many CLOs, each around 2.5% of the fund.
CLOD: Cloud computing companies in developed markets: the software, hosting and platform firms that rent computing power and tools over the internet. It is a focused technology bet: cloud names dominate, so it swings with tech spending and leaves out most other industries.
CLOI: Investment-grade slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of loans to companies that are packaged and sold as bonds. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, and its interest payments float with short-term rates, so it's less hurt when rates rise.
CLOO: The safest layers of collateralized loan obligations: investment grade debt issued by vehicles that bundle corporate loans together. It pays more than comparable plain bonds because of the structure's complexity, while sticking to the top rated slices where losses arrive last.
CLOU: Companies that sell cloud computing services, such as software over the internet, data storage and data center operators, with about 90 percent in technology. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing corner of tech, so it swings more than the broad market.
CLOX: Top-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of loans to companies packaged into bonds. It's meant for extra income with limited risk, and its payments float with short-term interest rates, so income rises when rates rise.
CLOZ: Bundles of loans made to lower-rated US companies, packaged as collateralized loan obligations, with ratings between BBB and B. It pays a high income that adjusts as interest rates change, but it carries real credit risk and can drop sharply in a downturn.
CLSE: Large US stocks, buying those expected to rise while betting against others expected to fall, led by technology among the holdings. It's meant to cushion drops and lower dependence on the market, but it can trail a plain stock fund in strong rallies.
CLSM: A rotating handful of US sector funds, currently concentrated in technology, big growth stocks and consumer staples, plus a little gold. It chases whichever sectors are leading while keeping a moderate stance, so the lineup can change completely as market leadership rotates.
CLUB: An actively managed global stock fund that buys companies where famous billionaire investors have large stakes. Holdings are spread widely, with Dell, SoftBank, Oracle and ArcelorMittal each around 4% to 6%, and technology is the biggest sector at roughly 30%.
CMAG: An actively managed fund holding the largest US-listed tech and tech-related giants, weighted by company size. NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 38% of it, and a large chunk sits in government cash funds, so it is very concentrated.
CMAY: S&P 500 exposure through options with a deeper cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. Compared with shallower buffers, it trades a lower cap on gains for protection that covers bigger drops.
CMBO: An interest rate strategy that shifts its bets as rates move, using derivatives to profit from rising or falling yields while keeping maturities very short. It aims to make money from rate swings themselves rather than simply collecting steady interest.
CMBS: Investment-grade bonds backed by pools of commercial mortgages on offices, apartments, shopping centers and similar properties. It's for steady income with a bit more yield than Treasuries, and it adds variety to a bond portfolio, though it can lose value when interest rates rise or property markets weaken.
CMCI: Raw materials across energy, metals and farm goods, reached through contracts tied to a broad commodity index that spreads bets across delivery dates. The steady-maturity approach aims for smoother commodity exposure than funds concentrated in the nearest futures contracts.
CMDT: Contracts that rise and fall with commodity prices such as energy, metals and farm goods, backed by a portfolio of bonds. It's used as a hedge when inflation heats up and to diversify away from stocks, but it can drop sharply when commodity prices fall.
CMDY: Futures contracts on 24 commodities, covering energy, metals and farm products, rather than owning any stocks or bonds. It's a hedge against inflation and a diversifier, but it swings with commodity prices and pays no dividends.
CMF: Longer-term municipal bonds issued in California, with interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It's for investors seeking tax-free income, and it's concentrated in one state's issuers, so its price drops when interest rates rise.
CNAV: About fifty US stocks chosen by a quantitative model that reads price momentum across the sub industries of the large stock market, currently leaning heavily into technology hardware. It tactically chases whichever corners of the market are rising, so its mix can change fast and it can whipsaw in choppy markets.
CNBS: US-listed companies tied to cannabis and hemp, such as growers, suppliers and cannabis-focused real estate firms. It is a narrow, volatile corner of the market, and Curaleaf is one of its biggest named stock holdings at about 16%.
CNEQ: A small group of large US growth companies, with technology over half and communication and industrial firms next. It's actively managed for growth, and because it owns far fewer companies than most funds, a few bad picks can move it more than the broad market.
CNQQ: China's biggest technology companies, from internet platforms and phone makers to battery and chip firms, chosen from the largest listed names. It is a focused bet on China's tech sector, so it swings with Chinese markets and with government policy there.
CNRG: Companies tied to clean power, split between industrials making equipment, utilities that generate renewable energy and technology firms, roughly a third each. It's a focused bet on the shift away from fossil fuels, so it swings more than the broad market and can react sharply to energy policy.
CNXT: The 100 largest companies on China's ChiNext board in Shenzhen, the country's startup-heavy exchange: battery makers, optical network gear, solar and medical firms, with technology over half. It is a focused bet on Chinese innovation, and ChiNext stocks are known for especially sharp price swings.
CNYA: Large and mid-sized companies listed on mainland China's domestic exchanges, with technology about a third, financials a fifth, and industrials and materials after that. It's a growth bet on China's home market, so it swings with Chinese policy and economic news, and moves differently from US stocks.
COAL: Coal companies worldwide, miners and shippers of both power plant coal and the metallurgical coal used to make steel. It is a narrow, old economy bet that rises and falls with coal prices and energy demand, and few other funds still offer this exposure.
COIW: Built around one stock, Coinbase, using swaps to deliver about 120 percent of its weekly move while paying out income every week. The leverage resets weekly and everything rides on a single crypto-linked stock, so it is a short-term trading tool, not a steady holding.
COLO: Companies in Colombia, with financials over two fifths and utilities, energy and materials making up much of the rest. It's a single-country bet, so it swings with oil prices and Colombian politics, and it's more volatile than a broad world fund.
COM: Futures contracts on commodities like energy, metals and farm goods, shifting toward cash when trends turn down. It's a diversifier that can hedge against inflation, and its trend-following rules can lag when markets reverse quickly.
COMB: Futures contracts on a broad basket of raw materials such as energy, metals and farm goods, with the rest held in cash and short-term bonds as backing. It's a hedge against rising prices, and a manager adjusts it actively, and it avoids the extra tax paperwork some commodity funds create.
COMD: Commodities of all kinds: oil, metals and farm goods, reached through futures and similar contracts under active management. It can diversify a stock and bond portfolio since raw materials often move on their own cycle, though commodity prices are famously volatile.
COMT: Commodities like energy, metals and farm goods, held through futures contracts, with the rest in cash and short-term bonds for backing. It can hedge against inflation and moves apart from stocks, and it adjusts which futures it holds to limit losses from rolling contracts forward.
CONY: Income from options tied to one stock, the crypto exchange Coinbase, with the rest held in Treasuries and cash. It's built to pay out high monthly income, but it gives up much of the stock's big gains and can still lose heavily when the stock falls.
COOL: Companies solving the AI data-center heat problem: cooling systems, power management and the electrical gear behind them, split between technology and industrials. It is a picks-and-shovels AI bet on infrastructure nobody sees, swinging with data-center construction rather than software hype.
COPA: A fund holding copper mining and refining companies from around the world, following an index of firms that earn much of their revenue from copper. Freeport-McMoRan is the largest holding at about 9%, and nearly everything is in materials companies.
COPJ: Smaller companies that mine, explore and produce copper, all in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on one metal, with fewer and smaller companies than a big miner fund, so it swings with copper prices and global growth more than the broad market.
COPP: Companies that mine copper, nearly all counted as materials. It's a focused bet on one metal, so it swings more than the broad market and moves with copper prices and global manufacturing demand.
COPX: Companies that mine copper around the world, nearly all in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on copper, a metal tied to construction and electrification, so it swings much more than the broad market and moves with the metal's price.
COPY: Small and mid-sized companies around the world, led by consumer brands, financials, industrials and energy, picked because they look cheap and the company's own leaders are buying shares. It's a value approach for patient investors, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
CORB: A mix of US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, chosen by a manager, with a small cash share and some foreign bonds allowed. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion against stock drops, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
CORN: Futures contracts on corn, held across three different delivery months rather than the physical grain. It's a direct bet on corn prices and a way to add farm commodities to a portfolio, but futures costs can make it lag the price of corn itself.
CORO: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, with financials and technology the biggest groups, followed by industrials. Managers shift money between countries over time, aiming for growth, so the mix can change instead of staying fixed like an index fund.
CORP: Bonds issued by US companies with solid credit ratings, spread across many industries. It's meant for steady income higher than Treasuries pay, though its price drops when interest rates rise, and it can fall when the economy weakens and companies struggle.
COSW: A single-stock fund that gets its exposure to Costco through swaps, contracts that pay the stock's returns, plus some direct shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and much of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing for those swaps.
COWG: Large US companies that produce lots of spare cash after expenses, with technology about 70 percent and health care next. It's a growth-leaning stock fund, so it behaves more like a tech fund and swings more than the broad market.
COWS: US companies that both pay dividends and generate strong free cash flow, spread across technology, industrial, energy and financial firms. The double screen aims for income backed by real cash, favoring mature businesses over fast growers with no payouts.
COWZ: Large and mid-sized US companies that generate a lot of cash compared with their price, led by technology, energy, health care and industrials. It's a value-style core holding, and it reshuffles regularly, so energy swings can move it more than the broad market.
COYY: Options tied to Coinbase, the big US crypto exchange, used through a related fund structure to produce boosted income payouts. It cashes in on the wild swings in crypto-linked shares, with gains capped and deep drops only partly softened by income.
CPAG: A basket of other bond funds that together mirror the US investment-grade bond market, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's a core bond holding built to deliver the market's total return without paying out regular income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
CPAI: US stocks of any size picked by a computer model, with technology about a third and energy near a fifth. It aims for growth from a quantitative stock screen, so its mix can shift over time and may look quite different from the broad market.
CPER: Futures contracts on copper, so it follows the metal's price instead of owning mining companies. It's a bet on industrial demand and the economy that swings a lot, and it pays no income.
CPHY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier kind often called junk bonds, held indirectly through other bond funds. Instead of paying the interest out, it is structured to keep returns compounding inside the fund, which can help investors in taxable accounts.
CPII: An actively managed fund built to protect against rising US inflation, using inflation-linked Treasury bonds along with inflation swaps and options. Most of it sits in a handful of inflation-protected Treasuries, so it is aimed at inflation rather than stock-like growth.
CPLB: A broad mix of bonds from governments, companies and mortgage pools, with some lower-quality bonds added to earn extra interest. It's meant as a core bond holding with a bit more income than a standard bond fund, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
CPLS: A broad mix of bonds, including corporate bonds, government-backed mortgage bonds and other debt, with some riskier bonds beyond the usual investment-grade core. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, with a bit of extra yield, though prices drop when interest rates rise.
CPNJ: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set up each June for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on the tech heavy growth basket while keeping a capped share of gains. It suits investors who want Nasdaq exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting smaller rallies.
CPNM: Options on the Nasdaq-100 structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in March, while taking part in gains up to a cap. It trades away the biggest rallies in exchange for a much softer landing when tech stocks fall.
CPNQ: Options on the Nasdaq-100 structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in December, while taking part in gains up to a cap. It trades away the biggest rallies in exchange for a much softer landing when tech stocks fall.
CPNS: Options on the Nasdaq-100 fund structured to protect against losses over the year starting each September, in exchange for a cap on gains. It applies Calamos's defined protection design to the tech-heavy index, so it suits investors who want Nasdaq growth potential without facing its full drops.
CPRA: Options on a Russell 2000 fund structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in April, while taking part in small-cap gains up to a cap. It trades away the strongest small-stock rallies for a softer landing in downturns.
CPRJ: Options on a small company stock fund, arranged to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each July, with gains capped in exchange. It targets small company exposure with a safety net, so it should fall less than small stocks in a downturn.
CPRO: Options on a small-cap index fund structured to protect against losses over the year starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. Small stocks fall harder than large ones in sell-offs, so pairing them with Calamos's full protection design targets a much smoother ride than small caps usually give.
CPRY: Options on a small company index fund, structured to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each January, with a cap on gains as the trade. It brings a safety net to the wildest corner of the stock market, small company shares.
CPSA: Options on the S&P 500 set up each August for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CPSD: Options on the S&P 500 set up each December for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CPSF: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to shield against losses over an outcome period that resets each February, with gains limited to pay for the shield. It is meant to be bought and held for the whole period, when the protection works as designed.
CPSJ: Options on the S&P 500 set up each July for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CPSL: US large-company stock exposure held through a ladder of twelve funds with staggered start dates, each built to limit part of the downside. It's for investors who want market growth with protection, though that protection comes with capped upside.
CPSM: Options on the S&P 500 set up each May for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock market exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CPSN: Options on the S&P 500 built to protect against losses over an outcome period resetting each November, trading away part of any gain for the shield. Bought at the wrong moment the protection can differ, so it is designed for buy-and-hold use.
CPSO: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CPSP: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CPSR: Options on the S&P 500 structured to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each March, with gains capped as the cost of protection. It suits holders who stay the full period, since the protection is designed around that fixed window.
CPST: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each September, with participation in gains limited in exchange. It offers big-company stock exposure with a safety net, designed to be held for the full period.
CPSU: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each June, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CPSY: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each January, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CPTL: Large US companies chosen for how well their bosses use cash, including buybacks, dividends and careful spending, spread across every major industry with technology the biggest slice at well over a third. It works as a core stock holding with a quality tilt toward disciplined money management.
CPU: The ten largest semiconductor companies, the designers and manufacturers behind the chips in every computer, phone and data center. Limiting the fund to ten giants makes it a concentrated bet on the chip cycle, so it swings hard when chip demand or AI spending shifts.
CQQQ: Chinese technology companies, with tech about half and the rest in internet, communication and online consumer businesses. It's a focused, high-risk bet on one country's tech sector, and Chinese government rules can hit these stocks hard, so it swings far more than the broad market.
CQTM: Companies building quantum computers and the security tools meant to withstand them, a small and speculative corner of technology. Holdings are concentrated in a few young companies, so single-stock news can drive the whole result.
CRAK: Companies that refine crude oil into gasoline and diesel, nearly all in energy, with firms in the US and abroad. It's a focused bet on refining profits, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on the gap between oil and fuel prices.
CRAM: Chinese memory and storage chip companies listed in mainland China and Hong Kong, covering the firms that make the memory inside phones, computers and data centers. It is a narrow, single-country bet on a strategic industry, so it carries both sharp industry swings and the political risks of investing in China.
CRBN: Companies from around the world, with technology at about a third and financials near a fifth, but with a tilt away from heavy carbon emitters and big fossil fuel reserves. It's a global core stock holding for those wanting a lower carbon footprint.
CRCO: An options income strategy tied to Circle, the company behind a major dollar pegged digital token, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting premiums for monthly payouts. It is an income play on one young, volatile crypto linked stock, with gains capped.
CRDD: Exposure to Cardano's ADA crypto token through regulated futures contracts, backed by cash and high-quality collateral. It lets traders bet on ADA's price in a brokerage account without holding the token, though futures pricing can drift from spot and crypto swings are large.
CRDT: A go-anywhere income portfolio spanning US and foreign bonds and other income securities, using leverage and derivatives to hunt for yield opportunistically. That flexible, amplified design can pay more than cautious bond funds, but it also magnifies losses and makes the fund harder to predict.
CRIB: Real estate companies from around the world, including the United States: property owners, developers and REITs across many countries. It is a global property holding for income and diversification, with currency swings and foreign housing markets added to the usual real estate risks.
CROB: Chinese companies building robots and automation systems, from factory machines to humanoid and service robots. It is a narrow, high-risk theme bet on China's robotics push: the fund is concentrated in one country and one industry, so policy and market swings hit it hard.
CRPT: Companies in the crypto industry and the wider digital economy, such as financial firms and technology, plus some direct crypto exposure. It's a high-risk, focused bet on digital assets, so it swings far more than the broad market.
CRSH: An options strategy that profits when Tesla's stock falls, using inverse exposure to the electric car maker plus income from sold options. It is a bearish single-stock tool: it gains in Tesla drops, loses when Tesla climbs, and pays income along the way.
CRTC: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries working on technologies seen as critical to national security and competitiveness, led by technology with communication, health care and industrials behind. It's a themed holding that swings more than the broad market.
CRUX: Investment-grade US dollar bonds, which are issued by borrowers rated as fairly safe, plus a little cash. It's meant as a steady income core for the bond part of a portfolio and a cushion for stocks, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
CRXP: A core-plus bond portfolio built on mortgage bonds, including agency pools and non-agency home loan trusts, plus corporate and other debt. The plus reach into non-agency mortgages lifts income above plain core funds, with more credit complexity underneath.
CRY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to Circle, the stablecoin company behind USDC. It stacks options on leverage on one newly public crypto-linked stock, so payouts can be fat but swings are extreme and holding periods should be short.
CSB: Small US companies that pay high dividends, led by financials and utilities, with each stock weighted by how steady its price has been. It's for income and a calmer ride within small companies, but it tends to trail in strong rallies led by growth stocks.
CSD: US companies recently split off from a parent company, with industrials over two fifths and technology about a quarter. It's a niche growth and value idea that holds mid-sized firms freed from their parents, and it can swing more than the broad market.
CSEN: Companies in energy, including traditional oil and gas, renewables and clean energy, plus utilities and related businesses. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, and an active manager picks the mix, so oil price swings and policy changes can move it sharply.
CSEP: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. The autumn start fixes its terms, so buyers later inherit only the protection time that remains.
CSHI: Very short-term US Treasury bills paired with a strategy of selling options on the S&P 500 to earn extra income. It's meant as a place to park cash for income above plain T-bills, though the option sales can cause occasional losses in sharp market drops.
CSHP: A mostly short-term, high-quality bond portfolio with some stocks and currencies mixed in, managed actively as markets shift. It's meant for people who want a bit more return than cash with limited swings, though the stock portion means it can dip more than a pure short-term bond fund.
CSIO: Infrastructure companies worldwide: utilities are over half, with transportation, energy and communications networks behind, all businesses owning essential physical systems. It targets income and steady growth from tolls, bills and fees people pay regardless of the economy, actively hunting opportunities across borders.
CSM: Large US companies, with a 130/30 approach: it bets on the stocks it likes most and shorts those it likes least. It's meant as a core stock holding that tries to beat the market, but shorting adds risk and cost.
CSMD: Small and mid-sized US companies, led by health care and technology at about a quarter each, with industrials around a fifth. A manager picks the stocks, aiming for growth, so it's a way to add smaller companies that tend to swing more than large ones.
CSNR: Companies tied to natural resources, split mainly between energy and materials, with some food and consumer staples firms. It's a focused bet on commodity-linked businesses and can serve as an inflation hedge, but it swings with commodity prices.
CSPF: Mostly income-paying securities from companies: preferred stock, which pays fixed dividends and ranks ahead of common shares, plus bonds and a few convertibles. It's built for high monthly-style income, and its price can fall when interest rates rise or when companies run into trouble.
CSRA: Real assets for income and inflation resistance: property companies, commodities, pipelines, utilities and gold, gathered through other funds and direct holdings. It aims to behave differently from plain stocks and bonds, especially when inflation is rising.
CSRE: Real estate companies, mainly trusts that own offices, apartments, warehouses and cell towers and pass rent income on, chosen by a manager. It's for income and property exposure, and it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
CSSD: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income bonds, mostly from banks and financial companies, with shorter maturities. The shorter terms are meant to make its price less sensitive to interest rate changes, and it focuses on investment grade issuers.
CSTK: Large US companies the managers see as unloved or out of favor, spread across financials, health care, technology and industrials. It's a value and contrarian choice for the stock part of a portfolio, and it holds a smaller group of names, so it can behave differently from the broad market.
CTA: Futures contracts across stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies, with trades that follow price trends and can bet on falls as well as rises. It's a diversifier meant to do differently from stocks and bonds, though trend following can lose money when markets keep reversing.
CTAG: Small and mid-sized US companies picked actively for growth, led by technology, industrial and health care firms. Smaller growers like these can rise fast, but they also fall harder than big companies when investors turn cautious about risk.
CTAP: US stocks, led by technology, combined with a managed futures strategy that bets on rising or falling trends in commodities, currencies and interest rates, backed by a large bond holding. The idea is a second source of returns that may help when stocks struggle, though it can lag in calm rallies.
CTAU: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection costs upside: the cap is low, so it trails badly in strong rallies.
CTEC: Climate technology companies worldwide: solar and battery makers, electric vehicle suppliers, grid and efficiency businesses, mostly industrial firms. It is a growth bet on the build-out of clean technology, concentrated in smaller companies whose fortunes follow green energy spending and policy more than the broad market.
CTEF: Mid-sized US stocks, with technology almost half, followed by financials and consumer companies. It's an actively managed growth-tilted holding, and since it may also use options and holds a concentrated mix, it can behave quite differently from a plain mid-cap fund.
CTIF: US companies with a history of growing their dividends, mostly industrials, technology and financials, paired with options that generate extra income. It aims for income plus some growth, though the options limit gains in strong rallies and the manager's picks can differ from the market.
CTJL: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to buffer the first 30% of losses over its outcome period, in exchange for a cap on gains. This July series resets each year, and the protection works as designed only for investors who hold through the full period.
CTJN: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to buffer the first 30% of losses over its outcome period, in exchange for a cap on gains. This June series resets each year, and the protection works as designed only for investors who hold through the full period.
CTMA: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection comes at a price: the cap on gains is low, so it trails badly in strong rallies.
CTSE: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection costs upside: the cap is low, so strong rallies mostly pass it by.
CTWO: European Union carbon allowances, the permits that factories and power plants must hold to emit carbon under the EU cap-and-trade system. It is a pure bet on carbon prices: the fund owns the allowances themselves, so it rises and falls with EU climate policy and energy markets.
CUST: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, so it is a low-risk way to hold government debt. Because the bonds are short, the price moves less when interest rates change than it would for long-term Treasuries.
CUT: Timber and forest product companies worldwide: forestry owners, lumber mills, paper and packaging makers. It is a focused bet on wood and the land under it, often used as a diversifier tied to housing and construction demand, and it moves with commodity and property cycles.
CVAR: An actively managed mix of US stocks the manager judges undervalued, spread across industries with health care, technology and everyday consumer goods the largest slices. It holds only a few dozen names, so each pick matters more than in a broad index fund.
CVGD: Dividend-paying companies in the US and abroad that a manager sees as financially strong, led by health care, financials and consumer staples. It's built for steady dividend income with a smoother ride, and it can trail when fast-growing tech stocks lead.
CVIE: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, led by technology and financials, then industrials and health care. It's a way to add international stocks, and it only includes companies meeting responsible-business standards, so some sectors are underrepresented compared with a standard international fund.
CVLC: Large US companies screened for strong environmental and social records, with technology about 40%, then financials, health care and industrials. It's a core US stock holding for people who want responsible investing, and it leaves out some businesses a plain index fund would own.
CVMC: US mid-sized companies, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care, screened for responsible business practices. It's a core mid-cap holding for people who want a values tilt, and the screen can make it differ slightly from a standard mid-cap fund.
CVNY: An options strategy built around a single stock, Carvana, the online used-car seller, using synthetic covered calls to generate income. It pays regular distributions from selling those options, but gains are capped and a sharp drop in the stock hits the fund hard.
CVRD: Dividend-paying US stocks with covered call options sold on a large share of the portfolio to collect premium income. The design targets steady income and a somewhat smoother ride than plain stocks, giving up part of the gains when share prices rise strongly.
CVRT: Convertible securities, the hybrid bonds that can turn into stock, chosen for the ones most sensitive to share price moves, plus related preferred shares. It aims to join in much of a stock rally while the bond side softens falls, a middle path between stocks and bonds.
CVSM: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by active managers, spread across finance, consumer, industrial and drug firms rather than concentrated in technology. It hunts for growth in the market's middle ranks, where companies are big enough to be proven but small enough to still expand quickly.
CVY: A blend of dividend-paying stocks, mainly financials, energy and real estate, plus some preferred shares and bonds, from the US and abroad. It's built for income, but it's heavy in a few cyclical industries and can drop in downturns.
CWB: Convertible bonds, which are company bonds that can be swapped for stock, with a smaller amount of preferred shares, mostly from technology and other growth companies. It aims for a middle path: it joins some of a stock rally while offering bond-like income and a bit less drop in sell-offs.
CWI: Large and mid-sized companies from around the world outside the US, led by financials and technology, followed by industrials. It's a way to add international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it includes emerging markets, which tend to be bumpier than developed ones.
CWS: A concentrated group of US mid-sized companies picked by a model, led by health care, industrials and technology. It's a core-style stock holding with only a limited number of picks, so it can behave quite differently from the broad market.
CWY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to CoreWeave, the AI data-center company. It stacks options on leverage on one young, volatile stock at the center of the AI buildout, so payouts can be large but swings are extreme and holding periods should be short.
CXSE: Chinese companies that aren't majority owned by the government, led by consumer discretionary and technology at roughly a quarter each. It's a focused bet on China's private sector, so it swings more than the broad market and reacts to Chinese policy changes.
CZA: One hundred mid-sized US companies chosen by a ranking system, with financials about a quarter, then industrials, health care and real estate. It adds the middle of the market to a portfolio, which is usually more volatile than giants and less than small companies, and it holds few tech names.
DABS: Bonds backed by pools of consumer and business loans, such as auto loans and credit cards, mostly rated investment grade. It's for steady income above Treasuries, and its price tends to swing less than long bonds, though it can drop if borrowers default.
DACL: Derivatives that follow an index of autocallable notes, structured products on stock markets that pay steady income and can end early when markets behave. The defensive design aims to soften falls, but the income comes with capped gains and note-style complexity.
DADS: An actively managed fund of debt, such as bonds, convertibles and preferred shares, from companies involved in digital assets like bitcoin mining. Core Scientific, Riot and Galaxy Digital are among its holdings, so it is tied to the crypto industry.
DAK: Large US stocks chosen actively, mostly held directly but partly through big index funds, with technology the largest slice. It blends stock picking with ready-made market exposure, so its results depend on the managers' picks beating a plain index fund.
DALI: A rotation among First Trust stock funds guided by relative strength, favoring whichever styles and sectors have been performing best recently. The lineup shifts as trends change, currently leaning industrial, making it a momentum strategy that can look very different from one season to the next.
DANA: High-quality bonds chosen to preserve capital: agency mortgage bonds, US government securities and corporate bonds rated AA or better. It aims for steady income with limited volatility, accepting modest yields as the price of safety.
DAPP: Companies built around digital assets and blockchain, such as crypto exchanges, miners and payment firms, with financials at about 60 percent and technology a third. It's a focused bet on this industry that holds no coins itself, and it swings sharply with crypto sentiment.
DAPR: Options tied to the S&P 500 that shield against a large part of losses over a one year period starting in April, in exchange for a limit on gains. It's for holders who want a deep cushion, and the protection only works if held from start to end.
DARP: A concentrated portfolio of thirty to sixty growth companies chosen for innovation and disruption, across technology, media, industry and energy, at home and abroad. It is a conviction driven growth bet, so it swings harder than diversified growth funds when its themes fall in or out of favor.
DAUG: Options contracts tied to an S&P 500 fund, so its exposure is to America's largest companies, with technology around 40 percent. It's built to cushion deep drops over a roughly one-year outcome period starting in August, and the trade-off is that gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
DAX: Germany's largest companies, with industrials about a third, financials about a fifth and technology around a seventh. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, so it moves with European exports and the euro and is more volatile than a broad world fund.
DBA: Futures contracts on farm goods such as corn, soybeans, sugar, coffee and livestock, with the rest held in cash and short-term safe assets. It's a way to bet on food prices or hedge inflation, and it can swing sharply with weather and harvests.
DBAR: Two strategies in one fund: a managed futures program that follows price trends across markets, and a US equity strategy. The blend aims for returns that do not depend on stocks rising, so it is meant to zig when a normal portfolio zags, though it can lag in calm, rising markets.
DBAW: Stocks from developed and emerging markets outside the US, led by financials and technology. Its currency hedge strips out swings from foreign money moving against the dollar, so it's for global stock exposure where only the stocks matter, not exchange rates.
DBB: Futures contracts on three industrial metals, aluminum, zinc and copper, backed by cash and short-term government securities. It's a way to bet on factory and construction demand, and since it holds metals contracts instead of company stocks, its prices can swing sharply.
