DBC: A basket of commodity futures covering energy, metals and farm goods, with Treasury bills held as backing. It's a hedge against inflation and a way to diversify beyond stocks and bonds, though commodity prices can swing sharply and it pays little income.
DBE: Futures contracts on energy: crude oil, heating oil, gasoline and natural gas, with the rest in cash-like holdings. It's a focused bet on energy prices rather than energy companies, so it can swing sharply and doesn't pay the way stocks do.
DBEF: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside North America, such as Europe and Japan, led by financials and industrials. It hedges the currency, meaning swings in foreign currencies against the dollar are largely removed, so returns follow the stocks alone.
DBEM: Stocks from developing countries across Asia, Latin America and beyond, with technology about two-fifths of the fund, plus currency contracts that cancel out most foreign money moves against the dollar. That hedge sets it apart: it aims to deliver emerging market stock results without the extra swings from exchange rates.
DBEU: Large companies across developed Europe, led by financials, industrials, health care and technology, with a currency hedge. The hedge removes the effect of euro and pound swings against the dollar, so it follows European stocks without gaining or losing from exchange rates.
DBEZ: Large companies from countries using the euro, following an MSCI Eurozone index, with currency swings against the US dollar hedged away. ASML is the largest holding at about 7%, and financials and industrials lead the sectors.
DBJP: Large Japanese companies, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer companies, with the yen's swings against the dollar hedged out. It's a way to own Japan's stock market, and hedging helps when the yen falls but hurts when it rises.
DBMF: Mostly cash and short-term bonds, paired with futures contracts that bet on trends in stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long or short. It's meant as a diversifier that may do well when stocks and bonds both fall, but it can lag when markets reverse sharply.
DBND: A broad mix of bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed, with a flexible manager who can shift between them. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion against stock drops, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
DBO: Futures contracts on West Texas crude oil, backed by a pile of cash and short-term bonds, so it follows oil prices instead of oil company stocks. It's a trade on the price of oil, and it can lose value over time even when oil holds steady because of how futures are rolled.
DBP: Futures contracts on gold and silver, held with cash and short-term Treasuries, rather than the metals themselves. It's a way to bet on precious metals or hedge against inflation, and futures roll costs can make it drift from the metals' actual price.
DCAP: Preferred shares issued by bitcoin treasury companies, the firms that hold bitcoin as their main asset, plus derivatives on those shares, all aimed at current income. It is crypto income at one remove: payouts depend on bitcoin-rich balance sheets, so bitcoin's swings drive everything.
DCMT: Broad commodity exposure managed actively: energy, industrial and precious metals and farm goods, held through futures and related investments with a view across a full market cycle. It aims to profit from commodity trends over time, offering diversification that moves differently from stocks and bonds.
DCOR: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology around 30 percent, then financials and industrials. It tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market fund, so it can behave differently from the broad market as a core holding.
DCRE: Loans and bonds backed by commercial real estate, such as office buildings, apartments and shopping centers, with a small cash cushion. It's for higher income than ordinary bonds, but it carries more risk if property values or borrowers' payments fall.
DDDD: Holds about 100 large US stocks like Abbott, Amgen, Merck and Coca-Cola while using options to pay out roughly double the usual income. The options mean it gives up some gains when stocks rise strongly.
DDEC: Options contracts tied to an S&P 500 fund, so its exposure is to America's largest companies, with technology around 40 percent. It's built to cushion deep drops over a roughly one-year outcome period starting in December, and the trade-off is that gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
DDFA: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year April period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 15 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
DDFD: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year December period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 15 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
DDFF: Options on the S&P 500 built to gain from moves in either direction over a one year period starting each February, up to a limit on down moves, while absorbing the first 15 percent of losses. It is a defined outcome holding for investors who want some return even if stocks drift down.
DDFG: A stock fund plus layered options designed to return gains whether the market rises or falls moderately, with a 15% buffer behind it, as the name says. The dual direction trick works only within limits: a plunge or a surge beyond the design undoes it.
DDFJ: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a 15% buffer against losses over a one-year period beginning in January. It also gains when the market dips slightly, but upside is capped and it fits the full period.
DDFL: A defined outcome fund holding options on the S&P 500 so it can gain whether the market rises or falls, within limits, over a set one-year period, with technology about 40 percent of the stocks behind it. It works best held for the full period, and it caps the upside.
DDFM: Options on the S&P 500 built to gain from moves in either direction over a one year period starting each March, up to a limit on down moves, while absorbing the first 15 percent of losses. It is a defined outcome holding for investors who want some return even if stocks drift down.
DDFN: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in November. It also tries to gain when the market falls a little, but gains are capped if it rises.
DDFO: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year October period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 15 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
DDFS: Exposure to the S&P 500 through options that cushion some losses and also gain when the market falls, up to a point, over a set period. It's for investors wanting a defined path, though upside is capped and the protection works best if held for the full period.
DDFY: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a 15% buffer against losses over a one-year period beginning in May. It also gains when the market falls slightly, but it caps the upside, so it only fits the full period.
DDFZ: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that set limits on gains and losses over a one-year period starting in June. It can gain whether the market rises or dips modestly, and the 15 percent buffer cushions drops, but upside is capped.
DDIV: About 50 US dividend-paying stocks picked for both high yield and strong recent price momentum, following a Dorsey Wright index. Financials and real estate make up about half, and the stocks are spread fairly evenly.
DDLS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US and Canada, with industrials the biggest slice, then financials and consumer companies. It's for international diversification weighted toward dividend payers, and it hedges currency, so swings in foreign currencies against the dollar matter much less.
DDNQ: An options structure on the Nasdaq-100 designed to gain in either direction over each quarter: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall, while buffering the first 5 percent of losses. The quarterly reset keeps windows short, and deep moves either way can still hurt.
DDSQ: Built to gain from moves in either direction over each quarterly period: it can profit when large US stocks fall modestly as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 5 in its name is the buffer against deeper losses, and the design resets every three months.
DDTA: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each April, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
DDTD: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from December, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTF: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each February, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
DDTG: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from August, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTJ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each January, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
DDTL: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year July period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 10 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
DDTM: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each March, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
DDTN: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from November, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTO: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from October, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTS: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from September, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDTY: A fund built to gain in two directions: it holds a big US stock fund plus options designed to profit from moderate falls as well as rises, with a 10% buffer as the name indicates. Big moves either way can break the design, so it suits range-bound markets.
DDTZ: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from June, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
DDV: Mostly Treasury securities and cash-like holdings, with a smaller slice of broad stock funds covering value, international and small companies. The mix targets a short, defined interest-rate profile, suiting cautious money that still wants a little growth.
DDWM: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, weighted by the dividends they pay. Financials are about a quarter and industrials a fifth, so it's a way to add international stocks with an income lean, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
DDX: A blended portfolio of Treasury bonds and US stocks, managed to keep the whole fund's overall sensitivity to interest rates at a set target, the 10 in its name. Stocks supply the growth and long bonds the rate exposure, so it behaves like neither a pure stock nor a pure bond fund.
DDXX: A basket of broad equity funds covering value stocks, low-volatility stocks, small companies and international markets, assembled by a rules-based discipline process. It aims to beat a plain market-weighted stock fund by tilting toward steadier corners of the market.
DECM: Options on the S&P 500 chasing the deepest available loss protection over a year starting in December, true to the Max Buffer label. With protection pushed to the max, only a small cap of gains remains, so it is about keeping money, not growing it fast.
DECO: Companies in the crypto business, including bitcoin miners, trading platforms, and chip and software firms, plus some direct bitcoin and ether exposure through futures and exchange-traded products. It captures the industry around crypto rather than one coin, and it is highly volatile.
DECP: Options on the S&P 500 meant to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in December, as the Buffer 12 name says. A moderate cushion for cautious investors, leaving more upside than the deepest buffer funds.
DECT: Options tied to a large-company US stock fund, set up to absorb the first 10 percent of losses over a year starting each December, with gains capped. It's meant as a modest cushion for stock exposure, and it trails in strong rallies, so it works best held the full year.
DECU: Options on the S&P 500 set each December for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual gain cap for a slow start, a different shape of protection.
DECW: Large US companies, led by technology, held through options that cushion a bigger share of stock market losses over a yearly cycle starting in December. It suits cautious stock investors, but the cushion has a price: gains are capped.
DECZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to soften part of a market drop over an outcome period that restarts each December, trading some upside for the cushion. It is one of a monthly series, so buyers can pick the starting month that suits their timing.
DEED: Bonds backed by pools of loans and mortgages: home loans, commercial property loans, asset backed securities and loan bundles known as CLOs, with at least half government backed. It aims for income with a quality tilt, and stands apart by staying in securitized debt rather than plain company bonds.
DEEF: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, screened by several factors at once, including value, quality and momentum, with industrials the biggest slice. The multifactor screen aims to beat a plain foreign index over time, though it can trail for stretches when its factors fall out of favor.
DEEP: The smallest and cheapest US companies: a deep value index of small and micro-cap stocks trading at low prices relative to their fundamentals. It is an aggressive bet that the market's most ignored leftovers will recover, and such tiny stocks can sit still or slide for long stretches.
DEFR: An actively managed fund that uses options, swaps and Treasury bills to earn a return meant to act like a bond, with tax-efficiency in mind, rather than holding bonds directly. It aims for steady, tax-aware income, but its derivatives make it more complex than an ordinary bond fund.
DEHP: Large emerging market companies picked for strong profitability compared to their peers, with technology close to half and communication around a tenth. It's a way to add developing economies with a quality tilt, and it swings more than developed market funds.
DEM: Emerging-market companies that pay high dividends, with financials about a quarter, technology nearly a quarter, plus energy and industrials. It's for income from developing economies, and it carries extra political and currency risks, so it swings more than a developed-market fund.
DEMZ: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen with a focus on firms that support Democratic Party causes and policies. It leans toward technology at close to half the fund, with chip names such as Lam Research, KLA and AMD among the top holdings.
DEPW: Companies in the ecosystem around Google's DeepMind AI lab: technology names, the utilities powering data centers, and media and finance firms touched by its research. It is a focused AI bet built around one lab's orbit, so it captures partners and suppliers, not just one stock.
DES: Small US companies that pay dividends, led by financials, consumer companies and industrials. It's built for income and value in smaller businesses, and because it's weighted by dividends paid it can trail when large growth stocks lead the market.
DESK: Office and commercial property companies: the trusts that own office towers, business parks and other workplaces in the US. It pays property income, but it is a narrow bet on offices at a time when remote work keeps demand for desk space uncertain.
DEUS: Mid-sized US companies picked for several traits at once, such as value, quality and momentum, and weighted to be spread across industrials, health care, financials and technology. It's a core stock holding with much less technology than the broad market, so it can trail when tech leads.
DEW: Global stocks that pay high dividends, led by financials and energy, with health care and real estate also large. It's built for income and is tilted to value companies, so it tends to trail in rallies led by fast-growing tech.
DEXC: Companies in developing economies, with technology about half, followed by financials and industrials, but with China deliberately left out. It adds emerging markets to a portfolio without China's policy risks, though it swings more than US stocks.
DFAC: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology about 30 percent, then financials and industrials. It tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market fund, so it can behave differently from the broad market as a core holding.
DFAE: A broad mix of emerging-market stocks of all sizes, with technology about 40%, followed by financials, industrials and consumer companies. It's meant as a low-cost core holding for developing economies, and its heavy tech weighting reflects chipmakers in places like Taiwan and Korea.
DFAI: Large and mid-sized companies across developed countries outside the US, led by financials at a quarter, then industrials at about a fifth. It's a core international holding that leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than a plain market-weighted fund, so it can behave differently from standard international funds.
DFAL: Large US companies across the whole market, with technology at about two fifths and financials, health care and communication behind. It's a core holding that follows the big-company market closely, with a slight tilt toward cheaper and more profitable firms.
DFAR: Companies that own, manage or develop real estate, such as apartment, office, warehouse and cell tower owners. It's a focused bet on property that pays income, and its prices tend to drop when interest rates rise.
DFAS: A broad group of small US companies, with financials, industrials, technology and consumer businesses making up most of it. It's a way to own the small-company slice of the market, and it swings more than large company funds, especially in a weak economy.
DFAT: Smaller US companies that look cheap relative to their value and are also profitable, with financials the biggest slice at about 30% and industrials, consumer companies and energy following. It's a bet on small value stocks, which can lag for long stretches but have historically behaved differently from big growth names.
DFAU: A broad slice of the US stock market, with technology about a third and financials, health care and consumer companies behind it. It works as a core holding, and it leans a little toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than a plain market fund.
DFAW: A mix of funds holding stocks from around the world, with technology at about a quarter and financials, industrials and consumer companies behind. It's a one-fund core holding for global diversification, built to spread across the world's stock markets in a single purchase.
DFAX: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, with financials and technology the largest groups and industrials close behind. It works as the international part of a core portfolio, and it leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than a plain index.
DFCA: Investment-grade California municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, whose interest is generally free from federal and California income taxes. It's meant for California residents in higher tax brackets seeking steady tax-free income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
DFCF: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, mostly of medium maturities. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, and managers adjust holdings based on where they see better pay for risk.
DFE: Small European companies that pay dividends, led by industrials with consumer, financial and materials businesses behind. It's a way to add small-company Europe exposure with a dividend tilt, and it swings with European economies and the euro, so US investors face currency movements too.
DFEB: Options contracts tied to an S&P 500 fund, so its exposure is to America's largest companies, with technology around 40 percent. It's built to cushion deep drops over a roughly one-year outcome period starting in February, and the trade-off is that gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
DFEM: A broad mix of emerging-market stocks, with technology around 40%, followed by financials, industrials and consumer companies. It's meant as a low-cost core holding for developing economies, and it can include smaller frontier markets, so it can swing more than funds focused on developed countries.
DFEV: Stocks from emerging market countries that look cheap compared with their size, with technology about 30 percent and financials a quarter. It's a way to add developing economies to a portfolio, and these markets swing more than developed ones.
DFGP: A mix of US and foreign bonds, mainly investment-grade, with currency risk hedged back to the dollar. It's a core holding for income that adds international bonds to a portfolio, and it tends to lose value when interest rates rise.
DFGR: Real estate companies from around the world, such as owners of offices, apartments, warehouses and shopping centers, plus other property businesses. It's a way to get property exposure and dividend income, and it swings with interest rates, since higher rates tend to hurt property prices.
DFGV: US Treasury and government agency bonds that mature in about five to fifteen years, with a little cash. It's a conservative holding for steady income and safety from default, and because the bonds are mid-length, its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise.
DFGX: Investment-grade bonds from the US and other developed countries, with maturities of twenty years or less. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, and it hedges foreign currencies back to dollars to keep exchange rates from adding risk.
DFIC: Companies of all sizes from developed countries outside the US, with financials about a fifth, industrials just under that, and materials and consumer companies following. It's a core international holding that tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a standard international fund.
DFII: Options contracts that give bitcoin exposure, combined with an income strategy that sells options to generate regular payouts. It offers a way to follow bitcoin with steadier cash flow, though bitcoin's sharp swings still drive the results.
DFIP: US government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, mostly maturing in five to twenty years. It's meant as a hedge against rising prices and a steady bond holding, though its value can still drop when interest rates climb faster than inflation.
DFIS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, with industrials the biggest group and materials, consumer and financial firms behind it. It's a way to diversify into smaller overseas businesses, and since small stocks and foreign currencies both move around, it swings more than large-company funds.
DFIV: Large companies outside the US that look cheap compared with their size, with financials the biggest slice, then energy, materials and industrials. It's a value tilt for international exposure, and it's actively managed to cut taxable gains, though foreign currency swings affect it.
DFJ: Smaller Japanese companies, led by industrials at about a quarter, with financials, consumer companies and materials each around 15%. It's a way to add Japan's smaller businesses, which tend to swing more than large ones and are affected by the yen.
DFLV: Large US companies that look inexpensive, led by financials, health care, energy and industrials. It's a value tilt for a core portfolio, with less technology than the broad market, so it can lag when growth stocks lead.
DFMC: A broad basket of US micro cap stocks, the tiniest public companies, spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care. It's a small-company growth play for diversifying a portfolio, and these stocks are less liquid and swing more than larger ones.
DFNL: Almost entirely financial companies such as banks, insurers and asset managers, chosen by an active manager who holds a fairly small group of them. It's a focused bet on the financial sector, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and the economy.
DFNM: Municipal bonds from across the US that mature in the medium term, with interest that is free from federal income tax, plus a little cash. It's meant for tax-free income with moderate swings, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
DFSB: Investment-grade bonds from companies and governments around the world, including mortgage-backed bonds, with the currency risk hedged back to dollars. It's a steady income and diversification holding that favors sustainable issuers, and it drops when interest rates rise.
DFSD: High-quality bonds that mostly mature within five years, mixing government and corporate debt. It aims for modest income with limited price swings, a steadier option than longer bonds, though it usually pays less than longer bonds.
DFSE: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about two fifths and financials next. It's a broad growth holding for developing economies, and it screens out companies that rate poorly on sustainability, which shifts it away from some typical emerging markets names.
DFSI: Stocks of companies in developed countries outside the US, spread across financials, industrials, technology and consumer businesses, with extra weight on smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms. It adds sustainability screens, so it's a broad international core holding with a slight value tilt.
DFSU: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology about a third and financials, health care and industrials following. It's a core stock holding that leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than the market and screens out companies with weaker sustainability records.
DFSV: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, with financials the biggest slice, then industrials, consumer companies and energy. It's meant to add a small-company value tilt to a portfolio, and it swings more than large company funds, especially in a weak economy.
DFTT: Thirty of America's hundred largest stocks, chosen by price momentum under a formula that also manages risk, currently led by chip and drug companies. Momentum means it buys what has been winning, which works until trends reverse suddenly.
DFUS: Nearly the whole US stock market, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, then financials, health care and communication. It's built as a simple core holding, and it moves with the overall US economy and market.
DFUV: US companies of all sizes that look cheap relative to their value, with financials about a fifth and health care, technology and energy making up much of the rest. It's a value-focused core holding that can lag when growth stocks lead rallies.
DFVE: America's 500 largest companies, but each one counts the same, so smaller members matter as much as the giants. That equal weighting makes technology a much smaller slice than in the usual market-weighted funds, giving a more balanced core holding.
DFVX: Large US companies spread across technology, communications, industrials and financials, with extra weight on smaller and cheaper stocks within the large-company group. It's meant as a core US stock holding, and that tilt means it can behave differently from a plain market-cap fund.
DGAP: Uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in April: a buffer against part of the losses, plus a fixed digital return if the market is up. Gains are limited, and the terms only apply if held for the full period.
DGCB: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US and foreign companies, rated mostly in the middle of the investment-grade range, that mature within twenty years. It's meant for income and as a steadier piece of a portfolio, with foreign currency risk hedged back to dollars.
DGIN: Indian companies that help power the country's digital economy, such as telecom, online services, payments and fintech, tracked through a benchmark index. It holds a small number of stocks, with Reliance, Bharti Airtel and Eternal each making up around 7% to 8%.
DGJA: US large-company stocks wrapped in options set to pay a preset digital return if the market ends the year starting in January roughly flat or higher. The first slice of losses is buffered, trading away some upside for a more predictable result.
DGJL: Large US stocks paired with options designed to pay a preset digital return when the market finishes the year starting in July at least roughly flat. A buffer absorbs the first slice of any fall, so results are steadier but big rallies are mostly given up.
DGLO: US companies set to gain as supply chains come home: manufacturers and industrial firms are 60 percent of the fund, with energy producers behind. It is a bet on factories, chips and goods being made in America again instead of overseas.
DGOC: Large US stocks with a twist: options are set so the fund aims to pay a preset digital return when the market ends the year starting in October roughly flat or up. A buffer softens the first slice of losses, but deep falls still hurt.
DGRE: Dividend-paying companies in developing countries that also show growth, with technology about 40 percent, then financials, industrials and materials. It's a way to add emerging market growth and income, though it swings more than US stocks and depends on a few big tech names.
DGRO: US companies with a record of raising their dividends, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer staples. It aims for growing income plus steady stock gains, and it tends to lag when fast-growing tech stocks lead a rally.
DGRS: Small US companies with a record of paying and growing dividends, led by financials, industrials and consumer companies, with some energy. It's a way to add small-company value stocks with income, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds.
DGRW: Large US companies with a record of paying dividends and growing earnings, with technology about a third and health care, communication and industrials making up much of the rest. It's built for a mix of income and growth, and it leans toward profitable, steady payers rather than the highest yields.
DGS: Small companies across emerging markets, led by technology at about a quarter, with financials and industrials each around a sixth. It's a way to add growth from developing economies, and small companies in these countries tend to swing more than large ones and the broad market.
DGT: 150 of the world's biggest and best-known companies, spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a simple way to own global blue chips, and it holds far fewer companies than a broad world fund, so it's less diversified.
DHDG: A defined outcome fund that uses exchange-traded FLEX options on the S&P 500 and resets every quarter, aiming to absorb losses between about 2.5% and 15%. Gains are limited, and nearly all the fund is in those options.
DHLX: An actively managed fund holding only a small group of large US companies that the managers believe are undervalued. It is concentrated: Microsoft, ConocoPhillips, Berkshire Hathaway and Amazon each make up around 6% to 8% of it.
DHS: US companies paying above-average dividends, with financials near a quarter and health care, consumer staples and energy behind. It's built for dividend income from large established firms, and it holds relatively little technology, so it can trail in tech-led rallies.
DHSB: It holds a broad US stock fund and layers option spreads on top, a smart buffer design meant to trim losses and add income. The options work means it will trail a plain stock fund in big rallies while aiming for a calmer path overall.
DIA: Thirty well-known US companies, led by financials with technology, industrials and health care behind. It's a narrow slice of big blue-chip stocks that works as a core holding, though it holds far fewer companies than a broad fund.
DIAL: A mix of bond types, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, spread across issuers with a rules-based tilt. It's meant for steady income and diversification beyond a single bond type, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
DICE: Companies that run trading platforms and prediction markets, mostly financial firms plus the technology providers behind them. It is a focused bet on betting and trading going mainstream: the theme is narrow and policy-sensitive, since gambling and event contracts draw regulatory attention.
DIEM: Emerging market stocks tilted to pay a higher dividend yield than the broad developing-world market, though Asian chipmakers still make technology the biggest slice at over two-fifths. It blends income with emerging market growth, favoring payers in Taiwan, Korea, Brazil and beyond.
DIHP: Large companies outside the US that earn high profits relative to their peers, led by industrials, then technology, health care and financials. It's a quality tilt on international stocks, and it leans away from the least profitable companies.
DIM: Mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US that pay dividends, led by financials and industrials with utilities and consumer businesses behind. It's a way to add dividend-paying international stocks, and it swings with foreign economies and currencies.
DINE: Income from many sources at once: dividend stocks, bonds, option spreads and currency trades, arranged with taxes in mind. The tax-aware mix aims to keep more of each payout after tax, which sets it apart from ordinary income funds.
DINT: A small, concentrated group of companies from outside the US, led by consumer, technology, financials and industrials, picked by active managers. It's meant to add international growth to a portfolio, and because few stocks drive results, it can differ a lot from broad foreign funds.
DIPR: Companies building space systems and satellite communications: the networks that provide connectivity, navigation, sensing and data from orbit. It is an actively managed growth bet on the orbital economy, mixing industrials with technology and even some private holdings, so valuations can be murkier than usual.
DIPS: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income while moving opposite to NVIDIA's share price, using options rather than owning the stock. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and its gains from falling NVIDIA shares are partly capped.
DISK: Memory chip companies: the makers of the DRAM, flash and storage chips that computers and AI data centers remember with, mostly in Korea, Japan and the US. Three Asian giants are about half the fund, so it is a concentrated bet on the memory cycle's booms and busts.
DISV: Small, lower-priced value companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, materials, financials and consumer businesses. It's a way to diversify into cheaper overseas small stocks, and it swings more than large-company funds and can lag when growth stocks lead.
DIV: Fifty high-dividend stocks held in roughly equal amounts, mostly energy, real estate, industrials and utilities, including pipeline partnerships and real estate trusts. It's built for income, and because no company dominates it, it looks very different from the broad market and has almost no big tech.
DIVB: US companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends or share buybacks, led by technology, financials and health care. It's built for income and value in a core stock portfolio, though it may trail in fast growth-led rallies.
DIVD: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, led by health care, banks and consumer staples, in a global value portfolio. It is an income holding that favors established payers across many countries, so it behaves more defensively than growth funds while still moving with world stock markets.
DIVE: A concentrated list of about twenty five to thirty five dividend paying US stocks across most industries, picked for income plus long term growth. Holding few names makes each pick matter, and the dividend focus tilts it toward proven, cash generating companies.
DIVG: US companies from the S&P 500 that have raised their dividends and pay relatively high yields, picked and weighted by an S&P index. It leans toward financials, technology, utilities and consumer staples, with no holding above about 3.5%.
DIVH: Dividend-paying stocks gathered for income, spread across technology, banks, energy and everyday consumer brands. It aims to harvest a steady stream of dividends from many industries at once, favoring reliable payers over chasing the single highest yields.
DIVI: Large companies in developed countries outside North America, led by financials and industrials, picked to pay higher dividends than the regional market. It suits investors wanting income and international diversification, but it holds few growth stocks and is tilted toward banks and older industries.
DIVL: US companies with market caps over $1 billion that have paid dividends and look able to raise them. It leans toward energy, financials and health care, and Johnson & Johnson, Exxon and Texas Instruments are about 14% of the fund.
DIVN: Dividend-paying large US companies, spread across consumer staples, energy, health care and financials, plus options that earn extra cash. It's aimed at steady income with a tilt toward stable businesses, though the option income can limit gains in strong rallies.
DIVO: Dividend-paying large US companies, with financials about a quarter, then technology, industrials and health care, plus an options strategy that sells some upside for extra income. It suits investors wanting income with steady growth, and it will usually lag in strong rallies because of those sold options.
DIVP: Dividend-paying US stocks, chosen on value, with covered call options sold on part of them to bring in extra income. Selling those calls can limit gains in strong markets, and the top holdings are spread across many sectors at about 4% or less.
DIVS: Dividend-paying companies from around the world chosen because the manager believes they can keep raising their payouts over the next few years. It favors proven dividend growers over the highest yields, aiming for income that climbs rather than income that is merely large today.
DIVY: Around thirty dividend-paying US companies, mostly midsize, spread across banks, health care, consumer firms and energy. It is an income holding built on stock picking rather than an index, favoring steady payers, and its mid-cap lean makes it somewhat steadier than small-cap dividend funds.
DIVZ: A concentrated group of 25 to 35 US dividend-paying companies spread across technology, energy, health care and utilities. It's aimed at income and steady dividend growth, and because a manager picks so few stocks, results can differ a lot from the broad market.
DJAN: A set of options tied to the S&P 500, so it follows large US stocks, with technology around 40%. It's built to absorb a deep share of market losses over a one year period starting in January, but it caps how much you can gain.
DJD: Dividend-paying stocks from the 30 companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, spread across consumer, health care, financials and technology. It's meant for income from big, established US companies, with the highest yielders given the most weight, so it leans toward value stocks.
DJIA: The 30 big US companies of the Dow, led by financials, technology, industrials and health care, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for monthly income. It's built for income, but it gives up gains in strong rallies and still falls when the Dow does.
DJUL: A fund using options on an S&P 500 fund, so it follows large US companies, with technology about 40 percent. It aims to absorb a deep portion of losses over a set one-year period in exchange for capping gains, so it suits cautious investors who accept limited upside.
DJUN: Large US companies, with technology around 40 percent, wrapped in options that absorb a deeper slice of losses over a one-year period starting each June. It's a cushion for cautious stock investors, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
DLAG: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to gain when the market moves up or down by a moderate amount over a one-year period ending each August. It is built for sideways or mildly trending markets, while a sharp move in one direction can leave it behind.
DLCU: Essentially the S&P 500, America's largest companies, with technology at about 40% and financials, communication and consumer companies each around a tenth. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US stock market.
DLFE: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to give a limited share of gains whether the market rises or falls slightly, while cushioning part of larger losses, over a one-year period starting in February. It holds options, not stocks, so timing of purchase matters.
DLMY: A fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to let investors gain when the market rises or falls modestly, over a set one-year period starting in May. It does not hold stocks directly, and its outcome only applies if you hold for the full period.
DLN: Large US companies that pay dividends, weighted by how much they pay out, so technology, financials, health care and consumer staples are the biggest groups. It's a core holding for investors who want dividend income, and because bigger payers count most, it leans toward mature, steady businesses rather than fast growers.
DLNV: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to gain when the market moves up or down by a moderate amount over a one-year period ending each November. It is built for sideways or mildly trending markets, while a sharp move in one direction can leave it behind.
DLS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US that look inexpensive, led by industrials, financials and consumer businesses. It's a way to add international small-company value stocks, and it swings more than large-company funds and carries currency risk.
DMAR: A set of options tied to the S&P 500, so it behaves like large US stocks, with technology around 40%. It's built to absorb a big share of market losses over a one year period starting in March, but the cost is a cap on how much you can gain.
DMAX: US large company stocks, held through options that reset each December, with technology about 40 percent of the underlying index. It's meant to cushion a large share of losses over a one-year period, but the options also cap your gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
DMAY: Large US companies, with technology around 40 percent, wrapped in options that absorb a deeper slice of losses over a one-year period starting in May. It's meant as a cushion for cautious stock investors, though the price of that protection is a cap on how much you can gain.
DMBS: Mostly mortgage bonds backed by US home loans, many guaranteed by government-sponsored agencies. It's meant for income above plain Treasuries, and it has a quirk: when rates fall, homeowners refinance and pay back early, and its price drops when rates rise.
DMX: An actively managed mix of bonds and loans from many corners of the debt market, including mortgage debt, bundled loans and corporate borrowing, chosen for income rather than safety. Managers roam across sectors hunting yield, so credit quality varies and the fund can fall when borrowers struggle.
DMXF: Large and mid-sized companies in Europe, Japan, Australia and other developed markets outside the US and Canada, with financials about a third and technology a fifth. It's meant to add international diversification, and it screens out companies with weaker environmental and social records.
DMXU: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US and Canada, such as Europe, Japan and Australia, tracking a Bloomberg index. It is spread widely: the largest holding, chip equipment maker ASML, is only about 5% of it, and financials are the biggest sector.
DNL: Quality companies from outside the US, led by technology at over a third, then consumer, industrials and health care. It's a growth-leaning way to add international stocks, and it picks firms with strong profits and growth, so it can differ from a plain international fund.
DNOV: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb a large share of stock market losses over a one-year period starting each November. In return it caps your gains, and the protection only fully works if you hold the whole period.
DOCK: Railroads, ports and freight companies: the infrastructure that moves goods across North America and through its harbors, almost entirely in the industrial sector. It is a bet on trade volumes and supply chains, so it tends to do well when the economy is shipping a lot of stuff.
DOCT: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb a large share of stock market losses over a one-year period starting each October. In return it caps your gains, and the protection only fully works if you hold the whole period.
DOGG: The ten highest-yielding stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the classic Dogs of the Dow list, paired with Treasuries and options to target income well above the Dow's own dividend yield. It is a concentrated income bet on ten blue-chip payers at a time.
DOJE: Direct exposure to Dogecoin, the meme-born cryptocurrency featuring a Shiba Inu dog, held rather than reached through futures. Dogecoin has no fixed supply cap and its price runs almost entirely on sentiment and social media attention, so it is among the swingiest assets in any fund lineup.
DOL: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials, then technology, industrials and health care. It gives broad international stock exposure to a core portfolio, and it weights companies by the dividends they pay rather than by size, which tilts it toward income payers.
DON: Mid-sized US companies that pay dividends, weighted by how much they pay out, with financials, industrials, consumer companies and real estate leading. It's built for income and steadiness from established businesses, and it holds less tech than most stock funds, so it can trail in growth rallies.
DPRE: Real estate income from several sources: property-owning trusts, preferred shares and real estate company debt. Mixing stock-like and bond-like real estate payers aims for higher, steadier income than a plain REIT fund, though property downturns still hurt.
DQJN: Options on the Nasdaq-100 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period ending each June. It is built for a choppy tech market, while a strong one-way run, up or down, can leave it behind.
DQSE: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to offer a set amount of protection from losses and a set amount of gains over a one-year period starting in September. Its gains are capped, and it pays off whether the index rises or falls, within limits.
DRAI: A tactical mix of other funds spanning US stocks, bonds, gold and leveraged index funds, shifted by an artificial intelligence model toward whatever looks most attractive. Because it can lean on leveraged funds, its risk level can change quickly from cautious to aggressive.
DRAM: Companies that make computer memory chips, so it's almost entirely technology, with a small portion held through derivatives. It's a focused bet on one corner of the chip industry, and memory prices go through sharp boom and bust cycles, so it swings a lot.
DRAY: Options on a single stock, DraftKings, arranged to pay current income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one sports-betting company, so the payout stream comes with that stock's sharp price swings.
DRES: US companies set to gain as supply chains come home: railroads, building material makers, industrial and energy firms that rebuild domestic capacity. It is GMO's bet on deglobalization and onshoring, a theme fund tied to trade and industrial policy.
DRGN: Chinese companies building generative artificial intelligence, from chip designers and server makers to internet platforms, with technology making up over three quarters of the fund. It is a focused bet on China's AI industry, so it swings sharply with sentiment toward Chinese tech.
DRIV: Companies building electric and self-driving vehicles, including carmakers, battery materials, parts makers and the technology behind autonomous driving. It's a focused bet on the future of transportation, so it swings more than the broad market.
DRKY: A concentrated, actively picked portfolio of growth companies, heavy in health care and technology, paired with an options program that sells contracts for income. It targets a high annual distribution rate of 15 percent, and the concentrated holdings mean individual stocks can move it a lot.
DRLL: US oil and gas producers, almost entirely energy companies. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil and gas prices and can behave very differently from the rest of the stock market.
DRMP: Companies in computer memory: makers of the chips and components that store data for phones, PCs and AI servers. The fund pairs that narrow chip bet with an income focus, so it aims for payouts alongside growth in one of tech's most cyclical corners.
DRMY: A fund of memory-chip and data-storage companies, such as SK Hynix, Samsung, Western Digital and Seagate, that also uses options to generate income. It is concentrated in one corner of tech, and the options can limit gains.
DRNZ: Companies that make drones and the technology behind them, mostly industrials such as aerospace and defense, plus technology. It's a narrow bet on one emerging industry, so it can swing far more than the broad market.
DRSK: Mostly investment-grade bonds, with a small slice used for stock options tied to large US companies. The options aim to add return while limiting losses, so it works as a bond holding with a bit of stock market upside, though bond prices still fall when rates rise.
DRUP: Large Nasdaq listed companies picked as disruptors, technology over half with health care innovators and media platforms behind. It concentrates on firms shaking up their industries, so it is a growth bet with bigger swings than a broad tech fund.
DRVR: S&P 500 companies chosen for the dividends they pay and the payout growth behind them, spread across financials, consumer and technology stocks. It is a large-cap income holding with a quality tilt: the screen favors firms whose dividends look sustainable, not just the highest yielders.
DSCO: Bonds backed by pools of mortgages, loans and other debts rather than by one company, chosen by active managers. It aims for higher income than regular bonds and is a step into riskier credit, so it can fall more than safe bonds when the economy weakens.
DSEP: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb a large share of stock market losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return it caps your gains, and the protection only fully works if you hold the whole period.
DSI: Large US companies that pass social and environmental screens, with technology about 45% and communication, financials and health care next. It's a core holding for investors who want broad US exposure with some companies filtered out, and it leans heavily on tech.
DSMC: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen for strong cash flow relative to their price, spread across consumer, technology, industrial and energy businesses. It's a value-minded way to own smaller companies, and it can lag when large growth stocks lead the market.
DSPY: US large companies weighted the way the S&P 500 looked in the past, so technology is about a third, followed by financials, health care and industrials. It's a core US stock holding with a twist, since the managers tilt away from today's most dominant companies.
DSTL: Large US companies with steady cash flow and strong balance sheets that look reasonably priced, led by technology, health care and industrials. It's a value-focused stock holding, so it can trail when fast-growing stocks lead the market.
DSTX: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized companies outside the US, chosen for steady finances and reasonable prices. It is spread across many countries and industries, with no single holding above about 3% of the fund.
DTAN: Large companies outside the US picked as undervalued once intangible assets like patents, brands and research are counted alongside factories and cash. Health care and technology lead the mix, and the intangible lens means it can favor very different stocks than a traditional value fund.
DTCR: Real estate companies that own data centers and cell towers, plus tech firms that build digital infrastructure, split about 57 to 41. It's a focused bet on the growth of cloud computing and data, so it swings more than the broad market and drops when rates rise.
DTD: US dividend-paying companies of all sizes, weighted by the dividends they pay, with technology near a fifth and financials, health care and consumer staples behind. It's built for dividend income with stock growth, and it tilts toward established, mature companies.
DTEC: Companies using disruptive technologies across ten areas such as healthcare, robotics, cybersecurity and clean energy, following an ALPS index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 2%, and technology is over half.
DTH: Large dividend-paying companies outside the US, led by banks and other financials, with industrials, utilities and energy next. It's built for income from developed overseas markets, and it leans toward value-style, slower-growing companies, so it has little in the way of tech growth stocks.
DTRE: Property companies behind disruptive technology: data center landlords, cell tower owners and e-commerce warehouse operators, worldwide. It collects rent from the physical backbone of the internet, so it behaves like a property fund with a tech accent.
DUBS: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials and communication behind, held through other ETFs. It uses swaps, which are contracts that add extra market exposure, to try for more return than the broad market, so it can rise and fall harder than a plain index fund.
DUHP: Large US companies chosen for earning high profits relative to their size, with technology about 40 percent, then industrials, health care and financials. It's a core stock holding with a quality tilt, and it skips less profitable companies that a plain market fund would own.
DUKH: A tactical rotation among high income bond funds, long-term Treasury funds and cash, run by Ocean Park's risk-managed process. It chases high yield when trends are friendly and shelters in Treasuries or cash when they are not, making income the goal but capital protection the governor.
DUKQ: A tactical rotation among US stock funds of different sizes and styles, from large growth to small value, moving to cash when trends weaken. The manager's timing calls drive results, which can help in downturns and hurt in fast rebounds.
DUKX: A tactical fund that moves between international stock funds and cash, following market trends to decide how much risk to take. When foreign markets look weak it can sit in cash, which can miss snap-back rallies but aims to dodge deep falls.
DUKZ: A tactical income fund that shifts between other bond funds and cash as its signals dictate, and it can sit mostly in cash equivalents when it sees danger. When it is invested it hunts yield across the bond market; the freedom to hide in cash defines it, and drags in rising markets.
DUNK: US stocks of companies using or poised to gain from disruptive technology, with tech near 60% and health care and consumer firms behind. It's built for growth, with a concentrated set of holdings, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
DURA: Companies paying high dividends that also pass tests for financial strength and reasonable prices, spread across health care, energy, everyday goods and utilities. The durability screen aims for income that survives downturns, not just the biggest yields on offer.
DUSA: A concentrated group of only a few dozen mostly US companies, led by financials, health care and communication, picked by a manager who looks for undervalued businesses. It's a bold core-style holding that can differ a lot from the broad market, for better or worse.
DUSG: Small US companies expected to grow, leaning toward profitable ones, with industrials, technology and consumer companies the biggest groups. It's meant for long-term growth, and small companies can swing more than large ones in both rallies and sell-offs.
DUTY: US companies earning at least half their money from defense: weapons platforms, military technology, logistics and cybersecurity, split between tech and industrial names. It is a focused bet on Pentagon spending, moving with defense budgets more than the wider economy.
DVAL: An actively managed fund of large, lower priced US companies, chosen by Brandywine as being good value. Financials make up about 30% of it, with companies like General Electric, Cisco, JPMorgan and Bank of America each around 4% to 5%.
DVDN: Mortgage REITs and business development companies, firms that lend on homes, commercial property and private businesses and pass most of their earnings out as dividends. It is an income holding with credit risk: payouts can be high, but values swing when loans sour or rates jump.
DVGR: US companies with a rare record: raising their dividends by double digits on average for at least ten straight years without a single cut. That strict screen favors proven growers across technology, health care and finance, and it rules out most dividend payers.
DVLU: About fifty US stocks chosen by blending two signals: strong price momentum and low prices relative to value measures, drawn from large and mid sized companies. The mix tries to buy cheap stocks that are already rising, and it reshuffles as the signals change.
DVND: Large US companies with long records of paying dividends, spread across technology, banks, health care, media and more, picked for income and steadiness. It works as a value leaning core stock holding, favoring proven payers over fast growers and collecting dividends along the way.
DVOL: About 50 US stocks picked for strong recent price momentum and low volatility, following a Dorsey Wright index. It leans toward financials, industrials and real estate, with no single holding above about 3%.
DVQQ: Nasdaq-100 exposure that dials itself up or down to hold annual volatility near a 22% target, adding cash when markets get wild. It is a risk-managed growth holding: the automatic throttle smooths the ride somewhat, but it can be underinvested right when rallies start.
DVSP: S&P 500 exposure that dials itself up or down to hold annual volatility near a 20% target, parking the rest in cash when markets swing. It is a risk-managed core holding: the throttle trades some upside for a steadier path, and can lag when markets snap back.
DVVY: Large US companies that pay dividends, picked with an emphasis on spreading across sectors rather than chasing the highest yields. It is a classic equity income holding: dividends provide a steady payout stream, though the fund still moves with the stock market and can fall in sell-offs.
DVY: US companies with a long record of high dividend yields, led by financials, utilities, consumer staples and energy. It's aimed at investors seeking income, and it has little technology, so it can trail in rallies driven by tech.
DVYA: Around 30 high dividend-paying companies from Australia, Japan, Hong Kong, New Zealand and Singapore, picked by dividend yield. Financial companies make up about a third of it, and miners like BHP and Fortescue are among the larger holdings.
DVYE: Companies in emerging markets such as Brazil, China, Taiwan and Mexico that pay some of the highest dividends, led by financials at about 30%, then industrials and energy. It's for income and international diversification, but it's volatile and tied to banks and commodities.
DWAS: Smaller US companies whose stock prices have been climbing fastest, with health care at nearly a third and technology about a fifth. It's a growth and momentum fund for trend-riding, and it can fall sharply when the trends reverse.
DWAW: A world fund of funds guided by Dorsey Wright's momentum research, rotating among stock factor funds from many countries, with the freedom to retreat into short-term bonds and cash. That defensive gear sets it apart: at times it can sit mostly in cash-like holdings.
DWLD: A concentrated group of stocks from the US and abroad, picked by managers who favor companies they see as undervalued, led by consumer discretionary names. It's an active global stock holding, and with few picks it may differ from the broad market.
DWM: Companies in developed countries outside the US, with financials and industrials leading, plus consumer and technology firms. It's a core international holding that favors dividend payers, so it adds global diversification.
DWMF: Companies from developed markets outside the US and Canada, selected by a model weighing several return factors like value, quality and momentum. Banks are the biggest group, and the multifactor tilt aims to beat a plain international index over time.
DWSH: An actively managed fund that bets against US stocks by short selling, borrowing shares and selling them so it gains when they fall. It holds many small short positions picked by a trend-following model, and it tends to lose when the stock market rises.
DWUS: A mix of US large-company stock funds, mostly technology, with the rest held in short-term bonds and cash. A fund of funds, it's meant as a core US stock holding that shifts between stocks and cash, so it can lag a fully invested market in rallies.
DWWN: An actively managed fund of long-term US government bonds, mostly Treasuries. Because the bonds mature far in the future, its price tends to swing more when interest rates move than a short-term bond fund's does.
DWX: 100 high-dividend stocks from outside the US, with financials the biggest piece at about a fifth, then industrials, real estate and communications. It's meant for income plus international diversification, with a value tilt that can lag in growth rallies.
DXIV: Smaller and mid-sized companies outside the US that look inexpensive, spread across industrials, financials, materials and consumer firms. It's a diversified way to add international value stocks, and it leans toward smaller, cheaper companies than a broad foreign fund, which can mean bumpier stretches.
DXJ: Large Japanese companies, mostly industrials, financials, consumer firms and technology, with the yen's moves hedged against the dollar. It's a bet on Japanese stocks that tends to do well when the yen weakens, and it can lag when the yen strengthens.
DXUV: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, tilted toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones, with technology, financials, industrials and consumer companies as the biggest groups. It's a core holding with a value and small-company flavor, so it can lag when big growth stocks lead the market.
DYFI: An actively managed fund of bond ETFs, spreading money across multisector bonds, fallen angel high yield, mortgage bonds, CLOs and inflation-protected Treasuries. It is a fund of funds, so it holds other ETFs instead of individual bonds, and the mix is adjusted by the manager.
DYLD: A go-anywhere income fund holding many kinds of debt at once: company bonds, government debt, bank loans, mortgage securities and even private loans. The dynamic approach shifts the mix toward wherever yields look most worth the risk, so its character changes over time.
DYLG: The 30 blue-chip companies of the Dow, paired with call options sold on part of the portfolio for extra income. Selling only some calls leaves room to grow, so it balances payouts and upside better than a fully covered strategy, while still trimming big rallies.
DYNB: A flexible bond portfolio that moves between investment grade debt and junk bonds as its managers see opportunity, currently leaning heavily on US Treasuries. It is built for income with freedom to roam, so its riskiness rises and falls with how boldly the managers reach for yield.
DYNF: Large and mid-sized US stocks, with technology around 40 percent, where a computer model shifts between styles such as value, quality and momentum. It's an actively managed core holding, so it can differ from the market, and the model may pick wrongly.
DYTA: A tactical mix of other stock funds that shifts between US and foreign markets, large and small companies, and even cash when its managers see risk rising. That flexibility sets it apart: it tries to lean into strength and step aside in downturns rather than stay fully invested.
EAFG: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, screened for strong free cash flow margins, led by technology and consumer stocks. It is a growth holding with a cash-generation filter: the screen favors profitable self-funding companies over flashier growers.
EAFH: Stocks from developed markets outside North America, Europe, Japan and their peers, with half of the currency exposure hedged back into dollars. The partial hedge is the twist: it softens currency swings without removing them, so returns split the difference between hedged and unhedged foreign funds.
EAGG: The US investment-grade bond market, including Treasuries, government-related bonds, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, with a tilt toward issuers that score well on environmental and social measures. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
EAGL: A hand-picked portfolio of large companies, led by technology at about a quarter, then financials, consumer and health care. It's an actively managed core holding, so the manager's choices decide results and it can differ a lot from the broad market, in either direction.
EALT: Large US companies across the S&P 500, led by technology, held through options that cushion a middle range of losses over each quarterly period. It's meant for investors wanting some protection on stocks, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
EAPR: Options on emerging market stocks, from Asian technology firms to banks and retailers across the developing world, arranged to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each April. It softens the famously rough ride of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
EART: Miners and producers of rare earths and other critical materials used in batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and electric motors, drawn from around the world. It is a focused bet on the raw ingredients of clean technology, and metal prices make it swing sharply.
EASY: Dividend paying US companies chosen for long records of raising their payouts, with health care the biggest slice at about a quarter, plus consumer staples, industrials and utilities. It is a defensive stock holding meant to grow income steadily while swinging less than growth heavy funds.
EBI: A manager's mix of US companies across industries, with technology about 30 percent, then financials, energy and consumer businesses. It's built as a core stock holding, but the manager's picks mean it can behave differently from the broad market.
EBIT: Small US companies that are profitable, picked by an index that screens for earnings. Holdings are spread thin, with no stock above roughly 1%, and it tilts toward financial companies, consumer businesses, industrials and energy.
EBIZ: Companies that sell and deliver online: internet retailers, marketplaces, payment and logistics enablers riding the shift to e-commerce. It is a growth bet on digital shopping habits worldwide, concentrated in consumer and technology names, so it moves with online retail sentiment rather than stores.
EBND: Government and other bonds from emerging market countries, paid in their own local currencies instead of US dollars. It's meant for higher income and diversification away from US bonds, but swings in those currencies against the dollar can drive big gains or losses.
EBUF: Options on an emerging markets stock fund, with a buffer meant to absorb roughly the first tenth of losses, resetting every quarter, as the 10 in the name indicates. It tempers the wild swings of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
ECH: Companies based in Chile, led by banks and other financials, then mining and materials, industrials and utilities. It's a focused bet on one small country whose economy depends on copper and other resources, so it swings more than the broad market.
ECML: Small US companies that managers using a rules-based, number-driven approach believe the market undervalues, spread across energy, consumer, health care and materials. It's a value-focused holding for long-term investors, and it can lag when growth stocks lead the market.
ECNS: Small Chinese companies, tracking the MSCI China Small Cap index, with shares listed in places like Hong Kong. It is widely spread across many tiny holdings, none more than about 4%, and health care and technology are among the biggest sectors.
ECON: Large and mid-sized stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, led by technology at over 40% and financials at about a quarter. It's for growth from developing economies, and it swings more than a developed market fund.
ECOW: About 100 large and mid-sized emerging market companies, spread over communication, energy, consumer, materials and other industries. It picks firms that generate lots of free cash (money left after running the business), so it's a value-style way to add emerging markets, and it can swing sharply with those economies.
EDEN: Large and mid-sized Danish companies, with health care at about a third, industrials near 30% and financials a bit under a fifth. It's a single-country bet on Denmark, and the drug makers that dominate it mean results hinge on a handful of big health care names.
EDGE: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to get stock market exposure, rather than owning the stocks directly. Nearly all of it is one long-dated option position on the SPY fund, so its returns can behave differently from owning the index.
EDGF: A flexible fund that moves between bonds, cash-like holdings and derivatives depending on the manager's view of interest rates. It aims for steady income with less rate sensitivity than a plain bond fund, but its mix changes, so it won't act like a fixed index.
EDGH: A mix of hard asset exposure, such as commodities and metals, held through funds and derivatives, with a large share in bonds and cash. It shifts its mix with market trends, aiming to benefit from inflation while cutting risk, but it can trail a pure commodity fund when prices climb.
EDGI: Stocks from several countries, mostly outside the US, led by technology, financials and industrials. It's an actively managed core international holding that shifts its mix of regions and sectors, so it can behave differently from a plain international index fund.
EDGQ: A fund that holds a Nasdaq-100 ETF and sells weekly call options on it to generate income. Selling those options limits gains when the Nasdaq-100 rises sharply, in exchange for regular payouts, and nearly all of the fund is the Nasdaq-100.
EDGU: A dynamically managed mix of US stock funds, currently heavy in technology and big growth names with a slice of small value companies. Managers shift sector and size exposures as their outlook changes, so the fund is a tactical core holding rather than a fixed index mix.
EDGX: About 500 large US companies, technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, paired with call options the fund sells for income every week. The option sales pay regular income but give up some gains in strong rallies, so it is built more for payouts than growth.
EDIV: Stocks of 100 high-dividend companies in emerging markets, led by financials at about 30%, then communication and consumer staples. It's for income and international diversification, but it's more volatile than developed market funds and swings with currencies.
EDOG: The highest dividend-paying stocks in each sector across emerging markets, from banks and energy to telecoms. It is an income-first way to hold developing markets, tilting toward mature, cash-generative companies, though high payouts in these markets often come with currency and political risk attached.
EDOW: The 30 giant US companies of the Dow Jones Industrial Average, with technology, financials, health care and industrials as the biggest groups. Each stock gets the same weight, so it works as a core holding that gives smaller Dow members more say than the usual version, where the highest-priced shares dominate.
EDV: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in 20 to 30 years, backed by the US government. It's a hedge against stock market drops, but its price swings a lot with interest rates and it falls sharply when they rise.
EEE: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in Ethereum, the blockchain network behind most smart contracts. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the Ethereum slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
EELV: The 200 steadiest stocks across emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with financials at about forty percent. It's built for a smoother ride in developing countries, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
EEM: Large companies from emerging countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology at over 40 percent and financials about a fifth. It's a growth-oriented way to add developing economies, and it swings more than funds holding only developed markets.
EEMA: Companies in emerging Asian countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about 46 percent and financials about a sixth. It's a growth-oriented way to add Asia's developing economies to a portfolio, and it swings more than US funds because of heavy tech and political and currency risks.
EEMO: Emerging market stocks chosen for momentum, meaning those with the strongest recent price trends, which currently puts Asian technology at about two thirds of the fund. It is a trend-following growth bet that rotates toward whichever developing markets are running hot, and it can cool just as fast.
EEMS: Small companies across emerging markets, with technology about a quarter, industrials nearly a fifth, and financials and consumer companies filling out much of the rest. It's a way to add growth from developing economies, but small stocks in these countries swing more than big ones.
EEMV: Emerging market stocks chosen to be less jumpy than the typical one, with technology about a third, financials a fifth and communication and consumer firms behind. It's a calmer way into developing economies, though it still swings more than US stocks and may lag in strong rallies.
EEMX: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, led by technology and financials, with companies that own fossil fuel reserves left out. It's a way to add growth markets with a climate filter, and it swings more than US funds.
EES: Small US companies weighted by their earnings, so profitable ones count more, with financials, technology and industrials leading. It's a value-leaning way to own small caps, and it swings more than large-company funds.
EETH: A fund that gives exposure to the price of ether, the cryptocurrency on the Ethereum network, by holding ether futures contracts rather than the coin itself. Futures can differ from ether's price, and crypto can swing sharply.
EFA: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside North America, such as in Europe, Japan and Australia, led by financials and industrials. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it has less tech than US funds, so it moves differently.
EFAA: Large companies in developed markets outside the US, led by financials and industrials, paired with an options strategy that trades some upside for extra income. The goal is income from international stocks, so it trails in strong rallies.
EFAD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada that have raised their dividends every year for at least 10 years, tracking an MSCI index. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3.5%.
EFAS: The 50 highest dividend-paying stocks in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, held in equal amounts. It leans toward banks, insurers, utilities and real estate, and no single company is more than about 3%.
EFAV: Stocks from developed countries in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, picked to be less jumpy than the market, with financials, industrials, consumer staples and health care leading. It's meant for international exposure with a smoother ride, though it can trail in strong rallies.
