EFAX: Large companies from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's a way to add international stocks, and it leaves out companies that own fossil fuel reserves, so there's almost no oil, gas or coal exposure.
EFFE: Stocks of emerging market companies that use resources like energy, water and materials more efficiently than their peers. It's meant as a growth holding in developing countries, and it swings more than US stocks.
EFFI: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, that use less carbon, water and waste than their industry peers. It's an international diversifier with an environmental tilt, so it can differ from a plain foreign index.
EFG: Growth-oriented companies from developed countries in Europe, Asia and Australia, excluding the US and Canada, with industrials at about a quarter and technology just under that. It's built for growth with an international twist, so it can swing more than broad foreign funds.
EFIV: The S&P 500 with companies screened for stronger environmental and social records, so it is about 40% technology, followed by financials, health care and communication. It's built as a core US stock holding, with the screen leaving out some businesses a plain S&P 500 fund would hold.
EFNL: Finnish companies of all sizes, with financials the largest slice at nearly a third, then industrials and technology at about a fifth each. It's a focused bet on one small European country, so it swings more than a broad global fund.
EFRA: Companies that build and run environmental infrastructure, mostly industrial firms with utilities behind them: water systems, waste handling and cleaner transport gear. It is a bet on the less glamorous side of going green, where spending comes from cities and long-term projects.
EFV: Cheaper-looking large companies from developed countries outside the US, with financials about 40 percent, plus industrials and consumer staples. It's a value tilt for the international part of a portfolio, with few tech companies and no US exposure.
EFZ: A fund that aims to go up about as much as the MSCI EAFE index of developed markets outside North America goes down, resetting each day. The money market holdings are collateral, and it is meant for short-term use as returns can drift over longer periods.
EGGQ: Fast-growing technology stocks, data storage, optical networking and AI power equipment, paired with an options portfolio that sells contracts against the positions for income. It aims to blend growth with a payout stream, and the options can trim gains when its high-flying holdings jump.
EGGS: An actively managed fund that holds growth stocks, either directly or through options, and sells options to generate income. This gives it some protection against falling prices, but it also limits how much it gains, and it is concentrated in tech hardware names.
EGGY: A stock portfolio heavy in technology, held partly through options, with an options strategy meant to generate high income and protect against very large market declines. It's built for income and a hedge against crashes, though the options limit gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
EGLE: S&P 500 companies that earn at least half their revenue inside the United States, so the fund leans toward domestic businesses across technology, financials and health care. It is a core holding with a homegrown tilt: multinational exporters weigh less here than in the plain index.
EGUS: US growth stocks screened for strong environmental, social and governance characteristics, with technology over half the fund. It pairs a growth portfolio with an ESG screen, suiting investors who want the big growth names but with the worst-rated companies on those measures left out or trimmed.
EHCC: Exposure to ether, the Ethereum network's token, through ether funds, combined with sold call options that generate income and cap the gains. It is an income twist on crypto: premiums pay regularly, but the fund still falls with ether and misses the biggest rallies.
EHLS: US stocks held both ways at once: a full book of long positions plus a shifting set of short bets against stocks the manager's algorithm expects to lag, from 10 to 90 percent of the fund. The hedge aims to smooth returns and rely less on the market's direction.
EHY: Ether, the second-biggest cryptocurrency, paired with an aggressive covered call strategy that sells options on ether funds for high income. It keeps some of ether's upside while paying out option premiums, though the selling caps gains when ether runs hard.
EIDO: Indonesian companies, with banks and other financials making up about half the fund, then mining and materials, energy and food and household goods. It's a focused bet on one emerging country, so it swings more than a global fund and depends heavily on Indonesian banks.
EINC: Energy companies that move and process oil and gas, mainly pipelines, following a VanEck index of them. They tend to pay income, and the top names are Williams, Enbridge, TC Energy and Kinder Morgan, about 30% of the fund.
EIPI: Mostly energy companies such as pipelines and producers, about two thirds, plus roughly 30% utilities. It's built for monthly-style income, using an options strategy that gives up some upside for extra payouts, so it can lag when energy stocks surge and still drop when they fall.
EIPX: Energy companies, about two thirds in oil, gas and pipeline businesses and nearly a third in utilities. It's an actively managed income-focused way to invest in the energy sector, and its value moves with energy prices and the shifts in the industry.
EIRL: Companies in Ireland, following the MSCI Ireland index. It has only a few big names: Ryanair, AIB Group and Bank of Ireland together are about 44% of the fund, so it leans toward banks and airlines.
EIS: Companies based in Israel, led by financials at about a third, then technology, health care and industrials. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, so it swings more than a broad international fund, and local politics and currency moves can affect it.
EJAN: Emerging market stocks, with technology a bit over 40 percent, held through options that cushion losses over a one-year period starting in January. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
EJUL: Emerging markets stocks, led by technology at over two fifths and financials near a fifth, wrapped in options that cushion some losses for about a year. In return it caps the gains, so it suits cautious investors who still want emerging markets, and the protection resets each July.
EKG: Digital health companies: firms bringing software, connected devices and online services to medicine, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on health care going digital, from remote monitoring to virtual visits, and swings with that young industry.
ELCV: Dividend-paying US companies, with energy about a quarter, plus technology, health care and utilities. It's meant for income and a steadier ride in a stock portfolio, and it has less technology than the broad market, so it can trail when tech leads.
ELD: Bonds from developing countries that are paid in their own local currencies rather than dollars. It aims for high income, and because returns depend on those currencies, it can drop when the dollar strengthens.
ELFY: Companies set to benefit from the shift to electric power, such as utilities, equipment makers, grid builders and energy firms, plus some technology. It's a focused bet on electrification, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on how fast that shift happens.
ELM: A fund of funds that mixes global stocks, bonds and a large cash cushion, with technology and financials leading the stock portion. A manager shifts the mix as conditions change, so it's meant as a one-fund, moderately aggressive portfolio, but its allocation can differ a lot from a fixed mix.
EMAG: Three giant emerging-market companies at the center of the artificial intelligence race, the Mag 3 of the fund's name, spanning chips and internet platforms in Asia. Owning just three stocks makes this one of the most concentrated funds anywhere, so single-company news can move it violently.
EMAU: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August, and gains capped in exchange. It adds late-summer defense to developing markets, where political and currency swings are part of the ride.
EMB: Dollar-denominated bonds issued by governments and government-linked companies in developing countries. It's a way to earn higher interest than US bonds pay, but it carries more risk, so it tends to fall harder than safe bonds in a crisis.
EMBD: Bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, mostly paid in US dollars. It's meant for higher income than US bonds, and it carries extra risk, so it can fall in a global downturn or when the dollar and interest rates rise.
EMBX: Bonds issued by emerging market governments and companies in developing countries, mostly priced in US dollars. It's meant for higher income than US bonds, and it drops more when investors get nervous or when interest rates rise.
EMC: Emerging market companies chosen for exposure to the rising consumer class, though in practice chipmakers and other tech hardware firms are the biggest slice, with banks next. It is a growth bet on shoppers in countries like China, Taiwan and Korea, held mostly through large well known companies.
EMCB: Corporate bonds from companies in developing countries, issued in US dollars by miners, banks, bottlers and telecom firms across Latin America, Asia and beyond. It pays more than developed-market corporate debt in exchange for emerging market risk, and dollar denomination removes direct currency swings.
EMCR: Large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets that meet certain environmental standards or have promised to cut greenhouse gas emissions. It is tech heavy, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix making up about 23% of the fund.
EMCS: Large stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology near half and financials about 30%. It's a growth-oriented way to own developing economies, screened for lower climate impact, and it swings more than developed market funds.
EMDM: Companies in emerging market countries that qualify as electoral democracies under Freedom House standards, led by Asian chip makers and banks. The democracy filter cuts out giants like China entirely, which sets it apart from ordinary emerging market funds.
EMDV: Companies in emerging markets with a record of growing their dividends, following the MSCI Emerging Markets Dividend Growers index. It holds many names, with the largest, such as Lotes and NAURA Technology, each only around 3%.
EMEM: Companies across emerging markets, from Asia to Latin America, picked by Sophus Capital's managers as a diversified core holding. Emerging markets offer faster growth than rich countries but come with sharper political, currency and market swings along the way.
EMEQ: A small group of emerging markets stocks, with technology a little over half and financials and energy next. It's a concentrated bet on growth in developing economies, and because it holds fewer companies and leans heavily on tech, it swings more than broad emerging markets funds.
EMES: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and China. It is heavy in tech, with Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and SK Hynix together over a quarter of the fund and Tencent around 4%.
EMET: Miners of copper and the other metals that electrification runs on, from global mining giants to smaller copper specialists. It is a focused wager on the buildout of power grids, electric vehicles and data centers, and metal prices make it volatile.
EMFI: Dollar-denominated bonds from emerging market governments and companies, including higher-yielding frontier countries in Africa, Latin America and beyond. It pays more than developed-market debt, and its borrowers include governments with real default risk, so credit news matters a lot.
EMGF: Large and mid-sized emerging market stocks, with technology about two fifths and financials a fifth. Stocks are weighted for momentum, quality, value, low volatility and size, so it's a rules-based growth holding for developing economies that aims for a smoother ride.
EMHC: Bonds issued in US dollars by governments and companies in emerging markets, the developing economies. It's meant to add extra income beyond US bonds, but it carries more risk of default and swings more than safer bonds, especially when global investors turn cautious.
EMHY: Higher-risk bonds from companies and governments in developing countries, paid in US dollars. It's meant for investors seeking more income than safer bonds offer, and the tradeoff is that it can fall sharply when investors get nervous about risky borrowers or emerging economies.
EMIF: Infrastructure in emerging markets: airport operators, water and power utilities and energy transport companies across Latin America, Asia and the Middle East. It collects tolls, fares and utility bills from growing economies, with political and currency risk attached.
EMJL: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, and gains capped in exchange. It adds mid-year defense to developing markets, where political and currency swings are part of the ride.
EMJN: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, and gains capped in exchange. It adds mid-year defense to a volatile asset class: EM and currency swings still show through.
EMKT: Stocks of companies in developing countries, with technology at about 40% and financials near a fifth. The managers hunt for shares they think are cheap relative to earnings, so it's a way to add emerging market growth with a value tilt, and it can swing a lot.
EMLC: Bonds issued by governments in emerging markets, paid in each country's own currency instead of dollars. It's meant for higher income and diversification from US assets, but it doesn't hedge currency, so it can fall sharply when those currencies weaken against the dollar.
EMLP: Companies that run pipelines, power utilities and other energy infrastructure across North America, split roughly evenly between utilities and energy. It's built for income from steady, fee-based businesses, and it's less tied to oil prices than drillers are, though it still sinks when interest rates jump.
EMM: An actively managed fund of stocks in emerging markets that leaves out China. It is tilted to tech and heavy in a few places: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and a Global X India fund make up around 40%.
EMMF: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials and consumer companies next. It picks stocks by traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a growth-market holding that swings more than US funds.
EMMY: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, and gains capped in exchange. It adds defense to a volatile asset class: EM swings and currency moves still show through.
EMNT: Very short-term bonds and cash-like debt, screened to avoid some companies on environmental and social grounds, run by active managers. It's meant as a place to park money for a little more income than cash, with only small price swings.
EMOP: Emerging market stocks picked by managers for strong profits and fair prices, with technology near half and financials about a fifth. It's a growth holding for developing economies, and because managers choose the stocks, results can differ a lot from the broad emerging market average.
EMOT: S&P 500 companies screened for durable competitive advantages, using strong profit margins, returns on capital and market share, spread across technology, consumer and health care stocks. It is a quality tilt on a core holding: the screen favors entrenched businesses over the plain index.
EMPB: An algorithm-driven long-short fund holding sector funds it expects to beat the market, plus bets against things like long-term bonds. Going both long and short makes it a hedge-fund-style product whose results hinge on the algorithm's calls.
EMQQ: Internet and online shopping companies based in emerging markets, led by consumer businesses, then communication and financial firms. It's a growth-oriented bet on the rise of the web in developing economies, so it swings more than a broad emerging markets fund.
EMSE: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, and gains capped in exchange. It adds autumn defense to developing markets, though their political and currency swings still show through.
EMSF: Emerging market companies that pass sustainability tests, chosen actively across Asian technology, banks, industry and consumer names in the developing world. It pairs growth in emerging economies with environmental and social screens, so some big state linked and heavy industry names are left out.
EMTY: A short-term trading tool that rises as brick-and-mortar retail chains fall, betting daily against physical stores. It is built on the idea that online shopping keeps hollowing out malls, but the daily reset makes it unsuitable for holding through rallies.
EMXC: Companies from emerging markets such as Taiwan, India and Korea, with technology over half, followed by financials. It leaves out China, which is normally the biggest emerging market, so it's a way to add developing economies without the China risk, though it swings more than US funds.
EMXF: Large and mid-sized companies in developing countries, with financials over a third and technology near a third. It screens for strong ESG ratings, which means environmental and social standards, and removes fossil fuel companies, so it's an emerging markets holding with a values tilt.
ENDW: A mix of asset classes including stocks, bonds and real assets like commodities and real estate, across US and foreign markets, using futures to add exposure. It's built like a college endowment for diversification, but it's actively managed, so it may behave very differently from the stock market.
ENFR: North American pipeline and storage companies that move oil and natural gas. It's a focused energy bet aimed at income, and it moves with energy volumes and interest rates, so it can swing more than the broad market.
ENHE: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks, with the managers choosing holdings to try to beat the market. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 27% of it, and technology is around 42%.
ENHI: Large companies across developed markets outside the US, spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care, picked actively while keeping overall risk close to the broad international market. It suits a core international holding, with stock picks meant to add a modest edge.
ENHU: An actively managed fund of large US companies that stays close to the Russell 1000 index but uses computer models to try to do a little better. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 20% of the fund, much like the broad market.
ENOR: Norwegian companies, with energy about a third, then banks and insurers, industrial firms and food producers. It's a single-country bet that adds international variety, and it leans on oil and seafood, so it can swing with energy prices and the Norwegian krone.
ENRG: Companies that explore for, produce and deliver oil, gas, coal and uranium around the world, gathered under a North American energy independence theme. It is a full-throated fossil fuel and nuclear fuel bet, swinging with energy prices and drilling activity.
ENZL: New Zealand stocks, tracking the MSCI New Zealand index, which covers the country's large and mid-sized companies. It is a small, concentrated market: Fisher & Paykel Healthcare is about 21% of the fund, and Infratil and Auckland Airport add roughly another 28%.
EOCT: Options on emerging market stocks, from Asian technology firms to banks and retailers across the developing world, arranged to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each October. It softens the famously rough ride of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
EPAI: Companies where artificial intelligence could change the business in a big way, led by technology at about 60 percent with industrials close behind. Managers hunt for firms at the turning point of adopting AI, so it is a growth bet wider than pure tech.
EPEM: An actively managed fund of stocks in developing countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, India and others. It is top-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 14% and Samsung about 8%, so chip companies make up a big part of the fund.
EPHE: Companies in the Philippines, led by industrials, financials, consumer businesses and utilities. It's a focused bet on a single emerging economy, so it swings more than a broad global fund and depends on one country's economy and currency.
EPI: Indian companies chosen by how much profit they earn, led by financials, with materials, industrials and energy also big. It's a way to invest in the Indian economy, so it swings more than a US fund and can be affected by currency changes.
EPIN: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Taiwan, the Netherlands, South Korea and the UK. It is spread broadly, with the largest holding, Taiwan Semiconductor, at only about 5% of the fund.
EPMB: Mid-sized US companies chosen by Harbor's managers as a core holding for the middle of the market. Actively picked rather than index-based, it aims to find mid-caps with room to grow into large companies, accepting more swing than big-company funds.
EPMV: Mid-sized US companies that look undervalued, spread across industrials, banks, technology and consumer firms. Harbor's managers pick them by hand, aiming for the middle of the market at reasonable prices, so it can lag when expensive growth stocks run.
EPOL: Polish companies, with banks and other financials close to half, then energy, consumer firms and materials. It's a focused bet on one emerging European economy, so it swings more than a broad international fund and leans heavily on the banking sector.
EPP: Companies in developed Asia Pacific countries outside Japan, mainly Australia, Hong Kong and Singapore, with financials making up nearly half and materials next. It's a way to add a specific region to a portfolio, and it's heavy in banks and miners rather than tech.
EPRF: Investment grade preferred stocks, which are shares that pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular shares, following an S&P index. All of them are financial companies, such as KKR, Ares, Voya and Northern Trust, and each is about 4% of the fund.
EPS: Large US companies chosen and weighted by their profits, with technology at over a third and financials, communication and health care behind. It's a core stock holding that leans toward earnings, so the biggest weights go to the most profitable firms rather than the biggest in price.
EPSB: Small and mid-sized US companies across industrials, technology, banks and health care, picked by Harbor's managers as a core holding. It covers the market's middleweights and up-and-comers in one fund, with more swing than large-company funds but more substance than microcaps.
EPSV: Small and mid-sized US companies that look undervalued, led by industrials at a bit over a quarter, with banks and technology behind them. It is a value bet on the market's smaller names, so it can trail while big growth stocks lead.
EPU: Companies tied to Peru, with materials (mostly miners) at roughly half and financials at nearly a third. It's a narrow bet on one small country's economy, so it swings widely with metal prices and local politics.
EQAL: About a thousand large US companies, each given roughly the same weight rather than being weighted by size. It spreads money across industries instead of leaning on a few giants, so it's a core holding that does better when smaller firms lead and trails when mega-caps rally.
EQIN: US companies that pay dividends, with financials the biggest piece at about a quarter, followed by energy, health care and consumer staples. It's meant for income and steady growth, and it holds fewer tech giants than the broad market, so it can trail when tech leads.
EQL: Large US stocks split evenly across the market's major sectors, such as technology, health care, energy and utilities, instead of letting big sectors dominate. It's a diversified core holding, and it gives smaller sectors more weight than the S&P 500, so it can trail when tech leads.
EQLT: A fund of emerging market stocks chosen for higher quality, such as strong profitability and stable earnings, than their peers. It is top-heavy in chips: SK Hynix and Samsung are together about 25% of it, with technology at around a third.
EQRR: Large companies chosen because their share prices have historically tended to rise when interest rates climb, led by energy, technology and financial stocks. It is a hedge for rising rate periods, the mirror image of rate-sensitive funds, so it can lag when rates fall.
EQTY: A concentrated mix of US and foreign companies, with technology about a quarter, financials just under that, and health care and industrials next. Managers pick a limited number of stocks they like, so it's a core style holding that can differ a lot from the broad market.
EQWL: The 100 biggest US companies, each given the same weight instead of letting the giants dominate, with technology about a quarter, then health care, financials and industrials. It's a core holding with less reliance on a few mega-caps, so it can trail when those giants lead.
ERET: Property companies and trusts in developed markets screened for stronger environmental performance, from warehouse and health care landlords to data centers. It tilts a global real estate portfolio toward greener buildings and operators, without leaving the property sector.
ERTH: Companies that offer products for a more sustainable economy, such as efficient buildings, clean industry and resource-saving consumer goods. Real estate, industrials, consumer and technology lead the mix, and it's a themed holding for environmental investing that can trail the broad market.
ESBG: Three asset classes in one fund, US large-cap stocks, intermediate Treasury bonds and gold, reached through futures on top of a Treasury base. It is a balanced diversifier: the gold and bonds are there to soften stock drops, though futures keep the mix more complex than it looks.
ESG: Large US companies chosen for better environmental, social and governance scores, with technology the largest slice at over a third, then financials and health care. It's a core stock holding for people who want to screen out weaker scorers, and it moves much like the broad US market.
ESGD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's meant as international exposure for a core portfolio, and it tilts toward companies with better environmental and social ratings while excluding some controversial businesses.
ESGE: Companies in emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India and Brazil, with technology the biggest slice at over 40% and financials next, screened for better environmental and social records. It's a growth-oriented way to diversify abroad, and it swings more than developed market funds.
ESGG: Large companies across the US and other developed countries, picked for better environmental, social and governance scores. Technology is about 40 percent and financials a fifth, so it's a core global stock holding for people who want a values screen, which can make it differ from the broad market.
ESGU: Large US companies screened and weighted to favor better environmental, social and governance scores, with technology at about 40% and financials, health care and communication each around a tenth. It suits someone wanting a core US stock holding with a values tilt, though it will not match the broad market exactly.
ESGV: US companies of all sizes screened to favor better environmental, social and governance scores, with technology at over 40% and financials, communication and health care following. It suits a core US stock holding with a values tilt, though it's heavier in tech than the broad market.
ESIM: Large companies outside the US spread across technology, industrials, finance and health care, picked by managers with a long-term, values-aware approach. It fills the international stock slot in a portfolio, with steadier established firms abroad rather than the faster, riskier end of foreign markets.
ESLG: Large US growth companies, over half in technology, picked by Eventide, a firm known for investing with a values lens on human flourishing. It plays the growth role with big innovators, and the managers' screening for companies creating genuine value sets it apart from plain growth index funds.
ESLV: Large US companies trading at value prices, balanced across finance, technology, industry and energy rather than concentrated in one sector. It is a steady, diversified value portfolio, the kind that tends to lag in go-go growth markets and hold up better in downturns.
ESML: Small US companies across technology, industrials, health care and financials, tilted toward firms with better environmental and governance scores. It's a way to own small companies for long-term growth, and they swing more than large ones, though the tilt keeps it close to the broad small-cap market.
ESMV: Large and mid-sized US stocks chosen to be steadier than the market, using the MSCI USA ESG Optimized Minimum Volatility approach, which also screens for environmental and social factors. It is spread out, with no holding above about 2% of the fund.
ESN: Forty blue-chip US companies, with technology, industrials, health care and financials leading. It's a concentrated large-company holding with only forty names, so each stock matters more than in a broad index fund.
ESPO: Video game makers, esports companies and the businesses that supply them, with communication companies about three quarters of the fund and some consumer and tech names. It's a themed bet on gaming around the world, so it swings with consumer spending and hit releases.
ESSC: Small US companies spread evenly across health care, technology, banks and industry, picked with Eventide's values-based research. Small firms offer more room to grow and more risk, and the values screen rules out businesses the managers see as harming people.
ESUM: US companies of any size, with technology over two fifths and financials, health care and industrials after that. It's an actively managed core stock fund, built for long-term growth, and it leans more toward technology than the broad market, so it can swing harder.
ETCO: An options strategy on an ether fund, built to squeeze high income out of the second-largest cryptocurrency while keeping some exposure to its price. Selling options caps the upside, and ether's deep drops can still bite through the income.
ETEC: Companies building breakthrough fixes for climate change: clean technology, environmental engineering and new energy ideas across industrials and tech. It is a growth bet on climate innovation rather than steady utilities, so it swings with funding and policy moods.
ETFT: An actively managed global stock fund run by Fundsmith, holding high-quality businesses it plans to keep for a long time, such as Waters, Amadeus and Mastercard. It holds relatively few companies, and about a tenth sits in a Treasury money fund.
ETH: Ether, the digital currency behind the Ethereum network, with the fund also earning staking rewards by helping run the network. It's a high-risk bet on a single digital asset, so its price can swing wildly, far more than stocks or bonds.
ETHA: A fund that holds ether, the digital currency behind the Ethereum network, so you get its price moves without setting up a crypto wallet. It's a high-risk bet on a single digital asset, and it can swing wildly in value and pays no income.
ETHB: Ethereum held by a trust, which also earns extra ether by helping run the network, known as staking. It's a bet on one digital currency, so the price can swing sharply in either direction and it behaves very differently from stocks and bonds.
ETHE: A fund that gives exposure to Ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, without having to buy it directly. It also earns staking rewards, which adds some income, but it's a high-risk bet on one crypto asset that can swing wildly.
ETHO: US companies, mostly in technology, health care, industrials and financials, chosen for having a smaller carbon footprint than industry peers. It's a core-style stock holding with a climate angle, and it leaves out many big polluters, so it can behave differently from the broad market.
ETHV: Ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, held directly by the fund. It's a speculative way to own crypto in a regular brokerage account, and its price can swing wildly and doesn't track stocks or bonds.
ETHW: Holds ether, the digital currency behind the Ethereum network, directly. It's a way to own ether without using a crypto exchange, but its price swings far more than stocks or bonds and can fall sharply.
ETTY: Ether, the second-biggest cryptocurrency, paired with option selling designed to pay out about 3 percent a month in premium income. It keeps part of ether's price moves while harvesting steady premiums, though big ether rallies are partly sold away.
EUAD: European makers of airplanes, defense systems and related equipment, all in the industrials sector. It's a focused bet on one industry that depends heavily on government defense budgets, so it can swing a lot, and it gives exposure to Europe rather than the US.
EUDG: European companies with high quality finances and a record of growing their dividends, picked by a WisdomTree index. It leans toward big names like Novartis, Nestle and Roche, which are each around 4% to 5% of the fund, and mixes industrials, financials and health care.
EUDV: European companies in the MSCI Europe index that have a record of raising their dividends steadily over time. It holds many companies in small slices, with Logitech, ACS, Halma and London Stock Exchange each around 3%, across industrials, health care and financials.
EUFN: Banks, insurers and other financial companies from across Europe, with almost nothing outside finance. It's a focused bet on European financials, so it leans heavily on interest rates and the health of the region's banks, and it holds no tech or consumer names to balance it.
EUHY: High yield corporate bonds issued in euros by riskier European and international companies, with a currency hedge that removes most euro swings against the dollar. It pays more interest than safer bond funds, and the hedge means returns hinge on the borrowers' credit rather than on exchange rates.
EUIG: Investment grade corporate bonds from across Europe, issued in euros but hedged back into US dollars. It pays interest income from big European companies while the currency hedge removes most of the euro's ups and downs from the result.
EUM: A daily inverse bet on emerging market stocks, designed to rise when developing-country shares fall. It resets daily, making it a short-term hedge or trade, and it bleeds value steadily whenever emerging markets trend upward.
EUSA: About 600 large and mid-size US companies, each given roughly the same weight, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care. It's a core holding that leans less on giant companies, so it can lag when the biggest stocks lead the market.
EUSB: A broad mix of US dollar bonds, mostly Treasuries and corporate bonds, with companies screened for environmental and social ratings. It's meant as a steady income core for the bond part of a portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise and the screens change what it holds.
EUV: Almost entirely technology companies in chip-making equipment and light-based technology, the tools behind advanced semiconductors. It's a focused, actively managed bet on one narrow corner of tech, so it swings more than the broad market and rises and falls with the chip cycle.
EVHY: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, which are corporate debt from companies with weaker credit that pay higher interest to make up for the risk. It is spread across hundreds of issuers, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
EVIM: Municipal bonds of medium length, issued by US states and cities, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income, mainly for higher earners, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
EVLN: Loans made to companies with weaker credit, whose interest rates reset as short-term rates change. It's meant for income that holds up when interest rates rise, but it can lose value in recessions when borrowers fail to repay.
EVLU: Value-priced stocks across emerging markets, with technology the biggest slice at over two fifths thanks to Asian chip and electronics makers, and a quality screen on top. It looks for bargains in developing economies, which adds currency and political risk to the value hunt.
EVMO: Mortgage-related bonds, including pass-through securities, commercial property loans and more specialized types. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, and since homeowners can repay early and the types are complex, its price can swing more than a plain bond fund.
EVMT: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to metals used in electric vehicle batteries, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and copper, mainly through futures. Most of the money sits in a Treasury money fund as backing.
EVNT: An event-driven long and short portfolio: stocks of companies facing mergers, spinoffs and other corporate changes, mostly held long with some shorts. It aims for returns driven by deal outcomes rather than market direction, and botched deals are the main hazard.
EVPF: Preferred securities and other income producers: the hybrid shares companies issue that pay steady dividends ahead of common stock, plus bonds, at home and abroad. It targets a higher income stream than plain bonds, sitting between stocks and bonds in risk and behavior.
EVSD: Short-term US dollar bonds from governments, companies and other issuers, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for modest income with limited ups and downs, because short maturities mean its price is less affected when interest rates move.
EVSM: Short-term municipal bonds, loans to US states and local governments whose interest is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income with a calmer price, since short maturities mean it reacts less to interest rate moves than longer municipal bond funds.
EVTR: A broad mix of US dollar bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, with some willingness to hold lower-rated ones for extra yield. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion against stock drops, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
EVUS: Large US value stocks (companies priced cheaply for their size), led by technology, financials and health care, screened to favor firms with better environmental and social records. It's a core-style value holding for those wanting an ESG tilt, and it tends to lag in growth-led rallies.
EVX: Companies that clean up: garbage collection giants, water treatment and drainage firms, recycling and environmental consultants, mostly industrial names. It is a focused bet on the unglamorous business of waste and water, which tends to grow steadily regardless of economic fashion.
EVYM: High yield municipal bonds, the riskier end of tax exempt debt, issued by cities, hospitals, housing projects and other public borrowers with weaker credit. The interest is generally free from federal income tax and pays more than safer munis, in exchange for more default risk.
EWA: Large and mid-sized Australian companies, with banks and financial firms making up about two fifths and miners and materials about a quarter. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, and it leans on banks and commodity prices, so it can swing more than a global fund.
EWC: Canadian companies, with financials about 40% of the fund, then energy, materials and technology. It's a way to add Canada to a portfolio, and its heavy tilt to banks, oil and mining means it moves with commodity prices.
EWD: Companies based in Sweden, with industrials the biggest slice at nearly half, then banks and other financials, and communication companies. It's a focused bet on one small developed country, so it moves differently from the US and swings with European markets and the Swedish krona.
EWG: German companies, with industrials the biggest slice at nearly a third, followed by financials, technology and health care. It's a focused bet on one European economy rather than a broad one, so it leans on exporters and can swing with global trade and the euro.
EWH: Large and mid-sized Hong Kong companies, with insurers, banks and exchanges at about 45%, plus property, utilities and industrial firms. It's a focused bet on one small market, so it swings more than a global fund and is sensitive to China's economy.
EWI: Large and mid-sized Italian companies, with banks and insurers making up more than half, plus utilities and industrial firms. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, so it swings more than a global fund and leans heavily on the financial sector.
EWJ: Large Japanese companies, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses. It's a way to add a major developed economy to a portfolio, and because it's priced in yen, its value also moves with the Japanese currency against the dollar.
EWJV: Large and mid-sized Japanese companies that look cheap compared to their size, led by financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's a way to add Japan with a value tilt, and because it avoids pricier growth stocks, it can trail when expensive tech names lead.
EWK: Belgian companies, led by health care, consumer staples and financials, with some real estate. It's a small single country bet on Europe, so it can be affected by one economy and the euro against the dollar, and it holds far fewer tech companies than US funds.
EWL: Large Swiss companies, with health care the biggest slice at nearly two fifths, followed by financials, consumer staples and industrials. It's a focused bet on one country with steady, defensive businesses, but with few companies and a strong currency, it can behave differently from the US market.
EWM: Malaysian stocks, with banks and other financials making up half, followed by industrials, utilities and materials. It's a focused bet on one emerging market, so it swings more than a global fund and is affected by the Malaysian currency.
EWN: Dutch companies, led by technology at about a third, then financials, food and household brands, and industrials. It's a concentrated bet on one small European country, heavy in chip equipment makers, and it moves with the euro.
EWO: Austrian companies, with almost half in banks and other financial firms, followed by industrials, energy and materials. It's a focused bet on one small European economy, so it swings more than a broad global fund, and it adds a way to diversify outside the US.
EWP: Spanish companies, with banks and other financials making up nearly half, utilities about a fifth and industrials most of the rest. It's a way to add a single European country to a portfolio, and with so much in banks and power companies it is less tech heavy than US funds.
EWQ: French companies, led by industrials, with financials, consumer businesses and health care next. It's a focused bet on one European country, so it swings more than a broad international fund, and the euro's moves against the dollar affect returns.
EWS: Singapore stocks, with financials a bit over half, mostly banks, followed by industrials and real estate. It's a focused bet on a small, trade driven economy, so it's heavy on banks and can swing with Asian and global markets.
EWT: Companies based in Taiwan, with technology about three quarters of the fund, mostly chip makers and electronics manufacturers. It's a concentrated bet on one country and one industry, so it swings a lot and carries political risk.
EWU: Large and mid-sized UK companies, with financials the biggest slice and consumer staples, industrials and health care close behind. It's a focused bet on one country's economy, with little tech, and its value also moves with the pound against the dollar.
EWUS: Small companies listed in the United Kingdom, spread across financial, industrial and consumer businesses. It offers a way into Britain's smaller firms, which move with the UK economy and the pound, and swing more than the country's big global companies.
EWW: Mexican stocks, with materials about a quarter, consumer staples another quarter, and financials and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a focused bet on one emerging market, so it swings more than a global fund and is sensitive to the peso and trade with the US.
EWX: Small companies in emerging markets, led by technology, industrials and consumer businesses, across many developing countries. It's a growth bet on small companies abroad, so it swings more than the broad market and than funds of big companies.
EWY: South Korean companies, with technology, mainly chip makers, making up over half, followed by industrials and financials. It's a focused bet on one country, so it swings more than a global fund and leans heavily on the health of the global chip industry.
EWZ: Brazilian companies, with financials about a third, then energy, mining and materials, and utilities. It's a focused bet on one emerging country, so it swings more than the broad market, and its returns also depend on the Brazilian real against the dollar.
EWZS: Small Brazilian companies, with utilities, consumer businesses, real estate and technology the biggest groups. It's a focused bet on a single emerging market, so it swings more than a broad fund, and moves with Brazil's currency and economy.
EXEQ: The 50 large US companies scoring highest on a leadership ranking that grades management quality and execution, spread across industrials, energy, health care and consumer stocks. It is a core holding with a management filter: the bet is that well-run companies win, whoever measures it.
EXI: Industrial companies from around the world, such as aerospace and defense, machinery, transportation and construction. It's a focused bet on one sector, tied to economic growth, so it tends to do well in expansions and fall harder when the economy slows.
EXPN: Large US companies its managers see as expansion leaders, technology at nearly half, plus an occasional options overlay for commodity-linked returns. The commodity twist sets it apart from plain growth funds, adding an extra engine that can help or hurt depending on raw material prices.
EXUS: A focused portfolio of large companies outside the US, from Asian chipmakers to European banks, aerospace and industrial firms, with technology about a third. Nomura's managers pick a select group rather than the whole market, making it an active core international holding with concentrated convictions.
EYEG: Investment grade bonds issued by companies, actively managed by AllianceBernstein across industries and maturities. It is a core corporate bond holding for interest income, with managers adjusting credit quality and maturity mix as conditions change rather than simply copying the corporate bond index.
EYES: Companies in data and surveillance technology: the firms that collect, secure and analyze information for monitoring, security and compliance. It is a focused technology bet on the watching economy, a theme with real demand and real controversy, which can bring regulatory swings.
EYLD: Emerging market stocks chosen for returning cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks, with financials the biggest group at about a quarter, followed by technology, industrials and energy. It aims for income plus growth abroad, and it can be volatile because emerging markets swing hard.
EZA: South African companies, with mining and materials around 40% and banks and other financials about a third. It's a focused bet on one emerging country, so it swings with commodity prices and the South African rand, and it's far less diversified than a global fund.
EZBC: Bitcoin itself, held directly by the fund, rather than stocks or bonds. It lets you own bitcoin in a regular brokerage account, but the price is very volatile and can swing sharply in either direction, so it's a high risk, speculative holding.
EZET: A fund that holds ether, the cryptocurrency behind Ethereum, so you can get its price moves in a regular stock account. Its value moves with ether, which can swing sharply, and it is not a proxy for owning ether directly.
EZM: Mid-sized US companies picked and weighted by their earnings rather than by their size, across financials, industrials, consumer businesses and technology. It's a value-leaning way to add mid-sized companies to a portfolio, and it can trail the market when large growth companies lead.
EZMO: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mostly one tracking the Nasdaq-100 and another tracking a broad market index, following an index built around momentum, meaning recent winners. About two thirds is in the Nasdaq-100 fund, so it leans heavily toward technology.
EZPZ: Only two cryptocurrencies, bitcoin and ether, held in roughly their market proportions. It is the simplest crypto basket: no other coins, no stock exposure, and full exposure to the boom and bust mood of digital assets.
EZRO: A defensive sector rotation system holding other US ETFs, shifting among stock sectors according to its AlphaDroid model's signals. It currently leans heavily on technology, but the point is the rotation: the model aims to favor stronger sectors and turn cautious when its measures of risk rise.
EZU: Companies from countries that use the euro, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and technology and consumer firms behind. It's meant to add European exposure to a portfolio, and its returns depend on the euro's value against the dollar and on the eurozone's economy.
FAAA: Top-rated slices of pools of corporate loans, called collateralized loan obligations, whose interest payments reset with short-term rates. It aims for steady income with little rate risk, so its price drops less than most bonds when rates rise.
FAAR: Commodity futures such as energy, metals and farm goods, with both bets on rising and falling prices, and most of the money held in cash and short-term holdings. It aims to hold up when stocks and bonds struggle, and may not rise with commodity prices.
FAB: Value-priced US stocks of every size, led by financials, energy and consumer companies, picked by a formula aiming to beat the market. It's a value tilt for a core holding, but results can trail the broad market for years when growth stocks lead.
FAD: US growth stocks of all sizes picked by a rules-based screen, with technology about 28% and industrials and health care next. It's for growth with a tilt toward smaller and mid-sized companies, so it usually swings more than the broad market.
FAI: Roughly 50 companies expected to benefit from artificial intelligence, with technology close to four fifths and the rest mostly communication and consumer companies. It's a focused bet on the AI theme, so it can swing more than the broad market, and it's concentrated in one industry.
FALN: Bonds from companies that were once investment grade but were downgraded to high-yield, the so-called fallen angels. It's meant for higher income than safe bonds, and these issuers are often large and established, though prices can fall sharply in recessions.
FAN: Companies in the wind energy business worldwide, split almost evenly between utilities that generate power and industrial firms that build turbines and equipment. It's a focused bet on one clean energy theme, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on government support and energy prices.
FAPR: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in April. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if held for that full period.
FARX: A conservative global mix of short-term bonds, trend-following futures funds, commodities and floating-rate Treasuries, run for absolute returns rather than against a benchmark. It aims to make modest progress in most markets, accepting that it will trail in strong bull runs.
FAUG: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in August, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FB: Large US stocks with an options buffer that resets daily, using one-day options to soften losses whenever the market falls. Unlike typical buffer funds with a fixed year-long period, this cushion is rebuilt every day, so protection is always fresh but never tied to a set outcome date.
FBCG: Well-established large US companies picked for growth, with technology more than half the fund and communication and consumer companies next. It's built for growth, and an active manager chooses the stocks, so it's heavily tied to tech and can swing more than the broad market.
FBCV: Well-known, large and mid-sized US companies the manager thinks are priced below their worth, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer businesses. It's a core value-style holding, and it may lag growth-led rallies when cheaper stocks are out of favor.
FBDC: Business development companies and specialty lenders, the firms that lend to mid-sized private companies and pass most earnings out as dividends. It is an income fund built on private credit, with high payouts and the risk that borrowers struggle in a downturn.
FBND: A broad mix of bonds that includes Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, plus a smaller slice of riskier, higher-yielding debt. It's built as a one-fund core bond holding for income, and the manager can shift between bond types, so it won't match a plain bond index.
FBOT: Companies building robots, automation and the chips and software behind them, split between industrials at half and technology at two fifths. It's a growth bet on automation worldwide, so it swings more than the broad market.
FBT: Thirty leading biotechnology companies held in roughly equal amounts, all in health care. It's a focused bet on drug research, so it swings more than the broad market, and because every company gets a similar share, smaller names matter as much as giants.
FBTC: Actual bitcoin held in storage by the fund, so there are no stocks or bonds inside. It's a way to own bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, and its price can swing wildly, with big moves up or down in a single day.
FBUF: Large US stocks chosen with quantitative analysis, paired with a dynamic options buffer that Fidelity adjusts as conditions change. It is an equity hedged design aiming to keep a good share of stock market gains while reducing the depth of falls, for investors who want stocks with a shock absorber.
FBY: A fund built entirely around Meta Platforms, using options to generate income, with most of its money parked in bonds and cash. It's for income seekers, but it gives up some of the stock's upside and can still lose money when Meta falls.
FBYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to Meta Platforms, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, rather than owning the stock itself. It aims to pay frequent distributions, but the leveraged options structure swings sharply, so it fits short holding periods more than steady investing.
FCA: Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong and China, selected by a quantitative model hunting for traits linked to better risk-adjusted returns across finance, technology and industry. It is a focused bet on China with a stock-picking twist, and it carries the political and currency risks of that market.
FCAL: Municipal bonds from California, whose interest is free of federal and California state income tax. It's meant for income for California residents in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
FCBD: A core bond portfolio built from other managers' bond funds, covering government, corporate and mortgage debt that is mostly investment grade. Using several outside funds spreads the manager risk, and the core-plus style reaches a little beyond plain vanilla bonds for extra income.
FCEF: A fund of funds that owns closed-end funds and ETFs spread across stocks and bonds, chasing income. Closed-end funds can trade above or below their underlying value, and the fund is actively managed, with no single holding above about 4%.
FCFY: S&P 500 companies with the highest free cash flow yield in each sector, so every industry is represented by its strongest cash generators. It is a value-leaning quality holding: the sector-by-sector design keeps it diversified, while the cash-flow screen favors profitable firms over story stocks.
FCG: Natural gas producers and related energy companies, nearly all of it in the energy sector, including some pipeline-style partnerships. It's a focused bet on gas prices and the energy industry, so it can swing sharply when energy prices jump or fall.
FCLD: Companies that sell cloud computing services and software, with almost all of it in technology. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing corner of tech, so it swings more than the broad market and can fall hard when growth stocks go out of favor.
FCLO: Bundles of corporate loans packaged into securities called CLOs, picked actively, spanning safer top layers and riskier lower ones. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, with the trade-off of credit risk if the borrowing companies run into trouble.
FCOM: US communication companies, such as social media, internet search, streaming, telecom and media firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giant companies drive most of its moves.
FCOR: Bonds from corporations, which are loans to businesses that pay interest, nearly all of its assets. It's meant for steady income above what government bonds pay, though its price drops when interest rates rise, and it carries more risk than Treasuries.
FCPI: Large and mid-sized US companies picked because they have tended to hold up when inflation rises, with technology, health care, energy and staples leading. It's a core stock holding with an inflation tilt, and it can lag when inflation is calm.
FCSH: An actively managed fund of investment grade corporate bonds with short maturities, issued by companies like Bank of America, Citigroup and JPMorgan. Short maturities mean the price should move less when interest rates change, and no one bond is more than about 3% of it.
FCTE: Roughly twenty large US stocks picked by a manager for quality and price trends, with technology about forty percent and industrials a quarter. It's a concentrated stock portfolio, so it can swing more than the broad market in either direction.
FCTR: Large US stocks sorted by investment factors like value, momentum, quality and low volatility, with the fund rotating its emphasis among four factor styles as its allocation model directs. It is one fund doing factor timing for you, so its fortunes ride on picking the right style at the right time.
FCUS: A focused portfolio of mid-sized US growth companies, with memory chip and data storage makers leading a technology slice of nearly three-quarters. Such concentration means a single industry's fortunes, especially the memory cycle, can drive the whole fund's results.
FCVT: Convertible securities, bonds and preferred shares that can turn into stock, issued mostly by technology and growth companies. Convertibles behave like a hybrid: they pay interest and fall less than stocks in downturns, but join in part of the rise when the underlying shares climb.
FDAT: A fund of other funds that moves between stock funds, high yield bond funds and cash as its managers judge the market's mood. It was sitting mostly in cash-like holdings at the last look, which shows how defensive this tactical fund can turn.
FDCF: Companies reinventing how people communicate and consume media: social platforms, streaming services, internet networks and the chipmakers behind them. Communication firms are about half and technology most of the rest, making it a growth bet on the future of media and connectivity rather than the broad market.
FDD: Thirty high-dividend European companies, with financials such as banks and insurers over half, and the rest in consumer, industrials and energy. It's meant for dividend income from Europe, and the heavy bank tilt plus currency swings between the euro and the dollar make it bumpier than a broad fund.
FDEC: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in December. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if bought at the start of that period.
FDEM: Large and mid-sized stocks from developing countries, tilted toward companies that look cheap, high quality or steady, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40%. It adds emerging-market growth to a portfolio, but it swings more than US stocks.
FDEV: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials, health care and energy. It picks stocks on traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a way to add international diversification with a modest tilt toward cheaper, higher-quality names.
FDFF: Companies reshaping how money is handled: digital banks, payment networks and new-style asset managers, mostly in finance with some technology firms. It is a bet that these disruptors keep taking business from traditional banks, so it is more volatile than a plain bank fund.
FDG: A concentrated group of 30 to 45 large growth companies, led by technology at nearly half, with communication and consumer companies next. It's built for growth and picked by an active manager, so it swings more than the broad market, rising faster in rallies and dropping harder in sell-offs.
FDHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, the so-called junk bonds, with a little cash. It's for higher income than safer bonds, and it leans toward the better quality end of junk, but it can still fall when the economy weakens.
FDIF: Five themed funds under one roof, each chasing a disruptive trend in areas like technology, health care, finance and communication, where new ways of doing business are displacing old ones. It is a growth bet on innovation themes rather than the broad market, so expect bigger swings.
FDIG: Companies in the crypto world, such as exchanges, miners and digital payment firms, mostly financials and technology. It's a focused bet on the crypto industry through stocks rather than coins, so it tends to swing sharply with the price of crypto.
FDIQ: The companies that run the plumbing of finance: stock exchanges, credit rating agencies, index makers and market data providers. They earn from trading and data fees rather than lending, so this is a focused bet on the business of financial information itself.
FDIS: US consumer companies that sell things people want rather than need, such as online retailers, carmakers, restaurants, hotels and home improvement. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to do well when the economy is strong and fall when people cut back.
FDIV: US companies that pay dividends, chosen with a focused, research driven process across banks, technology, industrials and food and drink makers. It aims for income plus growth from proven payers, holding a tighter list than broad dividend funds, so single stock moves matter more.
FDL: The 100 highest-yielding US stocks with a record of steady dividends, led by consumer staples, utilities, energy and financials. It's for dividend income, and it has little technology, so it can trail the broad market when growth stocks are leading.
FDLO: Large and mid-size US companies chosen for calmer share prices, with technology at roughly a third or more, then financials, health care and communication. It suits someone wanting a steadier core stock holding, though it usually lags in sharp rallies led by riskier stocks.
FDLS: A hundred or so smaller US companies picked using several stock traits at once, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials, and screened to fit faith-based values. It's a small company stock fund, so it swings more than large company funds.
FDM: Very small US companies, called micro-caps, with financials, mostly banks, making up over half. It's a concentrated bet on tiny, lightly followed businesses, so it swings more than large-company funds and does best when small banks are in favor.
FDMO: Large and mid-sized US stocks that have been rising lately, with technology about 40 percent and financials and health care each around a tenth. It's a growth-leaning holding that rides winning trends, and it can fall behind or reverse quickly when the market's leadership changes.
FDN: Internet companies, including online retailers, search and social media firms, streaming services and internet software, spread across technology, communication and consumer sectors. It's a focused bet on the web economy, so it swings more than the broad market and holds many companies that other tech funds class elsewhere.
FDND: A fund of internet companies, based on a Dow Jones internet index, that also uses options to produce extra income. Amazon, Meta and Cisco are about 28% of it, and the options income comes in exchange for giving up some of the upside.
FDNI: Internet companies from outside the US: online marketplaces, streaming, social platforms and digital services across emerging and developed markets. It skips American tech entirely, which is the point, offering the rest of the world's internet in one fund.
FDRR: Large and mid-sized US companies that pay dividends, led by technology, with financials, health care and communication next. It's built for dividend income, and it also screens for stocks that have historically held up better when interest rates rise.
FDRS: Fifty large US companies still run by the person who founded them, over half in technology, with social media, chips and car makers prominent. It bets that founders in charge keep their edge, so it concentrates in famous growth names and swings with them.
FDRV: Global companies building electric vehicles and future transportation: carmakers, battery and chip suppliers, charging and self-driving technology. It is a growth bet on the transport shift away from gasoline, concentrated in consumer and technology names, and it swings with the EV industry's fast-changing fortunes.
FDT: Companies from developed countries outside the US, with industrials the biggest slice at about a third, then financials, consumer goods and technology. It's for diversifying away from the US, picked by a scoring formula instead of by size, so its mix differs from standard international funds.
FDTS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, picked by First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value factors instead of simple size. It holds a very large number of stocks, none above about 1%.
FDTX: Mostly technology companies, with a small share in communication and consumer businesses, picked by a manager looking for firms that could reshape how products and services are delivered. It's a growth-focused fund for investors comfortable with big swings, since it leans far harder on tech than the broad market.
FDV: Large US companies with a history of paying and growing dividends, spread across utilities, consumer staples, health care and financials. It's built for steady income and a calmer ride, so it usually holds up better in sell-offs but can trail when fast-growing technology companies lead the market.
FDVV: Large US companies that pay higher-than-average dividends, with technology about a third and financials, consumer and staples firms behind it. It aims for income plus growth in one stock fund, and it holds far more tech than most dividend funds, which often lean toward utilities and banks.
FEAC: US companies of every size, large, mid and small, picked with Fidelity's research into long-term return drivers like value, growth and quality. Technology is the biggest slice, and the all-cap reach means it holds some smaller names most large-cap funds skip.
FEBM: Options on the S&P 500 set each February for a one year outcome period, designed to provide the maximum loss buffer the options market allows at the time in exchange for capped gains. It prioritizes protection above all, so it will lag badly in strong bull markets.
FEBP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each February, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every February.
FEBT: Options tied to US large companies, led by technology, designed to absorb the first 10% of losses over a one year period starting in February. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if held for the entire period.
FEBU: Options on the S&P 500 set each February for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual gain cap for a slow start, a different shape of protection.
FEBW: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that start a new one-year period each February. It's built as a cushion against drops, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses, but gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if you hold through the whole period.
FEBZ: Options on the S&P 500 that take part of a market loss for you over an outcome period restarting each February, paid for by giving up some gains. One of twelve monthly starting points in its series, letting investors choose when their year begins.
FECM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, actively managed by First Eagle. It targets steady tax-free income with moderate swings, the middle ground of the muni market.
FEDM: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked to follow an index that favors better environmental, social and governance scores and lower climate risk. It is widely spread, with ASML the biggest holding at about 3%, and tilts toward financials and industrials.
FEGE: A manager-picked mix of companies from the US and abroad, with consumer staples, technology, health care and financials as the largest parts. It aims for steady growth with less risk, favoring sturdy businesses, so it tends to hold up better in downturns but may trail in booms.
FEIG: Investment grade corporate bonds issued by companies that score well on environmental, social and governance measures and on climate readiness. It pays company bond interest with a values screen on top, so some big issuers are excluded even though the income looks much like a plain corporate fund.
FELC: Mostly the large companies in the S&P 500, with technology over 40%, but a manager tilts the weights toward stocks that look promising. It's a core holding that aims to modestly beat the broad market, so it should move much like it with some differences.
FELG: Large US growth companies, with technology about 60% and communication, industrials and health care behind it. It's a growth fund that leans heavily on tech, so it tends to rise faster in rallies and fall harder in sell-offs, and the manager makes modest adjustments to try to beat its benchmark.
FELV: Large US companies that look cheaply priced, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's meant as a core value holding, and the managers tilt the picks using their own research, so it can differ from a plain value index in both good and bad stretches.
FEM: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Brazil, with technology, industrials, energy and materials leading. It's a growth-oriented way to add developing economies, and it picks and weights stocks by a rules-based formula instead of size, so it swings more than the broad market.
FEMB: Government and company bonds from emerging markets, all paid in local currencies such as pesos or rupees rather than dollars. It's meant for higher income and diversification, but currency swings can cause losses, so it's far more volatile than typical bond funds.
FEMD: Mid-sized US companies bought with First Eagle's value approach, hunting for solid businesses priced below their worth. The patient, bargain-first style aims to protect against big losses while mid-caps compound, so it may trail in hot growth markets.
FEMG: Mid-sized US growth companies, led by technology at a little over a third, with industrials and health care behind. Fidelity starts from the mid-cap growth group and tilts toward stocks its research likes most, aiming for stronger growth than a plain index fund.
FEMR: Stocks from emerging markets, with technology nearly half and financials about a sixth. It's built for growth from developing economies, and the manager tilts toward stocks that look promising, so it's more tech-heavy than many emerging markets funds and can swing widely.
FEMS: Small companies in emerging markets, spread across technology, industrials, consumer firms and materials. It's picked with a rules-based screen favoring stronger growth and value traits, so it's a high-risk way to add developing-economy exposure that swings more than larger-company funds.
FEMV: Mid-sized US companies that look inexpensive, spread fairly evenly across technology, industrials, banks and health care. Fidelity starts from the mid-cap value group, then tilts toward stocks its research favors, aiming to beat plain value funds while staying diversified.
FENI: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, with technology and health care behind. It's an international core holding, and managers tilt the picks to try to beat a standard international index modestly.
FENY: US energy companies, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and equipment services firms. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it tends to rise and fall with oil and gas prices and swings more than the broad market.
FEOE: Companies outside the US, picked by managers who favor reasonably priced firms, spread across consumer staples, industrials, technology and financials. It's a way to own international stocks with a cautious style, so it may trail in strong rallies.
FEP: Stocks from developed European countries, with industrials the biggest slice at about a quarter, then energy, financials and materials. Stocks are picked and weighted by a rules-based screen for growth and value rather than size, so it's a way to add Europe and it can behave differently from a plain index.
FEPI: Big-name technology and internet companies, with tech about 70%, paired with an options strategy that trades some upside for monthly income. It's built for income, and it still swings with tech while giving up gains in strong rallies.
FESC: Small US companies bought with a value mindset: profitable little firms bought at prices the managers see as bargains. First Eagle's patient, bargain-hunting style sets it apart, aiming to lose less in downturns while small caps grow over time.
FESM: Small US companies from the Russell 2000, led by health care, technology, financials and industrials, picked by a manager using a computer-driven approach aiming to beat the index. It's a core small-company holding, and it swings more than large-company funds.
FETH: Ether, the digital currency that runs the Ethereum network, held directly rather than through companies or bonds. It's a high-risk bet on crypto, so it swings far more than stocks, and it pays no interest or dividends.
FEUS: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, screened to favor better environmental and climate records. It's meant as a core US stock holding for people who want a values tilt, and the screen can make it differ slightly from the broad market.
FEUZ: Stocks from countries using the euro, led by industrials, financials and energy, chosen by a scoring method rather than company size. It's a way to add European exposure, but it's tied to the eurozone economy and moves with the euro against the dollar.
FEX: Large US companies picked and weighted by a score for growth and value rather than by size, with technology near a fifth and industrials, financials and health care behind. It spreads money more evenly than the broad market, so it holds smaller weights in the giants.
FEZ: Fifty of the biggest companies in the eurozone, led by financials at about a quarter, then industrials and technology. It's a way to own big European firms in one fund, but it's concentrated in euro-area countries and tied to the euro's value against the dollar.
FFDI: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen with Fidelity's fundamental research, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It aims to beat plain international funds through stock picking, across Europe, Japan and other developed economies.
FFEB: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a one year period that starts in February. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, and the protection works best if bought at the start of that period.
FFEM: An actively managed fund of companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, chosen through in-depth company research. It is top-heavy in chips, as Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about a third of it.
FFF: One hundred US companies still run by their founders, heavily tilted to technology at well over half the fund. The idea is that founder-led firms think longer term and take bigger swings, so it is a growth bet with a distinctive selection rule.
FFGX: Growth companies outside the US, picked by bottom up fundamental research across developed and emerging markets, with technology and banks the largest slices. It is an actively managed foreign growth holding, so its fate rests on stock picking rather than any single country's market.
