FFIU: Medium term bonds of almost any kind, with the portfolio's average interest rate sensitivity held between three and ten years, managed without an index leash. The freedom to roam across bond types is the point, and results hinge on the managers' calls about rates and credit.
FFLC: Large US companies picked by Fidelity's analysts company by company, blending growth and value names across industries, with technology and internet giants currently prominent. It is a core-style holding whose results rest on fundamental research rather than a formula, so it can drift from the index for long stretches.
FFLG: Large US growth companies picked by Fidelity's analysts company by company, currently led by chipmakers, internet platforms and drug companies. It is a growth holding built on fundamental research, so it will rise and fall harder than the broad market when big growth stocks swing.
FFLS: US stocks held both long and short at once, buying companies the managers expect to rise and betting against those they expect to fall, across all sizes. The short book hedges part of the market risk, aiming for returns driven by stock picking rather than the market's direction.
FFLV: Large US companies trading at value prices, chosen with Fidelity's fundamental research across technology, finance, health care and consumer shares. It includes some big technology names bought when they looked cheap, so it is less strictly old-economy than many value funds.
FFLX: A flexible mix of company bonds, including riskier ones, and bank loans whose interest adjusts with rates. It's built to pay income and gives managers freedom to move among bond types, though lower-rated holdings can lose value in a downturn and it can lag safer bond funds.
FFND: Growth companies around the world picked by active managers, at least 30 percent of them outside the US, with technology about a third of the fund. It is one global growth portfolio rather than separate US and foreign funds, so stock selection drives everything.
FFOG: A small group of large US growth companies, with technology close to 60 percent and the rest in communication, consumer and health care. It's built for long-term growth, and with fewer holdings and so much tech, it swings more than the broad market.
FFOX: A manager's picks of mid-sized companies set to benefit from long-term trends, with technology, industrials and health care the biggest groups. It's a growth-oriented fund for patient investors, and since it holds fewer names, it can swing more than the broad market.
FFSM: Small and midsize US companies picked by Fidelity's analysts from the bottom up, company by company, rather than by formula. The mix ranges across industries, and smaller companies swing more than large ones, so this is a growth holding whose results depend heavily on the stock pickers' judgment.
FFTY: Holds about 50 fast-growing US stocks picked weekly from the IBD 50 index, a rules-based list built from growth and strength measures. The list changes often, and it leans toward health care and technology companies.
FFUT: Futures and other contracts across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, held alongside plenty of cash, following whichever markets are trending up or down. It's meant to diversify a stock and bond portfolio, but it can lose money when trends keep reversing.
FGD: High-dividend companies from around the world, led by financials at over a third, with industrials, energy and consumer companies behind. It's built for dividend income from global companies, and it holds little technology, so it can lag in tech-led rallies.
FGDL: Physical gold bars, sourced under responsible-mining standards, held in storage for the fund. It's a hedge against inflation and market turmoil that moves differently from stocks, though it pays no income, and its price can swing with the price of gold.
FGM: German companies selected by a quantitative AlphaDEX scoring system rather than by size, which tilts it toward mid-sized industrial, airline, materials and drug firms. It offers Germany exposure beyond the usual giant exporters, with stock selection, not the broad market, driving results.
FGSI: US stocks screened for growth strength, paired with sold call options on the S&P 500 to add a target level of income. It mixes growth and payouts: the options generate regular income but trim how much the fund gains when the market runs.
FGSM: Small companies from around the world, with at least 40 percent of its money outside the US across three or more countries, spanning industry, finance, consumer and technology names. It hunts overlooked little firms globally, carrying the extra swings and currency moves that come with small foreign stocks.
FHDG: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over each three-month period, in exchange for a limit on gains. The buffer is reset every quarter, so protection depends on when you hold it.
FHEQ: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%, combined with options that offset part of the market's drops. It's meant for stock growth with a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but gives up some gains in strong rallies.
FHIL: Leading companies from outside the US, picked by Federated Hermes across technology, industrials, banks and health care. It is a core international holding of established market leaders, aiming for steadier growth than narrower foreign bets.
FHLC: Nearly all US health care companies: drugmakers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms, of all sizes. It's a focused bet on the health sector, which tends to hold up better than most in recessions but is exposed to drug pricing and regulation.
FHYS: US dollar junk bonds, meaning bonds from lower-rated companies, chosen to mature sooner than most. Shorter bonds usually swing less in price than longer ones, and the fund is spread across many issuers, none above about 1%.
FIAT: An income strategy built to move against Coinbase stock: options give indirect inverse exposure to that single crypto exchange company while generating regular payments. It is a bearish, highly concentrated trade rather than an investment, designed for short holding periods and weekly or monthly income seekers.
FIAX: Mostly short-term US Treasury bonds, paired with an options strategy on stock indexes that earns extra income but can lose money when the market moves sharply. It's meant as a bond alternative for income with less interest-rate sensitivity, but the options add risk that regular bond funds lack.
FICS: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, then consumer staples. It picks firms with strong balance sheets, so it's a quality-focused way to add international stocks, and it has little technology compared with many international funds.
FID: Established companies outside the US that have kept or raised their dividends for at least ten years, led by financials, utilities and industrials. It's built for dividend income from abroad, and it leans toward steady, slower-growing businesses, so it can trail when fast-growing tech stocks lead.
FIDI: Large and mid-sized dividend-paying companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials, energy, food and household goods, and industrials. It's built for income from foreign stocks, so it can trail growth-driven markets.
FIDU: US industrial companies, including aerospace and defense, machinery, airlines, railroads and construction firms, with small slices of technology. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to rise when the economy is growing and factories are busy.
FIFT: Fifty large US companies picked from the biggest-company index by a quantitative model built with Ned Davis Research, favoring dividend payers. It works as a focused core holding, narrower than owning all 500, so its results depend on the model's picks rather than the whole market.
FIGB: Investment-grade bonds from companies and governments, spread across different types and maturities. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion when stocks fall, and a manager adjusts the mix actively, but its price still drops when interest rates rise.
FIIG: Investment-grade bonds from US companies, with medium-length maturities. It's meant for steady income above Treasury bonds, and the mid-length maturity means its price swings moderately, dropping when interest rates rise or when company credit worsens.
FIMU: Intermediate-term bonds from state and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It suits investors in higher tax brackets who want steady, tax-friendly income, though prices dip when interest rates rise.
FINA: Big companies across the US and Canada, with technology about two fifths and financials, communication and health care behind it. It's a low-effort core holding for North American stocks, though it leans heavily on tech and so swings with that one sector.
FINT: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs covering stocks outside the US, including emerging markets and international quality companies. It is a ready-made international mix, with Avantis Emerging Markets and two iShares funds making up about half of it.
FINX: Financial technology companies, like mobile payments, online lending and digital banking, split between software-style technology firms at about half and financial companies at over 40 percent. It's a focused bet on how money services are changing, so it swings more than the broad market.
FINY: An income fund that sells put options on a leveraged fund of financial stocks, one that aims for three times the daily move of its index. It aims to pay weekly distributions from option premiums, but the leveraged link means sharp drops in bank stocks can hit it hard.
FISR: Bonds from governments, mortgage pools and companies, shifted among sectors by a model that follows market signals. It's a core bond holding for income and a cushion in stock drops, and the rotation means it can differ from a plain bond fund.
FITE: Companies building security tools, like cybersecurity software, defense, surveillance and safety equipment, with technology about 60 percent and industrials around 30 percent. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
FITZ: Companies chosen as must-haves for the decades ahead, businesses positioned to benefit from long-running structural changes in technology, health and industry. It is an actively managed growth portfolio built around themes rather than sectors, so its results hinge on those long-term calls being right.
FIVA: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked because they look cheap, led by financials and industrials. It's for investors wanting overseas value stocks, and it tends to lag when fast-growing tech companies lead the market.
FIW: Companies that supply and clean drinking water and wastewater, mostly industrial firms like equipment and pipe makers, with health care, utilities and technology each around a tenth. It's a focused bet on the water theme, so it moves with industrial stocks more than with water utilities.
FIXD: A mix of mostly bonds, including government, mortgage-backed and corporate debt, plus a small slice of preferred stock. A manager picks the bonds, aiming for steady income as a core bond holding, and it can buy some lower-rated bonds, which adds more risk than a pure high-quality fund.
FIXP: An actively managed fund that owns other bond ETFs, such as short-term bonds, senior loans and mortgage real estate funds, with options layered on to boost income. It holds funds rather than individual bonds, so a handful of ETFs make up most of it.
FIXT: A manager-picked mix of bonds, mostly investment-grade, with a bit of cash on the side. It aims for steady income as a core bond holding, and because the manager can shift between bond types, it can differ from the broad bond market.
FIYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund of long-term US Treasury bonds, rather than on holding the bonds themselves. It aims to pay weekly distributions, but long-term bond prices swing hard when interest rates move, and the leveraged link magnifies that, so drops can be steep.
FIZY: An actively managed fund of US growth stocks, including Palantir, CrowdStrike, NVIDIA and Apple, which each make up around 5% to 7%. It also sells options on top of those holdings to earn extra income, which limits upside in strong markets.
FJAN: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in January, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FJP: Japanese stocks, led by industrials, consumer companies, technology and financials. It picks and weights stocks using a formula aimed at beating a standard index rather than simply following company size, so it's a way to add Japan with a tilt, and the yen's moves affect returns.
FJUL: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in July, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FJUN: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in June, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FKU: British companies picked by a scoring method hunting for growth and value, led by banks, consumer and industrial firms. It tilts away from the UK's giant global names toward mid-sized domestic businesses, so it leans more on Britain's own economy and the pound.
FLAG: The 50 highest-scoring companies in the S&P 500 on a market leadership ranking, all earning at least half their revenue in the United States, led by technology and health care. It is a concentrated core holding: fifty leaders instead of five hundred, so winners and losers matter more.
FLAO: Uses options on the S&P 500 to put a floor under losses over a six-month period that starts in April or October, in exchange for a limit on gains. It resets every six months, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
FLAU: Australian companies, led by banks and other financials at over a third, with mining and materials companies about a quarter. It's a way to add one country to a portfolio, and because it leans on banks and resources, it tends to move with commodity prices and Australia's economy.
FLAX: Large and mid sized companies across Asia with Japan left out, led by Taiwan and Korea, where chipmakers make technology nearly half the fund. It is a growth leaning bet on Asia's tech supply chain, with banks and consumer companies filling most of the rest.
FLBL: Senior loans to companies with weaker credit ratings, where the interest rate floats up and down with market rates. It aims for income and holds up better than ordinary bonds when rates rise, but it can drop if borrowers have trouble repaying.
FLBR: Brazilian companies, led by banks and other financials, with energy, mining and utilities next. It's a focused bet on one emerging economy, and it swings with commodity prices and the Brazilian real, so it is more volatile than broad international funds.
FLCA: Large and mid-sized Canadian companies, with financials about two fifths, then energy, materials and industrials. It's a way to add Canada to a portfolio, and because it leans on banks, oil and mining, it tends to follow commodity prices more than the US market does.
FLCB: A broad mix of US government, corporate, mortgage-backed and asset-backed bonds, mostly investment grade. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, and the managers can shift between bond types, though its price drops when rates rise.
FLCC: Large US companies, with technology about 40% and financials, health care and consumer firms behind. A computer model scores stocks and trades often to find bargains, so it's meant as a core stock holding that tries to beat the broad market, with no guarantee it does.
FLCE: A curated bundle of large-cap stock funds from big-name managers, mixing growth, value, dividend and factor approaches in one holding. Frontier assembles and rebalances the manager mix, so it is a fund of funds for investors who want active stock management without choosing managers themselves.
FLCG: Large US growth companies, with technology about 60 percent, then communication and consumer companies. It's built for growth and uses computer models to choose stocks, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
FLCH: Large and mid-sized Chinese companies, with consumer businesses, financials, communication and technology as the biggest groups. It's a way to add China to a portfolio, and it can swing widely with Chinese government policy and tension between the US and China.
FLCO: Investment-grade bonds issued by US and foreign companies, across a range of maturities. It's meant for steady income with more yield than government bonds, though prices drop when interest rates rise and companies can have credit troubles.
FLCV: Large US companies that look inexpensive compared with their earnings, spread across technology, financials, health care and consumer businesses. It suits investors wanting a value tilt inside a core stock holding, and a computer-driven selection process means it can lag when growth stocks lead the market.
FLDB: Mostly investment-grade bonds from companies and governments, kept to a duration of one year or less, which means they react very little to interest rate changes. It's a low-risk place to earn income while parking money, and it falls much less than regular bond funds when rates rise.
FLDR: Floating rate and short-term investment-grade bonds, whose payments adjust as interest rates change. It's meant as a place for cash-like money to earn a bit more than savings yields, and its price barely moves when rates rise because its payouts reset quickly.
FLDZ: US defense companies, mostly mid-sized and large industrial firms that supply the military. It is a focused bet on American defense spending, so it moves with government budgets and contracts rather than the wider stock market.
FLEE: Large and mid-sized companies across developed Europe, led by banks and industrial firms, with drugmakers and food giants adding a defensive streak. It offers one-holding access to Europe's stock markets, so results depend on European growth and on how the euro and pound move against the dollar.
FLEU: Large and mid-sized companies from the countries that use the euro, such as Germany, France, Spain and the Netherlands, tracking the FTSE Developed Eurozone Index. Dutch chipmaking equipment firm ASML is the largest holding at about 10%.
FLGB: Large and mid-sized UK companies, led by financials at about a quarter, then consumer staples, industrials and energy. It's a focused bet on one country, so it can swing more than a broad international fund, and the pound's moves against the dollar affect results.
FLGR: Germany's large and mid-sized companies: industrial and engineering giants, big insurers and banks, and its software leaders. It is a single-country bet on Europe's biggest economy, moving with German exports, the euro and European politics.
FLGV: Direct US government debt, including Treasury bonds, notes and bills plus inflation-protected ones, held across a range of maturities. It's a high-safety core bond holding for income and as a cushion for stocks, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
FLHY: Bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for the higher chance of default, with a small share from outside the US. It's for extra income, and it tends to fall alongside stocks in downturns more than safer bonds do.
FLIA: Bonds from governments and companies outside the US, almost all of it investment grade. It's for adding international income to a bond portfolio, and it hedges currency, so swings in foreign currencies against the dollar matter less, though the price still drops when interest rates rise.
FLIN: Large and mid-sized Indian companies, led by financials, with consumer, industrial and materials businesses behind them. It's a way to get exposure to a fast-growing emerging economy, and it can swing a lot with a single country's markets and currency.
FLJH: Japanese companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer firms, with the yen's moves hedged against the US dollar. It's for investors who want Japan's stocks without the swings of the currency.
FLJJ: Uses options on the S&P 500 to put a floor under losses over a six-month period that starts in January or July, in exchange for a limit on gains. It resets every six months, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
FLJP: Large Japanese companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer firms. It's a single-country holding that adds Japan to a portfolio, and its results also depend on the yen's value against the dollar.
FLKR: Large and mid-size South Korean companies, with technology, mainly computer chips, over half the portfolio, followed by industrials and financials. It's a focused bet on one country, so it swings more than a global fund and depends heavily on chip demand.
FLLA: Large and mid-sized companies across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Mexico, led by banks, miners and oil companies. It is a focused regional bet tied closely to commodity prices and local currencies, so it can rise or fall much harder than a global stock fund.
FLMB: Long term municipal bonds chosen to fund environmental projects, whose interest is free from federal income tax. The green label is the twist on a classic tax exempt income fund, and the long maturities mean its price moves more when interest rates change.
FLMI: Municipal bonds issued by US states and cities whose interest is free from federal income tax, chosen by an active manager who can adjust to changing conditions. It's meant for tax-free income, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
FLMX: Large Mexican companies, following the FTSE Mexico Capped Index. It is concentrated, with Grupo Mexico, Grupo Financiero Banorte, Fomento Economico Mexicano and America Movil about 40% of the fund, and it leans toward consumer staples, materials and banks.
FLN: Latin American companies screened for growth and value traits, led by banks with utilities, industrials and materials behind, across Brazil, Mexico and their neighbors. It is a focused bet on the region's economies, carrying extra political and currency swings on top of stock risk.
FLOT: Investment-grade corporate bonds whose interest payments reset regularly as short-term rates change. It's a cautious place for income, and because payments adjust, its price barely drops when interest rates rise.
FLOW: One hundred large and mid-sized US companies chosen for generating lots of free cash flow relative to their share price, led by technology, consumer and health care firms. It tilts toward cash-rich businesses, a value style that often holds up better when growth stocks stall.
FLQL: Large US companies picked for several traits at once, such as value, quality and momentum, with technology over 40 percent. It's a core stock holding that aims to beat the plain market, but because of that tilt it can lag it for a while.
FLQM: Mid-sized US companies spread fairly evenly across health care, financials, consumer companies and industrials. Stocks are chosen using several factors like value, quality and momentum, so it suits someone wanting a rules based way to add mid-sized companies to a core portfolio.
FLQS: Small US companies spread across many industries, with technology, consumer brands, health care and financials the biggest slices. It picks stocks using several measures at once, like value, quality and momentum, aiming for growth from smaller firms, which tend to swing more than big ones.
FLRG: Large and mid-sized US companies chosen for a mix of strengths like quality, value and momentum, with technology about two fifths. It's built as a core stock holding that leans toward certain traits, so it can trail the broad market when those traits fall out of favor.
FLRN: Investment-grade corporate and bank bonds whose interest payments reset as short-term rates change. It's meant as a cash-like cushion with income, and because payments adjust, its price barely drops when rates rise, though income falls when rates fall.
FLRT: Loans made to companies with lower credit ratings, whose interest rates reset as market rates move. It's meant for income that rises when rates rise, but the borrowers are riskier, so it can lose value when the economy weakens.
FLSA: Saudi Arabian companies, large and mid-sized, led by banks at over 40 percent with materials and energy firms behind. It is a single-country bet on the kingdom's economy and its push beyond oil, with extra political and currency risk.
FLSP: A mix of strategies that try to profit from well-known patterns such as cheap, rising and high-quality stocks, using stocks, commodity and currency positions, and plenty of cash. It's meant to diversify a portfolio and behave differently from the stock market, with no guarantee it will.
FLSW: Large Swiss companies, following the FTSE Switzerland Capped Index. It is top-heavy: Novartis, Roche and Nestle are about 39% of the fund, so it leans toward health care and food, and its holdings are priced in Swiss francs.
FLTB: Bonds that mature in the short to medium term, mixing investment-grade company and government debt with some higher-yield and emerging-market bonds. It's meant for steady income with smaller price swings than long bonds, though the lower-rated holdings add some risk.
FLTR: Investment-grade corporate bonds whose interest payments reset as short-term rates change, so income rises when rates rise. It's for earning more than cash with very little price swing, and it doesn't lose value when rates climb the way fixed-rate bond funds do.
FLTW: Taiwanese companies, with technology roughly three quarters (largely chip makers) and financials about an eighth. It's a single-country bet, so results depend heavily on one tech-driven economy and its currency, and it swings more than a broad world fund.
FLV: A concentrated group of large US value stocks (companies priced cheaply for their size) spread across financials, technology, health care and industrials. It's a value-focused core holding, and with fewer stocks than a broad index, it can differ noticeably from the overall market.
FLXI: An actively managed multisector bond portfolio that can roam across corporate, government, mortgage and other debt types as Invesco's managers see value. That freedom means its risk profile shifts over time, unlike a fixed core bond index fund.
FLXN: An actively managed fund that mainly holds lower-rated bonds, often called high yield or junk bonds, which pay more interest because the issuers are riskier. Nearly all of it is held through another State Street bond fund, so it is largely a single holding.
FLXR: An actively managed bond fund that moves flexibly among many bond types, such as mortgage-backed, corporate and government debt, to look for income wherever it seems best. Its manager has wide freedom, so what it holds can shift and it may not behave like a typical bond fund.
FMAG: US growth companies picked by Fidelity's active managers, with technology about 40% and industrials, financials and consumer companies behind it. It's a growth stock fund that doesn't show its full holdings daily, so it can swing more than the broad market.
FMAR: Options on the S&P 500 that are set up to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in March. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end of the period.
FMAT: US materials companies: chemical makers, miners, packaging and construction materials producers. It's a focused bet on one sector tied to the industrial economy, so it swings more than the broad market and lacks tech and health care entirely.
FMAY: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in May, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FMB: Municipal bonds from US states and cities, chosen by managers, that pay interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
FMCE: An actively managed fund holding just 25 to 35 US stocks, picked as companies the managers think can steadily grow their value. It is concentrated, with Intel, Microsoft, KKR and Amazon each making up roughly 5% of the fund.
FMCX: A focused group of about 25 to 35 US stocks, led by technology, industrials and consumer companies. It's a core-style holding with a high-conviction approach, so with so few stocks it can swing more than the broad market.
FMDE: Mid-sized US companies, with technology, industrials, health care and financials leading, and a manager tilts the mix toward stocks that look promising. It's a core holding for mid-sized companies that aims to modestly beat its benchmark, so it swings more than large-company funds.
FMED: Companies trying to disrupt medicine: new drug platforms, gene based treatments, advanced diagnostics and other approaches that could change how diseases are treated. All health care and innovation driven, it is a growth bet that can swing hard on research news, approvals and setbacks.
FMET: Companies building the metaverse, from chip makers and big platforms to the data centers that host virtual worlds, gathered from around the globe. It is a theme bet on virtual worlds taking off, so it moves with tech sentiment more than with actual metaverse profits.
FMF: Mostly cash and a wide range of futures contracts that bet on trends rising or falling in stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities. It's meant as a diversifier that tends not to move with the stock market, though it can lose money when markets keep reversing.
FMHI: Higher-yielding bonds from US cities, states and projects, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income, mostly for people in higher tax brackets, but these lower-rated bonds can lose value when the economy weakens or rates rise.
FMKT: An actively managed US stock fund that looks for companies expected to gain from lighter regulation, including in heavily regulated areas like health care and finance. Holdings are spread out, with no single stock above about 4% of the fund.
FMNY: Bonds from New York governments and public agencies, from the state dormitory authority to power and convention center issuers, including lower-rated ones for extra yield. The interest dodges federal, New York State and New York City taxes, making it a New Yorker's income fund.
FMQQ: Internet and e-commerce companies in emerging and frontier markets, from online marketplaces and food delivery to digital payments, led by consumer and finance names. It reaches younger, faster-growing online economies that the big emerging market funds often underweight.
FMTL: Miners and processors of critical metals: the lithium, cobalt, rare earths and other elements batteries and clean technology depend on. It is a focused bet on the raw materials of electrification, and small mining companies make it swing hard with metal prices and project news.
FMTM: US stocks that have recently been rising, concentrated in a small number of companies and led by technology and health care. It's a growth and trend-following bet, so it can run ahead in strong markets but may reverse sharply when leadership changes.
FMUB: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that pay interest typically free from federal income tax, with room for some lower-quality bonds that pay more. It's for tax-aware income, but the lower-quality part means more ups and downs than a plain high-quality muni fund.
FMUN: Municipal bonds from across the US, mostly medium-term, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It's aimed at investors in higher tax brackets looking for tax-friendly income, and its price falls when interest rates rise, so it's best as a steady piece of a portfolio.
FNCL: US financial companies such as banks, insurers, payment firms and asset managers, with nearly all in financials. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to do well when the economy is growing and rates are healthy.
FNDA: Small US companies picked and weighted by size of sales, cash flow and dividends rather than stock price, spread across industrials, financials, technology and consumer firms. It's a way to add small-company growth with a value tilt, and it swings more than large-company funds.
FNDB: US companies of all sizes across many industries, with technology about a fifth and financials, health care and industrials following. Instead of weighting by stock price size, it weights by business measures like sales and cash flow, giving a value tilt and less exposure to the priciest names.
FNDC: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, led by industrials, consumer companies, financials and materials. They're chosen by business size measures like sales and cash flow instead of stock price, so it's a diversifier that tilts toward bargains and can swing more than big company funds.
FNDE: Large emerging-market companies, led by financials at about a quarter, then technology, energy and materials. It's meant to add growth from developing economies, and it picks and weights companies by size of sales, earnings and assets rather than stock price, so it leans toward cheaper, established firms.
FNDF: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted by business size such as sales and cash flow, not stock price. Financials, industrials and energy lead, and it's a way to add international value stocks that also exposes you to foreign currency swings.
FNDX: Large US companies picked and weighted by business size, such as sales, cash flow and dividends, instead of by stock price. Technology, financials, health care and energy lead, and it's a core holding with a value tilt that leans away from the priciest stocks.
FNGS: An equal-weighted basket of about ten big internet and technology growth companies, packaged as a bank-issued note rather than a regular fund. It's a focused bet on mega-cap tech, and because it's a note, it carries the issuing bank's credit risk and swings more than the broad market.
FNK: Mid-sized US value stocks, led by financials at about a quarter, plus consumer, energy and industrial firms. It's a rules-based way to add cheaper mid-sized companies to a portfolio, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
FNOV: Options on the S&P 500 that are set up to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in November. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end of the period.
FNX: Mid-size US companies across financials, consumer firms, industrials and technology, picked by a scoring formula instead of by size. It's a diversifier between big and small stocks, so it's more volatile than large company funds but usually calmer than small ones.
FNY: US mid-sized growth stocks, picked by a rules-based screen, with health care, technology and industrials each around a fifth. It's a growth tilt for mid-sized companies, and since the stocks are picked by formula it can swing more than the broad market.
FOCT: Options on the S&P 500 that are set up to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end of the period.
FOPC: A fund of bond funds: roughly six to twelve other ETFs spanning US fixed income, chosen and shifted by its managers in search of extra yield. It plays a flexible core-plus bond role, reaching into credit corners a plain investment grade fund skips, which adds both income and risk.
FORH: Small and mid-sized companies worldwide, picked opportunistically across industry, technology, health care and energy, with some Treasury bills and volatility hedges alongside. The flexible, concentrated style means results depend heavily on the managers' calls.
FOTO: Companies in photonics, the technology of using light, such as lasers, optical fiber and sensors, almost all in the technology sector. It's a narrow bet on one theme, uses swaps for part of its exposure, and swings far more than the broad market.
FOWF: Defense companies from the US and its allies working on emerging warfare technology: missiles, aircraft, drones, sensors and cyber defense. Industry takes about three fifths and technology most of the rest, tying the fund to allied military spending.
FOXY: Currency contracts that bet on foreign currencies rising or falling against each other, held alongside cash and short-term bonds. It's an actively managed currency trade, not a stock or bond fund, so it can behave very differently from the rest of a portfolio.
FPA: Stocks from Asia outside Japan, led by industrials and technology, chosen by a scoring method rather than company size. It's for adding Asian growth to a portfolio, but it swings with emerging markets and currencies and is tilted away from the biggest companies.
FPAA: A global allocation portfolio from FPA's value-minded managers, holding about 61 percent stocks and 36 percent bonds worldwide, partly through other funds. It is a one-stop moderate portfolio run with a contrarian, bargain-hunting style, so its mix can drift from the usual balanced fund template.
FPAG: A small, hand-picked collection of companies from around the world, spread across health care, communication, materials and technology. It's an actively managed value approach, so it can hold a lot of cash and may look very different from the global market.
FPAS: Short-term debt issued or guaranteed by the US government and its agencies, kept brief in maturity to protect capital. It pays modest interest with very small price swings, suiting money that must be there when needed.
FPE: A mix of preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends and rank above common stock, and income-producing bonds, mostly from financial and utility companies. It's built for high regular income, and its price drops when interest rates rise, since its fixed payouts look less attractive then.
FPEI: Preferred shares and income-producing bonds, mostly from large institutions like banks and insurers. It's meant for higher income than regular bonds, but it can fall when interest rates rise and is more sensitive to financial sector trouble.
FPFD: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income-paying investments, which are stock-like shares that pay fixed dividends. Issuers include banks, pipelines and utilities, and the focus is on steady income.
FPRO: Real estate companies and trusts: warehouse landlords, data centers, cell towers, shopping centers and apartment owners, mostly in the US. It pays property income through a semi-transparent active fund, so the full holdings list is not published every day.
FPWR: Power infrastructure companies: regulated utilities at about two thirds, plus energy pipelines and related firms picked by energy income specialists. It is an income-oriented bet on electricity demand and grid building, steadier than most energy funds thanks to the utility core, and sensitive to interest rates.
FPX: Recent US stock market debuts and spin-offs, with technology about a third, health care about a fifth and industrials next. It's a growth bet on newer companies, so it swings more than the broad market, and the list is refreshed regularly as new ones come public.
FPXE: Recently listed European companies: the 100 largest and most tradable new stock market debuts and spin-offs across the continent. It is a bet on young public companies, led by health care and banks, so it carries the extra swing of fresh listings.
FPXI: Companies from developed and emerging markets outside the US, selected as the fastest growing and led by technology, health care and financials. It's a growth-oriented way to add international stocks, and it moves with foreign currencies as well.
FQAL: Large and mid-sized US companies screened for higher quality, meaning strong profits and healthy finances, with technology about two fifths. It's a core stock holding that favors steadier businesses, and it may trail in rallies led by weaker, riskier stocks.
FRDM: Stocks from emerging market countries that rank high on personal and economic freedom, with technology about half and financials a fifth. It's a way into developing economies that screens out less free countries, so it leaves out some major markets such as China.
FREI: A mix of bonds, preferred shares and stocks of real estate companies, with bonds about two thirds. It's aimed at income from real estate with less swing than a stock-only real estate fund, but it can still fall when interest rates rise.
FREL: Real estate companies, nearly all of the fund, such as those that own apartments, warehouses, offices, cell towers and storage. It's an income-oriented way to add property to a portfolio without buying buildings, and it usually drops when interest rates rise.
FRGN: Companies outside the US in both developed and emerging countries, with technology, financials, industrials and energy leading. It's a way to add international diversification, chosen by an active manager, so results can differ noticeably from a plain foreign stock index.
FRI: Real estate investment trusts, which are companies that own buildings like apartments, offices, warehouses and cell towers, and pay out most of their income. It's meant for income and property exposure, and it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
FRIZ: Companies with a record of paying steady or rising dividends, spread across technology, banks, health care and industrials. It is built to deliver income that can grow over time alongside stock gains, favoring reliable dividend growers over the biggest payouts.
FRNW: Clean energy companies worldwide: wind turbine makers, solar firms, renewable power producers and the utilities buying their output, with utilities the biggest slice at nearly half. It is a broad bet on the shift from fossil fuels, spanning both the builders and the operators of green power.
FRTY: About 40 mid-sized US companies, with health care the largest at over a third, then technology and industrials. It's a growth fund with few holdings and a heavy sector tilt, so it swings more than a broad mid-cap fund.
FRUT: A short named list of giant growth companies, the MANGOS group of mega-cap technology and tech-adjacent names, held through their stocks. It is a concentrated bet on a handful of market leaders: there is no diversification cushion, so it swings hard with those few names.
FRWD: Companies building new technologies such as AI, cloud and automation, with technology about three quarters and consumer firms behind. It's a growth bet on a single theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
FSCC: Smaller US companies spread across health care, financials, industrials and technology, each around a fifth or less of the fund. It's a way to add small-company growth to a portfolio, and a computer-driven model picks the stocks, so it swings more than large-company funds.
FSCS: Small and mid sized US companies picked for strong balance sheets and steady dividends, spread across banks, industrial firms, insurers and food companies in near equal weights. The focus on financially sturdy payers makes it a defensive way to own smaller companies, favoring steadiness over fast growth.
FSEC: Investment-grade bonds backed by pools of loans, including government-backed mortgage bonds and other asset-backed debt. It's meant for steady income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio with little company default risk, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
FSEG: Small US growth companies, with health care the biggest slice at about 30 percent and technology close behind. Fidelity begins with the small-cap growth group and tilts toward its research favorites, so it offers fast-growing small firms with extra stock picking on top.
FSEP: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to cushion some losses over a one year period starting in September, but it also caps your gains, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end.
FSEV: An actively managed fund of small US companies that look cheap, built around the Russell 2000 Value Index, with the manager adjusting weights to try to beat it. It holds many names, none above about 1% of the fund, and leans toward financials.
FSGS: Small and midsize US companies chosen for strong balance sheets and solid market positions, spread across technology, health care, finance and industry. It is a growth-leaning small company holding that favors financially sturdy firms over speculative ones, aiming for steadier performance within a volatile corner of the market.
FSIG: Investment-grade bonds from US companies, kept to short and medium maturities. It aims for steady interest income with less price swing than long-term corporate bonds, so it works as a calmer bond holding, though it still dips when interest rates rise.
FSMB: Short-term bonds from US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It's a low-swing place to park money for tax-free income, and because the bonds mature soon, prices barely move when interest rates change, but it pays less than longer bonds.
FSMD: Small and mid-sized US companies spread evenly across technology, industrials, financials and health care, chosen for good prices, quality, momentum and lower swings. It's a diversified core holding for smaller firms, aiming for a smoother ride than most small-company funds.
FSML: Small US companies, with health care the biggest slice at about a fifth, followed by financials, technology and industrials. It's meant for growth beyond big companies, and an enhanced selection approach tweaks the picks, but small stocks swing more than large ones.
FSOL: Holds the digital currency Solana directly rather than companies or bonds, so its value follows Solana's price. It's a speculative, focused bet on a single crypto asset, and it can swing sharply in either direction, far more than a stock or bond fund.
FSPC: Companies in the space economy: rocket and satellite makers, launch services and the industrial firms behind them, with industrials about three quarters of the fund. It is a growth bet on space going commercial, concentrated in one young industry that swings with contracts and launch headlines.
FSTA: Makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks, household products and groceries, nearly all of the fund. It's a defensive pick, because people keep buying these items in downturns, but it usually trails in strong rallies led by technology and growth stocks.
FSTB: Investment-grade bonds that come due in a few years, with interest rate sensitivity similar to a one to three year government and corporate bond index. It's a low-risk place for cash that pays modest income and barely drops when rates rise.
FSYD: High-yield bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, from companies with stronger environmental, social and governance records. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but it carries more default risk and tends to fall when the economy weakens.
FSZ: Swiss companies chosen by a scoring system that favors growth and value signals, spanning drug makers, industrial firms and big banks. It is a single-country fund on one of the world's richest, most stable markets, with returns also riding the Swiss franc.
FTA: Large US companies that look cheaply priced, with financials the biggest piece at a fifth, then energy, utilities and technology. It's a value tilt picked by a scoring formula instead of by size, so it holds more energy and utilities than the broad market.
FTAG: Agriculture companies worldwide: seed and crop chemical giants, fertilizer makers and farm machinery firms, with materials producers over half the fund. It is a bet on farm spending and crop prices, driven by weather, harvests and food demand.
FTBD: A go-anywhere bond fund that roams the whole debt market, from Treasuries to high yield and emerging market bonds, in dollars and hedged foreign currencies. The tactical freedom lets Fidelity chase income wherever it appears, so the risk level varies over time.
FTBI: A fixed-recipe blend of income ETFs: buy-write and target income stock funds plus other income strategies across three asset classes, in set proportions. It is a balanced income holding for investors who want one ticker that automatically keeps an income-focused mix of stock and bond funds.
FTC: Large US growth companies, with technology about a third and industrials a quarter, then health care and consumer firms. It's a growth tilt picked by a scoring formula instead of by size, so it's less tech heavy than many growth funds but swings more than the broad market.
FTCA: Investment-grade municipal bonds from California issuers, with maturities of three years or longer. Its interest is generally exempt from federal and California income tax, so it suits California residents in higher tax brackets, though prices drop when interest rates rise.
FTCB: A mix of high-quality US bonds, from corporations and the government to mortgage-backed debt, with a little cash. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and an active manager aims to do better than the standard bond market.
FTCE: One hundred US companies with the highest earnings quality in their sectors, chosen by forensic accounting research that checks whether reported profits are backed by real cash. Technology leads at about two-fifths, and the earnings capture screen sets it apart from plain index funds.
FTCS: Large US companies with strong balance sheets and large cash reserves, across financials, industrials, consumer staples and health care. It's a core-style holding with a quality tilt, and it holds roughly equal amounts of each stock, so it has less technology than the broad market.
FTDS: Companies with strong balance sheets and a record of raising their dividends year after year, led by banks, energy and industrial firms. The strength tests aim for dividends that keep growing through downturns, suiting investors who want income with staying power.
FTEC: US technology companies of all sizes, covering software, chip makers and computer hardware. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market, and internet and social media companies are classed elsewhere, so they aren't included.
FTG: Mid-sized US growth companies picked using behavioral finance, the study of how investor mistakes create mispriced stocks, with technology about half the fund. The managers look for overreactions to buy into, so it hunts bargains inside the growth world.
FTGC: Commodity futures covering energy, metals and farm goods, with most of the money parked in cash-like holdings to back the contracts. It's used to diversify away from stocks and bonds or hedge against inflation, and it's actively managed, so the mix of commodities shifts over time.
FTGS: Large US companies, with technology about 37 percent, then health care, financials and industrials, picked for strong growth with filters meant to avoid overpriced shares. It's a growth tilt in a core stock holding, and it swings more than the broad market.
FTHB: Bonds from issuers screened as biblically aligned, led by US Treasuries, with corporate bonds, mortgage bonds and preferred shares behind. It targets income for faith-based investors, and the values screen rules out some big borrowers entirely.
FTHF: Companies in emerging markets screened for how well they promote what the index calls human flourishing, with technology about half and financials about a quarter. It's a values-tilted way to add developing country growth, and it swings more than US stocks.
FTHI: Large US companies, led by technology, combined with an options strategy that sells away some of the upside in exchange for regular income payments. It aims for income and a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
FTIF: Companies picked because their businesses tend to hold up when inflation bites: energy producers are nearly half the fund, with industrial, materials and property firms behind. It is a defensive corner of the stock market meant to shine when prices elsewhere are rising fast.
FTKI: Small US companies with call options sold against the small-cap index in a buy-write program that collects premium income. Small stocks already swing plenty, and the option income is meant to smooth that ride and add cash flow, at the cost of capping gains when small caps surge.
FTLS: US stocks with about two thirds held in long positions plus some bets against stocks that the manager expects to fall, leaving a large cash portion. It aims for a smoother ride than the market, so it tends to lag in strong rallies but fall less in sell-offs.
FTMA: Investment-grade bonds from Massachusetts governments and agencies whose interest is free from federal and Massachusetts income tax. It's meant for tax-free income for state residents, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
FTMH: Municipal bonds, mostly lower-rated ones, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It's for investors in higher tax brackets looking for more tax-free income, and the tradeoff is more credit risk than safer munis, so it can fall in weak markets.
FTMN: Municipal bonds from Minnesota issuers that are investment-grade and mature in three years or more. It pays income free from federal and Minnesota state income tax, which suits Minnesota residents in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
FTMS: Short-term, mostly investment-grade municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It's a low-risk cushion for tax-free income, and because the maturities are short, its price moves less when rates rise.
FTMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds with intermediate to long maturities, mostly in the US. It's built for income that is exempt from federal income tax, which suits higher earners in taxable accounts, though its price falls more than short-term bonds when interest rates rise.
FTN: Investment-grade corporate bonds in the middle range: loans to solid companies with between five and ten years left until they come due. It sits between short and long bond funds in both interest paid and price swings, a middle-of-the-road core holding for the bond side of a portfolio.
FTNJ: New Jersey municipal bonds with medium to long maturities, whose interest is generally free from federal and New Jersey income tax. It's aimed at New Jersey residents seeking tax-friendly income, and because it holds one state's bonds, it is less spread out and drops when rates rise.
FTNY: Long-term municipal bonds from New York State and its cities, whose interest is generally free from federal, state and city income taxes. It's for New York residents in higher tax brackets seeking tax-free income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
FTOH: A fund of investment-grade Ohio municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal and Ohio income tax, though some may be subject to the alternative minimum tax. It is actively managed and focused on tax-free income for Ohio residents.
FTPA: Pennsylvania municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt issued by the state, its cities, school districts and authorities to fund public projects. The income is generally free of federal and Pennsylvania tax for state residents, which is the whole point, so it suits Pennsylvanians in higher tax brackets more than anyone else.
FTQI: Nasdaq-100 companies, led by technology at over half, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside in return for regular income. It's built for income from growth stocks, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
FTRB: Mostly investment-grade US bonds, including mortgage bonds and Treasuries, with some riskier bonds and foreign bonds mixed in by the manager. It's meant for steady income as the core of a bond portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
FTRI: Fifty high-dividend companies in natural resources, mainly materials like mining and chemicals, plus utilities and energy. It's for income and a hedge against rising commodity prices, but it swings with those prices and is concentrated in a few cyclical industries.
FTSD: Short-term bonds issued or backed by the US government, including Treasuries and agency mortgage bonds. It's meant to be a stable place to park money with modest income, and because the bonds are short-term, its price moves far less than longer bond funds when rates change.
FTSL: Loans that banks make to lower-rated companies, which pay interest that resets as short-term rates change. It's meant for income, and because payments float with rates it holds up better than most bonds when rates rise, but it can fall when the economy weakens and borrowers struggle.
FTSM: Short-term, high-quality US dollar bonds with a portion in cash, run by an active manager. It aims for a bit more income than plain cash holdings, with very small price swings.
FTWO: Companies tied to natural resources and national security, such as farm equipment, energy, mining and defense firms, following a Bloomberg-based index. Deere, Constellation Energy, ExxonMobil and General Electric make up about a third of it.
FTXG: US food and beverage companies selected from the Nasdaq by liquidity: packaged food makers, drink companies and producers that fill supermarket shelves. It is a defensive consumer staples bet, the kind of steady, everyday-spending industry that usually holds up better when the economy and markets wobble.
FTXH: US pharmaceutical companies, entirely health care, selected for how easily they trade and how they rank on a size screen. It's a focused bet on drugmakers, so it can swing on drug approvals and policy news more than a broad health care fund.
FTXL: Almost entirely chip companies: designers and makers of semiconductors and the equipment behind them. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market, rising hard when chip demand booms and dropping hard when it cools.
FTXN: US oil and gas companies, nearly all energy, covering producers, drillers and pipeline and refining businesses. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil and gas prices and often moves differently than the rest of the market.
FTXO: US banks, from big national lenders to regional ones, and nothing else, so every dollar sits in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on banking that swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and the health of the economy.
FTXR: US transportation companies, about two thirds industrials such as airlines, railroads and trucking, and about a third consumer companies like automakers and parts makers. It's a focused bet on how goods and people move, so it rises and falls with the economic cycle more than the broad market.
FUTY: US utilities, the companies that deliver electricity, gas and water. It's a lower-swing holding favored for steady dividends and as a cushion in rough markets, though its price tends to drop when interest rates rise.
FV: A fund that holds five other sector funds at a time, chosen by recent strength, so it shifts toward whatever is winning. Right now it leans on health care, energy, technology and industrials, and it's a momentum approach that can lag when leadership flips quickly.
FVAL: Large and mid-size US companies that look cheaply priced against their earnings and assets, with technology still around forty percent, then financials and health care. It's a value tilt inside a core stock holding, and it can trail when expensive growth stocks lead.
FVC: Five First Trust stock funds at a time, chosen by a momentum system that favors whichever market themes have been performing best lately. The mix shifts as trends change, so the fund is a rotation strategy that can look very different from one year to the next.
FVD: Dividend-paying US companies ranked highly by Value Line's research and screened for steady dividends, with financials, utilities, industrials and consumer staples leading. It's built for dividend income with lower swings, and it holds roughly equal amounts of each stock rather than favoring the biggest.
FWD: Actively managed stocks of global companies the manager thinks will profit from big changes in technology and the economy, with technology well over half. It's a growth fund for adding innovation, and it swings more than the broad market and can drop hard when tech sells off.
FXA: Actual Australian dollars held in a deposit account, packaged as a stock so investors can hold the currency in a brokerage account. It simply rises and falls with the Australian dollar, making it a direct currency bet tied to interest rates and commodity-rich Australia's economy.
FXB: Actual British pounds held in a deposit account, packaged as a stock so investors can hold the currency in a brokerage account. It simply rises and falls with the pound, making it a direct bet on Britain's currency, steered by interest rates and the UK economy.
FXC: Holds actual Canadian dollars in a bank deposit, so its price follows the exchange rate between the Canadian and US dollar. It owns no stocks or bonds, and gives a simple way to hold the currency without opening a foreign bank account.
FXD: US consumer discretionary companies such as retailers, restaurants, carmakers and travel firms, chosen and weighted by a scoring system rather than by size. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to swing more than the broad market and does best when people are feeling confident.
FXE: Euros held in a bank account, with nothing else mixed in. It's a bet on the euro against the US dollar, rising if the euro strengthens, so it serves as a currency hedge or trade and pays little or no income.
FXED: Income investments of many stripes: corporate bonds, preferred shares, lending companies and bond funds, blended to enhance the payout. Reaching across riskier corners of the bond world lifts the income, with correspondingly more credit risk than a plain investment grade fund.
FXF: Swiss francs held in bank deposits, so the fund's value follows the franc against the US dollar. It's used as a currency hedge or a safe-haven bet, since the franc often rises in turmoil, but it pays no income and can fall if the dollar strengthens.
FXG: US consumer staples companies, such as food, drink, household goods and grocery sellers, making up over four fifths of the fund. It's a defensive pick that tends to hold up better when the economy weakens, and it weights stocks by a score instead of size, so smaller names count more.
FXH: Health care companies from the Russell 1000, including drugmakers, device makers and insurers, chosen and weighted by a scoring formula rather than by size. It's a focused bet on one sector, and the equal-style weighting gives smaller names more say than a typical health care fund.
FXI: Roughly 50 of China's biggest companies, with financials about a third, consumer companies a quarter and internet and communication firms making up much of the rest. It's a focused bet on the Chinese economy, so it can swing sharply with Chinese policy and politics.
FXL: US technology companies, almost all in the sector, with a little industrials. Stocks are picked and weighted by growth and value scores rather than by size, so it isn't dominated by the giants, and as a one-sector bet it swings more than the broad market.
FXN: Almost entirely energy companies, such as oil and gas producers, drillers and pipelines. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, and it uses a scoring method that spreads money more evenly across stocks instead of favoring the biggest, so smaller names matter more.
FXO: US banks, insurers and other financial companies, picked and weighted by a formula that favors stronger growth and value traits instead of company size. It's a focused bet on one sector that moves with interest rates and the economy, and it holds smaller firms than most financial funds.
FXR: US industrial companies, about two thirds industrials plus technology and consumer firms in related fields, with stocks chosen by a rules-based score instead of size. It's a focused bet on the industrial economy, so it swings with business cycles and more than the broad market.
FXU: US utility companies, such as electric, gas and water providers, picked by a rules-based screen of growth and value instead of company size. It's a focused sector bet for income and steadier swings, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
FXY: The Japanese yen, held as cash, so its price follows the yen against the US dollar. It's used as a hedge or a bet on the currency, since the yen often rises in market panics, but it pays no real income and can drop when the dollar strengthens.
FXZ: Mostly materials companies, such as chemicals, metals and mining, with some industrials. It's a focused bet on raw materials, and it uses a scoring method that spreads money more evenly across stocks rather than favoring the biggest, so it can swing with the economy.
FYC: Small US growth companies, with health care the largest piece at about 30 percent, then technology and industrials. It's a growth bet on smaller businesses, picked by a scoring formula instead of by size, so it swings more than large company funds.
FYEE: Large US companies, with technology about two fifths, paired with an options strategy that collects extra income in exchange for giving up some gains. It aims to add income to a stock holding, but it can trail the market in strong rallies.
FYLD: Smaller and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by energy, financials and industrials, picked for returning cash through dividends and buybacks. It's a value-style way to add international stocks, and it tends to be cyclical.
FYT: Small US value companies, with financials about a fifth and consumer, industrial and energy firms behind. Instead of weighting by size, the index scores stocks on value and growth traits, so it's a way to tilt toward smaller, cheaper companies that can swing more than large stocks.
FYX: Small US companies across financials, health care, industrials and technology, picked by a scoring formula instead of by size. It's a diversifier beyond big names, and since smaller stocks are riskier, it swings more than large company funds.
GAA: A fund of funds that spreads money across many other ETFs covering stocks, bonds, real estate and commodities around the world. It is actively managed to hold a wide mix rather than follow a single index.
GABF: Financial services companies of all sizes: banks, insurers, asset managers, payment firms and brokers, nearly nine tenths of the fund. It is a focused bet on the money business, so it rises and falls with lending, markets and deal making.
GAEM: Bonds from governments and companies in emerging markets, borrowed in dollars or in local currencies, picked actively. It aims for higher income than developed market bonds, with extra risk from shakier economies and currency swings on the local currency debt.
GAIQ: Companies worldwide that the manager believes will grow thanks to technology, with tech around two fifths and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It's a growth fund with a global reach, and being actively managed, it can differ a lot from the market.
GAL: A one-fund portfolio: about 60% stocks, led by technology and financials, and the rest bonds with a little cash, spread worldwide. It's meant as a balanced core holding, and the manager can shift the mix, so the stock and bond split moves over time.
GALX: Space companies: rocket launchers, satellite makers and the firms supplying them, led by industrials at about 60 percent. It is a growth bet on the business of orbit, from broadband satellites to defense payloads, and swings on launches and contracts.
GAMR: The leaders of the video game business worldwide: game publishers, console and chip makers, and the platforms where games are played and streamed. It is a pure bet on gaming as entertainment, so it moves with game releases and player spending.
GANZ: A thematic fund that rotates into whatever themes the manager favors, holding US-listed stocks alongside options on individual companies and indexes. Nothing about its focus is fixed, so it is a bet on the manager's theme-picking and timing rather than on any one industry or style.
GAPR: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb a moderate share of losses over a one-year period that starts in April, with tech the biggest holding behind them. It's a cushion for cautious investors, but gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full year.
GARA: Real assets from around the world: infrastructure operators, utilities, property companies and data center owners whose value sits in physical things. It is built for income from toll-road-like businesses and rents, and what sets it apart is the global mix, so currency moves matter alongside the assets.
GARP: US companies that pass a quality screen and offer growth at a reasonable price, meaning solid finances without the steepest valuations. At the moment the mix leans toward technology and chipmakers, so it is a growth-leaning core holding that tries to avoid the most expensive corners of the market.
GARY: Mostly US growth companies, with technology making up well over half and smaller slices in health care and financials. A manager picks the stocks, so it's a growth holding that is much more tech-heavy than the broad market and tends to swing harder.
GASZ: An actively managed fund of companies tied to natural gas power, such as engine makers, turbine builders and pipeline companies. It is concentrated: Caterpillar and GE Vernova are about 25% of it, and nearly two thirds of the fund is industrials.
GAUG: Options tied to the S&P 500, the index of America's largest companies, which is about 40 percent technology. It's meant to cushion some losses over a one-year period that starts each August, but in return it caps your gains, and the protection only works if you hold through the full period.
GAVA: A fund that gives exposure to AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain, without having to buy and store the crypto yourself. It holds AVAX directly and may earn staking rewards, so its value moves with the price of one volatile crypto asset.
GBHI: Riskier corporate bonds, the high yield kind often called junk bonds, picked one by one by Gabelli's managers for interest income. It aims for high payouts from below-investment-grade borrowers, which means more chance of defaults and bigger price swings than safer bond funds.
GBIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills that mature within a year, plus some cash. It's meant as a place to park money with little risk and a cushion for stocks, and because its bonds mature quickly, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
GBND: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed debt. It's meant to be a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion when stocks fall, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
GBTC: A trust that holds Bitcoin, the digital currency, and nothing else. It's a way to get Bitcoin exposure through a regular brokerage account, but it swings far more than stocks and has no income or cash flow behind it.
GBUG: Gold and silver mining companies, plus royalty firms that finance mines, all in the materials industry. It's a focused bet on precious metals that the managers pick actively with a contrarian value style, and miners tend to swing much more than the metals themselves.
GCAD: Makers of aircraft, aircraft parts and defense equipment, from big prime contractors to smaller specialist suppliers. It is a focused bet on aviation and military spending, actively picked in Gabelli's value style, so it moves with defense budgets and air travel demand.
GCAL: Bonds from California governments and agencies, mostly intermediate maturities, plus a little cash. It's meant for income that is generally free from federal taxes, and often California taxes too, which suits high earners in the state, though bond prices fall when interest rates rise.
GCB: Intermediate-term bonds from governments and companies: a blend of Treasury and agency debt with investment-grade corporate bonds in the middle maturity range. It is a classic core bond holding, paying a little more than pure government funds while keeping maturities, and price swings, moderate.
GCC: Futures contracts on energy, farm products, industrial metals and precious metals, with most of the money parked in short-term bonds as backing. It's a way to add commodities, which often rise with inflation, and it holds no physical goods, so returns depend on futures pricing.
GCLO: An actively managed fund that invests in investment grade collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans to companies sliced into bonds. Investment grade CLOs are the safest slices, so they pay less than lower-rated ones.
GCOR: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
GCOW: Large global companies that pay high dividends and generate plenty of cash, led by consumer staples, health care, communication and industrials. It's built for dividend income from established businesses, and it holds little tech, so it can trail in growth rallies.
GCPB: A broad mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds, with room for some riskier bonds to earn extra income. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady interest, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
GCPU: Companies that supply computing power for artificial intelligence and bitcoin mining, including data center and cloud providers, following an index built around that theme. It is concentrated in a handful of volatile names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, DigitalOcean, Hut 8 and IREN.
GDE: Large US stocks, led by technology, combined with gold futures so you get both in one fund. It's a way to add a gold hedge to stock exposure without selling either, though gold can drag when it falls while stocks rise.
GDEC: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that absorb a moderate part of losses over a one-year period starting each December. It's meant to soften drops in the stock market, but the trade-off is a ceiling on gains in strong rallies.
GDIV: Large US companies with a record of paying and growing dividends, spread across financials, industrials, health care and technology. It aims for a mix of income and growth as a core holding, and the manager picks stocks actively, so it can differ from the broad market.
GDLC: A basket of five large cryptocurrencies, held directly rather than through companies, with bitcoin and ether the biggest. It's a single-fund way to bet on the crypto market, so it swings far more than stocks and can fall sharply in a short time.
GDMA: A manager-picked mix of stocks, bonds, currencies and real estate, with the stock side leaning toward technology, financials and health care. It aims to be a one-fund portfolio with a moderate tilt toward caution, and the manager can shift between asset types, so results depend on those choices.
GDMN: Gold mining companies, with gold futures layered on top to add exposure to the metal itself. It's a focused bet on gold, and because miners usually move more than gold, it swings harder than gold alone.
GDOC: Health care companies working on the field's future: gene-based medicine, precision treatments, robotic procedures and digital health, from giants to small innovators. It is a growth bet on medical innovation, so breakthroughs and trial failures can move it sharply.
GDOG: Direct ownership of Dogecoin, the meme-born cryptocurrency featuring a Shiba Inu dog, held as the fund's only asset. Its price is driven mostly by online enthusiasm and celebrity attention, making it among the most speculative assets in any brokerage account.
GDT: An actively managed mix of inflation-protected US Treasury bonds and gold, which the fund holds directly or through a subsidiary. It combines two traditional inflation hedges, so part of its movement follows the price of gold.
GDX: Companies that mine gold and silver, all falling in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on precious metals, and because mining costs are steady while metal prices move, it tends to swing much harder than gold itself and the broad stock market.
GDXJ: Smaller gold and silver mining companies, often exploring for new deposits rather than running giant mines. It's a focused bet on precious metals, so it swings far more than gold itself and the broad market, and it's used as a high-risk trade on gold prices.
GDXW: A fund that aims for about 1.2 times the weekly return of a gold miners stock group, using swaps and shares. It resets every week, so results over longer periods can drift from that, and it pays out income often.
GDXY: An income fund that uses options on a gold miners fund, with the cash and short-term bonds mostly sitting behind that strategy. It aims to pay out regular income, but in exchange it gives up part of the upside if gold mining stocks surge, while still taking losses when they fall.
GEEQ: An actively managed fund that holds stocks plus derivatives to give stock-like returns, and aims to pay out extra income from options. Selling options for income tends to cap gains in strong markets compared with owning the stocks alone.
GEM: Stocks from developing countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology the largest slice at over 40 percent, then financials. It's built for long-term growth and spreads across factors like value and momentum, but it swings more than US funds.
GEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and state-linked issuers, all in US dollars, screened for good governance and solid fundamentals. The screens aim to keep the higher income of emerging market debt while avoiding its most troubled borrowers.
GEME: A concentrated mix of large and mid-sized emerging market companies, with technology around 40% and financials about a fifth. A manager chooses a limited number of stocks, so it can be a growth-oriented way to add emerging markets that moves differently from broad index funds.
GEMQ: A fund of emerging market stocks that uses Goldman Sachs' data-driven models to choose and weight them rather than just tracking an index. It covers companies in developing economies, so it tends to be more volatile than funds of developed markets.
