GEND: Dividend-paying US companies in a focused portfolio of a few dozen stocks, spread across health care, banks, energy and industrials. It is built for steady income from established payers, favoring reliable dividends over fast growth or the very highest yields.
GENM: Intermediate municipal bonds rated A or better, issued by states, cities and public agencies across the US. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, so it is an income holding aimed at investors in higher tax brackets who want quality and a middle-of-the-road maturity.
GENT: Intermediate-term investment grade bonds, mostly US Treasuries with some corporate debt, chosen with a quality-first approach. It is a core bond holding meant for steady interest income, and because its bonds mature in the middle range, its price moves moderately when interest rates change.
GENW: Dividend-paying companies from outside the US, a focused list of a few dozen stocks led by banks at a bit over a third. It is built for income from abroad, favoring established payers over growth names, so it tilts toward value.
GENZ: Digital-native companies: video game makers, e-commerce platforms, ride-hailing, online brokers and social apps from around the world. It is a growth bet on businesses born on the internet, spread across gaming, shopping, finance and media rather than one app category.
GEQ: Large companies from around the world, with technology about a quarter, financials a fifth, and industrials and health care making up much of the rest. It's a global core holding that gives each position a similar weight, so smaller names count for more than in a typical size-weighted fund.
GEW: Large companies from around the world, with financials, technology and industrials leading. Each holding gets a similar-sized slice rather than weighting by company size, so it leans less on the biggest companies than a typical global fund.
GFEB: Large US companies, with technology around 40 percent, held through options that absorb a moderate part of losses over a one-year period starting each February. It's meant to soften stock market drops, but there's a cap on gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
GFGF: High quality companies favored by about twenty famous long-term investors whose portfolios the managers follow, bought at what they judge reasonable prices. It outsources stock picking to proven gurus, leaning toward big technology and financial names those investors love.
GFLW: About 100 growth companies that generate strong free cash flow, which is the cash left after running and investing in the business. Technology is nearly half, followed by health care and industrials, so it's a growth holding that swings more than the broad market and leans heavily on tech.
GGM: A fund of sector funds that rotates among industries like energy, staples, utilities and technology based on macroeconomic signals. The whole mix can shift as the outlook changes, so it is an active bet on the managers' reading of the economy.
GGME: Companies shaping next generation media and gaming: video game makers, streaming and social platforms, and the technology behind interactive entertainment, split between tech and communication names. It is a focused growth bet on how people play and watch, swinging with hit titles and user trends.
GGOV: Government bonds from around the world, actively managed, with currency exposure hedged back to US dollars. It's for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, and the hedge removes currency swings, though prices still drop when interest rates rise.
GGRW: An actively managed fund of stocks in companies it believes are driving innovation, mostly in technology and industrials. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon and Applied Materials are each about 5% to 9% of it, so a handful of big names drive much of the fund.
GGTL: Technology companies from around the world, chipmakers, software firms and electronics giants, picked actively by Gabelli. At nearly nine tenths technology it is a pure sector bet, so it rises and falls with the tech cycle.
GGUS: Large US growth companies, with technology at over half and communications next. It's built for growth, so it leans heavily toward a few industries and tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
GHTA: A tactical mix of other funds, currently leaning on bonds and floating rate Treasuries with a smaller stock slice, shifted by the managers' risk models. It can change posture a lot, from cautious to aggressive, depending on how dangerous the managers judge markets to be.
GHYB: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, spread widely across industries. It's meant to pay higher income than safer bonds, but it tends to fall alongside stocks in a downturn because these companies are likelier to default.
GHYG: Lower-rated corporate bonds from companies in the US and abroad, paying higher interest than safer bonds. It's meant for investors wanting extra income, but these companies are more likely to miss payments, so the price tends to fall harder than regular bonds in economic downturns.
GIAX: Global stock funds, led by technology, paired with an options strategy that sells call spreads for extra income. It's meant for income from stocks, but selling those options limits gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
GIEQ: Large and mid-sized companies from developed markets outside the US, spread across countries, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. Stock picking is driven by data models rather than a plain index, aiming for a core international holding with a quantitative tilt.
GIGB: US corporate bonds from financially healthy companies with investment-grade ratings. It's meant for steady interest income above Treasuries and a modest cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise and it can slip in a recession.
GIGL: Bonds issued by US companies, mostly investment-grade, with some lower-rated ones mixed in. It's for steady income beyond what government bonds pay, and it carries more credit risk, so it can fall when the economy weakens or interest rates rise.
GII: Roughly 75 of the world's largest infrastructure companies, with utilities about 40 percent, industrials (such as airports, toll roads and rail) about the same, and energy pipelines the rest. It's a sturdy, income-oriented way to own essential services worldwide, and it can slump when interest rates rise.
GINC: Mostly bonds from companies and governments, plus a bit of cash and preferred stock. It's an income-focused holding meant to pay more than a plain bond fund, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
GIND: Companies based in India, led by financials at about 30 percent, then consumer companies, industrials and health care. It's a focused bet on one emerging economy, so it's an add-on for growth that swings more than a global stock fund.
GINN: Companies around the world positioned to gain from new ideas, spanning technology, health care, consumer businesses and financials. It's a growth-oriented holding for investors who want exposure to innovation, and since it follows themes rather than the whole market, it can swing more than a broad global fund.
GINX: Dividend-paying companies around the world, banks the biggest slice at about a third, plus an options overlay that sells very short-dated contracts to add extra income. It is built for income first and growth second, and the fast-moving options strategy sets it apart from plain global dividend funds.
GISC: Securitized debt: bonds backed by home mortgages, commercial property loans and other pooled borrowing, actively selected across the securitized market. It aims for income with risks that differ from corporate bonds, since repayment depends on thousands of underlying borrowers rather than single companies.
GJAN: Options contracts tied to an S&P 500 fund, so its exposure is to America's largest companies, with technology around 40 percent. It's built to absorb part of any drop over a roughly one-year outcome period starting in January, and the trade-off is that gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
GJUL: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb some stock market losses over a one-year period starting each July. In return it limits how much you gain, and the protection only fully works if you hold from start to end of that period.
GJUN: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund, so it follows large US companies, with technology about 40 percent. It aims to cushion part of the market's losses over a set one-year period in exchange for capping the gains, so it suits cautious investors who accept limited upside.
GK: Actively managed growth stocks picked around long-running investment themes, with technology about 44 percent, plus industrial, media and health care names. It is a growth holding run on the managers' judgment rather than an index, so its fortunes depend heavily on the themes they favor at the time.
GKAT: A selective mix of US and foreign stocks that the manager believes have more room to rise than fall, led by health care, financials and technology. It's a long-term value approach for a core global holding, but with fewer holdings it can behave differently from the broad market.
GLAM: Companies in beauty, skincare and aesthetics: cosmetics brands, skincare makers and the retailers and clinics that sell them, mostly consumer staples and health care. It is an actively managed theme bet on the beauty business, riding consumer trends that can shift with fashion and social media.
GLBL: Large companies worldwide, tilted toward whichever industries are strongest in each country compared with a global benchmark, led by technology. It is a core global holding with an industry twist: the country-by-country industry bets set it apart from a plain world index fund.
GLCR: Icelandic companies: the banks, seafood and food firms, health care names and property companies of one small island economy. It is a single-country bet on a tiny market: a handful of stocks carry the fund, and the Icelandic krona adds currency swings on top.
GLD: Physical gold bars held in vaults, with no stocks or bonds inside. People use it as a hedge, a cushion that often holds up when stocks or the dollar fall, but it pays no income and its price can swing sharply.
GLDB: A blend of bitcoin and gold, adjusted dynamically as a model weighs risk signals like volatility and momentum, with small side positions in silver and ethereum. It is pitched as an alternative to paper money, and its mix shifts as the model's signals change.
GLDI: A note that pays based on gold shares combined with a covered call strategy, where monthly call options are sold to collect income. It's built to turn gold exposure into regular income, but it gives up gains if gold surges, and as a note it carries the issuer's credit risk.
GLDM: Physical gold bars held in a vault, rather than companies or bonds. It's used as a hedge when markets or currencies wobble, though it pays no income and its price can swing widely.
GLDN: Gold industry companies, mostly miners, combined with options sold on them and on gold funds to generate income. It aims to pay regular income from the gold business rather than just ride the metal's price, though miners still swing hard.
GLDW: Leveraged exposure to gold through swap agreements and shares, aiming to amplify a gold fund's return each week while paying weekly distributions. The weekly reset and leverage make it a trading tool, and the distributions are not the same thing as profit.
GLIN: Indian companies scored for growth and quality: the stock exchange itself, telecoms, retailers, defense and cable makers, with banks and finance at over a third. It is a single-country growth bet that favors fundamental strength over simply owning India's biggest names.
GLIX: Owners of essential infrastructure around the world: power and water utilities are about half, with railways, toll roads and airports making up most of the rest. It aims for steady income and steadier growth, since these businesses keep earning through good times and bad.
GLNK: A trust that holds Chainlink, a cryptocurrency used to feed real-world data to blockchain apps. It's a bet on a single digital token with no income, and its price can swing wildly in either direction, far more than stocks or the broad market.
GLOF: Large and mid-sized companies from around the world, with technology a third and financials about a sixth. It's a core global stock holding that favors stocks with five traits: momentum, quality, value, low volatility and smaller size, so it's rule-driven and can differ from plain market funds.
GLOW: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs to spread money across US and international stocks, with at least 40% of it in ETFs focused outside the US. Much of it sits in sector funds, with technology, financials and health care the biggest pieces.
GLRY: Mid-sized US companies, spread across technology, industrials, financials and consumer businesses, selected by a manager using faith-based screens that avoid certain industries. It's a growth-leaning middle-of-the-market holding, and the screens make it different from a standard mid-cap fund.
GLTR: A vault-held basket of gold, silver, platinum and palladium bars, with gold the largest part. It's used as a hedge against inflation and market turmoil, and since it pays no income and silver and platinum are industrial metals, it can swing more than gold alone.
GMAC: A global macro fund that can bet for or against stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities anywhere in the world, based on the managers' read of economies and valuations. Nothing about its mix is fixed, so it can move very differently from a normal portfolio, for better or worse.
GMAR: Options tied to the S&P 500, which is about 40 percent technology, set up to absorb some stock market losses over a one-year period starting each March. In return it limits how much you gain, and the protection only fully works if you hold from start to end of that period.
GMAY: Options contracts tied to an S&P 500 fund, so its exposure is to America's largest companies, with technology around 40 percent. It's built to absorb part of any drop over a roughly one-year outcome period starting in May, and the trade-off is that gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
GMEY: Options on a single stock, GameStop, arranged to pay current income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one of the market's most volatile meme stocks, so sharp swings come with the territory.
GMF: Stocks from emerging Asian countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology at about 40 percent, then financials and consumer companies. It's a growth-oriented way to add emerging markets to a portfolio, and it swings more than the broad market, with extra risk from politics and currencies.
GMIE: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside the US, with financials about a third and industrials about a quarter. Managers pick on value, so it's a way to add international exposure with a bargain tilt, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
GMMA: An actively managed fund that shifts between US stocks and safer short-term government bonds as market conditions change. The idea is to join rising markets and step aside when things turn rough, so its mix can look very different from one season to the next.
GMMF: Cash and very short-term US government debt, such as Treasury bills, held to keep the value steady. It's meant as a parking spot for money you may need soon, paying interest that moves with short-term rates, rather than something for growth.
GMNY: New York municipal bonds, debt from the state, its cities, transit systems, schools and other public projects, paying interest exempt from federal tax and usually New York state tax too. It is a tax smart income holding for New Yorkers, concentrated in one state's finances by design.
GMOD: A balanced portfolio that shifts among stocks, bonds and alternative strategies worldwide, run as a fund of funds by a famously valuation driven shop. It aims for steady long term growth with smaller drops than a pure stock fund, adjusting its mix as values change.
GMOI: Cheap-looking companies outside the US, led by financials at about a third, then energy, health care and consumer businesses. It's an international value fund run by managers, so it can trail when growth stocks are leading.
GMOM: A fund of funds from Cambria that owns other ETFs across stocks and assets around the world, favoring those that have been moving up recently, a style called momentum. It is actively managed and spreads money over several Cambria funds, mostly at 11% to 13% each.
GMOV: Large US companies that GMO's managers judge underpriced, spread across banks, drugmakers, technology and energy with an eye on quality as well as cheapness. It is an active value fund from a firm known for valuation discipline, so it often shuns whatever the market currently loves.
GMUB: Municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and agencies with medium maturities, which pay interest generally free of federal income tax. It's for steady, tax friendly income with moderate swings, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
GNMA: Mortgage bonds backed by the US government's Ginnie Mae program, which pool home loans into bonds that pay interest. It's meant for steady income with very low credit risk, though its price drops when interest rates rise and homeowners refinancing can change payouts.
GNMX: Companies in genomics and precision medicine: firms reading DNA to tailor treatments to each patient, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on medicine becoming personal, swinging on research results, approvals and health care politics.
GNOM: Companies working with the human genome: gene sequencing, genetic testing, gene-based medicines and the tools labs use to read DNA. It is a focused bet on genomics reshaping medicine, so it rides on scientific breakthroughs and trial results rather than the wider health care market.
GNOV: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb a moderate share of losses over a one-year period that starts in November, with tech the biggest holding behind them. It's a cushion for cautious investors, but gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full year.
GNR: Global companies that produce raw materials, with materials miners and chemical firms about half and energy producers about a third, plus some agriculture and timber. It's a hedge against rising commodity prices and inflation, so it swings with commodity cycles and can fall hard when demand weakens.
GOAU: Mining companies focused on gold and other precious metals, all in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on the metals industry, often used as a hedge against inflation, and it swings sharply because miners' profits rise and fall faster than the price of the metals themselves.
GOCT: US large company stocks tied to the S&P 500, with technology about 40%, wrapped in options that absorb part of the market's losses over one year starting each October. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and the protection only works if you hold through the full year.
GOEX: Companies that search for gold and other precious metals but are not yet big producers, all in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on mining discoveries and gold prices, and it swings far more than gold itself or the broad market.
GOIB: Income built around a single stock, Alphabet, Google's parent, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet: the income strategy rides on one company's stock, so its swings set the fund's fate.
GOLI: Income built on gold: Treasury-style holdings plus options giving indirect exposure to the big gold fund's share price, with gains on that exposure limited by design. It aims to turn gold's moves into regular payments, so it pays more like an income fund than a pure metal bet.
GOLS: Owners of sports teams, leagues and live entertainment: the companies behind the games, races and shows people pay to watch. It is a playful but real bet on live events and media rights, an asset class usually reserved for billionaires.
GOLY: Gold exposure paired with investment-grade corporate bonds, a mix designed so the bond side pays interest while the gold side chases the metal's price. The yield enhancement means it will not move exactly with gold, and it gives up some of gold's safe-haven purity for income.
GOOP: A single-stock income strategy on Alphabet, the parent of Google: options on its shares generate payments while keeping some exposure to the stock's movement. Everything rides on one technology giant, so income is the goal and gains are limited by the options sold against the position.
GOOW: A fund that seeks about 1.2 times the weekly move in Alphabet (Google) stock, using swaps and some shares, and pays out distributions every week. It is a bet on a single company, and the Treasury bills listed are backing for the swaps.
GOOY: An income strategy built on Google's parent company stock, using options to collect regular payouts, with most of the money in Treasury holdings. It pays high income but gives up much of the stock's upside, and can still lose money if the stock falls.
GOP: Stocks that Republican members of Congress and their families have reported buying, copied from public disclosure filings. It is a mirror of politicians' own portfolios, heavy in technology and industry, and it sets itself apart by following the money of one party's lawmakers.
GOVI: US Treasury notes and bonds with maturities running from short to 30 years, weighted equally across the range. It's a government bond holding for safety and income, with a wider spread of maturities, so it falls when interest rates rise.
GOVM: US Treasury bonds maturing over the next one to ten years, all backed by the federal government. It is a middle-ground bond holding: steadier interest than cash-like funds, with prices that dip when interest rates climb.
GOVT: US Treasury bonds across short, medium and long maturities, all backed by the federal government. It's meant as a safe core bond holding and a cushion against stock drops, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
GOVZ: US Treasury strips with roughly 25 years left, which are bonds sold at a discount that pay everything at the end. It's a hedge against stock market trouble, but it swings a great deal and drops sharply when interest rates rise.
GPIQ: Large Nasdaq-listed companies, with technology about 60% and communication and consumer companies making up much of the rest, paired with an options strategy that gives up some upside in exchange for extra income. It aims for income from growth-heavy stocks, but it trails in strong rallies.
GPIX: Large US companies across the S&P 500, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care behind it, combined with an options strategy that trades some upside for extra income. The goal is income and a smoother ride, though it trails in strong rallies.
GPRF: Preferred stock and similar hybrid securities, mostly issued by financial companies. They pay fixed dividends like a bond but rank below ordinary bonds, so it's built for income, and it drops when interest rates rise.
GPT: Global large companies picked by an artificial intelligence system and held in equal weights, spread across technology, industry, health care and energy. It is a core worldwide holding where the stock selection comes from a machine model rather than human analysts, and no single giant dominates the mix.
GPTY: Mostly technology companies tied to artificial intelligence, with smaller slices in communication and consumer businesses, plus an options strategy that sells some upside for income. It's built for high monthly payouts from tech, but gains are capped in big rallies and losses in a tech slump can still be steep.
GPZ: Companies that run private equity, credit and other alternative investment firms, all in financials. It's a focused bet on that corner of finance, so it tends to rise and fall with deal activity and market sentiment more than the broad market.
GQGU: A concentrated set of US stocks chosen by active managers, and unusually it leans toward consumer staples, utilities, financials and energy rather than technology. It's labeled growth but behaves defensively, so it can lag when tech leads the market.
GQI: High-quality US stocks, led by technology, combined with sold call options on a stock index, which give up some upside in return for regular income. It aims for income and a smoother ride, though it trails in strong rallies.
GQQQ: A concentrated group of US companies the managers see as high quality and fast growing, with technology near half and communication, consumer and health care firms behind. It's built for growth, with more tech than the broad market, so it tends to rise and fall harder.
GQRE: Real estate companies around the world, picked for quality, good value and recent momentum. It's a way to add property exposure beyond the US to a portfolio, and its picks are screened by those factors, so it behaves differently from a plain index of all real estate companies.
GREK: Greek companies, with banks and other financials over half, then industrials, utilities and energy. It's a focused bet on one small country, so it swings more than a broad international fund and depends heavily on Greece's banks and economy.
GRID: Companies that build and run the electric grid, mostly industrial firms making grid equipment and smart meters, plus utilities and some technology. It's a focused bet on upgrading the power network and electrification, so it swings more than the broad market.
GRIN: Growth-oriented companies outside the US, led by industrials and technology with consumer businesses and materials behind them. It's a way to add international growth stocks, and it favors firms that generate lots of cash after expenses, so it leans toward financially healthy names.
GRNB: Bonds sold to pay for environmentally friendly projects like clean energy and efficient buildings, issued by governments and companies around the world and paid in US dollars. It's meant for steady income with an environmental angle, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
GRNI: Large US companies picked from a well known market commentator's favorite themes, with technology about a third and industrials next, plus options strategies layered on for cash payouts. It blends growth stock picking with income, so it gives up some upside to pay distributions along the way.
GRNJ: Small and mid-sized US companies, led by technology at about a third and industrials about a quarter. It's a growth holding that focuses on stocks with major long-term themes, so it swings more than large-company funds and can lag the market for stretches.
GRNY: Large US growth stocks picked by an active manager, with technology about a third, industrials nearly a quarter, and financials and consumer companies next. It's built for growth, and its hand-picked approach means it can differ from the broad market, leading or lagging.
GROZ: Large US growth companies chosen for strong earnings potential, with more than half in technology and communication, health care and consumer names behind. It's built for long-term growth through a smaller set of stocks, so it swings more than the broad market.
GRPM: The 60 mid-sized US stocks with growth that still looks reasonably priced, spread over technology, financials, health care and consumer companies. It's a middle-ground blend of growth and value, and mid-sized companies tend to swing more than large ones.
GRPZ: About 90 small US companies chosen for growth at a reasonable price: strong growers that still score well on quality and value measures. It blends three styles that usually fight each other, aiming for small-cap growth without paying any price.
GRW: An actively managed fund of US and global companies the manager thinks will benefit from change driven by technology and shifting customer habits. It holds a small group of stocks, with TransDigm, Broadcom and General Electric around 20% of it.
GSC: Small US companies spread fairly evenly across financials, technology, health care and industrials, picked by active managers. It's for growth from smaller businesses, and it usually swings more than large-company funds, with results depending on the managers' stock picks.
GSEE: Large and mid-sized companies across emerging markets, with technology the largest slice at over a third, then financials. It's a low-cost way to add developing-country growth to a portfolio, and it swings more than US stocks, with a lot riding on a few tech firms.
GSEP: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500, whose stocks are about 40% technology with financials, communication and consumer companies behind it. It's meant for people who want stock exposure with a moderate cushion against losses over a set year, but gains are capped and it resets each September.
GSEU: Large companies across developed Europe, with financials over a quarter, then industrials, health care and technology. It tilts toward stocks with traits such as value and steadier prices, so it's a way to add European exposure, and moves in the euro against the dollar can add to the swings.
GSEW: The 100 largest US companies with each given the same weight instead of by size, led by technology, industrials, financials and health care. It spreads the risk away from the biggest firms, so it trails when mega-cap tech stocks lead.
GSG: A basket of raw materials such as oil, natural gas, metals and farm products, held through futures contracts rather than the physical goods, with the rest sitting in safe short-term holdings. It's a hedge against rising prices, but it is heavily weighted to energy, so it can swing sharply.
GSGO: Large US growth companies, with technology half of the fund and communication and industrial companies next. It's built for growth, with far more tech than the broad market, so it tends to rise and fall harder, and the manager picks stocks actively.
GSIB: The world's biggest banks, the ones regulators call systemically important because the whole financial system depends on them, spread across many countries. It is a focused bet on global banking giants, so it rises and falls with bank profits and financial stability worries.
GSID: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, with financials the biggest slice at about a quarter, then industrials, technology and health care. It's a core, broad way to own international stocks, and foreign currency moves affect its returns.
GSIE: Developed-market stocks outside the US, with financials the biggest group at nearly 30% followed by industrials, technology and health care. It's a way to add international diversification, and it tilts toward factors like value and low volatility, so it can behave differently from a plain international fund.
GSJY: Japanese companies across every major industry, weighted by four investing factors, value, momentum, quality and low volatility, rather than by size alone. Banks, carmakers, electronics and industrial giants all feature, giving broad Japan exposure with a rules-based twist on the usual index.
GSKH: Shares of one company, GSK, the British drugmaker, held through its US-listed depositary receipts rather than bought directly in London. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the stock itself as the main driver.
GSLC: Large US companies weighted by factors like value, momentum, quality and low volatility rather than just size, with technology at about 40%. It's a core US stock holding that aims to edge out the broad market, though it still moves closely with it.
GSOL: Solana, a cryptocurrency, held directly, with the coins also put to work in staking to earn extra Solana. It's a high-risk bet on one digital asset, and its price can swing dramatically in a single day.
GSPY: Mostly the same large US companies as the S&P 500, with technology about 40%, but a manager adjusts the mix instead of just copying the index. It's a core stock holding that tries to beat the market, so it may still lag.
GSSC: Small US companies, with health care the biggest slice at about a quarter, then financials, technology and industrials. It's meant as a way to add smaller, faster-growing businesses to a portfolio, and it leans on a rules-based tilt toward certain traits, so it swings more than large-company funds.
GSUI: A trust holding Sui, the token of a newer blockchain network built for fast, cheap transactions, that also stakes its holdings to earn extra tokens. It offers stock market access to a young cryptocurrency whose price is highly speculative and swings sharply.
GSUS: A low-cost slice of large and mid-sized US companies, with technology at about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care behind it. It works as a core holding for the broad US market, and its heavy tech weighting means it leans on that one sector.
GSWO: Stocks from around the world, weighted by four ActiveBeta factors, value, momentum, quality and low volatility, instead of by company size alone. It is a core-style global holding built to tilt toward the traits Goldman believes pay off, so it will not move exactly with the world market.
GTEK: Technology companies in the US and abroad that managers expect to lead future growth, with tech about 78% and the rest in industrials, consumer and communication companies. It's a growth bet on the sector that swings more than the broad market.
GTIP: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, whose principal rises when consumer prices rise. It's meant as a hedge against inflation within the bond part of a portfolio, though its price still drops when real interest rates rise.
GTND: Two big stock funds, one growth heavy and one broad market, with the mix between them steered by a trend following signal that can shift toward defense when prices weaken. It plays goalie for a stock portfolio: staying invested in uptrends, but ready to give up gains to limit losses.
GTO: A flexible mix of bonds of all lengths and credit qualities, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed debt. It's meant for income plus some price growth in the bond part of a portfolio, and managers can shift between safer and riskier bonds as conditions change.
GTOC: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, chosen by an active manager. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion against stock drops, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
GTOH: Short-term high yield bonds: below-investment-grade corporate debt that comes due soon, chosen by Invesco's managers. Short maturities soften the price swings that long junk bonds suffer, but the borrowers are still the riskier kind, so credit worries can move it more than safer short bond funds.
GTOP: Technology companies make up roughly 70% of this actively managed fund, with communication and consumer companies filling most of the rest. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, and because managers pick the stocks, it can differ a lot from a standard tech index.
GTOQ: A basket of high-yield corporate bonds, meaning below-investment-grade debt from companies with weaker credit. Managers pick using a rules-based approach, and it's meant for higher income than safer bonds, though prices can fall sharply in a downturn when more issuers struggle to pay.
GTOS: Short-term bonds from a mix of issuers, government debt alongside corporate bonds, chosen for total return rather than for safety alone. Keeping durations short means the price moves less when interest rates change, but reaching into corporate credit adds risk a Treasury-only fund would not have.
GTPE: Public stocks chosen to mimic the behavior of private equity investments, matching their regions and industries using an index built for that purpose. It offers private-equity-like returns in a fund that trades daily, though it is an approximation: there are no actual buyout funds or private companies inside.
GTR: An actively managed fund that uses options on global stocks to aim for returns within a target range, limiting both gains and losses. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills that support the options, so it is a hedged strategy.
GUNR: Companies that produce natural resources worldwide, about half materials such as miners and fertilizer makers, a third energy, plus agriculture and utilities. It's a hedge against inflation that spreads across several commodity industries, and it swings with commodity prices.
GURU: US stocks picked from the biggest positions reported by well-known hedge funds in their public filings. It tilts to health care and tech, and holds many smaller companies, with no single name above about 3%.
GUSA: The thousand largest US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US stock market, and because it's weighted by company size, the biggest companies matter most.
GUSE: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology around 40% and financials, communication and health care filling out the next tier. It's a core stock holding where managers tilt toward stocks they favor, so results can differ from the broad market in either direction.
GVAL: Stocks of cheap companies around the world, excluding the US, with financials making up nearly a third and materials, energy and utilities next. It's a value play for international diversification, and it can trail when growth stocks lead.
GVI: A mix of US Treasury and government-linked bonds along with investment-grade corporate bonds, with maturities mostly in the middle range of one to ten years. It's a steady core bond holding for income and stability, and its price dips a bit when interest rates rise.
GVIP: Large US stocks that hedge funds hold as their biggest positions, with technology at about a third plus communication, financials and industrials. It's a growth-leaning fund that copies professional crowds, so it swings more than the broad market when those favorites fall.
GVLE: Large US companies the managers judge cheap relative to their worth, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer firms. It is actively run value hunting in big stocks, so it will not mirror the index and can lag when pricey growth stocks lead.
GVLU: Mid-sized to large US companies that look cheap compared with their finances, spread across consumer, industrial, financial and technology businesses. It's a value-focused stock fund, and the managers pick holdings actively, so it can lag when expensive growth stocks lead the market.
GVUS: US large companies priced cheaply compared with their size, with technology, financials, health care and consumer companies the largest groups. It's a core value holding in one low-cost fund, and it usually holds up better than growth stocks in some markets but trails when growth stocks lead.
GWX: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, technology, materials and consumer businesses. It adds smaller, less-followed foreign companies to a portfolio for growth, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds and is affected by currency moves.
GXC: Chinese companies, led by consumer discretionary and financials at about a fifth each, with communication and technology following. It's a focused bet on one country, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to Chinese government policy.
GXDW: A fund of thematic funds: it holds other Global X ETFs picked by a momentum system that rotates toward the themes performing best. Technology, industrials and health care themes lead right now, but the mix changes as trends shift, adding a layer of active rotation.
GXIG: Investment-grade bonds from US companies, actively managed, which pay more interest than government bonds with only modest added risk. It's meant for steady income and as a more stable partner to stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise or companies' credit weakens.
GXLC: The 500 largest US companies in one fund, covering every major industry, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent. It works as a core holding that mirrors the broad US market, similar in spirit to S&P 500 funds.
GXPC: Nearly all communication services companies in the US, such as media, entertainment, telecom and online platforms. It's a focused bet on one sector, and its twist is a cap on the biggest companies so a few giants don't dominate, but it still swings more than the broad market.
GXPD: The full consumer discretionary sector in one fund: retailers, carmakers, restaurants, travel and media companies that depend on households having money to spare. It takes the sector at full market weight, giants and all, so it rides consumer confidence and spending cycles directly.
GXPE: US energy companies weighted by their full market value, with no size adjustments: oil and gas producers, pipelines and refiners at their natural weights. It is a pure sector bet, which means the giant integrated oil companies dominate and the fund swings with energy prices.
GXPS: Large US consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of everyday goods, from an MSCI index that caps each stock's weight. It is concentrated, with Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola about half of it.
GXPT: Only US technology companies, including software, chips and hardware, drawn from a broad US stock index. It's a focused bet on tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and it is built to hold fewer very large positions than a typical tech fund.
GXRP: A single cryptocurrency, XRP, held directly rather than through futures, giving brokerage-account exposure to the coin's price. Grayscale's trust format sets it apart from newer rivals, and like all single-coin funds it can swing violently with the crypto market's mood.
GXUS: Large and mid-sized companies from every developed and emerging country except the US, led by financials and technology. It's built to be the international half of a portfolio, and it adds a wide mix of countries at once, so it moves with global markets outside America.
GYLD: One hundred fifty of the highest yielding investments worldwide, gathered across property companies, energy partnerships, dividend stocks and bonds. Chasing the world's biggest yields pays high income, but high yield usually signals high risk somewhere, so holdings can be shaky.
HACK: Companies that make cybersecurity software and services, nearly all from technology with a small industrial slice. It's a focused bet on one theme as digital threats grow, and it swings more than the broad market because it holds so few kinds of business.
HAIL: Companies building smarter ways to move: electric vehicles, self-driving sensors, chips for cars, batteries and transport software. Technology and consumer vehicle makers split most of the fund, making it a growth bet on the future of transportation rather than on today's car industry.
HAKY: Holds the cybersecurity stocks of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF, such as CrowdStrike, Okta, Fortinet and Cloudflare, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. The options give up some of the upside when those stocks surge, and the fund is almost all technology.
HALX: Companies with heavy physical assets and slow-changing businesses, led by utilities and energy at about a fifth each, plus industrials and consumer staples. It is a defensive value-leaning holding: asset-heavy firms tend to be steadier, but they can lag when growth stocks are in favor.
HAP: Global companies that produce natural resources: materials such as metals and chemicals, energy, farming, industrial and utility firms. It's a way to add inflation-sensitive hard-asset exposure, and it tends to swing with commodity prices and the global economy.
HAPI: Around 150 large US companies, led by technology at about a third, then communication and financials. It's a core stock holding with a twist: companies are chosen for strong workplace culture and treatment of employees, so it differs from a plain market-weighted fund.
HAPS: About 200 small US companies chosen for strong workplace culture and employee focus, spread across health care, financials, technology and industrials. It's a small-company growth play with a people-based twist, so it tends to swing more than large company funds, especially in shaky markets.
HARD: Commodity futures covering energy, metals and farm goods, positioned by price trends so it can lean into rising markets and step back from falling ones. It packages that exposure without a K-1 tax form, which makes it simpler to hold than older commodity funds.
HAUG: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange for that protection. The August start matters: anyone buying later gets the remaining terms, not a fresh year of full protection.
HAUS: An actively managed fund of real estate investment trusts (REITs) whose income comes from housing-related property, including senior housing and medical properties. Its biggest holdings are Welltower, Ventas and Public Storage, and REITs pay out much of their income.
HAUZ: Real estate companies outside the US, such as property owners and developers, spread across many countries. It's meant to add global property to a portfolio for income and diversification, and since these stocks react to interest rates and currencies, it can drop when borrowing costs rise.
HAWG: Large US stocks, heavy in technology at about half the fund, paired with a hedging system that can pull back when its trend signals turn negative. It aims to stay invested for growth in good times and step aside in bad ones, though the hedge can also mute recoveries.
HAWX: Large and mid-sized companies outside the US, with financials, technology and industrials leading. It's a way to own international stocks, and it uses currency hedges so swings in the US dollar matter less, though it can still fall with foreign markets.
HBDC: Bonds issued by business development companies, the publicly traded lenders that finance mid-sized private businesses, all in one fund. It pays corporate-bond-like income with a twist: the borrowers are themselves lenders, so their health rises and falls with the private credit market.
HBIL: US Treasury bills, the shortest government IOUs, maturing in a few weeks or months. It works like a parking spot for cash that pays a little interest, with almost no price movement and the full backing of the US government.
HBIT: Bitcoin exposure with an active hedge: managers can pull back into cash-like safety when their risk signals warn of trouble. That sets it apart from plain bitcoin funds, trading some upside in strong runs for smaller falls in bad ones.
HBMX: A concentrated stack of memory chip companies, the makers of DRAM and flash storage, with derivatives adding to the exposure. Memory prices move in violent cycles, so this is an amplified bet on one of the most boom-and-bust corners of the technology industry.
HBR: A single cryptocurrency, HBAR, the token of the Hedera network, held directly as the trust's only digital asset. It gives brokerage-account exposure to a coin built for fast, cheap transactions, and like all single-coin funds it can swing violently with crypto sentiment.
HBRD: Hybrid corporate debt: subordinated bonds that sit between regular bonds and preferred stock in a company's pecking order, issued in US dollars. Hybrids pay more than senior bonds for the extra risk, a middle path between bond safety and stock-like returns.
HBTA: Large US companies, with technology about 40% and communication, consumer and industrial companies filling out the rest, combined with an options strategy run by active managers. It aims for stock growth with a bit of cushioning from the options, though that can limit gains in strong rallies.
HBTC: Exposure to bitcoin with a built-in hedge, meaning part of the fund is positioned to soften the drop when bitcoin falls sharply. Bitcoin is famously volatile, so the trade-off here is giving up some of the upside in rallies in exchange for a less bruising ride.
HCMT: An actively managed fund aimed at tracking the US stock market, mostly using futures and other derivatives rather than owning stocks outright. It's meant to deliver market-like returns with a boost, and because it can shift into cash and uses leverage, it can swing more than the market.
HCOW: Shares of a cash-flow-focused dividend fund, plus call options sold against that position to add a second layer of income. The double income design means high payouts, while the covered calls cap much of the growth when stocks rally.
HCRB: Mostly investment-grade US bonds, such as Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, picked by an active manager. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
HDEF: Stocks from developed countries outside the US that pay above average dividends, with financials about 28 percent, then consumer staples, health care and energy. It's meant for income and adding international stocks, and it has far less tech than the broad market.
HDG: Financial instruments engineered to copy the overall returns of the hedge fund industry, using liquid positions rather than actual hedge funds. It aims to deliver that alternative return pattern, steadier and less tied to stocks, inside an ordinary fund, though replication is approximate and cash collateral does much of the work.
HDMV: Developed-market companies outside the US chosen for low expected volatility, heavy in banks, utilities and property firms in places like Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia. It aims for a calmer international ride, often lagging when markets surge.
HDUS: Large US companies across every major industry, weighted by a rules-based system that balances growth, value and risk signals rather than pure company size. Technology is about a third, and the disciplined reweighting sets it apart from plain index funds that simply own the biggest firms.
HDV: Large US companies with high dividends that pass quality screens, concentrated in consumer staples, energy, health care and utilities. It's built for income and steadier stocks, so it usually holds up better in sell-offs but has little technology and can trail in tech-led rallies.
HEAL: Companies building health technology: digital health platforms, medical data, connected devices and software that modernize how care is delivered and paid for. It is a focused growth bet on the digital side of health care rather than drugmakers, so it swings with sentiment toward young tech companies.
HECA: A mix of stocks, bonds, cash and other assets such as commodities and currencies, with the manager shifting between them as conditions change. It aims to be an all-in-one diversified holding, but its results depend heavily on the manager's timing calls.
HECO: Companies tied to the digital asset economy, such as bitcoin miners and crypto-related businesses, with currency hedging aimed at reducing the effect of foreign exchange moves. It is concentrated: Riot Platforms, Keel Infrastructure and CleanSpark are about 31% of it, and it holds stocks, not crypto itself.
HEDG: Large US companies in the S&P 500, led by technology at about 40%, paired with call options that earn extra income and soften losses. It's designed for a smoother ride, so it should fall less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
HEDJ: European companies, led by industrials, financials and consumer staples, with currency hedging so euro swings against the dollar matter less. It's meant for owning Europe without exchange-rate risk, and it tends to do better when the euro falls.
HEEM: Large companies in developing economies, with technology the biggest piece at over forty percent, followed by financials. It adds emerging markets to a portfolio while hedging the currency, so swings in those countries' money against the dollar matter less.
HEFA: Large companies in developed markets outside North America, such as Europe, Japan and Australia, led by financials and industrials, with the currency risk hedged. It's a way to own international stocks without the ups and downs of foreign currencies against the dollar, which helps when the dollar rises.
HEFT: An actively managed fund that holds a mix of other funds and takes both bets that rise and bets that fall, with long exposure up to about 150% and short exposure up to about 50%. It is built around the manager's view of a cycle called the Fourth Turning.
HEGD: Large US stocks, led by technology, paired with options meant to cut losses when the market falls. It's built as a cushion for stock investors, and the protection costs something, so it usually trails in strong rallies.
HELO: Large US stocks, with technology about 40% and financials, consumer and communication companies making up much of the rest, paired with an options overlay that cushions part of the market's drops. It's a core stock holding with a smoother ride, though the hedge means it gives up some gains in strong rallies.
HELX: Companies advancing genomics: DNA testing firms, gene therapy developers and the labs and toolmakers behind them. It is a bet that reading and editing genes transforms medicine, concentrated in smaller biotech names whose fortunes turn on research results.
HEMI: US stocks chosen by Wellington researchers for improving quality and momentum, paired with option selling that harvests extra premium income. The premiums add a steady payout on top of dividends, in exchange for giving up part of the stocks' biggest gains.
HEQQ: Big Nasdaq-listed companies, heavy in technology at about 60 percent, combined with a laddered options overlay that hedges part of the market risk. It aims to keep much of the growth of tech-led stocks while softening falls, trading away some upside for a smoother ride than the unhedged index.
HEQT: US large companies, about 40% technology, paired with a collar of options that limits losses and also limits gains. It aims for a smoother ride than the stock market, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
HERD: Five Pacer funds under one roof, each hunting companies that generate lots of free cash flow for their size, across US and international markets. The cash cows idea favors profitable, cash-rich firms over fast growers, giving this fund-of-funds a value tilt and an income streak.
HERO: Companies around the world that make or benefit from video games and esports, such as game publishers, developers and hardware makers. Holdings are spread across the US, Japan, China and Korea, with no single name above about 7% of the fund.
HEWJ: Large Japanese companies, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses, with the yen's moves canceled out. It's a way to own Japan without the currency effect, so a falling yen doesn't drag it down, but a rising yen doesn't help.
HEZU: Large Eurozone companies, led by financials, industrials and technology, paired with a hedge against the euro's moves versus the dollar. It's a way to own European stocks without currency swings, so you don't gain when the euro rises against the dollar.
HF: An absolute return fund that mixes stock funds with positions betting against the market, aiming to make money in up and down markets alike. Its mix of long and short holdings means it can look nothing like a normal stock fund, and it will likely trail badly in strong bull markets.
HFEQ: A fund of funds that mostly holds other ETFs, including Vanguard value, mid-cap and momentum funds, and takes both long and short positions in stocks. It is actively managed, so the mix of what it owns changes over time.
HFGM: A mix of funds bought and sold short, aiming to copy the returns of global macro hedge funds, with stocks and other holdings across many sectors. It targets about twice the risk of that group, so it's a swingy diversifier, not a steady core holding.
HFGO: Large US companies the manager expects to grow for years, with technology nearly 60 percent and communication companies next. It's built for growth, with far more tech than the broad market, so it tends to rise and fall harder.
HFIX: High yield corporate bonds, the below-investment-grade kind that pay extra interest to make up for weaker borrowers, chosen for total return rather than yield alone. It aims to earn more than a plain Treasury fund, but these bonds fall when investors worry about defaults.
HFMF: Futures contracts across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, traded by trend and other systematic strategies to imitate the returns of hedge fund managed futures programs. It is a diversifier designed to zig when stocks zag, especially in long market slides, though it can drift in flat markets.
HFND: It builds long and short positions across dozens of stock and bond funds and futures, trying to copy the returns of hedge fund multi-strategy portfolios. Because it goes both long and short, it aims to depend less on whether markets rise or fall.
HFSI: An income fund that roams across bond types, government and mortgage bonds alongside corporate and riskier debt, shifting the mix as the managers see value. It aims to pay more than a plain government bond fund, and the price of that extra yield is more movement when credit markets wobble.
HFSP: Large US stocks paired with cash, managed by trading models that shift between being invested and sitting in cash. The equity-hedged approach aims to blunt big market drops by pulling back, though that also means it can lag when stocks rally while the models are cautious.
HFXI: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and technology under a fifth. It's a way to add international stocks, and about half of the currency swings against the dollar are hedged, so exchange rates matter less to results.
HGER: Futures on physical commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, chosen by a rules-based formula meant to work in different economic conditions. It's a diversifier that can help when inflation rises, but commodity prices are volatile and it holds no stocks or companies.
HGRO: US stocks picked for quality and growth, with technology nearly half and health care next. It's a growth-oriented core holding, but with its tech concentration and hand-picked approach, it can swing more than the broad market.
HH: High yield corporate bonds: dollar-denominated debt from companies with weaker credit, paying extra interest to compensate for the risk. It is an income fund whose fortunes follow the health of riskier borrowers, so it tends to fall when recession fears rise and defaults are in the news.
HIAI: A concentrated portfolio of US stocks chosen by artificial intelligence models hunting for high-conviction ideas across technology, retail, health care and more. The AI-driven picks mean the lineup can look unusual and change as the models change their minds.
HIDE: A mix of other ETFs holding intermediate-term Treasury bonds, real estate and commodities, shifted with market trends. It's built as a hedge for periods of high inflation or falling prices, so it can look quite different from a plain stock fund.
HIDV: US large companies chosen for their dividend payouts, with technology over a third and financials, consumer and communication companies after that. It's built for income plus growth, and actively picks stocks that look attractive, so it can differ from typical dividend funds, which often lean on banks and utilities.
HIGH: Short dated US Treasury securities form the base, and an options overlay on top aims to add extra income beyond what the bonds alone pay. The result targets steady payouts with limited interest rate risk, though the options add complexity and can trim returns in some markets.
HIMU: Bonds issued by US states, cities and local agencies, focused on lower-rated, higher-paying ones, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for income that is generally free from federal income tax, but the lower credit quality means it can drop more in a downturn than safer muni funds.
HINC: High yield corporate bonds chosen by Hartford's managers: below-investment-grade debt from companies that pay extra interest because their finances are weaker. It is an income fund that accepts credit risk for yield, so it falls when investors worry about the economy and defaults.
HIPS: Up to 40 US-listed securities built to pass their earnings straight to shareholders: energy partnerships, lending firms, property owners and income funds. That pass-through structure produces unusually high income, and it sets the fund apart, though payouts can shrink when energy and credit markets struggle.
HIS: A focused portfolio of large US companies, technology at over two-fifths, chosen by its managers rather than copied from an index. It works as an active core stock holding, so its results depend on a select set of picks and can differ noticeably from the broad market.
HISF: A blend of First Trust bond funds chosen to maximize income, mixing corporate debt, loans and other higher-yielding corners of the bond market. It is a fund of funds built purely for payout, so credit quality runs lower and price swings run larger than in core bond funds.
HIYY: An options income strategy on a single stock, Hims and Hers Health, the telehealth company known for hair, skin and weight-loss treatments. It converts a young, volatile stock's swings into distributions, with gains capped and sharp drops largely unprotected.
HJLY: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the defensive extreme of its series: principal protection for the period, paid for with a tight cap.
HJUN: The S&P 500 with a full shield: over the year starting in June, it is designed to protect against the whole of a market fall while capping gains. It offers the strongest cushion in this fund family, in exchange for giving up big rallies.
HLAL: Large and mid-sized US companies that pass Islamic law screens, so it excludes banks, alcohol and gambling, which leaves technology at nearly 60%. It's a core stock holding for people who follow those principles, and it behaves more like a tech fund than the broad market.
HLTH: An actively managed fund of health care companies that use artificial intelligence or data in areas like genetics, diagnostics and medical devices. It is concentrated, with 10x Genomics, Twist Bioscience and Illumina together making up about 20% of the fund.
HMAY: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the most defensive end of the buffer range: safety is total for the period, but the cap is tight.
HMOP: Municipal bonds from US states and cities, with interest that's generally exempt from federal income tax, chosen by a manager for attractive yields. It's for tax-free income, and it can hold some lower-rated bonds, which adds more risk than a high quality municipal fund.
HMYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to Hims and Hers, the telehealth company, rather than owning the stock itself. It aims for frequent distributions, but the leveraged options structure swings sharply, so it fits short holding periods and speculation more than steady income investing.
HNDL: A mix of stock, bond and other ETFs, about two fifths in stocks and a third in bonds, with real estate and energy along for the ride. It's built to pay a high monthly income from a balanced portfolio, and it pays out part of its own value, so share price can erode over time.
HODL: Actual bitcoin held by a trust, with nothing else mixed in. It's a bet on a single digital currency, so the price can swing sharply in either direction and it behaves very differently from stocks and bonds.
HOID: Companies building humanoid robots and the parts that make them work, motors, sensors, chips and software for machines shaped like people. Humanoid robots are still more promise than product, so this is a speculative bet on a young industry that swings with demos, deals and headlines.
HOLA: International stocks, led by financials and industrials, paired with options that offset part of the market's ups and downs. It's meant to give stock exposure with a smoother ride, but it will likely trail in strong rallies.
HOLD: Holds a fund that tracks the S&P 500 and layers a trend-following futures strategy on top, so each dollar gets both stock market exposure and a bet on price trends in other markets. About 40% is in an S&P 500 fund, with the rest in cash and futures.
HOMZ: One hundred companies across the US housing chain: homebuilders, housing real estate trusts, building suppliers and home improvement retailers. It is a focused bet on American housing, so it rises and falls with homebuilding, mortgage rates and the property market rather than the stock market as a whole.
HOOW: A bet on Robinhood stock that aims to deliver about 1.2 times its weekly move and pays distributions every week. It resets weekly, so it is for short holding periods, and it can lose value quickly if the stock drops.
HOOY: A fund built around the stock of Robinhood, using options on it to produce high monthly income, with cash and short-term Treasuries as backing. It gives up much of the stock's upside and still suffers when the stock falls, so it's for income seekers who accept big risk.
HOYY: An options strategy built on a leveraged fund tied to Robinhood stock, designed to turn big price swings into regular income. It is a high-risk, short-term style trade: the leveraged base resets often and the options cap gains, so losses can pile up fast.
HQDG: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends and have raised them over time. It is a concentrated group of about 30 or so stocks, with Microsoft, KLA, Texas Instruments and Casey's around 5% each.
HQGO: Large US growth companies screened for quality: strong, dependable businesses led by technology at a bit under half the fund. It aims for growth with a steadier foundation than go-go growth funds, holding profitable leaders rather than speculative names.
HRSK: Large US stock exposure built from index futures, funds and shares, with an active hedging program meant to cut losses in market falls. Toews built its name on avoiding deep drawdowns, so the fund accepts some cost and lag in rallies as insurance.
HRTS: Health care companies working on heart disease and weight related treatments, especially the GLP-1 drug wave and cardiovascular therapies. It is a focused bet on two huge treatment markets, so trial results and drug approvals can move it sharply.
HSBH: Shares of one company, HSBC, the British banking giant with a big Asian business, held through its US-listed depositary receipts. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the bank's own fortunes as the main driver.
HSCZ: Smaller companies in developed countries outside the US and Canada, led by industrials, financials and consumer firms. It uses currency hedges to cancel out swings in foreign currencies against the dollar, so returns follow the stocks more than exchange rates.
HSEP: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the defensive extreme of its series: the autumn start fixes the terms, and the cap is tight.
HSMV: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen for steadier share prices, leaning toward property, banking and utility stocks that usually move less. It aims to keep the growth potential of smaller companies while smoothing the ride, accepting that it will trail in strong rallies.
HTAB: US dollar bonds of good credit quality, aimed at income that is lighter on taxes, with a bit of cash. It's meant as a core bond holding for investors in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
HTAX: Municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments, with interest generally free from federal income tax. It focuses on higher-yielding, riskier issuers, including a notable share tied to Puerto Rico.
HTEC: Stocks of companies that use technology in healthcare, such as genetic testing, diagnostics and lab tools, following the ROBO Global healthcare technology index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 3% of the fund.
HTRB: A broad mix of bonds from the US government, companies and mortgage lenders, with a small slice allowed in lower-rated, higher-yield debt. It aims for income plus some price gains as a core bond holding, but its price drops when interest rates rise.
HTUS: Mostly US stocks, with technology around 40% and the rest spread across financials, communication and health care, plus a meaningful cash cushion of about a fifth. The manager shifts how much is invested based on market signals, aiming to soften drops, so it can lag when stocks rally steadily.
HULL: Shipping lines, couriers and freight companies that move goods around the world, mostly industrial firms with a large slice of energy in the tanker trade. It is a bet on global trade and freight rates, so it does best when the world economy is moving a lot of cargo.
HUMM: Companies building the power systems for AI data centers: the equipment that delivers high-voltage direct current to racks of AI chips, split between technology and industrial firms. It is a narrow bet on the plumbing behind the AI boom.
HUMN: Companies building humanoid robots and their parts: robot makers in China, Japan and Korea, the precision gears and joints inside them, and carmakers developing their own machines. It is an early-stage, concentrated bet that human-shaped robots become a real industry, so expect sharp swings.
HUSV: US stocks chosen for low expected future volatility, the calmer names across technology, banks, utilities and property companies, managed to keep swings down. It is a defensive stock holding that usually falls less in sell-offs and trails when markets race ahead.
HVAC: Companies that heat, cool and build: air conditioning giants, cooling specialists for data centers, contractors and industrial suppliers. It rides construction spending and the enormous cooling needs of AI data centers, making climate control a growth theme.
HWGV: Large companies from around the world bought when their prices look low compared with their underlying worth, in Hotchkis and Wiley's value style. Holdings span software, insurance, health care and industrial names, and the patient approach can lag for stretches before bargains pay off.
HWIV: An actively managed value fund of companies outside the US, bought when they seem cheap compared with what the managers think they are worth. It is spread over many countries and sectors, and its largest holdings include Akzo Nobel, SAP and Shell.
HWMV: Mid-sized US companies that look cheap compared to their worth, spread across technology, energy, financials and industrials. It's a value-focused way to add medium-sized companies, and it can lag when expensive growth stocks lead the market.
HWO: A flexible mix of mostly stocks of any size, with technology about 30 percent and energy, materials and industrials each around a tenth, plus some lower-rated bonds. The manager hunts for companies the market has overlooked, so it's a value-minded holding that can look very different from the broad market.
HWSM: Small and mid-sized companies the manager judges undervalued, spread across financials, consumer, technology and industrial stocks. It is an actively managed value holding: the stock picking aims to find bargains in the market's middle tier, which tends to swing more than large companies.
HXA: An arbitrage fund that trades around corporate events like mergers, restructurings and corporate spinoffs, using stocks, closed end funds, warrants and derivatives where the deals are. Most of the money waits in money market instruments between opportunities, so it aims for steady, deal driven gains rather than market returns.
HXC: A broad basket of commodities, from energy and metals to farm goods, held through futures and related contracts rather than physical goods. It is built as a diversifier and inflation hedge whose returns come from commodity price moves, and its managers use hedging techniques to try to smooth the ride.
HXE: A mix of US stock funds, from quality and large company funds to small caps, wrapped in an adaptive hedging program. The hedge can pull a large share into cash when risk looks high, so its stock exposure changes a lot over time.
HXF: An actively managed managed futures fund that takes long and short positions across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, trying to follow big market trends in either direction. It does not hold a fixed basket of stocks, and its results can differ a lot from stock markets.
HYBB: Corporate bonds rated BB, the highest tier of below-investment-grade debt. It aims for more income than safer bonds with less risk than the lowest-rated ones, though it can lose value if the economy weakens or interest rates rise.
HYBI: Bonds and bond funds, paired with an options strategy that sells insurance-like contracts on the S&P 500 to earn extra monthly income. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, but it can lose money in sharp stock market drops because of those options.
HYBL: High-yield debt from US companies, including junk bonds, floating-rate bank loans and the riskier slices of pooled corporate loans. It's for investors chasing higher income, and the tradeoff is credit risk, so it can fall in a weak economy.
HYBX: Actively managed high yield bonds chosen by TCW managers across lower-rated corporate debt. It is an income holding built on manager research into which junk borrowers look sound, so it aims to dodge the weakest credits that a plain high yield index holds by default.
HYD: Municipal bonds from state and local governments that carry lower credit ratings in exchange for higher interest, with income that is generally free of federal tax. It's for investors who want tax-friendly income and accept more risk, and it can fall when the economy weakens.
HYDB: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, picked by a rules-based model that aims to beat a plain high-yield index. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but it can fall in recessions when risky companies struggle to repay.
HYDR: Companies building the hydrogen economy: fuel cell makers, hydrogen producers and the industrial firms supplying them, mostly small and mid-sized names worldwide. Two holdings alone are nearly a third of the fund, so it is a concentrated bet on a young technology that still loses money widely.
HYDW: US dollar junk bonds, meaning corporate bonds from lower-rated companies, chosen to be less sensitive to swings in the broader high yield market. It holds many bonds, with the largest, EchoStar, around 1% of the fund.
HYEM: High-yield bonds issued by companies in emerging markets, denominated in US dollars. It aims for high income, but it's riskier than most bond funds because of the credit risk and exposure to developing economies.
HYFI: Mostly corporate bonds rated below investment grade, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the companies are riskier. It's built for extra income, and it tends to fall with stocks in downturns instead of cushioning them, since riskier borrowers may struggle to pay.
HYG: Bonds from US companies with weaker credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest to make up for the added risk. It's built for income, but it tends to fall alongside stocks in sell-offs, so it offers less of a cushion than safer bonds.
HYGH: A fund of riskier, higher-interest corporate bonds that uses futures to cancel out the effect of changing interest rates. It's built for income from junk bonds without the rate swings, though it can still drop when companies struggle.
HYGM: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier kind that pay more interest, held through a big bond fund plus an options overlay that sells call options expiring weekly. It targets the income level in its name, and the trade-off is bond risk: these borrowers are the ones most likely to struggle in a downturn.
HYGV: US-dollar corporate bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, screened for stronger finances and better value. It's meant for higher interest income than safer bonds, but these bonds can lose value in downturns when borrowers struggle, so it tends to act more like stocks than a cushion.
HYGW: A high yield bond fund paired with covered call options sold on it, so income comes from both junk bond interest and option premiums. The calls cap gains when bond prices jump, making this an income-first holding where the payout matters more than price growth.
HYHG: High-yield junk bonds paired with short positions on Treasuries, which offset the damage when interest rates rise. It's for investors wanting junk bond income with less rate risk, but it can still fall when the economy weakens and companies default.
HYIN: Listed vehicles that hold private credit and other alternative income assets: business development companies and closed end funds that lend to private businesses. It offers a doorway into private lending income through the stock market, with share price discounts and credit risk riding along.
HYLB: Bonds from US companies with weaker credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest to make up for the risk. It's built for income, but it tends to fall alongside stocks in downturns, since these companies struggle most when the economy weakens.
HYLS: Bonds from companies with credit ratings below investment grade, managed actively to adjust as markets change. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, and it can also hold loans and shift defensively, but it can fall in recessions when risky companies struggle.
HYMB: Municipal bonds from state and local governments that have lower credit ratings in return for higher interest, with income that is generally free of federal tax. It's for tax-friendly income and accepts more risk, so it can slide when credit worries grow or interest rates rise.
HYP: Fast-growing companies picked actively across technology, energy and health care, hunting for businesses expanding at hypergrowth speed. These are mostly smaller, less proven names, so the fund aims high and swings hard, a speculation rather than a core holding.
HYPG: The Hyperliquid cryptocurrency (HYPE), held in a way that earns staking rewards, which is like interest for helping run the network. It's a speculative bet on one coin, so its price can swing sharply, and it behaves very differently from stocks and bonds.
HYS: Short-term US company bonds rated below investment grade, with maturities of five years or less. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, and the shorter maturities mean it swings less than other junk bond funds, though it can still fall in recessions.
