HYSA: A fund built from three high yield bond funds sliced by credit rating, the stronger BB names, then B, then a small piece of risky CCC debt. Blending the slices gives broad junk bond income in one holding, with the mix actively adjusted as credit conditions change.
HYSD: High yield corporate bonds that come due soon, lending to below-investment-grade companies but only at the short end of the maturity range. Short maturities make its price steadier than a typical junk bond fund when rates move, though the borrowers' default risk remains.
HYTI: Treasury securities paired with an options strategy on high yield corporate bonds, selling call options to manufacture a target income stream. Instead of owning junk bonds directly, it harvests option premiums, so the payout depends on bond market volatility as much as on interest.
HYTR: A mix of high-yield junk bonds and Treasuries that shifts between them based on market trends, and right now it is mostly sitting in cash and short-term holdings. It's meant as a flexible income fund that tries to step back from junk bonds when they weaken.
HYUP: The higher beta slice of the high yield bond market: junk bonds that historically swing more than the junk market itself when credit conditions change. It pays junk level income with extra drama, amplifying both the good stretches and the sell-offs of ordinary high yield funds.
HYXF: Lower-rated US dollar corporate bonds from companies with better environmental, social and governance ratings, with some industries screened out. It's meant for extra income with an ethical filter, but these bonds can fall hard in downturns when companies struggle to pay.
HYZD: High-yield corporate bonds, the kind issued by less financially solid companies, paired with a hedge that offsets the effect of rising interest rates. The goal is high income with less sensitivity to rate moves, but it still loses value when credit worries spread.
IACL: Autocallable notes tied to the 100 largest US stocks, structured contracts that pay income and can end early if the market rises. It is an income holding with fine print: returns depend on the notes' terms, and losses arrive if the underlying stocks fall far enough.
IAGG: Investment-grade bonds from governments and companies around the world outside the US, with the currency risk hedged back to dollars. It adds global variety to a bond holding for steady income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
IAI: Investment banks, brokerages, stock exchanges and other firms that earn money from trading and markets, all within financials. It's a focused bet on one corner of finance, so it swings more than the broad market and rises and falls with market activity.
IAK: Nearly all insurance companies, including property and casualty, life and health insurers. It's a focused bet on one corner of financials, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to be steadier than banks since it doesn't depend on lending.
IALT: A mix of bonds, stocks and cash, run with strategies like those used by hedge funds, aiming to do reasonably well in both rising and falling markets. It's meant as a diversifier alongside stocks and bonds, and it may not keep up in strong stock rallies.
IAPR: Developed-market stocks outside North America, such as Europe and Japan, held through options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in April. It's meant for investors who want international exposure with some protection, but gains are capped and the protection only works if held the full period.
IAT: Small and mid-sized US regional banks, all in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on community and regional lenders, and it's sensitive to interest rates and credit worries, so it can drop sharply when banking stress hits.
IAU: Physical gold bars held in vaults, with no stocks or bonds inside. People use it as a hedge, a cushion that often holds up when stocks or the dollar fall, but it pays no income and its price can swing sharply.
IAUG: A defined outcome fund tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, using options over a set one-year period starting in August. It aims to cushion part of the losses, and in exchange gains are capped.
IAUI: A gold fund that holds gold-backed products and collects extra income from options, with the rest in Treasury bills. It's meant to pay income from gold, though the options cap some of the gains when gold surges.
IAUM: Physical gold held in a vault, so its price moves with the price of gold itself. It's meant as a hedge against inflation and stock sell-offs, but it pays no income and its price can swing for long stretches.
IBAT: Companies that help with energy storage, including hydrogen, fuel cells and batteries, tracking a global index. The holdings come from around the world, and Bloom Energy, Air Products, Air Liquide and BASF are each around 7% of the fund.
IBB: US biotechnology companies that develop new drugs and treatments, all within health care. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it can jump on drug approvals and fall on trial failures, swinging much more than the broad market.
IBBQ: Biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies listed on the Nasdaq, from large drugmakers with approved medicines to smaller firms betting on a single treatment. It is a focused health care bet where trial results and regulators' decisions can swing individual stocks, and the whole fund, sharply.
IBCA: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies that all mature in 2035. It's meant for steady interest income and for locking in a known end date, when the bonds pay back, though the price drops when interest rates rise.
IBCB: A basket of investment-grade US dollar corporate bonds that all mature around December 2036. It's meant for locking in income until a set date, and as the bonds near maturity the price tends to settle toward face value, though it drops when interest rates rise.
IBD: Investment-grade corporate bonds from large US companies, filtered by a faith-based screen. It's meant for steady interest income from company debt, and the screen leaves out some businesses, so it holds a narrower set of issuers than a regular corporate bond fund.
IBDR: Investment-grade corporate bonds that all come due in December 2026, so the fund is mostly cash as they mature. It's a short-term place to hold money with a known end date, and it pays interest until the fund closes.
IBDS: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all come due around December 2027, paying regular interest along the way. It's meant for steady income with a known end date, and the fund closes and pays out near the end of 2027 rather than running forever.
IBDT: Investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature by December 2028, when the fund winds down. It's for steady interest income with a known end date, and its price swings less as the bonds approach maturity.
IBDU: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all come due around December 2029, paying regular interest. It's meant for locking in income until a set date, and unlike a regular bond fund it winds down and returns the money at the end of 2029.
IBDV: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US and foreign companies that all come due in December 2030. It's built to pay interest and then return your principal near that date, so it works for a known timeline, though prices dip along the way if interest rates rise.
IBDW: A basket of investment-grade US company bonds that all mature in late 2031. It gives regular interest income and a known end date, when the fund winds down and returns the money, so it suits investors planning around a specific year.
IBDX: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in December 2032. The fund closes that year and returns the money, so it suits someone who wants predictable income for a set time horizon.
IBDY: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, held until the fund closes that year. It's for locking in income with a known end date, and its price drops when interest rates rise, though it recovers as the bonds approach maturity.
IBDZ: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US and foreign companies that all mature in 2034. Because the bonds expire together, the fund closes in December 2034 and returns the money, giving a more predictable income stream than an ordinary bond fund, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IBFR: Developed-market stocks outside the US, spread across banks, industry, technology and health care, paired with options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It aims for international growth with a softer landing in sell-offs, at the cost of some upside.
IBGA: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2044, held until the fund ends in December 2044 and pays back what is left. It behaves like one long bond, so its price moves a lot when interest rates change.
IBGB: A set of US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2045, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. A few big bond issues make up most of it, and because the bonds are long, its price swings a lot when interest rates move.
IBGC: US Treasury bonds that all mature around December 2046, packaged like a single very long government bond with a known end date. Its long horizon makes its price swing hard when interest rates move, suiting investors matching money to a far future goal.
IBGK: US Treasury bonds scheduled to mature in 2054, bundled in a fund with a set end date decades away. The long wait means steady government interest, but prices that jump around a lot whenever interest rates change.
IBGL: US Treasury bonds that mature in December 2055, held in a fund with a built-in end date three decades away. Such long bonds pay steady government interest but their prices swing hard when interest rates move, far more than shorter bonds.
IBGM: US Treasury bonds that all come due around the end of 2056, when the fund itself wraps up and pays out. With such long maturities, its price swings a lot when interest rates move, far more than ordinary bond funds.
IBHF: Corporate bonds rated junk or just above, all maturing in 2026, so the fund winds down and returns its cash at the end of that year. It pays higher income than safe bonds, but it carries more risk of companies not paying back.
IBHG: A basket of high-yield and lower-rated investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature during 2027. It's built for a known end date, giving regular income and a return of principal near maturity, though some of the companies could default.
IBHH: US dollar corporate bonds from lower rated and medium rated companies that all mature during 2028. It pays higher income than safe bonds and winds down in 2028, but the companies carry more risk of default, so it can fall when the economy weakens.
IBHI: A basket of high-yield and lower-rated investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature during 2029. It's built for a known end date, paying regular income and returning principal near maturity, though some companies could default.
IBHJ: A basket of lower-rated corporate bonds that all mature in 2030, so the fund is designed to wind down around that year. It's for income at higher yields than safer bonds, with the extra risk that some companies fail to pay, and its fixed end date makes it predictable.
IBHK: A basket of US dollar high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds because the issuers are riskier, that all mature in 2031. The fund is set to wind down around then, returning money as the bonds mature, and its holdings are spread across many small positions.
IBHL: High yield and other income-paying corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, so the fund behaves like a single bond with an end date. It is used to target income for a known future year, and when 2032 arrives the fund winds down and returns cash to holders.
IBHM: High yield and lower-rated investment grade corporate bonds that mature during 2033, when the fund is scheduled to wrap up. Blending junk with BBB bonds lifts the income, and the fixed end date makes planning easier than with an open-ended bond fund.
IBID: US Treasury inflation-protected securities that all mature in 2027, with payouts that rise with inflation. It's meant as a short-term place for cash that keeps up with prices, and as the bonds mature it winds down in October 2027.
IBIE: Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, all set to mature by October 2028. It's meant for holding until that date as a way to protect buying power, and because the bonds expire together, the fund winds down then and returns your money.
IBIF: Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that all mature in 2029, with payouts that rise with inflation. It's meant for people who want to protect buying power until a set date, and since the bonds mature, the fund winds down in October 2029 and returns the cash.
IBIG: Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, which adjust their value with inflation, that all mature in 2030 and pay back at that date. It's meant to protect buying power while holding to the end, though prices can still drop when interest rates rise.
IBIH: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, called TIPS, all maturing in 2031, whose principal rises with inflation. Because every bond matures the same year, it works like buying one inflation-proof bond: hold to 2031 and the inflation adjustment is locked in, while prices swing before then.
IBII: A basket of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that all mature in 2032, whose principal rises with inflation. The fund ends in October 2032, when it pays back what is left, so it behaves like one bond with a set end date.
IBIJ: A basket of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that mature in 2033, held until the fund ends in October 2033. Its payouts rise with inflation, and because the maturity is fixed it behaves more like one bond than an ever-rolling fund.
IBIK: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, called TIPS, all maturing in 2034, whose principal rises with inflation. Because every bond matures the same year, it works like buying one inflation-proof bond: hold to 2034 and the inflation adjustment is locked in, while prices swing before then.
IBIL: Inflation protected US Treasury bonds that all mature around 2035, packaged like a single TIPS bond with a known end date. Its payments and principal adjust with inflation until then, suiting savers protecting a future expense from rising prices, though market prices still swing with real interest rates.
IBIM: Inflation-protected Treasury bonds, known as TIPS, that mature around October 2036, so the fund has a set end date like a single bond. Its payments and principal adjust with inflation, making it a targeted way to protect a known future year's spending from rising prices.
IBIT: Bitcoin itself, held by the fund, with no stocks or bonds inside. It lets you invest in bitcoin through a regular brokerage account, but the price swings wildly, and it pays no income.
IBLC: Stocks of companies tied to blockchain and digital assets, such as crypto exchanges, bitcoin miners and chip makers, picked to follow an index. It is concentrated: Coinbase, Iris Energy and Hut 8 are about 26% of it, and it leans heavily toward financials and technology.
IBMO: A basket of investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in December 2026, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It's built for a known end date, like a bond held to maturity, so it works as a low-risk place to park money until then.
IBMP: Investment-grade municipal bonds from US states and local issuers that all mature in December 2027. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund is designed to wind down at that date, so it fits someone planning for a set year.
IBMQ: Investment-grade municipal bonds from US states and cities that all mature in December 2028. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund is designed to wind down at that date, so it suits someone planning around a set year.
IBMR: Municipal bonds from US state and local governments that all mature around December 2029. It's meant for income that is generally free of federal income tax, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down and returns your money, so it behaves like a single bond.
IBMS: Investment-grade municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments, that all mature in 2030. It provides income that's generally free from federal taxes, and the fund winds down around December 2030, so it's built for a planned end date.
IBMT: Investment-grade municipal bonds, meaning loans to US states and cities, that all mature by December 2031. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund winds down at the end date, so it works like a bond ladder rung that returns your money then.
IBMU: Municipal bonds that mature in December 2032, so the fund behaves like one tax-exempt bond with a known end date. It suits savers matching a future expense in that year, paying federal tax-free interest while its price swings shrink as 2032 gets closer.
IBMV: Municipal bonds that mature during 2033, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, in a fund set to close at the end of 2033. Like other term muni funds, it returns principal as bonds mature, suiting money with a known future use.
IBMW: A fund of US municipal bonds that mature in 2034, tracking an S&P index, so it is designed to wind down in December of that year. The income is generally exempt from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 2%.
IBMX: A basket of municipal bonds all maturing in December 2035, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds end around the same time, the fund closes down at that date and pays out the proceeds.
IBND: Bonds issued by companies outside the US, priced in many currencies. It's for adding international income to a portfolio, and because it doesn't hedge currency, swings in foreign currencies against the dollar can move its price, on top of the drop that comes when interest rates rise.
IBOT: Companies building robots and automation worldwide: factory robot makers, sensor and machine-vision firms, chip designers and industrial software, split between technology and industry. It is a focused bet on machines doing more physical work, tied to factory spending rather than consumer trends.
IBRN: Companies working on the brain and nervous system: drug makers and medical firms focused on diseases like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and depression. It is a narrow, focused bet on neuroscience, so it can swing hard on trial results and drug approvals.
IBTG: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2026, held until they end. It's for people who want safe, predictable interest and a known end date, and unlike most bond funds it winds down at maturity, paying out the cash.
IBTH: US Treasury bonds that all come due in December 2027, then the fund winds down and pays back the money. It's meant for people who want government-backed safety and a known end date, so its price wobbles with interest rates until then but drifts back toward face value.
IBTI: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2028, held until they end. It's for people who want safe, predictable interest and a known end date, and unlike most bond funds it winds down at maturity, paying out the cash.
IBTJ: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2029, with the fund ending in December of that year. It suits someone wanting government backed income toward a known date, though its price moves with interest rates until then.
IBTK: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2030, so the fund winds down then and returns the money. It's meant for safe, predictable income with a known end date, and its price dips if interest rates rise before then.
IBTL: US Treasury bonds that all mature during 2031, so the fund winds down and returns its cash that December. It's useful for planning around a known date with government-backed income, though its price still dips when interest rates rise before then.
IBTM: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2032, so the fund is built to wind down then and pay back like a single bond. It's very safe from default, though its price dips if interest rates rise before then.
IBTO: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2033. Because the bonds expire together, the fund is built to wind down on that date and return your money, giving a predictable income stream, though its price dips along the way when interest rates rise.
IBTP: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2034, so the fund ends that year and returns the money. It's meant for locked-in government-backed income aimed at a specific date, though its price falls when interest rates rise before then.
IBTQ: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2035. It pays steady government-backed interest, and because the bonds end in a set year, it works like a rung on a bond ladder, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IBTR: US Treasury bonds that come due around the end of 2036, when this fund itself ends and returns its money. Long-dated government debt like this pays income with no credit risk, but its price swings widely as long-term interest rates move.
IBUF: Developed-market stocks outside the US, held through options that cushion some losses over each quarter. It's for investors wanting some downside protection abroad, but gains are capped and the cushion resets every quarter.
IBUY: Global companies that earn much of their money selling online, mostly consumer discretionary names with some communication and technology. It's a focused bet on e-commerce growth, so it swings more than the broad market and does best when online shopping keeps taking share from stores.
ICAP: Dividend-paying US stocks plus a sizable slice of preferred shares, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular stock. It's built for income, and since it's actively managed and mixes asset types, it behaves differently from a plain stock fund.
ICF: Real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, offices, warehouses and cell towers and pay out most of their income. It's built for income and diversification beyond stocks and bonds, though it drops when interest rates rise.
ICLN: Companies around the world in clean energy, such as solar, wind and other renewable power makers and utilities, with utilities about 40 percent and technology and industrials most of the rest. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
ICLO: Floating-rate notes backed by pools of corporate loans, limited to the top AAA-rated slices. Its interest payments reset as short-term rates change, so it's meant for income with little rate sensitivity, though it still carries credit risk in a financial crisis.
ICMO: Foreign stock markets chosen by momentum: the fund holds country funds from outside the US and rotates toward whichever national markets have been rising most. Because it chases strength country by country, its mix of regions changes over time, and it can zig when markets suddenly reverse.
ICOM: Companies that produce commodities, miners, energy firms and farm businesses, chosen with an income tilt by Tema's managers. It offers raw-materials exposure through stocks rather than futures, so it pays dividends like a stock fund while still rising and falling with commodity prices.
ICOP: Mining companies that dig up copper and other metals, so everything it holds is in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on metal prices and the global economy, which makes it swing more than the broad market, especially when demand for copper slows.
ICOW: Large foreign companies in developed countries that produce a lot of cash relative to their price, spread across industrials, consumer, energy and communication. It's a value tilt for international exposure, and it may lag when growth stocks lead the market.
ICPI: Inflation-protected Treasury bonds with under a year to maturity, the shortest-dated corner of the TIPS market. It barely moves with interest rates, so it works as a cash-like parking place whose value adjusts with inflation, aimed at preserving purchasing power over short horizons.
ICPY: An actively managed fund of undervalued stocks outside the US, where company insiders are buying shares or the company is buying back its own stock. Tweedy, Browne picks them, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
ICVT: Convertible bonds, which are company bonds that can be swapped into the company's stock, and they often come from growth-oriented firms. It's meant to mix some stock upside with bond-like income, and it tends to fall less than stocks but more than ordinary bonds.
IDAU: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It pairs foreign diversification with late-summer protection terms: gains are capped, and currency swings still show through.
IDEC: Options giving exposure to large companies in developed markets outside North America, with a buffer against part of any loss over a period resetting each December. It pairs international diversification with a safety cushion, giving up some gains when overseas markets rally.
IDEF: Companies that serve the military and national security, with industrials like aerospace and defense contractors about three quarters and technology a fifth. It's an actively managed, focused bet on defense spending, so it rises and falls with government budgets and global tension.
IDEQ: Stocks of companies outside the US, with financials and technology the largest groups, followed by industrials. Managers actively choose the holdings, so it's built as a core international holding that can differ noticeably from the broad foreign market.
IDEV: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, with technology less than a seventh. It works as the international piece of a stock portfolio, and it has no US companies or emerging markets.
IDGT: Companies that own data centers and cell towers, plus related equipment, with technology about 60% and real estate about 40%. It's a focused bet on the physical backbone of the internet, so it swings more than the broad market.
IDHQ: High quality large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, led by industrials, technology, health care and financials. It's a growth-leaning way to add international stocks, picked for strong profits and healthy balance sheets, with foreign currency swings along the way.
IDJL: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It pairs foreign exposure with mid-year defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
IDJN: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It pairs foreign exposure with defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
IDLV: The 200 least volatile stocks in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials, utilities and consumer staples. It's built for a smoother ride abroad, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
IDMO: Developed-market stocks outside the US that have been rising recently, with financials nearly half and technology about a fifth. It's a momentum fund that chases winners, so its mix changes often and it can fall sharply when trends reverse.
IDMY: Developed-market stocks outside the United States, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It pairs foreign diversification with defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still matter.
IDNA: Health care companies working in genetics, immune therapies and related medical research, all in the health care sector. It's a focused growth bet on medical breakthroughs, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply when research disappoints.
IDOG: Foreign large companies from the highest-yielding stocks in each sector, spread evenly across industries. It's built for dividend income from abroad, and by favoring beaten-down payers it can lag in strong growth rallies.
IDRV: Companies in electric and self-driving vehicles worldwide, mostly carmakers and consumer firms, plus industrial and materials companies such as battery suppliers. It's a focused bet on the shift to electric and autonomous cars, so it swings more than the broad market.
IDSE: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It pairs foreign exposure with autumn defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
IDU: Electric, gas and water utilities, about nine tenths of the fund, plus some industrial companies. It's a steady income and defensive holding, since people pay these bills in any economy, but it's sensitive to interest rates and usually drops when rates rise.
IDUB: International stocks from developed and emerging markets, led by financials and technology, held through other ETFs. It adds options-style swaps to generate extra income, so it's meant for income from foreign stocks, though the strategy can limit gains when markets rally strongly.
IDV: Dividend-paying companies from developed countries outside North America, with financials about a third, followed by energy, utilities and communication. It's built for income, and it tilts toward banks, energy and utilities, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
IDVO: Dividend paying foreign companies, with financials about a quarter, plus technology, materials and energy. It also sells call options, trading some upside for extra income, so it suits income seekers but can trail in strong rallies.
IDVY: Dividend-paying companies outside the United States with records of growing their payouts, led by financials and industrials in developed markets. It is a foreign income holding: the rising-dividend screen favors established payers, and currency swings add a second source of movement.
IDVZ: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, with consumer staples, financials, health care and communication companies making up most of it. It's built for income plus steady growth from overseas stocks, and an active manager holds a concentrated list, so it can swing more than the broad international market.
IDX: Indonesia's listed companies, led by its big banks, with miners, energy firms and the national phone company behind them. It is a single-country bet on Southeast Asia's biggest economy, bringing currency risk and emerging market swings with it.
IDYN: Large companies outside the US, rotated by a computer model among investing styles like value, quality and momentum as conditions change. Banks are about a third and industrial firms a fifth, so it is an active international core holding whose style tilts shift over time.
IEF: US Treasury bonds that mature in seven to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road cushion for a stock portfolio, with moderate price swings, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IEFA: Companies in developed countries outside North America, such as in Europe, Japan and Australia, led by financials, industrials and technology. It is used to add international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it leaves out Canada and emerging markets.
IEI: US Treasury bonds that mature in three to seven years, all backed by the US government. It's meant as a middle-of-the-road cushion for a stock portfolio, with less price swing than long-term Treasuries, though its price still drops when interest rates rise.
IEMG: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology over 40 percent and financials next. It offers growth from developing economies, but it swings more than funds holding developed countries, and a few big tech and chip makers drive much of its movement.
IEO: Companies that find and pump oil and natural gas, with nearly the whole fund in energy. It's a focused bet on energy that rises and falls with oil prices, and it can offset inflation while swinging far more than the broad market.
IETC: US technology companies of all sizes, with tech about 85% and a bit in communication. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and its screen leaves out some familiar names.
IEUR: Large and mid-sized companies across developed European countries, with financials about a quarter, industrials a fifth and health care behind. It's a core way to add Europe to a portfolio, and its returns also depend on the euro and pound against the dollar.
IEUS: Small European companies, with industrials about a quarter, then financials, consumer firms and real estate. It adds smaller companies from across Europe to a portfolio, so it tends to swing more than big European stocks, and the currency moves against the dollar can add to the ups and downs.
IEV: Large European companies from across the continent, led by financials at about a quarter, with industrials, health care and technology behind. It's a way to add international diversification, and it moves with European economies and the euro and pound, not just US markets.
IEZ: Almost entirely oil equipment and services companies, the firms that supply drilling rigs, tools and field services to energy producers. It's a focused bet on oil industry spending, so it rises and falls with drilling activity and swings more than the broad market.
IFEB: Options on a developed markets stock fund covering Europe, Japan and other rich countries outside the US, set each February for a one year outcome period with a loss cushion and capped gains. It brings defined outcome protection to foreign stocks, adding currency swings on top.
IFED: US stocks selected by a rules based strategy that reads the Federal Reserve's policy stance, leaning into stocks when policy is loose and turning defensive when it tightens. It is an exchange traded note rather than a fund owning shares directly, so the issuing bank stands behind its value.
IFGL: Real estate companies in developed countries outside the US, following the FTSE EPRA Nareit Developed ex US Index. It includes landlords and developers like Goodman Group, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan, and is spread across many names.
IFLN: Bonds from companies that were once investment grade but were downgraded to junk status, known as fallen angels. It's aimed at higher income than safer bonds, and it can drop more than them during recessions when companies struggle to repay.
IFLO: Stocks of companies outside the US that generate lots of spare cash, spread across industrials, technology, energy and consumer firms. It's a value-style way to add international stocks, and its returns also move with foreign currencies.
IFLR: Stocks in developed markets outside the US, banks and industrial firms the biggest slices, paired with options arranged as a floor to limit how far the fund can fall. It aims for international growth with a built-in brake, giving up some upside to keep losses within a managed range.
IFRA: Companies that own and run the nuts and bolts of the US economy: utilities about two fifths, industrials a bit over a third, plus materials and energy. It's a focused bet on infrastructure spending, so it's heavy in slower, steady businesses and light on tech.
IFV: A fund that holds other ETFs, each covering a different country or region outside the US, with the five chosen based on recent strength. Its picks change over time, so it's a momentum-based way to rotate overseas, and it can lag if those trends reverse.
IG: A mix of bonds from companies with strong credit ratings, picked by active managers rather than a fixed list. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise and can slip if companies' finances weaken.
IGB: Investment-grade corporate bonds issued in the US market: loans to solid companies and other strong borrowers, paying interest until maturity. It is a core bond holding, steadier than stock funds but still sensitive to interest rates, and it pays a little more than government bonds of similar length.
IGBH: Long-term corporate bonds from US companies, paired with hedges that cancel out most of the effect of interest rate moves. It's built to earn the extra yield of company debt without the big price drops that usually come when interest rates rise, though it will not gain when rates fall.
IGCB: Corporate bonds of many maturities from companies in the US and abroad, including some in emerging markets, picked actively by TCW. It is a core-style bond holding aiming for income with moderate risk, though company debt falls when credit worries grow.
IGE: Oil and gas producers make up about 70% of this fund, with mining and materials companies close to a quarter, all based in North America. It's a focused bet on natural resources that can act as an inflation hedge, but it swings with commodity prices.
IGEB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds chosen with a rules based approach that favors qualities like value and momentum within the index. It aims for steady interest income as a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IGF: Companies that run the essential systems of the economy worldwide: utilities and infrastructure-style industrial firms such as toll roads and airports each about 40%, plus energy pipelines at about a fifth. It's meant to add steady, income-oriented real-asset exposure, and it spreads across many countries rather than only the US.
IGGY: Growth companies outside the US, spread across at least three countries and led by technology and industrial firms in equal measure. AllianceBernstein's managers pick the stocks actively, so it is a bet on their favorite foreign growers rather than a market index.
IGHG: Investment-grade company bonds, paired with short positions in US Treasuries that offset the effect of interest rate changes. It's meant to earn the extra interest of corporate bonds without losing much when rates rise, but it may not gain when rates fall.
IGIB: Bonds from financially sound companies that mature in five to ten years. It's meant for steady income with more yield than government bonds, but its price drops when interest rates rise, more than shorter corporate bonds.
IGLB: Investment-grade bonds from US companies that mature in ten years or more. It's meant for higher income than shorter bonds, but long maturities mean its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise, so it swings more than most bond funds.
IGLD: Short-term US Treasuries and cash paired with options that follow the price of gold. It's meant for gold-linked income without owning bars, and the options give up some of gold's gains in strong rallies while still losing when gold falls.
IGM: Technology companies plus internet, media and other tech-related businesses that standard tech funds leave out, with technology over 80 percent. It's a focused growth bet on the tech world, so it swings more than the broad market.
IGOV: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US, priced in local currencies instead of dollars. It's a way to diversify away from US bonds, but currency swings can add gains or losses, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
IGPT: Companies tied to artificial intelligence and next generation software, with technology about three quarters and communication companies about a fifth. It's a narrow growth bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
IGRO: Large companies outside the US with a record of raising their dividends, led by financials at about a third, then industrials, health care and consumer staples. It's for steady, growing income with international diversification, and it tends to hold up better than flashier growth funds in sell-offs.
IGSB: Bonds from financially sound companies that mature in one to five years. It's meant for steady income with less price swing than longer corporate bonds, so it acts as a calmer cushion, though it still pays less than longer or riskier bonds.
IGV: Software companies, from business applications to cloud and security programs, with nearly all in technology. It's a focused bet on one industry within tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and it holds no chipmakers or hardware firms.
IHAK: Companies that sell cybersecurity software, hardware and services, almost entirely technology. It's a focused bet on digital security, so it swings more than the broad market and rises or falls with software company sentiment.
IHDG: Quality dividend-growing companies outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer, financial and tech firms. It's a way to own international stocks for steady growth, and it hedges the currency, so swings in the dollar versus foreign currencies mostly don't affect returns.
IHE: US drug makers that sell prescription and over-the-counter medicines and vaccines. It's a focused bet on the pharmaceutical industry, so it's tied to drug approvals, patents and pricing rules, and it moves differently from the broad health care sector.
IHF: Health insurers, hospital operators and other companies that deliver or pay for medical care, all within health care. It's a focused bet on one corner of the sector, so it swings more than the broad market and can react sharply to government policy changes.
IHI: US companies that make medical devices such as heart valves, surgical tools, diagnostic equipment and diabetes monitors, all within health care. It's a focused bet on medical technology, which grows steadily but swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to hospital spending.
IHY: High yield bonds from companies outside the United States, issued in major currencies like euros and dollars. These junk bonds pay more than safer debt to make up for weaker borrowers, and adding foreign issuers spreads the risk across many economies.
IIGD: US investment grade bonds with the highest quality scores in their universe, emphasizing strong borrowers and defensive traits, in shorter maturities. It is a cautious income holding designed for capital preservation first, accepting lower yields than funds willing to own shakier corporate credit.
IINC: Large and midsize US stocks paired with an options program that sells contracts on holdings to collect premium payments. The point is monthly style income from a stock portfolio, with the trade-off that selling options gives away part of the upside when share prices climb quickly.
IJAN: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, held through options that cushion some stock market losses over a one-year cycle starting in January. It's meant for cautious investors wanting international exposure, but it caps the gains and the cushion only applies on that schedule.
IJH: Mid-sized US companies, led by industrials and technology with financials and health care next. It offers more growth potential than large companies with less risk than small ones, and it has far less tech than a large-company fund, so it behaves differently from the S&P 500.
IJJ: Mid-sized US companies that look inexpensive compared with their earnings and assets, led by financials, industrials and consumer firms. It's a value-leaning way to add mid-sized companies to a portfolio, and it can trail growth stocks when they lead the market.
IJK: Mid-sized US companies with growth traits, with industrials and technology each about a quarter, followed by health care. It's built for growth from companies bigger than small caps but nimbler than giants, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds.
IJR: Small US companies, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer companies, screened for profitability. It adds growth potential beyond large companies, but small firms are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market, though the profit screen filters out the weakest.
IJS: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, spread across financials, consumer companies, technology and industrials. It's a value tilt for the smaller end of the market, a way to diversify beyond large companies, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IJT: Small US companies expected to grow faster than average, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's a growth tilt for the smaller end of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds and can fall harder in downturns.
IJUL: Developed market stocks outside the US, mainly financials, industrials and technology, held through options that absorb part of the first losses over a one-year period starting each July. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full year.
IJUN: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in June. In return, the gains over that period are capped.
ILCG: Large and mid-sized US companies that are growing faster than average, with technology making up over half. It's built for growth in a stock portfolio, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market, and it has little exposure to slower-growing industries.
ILCV: Large and mid-size US companies that look cheaply priced, with technology about a quarter, then financials, health care and communication. It's a value tilt inside a core stock holding, with less tech than the broad market, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
ILDR: Large companies that benefit from new technology and scientific advances, with technology above half, then health care, industrials and consumer businesses. It's a growth fund for innovation, and it is concentrated in tech, so it swings more than the broad market.
ILF: Around 40 of the biggest companies in Latin America, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, led by financials with materials, energy and industrials behind. It's a focused bet on the region, so it moves with commodity prices and local currencies and swings more than US stocks.
ILIT: A fund holding lithium miners and producers around the world, picking the companies in a global lithium index. It is a narrow bet on one metal used in batteries, with Mineral Resources, Sociedad Quimica y Minera, Liontown and Albemarle each at about 7% to 8%.
ILOW: Stocks of companies outside the US that are picked to swing less than the market, with financials the biggest group, followed by industrials and technology. It's meant for a smoother international ride, though it may trail in strong rallies.
ILS: Bonds issued to cover insurers against natural disasters such as hurricanes, earthquakes and floods, so the interest investors earn is payment for taking on that disaster risk. It aims for income that moves independently of stock and bond markets, but a major covered catastrophe can cost it principal.
ILTB: US dollar bonds from government, agencies and companies, all with more than ten years left until they mature. It aims for high income and a cushion for stocks, but its price swings hard, falling a lot when interest rates rise.
IMAR: Options on large companies in developed markets outside North America, covering Europe, Japan and Australia, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It is built to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each March, in exchange for capped gains.
IMAY: Options on a developed markets stock fund covering Europe, Japan and other rich countries outside the US, set each May for a one year outcome period with a loss cushion and capped gains. It applies the defined outcome idea to foreign stocks, where currency moves add another layer.
IMCB: US mid-sized companies spread across industries, with technology near a fifth and industrials, financials and health care behind. It's a diversified core holding for the middle of the market, offering more growth potential than giant companies with more bumps than them too.
IMCG: Mid-sized US companies with above-average growth, led by technology and industrials at roughly a quarter each. It's a growth piece between large and small companies, so it can lag when value stocks lead and swings more than the broad market.
IMCV: Medium-sized US companies that look inexpensive, spread across financials, energy, health care and industrials. It's a value-style core holding for the middle of the market, and it tends to lag in growth-led rallies when expensive stocks do the winning.
IMF: Futures contracts that go long or short across stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies in over fifty global markets, following price trends. It's meant to diversify a stock and bond portfolio, since it can profit when markets fall, but it can also lag for long stretches.
IMFL: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by industrials, technology, financials and health care, with weights that shift toward whichever investing styles suit the economic cycle. It's an international core holding with a tactical twist, and results depend on those calls being right.
IMOM: About 50 companies in developed countries outside the US that have recently risen the most, led by financials and industrials. It's a bet on momentum, the idea that winners keep winning, so it can lag or reverse sharply when market leadership changes.
IMTB: US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, that mature in about five to ten years. It's for income with moderate sensitivity to rates, so its price drops when interest rates rise, more than short-term bond funds.
IMTG: Mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by US government agencies, pooling home loans of many maturities into interest-paying bonds. It offers steadier income than corporate debt, with returns shaped by how fast homeowners refinance when rates fall.
IMTM: Stocks outside the US that have been rising lately, with financials over a third and technology about a sixth. It's a momentum fund that chases recent winners, so its holdings turn over often and it can drop sharply when trends reverse.
IMVP: Large and mid-sized Indian companies screened on four factors at once: momentum, value, low volatility and profitability. The factor scoring sets it apart from plain India index funds, aiming for a steadier mix of Indian growth across banks, software, consumer and energy names.
INCE: A mix of dividend-paying stocks, about two thirds of the fund, plus preferred shares and bonds, spread across staples, financials, health care and utilities. It's built for income with a steadier ride than all stocks, though it will usually trail in strong rallies.
INCM: A flexible mix of bonds, preferred shares and dividend stocks from areas like consumer staples, energy and utilities. It's built for regular income, and the manager can shift between asset types, so it should be calmer than stocks but not as steady as plain bonds.
INCO: Indian consumer companies, with consumer discretionary around three fifths and consumer staples about a third. It's a growth bet on India's rising shoppers, so it swings with one country's economy and currency.
IND: India's 500 biggest traded companies in one fund, led by banks at about 30 percent, with consumer, industrial and materials firms behind. It is a broad bet on India's growth story, carrying the currency and political swings of a single emerging market.
INDA: Large Indian companies, with financials about 30% and consumer, industrial and materials businesses next. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing emerging economy, so it swings more than the US market and can be hit by currency moves and shifts in Indian policy.
INDE: Actively managed Indian companies, led by banks and financial firms, with consumer, industry and health care names behind. It is a single-country growth bet on India's expanding economy, with the currency and political risks that come with it.
INDH: Indian companies across banks, consumer brands, energy and technology, with a currency hedge that cancels out swings between the rupee and the dollar. The hedge means returns follow the stocks themselves, which can help or hurt versus unhedged India funds depending on the rupee.
INDQ: Indian companies screened for quality: the profitable, well-run firms of the subcontinent, spread across consumer, health care, industrial and financial names. It is an actively selected single-country growth bet: India's young consumer economy drives it, with currency and political swings on top.
INDS: Real estate companies in warehouses, distribution centers and self-storage, the property types behind online shopping and goods movement. Three big landlords make up nearly half the fund, so it is a concentrated income bet on industrial property rather than the whole real estate market.
INDY: The 50 largest Indian companies, with financials more than a third, then consumer companies, energy and industrials. It's a focused bet on one emerging country's economy, so it can swing more than a global fund and depends heavily on India's banks.
INDZ: Indian companies chosen by VanEck's managers, led by banks at about a third, with industrials, health care and materials behind. Unlike index funds for India, the hand-picked approach can lean into or away from sectors, so results depend on the managers' calls.
INEQ: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, led by banks at about a third, with oil, mining and industrial firms adding more income weight. It is built as an international income holding, favoring established payers in Europe, Asia and beyond over fast growers.
INFL: Stocks of companies expected to benefit from rising prices, such as energy, financial and materials firms along with commodity producers. It's a hedge against inflation that's actively managed, so it can look very different from the broad market.
INFO: Large US companies chosen by a computer-driven model that scores them on traits like value and momentum, with technology about 40% of the fund. It's a core US stock holding with an active twist, so it can differ from the broad market in either direction.
INKM: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across bonds, stocks, real estate and other assets, aimed at producing income. It is actively managed, with mostly bond funds and some dividend and options-income stock funds.
INMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds with medium maturities, chosen by active managers, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
INOV: Options tied to a fund of large companies in developed overseas markets, with a power buffer against part of any loss over a period resetting each November. It softens the bumps of foreign investing while capping the gains, and results depend on the full period.
INQQ: Indian internet and ecommerce companies: online shopping, food delivery, digital payments and the finance apps behind them. It is a narrow bet on India's digital growth story, so it swings with one country's young, fast-changing online sector.
INRO: Mostly US stocks, led by technology at over two-fifths, with financials, health care and consumer companies behind it. It's an actively managed fund that shifts toward the industries it expects to do best, so it can look quite different from the broad market over time.
INTF: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, with financials the largest slice, then industrials, technology and consumer companies. It picks and weights stocks by traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a way to add international diversification with a tilt toward those traits.
INTL: A fund that holds other ETFs of stocks outside the US, aimed at regions and sectors that look cheap compared with their history, with technology, financials and industrials leading. It's a foreign stock fund that leans toward bargains, so it's less like a plain international index.
INTM: Municipal bonds maturing in the intermediate range, from states, cities, schools and utilities across the US, actively managed for tax-exempt income. The interest escapes federal income tax, which sets it apart from taxable bond funds and suits investors in higher tax brackets.
INVG: US investment grade corporate bonds chosen by GMO's systematic process, scoring each bond on value, quality and other factors. It is a core corporate bond holding with a rules-driven twist, aiming to own the attractively priced, sound credits a plain index weights only by size.
INVN: A fund following an index of US companies the manager sees as innovative but not yet fully recognized by the market, mostly mid-sized. It leans toward technology at about 57%, with health care next, and no single holding is above about 3%.
INYY: A single-stock income strategy built on Intel shares, using options on that one chipmaker to generate regular payments. Because everything rides on one company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and the chipmaker's drops hit directly.
IOCT: Options on a fund of developed-market stocks outside North America, tilted toward financials, industrials and technology. It aims to cushion the first stretch of losses over a one year period starting in October, but gains are capped, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
ION: A fund of companies that mine lithium, cobalt and nickel, the metals used in batteries, picked from a broad global stock index. It is almost entirely mining and materials stocks, with Australian lithium producers like Liontown and PLS among the largest holdings.
IOO: Just 100 of the world's biggest companies, with technology about half and communication, financials and health care behind. It's a concentrated core holding of global giants, and because so much sits in tech, it can swing more than a broader world fund.
IOPP: An actively managed fund of Indian companies, picked by the manager from across the country's market. It leans toward consumer-focused businesses like Eternal and Indian Hotels, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 6%.
IOYY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to IonQ, a quantum computing company, harvesting its extreme price swings as payouts. Few income funds are riskier: leverage resets, option caps and a speculative underlying stock can combine into steep losses.
IPAC: Companies from developed Asia-Pacific countries such as Japan and Australia, led by financials, then industrials and technology. It's a way to add diversification beyond the US and Europe, and it leaves out China and emerging markets, so it moves with the Japanese economy.
IPAV: Companies that build infrastructure outside the US: construction, engineering and materials firms split about evenly between industrials and materials. It is a bet on roads, ports and power projects across developed and emerging markets, moving with government building programs.
IPAY: Companies that run digital and mobile payments, split roughly between technology firms and financial companies. It's a focused bet on how people pay, so it swings more than the broad market and depends heavily on consumer spending.
IPB: A trust certificate from a 2003 series: a fixed security that pays interest at the rate in its name and is backed by assets held in a trust. Securities like this trade more like a single bond than a diversified fund, so anyone holding it is exposed to that one structure's terms.
IPKW: Foreign companies that have been steadily shrinking their share counts by buying back their own stock. Financials, industrials and consumer companies lead the mix, and it suits investors who want international exposure with a tilt toward firms returning cash to shareholders.
IPO: Newly public US companies, mostly in the first few years after their stock market debut, with technology making up almost half. It's a growth-focused bet on fresh listings, so it swings more than the broad market and turns over as companies age out.
IPOS: Recently listed companies from outside the US, following an index of international IPOs. It is concentrated, with the top five holdings, like Kioxia, Galderma and CATL, making up about half of it, and tilts toward technology.
IQDF: Large companies outside the US that pay solid dividends and have strong financial quality, led by financials and technology with industrials and materials behind them. It's built for steady income from international stocks, and it carries currency swings and a heavy bank presence.
IQDG: Dividend-paying companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer brands, financials and technology. It aims for steady, growing quality companies abroad, which makes it a way to add international stocks, and it picks firms for earnings quality rather than just size.
IQDY: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, screened for quality as well as income, with banks the biggest slice at over a quarter and technology next. It aims to pay steadier dividends than a plain international fund by favoring financially strong firms across developed and emerging markets.
IQGR: Quality growth companies outside the US, picked actively across finance, technology and industry in developed and emerging markets. It looks for durable growers abroad, and currency movements add their own layer to the returns.
IQHI: High yield corporate bonds chosen by active managers rather than an index, lending to companies rated below investment grade in the US and abroad. It is built for income, and the managers can shift toward safer or riskier credit as conditions change, though defaults remain the key risk.
IQLT: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US with strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, led by financials at about a quarter. It's a core international holding that favors quality, so it may hold up better in rough markets but trail in speculative rallies.
IQM: Companies building intelligent machines: the chips, networking gear, testing equipment and power systems behind artificial intelligence and automation, with technology nearly three-quarters of the fund. It is a growth bet on the machinery of the AI era rather than on any single application.
IQMM: Short-term government debt and cash-like holdings run as a government money market fund, built to meet rules for the reserves behind payment stablecoins. It's a safe place to park cash and earn interest, so it's meant to hold its value and not to grow.
IQQ: The 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, with technology making up roughly 60% and communication, consumer and staples companies filling most of the rest. It's a growth tilt for a stock portfolio, and with no banks and so much tech it swings more than the broad market.
IQQQ: Mostly Nasdaq-100 stocks, about 60 percent technology, combined with a strategy of selling call options, which hands over some upside in exchange for cash. It's built for high monthly income from tech, but it gives up big gains when tech surges.
IQSI: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, technology, industrials and health care, screened for environmental, social and governance standards. It's a way to add international stocks with a values filter, so it leaves out some companies that broad foreign funds hold.
IQSM: Mid-sized US companies led by technology, industrials and health care, with financials a bit behind. It's a core mid-size stock holding, with the twist that companies are screened for environmental and social practices, so some businesses are left out.
IQSU: Large US companies led by technology at over 40%, with communication, consumer and financial companies next. It's a core large-company holding, with the twist that firms are screened for environmental and social practices, so it leaves out some businesses found in broad funds.
IQSZ: Large companies from around the world, with technology a third and financials, industrials and consumer firms behind. The managers favor companies cutting greenhouse gas emissions or planning to, so it's a global core holding with a climate tilt and may differ from the broad market.
IROC: High yield municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt from riskier local borrowers such as hospitals, utilities and development projects that must pay more to borrow. The interest is generally free of federal tax, but weaker borrowers mean more price movement and some default risk.
IRTR: A mix of about 40% stocks and 59% bonds, built from other iShares funds, aimed at people who are already retired. It is actively managed and adjusts the mix over time, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ISCF: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, consumer businesses, materials and financials. It's picked by factors like value and quality, so it adds international small caps, and it swings more than large-company funds.
ISCG: Smaller US companies with above-average growth, led by technology, industrials and health care. It's built for growth, with more small, fast-growing businesses than a typical fund, so it swings more than large-company funds.
ISCV: Small US companies that look cheap, led by financials, consumer businesses, health care and industrials. It's a value-leaning way to own small caps, so it swings more than large-company funds and can trail when growth leads.
ISEP: Options on large companies in developed markets outside North America, covering Europe, Japan and Australia, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It is built to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September, in exchange for capped gains.
ISHG: Short-term government bonds from developed countries outside the US, paid in their local currencies. It diversifies a bond portfolio abroad with little interest rate risk, but it doesn't hedge currencies, so a stronger dollar can erode its value.
ISHP: Online shopping companies from around the world: retailers and marketplaces are the biggest slice, with media, delivery and technology firms behind them. It is a growth bet on buying moving online for good, spread across countries rather than one market.
ISMD: Small and mid-sized US companies spread fairly evenly across financials, industrials, technology and health care, screened for a good score on social and ethical values. It adds smaller companies to a portfolio, and it swings more than large-company funds.
ISMF: Futures contracts across stock markets, bonds, currencies and commodities, traded long or short by following price trends wherever they appear around the world. Because it can profit from falling as well as rising prices, it is meant to diversify a portfolio and often holds up when stocks struggle.
ISPY: Large US stocks like the S&P 500, led by technology at about two fifths, with a cash cushion and options layered on top for a high income payout. The tradeoff is that it gives up some gains in strong rallies, so it suits income more than growth.
ISRA: Companies based in Israel, with technology over a third and financials over a quarter, plus health care and industrials. It's a focused bet on one small country's economy, so it can swing more than a broad international fund, especially during regional news.
ISRL: The 120 largest companies in Israel by market value, led by financials with real estate, technology and industrials behind them. It is a single-country bet on a small, export-driven market: currency swings, regional politics and a handful of giant firms drive most of the result.
ISTB: US investment-grade bonds from government and corporate issuers that mature in one to five years. It's a steady, lower-risk holding for income and a cushion for a stock portfolio, and because the bonds are short, its price drops less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates rise.
ISTM: A basket of futures on metals used heavily in rebuilding industry: power grids, AI data centers, factories, energy systems and defense. It holds futures rather than mining shares, so it follows metal prices directly, with the sharp moves commodities are known for.
ISVL: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, tilted toward cheap stocks, with industrials and financials making up about a quarter each. It adds small-company and value exposure abroad, and it swings more than large-company funds, with no US stocks at all.
ISWN: About nine tenths sits in US Treasuries, while roughly a tenth buys long-dated call options on developed overseas stocks. The BlackSwan design protects most of the money while keeping a leveraged ticket on foreign markets, so gains can surprise in strong years.
ITA: US makers of airplanes, defense equipment, weapons and aerospace parts, all from the industrial sector. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it depends on government defense budgets and air travel and swings more than the broad market.
ITAN: US stocks, mostly technology, health care and consumer companies, picked as bargains once things like brand value and research spending are counted. It's a value-oriented core holding, and because it's hand-picked it can differ noticeably from the broad market.
ITB: Homebuilders and the companies that supply them, such as building products and materials, with consumer discretionary names making up about three quarters. It's a focused bet on US housing, so it rises with home demand and falls when mortgage rates climb, swinging far more than the broad market.
ITDB: A fund that bundles other iShares funds in stocks and bonds, with the mix designed for people planning to retire around 2030. It is actively managed and gradually shifts toward bonds as 2030 approaches, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ITDC: A ready-made mix of about two-thirds stocks and one-third bonds, with technology the biggest stock sector. It's a target-date fund for someone retiring around 2035, so it gradually shifts toward bonds over time to become less risky as that date nears.
ITDD: A mix of other funds, about three quarters stocks and a fifth bonds, aimed at people retiring around 2040. It's an all-in-one retirement holding that shifts gradually toward bonds over time, so it takes less risk the closer the date gets.
ITDE: A retirement fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2045, mixing stock funds from around the world with a smaller slice of bond funds. Its mix automatically grows more cautious as 2045 approaches, shifting from growth toward income and capital preservation over time.
ITDF: A retirement fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2050, currently holding mostly stock funds from around the world with a small slice of bonds. Its mix automatically grows more cautious as 2050 approaches, shifting from growth toward income and capital preservation over time.
ITDG: A retirement fund of funds aimed at people planning to retire around 2055. It is actively managed and mostly holds other iShares funds, with the bulk in US stocks, and the mix is meant to gradually shift toward safer investments as that date gets closer.
ITDH: A target date fund for retirement around 2060, holding other funds that mix global stocks and bonds, starting growth heavy and gliding toward safety as the date nears. It is a whole retirement plan in one ticker for young savers, with the mix adjusting itself over decades.
ITDI: A target date fund for people planning to retire around 2065, holding other funds in a mix that starts heavily in stocks and shifts toward bonds as the date nears. It is a whole portfolio in one ticker, and its distant date keeps it aggressive for decades to come.
ITDJ: A target date portfolio for retirement around 2070, currently invested almost entirely in stock funds covering US large, small and international companies. The mix will glide toward bonds as 2070 approaches, so today it is built for maximum long-term growth.
ITEQ: Technology companies founded in Israel but listed around the world, heavy in cybersecurity, semiconductors and defense technology. It is a single-country tech bet known for security software expertise, so it concentrates risk in one small country's innovation scene rather than spreading it globally.
ITM: Municipal bonds from US states and cities with medium-length maturities, which pay interest that is generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
ITOT: Nearly every publicly traded US company, from giants to small firms, with technology around a third and financials and health care next. It works as a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and its small-company slice makes it slightly broader than an S&P 500 fund.
ITWO: Small US companies, spread across health care, financials, technology and industrials, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for income. It's built to pay out more than a plain small-company fund, but it trails in strong rallies and still falls in sell-offs.
IUS: Large US companies picked by measures like sales, cash flow and dividends instead of stock market size, spread across technology, health care, communication and consumer companies. It's a core US stock holding that leans value, so it holds fewer of the priciest stocks.
IUSB: A broad mix of US dollar bonds: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, plus some other types beyond the usual core bond fund. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
IUSG: Large and mid-sized US growth companies, with technology a little over half and communication about a seventh. It's built for growth, but with so much in tech, it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IUSV: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, led by technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's a core value holding that can lag when fast-growing stocks lead the market and hold up better when they stumble.
IVAL: Cheaply priced companies outside the US, with materials about a quarter, plus energy, consumer companies and industrials. It's meant to add international value stocks to a portfolio, and it leans on cyclical industries, so it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IVE: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, with technology at about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It leans toward established, lower-priced companies, so it tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech stocks sell off but can lag in tech rallies.
IVEP: Thirty companies supplying the power and infrastructure behind artificial intelligence: electrical equipment, data centers, cooling, utilities and energy firms. It is a picks-and-shovels bet on the AI buildout, profiting from spending on capacity rather than on any single AI winner.
IVES: Companies picked by one well-known tech analyst as winners of artificial intelligence, about three quarters technology, plus communication and consumer companies. It's a focused growth bet on a single theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
IVLU: Developed-market companies outside the US that look cheap on measures like price versus earnings, led by financials at nearly a third, then industrials. It's a value tilt for foreign stocks, so it can lag when growth stocks lead, and it has less tech than the broad market.
IVOG: Mid-size US companies with strong growth, led by industrials and technology, followed by health care. It's a growth holding that sits between big and small companies, so it can swing more than the broad market in both directions.
IVOL: Inflation-protected Treasury bonds paired with options that pay off when interest rates swing sharply. It's a hedge against rising inflation and rate turmoil rather than a plain income fund, so it can behave quite differently from ordinary bond funds.
IVOO: Mid-sized US companies, with industrials the biggest group at about a fifth and technology, financials and health care behind it. It's a way to add companies that are bigger than small caps but nimbler than giants, and it swings somewhat more than the large-company market.
IVOV: Mid-size US companies that look cheaply priced, led by financials at about a fifth, then industrials, consumer companies and technology. It's a value tilt in the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
IVSI: A fund of large companies in developed markets outside North America, in places like Europe, Japan and Australia. ASML is the largest holding at about 7%, followed by Roche, BHP and Novartis.
IVSS: A focused set of small and midsize US companies, as few as fifteen or so, chosen by Applied Finance for intrinsic value: what the business is truly worth versus its price. It is a concentrated value holding where thorough appraisal of each company drives results.
IVSX: Small and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside North America, led by industrials at about a third. Managers apply a valuation approach, hunting for firms priced below what their cash flows suggest, so it is a value-tilted way to own smaller foreign stocks.
IVV: Hundreds of the largest US companies across every major industry, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care following. It serves as a core holding for US stock exposure, and because bigger companies count for more, a few tech giants drive much of its movement.
IVVB: US large company stocks held through a ladder of options that reset each quarter, with a deeper cushion against losses. It's meant to protect against sharp drops, but the options cap your gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
IVVM: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, held through a ladder of staggered options that cushion moderate losses in each period. It's built for a smoother ride, though gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
IVVW: Large US companies in the S&P 500, about 40% technology, with a layer of options that earns extra income each month. It's built for income rather than growth, so it gives up some of the upside in strong rallies while softening small dips.
IVW: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, with technology over half and communication, financials and consumer companies next. It is built for growth, but it is concentrated in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IWB: About a thousand of the biggest US companies, with technology at roughly 40 percent and financials, communication and health care at about a tenth each. It works as a core holding that moves with the overall US stock market.
IWC: Tiny US public companies, the smallest slice of the stock market, with health care about a quarter and financials another quarter. It's a high-growth, high-risk diversifier that swings far more than large company funds, and its shares can be harder to trade.
