IWD: Large and mid-sized US value stocks, meaning companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials, technology and health care. It leans toward established, steadier businesses, and it has far less tech than the broad market, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
IWF: Large and mid-sized US growth companies, with technology close to 60 percent and communication, industrials and consumer companies next. It is built for growth and sits heavily in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IWFG: An actively managed fund of about 30 large US growth companies chosen by Winslow. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 26% together, and technology makes up over half of it.
IWL: The 200 biggest US companies, with technology over 40 percent and communication, financials and health care next. It's a core holding focused on giants, so it behaves like the big end of the US market and leans more on tech than a fund covering all sizes.
IWLG: Large US companies with strong growth, led by technology at about half, with communication, industrials and financials behind it. It's a growth fund, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market, with a heavy tech tilt.
IWM: Around two thousand small US companies, led by health care, financials, technology and industrials. It adds growth potential beyond large firms, but small companies are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market, and many of its health care holdings are unprofitable biotechs.
IWMI: Small US companies, with health care, financials and technology leading, paired with an options strategy that aims to pay high monthly income. The income comes at a price: gains are capped in strong rallies, and it still falls when small stocks drop.
IWMW: Small US companies held through a small cap stock fund, plus call options sold on that small cap basket each month to generate income. Selling the calls trades away part of small caps' upside, so it aims for steadier payouts from a jumpy corner of the market.
IWMY: An options strategy on small US companies designed to pay distributions every week, using the Russell 2000 group of smaller stocks as its engine. Weekly payouts are the point, and gains are capped, so it is an income tool built on a volatile corner of the market.
IWN: Smaller US companies that look cheap, with financials at about 28% and industrials, health care and real estate each around an eighth. It's a value-focused bet on small companies, which can swing more than large ones and lag for long stretches.
IWO: Smaller US companies with strong growth traits, with health care at about 30% and technology around a fifth, then industrials and consumer companies. It's built for growth, but small growth stocks swing more than the broad market and can fall hard in downturns.
IWP: Mid-sized US companies with fast-growing sales and earnings, with technology the biggest slice, then industrials, health care and consumer companies. It's built for growth, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply in downturns.
IWR: Mid-sized US companies, the ones just below the biggest names, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care. It fills the middle gap in a portfolio, and these companies often grow faster than giants but can be bumpier.
IWS: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaper than the market, spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care at roughly an eighth to a sixth each. It's a value-tilted way to add the middle of the market to a portfolio, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IWV: Nearly the entire US stock market, from the largest companies to small ones, with technology the biggest slice at about 38 percent. It's a simple core holding that moves with the overall US market and economy.
IWX: The cheaper-looking half of America's 200 largest companies, picked for low prices compared with their assets and earnings. Technology, financials, health care and consumer firms lead, and it's a core value holding that tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech slumps.
IWY: The largest US growth-oriented companies, with technology at close to 60%, communication around a sixth, and consumer companies and industrials making up the rest. It's built for growth, so it leans heavily on tech and tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
IXC: Large oil and gas companies from around the world, all in the energy sector. It's a focused bet on energy, so it rises and falls with oil prices and swings more than the broad market, though it often pays solid dividends.
IXG: Banks, insurers, payment companies and other financial firms from around the world, almost all of it in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on global finance, so it swings with banking and the economy, and it has no technology or health care to balance it.
IXJ: Health care companies around the world, such as drug makers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused sector bet that is often steadier than the broad market in downturns, but it can be hit by drug pricing and regulation news.
IXN: Technology companies from around the world, including software, chip and hardware makers, spread across the US and other developed countries. It's a focused bet on global tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and it caps the biggest names so a few stocks don't dominate.
IXP: Global communication companies, nearly all in the communication sector, such as phone and cable providers, media, and social media and streaming companies. It's a focused bet on one sector worldwide, and it swings more than the broad market.
IXUS: Thousands of stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by financials and technology at roughly a fifth each, with industrials not far behind. It works as the non-US half of a stock portfolio, and it has no US companies at all.
IYC: US companies that sell things people want rather than need: online retail, cars, restaurants, home improvement, and some media and streaming. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it swings more than the broad market and falls when the economy weakens.
IYE: Almost entirely US energy companies, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and drilling service firms. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil and gas prices and swings more than the broad market.
IYF: Nearly all US financial companies: banks, insurers, asset managers and payment and exchange firms. It's a focused bet on the financial sector, so it does well when the economy and lending are healthy and tends to struggle in credit scares, and it holds almost no other industries.
IYG: US financial companies, including banks, insurers, asset managers and payment and credit firms. It's a focused bet on the financial sector, so it tends to move with interest rates and the economy and swings more than the broad market.
IYH: US health care companies such as drug makers, device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused sector bet that is often steadier than the broad market in downturns, but it can drop on drug pricing and regulation news.
IYJ: US industrial companies like aerospace, machinery and transportation, plus payment and business services firms, with industrials about two thirds and financials near a fifth. It's a focused bet on one part of the economy, so it swings more than the broad market.
IYK: Makers and sellers of everyday goods, with consumer staples at over four fifths, such as food, beverage, tobacco and household products, and health care around a tenth. It's a defensive holding that tends to fall less in downturns, though it trails in strong rallies.
IYLD: A mix of bonds at about 60 percent, stocks at about a quarter and preferred shares, spread across other funds with a lean toward income-producing sectors like financials and real estate. It's meant for steady income with moderate risk, and bond-heavy mixes can lose value when interest rates rise.
IYM: Companies that make or dig up basic materials: mostly chemicals, gold and copper miners, and steel, with a small slice of industrials. It's a focused bet on one corner of the economy, so it tends to swing more than the broad market, especially when global growth shifts.
IYR: US real estate companies, nearly all real estate investment trusts that own things like cell towers, data centers, apartments and warehouses. It's for income and property exposure, and it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
IYRI: Stocks of real estate companies, paired with an options strategy that sells away some price upside to produce extra income. It's meant for high income from property, but it gives up gains in rallies and swings when interest rates move.
IYT: US transportation companies such as airlines, railroads, trucking and package delivery firms. It's a focused bet on one cyclical industry, so it tends to rise with the economy and fall hard when business slows or fuel costs jump.
IYW: US technology companies, with software, chip makers and hardware making up over 90 percent, plus a small slice of communication firms. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giant companies carry a large share of it.
IYY: Nearly the whole US stock market in one fund, from large companies down to some small ones, with technology at about 40 percent. It's built to be a core holding, and its heavy tech weighting means it leans on that one sector.
IYZ: US telecommunications companies, including phone and cable providers and the network equipment makers that supply them, split between technology and communication businesses. It's a focused bet on one sector, often valued for dividends, and it can lag when growth stocks lead.
IZRL: Israeli companies working on new technology, with about half in tech and the rest in health care, communication and industrials. It's a focused bet on one small country's innovators, so it swings more than the broad market.
JA: A pool of loans bundled into securities called CLOs, limited to the higher-rated tranches from AA down to A. They pay floating interest that adjusts with rates, so the fund suits income seekers wanting less sensitivity to rising rates, though prices can fall if loan defaults jump.
JAAA: Top-rated loans bundled into securities called CLOs, which are pools of loans to companies. It aims for higher income than regular short-term bonds with little price movement, since the floating payments adjust with interest rates, though it's less liquid than Treasuries.
JABS: A mix of asset-backed securities, which are bonds paid by pools of loans such as auto, credit card and student loans, with some cash. It's meant for steady income with less interest rate sensitivity than long bonds, though prices can drop if borrowers fall behind on payments.
JADB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each January to absorb a large share of any market fall over the following year. The protection costs upside, since gains are limited, so it targets cautious investors fearing a bad year.
JADE: Actively managed stocks across developing markets, from Asia to Latin America, with technology about 42 percent and banks about a quarter. It is a growth holding built on the managers' company research on the ground in those markets, and it carries the bigger swings emerging markets are known for.
JAJL: Options tied to the S&P 500 that cushion losses over a six-month period starting each January and July, with the fund's stocks led by technology. It's a hedge for people who want a measure of protection, but gains are limited and the protection works best if held for the full period.
JANB: Options giving structured exposure to large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to cushion losses over an outcome period that resets each January. The Aptus design trades gains past a cap for a buffer, aiming for stock market participation with a calmer ride.
JANH: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills plus options on the stock market to pay regular income, with a barrier that protects only as long as the market does not fall past a set level. Its gains are limited, and big drops can hurt.
JANI: International stocks wrapped in options that buffer the first 15 percent of losses over the year starting each January, with a twist: gains are uncapped. Most buffer funds trade protection for a ceiling, so this one suits investors who want a cushion abroad without giving up the rally.
JANJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
JANM: Options on the S&P 500 seeking the maximum loss buffer the market offers over a year starting in January, per the Max Buffer name. Protection that deep leaves only a thin slice of gains, so it is built for capital preservation, not growth.
JANP: Options on the S&P 500 set each January for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 12 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year ahead, paid for by giving up the top end of any strong rally.
JANT: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 10% of losses over a set one-year period starting in January, in exchange for a limit on the gains. The cushion and cap only apply if you hold for the full period.
JANU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in December 2026, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JANW: Options contracts tied to a large US stock fund, which is about 40% technology with financials, communication and health care behind it. It's built to absorb the first 20% of market losses over a year starting in January, and gains are capped.
JANZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to cushion part of a market fall over an outcome period that restarts each January, at the cost of some upside. It is actively managed rather than a strict formula, and results depend on when you buy during the period.
JAPN: Japanese companies run by owner-operators: founders and managers who own big stakes in the businesses they lead. Horizon Kinetics hunts for that alignment of incentives in Japan's market, making this a focused bet that owner-run firms compound better than hired-management peers over time.
JAVA: Large US companies that an active manager considers cheaply priced relative to their growth potential, across technology, financials, health care and consumer firms. It's a value-style core holding, and since the manager picks the stocks, it can differ from a standard value index.
JBBB: Lower-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of company loans packaged and sold as bonds, mostly in the BBB and BB range. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, with interest that floats with rates, but it can fall sharply in a credit scare.
JBND: A mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, chosen by a manager who tries to beat the broad bond market. It's meant for interest income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
JCAL: Mostly medium-term bonds issued by California cities and agencies, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for steady income that is generally free of federal and California income tax for state residents, and its price tends to dip when interest rates rise.
JCHI: Actively managed Chinese companies across mainland, Hong Kong and US listings, led by internet platforms and banks. JPMorgan's managers pick across China's share classes in one portfolio, carrying the region's regulatory and currency risks.
JCPB: A broad mix of US bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, with room for some lower-rated and foreign debt. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and stability, with managers aiming to beat a plain bond index, though its price drops when rates rise.
JCPI: Mostly bonds, including corporate, government and mortgage-related debt, managed to hold up when inflation rises. It aims to give steady income with some protection from rising prices, though its price can still fall when interest rates rise.
JDIV: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large companies from around the world that the managers see as leaders in their industries. Technology and financials are the biggest sectors, and Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor together make up about 12% of it.
JDOC: Large health care companies that the managers believe are leaders, including drugmakers, biotech, medical device and health services firms. It is actively managed, and AbbVie, Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth, Merck and Johnson & Johnson together make up about 30% of the fund.
JDVI: Large and mid-sized companies outside the US that look cheap, led by financials, industrials, technology and materials. It's a value-focused way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and it can lag growth-heavy markets while still carrying currency swings.
JDVL: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their fundamentals, spread across technology (about a quarter), financials, health care and consumer businesses. It's a value-style core holding for stock investors, and it can lag growth-heavy markets when the most expensive companies are leading the rally.
JEDI: Companies building drones, defense electronics and other modern military technology, with industrials making up about 60% and technology about 40%. It's a focused bet on one theme, and because it holds a limited set of stocks, it can swing much more than the broad market.
JELH: Income built from equity-linked notes, options and swaps tied to stocks and stock indexes, rather than from simply owning shares. It aims for high regular payouts, and the structured payoff means returns can behave quite differently from the stock market.
JELM: An actively managed fund that aims to pay regular income, using stock-linked securities and options. Its holdings are mostly cash and short-term instruments, so its returns come from the income strategy more than from owning stocks.
JEMA: Stocks from developing countries, with technology the largest slice at over 40 percent, followed by financials and consumer companies. Managers actively pick the holdings, so it's a growth holding that can differ from the broad index and swings more than US funds.
JEMB: Government and company bonds from emerging market countries, all paid in US dollars or other major currencies rather than local ones. It's for higher income than US bonds, and it avoids local currency swings, but it can fall when investors get nervous about riskier countries.
JEPI: Large US companies picked for steadier, lower-swing stocks across many industries, paired with an options strategy that trades some of the market's upside for monthly income. The goal is income and a smoother ride: it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
JEPQ: Large growth companies, mostly technology at around 60 percent, paired with an options strategy that gives up some upside in exchange for monthly income. It's for income from a tech-heavy mix, and it usually trails in strong rallies while still swinging with tech.
JETS: Airlines, plane makers, airports and travel services from the US and abroad, with industrials making up about nine tenths. It's a focused bet on air travel, so it swings far more than the broad market, rising fast when travel booms and dropping hard when it stalls.
JFLI: Income from everywhere: dividend stocks, bonds and convertible securities across the US and the world, blended flexibly by the manager as opportunities shift. It aims to pay steady income from many sources at once, so no single market's bad year decides its fate.
JFLX: A flexible mix of mostly bonds, loans and a few convertible securities across the credit spectrum, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for income with some adaptability, since the manager can shift between bond types, though it still loses value when interest rates rise.
JGLO: Stocks from companies around the world, mostly in developed countries, with technology about a third and financials, consumer and communication companies filling out much of the rest. It's a one-fund global core holding, and since the manager picks a concentrated set of stocks, it can differ noticeably from the world market.
JGRO: Large US growth companies chosen by a manager, with technology about half and communication, health care and industrials behind it. It's built for long-term growth, and because it's concentrated in fast-growing tech, it tends to fall harder than the broad market in sell-offs.
JGRW: An actively managed fund of large US companies with long records of steady profits and growth. It is fairly top-heavy, with Alphabet, Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA together around a third of the fund.
JHAC: US companies of every size, from giants to small firms, researched one by one and weighted by business fundamentals rather than market price. It is a core stock holding with a built-in tilt away from whatever happens to be most expensive.
JHAI: Companies around the world tied to artificial intelligence, with technology about three quarters of the fund and at least 40 percent invested outside the US. It is a focused growth bet on the firms building and using AI, from chipmakers to software, so it swings more than a broad global fund.
JHCB: Bonds issued by big US companies, banks, tech firms, utilities and drugmakers, all investment grade, with room for some bank loans alongside. It is a straightforward corporate income holding, paying more than government bonds in exchange for lending to companies rather than the Treasury.
JHCP: A broad mix of bonds, including corporate, government, mortgage-backed and some higher-yielding ones, managed actively. It's meant as a core bond holding that seeks a bit more income than a plain government bond fund, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
JHCR: Investment-grade bonds, meaning issuers rated as fairly safe borrowers, spread across government, corporate and mortgage-backed debt. It's meant as a steady income core for the bond part of a portfolio, though it is actively managed and its price falls when interest rates rise.
JHDG: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about a third, paired with a hedging strategy using options to soften market drops. It's meant as a smoother-riding stock holding, though the hedging usually means it trails in strong rallies.
JHDV: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized US companies chosen by a rules-based approach. Despite the income focus, it holds a lot of technology, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together about 16% of the fund.
JHEM: Companies in emerging markets such as China, India and Brazil, with technology about 30% and financials over a fifth. It's meant for growth from developing economies, with a tilt toward traits like value and smaller size, so it swings more than US or developed-market funds.
JHHY: High yield corporate bonds chosen by active managers, lending in US dollars to companies rated below investment grade across many industries. It is built for income, and active selection is meant to dodge the weakest borrowers, though defaults and price drops remain part of junk bond investing.
JHID: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, selected by a rules-based approach. Financial companies are about a third of the fund, and no single stock is more than roughly 2%.
JHLN: Floating-rate loans to lower-rated companies from around the world, plus a small cash cushion. It's meant for higher income than regular bonds, and because the interest adjusts with rates, its price holds up when rates rise, though it can drop if borrowers default.
JHMB: Bonds backed by pools of home loans, mostly issued or guaranteed by US government agencies, with some privately issued ones. It's meant for income above ordinary Treasuries and a cushion for stocks, but homeowners refinancing early can change payments, and prices fall when interest rates rise.
JHMD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, with financials about a quarter and industrials just under a fifth. It's meant to add international diversification, with a tilt toward traits like value and smaller size instead of weighting only by company size.
JHML: Large US companies with a lean toward cheaper, higher-quality and smaller names within the large-company group, with technology at about a third. It's a core stock holding with a slight tilt, so it can behave a little differently from a plain index fund.
JHMM: US mid-sized companies spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care, picked with a tilt toward cheaper, higher-quality and smaller stocks. It's a core mid-size holding that sits between big and small companies, and the factor tilts mean it can differ from a plain mid-cap fund.
JHMU: Municipal bonds from cities, states and public agencies across the US, actively chosen across maturities and mostly investment grade. The interest is exempt from federal income tax, and the manager can reach for extra yield with a minority of lower-rated bonds.
JHPI: Preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular stock, plus corporate bonds and a little cash. It's built for steady income, but its price tends to drop when interest rates rise, and it lags stocks in strong rallies.
JHSC: US small companies spread across financials, industrials, technology and consumer businesses, tilted toward cheaper, higher quality and smaller stocks. It's a way to own small caps in a diversified mix, and it swings more than large-company funds.
JIDE: Actively managed stocks from developed markets abroad, with banks the largest slice, chosen under a dynamic process that adjusts country and style tilts. It fills the international slot with manager judgment rather than an index, leaning on Europe and Japan style markets and their currencies.
JIG: Growth-oriented companies outside the US, including emerging markets, with technology about a third, then industrials, financials and consumer companies. It aims for capital growth and adds international exposure, but it tends to swing more than value-oriented foreign funds.
JIII: A mix of bonds from governments and companies in the US and abroad, picked for high income, along with some cash. It's an income fund where the manager chooses among bond types, and its price can still drop when interest rates rise.
JINT: Companies from developed countries outside the US, with banks the largest group at about a third of the fund. Managers use their own research signals to tilt toward stocks they expect to beat the pack, so it is an actively run core holding for international exposure.
JIRE: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's an international core holding, and researchers tilt the picks to try to beat a standard international index while keeping similar risk.
JIVE: Developed and emerging-market companies outside the US that look cheap, with financials about 40% and energy, industrials and technology around a tenth each. It's a value tilt for foreign stocks, so it may lag when growth stocks lead, and it leans heavily on banks.
JLCO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that holds a mix of stocks the managers think have good potential. It leans toward big tech, with Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon together about 21% of the fund.
JLQD: Mostly investment grade corporate bonds in US dollars, with some mortgage-backed securities mixed in, actively managed with sustainability criteria. It aims for core bond income while screening out issuers the managers judge weak on environmental and social grounds.
JLVP: Large US value stocks with a twist: alongside the shares it owns, the fund takes short positions betting against selected companies. That long-short overlay aims to add return and soften market drops, making it a more hedged value holding than a plain index of cheap big stocks.
JMBS: Mostly mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged into bonds, with a small slice of cash. It's meant for steady interest income and diversification from stocks, and because homeowners can repay loans early when rates fall, its income and price can shift in less predictable ways than ordinary bonds.
JMEE: Small and mid-sized US companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer businesses. It's an actively tuned version of a small and mid-cap index, meant to be a core holding that tries to beat the index, and smaller firms swing more than large ones.
JMHI: Municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments and projects, mostly lower-rated ones that pay higher interest, with a small cash slice. It aims for income that is free from federal income tax, but the lower credit quality means prices can fall hard in a downturn.
JMID: Midsize US growth companies picked by Janus Henderson with an active, systematic process hunting for an edge in that middle tier. Technology, industry, consumer and health care names share the lead, making it a diversified growth holding focused on companies past the fragile stage but not yet giants.
JMMF: A money market fund holding only US Treasury bills, notes and bonds, the safest corner of the cash world. Investors use it to park money with government backing and daily liquidity, earning a modest yield while aiming to keep a steady one-dollar share price.
JMOM: Large US companies whose share prices have recently been rising, with technology the largest slice at over two fifths. It's a growth-leaning core holding that rides winners, and momentum can fade fast, so it may fall sharply when market leadership changes.
JMSI: Municipal bonds from US states and cities, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, with an eye toward sustainable projects. It's meant for tax-friendly income for those in higher tax brackets, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
JMTG: Investment-grade mortgage-backed bonds, which pool home loans and pass along homeowners' payments, picked by an active manager. It's meant for steady income and diversification from stocks, though its price falls when rates rise and borrowers' refinancing changes the payments.
JMUB: Intermediate-term bonds issued by US states and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income, mostly for people in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
JNEU: Options on the S&P 500 set up to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period that starts each June, with a 15% buffer as the name says. Gains above a small spread are uncapped, unlike most buffer funds that limit the upside.
JNK: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, which pay higher interest because they are riskier. It's for extra income, and it tends to fall along with stocks in downturns when borrowers struggle to repay, unlike safer bonds.
JOET: Large US companies chosen for both strong business quality and recent price momentum, led by technology at about thirty percent. It's a core stock holding with a performance tilt, and it can lag when the market turns and recent winners fall out of favor.
JOJO: A bond fund that rotates between riskier corporate credit in calm times and safer ground when its signals flash warning. The switching sets it apart from buy-and-hold bond funds, aiming to dodge credit blowups, though the calls can be wrong.
JOUL: An actively managed fund of companies that make or build high-voltage power grid equipment. Eaton and GE Vernova alone are more than a quarter of the fund, and almost all of it is industrials.
JOYT: Large US stocks, led by technology at about two-fifths of the fund, combined with call options on a broad stock index to add option premium to dividends and growth. It aims for total return from three sources at once, though the options can trim gains in a strong rally.
JPAN: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in Japanese company stocks, chosen by the managers rather than an index. Tokyo Electron, Mitsubishi UFJ and Advantest are among the biggest holdings, and technology, industrials and financials make up most of it.
JPEF: A concentrated set of large US stocks picked by managers, with technology about a third of it. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and since it holds fewer companies than a broad index fund, it can differ a lot from the overall market.
JPEM: Stocks from emerging market countries, led by financials, with industrials, materials and consumer companies next. It's meant to add developing economy growth, picked using several factors to balance the mix, so it swings more than US stocks and moves with local currencies.
JPFP: A blend of US stocks, with technology the biggest slice, plus a managed futures strategy that bets on rising or falling trends in markets like bonds, currencies and commodities. It aims to add a second source of returns on top of stocks, and the trend bets can lose money when markets reverse.
JPHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for a higher chance of default, plus a little cash. It's meant for higher income, but it acts more like stocks than safe bonds and tends to fall when the economy weakens.
JPIB: Bonds from borrowers outside the US across many industries, including companies and governments, with currency risk hedged back to US dollars. It's meant for income and diversification beyond the US, and hedging means exchange rates matter less, though prices still fall when rates rise.
JPIE: A mix of bonds across several markets, including corporate bonds, mortgage-backed bonds and government debt, picked by managers. It's built for income above plain Treasuries, and managers can shift between areas, so it's less predictable than an index bond fund.
JPIN: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside North America, spread across industrials, consumer staples, financials and health care. It's a way to add international diversification, picked using several factors to balance the mix, and its returns also move with foreign currencies.
JPLD: Short-term bonds, mostly mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities. It's built for steady income with small price swings, a step up from cash that is less sensitive to interest rate changes than regular bond funds.
JPMB: Bonds sold by governments of developing countries, Brazil, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Colombia and others, all issued in US dollars. It pays higher interest than rich-country government debt in exchange for the risk that a borrowing government struggles, and dollar issuance removes local currency swings.
JPME: US mid-sized companies chosen to balance several traits like value and quality, spread fairly evenly across health care, real estate, consumer staples and industrials. It's a diversified middle ground between large and small companies, with far less technology than most US stock funds.
JPO: A single-stock income strategy built on JPMorgan Chase shares, using options on that one banking giant to generate monthly payments. Because everything rides on one company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and the bank's drops hit directly.
JPRE: Real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, offices, warehouses and cell towers. It's for dividend income and a way to add real estate to a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
JPRF: Preferred stocks and bonds that pay steady income, with at least a quarter in financial companies such as banks. It's meant for income, mixing hybrid securities that sit between stocks and bonds, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
JPSE: Small US companies chosen to balance value, quality and momentum rather than by size, with real estate, technology, industrials and health care all roughly similar. It's a diversified small-company holding, and small stocks usually swing more than large ones.
JPSV: Small US companies bought at value prices by JPMorgan managers, with banks the biggest slice at about 28 percent, plus industrial, consumer and property firms. It is an active small value holding where research into local lenders and overlooked businesses drives results rather than the small-cap index.
JPUS: US stocks of large and mid-sized companies spread evenly across health care, consumer staples, real estate, technology and more. It's a diversified core holding that picks stocks by factors like value and quality, so no single sector dominates the way tech does in the broad market.
JPXN: 400 Japanese companies picked for profitability and good governance, spread across industrials, technology, financials and consumer firms. It's a way to add Japan to a portfolio, and because it's priced in yen, currency moves can help or hurt returns.
JPY: Japanese companies picked by Lazard's managers, who rotate toward whichever industries look strongest at each stage of the economic cycle. Banks, chip equipment, electronics and trading firms all feature, giving actively managed Japan exposure rather than a plain slice of its market.
JQTY: US companies screened for quality: businesses with strong balance sheets and consistent profitability, led by technology at a bit over a third. It is a core holding with a sturdiness filter: the screen favors firms built to weather downturns, so it can lag speculative rallies.
JQUA: High-quality large US companies, meaning those with strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, with technology over 40%. It's meant as a core holding that aims for a smoother ride, though it can still trail in rallies led by riskier stocks.
JSCP: Mostly short-term investment-grade bonds from companies and governments, including mortgage-backed securities, with a small portion in riskier bonds. It's meant for steady income with a calm ride, and short maturities mean its price moves little when rates change.
JSI: Securitized debt, meaning bundles of loans like mortgages, car loans and company loans packaged into bonds, with a small cash cushion. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, though it can lose value when borrowers struggle to repay.
JSMD: Small and mid-sized US companies expected to grow, with health care and technology each about a quarter, then industrials and consumer companies. It's built for growth beyond the biggest names, and chosen by active managers, so it swings more than the broad market.
JSML: Small US companies chosen for growth potential, led by health care and technology, with industrials and financials next. It's a growth holding for people comfortable with bumpy rides, and managers pick stocks by a ranking method, so it can differ a lot from small-company benchmarks.
JSTC: Global companies across technology, financials, industrials and health care, picked because their business practices meet social justice standards. It serves as a worldwide core stock holding for values-minded investors, and its screens can steer it away from some well-known companies.
JTEK: US technology and tech-enabled companies picked by managers who think their growth is underappreciated, with technology about three quarters and communication, consumer and health care filling the rest. It's a growth bet on tech, so it swings more than the broad market.
JTNY: Investment-grade bonds from New York State and its cities, whose interest is exempt from federal, state and city income tax. It's for tax-free income, mainly for high earners living in New York, but it is concentrated in one state and its price drops when rates rise.
JUCY: Mostly Treasuries and government-linked bonds, paired with options and swaps that aim to boost monthly income beyond what bonds alone pay. It's meant for extra income from a conservative base, but the options add risks that plain bond funds don't have.
JUDB: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to absorb a deeper first slice of losses than standard buffers, over an outcome period that resets each July. The trade for that stronger cushion is a tighter cap on gains, and the protection only lines up if shares are held for the full period.
JUDO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that also uses options to earn extra income. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft making up about 21% of the fund, and the options can limit gains in strong markets.
JULB: Options on a large US stock fund in a structured outcome design that starts each July, absorbing a slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. It offers stock exposure with a planned cushion, suiting investors who prefer knowing the trade off in advance.
JULC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange. The July start fixes the terms: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap than deeper-protection editions.
JULH: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 20 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
JULI: Developed-market stocks outside the US, wrapped in options that absorb the first 15 percent of losses over a one-year period starting in July. Gains are left uncapped, which sets it apart from most buffer funds, though the cushion only counts at the end of the period.
JULJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
JULM: Options on the S&P 500 seeking the deepest loss protection available over a year starting in July, as its Max Buffer name promises. Maximum protection means minimal participation in rallies, so this is capital preservation first and growth a distant second.
JULP: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in July, matching the Buffer 12 name. The moderate cushion leaves more upside than deeper buffers, but gains are still capped.
JULT: Options on the S&P 500 set each July for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. Like other buffer funds it trades strong rally potential for a known cushion, and the clock restarts every July.
JULU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in mid 2027, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JULV: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the US stock market to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the outcome only applies if you hold the full period.
JULW: US large company stocks tied to the S&P 500, with technology about 40%, wrapped in options that shield against a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each July. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the protection works best if you hold the whole year.
JULZ: Options on the S&P 500 built to take part of a market drop for you over an outcome period that refreshes each July, while surrendering some gains. It is aimed at nervous stock investors, and what you receive hinges on when in the period you buy.
JUNC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. The June start fixes the terms: the shallower buffer suits investors who accept smaller drops in exchange for a higher cap.
JUNM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a larger set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each June. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold from the start to the end.
JUNP: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, with a buffer against a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each June (the 12 in its name). It trades gains past a cap for that protection, aiming for a calmer version of stock market exposure.
JUNT: Large US stocks, mostly technology, held through options that cushion some losses over a one-year period beginning in June. It's for investors seeking downside protection, but gains are capped and the protection works best if shares are held for the whole period.
JUNW: Large US companies, led by technology at about 40 percent, held through options that absorb a sizable chunk of losses over a one-year period starting each June. It's meant as a cushion for stock investors, though gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
JUNZ: Options on the big US stock index shape returns over a year starting each June, aiming to soften losses with a built-in buffer while keeping a share of gains up to a cap. It is a structured, defined-window stock holding, so when you buy relative to the June start matters.
JUSA: Large US companies, led by technology at about 40%, chosen by a research-driven manager who leans toward stocks with better outlooks. It's a core stock holding that stays close to the broad market while trying to edge past it.
JUST: Large US companies chosen for how they treat workers, customers, communities and the environment, with technology at around 40%. It's a core stock holding with a values screen, so it looks much like the broad market but overweights companies with strong social records.
JVAL: Large US companies that look cheap compared to their earnings and assets, though technology still makes up about 40%. It's a value-style core holding, and it can trail growth funds in rallies led by fast-growing companies.
JXI: Utility companies from around the world, such as electric, gas and water providers. It's a defensive, income-oriented holding because people keep paying their bills, but it's a one-industry bet, and its price tends to fall when interest rates rise.
JXX: A concentrated portfolio of about twenty to thirty companies Janus Henderson managers believe can ride transformational changes, mostly large firms across technology, health care and industry. With so few holdings, each pick drives results, making it a high-conviction growth holding rather than a diversified core.
KAIT: Asian technology companies built around artificial intelligence: chip makers, software firms and data companies across the region make up nearly the whole fund. It is a focused bet on Asia's AI industry, so it adds currency and regional political swings to tech's usual ups and downs.
KAMO: A tactical bundle of bond funds, currently parked mostly in very short-term Treasuries, top-rated loan bundles and ultra-short bonds, that can shift toward riskier credit when its managers see opportunity. It aims for income with flexibility, moving between safety and yield as conditions change.
KAPR: US small-company stocks wrapped in options that soften losses over a one-year period starting each April. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors who want small-company exposure with a cushion.
KARS: Global companies tied to electric vehicles and future mobility, including carmakers, battery makers and the miners of materials used in them. Panasonic, STMicroelectronics, Tesla and CATL are each about 4 to 6% of it.
KAT: A concentrated mix of US companies a manager thinks can grow with limited downside, led by financials, health care and technology. It's an actively managed core stock holding, and because the picks are few and chosen by judgment, results can differ a lot from the broad market.
KAUG: Uses options on a small company stock fund, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to protect against part of the losses over a one year period that starts in August. In return, the gains over that period are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
KBA: Fifty of the largest mainland China companies listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, led by technology and financials, with materials and industrials next. It's a way to own China's domestic market rather than the overseas-listed names, but it swings widely and is tied to Chinese policy and economic news.
KBE: US banks and nothing else, from large national lenders to smaller regional ones. It's a focused bet on the banking industry, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and credit worries.
KBFR: Small US companies across health care, finance, technology and industry, paired with options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It aims for small-cap growth with a managed cushion, giving up some upside to pay for the protection.
KBUF: Chinese internet companies, reached through a sister fund plus options built to absorb 90 percent of a drop over the period ending in January 2027. In exchange for that deep cushion, gains are limited, so it is a defensive way to hold a volatile corner of China.
KBWB: US banks only, from the biggest national names to smaller regional lenders, all in the financial sector. It's a focused bet on banking, so it moves with interest rates and the lending economy, and it typically swings more than the broad market, especially when worries about bank health arise.
KBWD: High-yielding financial companies, with about 60 percent in financials such as lenders and asset managers and about 40 percent in real estate firms. It's built for high dividend income, but those payouts can be cut in a downturn, so it can fall hard.
KBWP: US property and casualty insurers, the companies that cover homes, cars and businesses against damage. It's a focused bet on one corner of financials, so results hinge on storms, claims and pricing, and it has no banks in it.
KBWY: Small and mid-sized US real estate investment trusts, which are companies that own properties and pass rent income to shareholders, favoring those with higher payouts. It's for income, but it can drop when interest rates rise and swings more than larger REITs.
KCAI: Chinese companies held both long and short, aiming to beat the broad Chinese stock market whether it rises or falls. The short bets set it apart from ordinary China funds, though they can backfire when beaten-down stocks suddenly rally.
KCCA: Futures tied to the price of California carbon allowances, the permits companies need to emit greenhouse gases, with the rest held in cash and short-term bonds. It's a focused bet on carbon prices, so it can swing sharply and doesn't behave like stocks or bonds.
KCE: US capital markets companies such as brokers, asset managers and custody banks, nearly all financials. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market and rises and falls with trading activity.
KCHP: South Korean semiconductor companies, the chipmakers and equipment firms behind memory and processor production. It is a single-country, single-industry bet: it rides the global chip cycle and the Korean market at once, so currency and export swings both matter.
KCOP: Exposure to copper through mining companies, copper funds and derivatives, with option selling layered on to add income. Copper prices ride global construction and electrification demand, so the fund swings with the industrial cycle, while the options work pays extra along the way.
KDEC: Holds options on a fund of small US companies, the Russell 2000, aiming to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each December. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
KDEF: South Korean defense companies: makers of fighter jets, tanks, missiles, warships and ammunition, almost entirely industrial firms. It is a single-country bet on rising military spending in Asia and beyond, so it moves with defense budgets and geopolitics rather than the wider economy.
KDRN: A mix of bonds across types and maturities, actively shifted by the manager toward wherever the bond market looks most promising. It is a flexible core-plus income holding: the tactical freedom sets it apart from a plain bond index, and results depend on the manager's rate calls.
KDVD: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that pay and grow dividends, chosen by the manager rather than an index. Its biggest positions are each only a few percent of the fund, so it is fairly spread out across financials, consumer and industrial companies.
KEAT: A mix of roughly 70 percent stocks and 28 percent bonds, with stocks concentrated in energy, consumer staples and materials. It's an actively managed fund aimed at real-asset themes, so it can behave very differently from a typical balanced fund.
KEMQ: Internet and technology companies across emerging markets, including some privately held firms alongside listed ones, from KraneShares. Online shopping and consumer platforms dominate, making it a growth bet on the digital economies of China, Latin America and beyond, with extra risk from the private holdings.
KEMX: Emerging-market companies from every major developing country except China, with technology the largest slice at over a third and financials next. It's a way to own developing markets without China's weight, and it leans heavily on Taiwan and India.
KEO: Equity income built from Kurv's own option income funds and direct stock and option positions, aiming for regular payouts from share prices. It is a fund-of-funds income strategy: the payouts come from option premiums across several holdings, and gains are capped wherever the underlying funds cap theirs.
KFEB: Options on a small company index fund designed to absorb part of a loss over a year-long outcome period that resets every February. Gains are capped in return for the cushion, and the options structure means it will not behave exactly like owning small stocks.
KGLD: Gold exposure through gold funds and derivatives, with a large bond and cash holding on the side, plus an options strategy that generates extra monthly income. It aims to pay income from gold, but the options limit gains in big gold rallies.
KGRN: Chinese clean technology companies: solar panel makers, electric vehicle and battery firms, wind and clean power generators, with utilities the biggest slice. It is a focused bet on China's green buildout, swinging with energy policy and fierce price competition in that industry.
KHPI: Large US companies mirroring the S&P 500, with technology around 40 percent, paired with options that earn extra income and others that protect against sharp drops. It's meant for income with some downside protection, and the trade-off is that it trails in strong rallies.
KHYB: US dollar bonds from Asia-Pacific borrowers, including banks and companies in frontier markets like Mongolia, paying high income for the region. Dollar denomination removes local currency risk, but the borrowers include weaker credits far from the region's giants.
KIE: US insurance companies, including property and casualty, life and health insurers. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it can behave differently from the broad market, and it spreads weight more evenly across companies than a typical large-company fund.
KIQQ: Nasdaq stocks wrapped in a dynamic buffer strategy that aims for high income while cushioning part of any drop, with technology about 60% of the mix. It mixes growth and defense: the buffer softens losses in exchange for capped gains, and terms adjust as markets move.
KJAN: Options tied to US small company stocks that cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in January, in exchange for a cap on gains. It's a smaller-company bet with a safety net, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
KJUL: Small US companies, with health care, financials, technology and industrials the largest groups, held through options that cushion some losses over a yearly cycle starting in July. It's for cautious small-company investors, but gains are capped and small stocks still swing.
KJUN: Options on a small company stock fund, set each June for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. Small caps swing harder than large ones, so the cushion is the appeal, paid for by missing the biggest small stock rallies.
KLIP: Chinese internet companies, online shopping, social media, gaming and delivery platforms, with covered call options sold against the position for income. The calls generate a payout stream from a famously volatile sector, at the cost of giving up part of any sharp rebound.
KLMN: Large North American companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care filling most of the rest. It's a core stock holding with a climate tilt, favoring companies with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans over the heaviest polluters.
KLMT: Large global companies, with technology at about a third and financials near a sixth, chosen to favor lower carbon emissions and climate-friendly practices. It's a core world stock holding with a climate tilt, so it leans away from heavy polluters like oil and coal producers.
KMAR: Small US companies reached through options on a small-cap fund, with a power buffer designed to absorb a larger slice of losses over a year starting each March. Small stocks swing more than large ones, so the extra protection is the point, and in exchange the gains are capped.
KMAY: Options on a small company stock fund, set each May for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. Small caps swing harder than large ones, so the cushion is the appeal, paid for by missing the biggest small stock rallies.
KMCA: South Korean manufacturers, split between industrial firms at about half the fund and technology companies, mostly chip and electronics makers. It is a concentrated bet on Korea's export factories, so it moves with global demand for chips, batteries and machinery.
KMEM: A focused bet on memory chip companies: the makers of the DRAM and flash memory inside phones, computers and AI data centers. Memory is a famously boom-and-bust corner of semiconductors, so the fund offers concentrated exposure to that cycle rather than the steadier broad technology sector.
KMID: Mid sized US companies picked for quality and reasonable prices by a long tenured boutique manager, with industrials about half the fund. It aims to grow with mid caps while taking less risk than the mid cap market overall, favoring durable businesses over hot stories.
KMLM: Futures contracts on commodities, currencies and global bonds, following a rules-based trend approach that goes long or short depending on recent price direction. It's meant as a diversifier that can profit when markets fall, but it can lag badly when trends reverse quickly or stay choppy.
KNCT: Technology companies, with about 86% in tech and 10% in communication, that supply the equipment, chips and software behind faster networks, wireless and connected devices. It's a focused bet on one technology theme, so it swings more than the broad market when tech sentiment shifts.
KNG: Established US companies that have raised dividends for many years, led by consumer staples, industrials and financials, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for extra income. It aims for steadier payouts, but it trails in strong rallies.
KNGZ: Large US companies from the S&P 500 that have steadily kept paying dividends, picked by a First Trust index with limits to keep any one stock from dominating. It leans toward technology, with Qualcomm, HP and Texas Instruments each around 4% of it.
KNO: Companies picked from across the developed world for how much they invest in innovation and know-how, spread over industrial, technology and health care firms. It is an actively run stock-picking fund, so its country and industry mix shifts with where the manager finds ideas.
KNOV: Options on a small company index fund, set up to absorb part of any loss over a year-long outcome period that resets each November. In return, gains are capped, and it holds options rather than the small stocks themselves, so it behaves differently from owning them.
KNOW: An actively managed mix of stocks and some bonds, using a buy-and-hold approach and picking companies based on fundamentals. It holds a lot of industrials and energy as well as technology, and it can invest globally rather than only in the US.
KNRG: Debt and preferred shares issued by energy and infrastructure companies, such as pipelines and power producers, mostly bonds with some preferred and convertible securities. It aims to pay income from that corner of the market, so it can fall when energy prices or credit conditions sour.
KOCT: Small US companies with a built-in cushion: it absorbs a set amount of losses on the Russell 2000 over a year starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. Health care, financials and technology lead the mix, and the protection only works if held for the full year.
KOID: Companies building humanoid robots and the technology behind physical AI, such as chips, sensors and automation equipment, split between technology and industrials. It's a narrow bet on a young industry, so it can swing far more than the broad market.
KOKU: Large companies from developed countries other than Japan, mostly the US, with technology about a third, then financials, industrials and health care. It works as a core global stock holding for someone who already owns Japanese stocks separately.
KOMP: Companies tied to new technologies like artificial intelligence, robotics, genomics and 3D printing, spread across technology, industrials and health care. It's a bet on innovation and growth, with equal-sized stakes in many firms, so it swings more than the broad market.
KONG: Large and midsize US companies with fortress-like qualities: strong balance sheets, durable positions and steady cash generation, across technology, industry and health care. It is a quality-first core holding that favors companies built to survive storms, accepting it may trail flashier stocks in strong rallies.
KOOL: An actively managed fund that moves among US and foreign stocks, sector ETFs and stock market groups depending on where the manager sees opportunity. It spreads money widely, with no holding above about 6%, and the mix changes with views.
KORP: A broad mix of corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with a small amount of preferred stock. It's meant for steady interest income above Treasuries as part of a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
KPHO: Vietnamese stocks listed on the Ho Chi Minh City exchange, following a Vietnam index. It leans heavily on banks, which are about three quarters of the fund, and a Vietnam ETF alone is roughly a quarter of it.
KPO: An actively managed options fund that builds synthetic exposure to the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, taking part in some of their gains. Most of the fund sits in bonds and cash as backing, so returns come from the options rather than owning the stocks.
KPRO: Chinese internet companies held through a sister fund plus options designed to protect against the whole of a fall over the period ending in January 2027. In exchange, gains are capped, making it the most defensive way in this family to hold China's internet giants.
KQQQ: Large technology companies, with communication and consumer businesses behind them, plus options that earn extra income. It's built to pay income from tech stocks, but the options limit gains in big rallies and it still falls when tech sells off.
KRBN: Futures contracts on carbon emission allowances, the permits companies buy under government cap-and-trade programs, backed by Treasury bills and cash. It's a niche bet on carbon prices rather than a stock fund, so it can move very differently from stocks and bonds.
KRE: Regional US banks, from small community lenders to mid-sized ones, with almost nothing outside banking. It's a focused bet on the banking sector, so it swings more than big-bank funds and can drop sharply when there are worries about loans or deposits.
KROP: Companies modernizing farming and food: tractor and machinery makers, seed and crop science, fertilizers and food innovators around the world. It is a bet on feeding more people with fewer resources, tied to farm incomes and crop prices.
KRYP: The 20 largest and most traded crypto assets, reached through futures and other financial instruments rather than by holding coins directly. It is a broad crypto basket in one fund: bitcoin and its biggest rivals move it most, and futures pricing can drift from spot prices.
KSA: Saudi Arabian stocks, with banks and financials making up over 40%, followed by energy, materials and communication companies. It's a focused bet on a single country and a market tied to oil, so it can swing far more than a broad global fund.
KSEP: Options on a small company index fund that cushion part of any loss over a year-long outcome period resetting each September. The cushion costs upside, since gains are capped, and the options make it steadier but less responsive than owning small company stocks outright.
KSLV: Silver exposure through silver-linked funds and derivatives, with much of the money in bonds and cash, plus an options strategy for extra income. It's a bet on silver prices with income on top, but the options limit gains when silver surges.
KSMH: South Korean companies focused on artificial intelligence semiconductors: the chipmakers and equipment firms producing AI memory and processors. It is a single-country, single-industry bet even narrower than a general chip fund, riding both the AI boom and the Korean market.
KSPY: Large US companies with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths, paired with a hedging strategy that reduces exposure when a market signal suggests more risk. It's built to cushion drops in stocks, but it can trail in strong rallies if the hedge cuts gains.
KSTR: Chinese companies listed on Shanghai's tech board, with about 90 percent in technology, mostly chip makers and other advanced hardware and software. It's a focused growth bet on China's tech push, so it swings far more than the broad market and carries risks tied to China.
KTEC: The thirty largest technology companies listed in Hong Kong: internet platforms, e-commerce, phone and chip makers and other Chinese tech leaders. Consumer and media names bulk large alongside pure tech, making it a concentrated bet on China's internet economy and its regulators.
KURE: Health care companies from across China, including drug makers, medical devices and hospitals. It's a focused bet on one industry in one country, so it swings more than the broad market and is exposed to Chinese policy and regulation.
KVLE: Dividend-paying US companies selected using Value Line's research rankings, which favor financially steady firms with reliable payouts. Technology and property companies lead the mix, an unusual blend for an income fund, and the rules-based screen aims for dividends that can grow.
KWEB: Chinese internet companies such as online retailers, social media and gaming firms, with communication and consumer companies about 70% and technology about a sixth. It's a focused bet on one industry in one country, so it swings far more than the broad market and reacts to Chinese regulation.
KWH: Companies that build and run power infrastructure: utilities, grid equipment makers, engineering firms and energy suppliers, positioned for rising electricity demand worldwide. It is a focused bet on electrification, from data centers to electric vehicles, so it moves with energy and industrial cycles.
KWIN: An index fund of US stocks, in this case technology based, chosen to meet Islamic investing rules and designed to pay income. It is very concentrated: Sandisk alone is about 22%, and AMD, Fortinet and CrowdStrike add roughly another 26%.
KWT: Companies listed in Kuwait, following the MSCI All Kuwait Select Size Liquidity Capped Index, which limits how much any one stock can take up. It is concentrated in banks: National Bank of Kuwait and Kuwait Finance House are each over 20% of it, and financials are about two thirds.
KXI: Global makers and sellers of everyday goods, such as food, drinks, household products and grocery chains, almost entirely consumer staples. It's a defensive holding that tends to fall less in downturns, though it usually lags when the market is racing ahead.
KYC: Digital banking and fintech infrastructure: payment networks, app-based banks and the software firms that run modern finance behind the scenes. It is a focused bet on banking moving to phones and software, split between financial companies and technology firms, so it swings with both sectors.
KYLD: Listed stocks from around the world plus an active options program, combined to chase high income from premiums and dividends. Technology and industrial metals are among its larger stock slices, and the options overlay means it gives up some market gains to keep the payouts coming.
LADM: A ladder of twelve monthly buffer funds on the S&P 500, each with moderate protection and its own start date, held in one package. Laddering spreads the timing risk across the year: some protection is always fresh, and no single start date decides the whole outcome.
LALT: A mix of strategies meant to move differently than stocks and bonds, with about half in cash and the rest in stocks, bonds and other investments. It's built to diversify and soften swings, so it may lag when stocks soar.
LAPR: Holds Treasury bills and options on an S&P 500 fund to produce monthly income while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each April. The trade-off is that the options limit how much of the market's gains it can capture.
LATR: Payment networks, digital wallets and checkout lenders: the companies behind buy now, pay later and other installment credit offered when shoppers pay. Financial companies are about two-thirds of the fund, so it is a focused bet on shoppers splitting purchases into payments instead of using traditional credit cards.
LAZR: Companies that make lasers, optical chips and the light-based parts inside data centers, phone networks and factory sensors, almost entirely in technology. It is a narrow bet on photonics, the use of light to move data, so a small and fast-changing industry drives the whole fund.
LBAY: A long and short portfolio of income-producing alternatives to bonds, such as dividend stocks, preferred shares and property-related securities. Going both long and short aims to keep income flowing with smaller market swings, though it can lag when stocks climb steadily.
LBO: Publicly traded private equity firms: the big buyout managers whose shares anyone can buy, making up nearly the whole fund. It offers a way to own the private equity business itself, collecting fees and deal profits, without locking money up for years.
LBOX: Box spreads, combinations of options that lock in a small, known payoff at expiry, much like lending money until a set date. It is a cash-like parking spot: returns are modest and steady by design, and it deliberately avoids stock market direction altogether.
LCAP: Mostly large US companies picked by active managers, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40 percent, then financials and health care. It's a core growth-leaning holding, though the manager's picks can make it behave differently from the broad market.
LCDS: Large, established US companies chosen with a data-science-driven version of fundamental research, blending statistics with analyst judgment. Technology leads at about two fifths, making it a core holding with a growth tilt and an analytical edge as its claim to difference.
LCF: An actively managed fund holding a focused group of large US companies, picked by the managers rather than by an index. It leans heavily on tech and communication, with Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft together around 30% of the fund.
LCIV: Large foreign companies bought through US-listed depositary receipts, screened for value, with financials, energy, health care and consumer brands all represented. Using receipts avoids foreign exchanges and currencies directly, though the stocks still move with their home markets.
LCLG: Large US growth companies chosen by active managers, with technology about two-fifths and a meaningful slice of industrial and consumer firms alongside. It is a stock picker's growth fund rather than an index hugger, so results hinge on the managers' choices and can stray far from the market.
LCO: A contrarian mix picked by hand: a few dozen stocks the manager sees as out of favor, with technology, energy and materials on top, plus small helpings of bonds and metals. It goes against the crowd on purpose, so it can lag popular markets for long stretches before its picks pay off.
LCOW: Big US companies with a rare cash record: at least ten straight years of positive free cash flow, plus high cash margins and returns on capital. It is a quality-focused core holding that screens for proven cash generators rather than size or cheapness, and technology cash machines feature heavily.
LCR: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs covering US stocks, sectors and inflation protected bonds. The managers shift the mix over time based on their view of the market, so it is not a fixed index.
LCTD: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, picked by managers to lean toward firms better prepared for the shift to lower carbon. It's a core international holding that aims to beat its benchmark, but it behaves like the foreign stock market.
LCTO: Large US companies, reached mainly through a broad index fund, paired with municipal bonds and options in a structure designed to be tax-efficient. The idea is stock market growth with a smaller tax bill, so it fits taxable accounts, though the bond side can mute returns in strong rallies.
LCTU: Large US companies chosen by a manager to beat the broad market while tilting toward firms better prepared for a lower-carbon economy. Technology is about two fifths, so it's a core stock holding that is heavier in tech than the average fund.
LDDR: US Treasury bonds and government money market funds, arranged as an income bucket meant to pay out steady monthly income through 2035. Backed entirely by government debt, it trades growth for predictability, like a self-built pension with a fixed end year.
LDEM: Emerging market companies that score well on environmental, social and governance measures, led by Asian chip makers, internet firms and banks. The ESG screen trims the usual emerging market lineup, though it still swings like one, with extra movement from currencies.
LDRC: A ladder of corporate bond funds that each mature in a set year, spread evenly from 2027 through 2031, then rolled forward as years pass. Laddering spreads interest rate risk across maturities, giving a steadier, more predictable version of short-term corporate bond income.
LDRH: A ladder of iShares term bond funds holding high yield and other income corporate bonds maturing across the next one to five years. Spreading end dates smooths the ride versus a single-year fund, paying junk bond interest while each rung matures and rolls into new bonds.
LDRI: A ladder built from several inflation-protected bond funds, each maturing in a different year within a one to five year span. It spreads TIPS exposure across near-term dates for inflation-adjusted income with modest price swings, and the ladder rolls forward as the nearest funds reach their end.
LDRT: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to five years, spaced evenly like rungs on a ladder. It's a low-risk, short-term holding for stable income and safety, and since each rung matures and gets replaced, it reacts only a little to interest rate changes.
LDRX: Large US companies led by technology at nearly half, with communication, financials and consumer names behind it, plus an enhancement strategy managed by professionals. It's a growth-leaning stock fund, so it moves a lot like the tech-heavy market and can fall hard when tech does.
LDSF: A mix of other bond funds focused on short maturities of about three years or less, aiming for income with a steadier price. Because short bonds are less sensitive to interest rates, it falls less than longer bond funds when rates rise, though it earns less.
LDUR: Mostly bonds that mature soon, managed actively by PIMCO, with some flexibility to add other bond types for extra income. It aims for steady income with small price swings, so it's a cushion that is calmer than regular bond funds, but it earns less than longer bonds.
LEGR: Companies around blockchain technology, with about half in financial firms and a fifth in technology, plus communication and consumer names. It's a themed bet on how digital record-keeping reshapes business, and it swings with how excited the market is about crypto and blockchain adoption.
LEMB: Government bonds from emerging countries, issued in each country's own currency instead of dollars. It's built for high income and diversification, but its value swings with exchange rates, and a strong dollar tends to hurt it.
LEND: A mix of lower-rated corporate bonds and loans from alternative lenders, with real estate and communication companies among the borrowers. It's meant for high income, but the borrowers are riskier, so it can lose value when the economy weakens.
LENS: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies and assets tied to themes the manager thinks are poised for growth. Right now it leans heavily on gold, silver and energy: gold funds, miners and Chevron and Exxon make up much of the top holdings.
LEXI: A flexible mix of mostly stocks, led by technology, plus a good chunk of bonds, with the freedom to also hold commodities and real estate. It's a hands-on, all-in-one fund where the manager shifts between asset types, so its mix can change as markets do.
LFAI: US Treasury bonds arranged to pay a regular income meant to last through 2055, funding spending late into life. It is built for very long retirements: steady government-backed payments for decades, though its distant horizon means prices move with interest rates.
LFAO: US Treasury bonds arranged to pay regular income through 2055, designed to fund spending deep into later life. It offers decades of government-backed payments, though prices along the way move with interest rates and the horizon is very long.
LFAW: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income through the year 2060, like a pension you can buy in a fund. It is built for very long-term income planning: payments are the point, and the distant end date sets it apart.
LFBE: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income through the year 2065, the longest horizon in its family of income funds. It is built for lifelong income planning: the payments are the product, set on a schedule that runs for decades.
LFDR: Long-term US Treasury bonds, the safest borrowers in the market, held to pay a steady stream of income over many years. Because the bonds are long-term, the price moves a lot when interest rates change, even though the income itself is backed by the US government.
