LFEQ: Large US stocks when a trend model says be invested, and cash-like safety when it says step aside: the Ned Davis model behind it flips between long and flat. It is a defensive core holding for investors who want the market's gains with an automatic exit in downtrends.
LFGY: A basket of crypto and technology companies, bitcoin miners, payment firms and chipmakers, with call options sold against the holdings to generate income. It turns a volatile corner of the market into a payout stream, giving up some upside when crypto stocks surge.
LFSC: Life science companies, such as drug developers, medical technology and research firms, all in health care, chosen by active managers. It's a focused bet on innovation in medicine, and these smaller research-driven firms can swing more than the broad market.
LGDS: Large US growth companies chosen by a data-driven model that looks at company fundamentals, with technology at more than half and communication near a fifth. It's built for growth, so it swings harder than the broad market and is heavy in tech.
LGDX: Large US companies in the S&P 500, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent. A computer model adjusts weights to try to beat the index, so it works as a core stock holding that may behave differently from a plain index fund.
LGH: Mostly large US companies in the style of the S&P 500, led by technology at over 40%, with some money held in other assets that adjust its risk. It's a core stock holding that adds a defensive twist, so it may behave differently from a plain market fund in sharp drops.
LGHT: Healthcare technology companies from around the world, from medical software and devices to digital health services, at any company size. It is a focused growth bet on medicine going digital: it can grow fast, but health tech swings with regulation and hospital spending.
LGLV: Large US companies picked because their shares have swung less than most, with industrials, real estate, financials and utilities leading. It's built for a smoother ride and tends to fall less in sell-offs, but it often trails in strong rallies led by technology.
LGOV: Long-term US government and government-backed bonds. It's a bet on safety from default and a cushion when stocks fall, but with such long maturities its price swings a lot, dropping sharply when interest rates rise and gaining when they fall.
LGRO: Large US growth companies hand-picked by a manager, with technology a bit over half and consumer, communication and financial firms behind. It aims for growth, so it can rise faster in good times but fall harder than the broad market in sell-offs.
LIAE: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, known as TIPS, arranged to pay steady income that rises with inflation through 2050. It targets later-life spending decades away, protecting buying power over the whole journey rather than chasing the highest payouts today.
LIAM: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, known as TIPS, arranged to pay a steady income that keeps pace with inflation through 2055. It is built for very long horizons, funding later-life spending with payments designed not to lose buying power over the decades.
LIAU: Treasury inflation-protected securities arranged to pay out a stream of income through 2060, with payments that rise alongside consumer prices. It pairs a pension-style payout schedule with inflation protection: the point is dependable real income for decades, not growth.
LIBD: Treasury inflation-protected bonds set up to pay income through 2065, an unusually long runway aimed at funding spending very late in life. The payments adjust with inflation, so buying power is the priority, though the far-off horizon makes prices rate sensitive.
LIFT: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income ending in 2028, with the schedule set in advance. It is an income planning tool for a near horizon: the fixed end date makes payouts predictable, and it behaves more like a maturing bond than a regular fund.
LIGB: Long-dated investment-grade corporate bonds: loans to solid companies with at least ten years until they come due. Long maturities pay a bit more interest than shorter bonds, but the price swings much more when interest rates move, so it is a bolder core bond holding.
LIT: Companies across the lithium and battery chain, from miners and chemical makers to battery and electric vehicle parts makers. Materials are nearly half, with industrials and technology next, so it's a focused bet on one theme that swings far more than the broad market.
LITL: Small US companies, mostly health care, technology and banks, combined with an options overlay designed to add regular income. The mix aims for small-company growth plus payouts, a pairing most small-cap funds do not offer.
LITP: Lithium miners and explorers from around the world, the companies digging out the key ingredient of rechargeable batteries. It is a leveraged play on electric vehicle demand in effect, since lithium prices, and these small miners, swing violently with the battery cycle.
LJAN: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 to produce regular income while absorbing part of the market's losses over a set one-year period. Its gains are limited, so it will not fully follow a strong market rally.
LJUL: Uses US Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income and a cushion against part of the market's losses over a one-year period starting in July. Gains are limited, and the cushion only applies if you hold for the full period.
LKOR: Long-term US corporate bonds, all investment grade, screened by Northern Trust for sound credit, fair value and strong balance sheets. Picking quality long bonds is the twist: it aims for income with less credit risk than a plain long corporate fund, though long maturities still swing when rates move.
LLDR: US Treasury bonds in a ladder stretching from ten to thirty years, with slices maturing steadily along the way. Long government bonds pay dependable income and often rally when stocks crash, but their prices sink hard when long-term rates rise.
LLMA: Companies that build large language models, the AI systems behind chatbots: the firms researching, training and deploying their own models and products built on them. It is a focused bet on the model makers themselves rather than the wider AI supply chain, so it rides a young and fast-changing field.
LMBS: Mortgage-backed bonds and similar debt chosen to keep a short average life, with some cash. It's for income with less sensitivity to interest rates than regular mortgage bonds, though an active manager's choices mean it can differ from a standard index.
LMUB: Long-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments, nearly all investment grade, with interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It suits higher earners wanting tax-free income, but the long maturities mean its price falls noticeably when interest rates rise.
LNGX: US natural gas companies: the producers that drill for gas and the pipeline firms that move it, all energy stocks rather than gas futures. It rises and falls with natural gas prices and drilling activity, a direct industry bet that moves differently from the fuel itself.
LOCT: Holds Treasury bills and options on an S&P 500 fund to produce monthly income while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each October. The options also limit how much of the market's gains it can capture.
LODI: Short-term US bonds and income securities, mixing Treasuries with car loan bundles and corporate debt that matures soon, all actively managed. Short maturities mean its price barely moves when interest rates change, making it a steadier income holding than longer-term bond funds.
LOEV: A select portfolio of companies in developed markets outside the US, banks, oil, insurers and industrial leaders across Europe and Japan, picked for quality and growth at reasonable prices. Harding Loevner's managers hold a focused list with patience, so stock picking drives results.
LOGO: Leading consumer brands from around the world, the companies behind what people buy, eat, watch and wear, picked actively. Brand strength is the thesis: famous names can charge more and keep customers, making this a quality-tilted bet on global spending.
LOHA: Companies built on heavy assets that are hard to replace: pipelines, factories, stores, ships and other long lived physical plant, across industry, retail, energy and food. The idea favors businesses protected by the sheer cost of copying them, a sturdier corner of the stock market.
LONZ: Loans made to lower-rated companies, where the lender gets repaid before other creditors, with interest that adjusts as rates change. It aims for higher income than regular bonds, and its price holds up better when rates rise, but it can suffer when borrowers struggle to repay.
LOPP: US companies that pass Gabelli's sustainability guidelines, mostly industrial firms working in energy, water, waste and efficient equipment. It blends environmental goals with old-economy businesses, so it looks more like a factory and utility portfolio than a solar fund.
LOTI: A balanced tactical mix: dividend leaning stocks, with health care and utilities among them, plus bond funds, shifting the split as the manager reads markets. It aims for income with moderate growth, and the tactical freedom means its risk level can drift up or down over time.
LOUP: Companies working on new technologies like AI, cloud, robotics and data, with technology about two thirds and industrials next. It's a growth bet on the cutting edge, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply when tech falls out of favor.
LOWV: US large companies, led by technology at close to two fifths, then financials and health care, chosen for steadier price swings. It aims to be a smoother core stock holding that usually falls less in sell-offs, but it tends to trail in strong rallies.
LPRE: A hand-picked group of companies tied to real estate, with real estate firms like property owners about 60% and consumer businesses such as homebuilders and lodging about 40%. It's a focused bet on the property economy, and holding fewer stocks means it can swing more than a typical real estate fund.
LPSV: Small and midsize US companies that look cheap relative to their earnings and assets, picked one by one by an active manager. It aims for the long-run payoff of value investing in smaller companies, which can mean years of lagging the big growth stocks before the style comes back.
LQ: A mix of alternative strategies beyond plain stocks and bonds, chosen with taxes in mind for investors in higher brackets. It is a diversifier meant to zig when markets zag, and its tax-aware design sets it apart from most alternative funds, which often create messy tax bills.
LQAI: Large US stocks chosen with help from artificial intelligence models that scan company data for likely winners, led by technology at a bit over a third. It is a core equity holding with a machine doing the analysis: the AI tilt sets it apart, but it still moves with the market.
LQD: Bonds issued by large, financially sound US companies, spread across many industries. It's meant for steady interest income with more yield than government bonds, but it carries some risk of company defaults, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
LQDB: Corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade, issued by banks, carmakers, drug companies and other big borrowers across many industries. That bottom tier pays more interest than safer company debt, and it sits closest to junk status, so downgrades are the risk to watch.
LQDH: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds paired with interest rate swaps that cancel out most of the damage from rising rates. It's for people who want corporate bond income without as much interest-rate risk, though it gives up the gains when rates fall.
LQDI: Investment grade US corporate bonds, held mainly through another iShares bond fund, combined with contracts that offset the effect of rising inflation on bond prices. It aims to give the return of corporate bonds with less sensitivity to inflation and interest rates.
LQDM: Investment-grade corporate bonds, reached through a big bond fund, plus call options sold every week to target a 12 percent yearly income rate. It turns steady bond holdings into an aggressive payout machine, with the option selling adding risk plain bonds do not have.
LQDW: Investment-grade corporate bonds, which are loans to large, stable companies, combined with an options strategy that earns extra monthly income. It's for people wanting higher payouts from bonds, but it gives up some price gains when bond prices rise.
LQID: Ultra-short bonds and cash-like funds, Treasury bills, short bond funds and top-rated loan funds, plus an options strategy on bonds to add income. It aims to beat money market returns slightly, taking a small step up in risk for extra yield.
LQTI: Short-term investment-grade corporate bonds exposure, managed with a call options strategy for extra income. It aims for steady monthly payouts, but the options cap how much it gains when bond prices rise.
LRGC: Large US companies chosen by active managers, with technology about a third, then financials, communication and industrials. It aims to be a core stock holding that beats the broad market, but since managers choose the holdings, results can differ from the market.
LRGE: Large US growth companies chosen by a manager who also looks at environmental and social factors, with technology about half the fund. It's built for growth, so it can rise faster than the broad market, but it also drops harder when tech falls.
LRGF: Large US companies chosen for traits like value, quality, momentum and low size, with technology about two fifths and financials, health care and consumer companies behind. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward those traits, and it can trail the broad market when they fall out of favor.
LRGG: A small group of large US growth companies, led by technology at about 46 percent, with financials, health care and communication following. It's built for growth, and because it holds so few stocks, it can swing more than the broad market.
LRND: Large US companies that spend heavily on research and development, led by technology at about 60% and communication around a fifth. It's built for growth, with few companies from slow moving industries, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
LRNZ: Companies building artificial intelligence and deep learning tools, mostly software, cybersecurity and data firms, plus some health technology names. It is an actively managed, focused bet on AI, so its smaller technology stocks can swing sharply with the sector.
LSAF: Mid-sized US companies picked by a computer model that ranks stocks on several factors, spread across consumer, financial, technology and industrial businesses. It's a rules-based way to hold the middle of the market, and it can lag when the model's favored traits go out of style.
LSAT: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies, picked using a rules-based model that scores stocks on several factors. It is spread across financials, consumer and tech companies, with no single holding above about 5% of the fund.
LSCP: A core plus bond portfolio run dynamically by a veteran bond team: government, corporate and mortgage bonds of any maturity, with its interest rate stance kept near the broad bond market's. The active tilts aim to add return over a plain core fund, for better or worse.
LSEQ: Long and short positions in US stocks, buying companies the managers favor and betting against those they do not, across health care, materials and technology. The short side is meant to soften market drops, though it also trims gains in rallies.
LSGR: A concentrated mix of large US growth companies, with technology about a third, communication companies about a quarter, and consumer and health care firms filling out most of the rest. It's built for long-term growth, and because it holds relatively few stocks, it can swing more than the broad market.
LST: US companies of all sizes, with technology a third, health care a fifth, and financials and energy after that. A manager picks the industries that look most promising and skips the rest, so it's a growth-minded fund that can look quite different from the broad market.
LSTB: Bonds of all kinds picked by a storied bond shop: government debt, corporate bonds, mortgages and more, managed for total return rather than just income. The managers roam across sectors and maturities, making it a flexible core holding whose bets drive its results.
LSVD: Large US value stocks chosen by a computer model, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, then communication, consumer and financial companies. It aims for cheap-looking companies, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
LTAX: Long-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. The long maturities mean higher tax-free payouts but prices that move a lot when interest rates change, so it suits investors in high tax brackets.
LTB: US Treasury bonds with at least twenty years until they mature, the longest-dated debt of the world's safest borrower. Long bonds pay interest for decades and cushion stock portfolios in panics, but their prices swing the most of any Treasury fund when interest rates move.
LTCC: Direct ownership of Litecoin, a long-running cryptocurrency designed as a faster, lighter alternative to bitcoin, held as the fund's only asset. It moves with crypto sentiment generally and Litecoin's own adoption, and sharp daily swings are normal.
LTPZ: US government bonds that adjust with inflation, all with long lives of 15 years or more. It's a hedge against rising prices, but the long length means the price swings a lot, and it drops sharply when interest rates rise.
LTTI: Long-term US Treasury bonds, those maturing in more than 20 years, combined with options on a long Treasury fund to generate target income. Long Treasuries swing hard when rates move, and the option overlay adds payouts without removing that rate risk.
LUMA: A fund of companies working in photonics and optics, the technology that uses light for things like data transfer and sensors. Holdings include Soitec, Lumentum and Marvell, with the top few each around 6% to 7%, and nearly all of it is technology.
LUNC: A worldwide portfolio of what its managers call misclassified compounders: profitable companies they believe the market has filed in the wrong category. Unusually for a global fund, raw materials and energy together make up almost two thirds, so it behaves more like a resources fund than a broad world index.
LVDS: Large US companies picked with data-driven analysis of business fundamentals, hunting for stocks priced below what the numbers suggest they are worth. Technology is its biggest slice at about a fifth, unusual for a value fund, and it blends number crunching with old-fashioned company research.
LVHD: US stocks picked for steady prices and high dividends, so utilities, consumer staples and real estate dominate while technology is scarce. It's built for income and a smoother ride, which means it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
LVHI: Stocks from developed countries outside the US that pay high dividends and have steadier prices, led by financials, energy, industrials and consumer staples. It's built for income and a smoother ride abroad, and it hedges currency, so moves in the dollar matter less to returns.
LVIG: A mix of other bond funds that together cover mainly US investment grade bonds, with a small slice in other holdings. It's a core bond holding for income and stability, run by managers who adjust the mix, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
LYLD: About 100 large US companies chosen by Cambria's model for returning cash to shareholders through dividends, share buybacks and paying down debt. It is actively managed with no company above about 3%, and it leans toward financials, energy and health care.
LYTE: Technology companies that make lasers, optical parts and light-based communication gear used in data centers, sensors and similar devices. It's a focused bet on one corner of tech, so it swings more than the broad market and a small group of companies drives results.
MAAY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to MARA, a bitcoin mining company, built to harvest its huge price swings as payouts. It is a high-risk trade: leverage resets and capped gains mean a crypto downturn can produce steep losses.
MADE: US manufacturing companies: makers of farm and construction machinery, electrical equipment, engines, tools and factory gear, with industrials about three quarters of the fund. It is a direct bet on American factory output and the push to build more at home, so it rises and falls with industrial demand.
MAGA: US companies selected by a political lens: the index favors firms whose employees and political committees give most heavily to Republican candidates and America First causes. Industrials, banks and energy lead the mix, making it a values-driven bet that also tilts toward old-economy industries.
MAGC: China's answer to the Magnificent Seven: the seven giant Chinese technology companies, spanning e-commerce, gaming, electric vehicles and internet platforms. It is a highly concentrated bet on China's tech champions, so it swings with Chinese consumer spending, Beijing's regulation and the mood toward Chinese stocks abroad.
MAGG: An actively managed fund of US investment grade bonds, similar in scope to the broad US bond market. A large part is in US Treasuries, with the rest mainly in corporate and mortgage bonds, and the managers choose bonds rather than following an index.
MAGS: Roughly equal bets on the seven mega tech companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla. It's a concentrated growth bet on a tiny group, so it swings more than the broad market, and it can't spread risk the way a diversified fund does.
MAGY: The Magnificent Seven, the small group of giant technology stocks that dominate the modern market, with call options sold against them every week for income. Weekly option premiums are the point, so it pays out steadily while giving up part of the gains when those stocks jump.
MAMB: A mix of bonds across credit qualities and lengths, including corporate, high yield, Treasury and municipal bonds, with a small slice of convertibles. It aims to provide income from a wide range of fixed income, and the lower-rated bonds in it add extra risk compared with a pure investment-grade fund.
MANI: Debt across the whole credit spectrum, from sturdy borrowers to speculative ones, actively managed by Man Group including through derivatives. It is a flexible income holding that leans on the managers' judgment about where in the credit world the pay is worth the risk at any given time.
MARM: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged for the strongest level of loss protection in its family over a one-year period resetting each March. That max buffer comes with a lower cap on gains, suiting investors who put avoiding losses ahead of chasing rallies.
MARO: An options income strategy tied to MARA, a bitcoin mining company, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting option premiums for payouts. It rises and falls with one volatile crypto linked stock, and its gains are capped, so the income is the point.
MARS: Space industry companies: rocket launchers, satellite makers and operators, space infrastructure and the technology suppliers behind them, mostly industrial firms. It is a focused bet on the commercial space race, a young industry where a few contract wins or launch failures move prices sharply.
MART: Options on a fund of the largest US companies match its returns over one year from March, buffering the first 10 percent of losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms are set each March, so it is a defined-window holding for investors who want stock exposure with known protection.
MARU: Options on the S&P 500 set to absorb the first part of a market drop over a one-year period starting in March, with a 15% buffer in the design. Unlike capped buffers, gains beyond a small starting spread are unlimited, the feature in its Uncapped name.
MARW: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over a one-year period running from March to February. In exchange for that deep buffer it accepts a cap on gains, suiting investors who fear a serious downturn most.
MARZ: Options on the S&P 500 that cushion part of a market fall over an outcome period restarting each March, in exchange for some upside. It is part of a monthly series of structured outcome funds, each with its own starting point and protection level.
MATE: Mostly a big US stock fund at its core, with a trend-following program layered on top that trades futures across world markets. The overlay tries to add returns and soften drops by following market trends, making it more complex than a plain stock fund.
MATR: An actively managed mix of other ETFs spread across US stocks, international stocks and bonds, with the mix shifted based on the manager's view of the economy. About 70% sits in stocks, with the S&P 500 as the biggest piece.
MAUG: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. It is one edition of a monthly series, and the August start date matters because the protection terms were locked in then.
MAVF: Large US companies their managers judge undervalued, which in practice includes many big technology names alongside banks and consumer firms. It is an active value fund willing to buy growth stocks when they look cheap, so its lineup often resembles a blend fund more than a classic value portfolio.
MAXI: It aims for bitcoin exposure that can range from about half to twice the fund's size, held through bitcoin funds and options, alongside an income strategy. That variable leverage makes it far wilder than simply holding bitcoin, closer to a trading tool than an investment.
MAXJ: A mix of options and cash-like holdings tied to large US companies, built to absorb the first big chunk of losses over a one year period starting in June. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if held for the full period.
MAYC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. The May start fixes the terms: buyers later in the period get whatever protection time remains.
MAYM: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for the deepest loss protection the options market allows over a year starting in May, as the Max Buffer name suggests. With protection maxed out, the cap on gains is low, so it barely joins in during strong rallies.
MAYP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each May, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every May.
MAYT: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about forty percent, held through options that cushion some stock market losses. It's for people who want stock exposure with a built-in buffer, but it caps the gains, and the protection runs on a yearly cycle starting in May.
MAYU: Options on the S&P 500 set up so the fund absorbs the first part of a market drop over its one year period, which runs from May. In exchange, gains on the way up are unlimited past a small starting gap, unlike capped buffer funds.
MAYW: A set of options tied to large US companies, with technology around 40%. It's built to take the first 20% of losses over a one year period starting in May, but it caps how much you can gain, so it's meant to be held for the full period.
MAYZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to soften part of any market drop over an outcome period that restarts each May, at the cost of capped participation. Investors who buy mid-period get different protection than those who start at the reset date.
MBB: Bonds made of pooled home loans that are guaranteed by the US government or its agencies. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though its price drops when rates rise and homeowners refinancing can change its payments.
MBBA: Home mortgage bonds, mostly backed by government-linked agencies, chosen by an active manager. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though its price drops when interest rates rise and homeowners' refinancing patterns can shorten payouts.
MBBB: Corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest investment-grade tier, screened with Moody's analytics to favor issuers less likely to be downgraded. They pay more than top-rated bonds, and the quality screen sets it apart from plain BBB funds that buy the whole tier.
MBCE: Blue chip companies, the large established names picked by Monarch's index, which at the moment reaches well beyond old-economy giants into chipmakers and online retail. It is a core-style large company holding, though its current tilt toward technology makes it livelier than a traditional blue chip fund.
MBND: Intermediate municipal bonds from across the US, selected with Nuveen's muni expertise for a State Street fund. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, so it serves as a core tax-free income holding, with professional credit research doing the work an index cannot.
MBOX: US dividend-paying companies picked because the manager expects their payouts to keep growing, spread across financials, technology, energy and health care. It's meant for rising income over time, and its focus on payouts means it may trail in fast growth rallies.
MBS: Bonds backed by pools of home loans, with a limited amount of other asset-backed debt. It's meant for income above regular Treasuries and a cushion for stocks, but homeowners paying off early can change returns, and prices drop when interest rates rise.
MBSD: Mortgage bonds guaranteed by US agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the pooled home loans of American borrowers, managed with tight control over interest rate sensitivity. It aims for steady income a step above Treasuries, with its disciplined duration keeping price swings in check.
MBSF: Floating rate bonds backed by home mortgages, whose interest payments reset as short-term rates change. It's meant for income that adjusts to rates, with less price drop when interest rates rise than regular bonds, though it carries mortgage and credit risks.
MBSX: Fixed-rate mortgage bonds backed by US home loans and guaranteed by government-sponsored housing agencies. It pays monthly interest drawn from homeowner mortgage payments, with steadier quality than corporate debt but returns that shift as refinancing waves come and go.
MCDS: About 96% in mid-sized US companies, chosen by JPMorgan with data science models that rank stocks on value, quality and momentum. Holdings are very spread out, with no company much above 1% of the fund, across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
MCH: Actively managed Chinese stocks across Hong Kong, mainland and US listings, led by financials, with technology, internet and consumer companies behind. The managers hunt for companies that can keep growing for years, making it a core China holding with the usual political and currency risks.
MCHI: Large Chinese companies, with consumer businesses, financials, internet and communication firms and technology as the main groups. It's a focused bet on the Chinese economy, so it swings more than the US market and is sensitive to Chinese government policy and tensions with the West.
MCHS: Chinese companies picked as innovators in their products, technology or business models, mostly in industry and technology, from chip equipment to factory automation. It is a focused growth bet on China's inventive side, with the usual political and market risks of the region.
MCOW: Mid-sized US companies with at least seven straight years of positive free cash flow and strong cash returns, led by technology and industrials. It is a quality screen on the market's middle tier: the long cash-flow record is the filter, favoring proven mid-caps over speculative growers.
MCVT: Convertible bonds from companies with strong growth traits: debt that pays interest but can convert into stock if the company prospers. It is a hybrid holding that aims to join much of a growth stock's upside with a bond's floor under it, managed for total return.
MDAA: A mix that is mostly stocks right now, led by technology at about 40% and financials around 16%, with a manager free to shift between assets. It aims to be a flexible all in one holding, but its mix can change and may not match the market.
MDCR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in December, with gains capped in exchange. It is the December edition of a monthly series: the year-end start fixes its terms, and later buyers inherit what protection remains.
MDEV: Medical device companies: the makers of implants, surgical tools, scanners and patient monitors, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on medical technology rather than drug makers, growing with surgeries, aging populations and hospital spending.
MDIV: A mix of high-paying assets: about 60 percent stocks concentrated in energy and real estate, plus bonds and preferred shares, which are stock-like securities that pay set dividends. It's built for high income rather than growth, and it leans heavily on a few interest-sensitive industries.
MDLV: Large US companies that pay dividends and look cheaply priced, chosen by a small boutique manager across banks, industry, energy, utilities and more. It is an old fashioned value and income holding, favoring cash paying stalwarts over growth stories.
MDPL: Thirty US stocks in equal weights, chosen as dividend paying value stocks from a broad large and mid cap universe, spanning financial, technology, health care and other sectors. Equal weighting keeps any single company from dominating, and the dividend value tilt favors cheaper stocks that pay cash back.
MDST: Midstream energy companies that run oil and gas pipelines and storage, all counted as energy. It's built for high income, and an options strategy adds a bit more, but it moves with energy prices and can drop sharply in downturns.
MDY: Mid-sized US companies, larger than small caps but smaller than the giants, with industrials, technology, financials and health care leading. It's a core holding for the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
MDYG: Mid-sized US companies with faster growth, led by industrials and technology, followed by health care. It aims for growth beyond large companies without the full risk of tiny ones, and because growth stocks are priced for the future, it can drop hard when markets turn.
MDYV: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaply priced, led by financials and industrials, with consumer businesses and technology behind them. It's meant as a value-tilted core holding, and it often lags growth-driven rallies, since little of it is in high-flying technology.
MEAR: Short-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments, mostly investment grade, plus a bit of cash. It's meant as a stable place to park money with income that is exempt from federal income tax, and its short maturities keep price swings small.
MEDI: Health care companies of all sizes, from giant drug makers and biotech firms to device makers and drug distributors, picked actively. It is a focused bet on medicine and treatment spending, and a few large positions mean single company news can move it noticeably.
MEDX: Drugmakers and medical technology companies, from the biggest pharmaceutical firms to smaller research-driven names, mostly US and European. It is a concentrated health care portfolio, so drug trial results and pricing politics can move it more than the overall market.
MEIB: Income built around a single stock, Meta Platforms, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on one company: the strategy aims for income, but Meta's swings drive the result either way.
MEM: Emerging market stocks picked actively for sustainable growth, heavy in Asian technology with banks and consumer companies behind. It roams the developing world including China, so it offers broader emerging exposure with stock picking on top, and swings with those volatile markets.
MEMA: An actively managed fund holding stocks of companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and India, with some alternative strategy features. Chip makers dominate: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK hynix together are about 30% of it.
MEME: Meme stocks: companies caught up in social media frenzies, with heavy trading and extreme price swings driven by online attention. Holdings rotate toward whatever is trending, making this a speculation tool rather than an investment in the usual sense.
MEMS: Small companies across emerging markets, actively hunted by Matthews Asia specialists who look for undiscovered growers country by country. Industrials, technology and banks lead the mix, and the discovery approach means owning names most emerging market index funds have barely noticed yet.
MEMX: Emerging market stocks with China deliberately left out, led by Taiwan and Korean chipmakers, with banks the next biggest slice. It is a growth bet on the rest of the emerging world for investors who want that exposure without Chinese companies in the mix.
MEMY: Stocks that social media has turned into memes, the heavily hyped names retail traders pile into, paired with an options strategy for income. It is a deliberately speculative income trade: the underlying stocks swing on buzz rather than business results, so payouts and prices are both unstable.
METL: An actively managed fund of mining and metals companies, covering miners of copper and other industrial metals plus related firms such as drillers and steelmakers. The manager picks the stocks, and the holdings are fairly evenly spread, with no single company above about 5%.
METV: Companies building the metaverse, meaning virtual worlds and the games, social platforms, chips and hardware that power them. It's a narrow bet on a still-emerging theme, so it swings far more than the broad market and depends on that idea catching on.
METW: A single-stock trading fund aiming to deliver about 120 percent of Meta Platforms' return each calendar week, using swaps and shares, while paying weekly distributions. It resets its leverage weekly and rides entirely on one social media giant, so it suits short-term trades, not holding.
MFDX: Companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across industrials, financials, materials and technology. It picks stocks using several traits like value and size rather than just company size, so it's a way to add international stocks that differs from plain index funds.
MFEB: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in February, with gains capped in exchange. It is the February edition of a monthly series: the start month fixes the terms, so identical funds differ only by when their clock began.
MFEM: Stocks from emerging markets, with technology over a third, then financials and materials. It picks and weights companies using several measures such as value and quality, not just size, so it's a diversifier that can swing more than developed markets.
MFIG: A fund of large US companies the Motley Fool believes are innovative growth leaders, tracking a rules-based index. It is tilted to tech, with Broadcom, Amazon, Alphabet and Apple each around 5%, and technology is about half of the fund.
MFLX: Municipal bonds from states, cities and agencies across the US, reaching into lower-rated high yield munis as well as solid investment grade ones. The interest is exempt from federal income tax, and the flexible mandate lets the managers chase higher yields.
MFMO: US stocks with the strongest price momentum, picked by a Motley Fool index that favors recent winners, led by chip and technology names. Momentum strategies ride trends well but can crash when leadership flips, since yesterday's winners fall hardest.
MFSB: A manager-picked mix of corporate bonds, US government bonds, mortgage-backed securities and some riskier debt for extra yield. It's a core bond holding aiming for income and a bit more return than a plain index fund, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
MFSD: Short-term debt from governments, companies and securitized loans, managed by MFS for income with limited sensitivity to interest rate moves. It sits between a money market fund and a full bond fund: steadier than longer bonds, with a bit more yield and a bit more price movement.
MFSG: Large US growth companies chosen by a manager, with technology making up half the fund and communication about a seventh. It's built for growth, so it can rise faster than the broad market, but it also falls harder when tech stocks slide.
MFSI: Companies outside the US, led by financials at about a quarter, then technology and industrials, chosen by a manager rather than an index. It's for diversifying a US-heavy portfolio, and its results depend on the manager's choices and on currency moves.
MFSM: Municipal bonds from states, cities, schools and hospitals across the US, actively managed and mostly maturing in the intermediate range. Their interest is exempt from federal income tax, which sets this apart from taxable bond funds and makes it a common choice for higher earners investing outside retirement accounts.
MFSV: US companies that the managers believe are priced below their real worth, spread across financials, technology, health care and industrials. It's a core value holding that leans toward out-of-favor stocks, so it can trail growth-heavy funds when tech-led rallies run.
MFSX: Short-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. The short maturities keep price swings small when interest rates move, making it a tax-aware parking spot for cautious money.
MFUL: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and other ETFs, with a conservative tilt toward bonds, which are about 43% of the fund. It holds other ETFs such as floating-rate and 60/40 funds, so it is a ready-made blend in one ticker.
MFUS: US companies, led by technology, health care, financials and industrials, picked for several traits at once such as being cheap, high quality or rising in price. It's a core stock holding that favors cheaper companies, and its picks change with market conditions.
MFUT: An actively managed fund that follows market trends using futures contracts on things like stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long or short as trends change. It is meant to behave differently from plain stock and bond funds.
MFVL: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, chosen by a value approach across technology, health care, consumer and banking stocks. It is a bet that underpriced big companies catch up over time, so it can lag when growth stocks are hot.
MGC: The very largest US companies, with technology about 45 percent and communication, financials and health care behind. It's a core holding built around the giants, so it's more concentrated than a total-market fund and leans on a handful of big names.
MGIN: An actively managed fund of global companies that own or run infrastructure, such as utilities, transport and energy networks. The managers choose the holdings rather than following an index, so it can differ from a plain infrastructure index fund.
MGK: The very biggest US growth companies, with technology at nearly two thirds and communication and consumer firms behind. It's a concentrated growth bet on giants, so it can lead in tech rallies and fall harder than the broad market in sell-offs.
MGMT: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by a manager, spread across industrials, technology, energy and financials. It's a growth-oriented way to go beyond big companies, but smaller firms swing more than the broad market, and it can shift heavily into cash when the manager is cautious.
MGNR: Companies tied to natural resources, with more than half in miners and materials makers and about a quarter in energy, plus some food and paper businesses. A manager picks the stocks, so it's a focused bet on commodities and inflation that swings more than the broad market.
MGOV: Intermediate-term US government debt: Treasuries plus agency mortgage bonds issued by Fannie Mae and similar bodies, actively managed. Because the borrowers are the government and its agencies, credit risk is minimal, and the fund is built for steady income with moderate sensitivity to interest rates.
MGV: The biggest US companies that look cheaper than the market, with financials at about a quarter, then health care, technology and industrials. It's a steady value-tilted core holding, and it has less tech than the broad market, so it can trail in growth-led rallies.
MHIG: A multi-strategy fund built to guard against health care inflation, combining positions designed to grow when medical costs rise. It is a niche hedge holding, the sibling of a healthcare inflation fund: success is measured against rising medical bills, not against the stock market.
MHIP: A strategy built around health care costs, designed to grow faster than medical inflation by combining health-related investments with inflation-sensitive positions. It is a niche hedge holding: the target is beating rising health care bills, so it is judged against medical costs, not the stock market.
MHY: Actively managed high yield bonds: lower-rated corporate debt paying higher interest, in both fixed and floating rate forms. It is an income holding that takes real credit risk, so it tends to fall when investors worry about defaults, and the management team shifts holdings as conditions change.
MIDE: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400, screened and scored on environmental, social and governance measures to keep about three quarters of each industry. It offers the mid-cap market with an ESG filter, so the heaviest polluters and worst scorers are dropped.
MIG: Investment grade corporate bonds chosen with Moody's Analytics credit research, which looks for bonds priced attractively for their risk. It aims for a steadier, better-screened core corporate bond holding than a plain index of the whole market.
MIGO: Large US companies, with technology the dominant slice at over half, then communication, health care and financials. It's a growth-leaning stock holding that may use other ETFs too, and with so much in tech it swings more than the broad market.
MILK: Corporate bonds issued by companies in Pacer's Cash Cows stock indexes, firms picked for generating strong free cash flow. The idea is that cash-rich companies are dependable borrowers, so their bonds pay interest with less worry about repayment.
MILN: Companies selling to millennial consumers, the generation born between 1980 and 2000: phones, online shopping, travel stays, food delivery, sneakers and streaming. Consumer brands are over half the fund, making it a bet on one generation's spending habits as it reaches peak earning years.
MINN: Minnesota municipal bonds, debt from the state's cities, schools, hospitals and public projects, paying interest exempt from both federal and Minnesota state taxes. It is a hometown income holding for Minnesota residents, with the tax benefit worth most to those in high tax brackets.
MINO: Municipal bonds, mostly with interest that's exempt from federal income tax, chosen by a manager with room for some lower-rated bonds. It's for tax-free income and some extra yield, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
MINT: Short-term bonds and cash-like debt, mostly from companies and governments, that mature quickly. It's an actively managed place to park cash for a bit more income than a savings-like fund, and its price barely moves, though it isn't as safe as Treasuries.
MINV: Innovative companies across Asia outside Japan, with technology about half and industrials, consumer and communication firms making up much of the rest. It's a growth-focused way to add Asian exposure, run by a manager picking stocks, and it can swing sharply with emerging market sentiment.
MINY: An actively managed fund of US-listed strategic metals and mining companies, such as steel makers and copper miners, that also sells options for extra income. That income comes in exchange for capping some of the gains if those stocks rally.
MISL: Makers of aircraft, defense systems and space equipment, with industrials about 80 percent and technology the rest. It's a focused bet on aerospace and defense, so it depends on government spending and swings more than the broad market.
MIVL: Large foreign companies bought at value prices by MFS managers, with banks about a third, plus industrial, staples and energy firms. It is a patient international value holding, favoring established overseas businesses trading below what the managers think they are worth, dividends and all.
MJ: Cannabis companies from around the world: growers, retailers and makers of medical and recreational marijuana products, plus a large stake in a sister cannabis fund. It is a pure bet on legal cannabis, a young industry where regulation shifts can send the whole fund soaring or sinking.
MJSC: Small Japanese companies actively picked by MUFG managers, led by industrial firms, then technology, banks and consumer businesses. It is a focused bet on Japan's smaller domestic companies, a segment global investors often overlook, with the yen's moves adding to results for US holders.
MJUN: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. It is the June edition of a monthly series: buying it later means accepting the June terms, not a fresh set of protection.
MKAM: A simple two-part mix: about half in an S&P 500 fund and about half in Treasury bills maturing within three months, adjusted to soften drawdowns. Half the money always sits in cash-like safety, so it trails in bull markets and cushions bear ones.
MKOR: South Korean companies picked by a manager, led by technology, with industrials and financials behind. It's a focused bet on a single country, so it swings more than a global fund and depends heavily on the chip industry.
MKTN: Stocks the manager expects to rise are held long and stocks it expects to fall are sold short, aiming to cancel out overall market moves. It's meant as a diversifier that doesn't follow stocks closely, but it can lose money when its stock picks are wrong.
MLCC: Makers of multilayer ceramic capacitors and other electronic components, the tiny parts inside nearly every modern device, all within the technology sector. It is a narrow supply-chain bet: demand follows the global electronics cycle, so it can swing hard with chip and device sales.
MLDR: A ladder of US Treasury bonds with intermediate maturities, where bonds come due at regular intervals and are replaced as they do. Because it is spread evenly, the fund holds many Treasuries in small amounts, each around 4%, and has a middle level of rate sensitivity.
MLN: Tax-exempt bonds issued by US states and cities that mature far in the future. It's for investors seeking income that avoids federal income tax, and because the bonds are so long-dated, its price swings a lot when interest rates move.
MLPA: Master limited partnerships, which are companies that mostly own oil and gas pipelines and storage, almost entirely in energy. It's meant for high income from pipeline fees, and these partnerships tend to follow the energy sector, so it can fall hard when oil and gas slump.
MLPD: Master limited partnerships and energy infrastructure companies, the pipeline and storage operators of North America, wrapped in a covered call strategy. It stacks two income sources, partnership distributions and option premiums, making it a high-income energy holding that gives up some upside when oil and gas rally.
MLPI: Pipeline, storage and other energy infrastructure companies, nearly all in the energy sector, including master limited partnerships (businesses structured to pass most of their cash on to owners). It's built for high income from energy transport, and it moves with the energy industry, so oil and gas swings can hit it.
MLPX: Pipeline and energy infrastructure companies that move oil and gas around, all in the energy sector. It's built for income from the steady fees these businesses collect, but it still rises and falls with energy prices and swings more than the broad market.
MLRG: Large and mid-size US companies, covering roughly 85 percent of the market, with technology about 40 percent, then financials, communication and health care. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US stock market.
MMAR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in March, with gains capped in exchange. It is the March edition of a monthly series, chosen by investors who want their protection clock to start in spring.
MMAX: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion most of the losses over a one-year period starting in March. In exchange, gains are capped, and it only works as designed if held for the full period.
MMAY: The S&P 500 wrapped in an options strategy built to moderate the ride over the year starting in May, cushioning a middle slice of losses. It is a gentler stock holding from Pacer's Swan range, trading some upside for smaller falls.
MMCA: California municipal bonds maturing in the intermediate range, from the state's universities, airports, cities and clean energy authorities. Their interest is exempt from both federal and California income tax, a double exemption that sets it apart for California taxpayers in higher brackets.
MMF: Money market securities: very short-term, high-quality IOUs from governments and strong companies that mature in weeks or months. It is the closest thing to cash in fund form, built to hold value steady and pay a little interest, so its return trails anything that takes real risk.
MMHI: High income municipal bonds managed by MacKay Shields: lower-rated and longer city, hospital and project debt paying richer tax-exempt interest. It is the aggressive end of tax-free income, suiting high-bracket investors who accept that weaker muni credits fall more when markets get nervous.
MMID: Mid-sized US companies spread widely across industry, technology, finance and health care, picked actively by MFS. Mid-caps are the market's middle children: more established than small firms, more room to grow than giants, and this fund spreads its bets broadly among them.
MMIN: Municipal bonds issued by US states and cities that carry insurance, so the interest is generally free from federal income tax. It's for tax-conscious investors seeking steady income, and as longer-term bonds, their prices drop noticeably when interest rates rise.
MMIT: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments, nearly all with interest exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income with moderate price swings, falling between short and long maturity funds, and it still loses value when interest rates rise.
MMK: A prime money market fund holding very short-term bank obligations and other cash-like paper from high-quality borrowers. It is a place to park cash and earn a money market yield with minimal price movement, serving the same role as a savings sweep inside an investment account.
MMKT: A money market fund holding short-term US government debt, like Treasury bills, and repurchase agreements, which are very short loans backed by government securities. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, and the price barely moves.
MMMA: Municipal bonds from across the US, actively allocated by MacKay Shields specialists with a tilt toward longer maturities. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, making it an income holding for higher-bracket investors, and the active shifts between sectors and states set it apart from index muni funds.
MMSC: Small US companies managed by several outside stock picking firms at once, each running its own slice with its own style, across technology, health care and industrials. The multi manager setup spreads the bet on any one picker, aiming for steadier small cap results.
MMSD: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds issued by US states, cities and other local authorities, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. Holdings are spread thinly across many issuers, with no single bond above about 2%, and the short maturities keep price swings small.
MMTM: US large, mid and small companies, with technology about 43%, where stocks that have been rising lately are given extra weight. It's a core holding with a momentum tilt, so it can do well in trending markets but may drop hard when leadership suddenly reverses.
MN: Just six companies: Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI and SpaceX, a handpicked set of the biggest names in social media, chips and artificial intelligence. Three of them are not publicly traded, so exposure comes partly through derivatives, making this an extremely concentrated bet on a few giants.
MNA: Stocks of companies that are being bought by other companies, plus some cash, spread across industries like industrials, financials and health care. It tries to earn the small gap between the market price and the buyout price, so it aims for steadier returns but can lose if a deal collapses.
MNBD: Intermediate term municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and public projects, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It is built for steady tax exempt income with modest swings, suiting taxable accounts more than retirement accounts where the tax break is wasted.
MNVR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in November, with gains capped in exchange. It belongs to a monthly series: each edition's protection is set at its own start, so the November terms are the ones that count.
MNVT: An actively managed fund holding only about 15 to 35 stocks from around the world, making it very concentrated. Holdings include smaller, higher-risk names like CleanSpark, Lucid and Pagaya, so it can swing a lot.
MNZL: Large US companies that pass Shariah compliance screening, which rules out conventional banks, alcohol and other non-permissible businesses, leaving technology dominant. It gives Muslim investors a broad market fund aligned with Islamic principles, with the side effect of no bank exposure.
MOAT: US companies judged to have lasting competitive advantages, picked when their stock prices look cheap, spread across technology, consumer staples, consumer discretionary and health care. It's a quality-and-value approach that can trail in fast rallies led by expensive growth stocks.
MODL: US large companies spread across the market's sectors, with a manager shifting weight among them based on a model, now led by technology, health care and financials. It's a core stock holding with an active twist, so it can differ from the market.
MOO: Companies that earn most of their money from farming: food and consumer staples firms, fertilizer and chemical makers, farm machinery builders and animal health. It's a focused bet on global agriculture, so it moves with crop cycles and food demand more than with tech or banks.
MOOD: A fund that shifts among other funds holding stocks, bonds, commodities including gold, and currencies, based on market sentiment signals. It's meant to adapt to conditions instead of staying fixed, so its mix changes, and its results can differ widely from a regular stock fund.
MORT: Real estate investment trusts that own mortgages and mortgage bonds instead of buildings, earning money from the gap between borrowing and lending rates. It's built for high income, and it can drop sharply when interest rates swing or credit worries rise.
MOTG: Companies around the world with wide moats, durable advantages like brands, patents and networks that keep competitors at bay, selected by Morningstar's analysts. It blends growth and value across industries, looking for strong businesses at sensible prices.
MOTI: Companies outside the US that Morningstar rates as having durable competitive advantages, or moats, and that look reasonably priced. It spreads across many countries and industries, with no single holding above about 4% of the fund.
MOTO: Global companies that help build safer, cleaner or connected vehicles, from chipmakers to electric power and automotive suppliers. It is actively managed, leans toward technology, and its top holdings include Taiwan Semiconductor, Infineon, Quanta Services and Amphenol, each around 5% to 6%.
MPDB: Uses swap contracts to follow an HSBC index of large US stocks that is designed to limit part of the losses in falling markets. The cash holdings are collateral, and the buffer comes at the cost of some upside.
MPDY: Exposure through swap contracts to an autocall index tied to S&P 500 futures with a built-in volatility target. It aims to pay regular coupon income and can be called away early, with returns depending on the stock market staying above set levels.
MPIA: Exposure through swaps to an autocall index built on the Nasdaq-100 with an accelerator feature that can boost coupon payoffs. It aims for enhanced income tied to big tech, with early redemption possible and losses if the index falls far enough.
MPIM: Exposure to a structured autocall index built on US momentum stocks, gained through swap contracts rather than owning shares directly. It is designed to pay regular income and can end early when conditions are met, but the payoff depends on the index staying above set levels.
MPLY: Companies with monopoly-like positions, dominant firms facing little competition in their markets, led by big technology platforms. It looks for pricing power and durability, and its concentration in a few dozen winners makes it more focused than a broad index fund.
MPRO: A fixed mix of about half bond funds and half stock funds, with the stock side spread across communication, health care, technology and consumer companies. It's a one-fund balanced portfolio meant to grow with less swing than all stocks, though bonds can fall too.
MRA: An autocallable note tied to a single stock, MARA, the bitcoin mining company, a structured contract that pays income and can end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with heavy fine print: the underlying miner already swings wildly with bitcoin prices.
MRCP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each March, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every March.
MRGR: A merger arbitrage portfolio: shares of companies being acquired, bought after deals are announced in hopes of capturing the gap to the takeover price. It aims for steady, deal-driven gains mostly independent of the market, with the risk that a deal collapses.
MRNY: A basket centered on Moderna's stock, built using options rather than owning the shares outright, plus Treasuries. It aims to pay high monthly income, but it gives up much of Moderna's gains and still loses money when the stock falls.
MRSK: Mostly S&P 500 stocks and futures, about 40% technology, plus put options, which gain value when markets fall. It aims to soften big drops, but the hedging costs money and shifts around, so it usually trails the market in strong rallies.
MSBT: Holds bitcoin and nothing else, with a major bank as the sponsor. It's a speculative bet on one digital currency through a regular brokerage account, and its price can swing wildly since there are no earnings or interest behind it.
MSEP: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged to give moderate protection against losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. It is a cautious equity holding: the September start date matters, because the protection terms were set then, not when you buy.
MSFO: An options strategy built on one stock, Microsoft, selling call options against its price moves to turn them into monthly income. The trade-off is capped gains when the stock jumps, and income that rises and falls with how jumpy the market expects Microsoft to be.
MSFW: A single-stock trading fund aiming to deliver about 120 percent of Microsoft's return each calendar week, using swaps and shares, while paying weekly distributions. It resets its leverage weekly and rides on one company, so it is a short-term trading tool, not a buy-and-hold investment.
MSFY: An actively managed fund that aims for regular income from options on Microsoft stock while keeping some exposure to the share price. Mostly Treasury bills sit behind the options, and the strategy limits gains if Microsoft rises sharply.
MSLC: Large US companies with technology about 37% and financials, communication and industrials next. It's an actively managed core holding, so results depend on the managers' picks and can lead or lag the broad market.
MSML: Smaller US companies spread evenly across technology, industrials, financials and health care. It's a broad way to add small-company exposure to a portfolio, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds, though it can lead when smaller firms are in favor.
MSMR: A mix of about 80% stocks and the rest in cash, with technology near 40% and health care about a quarter of the stock side. The manager shifts between sectors and cuts risk when trends turn down, aiming for a smoother ride that may lag in fast rallies.
MSOL: A trust that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, directly and tries to track its price. It also earns some staking rewards on part of its holdings, and its value rises and falls with SOL, which can swing sharply.
MSOS: Companies that earn most of their revenue from US cannabis and hemp, including landowners, industrial suppliers and consumer firms, plus a large cash and derivatives portion. It's a speculative bet on one industry whose legal status is still shifting, so it swings far more than the broad market.
MSR: A fund built on autocallable notes tied to MicroStrategy, the software company that has become a bitcoin proxy, using derivatives rather than the stock itself. Autocallables pay coupons and can be called away early when the stock cooperates, so the income comes with complicated, capped upside and real downside if the stock sinks.
MSSE: A trust that holds ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, and stakes part of it, locking it up to help run the network in exchange for extra rewards. It gives stock market access to ether's price, which swings far more than most investments.
MSSM: Small and mid-sized US companies, led by technology, industrials and health care, chosen by a manager rather than an index. It's for growth beyond the biggest stocks, so it swings more than large-company funds, and a manager's picks can differ widely from the market.
MSSS: A fund made of ten equally weighted ETFs, each covering a US sector or industry slice, with health care, technology and financials leading. It's a way to tilt toward chosen sectors, and the pick of slices means it can behave very differently from the broad market.
MSST: An options strategy built around MicroStrategy, the company famous for holding huge amounts of bitcoin, aiming for income at a target 25 percent yearly rate. Its payouts ride on one of the market's wildest stocks, so the price can swing violently.
MSTB: Mainly S&P 500 exposure, with technology about 40 percent, built through funds and derivatives tied to the market and its volatility. It shifts its stance based on statistical signals about whether the market is likely to rise or fall, aiming to limit losses, though the timing calls can be wrong.
MSTI: Short term bonds for strategic income: a mix of government, corporate and other bonds kept on short maturities to limit interest rate swings. It aims to pay more than cash and money market funds while keeping price moves modest, a cautious step up in yield.
MSTQ: Mostly the big Nasdaq growth stocks, held through a large index fund, with the amount adjusted by statistical signals about the market's direction. The tactical overlay can dial exposure up or down, so it will not always be fully invested in stocks.
MSTW: An options and swap strategy built on one very volatile stock, MicroStrategy, the software company famous for holding bitcoin, designed to pay income weekly. Weekly payouts from such a jumpy stock can be large, but the same swings that create the income can slash the fund's value.
MSTY: A bet on the stock of MicroStrategy, a company known for holding lots of bitcoin, paired with options that bring in income but cap how much of a rise you share in. It's for high income and not for steady growth, and it can fall sharply when the stock does.
MTAW: Companies tied to Meta's artificial intelligence ecosystem, from technology and social media to the utilities that power data centers. It is a focused AI bet organized around one company's orbit: it captures suppliers and partners, not just Meta itself, and swings with the AI trade.
MTBA: Mortgage-backed bonds, which are bundles of home loans that pay interest and principal to investors, actively managed with some borrowing and derivatives. It's meant for higher bond income than Treasuries, and it can lose value when interest rates rise or people refinance loans.
MTGG: Growth companies from around the world, with a large share outside the US in foreign markets across Asia, Europe and beyond. It is a growth holding that adds currency moves and foreign market moods to the usual stock swings, so it will not move in step with a US-only fund.
MTGP: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans, many backed by Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae. It can also hold other securitized debt, and the managers choose holdings rather than tracking an index.
MTRA: Growth-oriented companies outside the US, led by technology, then industrials and health care. It's a focused pick of overseas growth stocks to complement US holdings, and it can lag when cheaper, slower-growing companies lead.
MTUM: US stocks that have been rising fastest lately, with technology making up over half the fund. It's a bet that recent winners keep winning, and since it reshuffles as trends shift, it can fall sharply when market leadership turns.
MTYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to Strategy, the software firm turned bitcoin holding company. It stacks options on leverage on a stock that already amplifies bitcoin, so the swings are extreme in both directions and holding periods should be short.
MUB: Bonds from states, cities and local agencies, with interest that is generally exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for steady, tax-free income in a regular account, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
MUIB: An options strategy on Micron Technology, the memory chip maker, designed to define the outcome in advance and boost income from the stock. It rides on one cyclical chip company, so payouts and prices swing with memory prices and AI demand.
MULT: An actively managed bond fund spread across many types of debt, including US and foreign government bonds, corporate bonds and loans. The manager shifts between sectors to find income, so it is more flexible than a fund tracking one bond index.
MUNA: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature by 2030, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. As bonds mature, the money is returned and the fund winds down, and it spreads across many local issuers, none above about 2% of the fund.
MUNB: A ladder of tax-exempt municipal bonds maturing in the years running up to 2035, paying out as each rung comes due. It is designed to fund a future goal around 2035 with federal tax-free income along the way.
MUNC: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature by 2045, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. As bonds mature, the money is returned and the fund winds down, and it spreads across many local issuers, none above about 3% of the fund.
MUND: Tax-exempt municipal bonds in a long ladder reaching to 2055, paying federal-tax-free interest in distributions as the rungs mature. It is built for savers planning spending in the mid 2050s who want steady income the tax man mostly leaves alone.
MUNF: Tax-exempt municipal bonds in a ladder stretching to 2036, paying federal-tax-free interest in regular distributions as bonds mature along the way. The long ladder suits savers funding spending in the mid 2030s who want income without the tax bite.
MUNG: A fund of tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, built as a ladder of bonds maturing around 2046. It pays out income regularly and winds down as the bonds mature.
MUNH: A fund of tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, built as a ladder of bonds maturing around 2056. Its bonds are very long-term, so the price is more sensitive to interest rate changes.
MUNI: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from state and local governments that pay interest free of regular federal income tax, with a small share that may be taxable under minimum tax rules. It's built for tax-advantaged income, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
MUNJ: Tax-exempt municipal bonds arranged in a ladder ending around 2031, paying interest free of regular federal income tax along the way. It is designed to hand money back in stages for planned spending, rather than locking everything into one maturity date.
MUNX: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, managed by a specialist muni team. It targets steady tax-free income with moderate price movement, sitting between short-term safety and long-term yield in the muni market.
MUNY: Municipal bonds issued by New York State and local governments, with intermediate maturities. Their interest is generally exempt from federal and New York income taxes, so it suits New York residents seeking tax-free income, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
MUSE: Credit of many kinds from around the world: high yield bonds, bank loans and foreign debt including emerging markets, mixed actively by TCW. Spreading across credit sectors hunts for income wherever it looks best paid, with more risk than a plain corporate bond fund.
MUST: Municipal bonds from state and local governments across the country, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It aims for tax-free income at intermediate maturities, and it mixes bond types, so prices drop when interest rates rise.
MUY: Options on a single stock, Micron, the memory chipmaker, arranged to pay income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one cyclical chip stock: payouts come from its swings, and memory downturns hit it hard.
MUYY: A fund that aims for high income from options tied to Micron stock, using a leveraged Micron fund as its reference. It does not simply own the shares, and Treasury bills back the options, so it follows one volatile company with limited upside.
MVAL: Large US companies that Morningstar analysts judge both undervalued and protected by durable competitive advantages, tilted toward consumer staples and health care. It is a value holding with a quality screen: the moat test keeps out cheap-but-fragile firms, though it can lag in growth-led markets.
MVFD: Forty equal-sized US stocks that generate positive cash flow and can pay dividends, with energy the largest slice at about two fifths. If cash flow turns negative, it can swap into bond funds, giving it a blended approach that can shift between stocks and safer holdings.
MVFG: A fund of up to 25 equal-sized stock funds spread across the world, with financials, technology and industrials each making up a large share. It picks funds with positive cash flow and can switch into Treasuries when trends turn negative, so it aims to avoid long downturns but may lag in rebounds.
MVPA: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies that the managers believe are undervalued and have room to grow. It is fairly concentrated, with Crocs, Bread Financial, Bloomin' Brands and Crescent Energy each around 6% of it.
MWHS: Electricity prices themselves, traded through futures contracts on power markets rather than shares of utility companies. Power prices spike with heat waves, cold snaps and grid strain, so this is a volatile trading tool whose moves have little to do with the stock market.
MXI: Materials companies around the world, such as miners, chemical makers and steel and packaging producers, making up nearly all of the fund. It's a focused bet on raw materials, so it swings with global growth and commodity prices and tends to do better when the economy is strong.
MYCF: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2026, so the fund behaves like a single bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature and return their principal. As 2026 runs out the fund winds down, suiting savers matching money to a near term goal.
MYCG: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2027, packaged like a single company bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature and return principal. It suits savers matching money to a goal around 2027, and its swings shrink as the date nears.
MYCH: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2028. Because the bonds expire together, the fund closes in 2028 and returns the money, giving a more predictable income stream than an ordinary bond fund, though a company's credit trouble can still hurt.
MYCI: Corporate bonds that come due in 2029, from big issuers across industries, gathered into one target-year package. Like a single bond with many borrowers, it suits investors saving toward a 2029 expense who want company debt rather than government debt.
MYCJ: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2030, packaged like a single company bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature. It suits savers matching money to a goal around 2030, and its price swings fade as the date approaches.
MYCK: Corporate bonds that mature in 2031, part of a series of target-year bond funds, so the holdings roll down toward cash as 2031 approaches. It works like a ladder rung for a known future expense, paying company bond interest with less and less rate sensitivity as the end nears.
MYCL: A fund of US corporate bonds that mature in 2032, so it is designed to wind down around that year. It holds many companies, such as IBM, Philip Morris, Church & Dwight and AT&T, each only about 3% of the fund.
