MYCM: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, so the fund is designed to wind down around then and return the money. Holdings are spread thin, with no single issuer above about 4%, across companies like CVS, Marvell and Verisk.
MYCN: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2034, so the fund is designed to wind down around then and return the money. Holdings are spread thin, with no single issuer above about 3%, from companies like General Motors Financial, BP and AT&T.
MYCO: Corporate bonds from many industries that all come due in 2035, so the fund behaves more like a single bond with a known end date. It suits savers aiming at a goal around that year, and its price still moves as interest rates change along the way.
MYCP: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2036. The fund is set to close around that year, so it behaves more like a single bond that returns your money at the end.
MYHA: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk-rated kind, bundled so they come due around 2027. The near end date makes it work like a single short bond: higher interest than safer funds, with principal due back soon if issuers stay healthy.
MYHB: Riskier corporate bonds rated below investment grade, grouped so that nearly all of them mature in 2028. It behaves like one junk bond with a set finish line, paying extra interest to compensate for the higher chance some issuers fail.
MYHC: High yield corporate bonds, rated below investment grade, that nearly all come due in 2029. Maturing together gives it a set end date like a single bond, paying higher interest in exchange for the risk that some issuers cannot pay.
MYHD: Riskier corporate bonds, known as high yield or junk bonds, that nearly all come due in 2030. Because the bonds mature together, it works like a single bond with a set end date, paying higher interest in exchange for more credit risk.
MYHE: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk-rated kind, bundled so that nearly all of them mature in 2031. The shared end date makes it act like one big bond: higher interest along the way, then principal back at the finish if issuers stay solvent.
MYHF: Junk-rated corporate bonds, the high yield kind, bundled so nearly all of them mature in 2032. The shared end date makes it act like a single bond with higher interest, built for a goal in the early 2030s if issuers hold up.
MYLD: Tiny and small US companies chosen for shareholder yield: firms returning cash through dividends and share buybacks, across banks, shops, industrials and energy. It favors cash returning small fry over growth stories, a value tilt in the market's smallest corner.
MYMF: Municipal bonds with income generally exempt from federal income tax, all maturing in 2026, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. Because that date is so near, most of the fund now sits in cash while the last bonds mature.
MYMG: Municipal bonds with income generally exempt from federal income tax, all maturing in 2027, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It is spread over many issuers like school districts and transit authorities, with none above roughly 4%.
MYMH: A basket of US municipal bonds that all mature in 2028, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. The fund is set to close around that year, spreading its money across many state and local issuers.
MYMI: Municipal bonds maturing in 2029 from states, schools and local agencies across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. It suits money with a known 2029 purpose, and prices settle down as the maturity year approaches.
MYMJ: A fund of US municipal bonds that mature in 2030, so it is designed to wind down around that year. The income is generally free from federal income tax, and the bonds come from many issuers, with no single one above about 4%.
MYMK: A basket of municipal bonds that mature in 2031, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It holds many bonds from issuers like toll roads, hospitals and water utilities, and the fund winds down as the bonds mature.
MYML: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that come due around 2032, paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax. The shared maturity makes it act like a single tax-free bond, handy for planning a goal in the early 2030s.
MYY: A short-term trading tool that rises when mid-sized US companies fall, resetting its inverse bet every day. The daily reset steadily erodes value over longer stretches, so it suits brief bearish trades rather than a lasting hedge.
NACP: Large US companies picked by an index that scores them on diversity and inclusion, tied to the NAACP's goals. It looks a lot like the broader market, with technology the largest sector at around 40%.
NANC: US stocks that sitting Democratic members of Congress or their families have reported owning, with technology about half. It's an unusual actively managed stock fund built around a theme, and it leans harder on tech than the broad market.
NANR: Companies in oil, gas, mining, forestry and agriculture across the US and Canada, with energy and materials making up almost nine tenths. It's a focused bet on natural resources that can hedge against inflation, but it swings with commodity prices.
NAPR: Large growth stocks from the Nasdaq 100, led by technology at about three fifths, wrapped in options that cushion some losses over a year starting each April. The trade-off is capped gains, so it's for people who want tech exposure with some protection.
NASA: Companies tied to the space economy, with industrials like aerospace and defense contractors making up over half and technology about a third. It's a focused, growth-style bet on a young industry, so it swings more than the broad market and holds a small group of firms.
NATO: Defense companies headquartered in NATO member countries: American and European makers of fighter jets, missiles, warships and aircraft engines, nearly all industrial firms. It is a transatlantic bet on rising military budgets across the alliance, tied to geopolitics rather than consumer demand.
NAUG: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ fund, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period beginning each August. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
NBCE: Chinese companies across mainland A-shares, Hong Kong listings and US-listed receipts, actively picked with technology the biggest slice. It spreads across China's listing venues in one fund, carrying the region's regulatory and currency risks.
NBCM: Commodity-linked contracts covering energy, metals and farm products, paired with mostly short-term investment-grade bonds. It's meant to diversify a stock and bond portfolio and hedge against inflation, though commodity prices can fall sharply and swing a lot.
NBCR: Large US companies chosen by a manager, with technology about a third, then financials, communication and consumer firms. It's meant as a core stock holding that mostly moves with the broad US market, though the manager's picks can make it differ from an index fund.
NBDS: Companies the managers think are shaking up their industries, with technology over half and health care about a sixth. It's built for growth and holds a concentrated set of names from around the world, so it swings more than the broad market and can fall hard when growth stocks sag.
NBET: Companies driving the energy transition and rebuilding infrastructure: traditional energy firms cutting carbon, clean power builders, and grid and pipeline operators, mostly energy with some utilities. It bets on the decades long shift in how the world makes and moves energy, with commodity swings along the way.
NBFC: Credit of almost every kind, corporate bonds, bundled loans, mortgage debt and other securitized borrowing, chosen flexibly by active managers hunting income. It can roam wherever lending looks attractive, which means credit quality and risk vary as the managers trade safety for yield.
NBFR: Exposure to the Nasdaq-100's big technology and growth companies, combined with options designed to buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It suits investors who want tech-led growth with a cushion, though gains are reduced by the cost of that protection.
NBGX: Large US growth companies picked through research that mixes number crunching with judgment, led by the biggest technology names. It is a concentrated growth portfolio, so it lives and dies by a few dozen large stocks.
NBIE: Stocks of companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials at nearly a third, with industrials and technology next. It's a way to add international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and the managers pick holdings actively rather than following an index.
NBJP: Japanese companies picked by managers for durable growth, with industrials the biggest slice at about a third, followed by financials, technology and consumer businesses. It's meant to add Japan to a portfolio, and its returns are also affected by moves in the yen against the dollar.
NBOS: A fund that sells put options on US stock indexes, collecting premiums, while holding mostly short-term bonds as collateral. It aims for income and equity-like returns with a lower level of swings, but it can lose money in sharp stock market drops and trails in strong rallies.
NBSD: Mostly investment-grade bonds from governments and companies, including mortgage and asset-backed securities, with a bit of cash. It aims for extra income without taking on much price swing, so it fits as a calmer bond holding, though it can still lose value when interest rates climb.
NBSM: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by active managers for growth, spread across industrial firms, banks, health care and technology. It aims to catch tomorrow's large companies while they are still mid-sized, which means more room to grow and more price swings than big-company funds.
NBTR: A broad bond mix led by US government debt, with corporate bonds, mortgage backed and asset backed securities filling out the portfolio. It works as a core income holding, and managers can tilt toward whichever bond corner looks best, adding flexibility a plain index fund lacks.
NCIQ: A basket of major cryptocurrencies, with no stocks or bonds inside. It's a high-risk bet on digital assets in a single fund that spreads across several coins, and its price can swing wildly, far more than the stock market.
NCLD: Neocloud companies, the new breed of cloud firms renting out powerful graphics chips for artificial intelligence training, many of them converted bitcoin miners. It is a narrow, young and concentrated bet on AI computing demand, so sharp swings are part of the package.
NCLO: Bonds backed by pools of corporate loans, called collateralized loan obligations, from the higher-rated AA to BBB layers. It's for income above regular bonds, with interest that adjusts as rates change, but it can lose value when credit worries rise.
NCPB: A core bond portfolio with extra reach: investment grade bonds form the base, and managers can add higher yielding debt for more income. It aims to beat plain core bond funds over time by flexing across sectors, accepting somewhat more credit risk.
NDAA: A fund of funds that mixes mostly stocks with some bonds and cash, using a research firm's models to shift between them as conditions change. It's meant as a moderate, all-in-one portfolio, and its stock side leans toward technology, financials and health care.
NDEC: Uses options tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in December. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
NDIA: Indian companies picked actively, led by banks and other financial firms with consumer, industrial and energy names behind, all in one fast growing economy. It is a single country growth bet, so it swings with India's markets, politics and currency.
NDIV: Energy and natural resource companies, mostly oil and gas producers and pipelines, wrapped in a covered call program that sells options on the holdings for extra income. It is built for high income from the energy sector, trading away some upside when fuel prices surge.
NDOW: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and other funds spread across many asset types, such as international stocks, emerging market debt and managed futures. It aims for a more conservative balance than an all-stock fund.
NEAR: Investment-grade US dollar bonds that mature in the short term, with the manager actively adjusting holdings. It's a low-risk place to earn income above cash while keeping money fairly stable, and because maturities are short, its price drops far less than other bonds when interest rates rise.
NECK: The bottleneck suppliers of the AI buildout: makers of memory chips, optical networking gear and other scarce parts that data centers cannot do without. It skips the famous AI names to own the chokepoints instead, so it is a focused, fast-swinging bet on one supply chain.
NEHI: Exposure to Ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, through funds that hold it, paired with an options strategy that sells puts for monthly income. It's an income-focused crypto bet, but it can lose money when Ether falls and gives up gains in big rallies.
NELS: An actively managed fund that mixes individual stocks and other ETFs to cover a broad range of US companies. Its biggest positions are NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, which together make up around 20% of the fund.
NEMD: Government and company bonds from developing countries, all paid in US dollars or other major currencies, with a little cash. It aims for higher income than US bonds, and it carries extra risk because those borrowers are more likely to struggle to repay in a crisis.
NERD: Video game companies worldwide: publishers, console makers, mobile game firms and the platforms where games are sold and streamed. It is a pure entertainment growth bet whose fortunes follow game releases, player spending and hit titles.
NETL: Net lease real estate companies, landlords whose tenants sign long leases and pay the taxes, insurance and upkeep on top of rent. Those leases make income steadier than most property stocks, so it is a defensive corner of real estate, still sensitive to interest rates.
NEWZ: US companies of all sizes chosen by an artificial intelligence system that scores the sentiment of news coverage about each stock. Financials and technology lead the current mix, and the lineup changes as news flow shifts, so it can turn over quickly.
NFEB: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each February. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
NFLP: An income strategy wrapped around Netflix stock, selling options to turn the streamer's price swings into regular payouts. It keeps some exposure if Netflix rises, but option selling caps the gains, and a sharp drop in the stock still hurts.
NFLT: A flexible mix of bonds from many parts of the bond market, including corporate and higher-risk bonds. It's meant for extra income compared with plain government bonds, and the managers shift between bond types as conditions change, so it carries more credit risk than a typical bond fund.
NFLW: A fund meant to return about 1.2 times the weekly move of Netflix stock, using swaps (contracts that pay a stock's returns) and some shares. It pays distributions weekly, and because it is leveraged and tied to a single stock, it can swing sharply.
NFLY: A single-stock income fund built on Netflix: options mimic owning the shares while covered calls are sold against them for income. The sold calls cap the upside, so it harvests the streaming giant's swings as income rather than riding its full growth.
NFRA: Companies that run the roads, power grids, pipelines and communication networks that economies depend on, from developed and emerging countries. It's a diversifier meant to add steady, real-world assets, and it leans toward industrials, utilities and communication.
NFRX: Infrastructure companies picked by active managers: electric and gas utilities are about half, with railroads, pipelines and other transport and energy networks making up the rest. These businesses run essential services with steady demand, so the fund is built as a defensive income-leaning stock holding.
NFTY: India's 50 largest listed companies, held in equal weights so mid-sized names count as much as the giants, across banks, consumer brands, materials and drugmakers. Equal weighting sets it apart from most India funds and makes it a balanced single-country bet on Indian growth.
NGHT: A rotation between bitcoin exposure, emphasized during overnight hours when the fund's research says crypto tends to move most, and US Treasury bills the rest of the time. It is a quirky, tactical way to hold bitcoin: part crypto bet, part cash-like safety, switching on a daily rhythm.
NGIF: Companies that own and run infrastructure around the world, with utilities at about half, industrials about 30% and energy about a fifth. It aims for steady income and inflation resistance, with at least 40% in foreign companies, and it can lag in strong stock rallies.
NHYB: US company bonds rated below investment grade, which pay higher interest because the companies are riskier. It's meant for extra income, but it can fall in bad economies when more issuers struggle to pay, and no single issuer is allowed to dominate.
NHYM: Lower-rated municipal bonds from across the US that pay interest free of regular federal income tax. It aims for higher tax-free income than safer municipal bonds, though it can drop more in a downturn because these issuers are riskier.
NICO: Tobacco and nicotine companies worldwide: cigarette makers, vaping and pouch brands, and others earning most of their revenue from nicotine products. It is a deliberately concentrated bet on a controversial industry: these stocks often pay fat dividends, but regulation and lawsuits hang over them permanently.
NIHI: Large companies from developed markets outside the US, led by financials, industrials, technology and health care, plus an options strategy to produce extra income. It's for income, but the options cap gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
NIKL: Nickel mining companies, the explorers and producers of the metal used in stainless steel and electric vehicle batteries. It is a narrow commodity stock bet, so it swings with nickel prices and battery demand rather than the broad mining market.
NISM: Small and midsize companies from markets outside the US, spanning developed and emerging economies, chosen by New York Life's investment managers. It fills the smaller-company corner of an international stock holding, a segment that tends to swing more than big foreign blue chips and gets less analyst attention.
NITE: A concentrated handful of about twenty US growth stocks, led by big technology, consumer and financial names, picked with conviction. With so few holdings, each one matters a lot, so it will look and behave very differently from a broad index fund.
NIXT: Small and mid-sized US value stocks, built around companies dropped from big stock indexes, which often leaves them temporarily unpopular and cheap. The bet is that yesterday's index castoffs recover, a contrarian corner of the market most funds ignore.
NJAN: Options contracts tied to a fund of the 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq companies, with technology around 60%. It's built to absorb a set amount of losses over a year starting in January, but the cap on gains means it trails in strong rallies.
NJNK: Bonds from US companies rated below investment grade, the so-called junk bonds, picked across industries by Columbia's managers. They pay higher income to compensate for weaker borrowers, and prices can drop hard when investors worry about defaults in a downturn.
NJUL: Large US growth stocks through a Nasdaq-100 based fund, with technology at about 60 percent, plus a buffer that cushions part of the losses over a one-year period starting each July. It caps the gains, and it works as designed only if held through the full period.
NJUN: Nasdaq 100 exposure, about 60% technology, wrapped in options that cushion the first stretch of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the protection only works fully if you hold from the start date to the end date.
NLR: Companies tied to nuclear power, including uranium miners, nuclear utilities and equipment makers, spread across energy, utilities and industrials. It's a focused bet on nuclear energy, so it swings more than the broad market and rides on policy and demand for clean electricity.
NLSI: A long-short stock strategy: it owns US companies it likes and bets against ones it does not, across technology, banks and energy, while selling options for income. The short side can soften market falls, though wrong bets on either side drag results.
NMAR: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each March. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
NMAY: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big growth stock basket, set each May for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It offers a cushioned way to hold tech heavy stocks, with technology over half the underlying exposure.
NMB: Investment grade municipal bonds from across the US, picked actively for the best balance of income, quality and value, with interest generally free from federal income tax. As an actively managed national muni fund it can roam maturities and issuers that index funds cannot.
NMBL: A flexible global mix that currently holds about 58 percent stocks and 27 percent bonds, plus commodities, across many countries including emerging markets. NovaTide managers shift the blend actively, making it a one-fund moderate portfolio whose risk level moves with their outlook rather than staying fixed.
NNOV: A defined outcome fund tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, using options over a one-year period starting in November. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and in return gains are capped.
NOBL: S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividends for at least 25 years in a row, spread across consumer staples, industrials, financials and health care. It's for steadier dividend income, and with little technology it can trail in tech-led rallies.
NOCT: Large Nasdaq companies, led by technology at well over half, held through options that cushion some stock market losses over a yearly cycle starting in October. It's for growth investors wanting a safety net, but gains are capped and tech swings still matter.
NODE: Companies building the digital asset economy, such as bitcoin miners and crypto-related businesses, plus some bitcoin-linked funds. It is a concentrated, volatile theme, with the largest holding being a VanEck bitcoin fund at about 7%.
NOEQ: A broad portfolio of US stocks across many industries, managed to serve as a general-purpose stock holding. It's meant to be a core piece of a portfolio that moves with the overall US market, and its returns will rise and fall with stock market swings.
NORW: Companies of Norway, one country's whole market: oil and gas producers are about a third, with banks, salmon farming, shipping and defense firms behind. It is a single-country bet on a wealthy, energy-rich economy, so oil prices and the krone steer results.
NOVM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each November. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
NOVP: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, per the Buffer 12 name. It is a middle-ground buffer: less protection than the deep versions, more room to gain than they allow.
NOVZ: Options on the S&P 500 meant to absorb part of a market decline over an outcome period that restarts each November, while keeping a share of the gains. Actively managed, it trades some upside for peace of mind, and timing your purchase affects the result.
NPFE: A manager's mix of large US companies, with technology about a third and the rest across consumer, health care and financial firms. It's a core stock holding aimed at income and growth, though picks can differ from the broad market.
NPFI: A mix of preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends and rank above common stock, and income-producing bonds. It aims at steady income above ordinary bonds, but its price can drop when interest rates rise, and it is generally concentrated in financial companies.
NQLT: Mid and large sized companies chosen for quality: strong finances, reliable profits and durable businesses, spread across technology, consumer, financial and health care names. It is a plain spoken core stock holding that favors proven operators over speculative growers, at home and some abroad.
NRAM: Companies making computer memory: the chip firms that produce the DRAM, flash and next-generation memory AI systems are hungry for. It is a narrow slice of the semiconductor industry, so it swings with memory prices, which are famously cyclical and brutal in downturns.
NRES: Companies that dig, drill and grow the world's raw materials: miners, oil and gas producers, fertilizer and timber firms from many countries. It is a bet on commodity demand and inflation, since resource stocks often rise when the prices of what they produce climb.
NRR: This fund simply holds NEAR, the token of the NEAR blockchain network, and stakes part of it to earn extra tokens as rewards. Its value is the price of one cryptocurrency, nothing else, so it carries the full boom and bust swings of crypto.
NRSH: Companies positioned for nearshoring, the shift of supply chains toward North America: industrial landlords, logistics and transport firms across the US, Mexico and Canada. It bets factories moving closer to home lift these businesses, a theme tied to trade policy.
NSCI: Securitized bonds, which are pools of loans like home mortgages, car loans and commercial property debt. It's meant for income beyond Treasuries, and it can fall in credit stress or when interest rates rise.
NSEP: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
NSI: Emerging market stocks screened to leave out companies the sponsor sees as a threat to US national security. What remains leans heavily toward Asian chip makers and banks, so it still swings like an emerging markets fund, just with a security filter.
NSIG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Apple make up about 34% of it, and technology is well over half the fund.
NSIV: An actively managed fund of US companies the manager considers undervalued, using a disciplined, research-driven approach. It is diversified across financials, technology, health care and industrials, with no single stock above about 7%.
NTRL: A market neutral event strategy: long and short positions in companies caught up in announced mergers and other big corporate events, balanced so market direction matters little. It aims for steady, deal-driven returns, with losses when deals fall apart or spreads widen.
NTSD: Large US stocks held directly, with international stock futures layered on top so each dollar carries both home and foreign exposure. The stacked design aims to squeeze more diversification from the same money, and the leverage means losses can outrun a plain global fund.
NTSE: Emerging market stocks, heavy in Asian technology, layered with US Treasury futures on top so each dollar works twice. The stacked design aims for stock growth plus bond returns from the same money, and the leverage can magnify losses as well as gains.
NTSI: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside the US and Canada, led by financials, industrials and technology. It's a way to add international stocks, and it uses currency contracts to hedge foreign currencies, so dollar moves matter less than in an unhedged fund.
NTSX: Mostly large US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, plus Treasury futures that add bond exposure on top. The goal is stock and bond exposure in one fund while using less cash, so it's a core holding that can fall when interest rates jump.
NUAG: The broad US investment grade bond market, Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, tilted to squeeze out a bit more yield than a plain core bond fund. It is meant as a portfolio's main bond holding, offering steady income with slightly more credit risk than the plainest version.
NUBD: Investment-grade US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds, screened for environmental and social standards. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
NUDG: Dividend-paying US stocks, with technology about a third and financials, health care and consumer companies behind it, plus a small amount of cash. It aims for growing income and a steady core holding, and it focuses on companies that raise dividends over time instead of simply paying the highest yield.
NUDM: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, screened for environmental and social practices. It's a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and the screen means it avoids some companies the regular index holds.
NUDV: US companies that pay high dividends and also pass environmental, social and governance screens, led by banks, health care and industrials. It pairs income with values screening, so heavy polluters and poor governance scorers are left out even when their dividends are tempting.
NUEM: Companies from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, led by technology at about 40 percent and financials about a fifth. It's a way to add emerging-market growth, and it screens for environmental and social standards, so it differs from a plain emerging-markets fund.
NUGO: Large US growth companies, with technology making up nearly two thirds and communication and industrials next. A manager picks the stocks to seek capital growth, and with such a heavy tech tilt, it can swing more than the broad market.
NUGY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged gold miners fund, harvesting the miners' big price swings as regular payouts. It is a high-risk trade rather than a way to own gold: leverage resets and option caps can turn a miners' slump into steep losses.
NUHY: Lower-rated corporate bonds, the kind that pay high interest because the borrowers carry more default risk, screened with environmental, social and governance criteria. It is built for income, and the screen sets it apart from plain junk bond funds, though the bonds can still fall hard in a recession.
NUIB: Investment-grade bonds chosen for impact: government, corporate and mortgage bonds whose proceeds fund projects meant to do measurable environmental or social good. It still behaves like a core bond fund, paying interest and cushioning stock swings, with the bond picking screened for impact on top.
NUIF: US infrastructure companies: power utilities at about half the fund, energy pipelines and industrial operators making up most of the rest. It is built for steady, fee-and-bill-based income from essential systems, so it tends to move less than the broad market but still feels interest rate changes.
NUKX: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the nuclear industry, including utilities, uranium miners and equipment makers, with a goal of paying income. About 12% sits in a uranium ETF, and it may also use options to add income.
NUKZ: Companies tied to nuclear power, including uranium miners, reactor builders and utilities, mostly industrials and utilities with some energy. It's a focused bet on the nuclear industry, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on energy policy.
NULC: Large US companies selected from an index that screens for environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors. It looks much like the broad market, with technology around 40% of the fund and NVIDIA the largest holding.
NULG: Large US growth companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, with technology about half. It's a growth holding for people who want fewer companies they find objectionable, and it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
NULV: Large US companies that look reasonably priced, with technology, financials, health care and industrials as the biggest parts, screened for environmental and social standards. It's a value-tilted core holding with a values filter, and it may trail when growth stocks lead.
NUMG: Mid-sized US growth companies, led by technology, with industrials, health care and consumer businesses next. It's a growth holding for the middle of the market, and it screens for environmental and social practices, so it leaves out some businesses.
NUMI: Municipal bonds from across the US, toll roads, schools, universities and towns, actively chosen for tax-exempt income. The interest escapes federal income tax, which sets it apart from taxable bond funds and makes it a staple for higher earners investing outside retirement accounts.
NUMV: US mid-sized companies priced cheaply compared with their size, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer staples. It's a value holding that screens out companies with poor environmental and social records, so it leaves out some of the broad market's biggest polluters and controversial firms.
NURE: Property trusts whose leases are short: apartment buildings, hotels and rental home companies that can raise rents quickly. Short leases let landlords reprice with inflation, which is the appeal, though occupancy swings hit hotels and apartments fast in downturns.
NUSA: Short-term US bonds that pass environmental, social and governance screens: Treasuries, government-backed bonds and company debt all due within about five years. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it is a cautious income holding for investors who want ESG rules applied to bonds.
NUSC: Small US companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, spread across technology, health care, industrials and financials. It's a growth-oriented slice of the market that adds smaller businesses to a portfolio, and it tends to swing more than large company funds.
NVBT: Options on a fund of the largest US companies match its returns over one year from November, buffering the first 10 percent of losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms are set each November, so it is a defined-window holding for investors who want stock exposure with known protection.
NVBU: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, with a 15% buffer in the build. Gains past a starting spread are uncapped, so it keeps more of a rally than capped buffers do.
NVBW: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over a one-year period running from November to October. In exchange for that deep buffer it accepts a cap on gains, suiting investors who fear a serious downturn most.
NVDW: An income strategy wrapped around one stock, Nvidia, the AI chip leader, using options and Treasury bills rather than simply holding shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and the trade-off is that everything rides on one very volatile stock, with options capping some of its biggest jumps.
NVDY: A fund built around a single stock, NVIDIA, using options rather than owning much of the shares, with most assets in Treasuries and cash. It pays out big monthly income but gives up much of the stock's upside, and it can still lose a lot when NVIDIA falls.
NVIB: Income built around a single stock, NVIDIA, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on the chip giant: the income strategy cannot remove the sharp swings that come with one high-flying stock.
NVII: A single-stock fund built around NVIDIA, the chip maker, combining exposure to its shares with an options strategy that sells some upside for monthly income. It's for income from one company's stock, so it can fall sharply when NVIDIA drops and trails when it surges.
NVIR: Energy companies plus the firms that clean up after the industry: drillers and producers alongside businesses that remediate old oil and gas sites. It is an actively managed bet that carbon energy stays essential while its cleanup becomes a business of its own.
NVIT: An actively managed fund built around NVIDIA stock that uses options to aim for a target yearly payout of about 25%, while also seeking some growth. Much of the fund sits in Treasury bills, and the options strategy means it will not fully share in NVIDIA's big gains.
NVOH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of Novo Nordisk, the Danish drug maker behind famous diabetes and weight loss treatments. A currency hedge softens swings between the krone and the dollar, leaving returns riding on one pharma giant.
NVPS: The picks and shovels of the Nvidia world: suppliers and partners that sell the chips, cooling, power and parts AI data centers need, rather than Nvidia itself. Technology is over 80 percent, so it rides the AI build-out one step removed.
NVYY: An income strategy built on derivatives referencing a fund of Nvidia shares, designed to convert that one chip giant's big price swings into regular payments. It is highly concentrated by design: the income aim is generous, but Nvidia's sharp drops pass through and gains are limited by the strategy.
NXTE: Companies worldwide picked for sustainability, from clean technology and health care to industrials and real estate, with technology about half the fund. It is a values driven growth holding: the screen favors firms judged greener than their peers, which tilts it toward tech and away from heavy polluters.
NXTG: Companies building and using next-generation wireless networks like 5G: equipment makers, chip companies and telecom operators, with technology about two thirds. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
NXTI: US companies rich in intangible capital: research, brands, software and know-how that outweigh their physical assets relative to book value. That lens favors modern, asset-light businesses across technology, retail and health care over factories and heavy industry.
NXUS: Investment-grade bonds from governments, companies and mortgage pools outside the US, with currency swings hedged back to dollars. It's for income and diversification away from US bonds, though prices drop when interest rates rise.
NYF: Tax-exempt bonds issued by New York State and local governments, nearly all investment grade. It suits New York residents who want income that is mostly free of federal and state income tax, though longer maturities mean its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise.
NYM: Municipal bonds from New York State and its cities and agencies, mostly high quality, with medium-term maturities. It's built for investors in that state who want income that is generally free of federal and New York income tax, and it is concentrated in one state's finances.
NYNY: Companies headquartered in or with major operations in New York City, led by big banks and financial firms at about two-thirds of the fund. It is a playful, concentrated bet on one city's economy, so it leans heavily on Wall Street's fortunes rather than spreading across the country.
NYSX: The one hundred largest companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange, led heavily by technology with media and consumer growth names behind. Despite the old exchange's blue chip image, the list is growth tilted today, so it behaves much like a big tech heavy growth fund.
NYYY: Daily income built around NVIDIA, using Treasury bills and short-term funds as ballast while options on the chip giant generate payouts. It is an income machine bolted onto one volatile stock: the bills keep most of the money steady, but the payouts rise and fall with NVIDIA's swings.
NZAC: Large companies worldwide, with technology close to two fifths and financials about a sixth, tilted away from heavy carbon emitters. It's a core global stock holding for people who want lower climate impact, so it holds fewer oil and gas companies than the broad world market.
OACP: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds, including US government, corporate, mortgage-backed and municipal bonds, run by active managers. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion for stocks, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
OAEM: Companies in emerging markets such as developing countries in Asia and Latin America, with technology the largest slice at about two fifths and financials next. It's a growth holding for adding emerging-market exposure, so it swings widely.
OAIM: Medium and large companies outside the US, with financials at about a third, then industrials, technology and energy. It's a core way to add international stocks, and an active manager picks them, so results can differ from a plain international index fund.
OAIW: Companies tied to the OpenAI ecosystem: the chip makers, cloud providers and software firms that power or build on its AI tools. Technology is about two thirds of the fund, making it a focused bet on one company's orbit within the AI boom.
OAKG: Large companies worldwide bought at prices Oakmark's managers consider below their true worth, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer firms. It is a patient value portfolio of a few dozen picks, and the mix of US and foreign stocks changes as bargains shift.
OAKI: Large companies outside the US bought when their prices look depressed, from European banks and sportswear brands to caterers and hotels. Oakmark's managers are patient contrarians, so it is a value fund that often buys what others are avoiding and holds for years.
OAKL: A concentrated handful of US stocks that Oakmark's managers judge to be trading well below what the businesses are worth. With few holdings it is a high-conviction value bet, so it can trail the market for long stretches when cheap stocks stay out of favor.
OAKM: A concentrated group of large US companies the manager thinks are priced below their worth, with financials the biggest piece at about 30%. It's a value-style core stock holding picked by a manager, so it can look quite different from the market and lag during growth rallies.
OALC: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths, followed by financials, consumer and industrial firms. It's a core stock holding run by active managers, and its results depend on their stock picks, so it can differ from a plain index fund.
OARK: A synthetic covered call fund built on an innovation fund of disruptive growth companies, using options to harvest their price swings as income. The payouts can be large because the underlying stocks are volatile, and the strategy caps gains while keeping most losses.
OASC: Small and mid-sized US companies spread across finance, technology, health care and consumer firms, actively enhanced beyond a plain index approach. Smaller companies offer more growth potential and more volatility, and this fund's active selection aims to tilt those odds in the investor's favor.
OBIL: US Treasury bills that mature in about a year, the government's short-term debt. It's a place to hold cash-like money with income from interest, and because the maturity is short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
OBND: A go-anywhere bond portfolio run by Loomis Sayles managers, spanning government, corporate, mortgage and other debt, with room for preferred and convertible securities. It is a flexible income holding that leans on manager judgment to hunt for value across bond markets, including through other funds.
OBOR: Companies positioned to benefit from China's Belt and Road building program across Asia, Africa and beyond, led by banks, materials and industrial firms. It is a bet on Chinese-led infrastructure spending, with the political and currency risks that follow it.
OBTC: A trust that holds bitcoin directly, so its value follows the price of bitcoin, less costs. Bitcoin is a volatile digital currency, and the trust holds the coins instead of stocks, so it moves very differently from a stock fund.
OCDB: Large US stocks wrapped in a deep options cushion, set up each October to absorb a large share of a market fall over the following year. In return, gains are limited, making it a defensive pick for investors bracing for trouble.
OCIO: A blend of about 80% stocks, with technology around 40% of that part, plus bonds and some cash. It's a one-fund, balanced approach that holds other funds and shifts the mix with the market, so it aims to be steadier than all stocks, but it will lag in strong rallies.
OCT: A defined-outcome fund that follows US stocks through options, built to absorb a first slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. The October series runs on a yearly cycle that resets each fall, so the protection on offer depends on when in that cycle shares are bought.
OCTB: Options on a large US stock fund in a structured outcome design that starts each October, absorbing a slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. It offers stock exposure with a planned cushion, suiting investors who prefer knowing the trade off in advance.
OCTH: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay income unless the index falls past a barrier set 20 percent below its starting level. If the barrier breaks, the income stops cushioning and the fund shares the market's decline.
OCTI: Developed-market stocks outside the US, wrapped in options that absorb the first 15 percent of losses over a one-year period starting in October. Gains are left uncapped, unusual for buffer funds, though the cushion is only measured when the period ends.
OCTJ: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay income unless the index falls past a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. The deeper barrier keeps income flowing through moderate sell-offs, but a crash still passes losses through.
OCTM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each October. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
OCTP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to stay invested in stocks with some protection when markets fall.
OCTT: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. It suits investors who want large US stock exposure with a planned cushion, and the terms reset every October.
OCTU: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped once stocks climb past a small starting hurdle. It trades the usual gain cap for that opening flat stretch, a different shape of protection.
OCTW: Options tied to the US large company stocks, heavy in technology, that shield the first 20% of losses over a one year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped, and the cushion only applies if you hold from the start to the end of that period.
OCTZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb part of a market decline over an outcome period that restarts each October, in exchange for capped participation in big rallies. It suits investors who want a measure of protection, but results vary with when shares are bought.
ODDS: Digital entertainment companies worldwide: video game makers, streaming services and esports firms, split between media and consumer stocks. It is a focused bet on how people play and watch now, riding game releases, subscribers and advertising.
ODDZ: Casinos, sportsbooks and online betting platforms: consumer companies built on gambling, from Las Vegas resorts to phone-based wagering apps. It is a focused bet on betting becoming a mainstream pastime, so it swings with consumer spending and with state-by-state legalization decisions.
ODHY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk kind, chosen with a defensive slant that favors sturdier borrowers over the highest payouts. It aims for bond income with fewer blowups than typical junk funds, though defaults and price swings still come with the territory.
ODTE: Option premium income built on three big US stock indexes at once, the S&P 500, the Nasdaq-100 and the small-cap Russell 2000. It is an income strategy rather than a growth one: selling options pays regularly, but caps how much it gains when stocks climb.
OEF: The 100 biggest companies in the S&P 500, with technology at nearly half, followed by communication, financials and health care. It's a core large-company holding, but it's more concentrated and tech-heavy than the broader index, and it leaves out smaller firms.
OEFA: Dividend-paying companies across Europe that pass quality, steadiness and yield tests, spanning drug makers, industrial giants and banks. It favors reliable payers over the highest yields, aiming for international income with fewer nasty surprises.
OEI: Large US stocks picked and managed for income, spanning technology, banks, health care and media, with the portfolio organized around producing payouts. It aims to pay more than a plain large cap fund while still holding familiar big names, trading some growth for income.
OGIG: The world's internet giants, screened for quality and growth: online shopping, search, social media, cloud software and streaming across the US, China and beyond. Technology and communication firms together are over four-fifths of the fund, making it a concentrated bet on the biggest platforms.
OGSP: High-grade structured bonds: top-rated pieces of mortgage, asset-backed and other securitized loan pools, actively selected by specialists in that market. It is an income holding for the cautious side of a bond portfolio, aiming for a bit more yield than plain government bonds with limited credit risk.
OIH: Companies that supply drilling rigs, equipment and services to oil and gas producers. It's a focused bet on the energy industry, so it swings widely with oil prices and drilling activity, and it can rise or fall much more than the broad market.
OILK: Futures contracts on West Texas crude oil, with most of the money parked in cash and short-term holdings to back them. It's a focused bet on oil prices that avoids the extra tax paperwork of some other oil funds, and it can swing hard when oil moves.
OILT: A fund holding oil and gas companies based in Texas, tracking an index of those firms. It is a narrow energy bet, with ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips, Occidental and Diamondback each around 7% of the fund and energy at over 90% of it.
OMAH: A concentrated group of stocks drawn from Berkshire Hathaway and its biggest holdings, mostly financials, communication, technology and consumer staples, paired with options that sell some upside for monthly income. It's built for income, and it can trail when the stocks rally hard.
OMFL: Large US companies reweighted by size, value and volatility factors depending on the stage of the economic cycle, with technology about a third and health care and industrials next. It's a core stock holding with a twist, since its tilts shift over time instead of staying fixed.
OMFS: Small US companies, led by financials, health care, technology and real estate, chosen using several traits like value and momentum. The mix of traits shifts over time based on what's working, so it's a rules-based way to hold small stocks that can swing more than large-company funds.
ONEH: A hedged stock strategy built from options on the big US index: put options set a floor under losses while call options keep a share of the upside. It aims for stock-like growth with smaller drops, acting as a defensive equity holding for investors who fear a sharp sell-off.
ONEO: Large US companies picked for momentum: stocks whose prices have been rising strongly, drawn from the thousand biggest names. It is a growth-tilting core holding, and because momentum leadership rotates, the fund can lag when the market suddenly reverses and yesterday's winners fall out of favor.
ONEQ: Nearly every stock on the Nasdaq exchange, with technology over half the fund and communication, consumer and health care companies behind. It's built for growth, and with much more tech than the broad market it tends to rise and fall harder.
ONEV: Mid-sized and large US companies with relatively steady prices and decent value, spread across financials, industrials, health care and consumer businesses. It aims for a smoother ride than the broad market, so it tends to hold up better in drops but lag in strong rallies.
ONEY: Large and mid-sized US companies that pay above-average dividends, spread across financials, consumer firms and real estate. It's for dividend income with a value tilt, and it holds little in technology, so it can lag when tech leads the market.
ONEZ: A mix of other buffered funds, which cushion stock losses over a set period, plus a smaller amount of hedged funds, tied to large US companies. It staggers the reset dates and picks funds by calendar patterns, aiming for a smoother ride but with limited upside.
ONLN: Companies that sell through the internet: big e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, car buying sites and pet and home goods retailers, almost all consumer discretionary. It is a concentrated bet on shopping moving online, so a few giant platforms drive most of its performance.
ONOF: US large company stocks that the index shifts between fully invested and partly hedged depending on market signals. It's meant to smooth out big drops, but it can lag in quick rebounds because it may be out of the market at the wrong time.
OOSP: Almost entirely securitized bonds, which are pools of loans like mortgages and car loans bundled into bonds. It's meant for income beyond regular bonds, and managers pick opportunistically, so it carries more credit risk than a plain Treasury or corporate bond fund.
OPPE: European stocks, led by financials and industrials, with materials and technology behind them. It's a way to add Europe-based companies to a portfolio, and it has far less technology than US funds, so it moves with the European economy and the euro.
OPPG: Companies around the world chosen using geopolitical analysis, spread across industrials, technology, consumer and media stocks. It is an actively managed global growth holding: the manager shifts toward countries and industries expected to benefit from world events, so results depend heavily on those calls being right.
OPPJ: Japanese companies, with nearly half in industrials and the rest in technology, financials and materials. It's a focused bet on Japan's economy, and it picks stocks using a rules-based method that leans toward profitable firms, so it can differ from a broad Japan fund.
OPTO: Photonics companies, the firms working with light itself: lasers, fiber optics, sensors and optical chips, with swaps and options used to add an income blast. It is a narrow bet on light-based technology, a small and fast-moving field, so it swings far more than a broad tech fund.
OPTZ: US stocks led by technology at nearly half, with financials, health care and consumer companies behind it, picked by a rules-based method that aims to beat the broader market over a full economic cycle. It leans heavily toward tech, so it can swing more than the broad market.
ORBX: Companies developing space technology: rocket builders, satellite makers and the firms turning orbit into a business. It is concentrated in a small, young industry, with a few names carrying much of the weight, so news about launches and contracts moves it sharply.
ORO: A tactical mix that shifts between bitcoin futures, gold futures and cash, guided by computer models watching price trends. It aims to catch much of bitcoin's rises with fewer of its crashes, though the signals can whipsaw in choppy markets.
ORR: A mix of long positions, which gain when stocks rise, and short positions, which gain when stocks fall, mainly in industrials, financials and consumer businesses. It aims to reduce swings versus the market, but results depend heavily on the managers' picks.
OSCV: Smaller US companies that look cheap, led by financials, with industrials, energy and consumer firms next. It's an actively managed value bet on small caps, and since small companies are less stable, it swings more than large company funds.
OSEA: International companies, including some from emerging markets, chosen because they should keep growing earnings for years, led by technology, financials, industrials and consumer companies. It's a growth way to add foreign stocks, and it can fall hard when growth stocks sell off.
OTAX: An actively managed fund of US stocks across company sizes, built to hold broad-market exposure while cutting taxes by selling losing stocks. It mostly holds other funds and stocks like NVIDIA and Apple, tilted toward technology.
OTGL: Latin American stocks, led by Brazilian and Mexican banks, miners and consumer staples companies. It is a focused regional bet whose fortunes ride on commodity prices, local politics and currencies like the real and peso, so it is markedly more volatile than a broad emerging market fund.
OUNZ: Physical gold bars held in a vault, so the price follows gold itself rather than a company. It's used as a hedge against inflation and market turmoil, but gold pays no interest or dividends, and its price can swing sharply for long stretches.
OUSA: Large and mid-sized US companies that pay dividends, chosen for high quality and low swings, led by technology, financials and communication. It's built for steady dividend income with a smoother ride, though it can trail in fast-rising markets.
OUSM: Small US companies that pay dividends and score well on quality and low swings, led by industrials, financials, technology and consumer firms. It's a way to add smaller companies with a steadier tilt, though small stocks still swing more than large ones.
OVB: Investment grade US bonds held through other funds, with an options overlay sold on top to add extra income beyond the bonds' own interest. The overlay is the twist on a core bond holding: more payout potential, paid for with added complexity and some upside given away.
OVF: An actively managed fund that holds other iShares ETFs covering stocks outside the US, from developed and emerging markets. It also uses an options overlay meant to manage risk, so it differs from simply buying a plain international index fund.
OVL: Large US companies, led by technology at about 40%, combined with options that adjust how much of the market's ups and downs you feel. It's a core US stock holding with a twist: the options overlay can soften or change returns, so it won't simply mirror the market.
OVLH: Large US stocks across every major industry, paired with put options, which are insurance contracts that pay off when the market drops sharply. It aims to smooth out crashes for stock investors, and the cost of that insurance quietly trims returns in calm, rising markets.
OVM: Investment grade and some lower-rated municipal bonds, held through another bond fund, with an options overlay that sells put options to add income. The bond interest is tax-free at the federal level, but the option selling adds extra ups and downs on top.
OVQ: The Nasdaq 100's big growth companies, technology-led, with an options overlay on top that sells options to generate extra income. The overlay trades some of the index's upside for payouts, so it behaves like a slightly tamer, income-paying version of a very growth-heavy fund.
OVS: US small company stocks, held through a broad small cap fund, with an options overlay that sells put options to add income. Small caps bring extra growth potential and extra swings, while the option premiums aim to smooth the ride and pay along the way.
OVT: Almost all of this fund sits in one short-term corporate bond ETF, and it sells put options on top to bring in extra income. That options income comes with added risk, because the fund takes on losses if bonds fall sharply.
OWN: One hundred big US companies where insiders, the executives and directors, own the most stock, drawn from the S&P 500. The idea is that leaders with serious money in their own company run it harder, so ownership itself is the selection rule.
OWNB: Companies that hold large amounts of bitcoin on their own balance sheets, the so-called bitcoin standard firms, including miners and software companies turned bitcoin treasuries. It rises and falls with bitcoin's price, with extra company-specific risk on top.
OWNS: Government-backed mortgage bonds whose loans were made to minority, lower-income and workforce families and to neighborhoods with persistent poverty. It pays interest like other mortgage bond funds, and it sets itself apart with an affordable housing mission behind every loan it finances.
OZEM: Drug companies working on GLP-1 and weight loss treatments, from the two big makers of today's hit medicines to small developers still testing theirs. It is a concentrated bet on one drug boom, all health care, so it can swing hard on trial results and rival launches.
PAAA: Bonds backed by pools of corporate loans, called collateralized loan obligations, limited to the top AAA rating. It's built for income with low credit risk and little price swing, since its payments adjust with short-term interest rates rather than falling when rates rise.
PAB: The broad US investment grade bond market, Treasuries, government mortgage bonds and corporate debt, actively managed rather than indexed. Managers adjust maturities and credit as they see value, making it a flexible core bond holding whose results depend on those calls as much as on rates.
PABD: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, led by financials, industrials and technology, weighted to cut carbon emissions in line with the Paris climate goals. It's a climate-minded core international holding, and it behaves like the broader foreign stock market.
PABU: Large and mid-sized US companies, with technology over half and real estate around 15 percent. It's a core stock holding with a climate twist: companies are weighted so the group cuts its carbon footprint each year, which makes it lean even more heavily toward tech than the broad market.
PALC: US large companies, with financials a quarter, communication a fifth and technology about a fifth, with a rules-based approach that switches between different stock styles. It's a core stock holding with a tactical twist, so its mix can look quite different from the broad market.
PALL: Physical palladium metal held in a vault, so it holds no stocks or bonds and pays no income. It's a focused bet on one industrial metal, mostly used in car exhaust systems, and its price can swing sharply with auto demand and supply news.
PAMC: Mid sized US companies whose style exposure alternates between two factor approaches, low volatility and momentum, switching as the model's signals change. It is factor timing for the middle of the market, so results depend on the switches landing on the right style at the right time.
PAPI: US stocks spread across many industries, including technology, consumer, health care and energy, with no single sector dominating. It pairs them with options that trade some upside for monthly income, so it's meant for income and usually trails in strong rallies.
PAPR: S&P 500 exposure with built-in protection: options cushion part of any loss over a one-year period that starts each April, while capping how much gain you can capture. It's for people wanting a smoother ride in stocks, and the cap means it trails in strong rallies.
PATN: Large companies outside the US that own highly valuable patents, led by technology, with industrials, consumer and health care firms behind it. It's a bet that strong inventions give companies an edge, and it includes many foreign firms, so currency moves matter.
PAUG: An options-based fund tied to the S&P 500 that shields against losses beyond a small initial drop for one year starting in August, in exchange for capped gains. It's for investors wanting stock exposure with a cushion, and it must be held through the full period to get that shield.
PAVE: US companies that build and supply infrastructure, with industrials about three quarters and materials about a fifth, including construction, engineering, equipment and steel and cement makers. It's a focused bet on infrastructure spending, so it swings more than the broad market and has little technology.
PAWZ: Companies that earn from pet ownership: animal health and drug makers, pet food brands, retailers and veterinary services. It is a focused bet on steady spending on pets, mixing health care, consumer staples and shops, so it moves with that industry rather than the broad market.
PAYH: Exposure to an index built from autocallable notes, structured products that pay high coupons as long as markets behave and can end early when conditions are met. It chases high income, and the notes are linked to a volatility measure, so sharp market stress can cut both income and principal.
PAYM: Mostly Treasuries and cash, plus swaps that give exposure to a basket of autocallable notes, which are bonds that pay a coupon and get redeemed early when markets hold up. It aims for steady income with defensive intent, but the notes can lose value if stocks fall sharply.
PAYR: An actively managed fund of high dividend-paying US and international stocks, with an options strategy added to bring in extra income. The options can limit gains in strong markets, so it focuses on income over growth.
PBAP: Options on big US stocks built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in April, as its Buffer 20 name states. It favors protection over growth, so expect it to sit out much of any strong rally.
PBAU: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in August, in line with the Buffer 20 name. That deep protection costs upside: gains above the buffer design are capped, so it lags in rallies.
PBCS: Consumer staples companies from around the world: the food, drink, household goods and personal care makers people buy in good times and bad. It is a defensive sector building block: staples are famous for steadiness, and the global spread adds currency swings to an otherwise calm holding.
PBD: Companies working in clean energy, such as solar, wind and related equipment, mostly industrials, technology and utilities from around the world. It's a focused bet on the energy transition, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on policy and rates.
PBDC: Business development companies, which are lenders to mid-sized private US businesses, all counted as financials. It's built for high income because these companies pass most earnings to shareholders, but it can fall sharply when the economy weakens and borrowers struggle to pay.
PBDE: Options on the S&P 500 set to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in December, the deep protection its Buffer 20 name describes. Investors give up part of any rally in exchange, making it a defensive, low-drama holding.
PBE: Entirely health care, specifically biotechnology and genome companies that research and develop new drugs and treatments. It's a focused bet on medical breakthroughs, so it swings more than the broad market, and the outcome of drug trials can make individual holdings jump or crash.
PBEU: Banks in developed Europe, so everything it holds is in financials. It's a focused bet on the European banking industry, which swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates, the economy and the euro.
PBFB: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in February, as the Buffer 20 name suggests. In exchange for that deep cushion, gains are capped, so it trails in strong years.
PBFR: Large US companies, led by technology, held through a ladder of twelve funds with options that cushion a bigger share of stock market losses on staggered yearly cycles. It suits cautious investors, and the staggered timing smooths protection, though gains are capped.
PBJ: US food and beverage companies: soda and energy drink giants, coffee chains, snack and chocolate makers, grocery stores and farm suppliers. Food is a classic defensive industry, since people eat in good times and bad, so the fund tends to swing less than the broad market.
PBJA: Uses options that follow the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period that starts in January, while capping how much of the gains it can capture. The buffer is 20% as named, and it only works if shares are held for the full period.
PBJL: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cover the first 20% of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, so it only works as designed if held for the full period.
PBJN: Options on the S&P 500 set each June for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is certainty about the downside for that year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PBL: An actively managed fund that aims to capture part of the stock market's gains while limiting swings and losses. It mostly avoids buying stocks directly, instead using other funds, options and Treasuries to get stock exposure with a cushion.
PBMR: Options on the S&P 500 designed to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in March, the deep protection its Buffer 20 name describes. The price of that safety is a cap on gains when markets climb strongly.
PBMY: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in May, matching the Buffer 20 in its name. The deep cushion is the draw, paid for with a cap on gains during strong market years.
PBNV: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, the promise in its Buffer 20 name. Deep protection like this means muted gains, suiting investors who fear losses more than missing rallies.
PBOC: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PBOG: Oil and gas producers and explorers, so everything it holds is in the energy sector. It's a focused bet on energy prices, tilted toward companies that pull oil and gas out of the ground, so it swings more than the broad market.
PBOT: Artificial intelligence and automation companies worldwide: chip designers, equipment makers, software platforms and cybersecurity firms. Technology makes up about nine tenths of the fund, so it is a broad AI wager rather than a bet on one kind of AI business.
PBP: The stocks of the S&P 500, America's largest companies, with about 40 percent in technology, while selling call options on the index for extra income. It's meant for income and a smoother ride, but it gives up big gains in strong rallies.
PBPH: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies from developed countries around the world, all in health care. It's a focused bet on drug development, with global reach, so its results swing on drug approvals and carry currency effects.
PBQQ: Four Nasdaq-100 buffer funds layered together, each with its own one-year protection period starting a quarter apart, so part of the fund resets every three months. The ladder smooths the timing risk of a single reset date while keeping a buffer against a first slice of losses.
PBSC: Debt that is secured by collateral: bundles of loans and other asset-backed borrowings, actively managed so the mix can flex across secured credit markets. It is an income fund built on loans with assets behind them, which cushions losses compared with unsecured debt but still carries credit risk.
PBSE: Options on the S&P 500 set each September for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PBTP: US Treasury bonds with up to five years left, whose principal rises with inflation. It's meant to protect buying power with small price swings, as the short maturities make it less sensitive to interest rates than longer inflation-protected funds.
PBUB: US banks of all sizes, from giant money-center lenders to regional banks, and nothing else. It is a pure sector building block: the whole fund rises and falls with bank profits, interest rates and credit quality, with no other industries to soften a banking slump.
PBUS: Large and mid-sized US companies across the whole market, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care behind. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, much like other broad market funds.
PBW: Smaller US companies in clean energy: industrials, technology, materials and consumer makers, each with roughly a fifth to a third of the fund. It's a focused bet on the shift to cleaner power, and it swings much more than the broad market, with sharp drops and rebounds.
PBWN: Industrial companies from outside the US: engineering, electrical equipment and machinery giants of Europe and Japan, with industrials at nearly the whole fund. It fills the industrial corner of a foreign stock portfolio, so it swings with global manufacturing and with currencies other than the dollar.
PCEB: Below-investment-grade corporate bonds issued in Europe and denominated in euros, actively chosen for their higher yields. Along with the usual junk bond default risk, its results depend on the euro's value, since the bonds pay and trade in euros.
PCEF: A fund that holds other income-focused closed-end funds, mixing stocks and bonds, with preferred shares as a smaller piece. It's for high monthly income, but those funds often use borrowing, so it can swing more than a regular balanced fund.
PCFI: Floating rate loans and securities, mostly bank loans made to companies, whose interest payments reset as market rates change. When rates rise its income rises too, making it a rare bond fund that can welcome higher rates, though the borrowers are often leveraged firms.
PCHI: High yield corporate bonds, the below-investment-grade debt often called junk bonds, chosen actively by Polen's credit team. It aims to beat the broader high yield market over a full credit cycle, accepting default risk in exchange for higher interest income.
PCI: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies, mostly maturing in five to ten years. It's meant for steady income, and since it holds only company debt rather than government bonds, it takes more credit risk, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
PCL: Bonds issued by US companies that mature in ten years or more, from big names like JPMorgan, UnitedHealth and Wells Fargo. Long maturities mean the fund's price swings more when interest rates change, in exchange for higher interest payments.
PCLC: A focused portfolio of large growth companies, with technology over half, picked by a manager looking at businesses from several angles. It is an actively managed growth holding: concentration in tech gives it punch, and bigger swings than a broad index fund.
PCLG: A focused portfolio of about two dozen large companies with durable competitive advantages, picked by Polen Capital for steady, compounding growth. Concentration is the point: software, payments and chip leaders dominate, and each holding is expected to earn its place for years.
PCLN: Companies whose products clean up the planet: chip-making equipment, industrial technology, water and efficiency specialists from around the world. Technology and industry dominate, making it an environmental theme expressed through engineers rather than solar panels and wind farms.
PCLO: The safest slices, rated AAA, of collateralized loan obligations backed by private company loans. It offers income from private credit with the protection of sitting at the top of the payment line, though the underlying loans are not traded publicly.
PCMM: Bundles of loans to private companies, packaged into securities called CLOs. It's meant for higher income than ordinary bonds, and since the payments float with interest rates, it holds up better than most bonds when rates rise, though it carries more credit risk.
PCOV: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying stocks that also uses options to generate extra income. Apple, Microsoft and JPMorgan are the biggest holdings at roughly 4% to 5% each, and the options income limits some upside.
PCPC: Property and casualty insurers: the companies that insure homes, cars and businesses against accidents and disasters, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on one steady corner of finance, moving with premiums, storms and claims costs.
PCPI: Inflation-linked bonds from governments and companies, whose values adjust as prices rise, held with derivatives for flexibility. It's meant as a hedge against inflation with relatively short maturities, though it can still lose value when interest rates rise.
PCPP: A ready-made balanced portfolio following a published model index: a bit over half in global stocks, plus bonds, cash and other assets. One fund covers several asset classes at a moderate risk level, with financial stocks the biggest single theme inside the equity side.
PCR: Private credit exposures, meaning loans to companies made outside the banking system, reached through index-linked instruments rather than direct lending. It is an income holding with less transparency than regular bonds: the loans are hard to value daily, and losses land when borrowers struggle.
PCS: Short-term bonds from companies, mostly large banks and other businesses, with maturities of up to five years. It's meant for income with less swing than longer bonds, though it still falls when rates rise.
PCSG: A focused portfolio of small and mid-sized growth companies, led by technology at about a third, with industrials and health care behind it. It is an actively managed growth holding: smaller companies offer more room to run, but they swing more than large stocks.
