PCY: Government bonds issued by emerging market countries, all priced in US dollars. It pays higher interest than US government bonds to make up for higher risk, so it's for income, but it can fall sharply when investors get nervous about developing economies.
PDBA: Agriculture commodities such as crops and livestock, held through futures contracts rather than physical goods, with the rest in short-term cash-like holdings. It's a way to add farm prices to a portfolio, and it avoids the K-1 tax form, though prices can swing sharply with weather and supply.
PDBC: A mix of the most heavily traded raw materials, such as oil, metals and farm products, gained through futures contracts, with the rest held in cash-like safe assets. It's a hedge against inflation and a way to diversify away from stocks and bonds, though commodity prices can swing sharply.
PDEC: S&P 500 exposure with built-in protection: options cushion part of any loss over a one-year period that starts each December, while capping how much gain you can capture. It's for people wanting a smoother ride in stocks, and the cap means it trails in strong rallies.
PDN: Small and mid-sized companies outside the US across developed countries, led by industrials and financials, with consumer businesses and materials behind them. It adds international small-company exposure, and it picks stocks by size of business, such as sales and cash flow, rather than stock price.
PDP: Large and mid-sized US stocks picked for strong recent price momentum, with technology the biggest slice at over a third and industrials about a quarter. It's a growth tilt that chases winners, so it can fall hard when market leadership suddenly changes.
PEJ: US leisure and entertainment businesses: consumer companies such as restaurants, hotels, cruise lines and retailers make up about half, and media and communication firms about a third. It's a focused bet on how freely people spend, so it tends to drop when the economy weakens.
PEMX: Actively picked companies across emerging markets, with China and Hong Kong left out entirely, so chipmakers and banks in Taiwan, South Korea and India dominate and technology is over half the fund. It is a growth holding for investors who want developing markets without the China exposure most such funds carry.
PEPS: Large US stocks matching the broad market's shape, with technology about 40 percent, plus an options overlay run by Parametric managers to add extra return on top. It is a core equity holding with a derivative twist, aiming to squeeze out a bit more than the plain stock portfolio.
PEPT: Companies advancing peptide-based products: medicines, supplements and cosmetics built from short chains of amino acids, plus the technology that makes them. It is a narrow bet on one corner of biotechnology, the field behind many new weight-loss and metabolic drugs, so it swings with drug trial news.
PEVC: Public stocks, funds and futures combined to mimic how private equity and venture capital portfolios perform, led by technology at nearly half. It is a growth holding for investors who want private-market style exposure they can trade daily, though the match to real private funds is only approximate.
PEX: Companies that invest in private businesses, like Ares Capital, 3i Group and Onex, which are listed on stock exchanges so they can be bought like any stock. It is a way to get private equity style exposure, and the top five holdings are about 40% of it.
PEXL: About one hundred large and mid sized US companies in equal weights, screened for earning a high share of their sales abroad and for fast growing free cash flow. It tilts toward technology and global brands, offering exporters' earnings without leaving the US stock market.
PEY: US companies with long records of raising dividends and above-average yields, led by financials, consumer staples and utilities. It's meant for dividend income and a steadier ride than growth stocks, but it tends to trail when technology leads a rally.
PEZ: Consumer companies selling discretionary goods and services, from online retail and airlines to hotels, restaurants and carmakers, chosen for strong recent price momentum. The momentum focus means the lineup changes as trends shift, and it can lag when out-of-favor stocks suddenly rebound.
PFDE: US stocks picked by a manager, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%, then consumer, financial and health care companies. It's meant as a core stock holding, but with relatively few holdings and a heavy tech tilt, it can swing more than the broad market.
PFEB: Gives you exposure to the S&P 500, which is led by technology, using options that cushion part of any losses over a one-year period starting in February. In exchange, gains are capped, so it's built for investors who want a smoother ride and will trade away upside, and results depend on when you buy.
PFF: Preferred stocks, which are hybrids that pay fixed dividends like bonds but trade like shares, mostly issued by banks and other financial companies. It's built for high income, though its price drops when interest rates rise and can fall hard in a financial crisis.
PFFA: Preferred stocks, which are hybrids that pay fixed dividends like bonds but trade like stocks, mostly from real estate and financial type companies. It's meant for high income, and uses borrowed money to boost payouts, so it swings more than other preferred funds and drops when interest rates rise.
PFFD: Preferred stocks, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pays fixed dividends, mostly from US banks and other financial companies. It's built for high monthly-style income, but its price tends to fall when interest rates rise and it shares less in stock market gains.
PFFR: Preferred shares issued by real estate investment trusts, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular stock. It's for income, but its price drops when interest rates rise and it depends on the health of real estate companies.
PFFV: Preferred stocks, which are hybrids that pay set dividends and rank above regular stock, whose dividend rates float with interest rates. It's built for income, and because the payouts adjust, it holds up better than fixed-rate preferreds when rates rise.
PFI: Financial companies only: banks, insurers, asset managers and real estate firms, narrowed to a few dozen names showing the strongest recent price momentum. Concentrating on one sector and chasing its hottest stocks makes it a focused, jumpier bet than a plain financial fund.
PFIG: Investment grade US corporate bonds, chosen and weighted by company size and financial strength instead of by how much debt each issues. It's meant for steady income above Treasuries, and its price drops when interest rates rise or when companies' credit worsens.
PFIX: Interest rate derivatives that gain when rates rise, plus a pile of Treasuries and other bonds for income. It's a hedge for portfolios hurt by rising rates, and it usually loses value when rates fall, so it works like insurance.
PFLD: Preferred shares (stock-like securities that pay fixed income) and hybrid bonds, mostly issued by banks and utilities, picked for shorter durations. It's meant for regular income, and the shorter duration makes its price drop less than typical preferred funds when interest rates rise.
PFM: Large US companies that have raised their dividends for at least ten years in a row, with technology, financials, health care and consumer staples leading. It's a core holding for dividend growth and steady companies, and it can lag in fast, tech-led rallies.
PFOE: Fifteen to thirty companies worldwide that its managers judge to be high-quality growers, from music and streaming platforms to chip equipment and health insurers. Such a short list makes it a conviction portfolio: each pick counts, for better or worse.
PFRL: Loans to companies with lower credit ratings whose interest rates reset as short-term rates change. It aims for income that rises with rates, so it holds up better than most bonds when rates climb, but it can fall in a downturn when borrowers struggle.
PFRX: A focused portfolio of US stocks drawn from Putnam's own analyst research, concentrating on the team's highest-conviction ideas across industries. With fewer holdings than a broad fund, each pick matters more, so results depend on the analysts' calls rather than on the market as a whole.
PFXF: Preferred stocks and similar hybrid securities, which pay steady fixed dividends like bonds, with utilities about three quarters. It's meant for income, and by leaving out banks it avoids financial sector trouble, though its price still drops when interest rates rise.
PGF: Preferred shares issued by banks, insurers and other financial companies, which pay fixed dividends and sit between bonds and stocks. It's for high income, and since it's concentrated in finance, it's hit hard by banking trouble and rising interest rates.
PGHY: Below-investment-grade US dollar bonds issued by companies outside the US, nearly all from energy businesses. It's meant for high income and international credit exposure, but the bonds are riskier than safe ones, so it can fall hard in a weak economy.
PGJ: Chinese companies listed on US exchanges: online shopping, gaming, search, restaurants and delivery platforms headquartered in China but traded in New York. It is a bet on China's consumer internet through American-listed shares, carrying both China policy risk and US listing risk.
PGRI: Large growth companies from outside the US, led by technology at about a third and industrials close behind. Managers pick the stocks by hand, looking for fast growers in developed and emerging markets, so results depend heavily on their choices.
PGRO: A concentrated group of large US growth companies, with technology a bit over half and communication around a sixth. It's meant for growth, and with fewer holdings and so much tech it can swing harder than the broad market.
PGX: Preferred stocks, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of regular stock when a company is in trouble. It's for income seekers, and its price drops when interest rates rise, with issuers heavily from banks and other financial firms.
PHDG: The S&P 500 paired with a hedge that uses volatility futures, plus some cash, so it tries to lose less when markets drop sharply. It holds the big index names like NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, but the hedge can hold back gains in rallies.
PHEQ: Large US stocks, with technology over 40 percent, combined with an options strategy meant to cut losses in market drops. It aims for a smoother ride than a plain stock fund, but it usually trails in strong rallies.
PHO: US companies that clean, filter and move water, mostly industrials such as equipment and utilities makers, plus health care and technology firms. It's a focused bet on the water industry, so it follows that theme rather than the whole market.
PHOX: Companies working in photonics and optics: lasers, fiber optics, sensors and the light-based technology inside data centers and medical devices. It is a narrow technology bet on the hardware of the AI buildout, so it swings with data-center spending and chip demand.
PHYL: High yield bonds, which are loans to companies with weaker credit ratings, spread across many industries. It aims for higher income than safer bonds, but these companies are likelier to default, so it can fall sharply when the economy weakens.
PHYS: Actual gold bullion held in vaults, so the shares move with the price of gold itself rather than with mining companies. It is a direct way to own the metal as a safe-haven asset, and it tends to be steadier than silver or gold miners, though it still follows gold's price swings.
PICB: Investment-grade bonds from companies outside the US, paid in currencies such as the euro, pound and yen, and mostly from banks and other financial firms. It diversifies a bond portfolio abroad, but foreign currency swings against the dollar can hurt or help returns.
PICK: Companies that dig up metals and minerals around the world, such as iron ore, copper and steel inputs, almost entirely in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on mining, so it swings with commodity prices and global demand, especially from China, and moves much more than the broad market.
PID: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, led by financials, utilities, communication and energy firms that have raised their payouts year after year. It's meant for steady income from international stocks, and it leans toward slower, mature businesses, so it often lags when growth stocks lead.
PIE: Large companies in emerging markets such as India, Taiwan and Brazil, with technology at almost half and financials, industrials and materials behind it. It's a growth bet on developing economies, picking stocks whose prices have been rising, so it swings far more than US stocks.
PIEL: Companies outside the United States that lead their industries in exports: the manufacturers and brands that sell heavily into world markets. It is a foreign growth holding built on trade strength: export champions ride global demand, so a strong dollar or a trade slowdown hits it directly.
PIEQ: Stocks from outside the US, including emerging markets like China, led by financials and technology, then health care and consumer companies. It's actively managed and meant as a core international holding, so a manager's choices, not an index, decide what it owns.
PIFI: Intermediate US bonds, mostly Treasuries and government agency debt, actively managed with maturities kept between zero and ten years. It is a quality-first core bond holding, and active management of its maturity mix is meant to soften the blow when interest rates rise.
PINC: Securitized bonds actively picked by PGIM: mortgage-backed, asset-backed and commercial mortgage securities rather than ordinary company or government bonds. It is an income holding built on loan pools, where specialist credit work on the underlying mortgages and assets is the main way it tries to beat plain bond funds.
PINK: US health care companies, from drugmakers to medical device makers and insurers, with a small slice of industrials. It's a focused bet on health care, and the managers pick a limited number of stocks, so it can behave differently from the broad health care sector.
PIO: Companies tied to water, from industrial makers of pipes and filtration equipment to water utilities, with some health care and materials firms. It's a focused bet on the water theme, spread across countries, and it moves with industrial activity more than with the broad market.
PIPE: Master limited partnerships (MLPs) and other companies that run oil and gas pipelines and related energy infrastructure, mostly in North America. It is all energy, and Targa, Plains, Williams, TC Energy and Cheniere are about 30% of it.
PIT: A spread of commodity futures, such as energy, metals and farm products, with most of the money held in cash like instruments. It's a hedge against inflation that moves differently from stocks and bonds, but it can swing widely when commodity prices drop.
PIZ: Large developed-market companies outside the US that have been rising lately, led by financials and industrials. It's a momentum fund, so it chases recent winners and can reverse fast when trends change.
PJAN: US large company stocks, mostly technology, reached through options on an S&P 500 fund. It's built to absorb a large share of losses over a one year period starting in January, but gains are capped, and the full protection only applies if held from start to end.
PJFG: A concentrated group of US growth companies, with technology over half, followed by communication, consumer and health care. It's built for growth, with fewer holdings than most funds, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
PJFM: Mid-sized US companies picked through a mix of fundamental research and systematic portfolio building, spread across technology, finance, industry and health care. It is a focused mid-cap portfolio, so the managers' stock choices matter more than the mid-cap market itself.
PJFV: A concentrated group of US stocks a manager thinks are priced below their worth, with technology about a quarter, then financials and industrials. It suits someone wanting a value-tilted core holding, but with fewer stocks than a broad fund, it can swing away from the market.
PJIN: Companies from around the world, picked by PGIM's Jennison team as a core international holding. Managers choose stocks across developed markets rather than copying an index, so the mix shifts with where they find the strongest businesses.
PJIO: An actively managed fund of growth companies outside the US, including some in emerging markets. It is concentrated and tech heavy: SK Hynix, Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor are about 20% of it.
PJP: About 30 US drug companies that research, develop and sell pharmaceuticals, so it's entirely health care. It's a focused bet on one industry, with fewer companies than a broad health fund, and it can swing on drug approvals, patent expirations or pricing rules.
PJSM: Small and medium-sized US companies picked by PGIM's Jennison team across all industries, aiming for a mix of steady growers and undervalued names. It is an actively managed core holding for the smaller end of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds.
PJUL: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, wrapped in options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period that starts in July. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it's for cautious investors, who should note that the protection works best if held to the end.
PJUN: Gives you exposure to the S&P 500, which is led by technology, using options that cushion part of any losses over a one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are capped, so it's built for investors who want a smoother ride and will trade away upside, and results depend on when you buy.
PJUS: A hand-picked basket of large US companies across industries, with technology the biggest slice at a little over a third. Managers choose the stocks instead of copying an index, aiming for a core holding that can do a bit better than the broad market.
PKB: US companies that build things: industrial firms such as contractors and engineering businesses make up under half, materials like cement and lumber about two fifths, and homebuilders and related consumer names the rest. It's a focused bet on construction, so it rises and falls with housing and building activity.
PKW: US companies that have been buying back their own shares, with financials making up about two fifths and technology, consumer companies and energy behind. It's a tilt toward firms returning cash to shareholders, and it is heavy in financials compared with the broad market.
PLA: A note-like bet on Palantir stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or rises. If Palantir falls hard, the fund can drop sharply too, and steady payouts come with a ceiling on gains.
PLGI: A tactical mix of growth stocks and income producing securities and options, traded actively and often as the manager shifts between offense and income. The flexibility is the point: it can chase growth or lean on payouts, and results depend entirely on the manager's timing.
PLIB: Income built around a single stock, Palantir, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost the payout from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet: everything depends on one company's stock, so it can swing sharply even though the goal is income.
PLTM: Physical platinum bars held in storage, so the price follows the metal itself. It's used as a way to own an industrial and jewelry metal outside of stocks, but it pays no income and the price can swing sharply with factory demand, particularly for car exhaust parts.
PLTW: A bet on Palantir stock that aims for about 120 percent of its weekly moves, paying out distributions every week. It resets weekly so it's for short holding periods, and it can lose a lot quickly if that single stock falls.
PLTY: Income from options tied to one stock, the data software company Palantir, with the rest in Treasuries and cash. It's built to pay high monthly income, but gives up much of the stock's big gains and can still lose a lot when the stock falls.
PLYY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged Palantir fund, stacking options on top of a fund that already amplifies the stock's daily moves. It is an aggressive short-term income trade: the double leverage makes swings extreme, so it suits active traders, not steady savers.
PMAP: Large US stocks matching the S&P 500 mix, paired with an options cushion over the one-year period starting in April. It trades some upside for protection: gains stop at a cap, while the first slice of any market fall is absorbed.
PMAR: Options on a large-company US stock fund, set up to cushion losses over a one-year period that starts each March. In exchange, gains are capped, so it's built for people who want some protection in drops and accept limited upside.
PMAU: Large US stocks, the same broad mix as the S&P 500, wrapped in options that cushion the first chunk of a fall over a one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are capped, so it suits cautious investors who want stocks with a softer landing.
PMAY: Large US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that absorb part of the market's drops over a one year period that starts each May. It's for cautious investors who want stock exposure with some protection, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
PMBS: Mortgage-backed bonds, which pool home loans and pass the payments to investors, managed actively by PIMCO. It's meant for steady income and diversification from stocks, though it can lose value when interest rates rise or when homeowners refinance or repay early.
PMDE: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a large part of the index's losses over a one-year period that starts in December, while capping how much of its gains you can keep. It is actively managed, and the protection only works if held through the full period.
PMFB: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, combined with options that absorb an opening slice of losses over the year starting in February. The trade-off is a cap on gains, making it a cautious way to stay invested in stocks.
PMIO: Municipal bonds from across the US, actively hunted for income opportunities in issues other buyers overlook, with interest generally free from federal income tax. It aims to pay more than plain muni index funds by taking selective credit risks within the tax exempt market.
PMJA: Large US stocks matching the broad S&P 500 mix, wrapped in options that cushion the opening slice of any fall over the year starting in January. The cushion costs some upside, since gains are capped, making it a gentler way to hold stocks.
PMJL: Uses options on the S&P 500 to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in July, with a maximum buffer meant to absorb a large share of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
PMJN: An actively managed fund tied to the S&P 500 that uses options to cushion a large part of the losses over a set period starting in June, in exchange for a limit on gains. The protection only applies if shares are held for the full period.
PMMF: Short-term, high-quality loans to governments, banks and corporations, plus overnight lending agreements, so it holds nearly all cash-like assets. It's a place to park money you may need soon, with a stable price and interest that rises and falls with rates.
PMMR: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, combined with an options cushion that absorbs the first slice of losses over the year starting in March. Gains are capped in exchange, so it suits investors who want stocks with some protection underneath.
PMMY: Large US stocks, the same broad mix as the S&P 500, paired with options that cushion the first chunk of a fall over the one-year period starting in May. Gains are limited in exchange, making it a cautious route into the stock market.
PMNV: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, wrapped in options that cushion the opening slice of a fall over the year starting in November. Because gains are capped, it is built for investors who want to stay in stocks with a softer landing.
PMOC: The S&P 500's big US companies, combined with an options cushion over the one-year period starting in October. The cushion absorbs the opening slice of a fall while capping gains, so it is built for a smoother stock market ride.
PMSE: Uses options on the S&P 500 to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in September, with a maximum buffer meant to absorb a large share of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
PMTL: Mining companies that dig up gold, silver and other precious metals, screened for quality by profitability and balance-sheet measures. It is a leveraged-feeling bet on metal prices: miners usually rise faster than gold itself when prices climb, and fall harder when they drop.
PNOV: Large US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that cushion part of the market's drops over a one year period that starts each November. It's for cautious investors who want stock exposure with some protection, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
PNQI: Internet companies listed on the Nasdaq, with technology at about 40%, communications about a third and online retailers about a quarter. It's a growth-oriented bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
POCT: S&P 500 exposure with built-in protection: options cushion part of any loss over a one-year period that starts each October, while capping how much gain you can capture. It's for people wanting a smoother ride in stocks, and the cap means it trails in strong rallies.
POMG: Growth companies in the small and midsize range, actively hunted by PRIMECAP, a manager known for patient, research-driven stock picking. It aims for tomorrow's large companies before they are obvious, so it accepts years of uneven results and bigger swings than a large-company fund.
POW: An actively managed fund of global companies that benefit from the growing need for electricity, such as makers of electrical equipment, power components and utilities. It holds companies like LS Electric, Delta Electronics and Powell, and industrials are about 60% of it.
POWA: US large companies chosen for having steady profit margins over time, which hints they can raise prices without losing business. It spreads across technology, health care, industrials and consumer companies, and works as a core holding with a quality tilt that may lag in speculative rallies.
POWR: Companies that power the US electric grid, about half utilities, a third industrial firms that build the equipment, and some energy producers. It's a themed bet on rising electricity demand, and because utilities are a big part, it is sensitive to interest rates.
PPA: Aerospace and defense companies, mostly industrials such as makers of aircraft, weapons, military electronics and space systems. It's a focused bet on government defense spending, so it swings with budgets and global tensions rather than the broad market.
PPH: Drug companies, all from the health care sector, including big makers of prescription medicines. It's a focused bet on one industry that tends to hold up better in slowdowns, though it can swing on drug approvals, patent expirations and pricing rules.
PPI: Companies tied to real assets that tend to hold value when prices rise, including industrials, energy, materials and real estate. It's meant as an inflation hedge to pair with regular stocks, and an active manager picks the mix, so commodity swings can move it.
PPLT: A fund that holds physical platinum bars in a vault, so it owns a metal rather than companies or bonds. It's a focused bet on platinum prices, which are used in cars and industry, so it can swing sharply and pays no income.
PPTY: US real estate companies diversified deliberately across property types, from apartments and warehouses to shops, offices and data centers. The mix is set by property market fundamentals rather than company size, aiming for a more balanced property holding than the big-REIT-heavy indexes provide.
PQAP: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
PQDI: Preferred shares and other income-paying securities, roughly half preferred and half bonds, mostly from financial companies. It's for steady income, but its price drops when interest rates rise and it can fall when credit worries grow.
PQJA: Options on the Nasdaq-100 built to absorb about the first eighth of a loss over a one-year period starting in January, matching its Buffer 12 name. Buffering tech-heavy growth stocks tames their famous swings, with capped gains as the cost.
PQJL: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each July, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
PQNT: An actively managed fund of large companies outside the US, where artificial intelligence tools help pick and weight the stocks. It is spread widely, with the biggest holding, ASML, only about 4% of the fund.
PQOC: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100 create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. Because the underlying stocks lean heavily on technology, it pairs that protection with more growth and more swing than broad market buffers.
PQUS: US large companies chosen by a manager using artificial intelligence to rank stocks, with technology the biggest slice at about 43%. It's meant as a core stock holding that tries to beat the market, but it can swing as much as tech-heavy markets do.
PQV: Large US stocks through options on the S&P 500, with a built-in cushion that absorbs the first 5% of losses over each quarterly outcome period. It suits cautious investors: the smaller buffer means a higher cap on gains than deeper-protection funds, and terms reset every three months.
PQX: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses, with the protection resetting every quarter instead of once a year. The shorter cycle keeps the cushion fresh, in exchange for capped gains each quarter.
PQXV: Large US stocks through options on the S&P 500, with a built-in cushion that absorbs the first 15% of losses over each quarterly outcome period. It is made for cautious stock investors: gains are capped, and the protection resets every three months rather than lasting all year.
PQXX: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 20 percent of losses, with the shield resetting every quarter. The deeper cushion and fast resets suit especially cautious investors, paid for with capped gains each quarter.
PRAB: Investment grade asset-backed securities, including harder-to-buy private issues alongside public ones, in a State Street portfolio. It earns income from pools of consumer and business loans, and the access to private asset-backed deals, usually reserved for big institutions, is what sets it apart.
PRAE: Global stock funds covering value, small companies and international markets, plus an alternatives overlay of futures, commodities and currencies. The overlay is meant to diversify the stock exposure and soften drops, adding complexity most plain portfolios skip.
PRAM: A fund focused on companies tied to computer memory chips and photonics, the use of light to move data. Much of its exposure may come through derivatives rather than owning the stocks directly, and it is a narrow, concentrated theme.
PRAY: An actively managed fund of US and international stocks screened to fit Christian values, excluding companies that conflict with them. It is a mix of big and small names, with technology the largest sector at around 30%.
PRCS: A concentrated group of US companies, with technology about a third, then industrials, consumer companies and financials. The managers pick on quality and responsible business practices, so it can serve as a core holding with fewer names, and it may behave quite differently from the broad market.
PREF: Mostly preferred stocks and bonds issued by banks and other financial companies, which pay fixed income and rank ahead of regular shares. It's meant for steady income, but prices fall when interest rates rise and can drop sharply if the financial sector struggles.
PRF: Large US companies picked and weighted by size of sales, cash flow, dividends and book value instead of stock price. Technology is about a fifth and financials and health care follow, so it works as a core holding with a value tilt that can trail in growth-led rallies.
PRFD: Preferred shares and similar capital securities, mostly issued by banks and insurers, which sit between bonds and stocks. It's built for regular income, but its price can fall when interest rates rise, and it depends heavily on the health of financial companies.
PRFZ: About 1,500 small and mid-sized US companies, chosen and weighted by sales, cash flow, dividends and book value rather than by market size. It's a broad core holding for smaller companies that avoids loading up on the priciest stocks, though smaller firms swing more.
PRIV: Investment-grade bonds, including a mix of regular public corporate bonds and loans made privately to companies. It aims for more income than a typical bond fund, but the private loans are harder to sell quickly, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
PRIZ: Preferred shares, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pays set dividends, mostly issued by banks and other big companies. It is built for steady income that usually pays more than regular bonds, though preferred prices still dip when markets fall.
PRMR: An actively managed, frequently traded portfolio of large US companies, spread across technology, finance, consumer and health care names. Frequent trading sets it apart from buy-and-hold funds: the managers act on shorter-term signals, so the lineup and results can change character quickly.
PRN: Industrial companies, such as aerospace, machinery and transportation, making up almost three quarters, with technology about a quarter. It's a focused bet on industrials, and it picks stocks that have recently been rising fastest, so it can swing hard when trends reverse.
PRNT: Companies involved in 3D printing, from the software and design tools to printers, materials and medical uses. It tracks an index of companies spread across the US and Europe, with no holding above about 6%.
PRSD: Investment-grade bonds that mature soon, mixing publicly traded company debt with privately arranged loans. It's built for steady income with little price swing, and since private credit is hard to sell quickly, it behaves a bit differently from plain short-term bond funds.
PRTO: A tactical portfolio steered by trend and momentum signals, currently heavy in small-cap stock funds and gold, with some big-index exposure. The mix shifts as trends change, aiming to ride what is working and step aside from what is not.
PRVS: A concentrated portfolio of large US companies bought at value prices, run by Parnassus, a firm known for responsible investing. With fewer holdings than most value funds, each pick matters more, and the approach favors established companies its managers judge temporarily out of favor.
PRXG: Large US growth companies screened to align with the manager's stewardship values, though technology giants still dominate at nearly three-fifths of the fund. It pairs mainstream growth exposure with a values filter, which can exclude or favor companies on more than financial grounds.
PRXI: Stocks from countries outside the US, screened through a faith-based impact lens, with banks about a quarter of the fund and industrials and technology behind them. It gives international diversification with social screens applied, so some industries common abroad are left out.
PRXV: Large US value companies screened to align with the manager's stewardship values, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer brands. It pairs dividend-leaning value exposure with a values filter, which shapes the lineup beyond the usual cheapness and profitability tests.
PSAI: The 100 S&P 500 companies with the strongest artificial intelligence exposure, chosen by an AI-driven scoring approach across all industries. It is a concentrated growth bet on the AI leaders among big US companies, so it swings more than the full index.
PSC: Small US companies, led by health care and financials, with technology and industrials behind them. It's an actively managed fund that picks individual small-cap stocks, aiming to beat the small-company index, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones.
PSCC: Small companies in consumer staples: food makers, grocery distributors and household goods firms serving everyday needs. Staples are usually the calmest corner of the market, but small size adds wiggle, so this is defensive with a small-company twist.
PSCD: Small US consumer discretionary companies: the retailers, restaurants, car-related and leisure firms selling things people buy when they feel flush. It is a focused bet on the American consumer's mood, and small discretionary stocks are among the first to fall when shoppers pull back.
PSCE: Small US energy companies: oil and gas drillers, equipment and service firms, and pipeline operators outside the industry giants. It is a focused bet on smaller energy names, which swing harder than big oil stocks when fuel prices and drilling activity move.
PSCF: Small US financial companies: community and regional banks make up about two thirds, with small real estate trusts most of the rest. It is a focused bet on local American finance, so it depends on small-town lending health and property markets rather than Wall Street giants.
PSCH: Small US health care companies, from drug and biotech makers to medical device and service providers. It's a focused bet on one industry's smaller players, so it swings more than the broad market and than big pharma funds, while ignoring every other sector.
PSCI: Small US industrial companies such as machinery makers, airlines, building suppliers and staffing firms, with a bit of technology and consumer businesses. It's a focused bet on small industrial firms, so it swings more than large-company funds and follows the health of the economy.
PSCJ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged conservatively to keep most of the money safe while taking a modest part in market gains, over a period resetting each July. It aims for a smoother ride than stocks, accepting smaller gains in strong years in exchange for protection.
PSCM: Small US materials companies: chemical makers, metal miners, packaging, paper and specialty materials producers. It is a narrow bet on the raw-materials economy through small stocks, so it tends to swing hard with commodity prices and factory demand.
PSCQ: Options on the S&P 500 in a conservative structured outcome design starting each October, cushioning losses while keeping only part of any gains. The conservative tilt favors protection over participation, suiting investors who want stock exposure on a leash.
PSCT: Small US technology companies, nearly all in software, hardware and related tech businesses. It's a focused bet on one sector among smaller firms, so it swings more than the broad market and more than large-company tech funds.
PSCU: Small US companies in two steadier industries, utilities and communication services, from rural power and water firms to satellite and media names. Small size makes these normally calm industries livelier than usual, an unusual mix of caution and spice.
PSCW: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to protect part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in April, with a limit on the gains. This is the conservative version, which uses a bigger cushion and a lower cap on gains.
PSCX: Options on the S&P 500 in a conservative structured outcome design starting each January, cushioning losses while keeping only part of any gains. The conservative tilt favors protection over participation, suiting investors who want stock exposure on a leash.
PSDM: Bonds with short lifespans from many sources, including government, corporate and mortgage debt, picked by active managers. It aims for more income than cash with less price risk than a typical bond fund, since short bonds react less to interest rate changes.
PSEP: Options on the S&P 500 that are set up to absorb a large part of any losses over a one-year period starting in September. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, and the protection works as designed only if you hold from the start date to the end.
PSFD: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to protect part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in January, with a limit on the gains. This is the flex version, which balances the cushion and cap more evenly.
PSFF: A fund holding other buffer ETFs, which use options to cushion part of the loss in the US stock market and cap part of the gain, over a set period. It's meant for investors who want some protection from drops, and the cap means it trails in strong rallies.
PSFJ: Options on the S&P 500 in a flexible structured outcome design that starts each July, with room to reset the outcome terms during the year rather than locking them for a full term. It offers large stock exposure with a built in cushion, traded for a cap on gains.
PSFM: Options referencing the big US index fund shape a defined outcome over the year from April, under Pacer and Swan's structured SOS options approach. The design targets a buffer against losses with capped gains, using a flexible options mix that can be adjusted as markets move during the period.
PSFO: Options on the S&P 500 in a flexible outcome design, meant to join in market gains while keeping a measure of protection against losses, over a period ending each October. Flexibility means the protection level can vary, unlike the fixed promises of plain buffer funds.
PSH: Mostly bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, often called high-yield or junk bonds, but focused on ones that mature soon. It's for extra income with less sensitivity to interest rate changes than longer high-yield funds, though it can still lose value when the economy sours and defaults rise.
PSI: Thirty US companies that make semiconductors, so it is all chips and nothing else. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market, and with only 30 stocks, a few firms can drive the results.
PSIL: Companies developing psychedelic medicines, small drug developers working on treatments for depression, addiction and other mental health conditions using compounds like psilocybin. It is a speculative corner of health care: tiny, early stage firms whose prices swing on trial results and drug regulators' decisions.
PSK: Preferred shares, which sit between bonds and stocks and pay fixed dividends, mostly from banks and other financial companies. It's meant for steady income above typical bonds, but its price drops when interest rates rise, and it can fall hard in banking stress.
PSL: US consumer staples companies, such as food, grocery and household product makers, chosen by recent price momentum under a Dorsey Wright method. It holds about the same weight in each top name, with Casey's, US Foods and Costco each around 5%.
PSLV: Actual silver bullion held in vaults, so the shares move with the price of the metal itself rather than with mining companies. It is a direct way to own silver as a store of value, and silver swings more than gold because it is also an industrial metal.
PSMD: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each January. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
PSMJ: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each July. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
PSMO: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each October. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
PSMR: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each April. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
PSOX: Two unglamorous but essential parts of electronics: multilayer ceramic capacitors, the tiny components on every circuit board, and power semiconductors that manage electricity. It is a supply-chain bet on the components AI data centers and electric vehicles cannot do without, far from the famous chip names.
PSP: Publicly traded companies that run or invest in private equity, mostly asset managers and investment firms across the world. It's a way to get private equity exposure without locking money up, and it swings with markets and deal activity more than the broad market.
PSQA: Top-rated, AAA and AA, bonds backed by pools of corporate loans, called CLOs. It aims for higher income than ordinary safe bonds, while its payments float with interest rates, so it holds up well when rates rise, though it can lose value in credit scares.
PSQO: Mostly loans and bonds of companies, including lower-rated ones and some from abroad, picked by an active manager hunting for extra yield. It's for income beyond what safer bonds pay, but the lower-rated debt can lose value when the economy weakens.
PSR: US real estate investment trusts and property companies, picked actively rather than by index, spanning apartments, warehouses, offices, malls and other property types. It pays income from rents collected across the property market, and it rises and falls with real estate values and interest rates.
PSTP: US large company stocks, through options, with a stepped-up cushion against losses over each one-year period. It's meant to protect against moderate drops, but your gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
PSTR: An actively managed fund that rotates between US sector funds, such as financials, technology and health care, holding mostly other ETFs. It also uses options to bring in extra income, which can limit some of the upside when markets rise.
PSWD: Cybersecurity companies screened for strong business quality, with technology names making up about 90 percent of the fund. It is a focused bet on spending to stop hackers and data breaches, a corner of tech that grows even when other budgets tighten.
PTBD: A trend-following bond strategy that switches between high yield corporate bonds and intermediate Treasuries, fully in one, half and half, or fully defensive, depending on which way bond markets are trending. The rule-based switching aims to ride good times and sidestep credit downturns.
PTEU: Big Eurozone companies, banks, industrial and energy firms among them, with a trend rule that can move half or all of the money into Treasury bills when European stocks fall. The Trendpilot switch aims to dodge long slumps, at the risk of rejoining rallies late.
PTF: Technology companies chosen because their stock prices have recently been rising fastest, nearly all in the tech sector. It's a focused bet on tech momentum, and the holdings get reshuffled as leaders change, so it can fall hard when trends reverse.
PTH: Health care companies, such as drug makers, medical device firms and biotech, chosen because their shares have been rising faster than their peers. It's a focused bet on one industry, and the momentum approach can reverse quickly when trends change.
PTIN: Developed-market stocks outside the US, led by financials at roughly a quarter and technology at a fifth, with industrials and health care behind. A trend rule moves it into Treasury bills when the market weakens, so it aims to cushion big drops but can miss part of a rebound.
PTL: Large US companies chosen by a faith-based screen that scores them on values, led by technology at about a third, with industrials, energy and financials behind. It's a core stock holding for investors who want their money to match their beliefs, and it moves roughly with the broad market.
PTLC: Large US stocks, about 40 percent technology, with a rule that moves part or all of the money into Treasury bills when the market's trend turns weak. It's meant to soften big drops, but it can lag when the market bounces back after a slide.
PTMC: Mid-sized US companies that shifts to Treasury bills when the market trend turns down, using a moving average signal. It's built to cushion big drops while joining most rallies, but it can lag when the market whipsaws or rebounds quickly.
PTNQ: The Nasdaq 100, led by technology at about sixty percent, with a trend rule that moves half or all of the money into Treasury bills when prices slide below their long-term average. It aims to limit big drops, but it can lag in quick rebounds.
PTNT: Companies that earn money from intellectual property: patent holders, brand owners and entertainment firms paid royalties when others use their ideas, characters and inventions. It is a global bet on owning the rights rather than the factories, so income depends on licensing deals and legal protection holding up.
PTRB: A manager-picked mix of bonds, including government debt, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate debt, with room to take on some riskier credit. It's meant as a core bond holding for income and a cushion for stocks, though prices fall when interest rates rise.
PUI: Utility companies chosen by momentum: at least thirty power, gas and water providers showing the strongest recent price trends, rebalanced as leadership rotates. Chasing the hottest names in a normally sleepy sector makes it livelier than a plain utilities fund, for better or worse.
PVAL: A concentrated group of large US companies chosen by managers for looking cheap, with technology about a quarter and health care, financials and consumer companies following. It's a value-focused holding, and because it owns fewer stocks than an index fund, individual picks matter more.
PVEX: A defensive blend that keeps partial exposure to large US stocks through stock funds, while much of the money sits in Treasury bills and high quality bond funds. It aims to capture a good share of stock gains yet give back far less in sell-offs, playing goalie for a stock portfolio.
PVI: Municipal bonds whose interest rates reset daily, weekly or monthly, issued by states, cities and public agencies across the US. Floating rates keep the price nearly still when market rates move, and the income is tax-exempt, making it a calm, cash-like corner of the muni market.
PWB: Fifty large US growth companies, with technology about half and industrials about a fifth. It's built for capital growth rather than income, and with only 50 stocks packed toward tech, it swings more than the broad market and can drop hard when growth stocks fall.
PWER: A fund of companies tied to the shift away from fossil fuels, including utilities, metals and mining firms, and energy producers. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Steel Dynamics, Hudbay, ERO Copper and Valero each around 5% to 6%.
PWRD: Companies helping change how energy and power are produced and used, with industrials more than half and technology about a third. Managers pick the stocks themselves, so it's a focused growth theme on electrification and power infrastructure that can swing more than the broad market.
PWRX: Power and infrastructure companies: utilities, energy firms and the industrial builders behind the grid, in roughly equal thirds. It is an actively managed bet on the world's electricity build-out, with an income-friendly tilt from steady infrastructure cash flows.
PWRZ: Companies that own and run renewable power plants, mostly utilities generating wind and solar electricity around the world. It is built for income from selling clean power, so it behaves more like a steady utility than a high-growth green tech bet.
PWS: A systematic strategy that shifts between US stocks and Treasury securities based on risk signals in its index, aiming to sidestep major market falls. It currently sits fully in stocks, spread across technology, energy, health care and property, but the WealthShield design can retreat to Treasuries when danger flashes.
PWV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with what they earn, led by financials and energy, with health care and communication next. It's a value holding meant for steady growth and dividends, and it may trail when technology leads the market.
PWZ: Long-term bonds issued by California and its local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax and AMT, the alternative minimum tax. It's meant for tax-free income for California residents, though prices fall when interest rates rise and it leans heavily on one state.
PXE: US companies that find and pump oil and natural gas. It's a focused bet on energy producers, so it rises and falls sharply with oil and gas prices and can behave very differently from the broad market.
PXF: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, chosen by size measures like sales and cash flow instead of stock price. It leans toward financials, industrials, technology and energy, and it's a value-tilted way to diversify beyond US stocks.
PXH: Emerging market stocks chosen by company size in sales, cash flow and dividends rather than stock price, led by financials and technology, with energy and materials next. It's a way to own developing economies with a value tilt, and it's less tech-heavy than most funds here.
PXI: US energy companies that have shown strong recent price momentum, selected by a Dorsey Wright index of at least 30 stocks. It tilts toward refiners and pipeline companies like Marathon Petroleum, Cheniere and Targa, and the list gets reshuffled regularly.
PXJ: Companies that serve oil and gas producers, such as drilling services, equipment and field support, almost entirely in the energy sector. It's a focused bet on oil industry activity, so it swings sharply with oil prices and drilling budgets, more than the broad market.
PY: Large US companies that look cheaply priced, with technology the biggest group at about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It's a core stock holding with a value tilt picked by active managers, so it can lag when growth stocks lead.
PYLD: A wide mix of bonds actively managed across sectors, including corporate, government-backed mortgage and foreign debt, using derivatives to adjust exposure. It's built for monthly-style income beyond what plain bonds pay, but the managers' choices add risk, and it can fall when credit worries or interest rates rise.
PYPY: An actively managed fund that tries to earn high monthly income from PayPal's stock price moves by using options, rather than owning much PayPal stock directly. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills, and the options approach limits how much it gains if PayPal rallies.
PYZ: US basic materials companies, such as steel makers, specialty metals and chemicals, that have shown strong recent price momentum, picked by a Dorsey Wright index. ATI and Carpenter Technology are each about 7% of the fund, and the list is reshuffled regularly.
PZA: Long-term municipal bonds from across the US with interest exempt from federal income tax and the alternative minimum tax. It's for tax-free income, though long maturities make its price drop noticeably when interest rates rise.
PZIV: Non-US companies trading at deep discounts to what the managers believe they are truly worth, spread across finance, industry, health care and consumer shares. Pzena's patient value style can look out of step for years before bargains pay off.
PZLV: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers think are cheap compared to what they are worth. It leans toward health care and financials, with Humana, Baxter and Skyworks among its biggest holdings.
PZT: Tax-exempt bonds issued by New York State, its cities and other local governments, nearly all investment grade. It's meant for steady income that is generally free of federal and New York taxes, which suits higher earners in the state, and its price falls when interest rates rise.
QABA: Community banks: the small and mid-sized local lenders listed on US exchanges, from regional banking groups to hometown institutions. It is a pure bet on Main Street banking, so it moves with local economies, loan demand and interest rates rather than with the giant money-center banks.
QAI: A mix of other funds that copy the approaches of hedge funds, with about half in bonds and a third in stocks, plus some cash and other holdings. It's meant to smooth out the ride and diversify, so it usually moves less than stocks but gives up some upside.
QALT: A mix of long and short bets across stocks, bonds and currencies, using futures and other derivatives, so most of the fund sits in cash backing those positions. It's meant to move differently from the stock market as a diversifier, though it can lag when markets surge.
QARP: Large US companies that look high in quality yet are reasonably priced, picked by a Russell index. It is top-heavy, with Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon and Alphabet about 22% of the fund, and it leans toward technology.
QAT: Stocks listed in Qatar, where banks and other financial companies make up over half the fund, with energy, materials and telecom behind them. It is a single country bet on a wealthy gas exporting economy, so bank earnings and energy prices drive most of what it does.
QAU: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It is tech growth with late-summer protection terms: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains.
QB: The Nasdaq 100 growth giants wrapped in a buffer that adjusts daily, using very short-term options to keep a cushion under the fund as markets move. It aims to keep most of the Nasdaq's upside while softening falls, with the protection rebuilt every day.
QBF: Bitcoin exposure with a floor under losses over each three-month period, while leaving gains uncapped above that floor. The floor is set 20 percent down, so deep quarterly crashes are trimmed while ordinary dips are still felt in full.
QBIF: Tracks international developed-markets stocks through options on an EFA ETF, with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
QBIG: The very largest companies in the Nasdaq-100, the mega-sized top of the growth index, gathered into one concentrated fund. It doubles down on the giants that already dominate the Nasdaq, so it is technology-heavy and rises or falls with a handful of names.
QBIV: Tracks the performance of an international developed-markets stock ETF (EFA) using options, with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 5% of losses over a set one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies to investors who hold for the full period.
QBKF: Tracks small US companies through options on a Russell 2000 ETF (IWM), with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
QBKV: Tracks small US companies through options on a Russell 2000 ETF (IWM), with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 5% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held through the whole period.
QBQF: Uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year outcome period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold the fund for the whole period.
QBQV: Options on the Nasdaq-100 growth basket set for one year outcome periods, absorbing the first 5 percent of losses in exchange for capped gains. The cushion is thinner than most buffer funds offer, which leaves more upside room but less protection when tech stocks slide.
QBSF: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period, in exchange for a limit on the gains. The cushion and cap only apply if you hold from the start to the end of that period.
QBSV: Options on large US companies structured to buffer the first 5 percent of losses over each outcome period, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the lightest protection in the AllianzIM buffer range, a small cushion for investors who want to give up as little upside as possible.
QBUF: Nasdaq-100 companies, led by technology, held through options that cushion a set amount of losses over each quarterly period. It's meant for investors wanting some protection on a tech-heavy index, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
QBY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged fund tied to D-Wave Quantum, a quantum computing company. It stacks options on leverage on one speculative stock, so payouts can be large but swings are extreme and it is built for short holding periods.
QCAP: Options linked to the Nasdaq-100, which is heavy in technology, set up to absorb a limited amount of losses over a year starting each April. It's for investors who want tech exposure with a cushion, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies and protection needs a full-year hold.
QCJA: Options contracts tied to the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, that aim to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in January. Gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
QCJL: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big non-financial technology and internet companies, with a conservative cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each July. It tempers one of the market's swingiest indexes, trading away some upside for a calmer ride.
QCLN: Clean energy companies such as solar, wind and electric vehicle makers, along with the technology and industrial firms supplying them. It's a focused bet on the shift away from fossil fuels, so it swings far more than the broad market.
QCOC: Uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100 to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in October, with a conservative level of protection. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
QDEC: A package of options tied to the Nasdaq-100, so it follows technology-heavy large companies, with technology about 60 percent. It's built to cushion some losses over a one-year period that resets each December, but it also caps the gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
QDEF: Large US companies chosen for steady dividends and quality, with about a third in technology and the rest spread over health care, financials and communications. It aims to be defensive, targeting less market swing than average, so it usually trails in strong rallies.
QDF: Large US companies with strong profits and steady dividends, with technology about 38 percent and financials, industrials and health care next. It's meant for dividend income plus growth with a market-like ride, and it holds up a little better than average when markets fall.
QDIV: Companies from the big US index that score well on both quality measures and dividend yield, spread across staples, finance, industry and health care. It is a defensive income-tilted core holding, favoring profitable steady payers and avoiding the weakest balance sheets in the index.
QDPL: S&P 500 companies, with technology about 40 percent, plus futures that add extra exposure to the dividends they pay. It's built to boost dividend income from large stocks, but it carries more market swings than the plain index when stocks fall.
QDTE: Exposure to the Nasdaq-100, the large tech-heavy US index, combined with options that are sold daily to generate income paid weekly. It's built for income, but the short-term options limit gains in rallies while leaving most of the downside, so it can lose a lot.
QDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the Nasdaq-100 using options that expire the same day they are bought, designed to pay income weekly. The tech-heavy index means bigger swings than a broad market version, and the same-day calls give up most gains on strong rally days.
QDVO: Growth-minded US companies, with technology about half, paired with options that trade some of the upside for extra income. It aims for growth plus income, so it should hold up better than a plain growth fund in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
QEFA: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, with financials the biggest slice at about a fifth, then industrials and health care. It's meant to add international diversification, and it tilts toward traits like value and lower swings instead of weighting by size.
QEMM: Large and mid-sized stocks across 26 emerging markets, picked and weighted for value, low volatility and quality instead of just company size. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 7% of it, and tech and financials are the biggest sectors.
QETH: A single-cryptocurrency trust holding ether, the token of the Ethereum network, and valuing it daily at market prices. It gives brokerage-account access to the second-largest digital asset without a crypto wallet, and it moves exactly with ether, whose swings dwarf those of stock funds.
QEW: The Nasdaq-100 spread evenly: every one of the hundred non-financial giants gets roughly the same weight instead of the biggest names dominating. Technology still leads at about 46 percent, but smaller members matter far more here, so it behaves a bit less like a big-tech fund.
QFF: US growth companies chosen as quality compounders: businesses with durable advantages, high returns on capital and managers who reinvest profits wisely, led by technology, banks and consumer names. The focus on proven operators makes it a steady handed growth holding that depends on a focused list of stocks.
QFHD: Dividend-paying companies from the 500 biggest US stocks, screened for strong free cash flow and quality, then weighted toward the highest yields. It is built for income with a quality filter, so it owns more banks, utilities and staples than the broad market and less fast-growing technology.
QFLR: Nasdaq-100 stocks, mostly technology and communications, combined with options designed to limit how much you can lose over a set period. The cost is that gains are likely smaller than in the plain Nasdaq-100 when markets surge.
QFRD: S&P 500 companies that combine strong free cash flow with heavy research spending, which tilts the fund heavily to technology at about two thirds, plus health care. It is a growth holding with an innovation filter: it favors firms that fund their own future, and swings with tech.
QGRD: Nasdaq 100 stocks, about 60% technology, combined with an options strategy that aims to generate income and soften losses. It's meant for a smoother ride than owning the index outright, but the options limit gains in strong rallies, so it trails the index when tech surges.
QGRO: Large and mid-sized US companies with strong profits and growing sales, with technology about half. It's a growth-focused stock holding, so it can swing harder than the broad market, especially when tech falls.
QGRW: Large US companies with strong profits and growth, with technology over half and communication and consumer companies next. It's a growth holding that favors financially healthy businesses, so it tends to swing more than the broad market and leans heavily on tech.
QHY: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the risk of default is greater. It's for extra income, and it tends to fall with stocks in a downturn, more than safer bonds do.
QIDX: Companies of many sizes chosen for steady, growing earnings, led by technology, industrial and health care firms. The quality earnings focus aims for a dependable core holding, favoring businesses whose profits are consistent over flashy growers with uneven results.
QIG: Investment grade corporate bonds from US banks, hospitals, insurers and other issuers, selected for healthy fundamentals and income. It aims to be a core corporate bond holding with a quality tilt, avoiding the weakest borrowers in the market.
QINT: Large and mid-sized companies outside the US, led by financials, industrials, consumer firms and technology, picked for quality, growth and good value. It's a way to add international stocks, and its screens tilt it toward healthier companies than a plain index.
QIS: A bundle of outside quantitative trading strategies, accessed through swaps, spanning stocks, interest rates, commodities and currencies all at once. It aims for hedge fund like returns that move independently of a normal portfolio, with layers of strategies most investors could not reach directly.
QJL: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It is tech growth with a mid-year safety net: the shallower buffer leaves more room to gain than deeper versions.
QJN: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It is tech growth with a mid-year safety net: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains than deeper versions.
QJUN: Options on a fund holding the 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq companies, set up to absorb some losses over a one-year period starting each June. The tradeoff is capped gains, so it suits people who want tech exposure with a partial cushion.
QLC: Large US companies chosen for high quality, value and momentum, with technology the biggest slice at nearly 40%, then financials, communication and health care. It works as a core stock holding with a tilt toward strong, reasonably priced firms, and it leans more on tech than most value funds.
QLDY: Options on the Nasdaq-100 traded through daily call spreads, a strategy designed to harvest small amounts of income every day and pay distributions twice a week. It barely owns the underlying stocks' upside, so it is an income machine built on tech volatility, with daily resets and high turnover.
QLTA: Corporate bonds from US companies with the highest credit ratings, from the top grade down to A. It's meant for steady interest income with lower default risk than other corporate bonds, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
QLTI: Companies outside the US that the managers consider high quality, meaning financially strong and consistently profitable, across technology, industrials, consumer staples and health care. It's an actively run way to add international stocks, with a steadier, defensive flavor than a typical foreign growth fund.
QLTY: Large US companies the manager sees as high quality, with technology about 40% and health care a notable quarter, followed by communication and financials. It's an actively managed core holding that holds a concentrated set of stocks, so it can differ noticeably from the broad market.
QLV: US large and mid-sized companies chosen for strong financial quality and steadier price swings, led by technology with health care, financials and consumer staples behind. It's meant as a smoother core holding that usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in sharp, fast rallies.
QLVD: Large companies in developed markets outside the US, screened for quality and low volatility, with banks and industrials the biggest slices. The twin screens aim for a calmer foreign stock holding that still pays its way, accepting that it will trail in hot rallies abroad.
QLVE: Emerging market stocks screened for quality and lower volatility, led by Asian technology, with finance, communications and energy behind. It aims for a calmer version of emerging market growth, though calmer is relative in markets that can drop fast.
QMAG: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a moderate cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each August. It softens one of the market's most growth-heavy indexes, trading away some upside for a calmer ride.
QMAR: Uses options on the Nasdaq-100, where technology makes up about 60 percent, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each March. In exchange, gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies and works best when held through the full period.
QMFE: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set each February for a one year outcome period, absorbing a moderate slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It cushions the tech heavy growth basket's famous swings, suiting investors who want Nasdaq exposure with a softer landing.
QMID: Mid-sized US companies screened for both quality and growth, spread across technology, health care, industrials and consumer stocks. It is a growth holding in the market's middle tier: the quality screen aims for sturdier growers, but mid-caps still swing more than large companies.
QMMY: Options tied to the Nasdaq-100, which is about 60 percent technology, set up to absorb a moderate part of losses over a one-year period starting in May. In exchange, your gain is capped, so it's for people who want some protection and hold for the full period.
QMNV: Options on the Nasdaq-100 set each November for a one year outcome period, absorbing a moderate slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It cushions the tech heavy growth basket's famous swings, suiting investors who want Nasdaq exposure with a softer landing.
QMOM: About 50 US stocks chosen because their prices have been rising fastest, led by health care, technology and energy at roughly a fifth each. It's a growth-seeking fund for riding trends, and it can fall hard when the market's leaders suddenly change.
QMY: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It is tech growth with a safety net: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains than deeper versions.
QNDX: The 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, with technology at about 60 percent plus communication and consumer companies. It's built for growth as a core or satellite holding, and with no banks and far more tech than the broad market, it tends to rise and fall harder.
QNXT: The Nasdaq-100 with its thirty biggest members removed, leaving roughly seventy smaller companies from that index across technology, consumer, health care and industry. It is a growth holding for investors who already own the giants elsewhere and want the index's next tier to get its own room to run.
QOWZ: A fund following a Nasdaq index of US-listed companies with steady, growing free cash flow, meaning the cash left over after running the business. It is heavy in technology at about two-thirds, and NVIDIA and Broadcom together are close to 18%.
QPX: A dynamic fund of funds that rotates among stock funds, bond funds, gold and even volatility products as its managers chase growth. At the last look it leaned on technology funds and gold, a mix that shows how far this flexible fund can roam.
QQA: Large Nasdaq-100 companies, with technology about 60 percent, plus an options strategy that sells some of the upside for regular income. It aims to pay more income than a plain Nasdaq fund, but it will likely trail in strong rallies and can still fall hard in tech sell-offs.
QQAU: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It blends tech growth with late-summer defense: gains are capped, and the August start fixes the protection terms.
QQBF: Nasdaq-100 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over each quarterly outcome period, with gains capped in exchange. The quarterly reset sets it apart from year-long buffers: protection terms refresh four times a year, so timing matters less.
QQDH: Exposure to the Nasdaq 100's big innovators, wrapped in two options overlays: one sells put spreads for income, the other buys cheap daily crash protection. The design tries to pay income and blunt sudden drops, at the cost of some upside and a more complicated risk profile.
QQEW: Fifty Nasdaq-100 companies chosen for quality and growth, with technology about 70 percent and health care next. Every company gets the same weight, so the biggest names matter less than in the usual Nasdaq funds, which makes it a growth holding with a different mix.
QQH: Large US growth companies, with technology over three fifths and the rest in communication and consumer firms. It follows a tech-heavy list with a manager's rules for stepping back to cash, so it can swing less than a plain tech fund but still more than the broad market.
QQHG: A fund that holds the stocks of the Nasdaq-100 and adds an options hedge meant to soften sharp drops. NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet are about 28% of it, and technology is around 60%, so it is very tech-heavy.
QQI: One hundred innovative companies from outside the US, chosen from the Nasdaq stable of growth names, led by technology and health care. It is the international cousin of the famous Nasdaq 100 approach, so it leans into growth and swings harder than broad foreign funds.
QQJL: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It blends tech growth with mid-year protection terms: gains are capped, and the July start fixes what protection remains.
QQJN: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It is tech exposure with mid-year protection terms: the cap limits rallies, and the June start fixes the buffer.
QQLV: The calmest slice of the Nasdaq-100: the large stocks that swung the least over the past year, which tilts it toward consumer staples, industrials and utilities. It is a defensive growth holding, built to fall less in sell-offs while giving up some punch in rallies.
