QQMG: Nasdaq 100 companies screened for environmental, social and governance standards, with technology about two thirds. It's a growth holding for people who want large tech-heavy US stocks with an ethical filter, and it swings about as hard as the Nasdaq.
QQMY: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It blends tech growth with defense: gains are capped, and the May start date fixes the protection terms.
QQQ: The 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, led by technology, with internet, consumer brands and health care making up most of the rest. It's built for growth: there are no banks and far more tech than the broad market, so it tends to rise and fall harder.
QQQA: Just twenty one stocks at a time: the members of a big Nasdaq growth index with the strongest recent price momentum, swapped as momentum shifts, with technology usually dominating. Concentrating on the hottest slice of a growth index makes it a turbocharged, swing heavy bet.
QQQB: Nasdaq-100 exposure with an options shield designed to protect more of the downside than a typical buffer, while keeping a share of the upside. It is tech growth with armor: the shield softens drops in a volatile index, paid for by giving up part of strong rallies.
QQQE: The roughly 100 large non-financial Nasdaq companies, each held in about equal amounts instead of by size. Technology is under half, so it's a growth fund with less lean on the biggest tech names than the usual version, and it still swings more than the broad market.
QQQG: The fifty strongest cash generators among a big Nasdaq growth index's leaders, screened by projected free cash flow and earnings, with technology over four fifths of the fund. It filters a growth index down to its proven money makers, so it is less speculative than the full basket.
QQQH: Nasdaq-100 stocks, about 60 percent technology, paired with an options collar that gives up some of the biggest gains to soften losses and produce income. It's built to be a smoother tech-heavy holding, so it usually falls less than the Nasdaq-100 but trails in strong rallies.
QQQI: The stocks of the Nasdaq-100, with technology at about 60%, paired with a strategy of selling call options, which trades some of the upside for regular income. It's built for monthly income from big tech and growth companies, but it will trail in strong rallies.
QQQJ: The next 100 largest Nasdaq companies after the ones in the Nasdaq-100, with technology at about a third and health care at about a quarter. It's a growth fund for mid-sized innovators with no banks, and it tends to swing more than the broad market.
QQQM: The 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, with technology about 60 percent and communication, consumer companies and health care next. It is built for growth, and with no banks and far more tech than the broad market, it tends to rise and fall harder.
QQQS: The next generation of Nasdaq companies: about two hundred smaller listed firms not in the Nasdaq-100, with health care over half thanks to young biotech and medical firms. It is a growth bet on tomorrow's Nasdaq names before they graduate, and small biotech makes it extra volatile.
QQQT: Shares in Nasdaq-100 index funds plus daily credit call spreads sold on that index, a machine for turning tech stock volatility into regular income. It targets a set income level rather than growth, so its payout focus means it will not keep pace when tech stocks surge.
QQQY: Large Nasdaq companies, with technology over 60 percent, paired with an options strategy that sells upside in exchange for income paid weekly. It's built for high regular payouts, but gains are limited in strong rallies while big drops in the Nasdaq still hit it.
QQSE: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It blends tech growth with autumn defense: gains are capped, and the September start fixes the protection terms.
QQWZ: Large Nasdaq-listed companies, with the mix rotating by rule between the growth-heavy Nasdaq 100 lineup and a version tilted to firms with strong free cash flow. The switching rule is the point: it tries to favor whichever style is in favor at the time.
QQXT: Nasdaq-100 companies with the technology firms removed, spread fairly evenly across industrials, health care, consumer businesses and more. It's a way to own big growth names without the tech weighting, and because each company gets the same size slice, smaller members matter more than usual.
QRMI: The Nasdaq-100's technology-led stocks wrapped in a collar: put options bought for protection and call options sold to pay for them and add income. The collar trims both the worst drops and the best rallies, suiting investors who fear big tech's swings.
QSE: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It is tech growth with autumn protection terms: gains are capped, and the September start date fixes the buffer.
QSIG: Short term corporate bonds chosen through a rules based index of short dated company debt, coming due within a few years. It pays a bit more than Treasury bills and cash funds while keeping price swings small, a step up in yield for cautious money.
QSIX: Stocks from the Nasdaq-100, mostly big technology names, paired with futures contracts tied to the dividends those companies pay. It aims for stock growth plus a multiplied dividend stream, so the income side is amplified well beyond what the stocks alone would pay.
QSML: A fund of small US companies picked by an index that favors strong profitability and growth. It holds hundreds of stocks, with none above about 1%, so it is very spread out, and technology and consumer discretionary are the largest sectors.
QSOL: A fund that holds Solana, a cryptocurrency used on a fast blockchain network, rather than stocks or bonds. Most of the Solana is staked, meaning locked up to help run the network in exchange for rewards, which adds a little extra return on top of the coin's price moves.
QSPT: Options on a fund holding the 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq companies, set up to absorb some losses over a one-year period starting each September. The tradeoff is capped gains, so it suits people wanting tech exposure with a partial cushion.
QTAC: A tactical mix built mainly on futures tied to big US stock indexes, plus leveraged funds, Treasuries and cash for ballast. It shifts with the seasons of the market, aiming to press gains in good times and protect capital when conditions turn rough.
QTAP: Options on the Nasdaq-100 that aim to deliver accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each April. It is a leveraged-style bet on big tech rising, and losses are not cushioned when the index falls.
QTEC: Technology companies from the Nasdaq-100, with technology about 86%, where every stock gets equal weight so smaller names matter as much as giants. It's a focused growth bet on tech that swings more than the broad market and behaves differently from size-weighted tech funds.
QTJA: Options on a Nasdaq-100 fund structured to amplify gains over the year starting each January: returns aim for a multiple of the underlying fund's rise, up to a cap. Losses land closer to one-for-one, so it is an aggressive defined-window growth trade rather than a plain holding.
QTJL: Options on a Nasdaq-100 fund structured to amplify gains over the year starting each July: returns aim for a multiple of the underlying fund's rise, up to a cap. Losses land closer to one-for-one, so it is an aggressive defined-window growth trade rather than a plain holding.
QTOC: Options on the Nasdaq-100 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each October. It is a leveraged-style bet on big tech rising, with no cushion when the index falls.
QTOP: The 30 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq, with technology about two thirds of the fund. It's a concentrated growth fund with no banks, and since it holds so few names and so much tech, it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
QTPI: An actively managed fund of preferred stocks and bonds whose dividends are meant to qualify for lower US tax rates. Preferreds pay steady income, and the biggest holdings are large US banks like Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and Citigroup at about 3% each.
QTR: The Nasdaq-100 stocks combined with protective put options that pay off if the index drops sharply. The options act as insurance against big falls, which costs some return, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
QTUM: Companies working on quantum computing and advanced machine technology, mostly in technology with some industrial and communication firms, held in roughly equal amounts. It's a focused bet on an early-stage technology theme, so it swings more than the broad market and some holdings are still unproven.
QTUP: Small, specialized companies whose business is mainly quantum computing, from hardware builders to software and encryption firms. It is a pure-play bet on an early-stage technology, so holdings are mostly young companies and the price can swing violently.
QUAL: Large US companies chosen for strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, with technology at about 40 percent. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward financially sturdy firms, and it may trail when riskier stocks lead a rally.
QUIZ: Quality companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen by Zacks for strong fundamentals, with banks the biggest slice at nearly a third. It is a core international holding with a quality filter, favoring steady earners in Europe and Japan over speculative names.
QUS: Large and mid-sized US companies weighted by quality, value and low volatility, with technology near a third and financials and health care each near a sixth. It's a core stock holding built to be steadier than the broad market, though it can trail in sharp rallies.
QUSA: Quality US companies, heavy in technology, paired with an options program built to pay a targeted level of monthly income, the 15 in its name. It aims to pair sturdy stock holdings with unusually high cash distributions, giving up some stock gains to keep the payments flowing.
QVAL: US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and strength, with energy and consumer firms the biggest groups. It's a rules-based value approach, so it tends to lag when growth stocks lead, and it holds many fewer tech companies than the broad market.
QVML: Large US companies from the S&P 500 weighted toward those with better quality, value and momentum, with technology at over two fifths. It's a core stock holding with a tilt, so it leans harder on tech than a plain S&P 500 fund and can behave differently from it.
QVMM: US mid-sized companies chosen for quality, value and momentum, led by industrials, then technology, financials and consumer companies. It's a core mid-size holding that tilts toward healthier, better-priced businesses, so it can trail a plain mid-cap fund in broad rallies.
QVMS: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, with the weakest scorers on quality, value and momentum removed. Financials, industrials and technology are the biggest groups, so it's a small-company core holding that tries to avoid the shakiest stocks.
QVMT: One hundred large US companies from the S&P 500 chosen for quality, low prices and recent strength, with technology, industrials, energy and financials the biggest groups. It suits someone wanting a value-leaning core stock holding, and it is more concentrated than the full index, so it can behave differently.
QVOL: Nasdaq listed growth stocks, technology about two thirds of the fund, with an options program that sells calls against the holdings to turn part of their upside into income. It targets frequent payouts from volatile tech names, accepting smaller gains when those stocks run hard.
QVOY: A fund of funds that rotates money among four sleeves: core stocks, actively picked stocks, bonds and alternatives, shifting the mix as its process directs. The appeal is one ticker doing the rotating for you, though the layers of funds mean its results trail whichever sleeve is hottest.
QWLD: Large and mid-sized companies from 23 developed countries, with technology about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It leans toward cheaper, steadier, higher-quality stocks, so it's a global core holding built to fall a bit less in drops but it may trail in strong rallies.
QXQ: Nasdaq-100 companies, the big technology and internet names, paired with an actively traded options strategy that sells contracts to generate current income. It aims to pay more than the growth index yields on its own, giving up some upside when tech stocks surge.
QYLD: Large Nasdaq-listed companies, led by technology at about 60%, combined with a strategy that sells options on them each month. It's built for high monthly income, but it gives up most of the upside in strong rallies while still being exposed to drops.
QYLG: Nasdaq 100 stocks, about 60% technology, with covered calls written on half of the portfolio. Selling those options brings in monthly income and softens some drops, while still leaving room for gains on the rest, so it's a middle path between growth and income that trails in big rallies.
RAA: A mix of about 60 percent stocks, a fifth in bonds, and the rest in cash and alternatives such as commodities. It leans toward real assets, things like energy, materials and commodities that tend to hold value with inflation, and it's a one-fund balanced portfolio that shifts actively.
RAAA: The safest top slice of CLOs, the AAA-rated layers of bundled corporate loans, with borrowed money added to enhance the yield. AAA layers have historically been well protected, but the leverage and the complexity of loan bundles add risks ordinary bond funds do not have.
RAAR: Leveraged exposure to AAA collateralized loan obligation slices, the safest layer of bundles of company loans, with distributions reinvested rather than paid out. Reinvesting compounds the yield over time, while the leverage still magnifies every price move.
RAAX: A blend of real assets, including energy, industrial and mining stocks, commodities, real estate and inflation-protected bonds, plus some cash. It's meant as a hedge against rising prices, and it won't move in step with regular stock and bond funds.
RAAY: Leveraged exposure to the safest AAA slices of collateralized loan obligations, bundles of company loans, with leverage used to enhance the yield. The top-rated collateral keeps credit risk low, but the borrowed money magnifies price moves in both directions.
RACK: Companies that supply what data centers need, such as memory chips, cables and connectors, power equipment and electricity-related firms, following a VanEck index. It is spread across many names, with Micron, Amphenol and Sandisk each around 5% of it, and it leans heavily toward technology.
RAFE: Large US companies chosen by size measures such as sales and cash flow rather than market value, with technology near 30% and health care a quarter. It tilts toward companies with strong ESG scores, so it suits a core value style holding with a values angle.
RANK: A fund that follows an index of large US stocks chosen using Wall Street analyst ratings and forecasts. Technology makes up over 40%, and Micron, Applied Materials, Walmart and General Electric are each roughly 5% to 7% of it.
RAUS: US listed companies weighted by fundamentals such as sales, cash flow and book value, instead of by market size like most index funds. It still holds the big names, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet about 20% of the fund.
RB: Small US companies with an options buffer that resets daily, using one-day options to soften losses whenever the small-cap market falls. Unlike year-long buffer funds, its cushion is rebuilt every day, so protection is always fresh but never promised for any set period.
RBLD: US companies that build, own and run infrastructure, from construction and utility firms to the data and technology names behind modern networks. It leans toward the builders of next generation infrastructure, so it has a growth flavor compared with sleepy utility funds.
RBLY: An options strategy wrapped around Roblox stock, the gaming platform company, built to turn its price swings into regular income. It never simply holds the shares for growth, and if Roblox drops hard the fund can fall nearly as much while its gains stay capped.
RBTX: Robotics companies and the technology around them: makers of robots, automation systems and the sensors and software that guide them, actively picked worldwide. It is a focused bet on machines taking over more physical work, so it swings with industrial spending and tech sentiment.
RBUF: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a buffer built to absorb the first slice of losses each quarter (the 10 in its name). It resets every three months instead of yearly, trading capped gains for frequently renewed protection on small caps.
RCGE: Companies around the world chosen for a demonstrated commitment to gender balance in management and across their workforce, spread across finance, consumer brands, health care and industry. It is a values-screened global core holding, so the equality commitment, not sector bets, is what sets it apart.
RCLO: The middle layers of collateralized loan obligations: debt tranches rated in the BBB to B range, issued by vehicles bundling corporate loans. Those layers pay notably more than the safest CLO slices because losses reach them sooner, making this a yield hungry, credit heavy holding.
RCLR: Middle slices of collateralized loan obligations rated from BBB down to B, with income reinvested rather than paid out. Reinvestment compounds the higher yields of these riskier CLO layers, and losses can mount if the underlying company loans sour.
RCLY: Middle slices of collateralized loan obligations, bundles of company loans, rated in the BBB to B range where yields are higher and risk is real. It pays stronger income than top-rated CLO funds, and it can fall hard if loan defaults climb.
RCTR: Companies across the nuclear power chain: utilities running reactors, engineering and equipment firms, and uranium-linked businesses. It is a focused bet on nuclear energy's revival as a source of steady, carbon-free electricity, mixing steadier utility stocks with more volatile suppliers and miners.
RDFI: Closed-end bond funds bought for their income, many trading at discounts to the assets they hold, with a heavy lean toward emerging market debt funds. Buying discounted funds can add extra yield, though the discounts and the underlying loans add layers of risk and complexity.
RDOG: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) chosen for their high dividend yields, with the highest payers from each property type held in roughly equal amounts. That equal weighting leaves it spread out, with no holding above about 3%.
RDTE: Exposure to small US companies, spread across health care, financials, technology and industrials, paired with covered calls that expire within a day. Selling those options produces frequent income, but it caps upside in rallies and still takes losses in downturns, so it's for income seekers.
RDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the Russell 2000 small-cap index using options that expire the same day they are sold. It targets weekly income from small-cap volatility, with gains capped and losses close to the index's own when small stocks fall.
RDVI: Large US companies with long records of raising dividends, led by financials and technology, paired with an options strategy that gives up some stock gains for extra monthly income. It's for income seekers, and it usually trails in strong rallies.
RDVY: Large US companies that have steadily raised their dividends and have room to keep paying them, led by financials and technology. It's meant for a blend of growth and rising dividend income, and it holds up well in steady markets but can lag in sharp rallies led by non-payers.
RDYY: A single-stock income strategy built on Reddit shares, using options on that one social media company to generate regular payments. Because everything rides on one young, volatile company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and drops hit directly.
REAI: Real estate stocks picked with artificial intelligence: property companies and REITs chosen by models scanning rents, prices and company data. It is an actively run property income holding where the algorithm does the picking: the AI angle sets it apart, but it still rises and falls with property markets.
RECI: A US stock fund chosen with in-house research that also uses options to bring in extra income. Technology is about 40% of it, with NVIDIA and Apple each around 10%, and the options income comes in exchange for limiting some gains.
RECS: Large and mid-sized US companies, with technology about 40% and communication, financials and health care next. It's a core holding that follows the broad US market but tilts toward stocks that research scores favor, so it can drift modestly from a plain market fund.
REET: Real estate investment trusts around the world, companies that own properties like offices, apartments and warehouses and pass most rental income to shareholders. It's for income and real estate exposure beyond the US, though it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
REFA: Companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across drug makers, chip equipment, mining, banks and machinery firms. Columbia's research models tilt the mix toward their highest-rated names, aiming for a core international holding that does a bit better than plain index funds.
REGL: Mid-sized US companies that have raised their dividends for at least 15 years in a row, with financials near a third and industrials and utilities behind. It's built for steady dividend income with some stability, and it has little technology compared with the broad market.
REGS: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen for above-average growth potential. It leans heavily on technology, and NVIDIA, Apple, Broadcom and Alphabet together make up about 30% of it.
REIT: US real estate investment trusts picked actively across property types like apartments, warehouses, shopping centers and offices. Active picking is the difference from index REIT funds: managers can dodge weak property sectors, and the income comes from rents the trusts collect.
REIX: Real estate and infrastructure companies worldwide: property trusts at about half, plus utilities, industrial operators and energy infrastructure. It is an income-leaning holding on the world's buildings, toll roads, pipelines and data centers, and it tends to react strongly to interest rate moves.
REK: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of the daily move in a US real estate stock index, so it tends to rise when real estate falls. It resets every day, which makes it a short-term tool that can drift from the index over longer periods.
REM: Mortgage real estate investment trusts, companies that own home and commercial mortgages rather than buildings. It's meant for high dividend income, but those payouts can be cut, and its price swings with interest rates and credit worries more than regular stock funds.
REMC: Mid-sized US companies, led by technology at about a fifth, with industrials, health care and banks behind them. Columbia's research models tilt toward their favorite names, aiming for a mid-cap core holding that edges past a plain index.
REMG: Companies in emerging markets such as developing countries in Asia and Latin America, with technology the biggest slice at over two fifths and financials next. It's a growth holding that adds developing-economy exposure, and it swings more than developed-market funds.
REMX: Companies that mine, refine and recycle rare earth and other strategic metals used in magnets, batteries and electronics. It's a focused bet on materials, so it can swing sharply with metal prices and changes in global supply, especially from China.
RESM: Small US companies across health care, technology, banks and industrials, chosen with Columbia's research models tilting toward the names scored best. It aims to beat a plain small-cap index by quiet stock picking rather than big sector bets.
REVS: Large US value companies, which are stocks that look cheap compared with their size, led by technology and financials, with health care and consumer next. It's a core value holding that tweaks the standard index using research, so it can differ from broad value funds.
REXC: Mining and processing companies for rare earths, the metals used in magnets, electronics and electric motors, outside of China. It is very concentrated: MP Materials and Lynas Rare Earths together are about 39% of the fund, so it rides on a few producers.
REZ: US real estate companies focused on homes, including apartment landlords, manufactured homes, health care properties and self-storage. It's for rental income and diversification away from regular stocks, and it can fall when interest rates rise.
RFCI: An actively managed bond fund that mixes US Treasuries, corporate bonds and some preferred stocks, from the US and abroad. Managers shift between these types as conditions change, so it differs from an index fund that tracks one fixed slice of the bond market.
RFDA: US dividend-paying stocks and real estate investment trusts, picked using a dynamic approach by ALPS. It is a fairly spread-out large-company fund, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft each around 4%, and financials, technology and health care the biggest areas.
RFFC: Actively managed US stocks across all major industries, with technology the largest slice at about a third, chosen by managers hunting for opportunities rather than copying an index. It is a flexible core style holding whose results depend on stock picking, and it can hold real estate trusts too.
RFG: Mid-sized US companies with the strongest growth, spread across industrials, health care and technology at about a quarter each. It's for growth in the middle of the market, and since it's all growth stocks, it can fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
RFLR: US small company stocks paired with an options floor designed to limit how far the fund can fall over each period. Small caps offer growth with rough swings, and the managed floor aims to soften the worst of them, giving up some upside for the brake.
RFV: Mid-sized US companies that look cheapest on value measures, spread across consumer, financials, energy and technology. It's a value-tilted way to own the middle of the market, and it tends to swing more than the broad market, especially in economic slowdowns.
RGEF: Companies from around the world, mostly in developed markets, with technology about a third, then financials, industrials and communication. It's meant as a core global stock holding, and a manager picks the stocks, with a small share allowed in emerging markets.
RGLO: Stocks of companies around the world, including the US, led by technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's a one-fund core holding for global diversification, picked by an active manager, and its returns move with foreign currencies as well as stock prices.
RGYY: Weekly income from selling put options on a twice-leveraged fund tied to Rigetti Computing, a quantum computing company. It is an extreme trade: double leverage on a speculative stock means losses can be brutal when the stock falls.
RHRX: A rotating basket of other stock funds: broad market funds form the base, with sector and industry funds like semiconductors dialed up or down as the manager's rotation process directs. It is active allocation in one ticker, chasing stronger areas of the stock market while trying to dodge weaker ones.
RHTX: An actively managed mix of other ETFs, shifting between US stocks, gold, silver and cash depending on the manager's view of the market. About two-thirds of it sits in two S&P 500 ETFs, so its results depend on the manager's timing calls.
RIET: One hundred US real estate securities chosen for high dividend yields: warehouse, storage, hotel and casino landlords, plus some preferred shares. It is built purely for property income, so it leans on the highest payers, which can mean more risk when property markets cool.
RIFR: Infrastructure owners worldwide: utilities are the biggest slice at over two fifths, with railways, toll roads, airports and energy pipelines behind them. It is built for steady income and growth from assets everyone needs, across many countries rather than just the US.
RIGS: A worldwide mix of income bonds: government debt, company bonds and other fixed income of many maturities, ratings and currencies, steered actively toward the best yield opportunities. It aims to be a flexible income core, reaching abroad and down the quality scale where plain US bond funds do not.
RILA: Growth stocks of any size picked aggressively, technology nearly half the fund with health care and consumer names behind, all chosen for their potential to expand fast. It is a go for growth holding that accepts big swings, suiting investors comfortable with an aggressive ride.
RINF: A position built to gain when the market's expected inflation rate rises, using the gap between regular Treasury yields and inflation-protected Treasury yields. It is a targeted hedge against inflation surprises, and it loses ground when inflation expectations cool.
RING: Companies around the world that mine gold, all in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on gold prices, so it tends to rise when gold does and often gains more than gold itself, but it also falls harder and swings far more than the broad market.
RINK: Bonds from many sectors at once, corporate, government, mortgage and riskier high yield among them, with the mix shifted as conditions change. Russell builds it from several specialist bond managers, so it works as a one-fund bond core whose bets are spread across styles.
RINT: Stocks of developed countries outside the US, led by financials, followed by industrials, technology and health care. It's a plain way to add international diversification to a portfolio, and an investment manager actively adjusts the mix.
RISE: Emerging market stocks chosen by Pictet managers in what they call rising economies, with banks about a third, plus materials, technology and consumer firms. It is a developing markets holding from a Swiss active shop, spread across regions rather than dominated by the usual Asian giants.
RISN: An actively managed fund that uses chart-based signals to move between US large company stocks when the market trends up and safer assets like short-term Treasuries when it does not. It currently holds a sizable chunk in a short-term Treasury fund.
RISR: Interest-only mortgage securities and US Treasury bonds, an unusual mix that tends to gain when interest rates rise. It's meant as income plus a hedge against rising rates, which hurt most bond funds, but it can lose value when rates fall.
RITA: Real estate investment trusts from developed countries that pass green building and social responsibility screens. It pays out property income like other real estate funds, but sets itself apart by favoring landlords with greener, better-run buildings.
RIZE: Mostly short-to-medium term US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, whose value adjusts with inflation. It is actively managed, and the top holdings are Treasuries of about 6% each, so it is very low in credit risk.
RJCA: US stocks of companies expected to grow earnings, with technology over half and communication and health care next. It's built for long-term growth, and its heavy tech tilt means it swings more than the broad market.
RJDI: Dividend-paying companies picked by a manager, led by technology, industrials, health care and financials. It aims for dividends above the S&P 500's, with growth that beats inflation and swings no bigger than the market.
RJMI: Municipal bonds from states, cities, schools and public agencies across the US, picked actively by Raymond James for tax-free income. The interest escapes federal income tax, and the active approach hunts for value among thousands of small local issuers.
RJVI: Income gathered from every layer of a company's finances, its bonds, preferred shares and common stock, mostly investment grade corporate debt. This vertical approach lets the managers pick whichever layer of a trusted company pays best at the time.
RKNG: Stocks that individual traders crowd into most, drawn mainly from technology with some industrial and health care names mixed in. It is a bet on the crowd's favorite companies, so it chases popular momentum names and can move sharply.
RKSG: US growth stocks picked by a rules-based screen, led by technology at about a third, with health care, financials and energy behind it. It is built for growth as a core equity holding, and its index rules, not a manager, decide what gets in or out.
RLY: A mix of assets that tend to hold up when prices rise: commodity and natural resource stocks, inflation-protected Treasuries, real estate and some cash. It's meant as an inflation cushion alongside regular stocks and bonds, and because it spreads across so many areas, it won't track any one market.
RMCA: California municipal bonds from schools, housing agencies, airports and hospitals across the state, paying interest exempt from both federal and California income tax. It is aimed at California taxpayers, and the single-state focus means state finances matter more than in a national fund.
RMHY: High yield corporate bond exposure gathered through other bond funds, with an adaptive overlay designed to dial risk down when markets turn hostile. It chases junk bond income with a safety switch, though the shifts can arrive late, after trouble has already started.
RMME: A money market fund holding only cash, US government securities and loans backed by them, all maturing within about a year. It aims to keep a steady one dollar share price and pay modest interest, the lowest-risk corner of the fund world.
RMNY: New York municipal bonds with long maturities, actively managed for income that is exempt from both federal and New York state taxes. It is aimed squarely at New Yorkers in higher tax brackets, and the long maturities mean its price moves more when interest rates change.
RMOP: Municipal bonds from US states and local governments, including lower rated ones, with interest generally free of federal income tax. A manager picks them for tax friendly income and some growth, but the lower rated bonds are riskier and can fall when markets get nervous.
RMRC: An actively managed fund that spreads money across ETFs for the S&P 500's sectors, such as consumer staples, utilities and health care. It can shift between them to manage risk, and it owns funds rather than individual stocks.
RND: A fund following a Bloomberg index of US companies that pour money into their own growth through research and development. Alphabet, NVIDIA, Amazon and Apple are each around 8% of it, and technology is about 46%.
RNEM: Large and mid-sized emerging market companies selected from a broad index, with financial firms the biggest slice at over a third. It holds consumer, materials and technology names across Asia and beyond, carrying the usual currency and political risks of developing markets.
RNIN: US small and mid-sized companies, with technology close to a third, consumer businesses over a fifth, and energy and health care after that. It leans toward stocks that look cheaply priced, so it aims for growth with a value tilt, and smaller companies tend to swing more than large ones.
RNMN: A market neutral fund that pairs long and short positions, with much of the book in SPACs, the blank-check companies holding cash while they hunt for a merger. It aims to earn from deal mechanics and price gaps rather than market direction, a specialist strategy whose returns can look odd next to stocks.
RNRG: Companies that produce power from renewable sources: wind, solar, hydro and geothermal generators, mostly regulated-style utilities worldwide. It is a steadier way into clean energy than panel or turbine makers, since these firms sell electricity under contract, though their shares still follow interest rates closely.
RNTY: US real estate companies, mostly property-owning trusts, paired with an options program built to pay income at a target rate of 12 percent a year. It aims for rent-like payouts with extra option income, though property stocks still swing with the housing and rate cycle.
ROAM: Emerging market stocks scored on several investing factors at once, balancing value, quality and momentum rather than simply owning the biggest companies. Technology is about a third and banks about a fifth, giving diversified developing-world exposure with a deliberate tilt toward steadier, better-run firms.
ROBO: Companies making robots, factory automation and related technology, split between industrials at about two fifths and technology at about as much. It's a focused bet on automation as a theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
ROBT: Companies building artificial intelligence and robotics, with technology over half, then industrials and health care. It's a focused bet on automation and AI, so it swings more than the broad market, and it holds many smaller names too.
ROBX: The ten standout companies in robotics, from factory automation to surgical and warehouse robots, mostly industrials with a technology slice. It is a concentrated bet on machines doing physical work: ten names carry the fund, so it swings with automation headlines and orders.
ROCQ: Large Nasdaq-listed companies, with technology about 60 percent, paired with an options strategy that gives up some upside in exchange for regular income. The goal is monthly income from tech-heavy stocks, so it usually trails in strong rallies but cushions some small drops.
ROCY: Large US stocks, with technology about 40%, combined with an options strategy that gives up some of the market's upside in exchange for regular income. It's built for investors wanting income from stocks, and it usually lags in strong rallies while cushioning small dips.
RODM: Developed-market companies outside the US, picked using several factors such as value, quality and low volatility, with financials at over a quarter and industrials behind. It's meant for international diversification with a tilt toward steadier, cheaper stocks, and returns also move with foreign currencies.
ROE: Large US companies chosen for quality, such as strong profits and low debt, with each stock given about equal weight. It's a core stock holding, and because small and large companies count equally, it behaves differently from funds dominated by the biggest tech names.
ROKT: Companies pushing into space and the deep sea, mostly industrials such as aerospace and defense, with technology about a fifth and some energy. It's a focused bet on exploration themes, so it swings more than the broad market and has few close peers.
ROMO: US stocks selected by a robust momentum system from Newfound and ReSolve that favors strong, steady price trends and builds in risk controls. It is a core style equity holding with a defensive streak, designed to cut exposure when momentum breaks down rather than ride every fall to the bottom.
RONB: An actively managed mix of US growth companies of any size, led by industrials at over 40%, then consumer, financial and a little technology firms. It aims for long-term growth, and it holds a limited number of companies, so a few picks can drive results.
ROPE: One hundred actively chosen US stocks with a defensive escape hatch: the managers can move up to everything into cash when conditions look dangerous. It aims to join stock gains in good times and dodge deep falls in bad ones, so its success depends on the managers' timing calls.
ROSC: Small US companies screened by several factors at once, quality, value and momentum signals blended to manage the risks small caps carry. The multifactor approach aims to smooth the small cap ride, though it can trail simple small cap funds when one factor runs hot.
ROUS: Large US stocks picked using several factors at once, such as value, quality and momentum, with technology about a third. It's a steady core-style holding that leans on rules instead of size, so it can behave differently from the broad market.
RPAR: A mix of stocks, inflation-linked and regular government bonds, and commodities, weighted so each type contributes a similar amount of risk rather than a similar amount of money. It's meant as an all-weather portfolio, but it can fall when stocks and bonds drop together.
RPG: Large US companies with the fastest sales and earnings growth, with technology about half and industrials and consumer firms next. It's built for growth, so it swings harder than the broad market and can fall sharply when growth stocks sell off.
RPV: The cheapest-looking stocks in the S&P 500, with financials and health care each near a fifth and consumer staples and energy behind. It's a value tilt with far less technology than the broad market, so it tends to lag in growth-led rallies.
RSBA: Two strategies stacked in one fund: an actively managed bond portfolio, plus merger arbitrage, which buys companies being acquired and profits when deals close at the agreed price. The stacking puts each dollar to work twice, and broken deals are the distinctive risk riding alongside bond market moves.
RSBT: Two strategies stacked together: a bond portfolio plus a managed futures strategy that follows rising or falling trends in markets like commodities and currencies. Using leverage, it aims to give you both returns on one dollar, so it can swing more than bonds alone.
RSBY: Two strategies stacked in one fund: a core of US bonds, plus a futures program that harvests yield like returns from rolling futures contracts across markets, layered on top with borrowing. The stacking aims to earn more from each dollar invested, at the cost of leverage and complexity.
RSDE: Exposure to an equal weight version of the big US stock index, where every company counts the same, wrapped in options that buffer a slice of losses over a year starting each December. Smaller index members matter more here than in the usual market-weighted funds, and gains are capped.
RSEE: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs covering US large and small companies, developed markets outside the US, and emerging markets, shifting the mix using its own rules. It also uses a hedging approach meant to reduce losses in rough markets, so it differs from a plain stock index fund.
RSIT: A stacked fund that holds international stocks and a managed futures strategy at the same time, so each dollar gets both exposures. The futures use leverage, meaning borrowed-style exposure, so it is more complex than a plain international stock fund.
RSJN: Options on an equal-weight basket of large US stocks, where every company counts the same, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each June. Equal weighting shrinks the tech giants' dominance compared with ordinary large-cap funds.
RSMC: Small and mid-sized US companies across industrials, financials, technology and consumer staples, picked by an active manager. It's a growth-leaning holding, and these smaller companies tend to swing more than large ones in both rallies and sell-offs.
RSMR: Uses options on an equal-weighted S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each March. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if you hold the full period.
RSMV: US growth companies chosen for relative strength, meaning their prices have been outrunning peers, with volatility management that can trim risk when markets get rough. The approach leans into winners, so it can be caught out when market leadership suddenly flips.
RSP: The same companies as the S&P 500, but each one gets an equal share instead of the biggest getting the most. That spreads money across technology, industrials, financials and health care, so it has far less tech weight and often lags when a few giants lead the market.
RSPA: US stocks weighted equally, so small names count as much as giants, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care, with an options strategy layered on top for extra income. It's for income seekers, but the options give up some gains in strong rallies.
RSPC: The communication services companies of the large US stock market, internet platforms, media, entertainment and telecom, held in equal weights rather than by size. Equal weighting gives smaller names a real voice next to the giants, so it behaves differently from the usual giant led sector fund.
RSPD: All the consumer discretionary companies in the S&P 500, which are makers and sellers of things people want but don't need, like cars, restaurants and online shopping. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, and equal weighting means smaller companies matter more, so it swings more than the broad market.
RSPE: About 500 US companies from the S&P 500 that pass environmental, social and governance screens, each held in roughly equal amounts. Because every company counts about the same, it leans less on the biggest tech names than a regular index fund.
RSPF: The financial companies in the S&P 500, such as banks, insurers and asset managers, with each company given the same weight rather than favoring the biggest. It's a focused bet on financials, and the equal weighting gives smaller firms more influence than in standard financial funds.
RSPG: Every energy company in the S&P 500, such as oil and gas producers and service firms, each given the same weight. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, and equal weighting gives smaller companies more say, so it swings more than the broad market.
RSPH: All the health care companies in the S&P 500, such as drugmakers, medical device makers and insurers, each given an equal weight. It's a focused bet on one industry, and the equal weighting gives smaller companies more influence than they would get in a typical health care fund.
RSPM: The materials companies in the S&P 500, such as chemicals, metals and mining, and packaging, with each company given the same weight. It's a focused bet on one sector, and equal weighting means smaller names matter more than in a typical fund, so it swings more than the broad market.
RSPN: Industrial companies in the S&P 500, such as machinery, aerospace, airlines and transport, held in equal amounts instead of by size. It's a focused bet on one sector, and equal weighting gives smaller companies more say than in a typical industrials fund.
RSPR: Every real estate company in a major US large-cap index, held in equal weights: senior housing, malls, offices, hotels and data centers alike. Equal weighting keeps the giants from dominating, giving smaller landlords the same say as the biggest property owners.
RSPS: Nearly all consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products. It's a defensive holding that tends to fall less in downturns, and because each company counts equally, it gives smaller firms more weight than the usual version does.
RSPT: Every technology company in the S&P 500, held in equal amounts instead of weighting by size, so smaller tech names matter as much as the giants. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, and it swings more than the broad market but is less dominated by a few mega companies.
RSPU: Every utility company in the S&P 500, such as electric, gas and water providers, all weighted equally. It's a steady, dividend-friendly corner of the market that cushions stock portfolios, though its price drops when interest rates rise and it trails in strong rallies.
RSSB: Two investments in one fund: global stocks, led by technology, and US Treasury bond exposure through futures on top of the same money. It's a way to own stocks and bonds together without splitting your money, and the extra leverage means bigger swings than a typical balanced fund.
RSSE: Options on an equal-weight version of the S&P 500, where every company counts the same, with a buffer against part of any loss over a year to September. Equal weighting softens the mega-cap dominance of the usual index, and gains are capped in exchange for the cushion.
RSSL: Small US companies across many industries, with health care about a fifth, financials just under that, and technology and industrials following. It's a way to add small company growth to a portfolio, but small stocks swing more than large ones and often fall harder in downturns.
RSST: Two strategies on the same money: US large company stocks, led by technology, plus a managed futures strategy that bets on trends in commodities, currencies and bonds. The goal is more than one fund's worth of exposure, which also means bigger swings than stocks alone.
RSSX: Two strategies stacked in one fund: full exposure to large US stocks, plus an equal second layer split between gold and bitcoin, built with futures. That stacking means every dollar does double duty, which can boost diversification but also magnifies moves in both layers.
RSSY: Two strategies stacked in one fund: full exposure to large US stocks, plus an equal second layer of futures across bonds, commodities and currencies run for yield. The stacking lets every dollar work twice, aiming for stock growth alongside a futures income stream that does not depend on the market's direction.
RTAI: Closed-end funds that hold municipal bonds, bought when they trade at discounts to the value of their bonds, paying tax-advantaged income. The closed-end structure adds a second layer of movement, since discounts can widen or narrow on top of bond prices.
RTH: Companies that earn most of their money from retail, with consumer discretionary stores about half, then grocery and drug sellers, with some health care businesses. It's a focused bet on how shoppers are spending, so it tends to move with the consumer economy.
RTHY: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds with at least twenty years left to run, whose principal rises with inflation so the payments keep their buying power. The long maturities make the price very sensitive to interest rates, so this protects against inflation while still swinging a lot.
RTOO: Robotics companies: the makers of factory robots, warehouse automation and the technology behind them, led by industrials at about 60 percent. It is a growth bet on machines doing more of the world's physical work, a fast-moving and sometimes frothy theme.
RTRE: An actively managed bond fund that mixes corporate, mortgage, government and other bonds. Some of its money is held in other Rareview funds and long Treasury funds, so it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
RTYY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to Riot Platforms, a bitcoin mining company, converting its wild swings into payouts. It is a very risky trade: the leverage resets and options cap gains, so a crypto slump can hit hard.
RULE: A flexible portfolio that currently leans hard into chip and technology stocks, with room to hold bonds, cash and other funds as conditions change. Few rules bind the managers, so it can adapt quickly, for better or worse, when markets shift.
RUNN: Large and mid-sized US companies, 50 to 75 stocks held at roughly equal amounts, led by industrials at about a third, then technology and health care. It's a growth fund chosen for efficient companies, and it can trail when mega-sized tech leads the market.
RUSC: US small companies, aiming to track the performance of smaller US stocks, with thousands of holdings spread thinly. No single stock is above about 1%, so it is very diversified, with health care, industrials and financials the biggest areas.
RVER: A concentrated group of US stocks chosen by a manager aiming to beat the S&P 500, led by technology and industrials, with some cash. It's a growth-oriented bet with few holdings, so it can swing much more than the broad market.
RVNU: Municipal bonds that fund public projects like airports, toll roads and utilities and are repaid from their own revenue. It's built for tax-free income, and its price drops when interest rates rise because the bonds run long.
RW: A focused portfolio of durable global companies, mostly mid and large sized, with industry and technology leading, picked for steady compounding. It holds a modest cash cushion and buys businesses meant to grow through good times and bad.
RWEM: Emerging market stocks chosen with a systematic, data-driven approach that favors cheaper, higher-quality companies. It is top-heavy in chip makers, with TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung together about a quarter of the fund.
RWIN: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen with a next-generation multifactor process that blends traits like value, quality and momentum. Financials lead the mix, and the factor tilts mean it will not mirror a plain international index fund.
RWJ: Small US companies weighted by how much they sell rather than by their stock price, led by consumer companies, industrials, financials and technology. It's a value-leaning holding for smaller businesses, so it swings more than large company funds.
RWK: Mid-sized US companies, with industrials and consumer businesses making up about two fifths and technology and financials adding more. Companies are weighted by how much revenue they bring in rather than by size, so it leans toward big sellers like distributors and retailers, and it can trail in growth-led rallies.
RWL: The 500 big US companies in the S&P 500, but weighted by how much revenue they bring in rather than by stock market value. Health care, technology and financials lead, so it works as a core holding that leans less on today's most expensive stocks and can trail in tech-led rallies.
RWLC: Large US companies with an active tilt toward businesses seen as next-generation leaders, which leaves technology at over two-fifths of the fund. It is a growth-leaning core holding that reweights away from simply owning the biggest firms, so results can differ noticeably from a plain index fund.
RWO: Real estate companies from around the world, mostly REITs that own health care buildings, warehouses, data centers, malls and storage, with a majority in the US. It's for income and diversification beyond stocks and bonds, and it drops when interest rates rise.
RWR: US real estate investment trusts, which are companies that own buildings such as apartments, offices, warehouses and cell towers. It's meant for income and property exposure, and it tends to be sensitive to interest rates, falling when they rise.
RWX: Real estate companies and property trusts outside the US, spread across developed and some emerging markets. It's a way to add international property to a portfolio for income and diversification, and it's sensitive to interest rates and currency moves against the dollar.
RXI: Global makers and sellers of things people buy by choice, such as cars, clothing, travel, restaurants and online shopping. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to rise in good economies and fall harder when people cut back.
RYLD: Small US companies, with health care, financials and technology leading, paired with an options strategy that trades some of the upside for regular monthly income. The goal is income, but gains are capped in strong rallies and it still falls when small stocks drop.
RYLG: Holds a Russell 2000 small-company stock ETF and sells call options on part of it to generate income, while keeping some of the upside. The options bring in extra payouts but cap some gains, and small-company stocks can swing a lot.
RZG: Small US companies chosen for the strongest growth traits, spread across health care, industrials, financials and technology. It's a growth-focused bet on smaller firms, so it tends to swing more than the broad market, and it only holds the most growth-heavy picks from its index.
RZV: Small US companies that look cheap on measures like price compared to assets and sales, spread across consumer, industrial, technology and food-related businesses. It's for investors tilting toward bargain-priced small stocks, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds, especially in a weak economy.
SAGP: An actively managed fund of US and international stocks of companies that are active in influencing public policy, such as through lobbying. It is spread widely, with health care and industrials the biggest sectors.
SALI: Income from a ladder of autocallable notes reached through swap contracts: structured notes linked to stock indexes that pay coupons and can end early when markets rise. Laddering staggers the notes' dates, and the fund aims for high regular income, with returns tied to how those notes perform.
SAMM: Stocks chosen with a macro lens by Strategas, tilting toward whatever parts of the market its research sees as having momentum, currently technology and health care. The willingness to roam across company types, even other funds and partnerships, makes it a flexible all-in-one equity bet.
SAMT: US stocks chosen by a manager to fit big economic trends, with technology about a quarter, then health care, consumer staples and industrials, plus some cash. It's a flexible, actively managed stock holding, so results can differ a lot from the broad market.
SAPH: Shares of one company, SAP, the German business software giant, bought through its US-listed depositary receipts. What sets it apart is a built-in currency hedge, which strips out most of the effect of euro moves against the dollar, so the fund rises and falls mostly with the stock itself.
SASS: An actively managed fund holding a small group of US companies the manager thinks are undervalued. It is concentrated, with top names like Henry Schein, Primo Brands, AMETEK and Williams each about 6 or 7%.
SATO: Companies in the crypto economy, such as bitcoin miners and firms holding crypto, tracked by an Alerian Galaxy index, plus some direct bitcoin exposure through a bitcoin ETF. About 10% is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust, and it can swing sharply with crypto prices.
SAUG: Options tied to the Russell 2000, an index of small US companies. It absorbs a moderate amount of losses over a year starting each August, in exchange for capped gains, so it trails in strong rallies and works best if held for the full year.
SAWG: Large US companies picked for quality growth: profitable firms with strong track records, led by technology at close to half the fund. Sawgrass's managers favor durable earners over speculative names, aiming for growth with a steadier foundation than most growth funds.
SAWS: An actively managed fund of small US growth companies that the manager considers high quality. It spreads across health care, industrials and technology, with no holding above about 4% of the fund.
SBAR: Mostly short-term Treasury-style bonds and cash, plus an options strategy that collects extra income by selling put spreads, which are bets that the market won't fall past a set level. It's built for monthly income, but it can lose money if the market drops sharply.
SBB: A short-term trading tool that rises when small US companies fall, resetting its inverse bet every day. The daily reset steadily erodes returns over longer periods, so it suits brief bearish trades rather than a lasting hedge.
SBIL: Short-term US government debt and cash-like holdings run under the rules of a government money market fund. It's meant for parking cash and earning short-term interest, so its price barely moves, but its income falls when interest rates fall.
SBIO: Small and mid-sized biotech companies that are still developing breakthrough drugs, all in health care. It's a high-risk growth bet, since many hold unproven drugs and trial results can send prices up or down sharply.
SBND: Mostly short-term US investment-grade bonds, including government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, plus a bit of cash. It's meant for steady income with small price swings, and because the bonds mature soon, it drops less than longer bond funds when interest rates rise.
SCA: An autocallable note tied to a single stock, Super Micro Computer, a structured contract that pays income and can end early if the stock behaves. It is concentrated income with fine print: everything rides on one volatile AI hardware stock, and losses arrive if it falls far enough.
SCAP: Small US companies chosen for income, including dividend-paying stocks and a large slice of preferred shares across industry, technology, retail and finance. Income from small caps is uncommon, and the preferred holdings add both yield and interest-rate sensitivity.
SCAU: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in August. It adds late-summer defense to the market's jumpiest tier: the buffer helps, but small-cap swings and the gain cap both bind.
SCCR: Investment-grade US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds, with medium-length maturities. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCDS: About 95% in small US companies, picked by JPMorgan using data science models that score each company on measures of value, quality and momentum. It is spread thin: no holding is much more than 1% of the fund, across health care, financials and technology.
SCDV: Small US companies that pay dividends, led by industrials and health care, with financials and technology behind. It's meant for income and growth from smaller firms, and it can swing more than large-company funds while holding fewer tech stocks than most small-company funds.
SCEC: A diversified mix of US government bonds, corporate bonds and other debt such as mortgage-backed securities, with a manager allowed to lean into higher-yielding corners. It aims for steady income as a core bond holding, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCEP: Large and mid-size US companies, with technology about 40%, combined with options that bring in extra income and soften some losses. The trade-off is that it gives up some gains in big rallies, so it aims for a smoother ride than plain stocks.
SCHA: Small US companies spread fairly evenly across health care, financials, technology and industrials. It's a broad way to own the small-company slice of the market, and it swings more than large company funds, especially in a weak economy.
SCHB: Roughly the 2,500 largest US companies in one fund, with technology at about 38 percent and financials, health care and communication behind it. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the whole US stock market.
SCHC: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, with industrials the biggest group and materials, financials and technology behind it. It's a way to diversify into smaller overseas businesses, and it swings more than large-company funds because small stocks and foreign currencies both move around.
SCHD: Quality US companies with strong records of paying dividends, led by consumer staples, health care, technology and energy. It is built for dividend income and steady growth, and with little in the tech giants, it often trails in strong growth-led rallies.
SCHE: Large and mid-sized companies in developing countries such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials about a fifth. It's meant for growth and global variety, but it swings more than US funds and carries political and currency risk.
SCHF: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, such as in Europe and Japan, led by financials, technology and industrials. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it leaves out emerging markets and small companies.
SCHG: Large US growth companies, with technology over half and communication, consumer companies and industrials next. It is built for growth, but it is concentrated in a few tech leaders, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
SCHH: US real estate investment trusts that own buildings like apartments, offices, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers, leaving out those that lend money. It's for income and property exposure, and its price tends to drop when interest rates rise.
SCHI: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that mature in about five to ten years. It's meant for steady income above Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise and can slide if companies' credit quality weakens.
SCHJ: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies that mature in one to five years. It's meant for steady interest income with less price swing than long-term bonds, though it pays a little less than longer maturities and can still lose value when interest rates rise.
SCHK: Essentially the 1,000 largest US companies, with technology near 40% and financials, health care and communication next. It's a core holding that covers the large and mid-sized US stock market in one fund, so it moves with the overall economy and leans heavily on tech.
SCHM: Mid-sized US companies, ranked roughly 501st to 1,000th in size, spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care. It's a way to add the middle of the market, which sits between the stability of large companies and the swings of small ones.
SCHO: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to three years, all backed by the government. It's a place to park money safely while earning interest, and because the bonds are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
SCHP: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, covering a range of maturities beyond one year. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a stock and bond mix, though its price still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
SCHQ: US Treasury bonds that mature in ten years or more, backed by the federal government. It's used as a cushion when stocks fall and for steady interest income, but because the maturities are so long, its price drops sharply when interest rates rise.
SCHR: US Treasury bonds that mature in roughly three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road choice for steady interest income and a cushion when stocks fall, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SCHV: Large US companies that look cheaper than the market, with financials at about a fifth, then technology, health care and industrials. It's a value-tilted core holding, and it usually has less tech than the broad market, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
SCHX: Large US companies across every major industry, with technology about 40 percent and financials, health care and communication next. It is a core holding for big-company US stocks, and a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
SCHY: High-dividend companies outside the US, in developed and emerging countries, spread among consumer staples, financials, communication and industrials. It's built for income and international diversification, and it leans toward mature, slow-growing businesses, so it often trails in growth-driven rallies.
SCHZ: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCIN: Bonds issued outside the US: government and corporate debt from developed markets overseas, in a single Schwab fund. It diversifies a bond portfolio beyond US borrowers, and because the bonds are priced in foreign currencies, exchange rate moves can add to or subtract from the interest earned.
SCIO: Bonds backed by pools of loans and mortgages, such as asset-backed and mortgage securities, rather than by a single company. It aims for higher income than ordinary bonds, with the tradeoff that it carries more credit risk and can drop sharply when borrowers struggle.
SCJ: Smaller Japanese companies, spread across industrials, consumer goods, financials and technology. It's a way to add Japan's small companies to a portfolio for diversification, and it moves with the Japanese economy and the yen against the dollar.
SCJL: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in July. It adds mid-year defense to smaller stocks: gains are capped, and the July start fixes how much protection remains.
SCJN: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It adds mid-year defense to the market's jumpiest tier: the buffer helps, but small-cap swings and the gain cap both bind.
SCLZ: Dividend-paying US companies, mostly large and mid-sized, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths of the fund. It aims for growing dividend income with growth potential, and its tech weight makes it livelier than a traditional dividend fund.
SCMB: Investment-grade municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and other local governments, paying interest free of regular federal income tax. It's meant for steady, tax-friendly income in a bond mix, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCMC: A manager's mix of bonds from many parts of the bond market, with a small slice of preferred shares. It aims for steady income spread across several bond types, and its price can still drop when interest rates rise.
SCMY: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It adds defense to the market's most volatile tier: small-caps swing hard, so the buffer does real work here.
SCNM: Municipal bonds from across the country, mainly intermediate-term, whose interest is generally free of regular federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income, mostly for investors in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
SCOP: Actual copper metal held in storage, so the units move with the price of copper rather than with mining companies. Copper is the wiring metal of electrification, used in grids, motors and data centers, so its price swings with industrial demand and construction.
SCOW: Small US companies with at least seven straight years of positive free cash flow and strong cash returns, spread across technology, financials and consumer stocks. It is a quality screen on the market's smallest tier: the long cash-flow record is the filter, favoring proven survivors over young growers.
SCSB: Short-term, mostly investment grade bonds from governments, companies and municipalities, with a small allowance for lower-rated debt. It is built for income with modest price swings, since short maturities react less when interest rates move, though its yield is lower than riskier bond funds offer.
SCSE: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in September. It adds autumn defense to the market's most volatile tier: small-caps swing hard, so the buffer does real work here.
SCYB: Corporate bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the issuers are riskier. It's meant for extra income, but it can fall alongside stocks in downturns, so it isn't as steady as high-quality bonds.
SCZ: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, led by industrials, with financials, consumer companies and materials next. It adds smaller-company growth potential to a global portfolio, but it swings more than large-company funds.
SDCI: A diversified basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, held through futures contracts with the rest in cash and short-term bonds. It can hedge against inflation and moves differently from stocks, and it picks commodities by a rules-based method and avoids tax form K-1.
SDCP: Short-term bonds, mostly investment grade US corporate, government and asset-backed debt kept within one to three years of maturity. It emphasizes low volatility income, a step up from cash for money that still needs to stay fairly steady.
SDEM: Fifty emerging market companies in equal weights, chosen for ranking among the highest dividend payers in their markets, led by banks with consumer and energy names behind. Equal weighting lifts smaller payers to the same footing as giants, and the yields come with emerging market swings.
SDFI: Short-term bonds with an average length under three years, mostly investment-grade, from companies and governments. It's meant for steady income with less price swing than regular bonds, and it makes a calmer place for money you may need soon, though it pays less than longer bonds.
SDG: Global companies earning most of their revenue from products addressing world needs like health, clean energy and food, spread across technology, consumer staples, health care and industrials. It suits investors wanting a values-based global stock holding, and it may differ noticeably from the broad market.
SDIV: About 100 of the highest dividend-paying companies around the world, weighted equally, with real estate at about a third and financials and energy next. It's for high income, but the payout can be cut, and prices may swing more than the broad market.
SDMF: It copies a managed futures strategy that follows price trends across markets like currencies, commodities, bonds and stock indexes, using futures contracts. Such strategies aim to make money in long up or down moves and to zig when stocks zag, adding a diversifier.
SDOG: Fifty large US companies, five from each of ten sectors, that pay the highest dividends, spread across consumer goods, technology, health care and more. It's an income-focused fund, and since the highest payers are often out-of-favor stocks, it can trail in strong rallies.
SDSI: A mix of short-term corporate, government and mortgage-backed bonds, including some higher-yielding ones, managed actively. It aims for income with less price swing than longer bonds, since short maturities react less to rate changes, though the lower-rated holdings add some credit risk.
SDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the big US stock index using options that expire the same day they are bought, aiming to generate income weekly. Using same-day options makes the income stream depend heavily on day-to-day market calm, and the strategy gives up most index gains beyond the calls.
SDUR: Short-term investment grade debt: corporate bonds, asset-backed and mortgage securities and government bonds with brief maturities. It aims for income a step above cash with low volatility, suiting money that cannot afford big price swings.
SDVD: Small and mid-sized US companies with a record of raising dividends, led by financials and industrials, plus an options strategy that adds extra monthly income. It's built for income, but selling options limits gains, so it can trail in strong rallies.
SDVY: Small and mid-sized US companies with long records of growing their dividends, led by financials and industrials. It's built for dividend income plus growth, and because the companies are smaller, it swings more than funds of large dividend payers.
SDY: US companies that have raised their dividends for at least 20 years in a row, with industrials, consumer staples, utilities and financials leading. It's aimed at steady, growing income, and it holds little technology, so it can trail in tech-led rallies.
SEA: Global cargo companies: container lines, oil tankers, ship owners, air freight and port operators. It is a bet on world trade volumes and shipping rates, which are famously cyclical, booming when ships are scarce and slumping when fleets grow.
SECA: Mostly US stocks, led by technology at over two-fifths, followed by financials, consumer companies and industrials. It's an actively managed fund that rotates among sector ETFs, so it aims to lean into whichever industries look strongest and can differ a lot from the broad market.
SECR: Bonds backed by pools of loans, such as commercial property mortgages, home mortgages and consumer debt like car loans. It's built for income above regular government bonds with a diversified feel, though it takes more credit risk than Treasuries and can drop when borrowers struggle.
SECT: A fund that holds other sector funds and shifts between them, with technology about half, then financials, industrials and health care. Its purpose is to chase whichever sectors look strongest, so results depend on the manager's calls and it can lag a plain index.
SECU: Bonds backed by pools of loans, such as home mortgages, car loans and commercial property, picked by an active manager. It's meant for income higher than plain government bonds, and it carries more risk if borrowers fall behind on payments.
SEEM: Companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, Korea and China, with technology about 40 percent and financials next. It's for growth from developing economies, run by managers who pick stocks, so it swings more than US funds.
SEF: A daily inverse bet on financial stocks, designed to rise when bank and finance shares in the S&P 500 fall. It resets daily, so it is a short-term hedge or trade, and it steadily loses ground when financial stocks climb.
SEIE: Stocks from companies in many countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, then consumer and health care firms. It's actively managed and meant as a core international holding, so a manager's picks, not an index, decide what it owns.
SEIM: Large US stocks that have recently been rising fastest, with technology at over two fifths and industrials, financials and consumer companies behind. It's a momentum bet, so it can surge in trending markets but may fall hard when leadership suddenly changes.
SEIQ: Large US companies chosen for strong profits and sound finances, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%. It's a core stock holding with a quality tilt, so it may hold up better when markets are shaky but lag in junk-driven rallies.
SEIS: Small US companies chosen by active managers, spread across technology, health care, financials and industrials at roughly a fifth each. It's a growth-oriented slice of the market for a portfolio's smaller-company exposure, and small companies usually swing more than large ones.
SEIV: Large US value stocks selected for cheapness and other quality traits, with technology at a third and financials and health care behind. It's a core stock holding with a value tilt, so it can trail growth-heavy funds when expensive stocks lead.
SEIX: Senior loans made to companies with lower credit ratings, which have interest payments that float up and down with market rates. It's for income that rises when rates rise, but the borrowers are riskier, so it can lose value in a weak economy.
