SELV: Large US companies chosen for steadier price swings, with technology, health care, consumer staples and industrials the biggest groups. It aims to be a calmer core stock holding that typically falls less in sell-offs, but it may trail the market when stocks surge.
SEMG: An actively managed fund of high quality US growth companies. It is top-heavy: Alphabet, NVIDIA and Microsoft together make up about 30% of the fund, and technology is the largest sector at around 45%.
SEMI: Chip makers and the companies that supply them, plus other large technology names, with semiconductors at the center. It is a concentrated bet on the chip industry, so it rises and falls harder than the broader tech sector when chip demand shifts.
SEMY: An income strategy built on options tied to a leveraged semiconductor fund, collecting premiums from the chip sector's big price swings to fund payouts. It doubles down on volatility: a leveraged underlying plus options means sharp moves both ways, with gains capped by design.
SEPC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. The autumn start fixes its terms: later buyers get the remaining protection, not a fresh period.
SEPI: Large US stocks, with technology about a third and financials, communication and consumer companies next, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside for regular income. It aims for income and a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
SEPM: Options on the S&P 500 that aim for the maximum buffer against losses over a year starting in September, per the Max Buffer label. The trade is stark: near-total shelter from falls, with only a small slice of any rally kept.
SEPP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each September, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every September.
SEPQ: A tactical mix that rotates among big Nasdaq-listed growth stocks, long-term Treasury bonds and cash-like Treasury bills as conditions change. It aims to lean into growth when markets cooperate and shelter in bonds and cash when they do not, a flexibility plain stock funds lack.
SEPT: Options on big US stocks that absorb the first 10% of a market loss over a year starting in September, exactly what the Buffer10 in the name promises. Gains above that are capped, so it is a cautious way to stay invested.
SEPU: Options tied to a fund of 500 large US companies, led by technology, designed to absorb the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in September. Gains have no set cap but fall short of the market by a small amount, and the protection works only if held to the end.
SEPW: US large company stocks, held through options that reset each September, with technology about 40 percent. It aims to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over each one-year period, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
SEPZ: Options on the S&P 500 that are set up to follow the index's gains up to a limit, with some protection against drops over a one-year period starting each September. It's a cushion for stock exposure, but it gives up the biggest rallies and works best held the full period.
SEQ: An actively managed portfolio of a small number of global companies picked for long-term growth, spread over industrials, health care, communication and technology. It's a concentrated bet on the manager's picks, so it can look very different from the market and swing more.
SETH: An inverse fund that aims to move opposite to the price of ether, the second largest cryptocurrency, on a daily basis. It rises when ether falls and falls when ether rises, and because it resets each day, it is a short-term trading tool rather than a long-term hold.
SETM: Miners and processors of materials used in the energy transition, such as lithium, copper and uranium, with materials near three quarters and energy about a quarter. It's a narrow bet on one theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
SEUS: US companies of all sizes, with technology about a third and health care, financials and consumer companies each making up roughly a tenth. A manager tilts toward traits like value, quality and momentum, so it's a core stock holding that may behave a little differently from a plain market fund.
SFEB: Options tied to the Russell 2000, an index of small US companies led by health care, financials and technology. It absorbs a moderate amount of losses over a year starting each February, in exchange for capped gains, so it trails in strong rallies and works best held for the full year.
SFGV: Global stocks that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, spread across industrials, financials, technology and consumer companies. It's a value-focused core holding for world stock exposure, and it can lag when fast-growing companies lead the market.
SFLO: Small US companies that generate a lot of spare cash after their expenses, with technology, energy, consumer firms and health care leading. It's a value-minded way to add smaller companies to a portfolio, and it swings more than large company funds.
SFLR: Large US companies, with technology about 40 percent, paired with options that aim to limit how much it can lose over a set period. It's built for a cushion against big drops, so it should fall less than the market in sell-offs but gives up some gains in strong rallies.
SFTX: Stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, led by technology, financials, industrials and energy, paired with a strategy that cuts exposure when markets turn shaky. It aims for a smoother ride, but that protection can lag in quick rebounds.
SFTY: US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, paired with a risk-control strategy that cuts stock exposure when markets turn shaky. It aims for a smoother ride than the broad market, but that protection can lag in quick rebounds, and it follows an actively managed plan.
SFY: Five hundred of the largest US companies, with technology about half, weighted by both size and company fundamentals instead of size alone. It's a core growth-leaning holding that looks like the S&P 500 but leans harder into tech.
SFYF: The 50 stocks most widely held by everyday investors in SoFi brokerage accounts, led by big technology and consumer names. Because it follows what retail investors actually own, it leans heavily into popular growth stocks and can change character as fashions shift.
SFYI: The 50 most widely followed stocks on social media and brokerage platforms, paired with options to generate income from them. It is a popularity contest turned into a portfolio: holdings follow retail investor buzz, so the mix can chase whatever is trending.
SGDJ: Small gold mining companies, mostly in the US, Canada and Australia, so the whole fund sits in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on gold, and because these miners are small and less established, it swings far more than the broad market or bigger gold producers.
SGDM: Gold mining companies in the US and Canada, all in the materials sector, from large producers to smaller ones. It's a focused bet on gold, so it swings far more than gold itself and than the broad market.
SGLC: Large US companies chosen by an actively managed process, with technology about two fifths and financials, communication and health care next. It's a core holding for broad market exposure, and the managers' stock picks mean it can differ from the S&P 500.
SGOL: Physical gold bars held in vaults, so the fund simply follows the price of gold. It's a hedge against inflation and market stress that can diversify a stock and bond mix, but it pays no income and the price can swing a lot.
SGOV: US Treasury bills that mature in three months or less. It's a place to park cash that earns interest close to short-term rates, and its price barely moves, but its income falls when interest rates are cut.
SGRT: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked for strong earnings growth. It is concentrated and tilted to tech hardware: Vertiv, Western Digital and Micron are roughly 31% of it, with Energy and health care names making up the rest.
SGRW: Small US growth companies picked by Granahan managers, concentrated in technology and health care innovators. It is an aggressive growth holding: small companies with fast-growing sales can multiply in value, and they also fall hardest when investors turn away from risk and growth stories.
SGVT: Short-term US government debt such as Treasury bills, held much like a money market account. It's a place to park cash that pays interest with very little price movement, but it won't grow much and may not keep up with inflation.
SHAG: Short-term US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate debt, following an index of those bonds with a tilt to boost yield. Because the bonds mature soon, the fund's price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds.
SHDG: US large-company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, combined with a hedging strategy aimed at limiting losses in market drops. It aims for a smoother ride than a plain stock fund, though that protection usually means it lags in strong rallies.
SHE: Large US companies chosen because they have stronger gender balance in leadership, with technology about 40% and financials, health care and communication following. It's a core-style stock holding with a values screen, and it behaves much like the overall US market.
SHEH: Shares of one company, Shell, the global energy giant, held through its US-listed depositary receipts rather than bought on the London exchange. Like others in this series, it is built to soften the effect of currency moves between the pound and the dollar, leaving the stock itself as the main driver.
SHLD: Companies building defense technology, such as aerospace, cybersecurity, drones and military electronics, mostly industrials with some technology. It's a focused bet on rising defense spending, so it moves with government budgets and global tensions more than the broad market.
SHM: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments across the US, paying income that is generally free of federal tax. It's a low-risk tax-friendly place to hold money, and because maturities are short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
SHOC: Companies that design and make computer chips and the equipment to produce them, all within the US market. It's a focused bet on semiconductors, so it can rise sharply when chip demand is strong and falls harder than the broad market when it cools.
SHPP: Industrial and logistics companies from around the world: airlines, shipping, trucking, rail and warehouse operators that keep goods moving. It is a focused bet on global trade and transport, so it rises and falls with shipping volumes and the world economy.
SHRD: Core bonds, mostly US Treasuries and agency securities, in an index screened to align with Catholic values. It targets plain investment grade income for faith-based investors, and the screen removes issuers whose business conflicts with Catholic teaching.
SHRT: An actively managed fund that both buys stocks it likes and bets against stocks it expects to fall, a strategy called long/short. It is built to hold up better than the market when stocks drop, and no single position is more than a small slice.
SHRY: Large and mid-sized US companies that return the most cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks combined. That shareholder yield focus tilts it toward mature, cash-generating firms in finance, media and technology rather than fast growers.
SHUS: Large US stocks weighted by business risk rather than company size, using Syntax's stratified method to keep any one industry from dominating, plus index options for hedging. It aims for a more balanced big-stock portfolio than market-cap indexes give, with the options softening market drops.
SHV: US Treasury bills and notes that mature in under a year, about half of them held as cash-like short-term debt. It's a place to park cash with almost no risk, earning interest that follows short-term rates, and its price barely moves.
SHY: US Treasury bonds that come due in one to three years, so they're backed by the government. It's a low-risk place to park money for income and stability, and because the bonds are short, its price moves very little when interest rates change.
SHYD: Short-term municipal bonds from US state and local governments that carry lower credit ratings, so they pay higher interest. It's meant for income that is generally free of federal income tax, and the short maturities soften rate swings but credit risk remains.
SHYG: Short-term bonds from US companies with weaker credit ratings, maturing within about five years. It aims for higher interest income than safe bonds, with less sensitivity to interest rate moves than longer high-yield bonds, but it can still fall when the economy sours and defaults rise.
SHYL: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings that mature in a few years. It's for higher income than safer bonds, and its shorter maturities make its price less sensitive to interest rates, though it can still fall when the economy weakens and defaults rise.
SHYM: Short-term municipal bonds from riskier borrowers, cities, hospitals and projects that pay higher interest because their credit is weaker. The interest is generally free of federal tax, and keeping maturities short limits how much the price moves when interest rates change.
SIFI: A systematic income portfolio run with Ares, a major credit manager, spanning many bond sectors and using derivatives like credit default swaps and Treasury futures. It applies institutional credit machinery to a multisector income role, shifting exposures by model rather than by a single manager's hunches.
SIHY: Corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, often called junk bonds, selected with a rules-based approach. It pays higher income than safer bonds, but it can fall in recessions when companies struggle to repay, so it acts more like stocks than Treasuries.
SIL: Companies that mine silver, all classified as materials. It's a focused bet on silver prices, so it often swings more than silver itself and can behave very differently from ordinary stocks.
SILJ: Smaller companies that mine silver and other precious metals, all in the materials sector. It's a high-risk bet on silver prices, and because the miners are small and borrow to operate, it swings much harder than silver itself or the stock market.
SIMS: About 100 US-listed companies worldwide that build and run smart infrastructure, such as clean power, smart grids, water systems and automation, following the S&P Kensho Intelligent Structures Index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above roughly 3% of the fund, and leans toward industrial and tech names.
SIO: A mix of bonds, mostly corporate, spread across health care, industrials, financials and technology issuers, including some riskier junk bonds. It's built for income from a manager choosing across the bond market, and it can fall more than safer bonds in a downturn.
SIOO: The hundred largest US companies, spanning technology, banks, health care and consumer brands, paired with an options overlay that sells contracts for income. It targets an annual distribution rate of 15 percent, trading some upside in strong rallies for steady payouts.
SIVR: Physical silver bars held in a vault, so it holds no stocks or bonds. It's a way to own silver without storing metal, used as a hedge against inflation or market stress, but silver pays no income and its price swings a lot.
SIXA: The very largest US companies, spread across consumer staples, technology, health care and communications. It aims to be a core holding focused on stable giants, with a tilt toward food and household names that makes it look different from a standard large-company fund.
SIXD: Large US companies, mostly technology at about 40 percent, using options that cushion part of the first losses over a six month period, with a reset each June and December. It suits someone wanting some protection, but gains are capped and you give up part of a strong rally.
SIXF: Options on the S&P 500 in six month outcome periods starting in February and August, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The twice yearly reset keeps the cushion fresh, suiting investors who want defined outcomes on a shorter clock.
SIXH: US stocks, led by consumer staples, technology and health care, paired with index options that cushion some losses. It's meant for a smoother ride than the market, and the hedge limits gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
SIXJ: Options on a large US stock fund set to absorb the first 10 percent of losses over six-month periods starting January and July, while capping gains. It's for cautious investors, and the protection only applies if held the whole period.
SIXL: Mid-sized and other US companies picked for lower-than-market swings, leaning toward financials, consumer staples, utilities and energy. It's built for a smoother ride that falls less in sell-offs, but it tends to trail in strong rallies led by growth stocks.
SIXO: Large US stocks, mostly technology, financials and health care, held through options that cushion some losses over a six-month period. It's for investors who want some downside protection, but the cushion resets twice a year and it caps gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
SIXP: Options on the S&P 500 in six month outcome periods starting in March and September, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The shorter cycle refreshes the terms twice a year, suiting investors who want a cushion without a full year commitment.
SIXS: Small US companies spread across real estate, health care, energy and financials, picked by a manager for low prices and solid business quality. It's a value approach to smaller stocks, and with only a modest number of holdings it can swing more than the broad market.
SIXZ: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over six months, from November to May and May to November. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it is designed to be held for the full period.
SIZE: US mid-sized companies spread fairly evenly, with technology at about a fifth, then financials, industrials and health care. It leans on the idea that medium companies can grow faster than giants, so it works as a core holding that adds mid-size exposure.
SJB: A short term trading tool that moves opposite to high yield corporate bonds each day, gaining when junk bonds fall and losing when they rise. Because the inverse exposure resets daily, it is built for brief hedges or bets, not for holding through long stretches.
SJCP: An actively managed bond fund holding mostly investment-grade US corporate and government bonds, plus some preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends. US Treasuries are about a third of the fund, so it is aimed at steady income.
SJLD: Short-term investment-grade bonds and some preferred shares, actively managed to keep the portfolio's average maturity under two years. It is a low-drama income holding: the short maturities mean its price barely moves when interest rates change, though payouts stay modest.
SJNK: Short-term bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay higher interest than safer bonds. It's for extra income with less sensitivity to interest rates than longer junk bonds, but these companies are more likely to default, so it can drop in recessions.
SKOR: US corporate bonds from companies with solid credit ratings, medium in length, screened for better value and financial strength. It's meant for steady interest income above Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
SKYY: Companies that sell cloud computing, meaning software and services delivered over the internet, almost all in technology. It's a focused bet on one fast-growing corner of tech, so it tends to swing more than the broad market, especially when growth stocks fall out of favor.
SLDR: US Treasury bonds arranged in a ladder, with pieces coming due steadily over the next one to three years. The ladder keeps income rolling in and money regularly freeing up, a conservative parking place that barely flinches when interest rates move.
SLJY: Holds shares of junior silver mining companies, mostly through another Amplify silver miners ETF, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. The options cap gains when silver miners surge, while the miners can still fall sharply.
SLNZ: Loans to companies with weaker credit, which are senior secured, meaning lenders are paid first, plus some cash. It pays higher income than most bonds, and since the payments float with interest rates, its price holds up when rates rise.
SLQD: Short-term bonds from financially solid US companies, all coming due within five years, plus a little cash. It's meant for modest, steady income with a gentler ride than longer bonds, so it rises less than the broad bond market when rates fall but also loses less when they rise.
SLV: Physical silver held in a vault, rather than companies or bonds. It's used as a hedge and a bet on metal prices, but it pays no income and swings more than gold because industry demand also moves it.
SLVI: Income built on silver: the fund holds silver funds that own the metal and sells options on them to generate payouts. Silver swings far more than gold, and the options cap part of the upside, so the distributions come with a bumpier ride than most income funds.
SLVO: A note from a bank that pays you based on silver prices plus income from selling call options on silver, which trade away big price gains for cash. It's meant for monthly income from silver, but it's a loan to the bank rather than a fund, so it carries the bank's credit risk.
SLVP: Mining companies focused on silver and other metals, all classed in the materials sector. It's a focused bet on the miners rather than on metal itself, so it swings more than the broad market, and its price tends to follow silver and metals prices up and down.
SLVR: Silver mining companies, plus some physical silver bars, with the stock part nearly all in materials. It's a focused bet on silver prices that can work as an inflation hedge, but it swings far more than the broad market.
SLVX: Silver mining companies, a silver trust, and options on silver stocks, aimed at producing income. About 15% of the fund is a physical silver fund and the rest is miners like First Majestic, SSR Mining and Silvercorp, and selling options caps some of the upside.
SLVY: Exposure to silver through funds and income-producing investments, aiming to pay a target level of income while following the metal's price. It blends a commodity bet with payouts: silver swings harder than gold, and the income layer trades some of that movement for steadier cash.
SLWS: Mostly short-term bonds from many types of borrowers and countries, plus a small amount of cash. It's meant for steady income with little price movement, as a parking spot for money you may need soon, though it can still lose a little value when rates rise.
SLX: Steel makers and the miners, processors and recyclers that supply them, with materials making up over 90%. It's a focused bet on one cyclical industry, so it swings far more than the broad market with construction and manufacturing demand.
SLYG: Small US companies with faster growth, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, each roughly a fifth or less. It's for long-term growth, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones and can lag in downturns.
SLYV: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, led by financials at about a fifth, then consumer, technology and industrial companies. It's a value-oriented piece for a portfolio, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones and can struggle in downturns.
SMAX: Options on large US stocks arranged for the maximum buffer in its family over a year running from September, built to shield against nearly the whole of a market drop. That near-total protection comes with a modest cap, so it suits capital preservation more than growth.
SMAY: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each May. It is built for gentler exposure to small caps, trading away gains past a cap for that protection.
SMB: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments, with interest that's generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly income and stability, and because the maturities are short, its price moves less than longer municipal funds when rates change.
SMBS: Nearly all bonds backed by pools of home mortgages that are issued or guaranteed by US government agencies. It's meant for steady interest income with high credit quality, but its price falls when interest rates rise, and homeowners paying off loans early can change how long the income lasts.
SMCO: A manager's picks of 50 to 75 small and mid-sized US companies, led by industrials, technology and health care. It's a growth-leaning way to own smaller companies, and these stocks tend to swing more than large ones.
SMCP: An actively managed fund of mid-sized companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. It is a concentrated mix of miners, energy and drug companies, with the largest few holdings each around 6% to 8% of the fund.
SMCY: A bet on Super Micro Computer stock that uses options to pay out high monthly income instead of owning the shares fully. It gives up gains if the stock soars while still taking much of its losses, and the payouts can swing widely.
SMDV: Small US companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least ten years, led by financials and industrials. It's a steadier small-cap fund for dividend growth, so it trails in strong rallies led by risky stocks.
SMDX: Small and mid-size US companies, actively managed to beat a small-mid cap index while spreading out the risk. It's a diversified way to hold smaller companies for growth, so it swings more than large company funds and its results depend on the managers' stock choices.
SMH: Companies that design and make semiconductors, the chips that power computers, phones and AI, with all of it in technology. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market, and a few big chip makers dominate it.
SMHC: Twenty-five of the largest, most traded Chinese semiconductor companies, from chip designers to equipment makers, bought mainly through mainland A-shares. It is a direct bet on China's push for chip independence, and tensions with the US can move it sharply.
SMHX: Chip designers that don't build their own factories, instead leaving manufacturing to others, all in the semiconductor business. It's a concentrated bet on one corner of technology, so it swings far more than the broad market.
SMIG: Small and mid-sized US companies that pay and grow dividends, spread across financials, industrials, consumer companies and energy. Managers pick the stocks themselves, so it's meant for steady growth with some income, and tends to hold up better in downturns than rallies.
SMIN: Small Indian companies spread across industrials, consumer companies, financials and health care. It's a high-growth bet on one emerging market, so it swings more than large-company funds and is affected by currency moves.
SMIZ: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by a ratings model, with technology, industrials and financials leading. It's a growth-oriented stock holding for the smaller end of the market, so it tends to swing more than large company funds.
SMLF: Small US companies picked for four traits: momentum, quality, value and low volatility, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's a diversified small-company holding with a built-in tilt, so it can swing more than large-company funds.
SMLL: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies chosen by the managers rather than an index. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Pool Corp, Morningstar, WillScot and Wintrust each around 4% to 5%, and industrials and financials are the largest sectors.
SMLV: Smaller US companies chosen for steadier price swings, with financials the biggest group at about a third, along with industrials, technology and real estate. It's for smoother small company exposure, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but may trail in strong rallies.
SMMD: Small and mid-sized US companies spread evenly across industrials, technology, health care and financials. It adds the part of the market the biggest companies miss, so it tends to swing more than a large-company fund.
SMMU: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments, mostly high quality, with a bit of cash. It's a low-risk place to park money for income that is generally free of federal income tax, and because maturities are short, prices move less when interest rates change.
SMMV: Smaller US companies chosen for lower price swings, spread across health care, industrials, financials and real estate. It's built for a calmer ride in small stocks, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails when risky small companies surge.
SMNG: The Samsung group in one fund: companies of the South Korean conglomerate spanning memory chips and phones, batteries, construction, insurance and biotechnology. It is a single-conglomerate bet, so it concentrates in one country's corporate giant and swings with both the chip cycle and the Korean market.
SMOG: Companies in clean energy, mostly utilities and industrials, plus some consumer businesses such as electric vehicle makers. It's a focused bet on the shift away from fossil fuels, and it can include smaller and foreign firms, so it swings more than the broad market.
SMOM: An actively managed fund of funds that holds sector ETFs from the S&P 500, shifting toward the sectors with the strongest recent momentum. This means it can be heavily tilted, with technology and energy funds being about half now.
SMOT: Small and mid-sized US companies that Morningstar says have lasting competitive advantages, spread across health care, industrials, consumer staples and consumer discretionary. It's a quality-minded way to own smaller companies, though they still swing more than large ones.
SMOX: Small and mid-sized US companies, including real estate trusts, led by industrials, financials and technology. It aims for growth beyond the biggest companies, and these smaller firms swing more than large-company funds, especially in downturns.
SMRF: Nuclear energy companies: uranium miners, reactor builders and firms developing small modular reactors, plus the technology around them. It is a bet on nuclear power's comeback as grids hunt for clean, always-on electricity for data centers and industry.
SMRI: Mid-sized US value stocks, led by technology and health care, with energy and consumer companies behind them. It's a manager-picked stock fund for growth beyond the largest companies, and it swings more than the broad market.
SMRZ: Companies developing small modular reactors, the next-generation nuclear plants designed to be built in factories and shipped to sites, plus their suppliers. It is a speculative bet on a technology still proving itself commercially, so it can swing hard on policy news and project milestones.
SMTH: An actively managed mix of high-quality bonds, mainly mortgage-backed and other government-related debt along with some corporate bonds. It's a core bond holding aimed at steady income, and the manager has room to depart from the broad bond market, so results can differ.
SMTJ: Japanese companies across the economy, led by industrial firms at about a quarter, banks and technology names, picked for those set to gain from long-term changes in Japanese society and industry. It is a single-country fund, so it swings with Japan's market and with the yen.
SMYY: An options strategy on a leveraged fund tied to Super Micro Computer stock, built to convert the stock's wild swings into income payments. It is a risky short-term trade: leverage resets and option caps mean losses can mount quickly when the stock falls.
SNAV: A tactical fund that navigates among the sectors of the S&P 500, shifting money toward whichever industries look strongest, through sector and index funds. It accepts full stock market risk, so the navigation is about which sectors to ride, not whether to be in stocks.
SNOV: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each November. It is built for gentler exposure to small caps, trading away gains past a cap for that protection.
SNOY: A fund that gives income and partial exposure to Snowflake's stock price using options, rather than owning the shares. Its option strategy caps how much it gains if Snowflake rises, while losses can still be large, and most assets are held in Treasury bills.
SNPD: Companies with long records of raising dividends, drawn from an S&P dividend aristocrats list and screened further, led by everyday consumer brands, industrials and utilities. It is a steady income holding built on dependable payers rather than the highest yields.
SNPE: Large US companies in roughly the same industry mix as the S&P 500, with technology about two fifths, after screening out firms that score poorly on environmental and social measures. It's a core stock holding with a values filter, so it behaves much like the broad market.
SNPG: Growth companies from the S&P 500, screened and scored so each industry favors firms with stronger environmental, social and governance records than their peers. It keeps the shape of a standard growth fund while tilting toward better-rated corporate citizens.
SNSR: Companies that make the sensors, chips and software connecting everyday objects to the internet, with technology about four fifths and industrials next. It's a focused growth bet on connected devices, so it swings more than the broad market.
SNTH: Mostly Treasury bonds, with stock market exposure created through options on the S&P 500 so that only part of the fund is truly in stocks. It aims for stock-like growth while using the bonds as ballast, so results can differ from owning the index outright.
SNTQ: Nasdaq-100 exposure built synthetically from options, with US Treasuries making up most of the fund as backing. This engineered approach aims to reshape the ups and downs of big tech stocks, though the outcome depends on the option positions in place at any time.
SOCL: Social media companies worldwide: the platforms behind messaging, short video, social networking and online communities in the US, China and Korea. It is a focused bet on the attention economy, and these firms swing with advertising spending, regulation and user growth headlines.
SOEZ: Direct exposure to Solana, the cryptocurrency of a fast blockchain network, held as the fund's sole asset. It lets investors follow Solana's price through a brokerage account, and that price is extremely volatile, driven by crypto sentiment and network adoption.
SOFR: Short term cash style investments that aim to earn the overnight SOFR rate, a key benchmark for short term US borrowing. It's a place to park money with very little price movement, and its income rises and falls with short term interest rates.
SOLC: Holds actual Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, in a trust, so its price follows the price of the coin. A portion of the coins may be staked through Marinade to earn extra rewards, and the value can swing sharply, as with other crypto.
SOLM: Exposure to Solana's SOL token through regulated Solana funds, combined with selling options on them to generate monthly income. It pairs a volatile crypto asset with an income overlay: option premiums add payouts, but capped gains mean it trails a straight SOL rally.
SOLZ: Solana, a digital currency, held directly and through related investments, with some cash. It's a speculative bet on one crypto coin, so its price can swing wildly and doesn't move with stocks or bonds.
SOVF: Mid-sized US companies picked by active managers, leaning toward technology and payment firms alongside health care and industrial names. It is a stock picker's mid-cap fund, aiming to catch companies in the sweet spot between small and large, with the growth potential and volatility that implies.
SOXQ: The 30 largest chip companies listed in the US, all in semiconductors. It's a focused bet on the engines behind computers, phones and artificial intelligence, so it swings far more than the broad market and rises and falls with the chip industry's cycles.
SOXX: Computer chip designers and makers, including companies that build the equipment used to produce chips. It's a focused bet on one fast-moving industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and does best when chip demand is booming.
SOXY: Holds semiconductor stocks such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and ASML, and sells options on them to generate income. Those options cap how much it can gain when chip stocks rise, so it trades some upside for monthly payouts.
SOYB: Soybean futures contracts, rolled as they expire, giving direct exposure to the world soybean price without owning any physical beans. It is a single crop trading tool that swings with harvests, weather and export demand, and futures rolling costs can drag on long holdings.
SPAB: Nearly the whole US investment-grade bond market in one fund, mostly Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate bonds. It's meant for steady interest income and as a cushion for a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
SPAM: Companies in the cybersecurity industry, such as Palo Alto Networks, Okta and CrowdStrike, following a Themes index. It is concentrated in tech, and each of the top holdings is around 6% of the fund.
SPAQ: An actively managed fund of SPACs, shell companies that raise money in a stock market listing so they can buy a business later. It aims to beat what bank CDs pay, and holds many SPACs, each around 4% to 5% of the fund.
SPBC: Broad US stocks make up about nine tenths of the fund, with the rest in bitcoin funds for a measured dose of crypto. It is for stock investors who want some bitcoin exposure in the same ticker, with crypto adding extra volatility on top.
SPBO: Bonds issued by US and international companies, mostly investment grade, meaning borrowers rated fairly safe. It's meant for steady income and to diversify a stock portfolio, and it pays more than Treasuries but its price drops when interest rates rise.
SPBU: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through a ladder of twelve buffered funds, one for each month. It cushions the first 15 percent of losses over each period but has no cap on gains, so it can keep rising in rallies, though protection is partial.
SPBW: Twelve large-cap buffer funds layered together, each running its own one-year period starting a month apart, each absorbing the first 20 percent of losses for its slice. A slice resets every month, so protection is always fresh somewhere in the fund, with gains capped in exchange.
SPBX: Six large-cap buffer funds layered together, each running a six-month protection period starting a month apart, each absorbing the first 10 percent of losses for its slice. A new slice resets every month, spreading timing risk while the buffers trade away gains past caps.
SPCI: A fund giving exposure to space industry companies using stocks, call options and synthetic positions, and earning extra income with a put spread, a paired options trade. The options strategy trades away some upside in exchange for that income.
SPCK: Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs), empty shell companies that raise money to buy a business later, plus companies that recently went public. Because SPACs are mostly cash waiting for a deal, its holdings are small, with none above about 5%.
SPCT: Large US companies with a strong record of raising their dividends, picked by the managers rather than an index. It is spread widely, with the top names such as Apple, Amazon, Caterpillar and Eli Lilly each around 3% of the fund.
SPD: Large US stocks across every major industry, plus a put options overlay designed to gain value quickly in a sharp crash, which traders call downside convexity. The insurance can pay off in panics, but its cost quietly trims returns during long calm stretches.
SPDF: Large US stocks bought through a broad index fund, with a technical risk overlay that can pull money out when market signals turn bad. The defender design aims to sidestep deep crashes, though the signals can also pull it out just before rebounds.
SPDG: US dividend-paying large companies, weighted so that no sector gets far bigger than the others, tracking an S&P index. Even so, tech is the largest sector at about 40%, with Cisco, Verizon, IBM and Texas Instruments among the biggest holdings.
SPDV: Large US companies from a major index, screened for dividends that are both high and sustainable, then held in equal weights. It is an income-tilted value fund, so it favors steady payers like energy, retail and tech hardware firms over the fastest growers.
SPDW: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, such as Europe, Japan and Canada, led by financials, industrials and technology. It works as the international portion of a stock portfolio, and it has no US companies or emerging markets.
SPEM: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials a fifth. It's a way to add faster-growing but riskier economies to a portfolio, and it can swing more than developed-market funds because of politics and currency moves.
SPEU: Companies across developed Europe, led by financials and industrials, then health care and technology. It's a way to add European stocks to a portfolio, with much less tech than US funds, and it's affected by the euro and pound.
SPFF: Preferred shares, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pay fixed dividends, almost all issued by banks and other financial companies. It's built for high income, but it drops when interest rates rise and leans heavily on the financial sector.
SPGM: Companies from around the world, both developed and emerging countries, with technology the largest slice at about a third and financials next. It's a one-fund core holding for global stock exposure, with a large share in US companies.
SPGP: Large US companies chosen for steady growth at reasonable prices, with financials about a third and technology about a fifth. It's a blend of growth and value for a stock portfolio, and it holds far less tech than the broad market.
SPHB: The 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have swung the most compared to the market, with technology over half and industrials about a seventh. It's a bet on rallies, built to rise faster in good times, but it also falls harder in sell-offs.
SPHD: The 50 S&P 500 stocks with high dividends and low price swings, led by real estate, consumer staples, utilities and financials. It's built for income and a calmer ride, but it holds little technology, so it tends to lag when growth stocks lead.
SPHQ: The 100 S&P 500 companies with the strongest profits, steady earnings and low debt, led by technology, industrials and financials. It's a core holding built around company quality, and it can lag when riskier stocks lead a rally.
SPHY: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, that pay higher interest because they are riskier. It's built for extra income, but it tends to fall alongside stocks in a downturn, so it's a weaker cushion than safer bonds.
SPIB: Investment-grade bonds from US companies that mature in roughly three to ten years. It's built for steady income that pays more than Treasuries, though it falls when interest rates rise or when company credit worries grow.
SPIN: Large US stocks across every major industry, technology the biggest slice, paired with selling call options against the portfolio to collect premium income. It aims for stock market participation with fatter payouts, trading away part of strong rallies to keep the income coming.
SPIP: US government bonds whose payments rise with inflation, across a range of lengths. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a stock portfolio, though its price drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
SPIT: Companies in special situations, events like spinoffs, restructurings or turnarounds that can unlock hidden value, mostly mid-sized and smaller firms. Event-driven picking like this depends on the managers reading corporate dramas well, and situations can take years to play out.
SPLB: Long-term US corporate bonds, all maturing in ten years or more. It pays higher interest than shorter bonds, but its price swings widely when interest rates change, falling sharply when they rise, so it's for income seekers who can ride out the swings.
SPLS: A fund that holds S&P 500 stock exposure and adds an actively managed bond portfolio on top, using funds, futures and swaps to do both at once. It gives stock market returns plus a bond manager's attempt to earn extra, so it differs from a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPLV: The 100 S&P 500 stocks that have swung the least over the past year, heavy in utilities, financials, real estate and industrials. It's built for a smoother ride and falls less in sell-offs, but it trails in strong rallies.
SPMB: Mortgage-backed bonds, which pool home loans backed by government-sponsored agencies and pay out homeowners' monthly payments. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, though it falls when rates rise and homeowners' refinancing can change the payments.
SPMD: Mid-sized US companies, larger than small caps but smaller than the giants, with industrials, technology, financials and health care leading. It's a core holding for the middle of the market, and it usually swings more than large company funds but less than small ones.
SPMO: About 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have been rising fastest lately, with technology making up over half the fund. It's a bet that winners keep winning, and since it reshuffles as trends change, it can drop sharply when market leadership turns.
SPPP: Physical platinum and palladium held in vaults, two rarer precious metals used heavily in catalytic converters and industry. Their prices depend more on car production and mining supply than on investors, so they can swing sharply and move very differently from gold.
SPRE: Real estate investment trusts from around the world, companies that own property such as offices, warehouses and apartments, filtered to follow Sharia (Islamic) rules. It's for property income and diversification, and screens out companies tied to interest-based debt, so it is narrower than typical real estate funds.
SPRX: Mostly technology companies, with some industrials, that a manager thinks will benefit from new industrial innovation such as robotics and automation. It's a focused growth bet on emerging technology, and it can swing more than the broad market.
SPSB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that mature in one to three years. It's a low-risk choice for income that pays more than Treasuries, and because the bonds mature soon, its price moves very little when interest rates change.
SPSK: Investment grade sukuk, which are bond like certificates structured to follow Islamic law, issued in US dollars around the world. It's for steady income that fits Sharia principles, and its price drops when interest rates rise like ordinary bonds.
SPSM: About 600 small US companies that meet profitability screens, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer companies at roughly an eighth to a sixth each. It's a way to add smaller-company growth to a portfolio, but it swings more than large-company funds.
SPTB: US Treasury bonds across short and medium lengths, backed by the government. It's meant for safe, steady interest income and as a cushion when stocks drop, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SPTE: Large technology companies from around the world, nearly all in the tech sector, screened to follow Islamic investing rules. It's a focused bet on global tech, so it swings more than the broad market, and the screens leave out companies that break those rules.
SPTI: US Treasury bonds that mature in roughly three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a middle-of-the-road choice for steady income and a cushion when stocks fall, though its price slips when interest rates rise.
SPTL: US Treasury bonds that mature in over ten years, backed by the federal government. It's a cushion that often rises when stocks fall, but with such long maturities its price swings sharply when interest rates change.
SPTM: The whole US stock market in one fund, from large to small companies, with technology around 40% and financials, health care and communication following. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, with a bit of small company exposure.
SPTS: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to three years. It's a very safe place for money that wants some income, with small price changes when interest rates move, though it pays less than longer bonds.
SPUC: Large US companies, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care behind it, plus an options overlay that gives up some gains in big rallies for extra income and protection. It's a stock fund for people wanting income and a smoother ride than a plain stock fund.
SPUS: Large US companies screened to follow Islamic investing rules, with technology making up over half and health care a distant second. It fits investors who want a stock fund that avoids things like banks and alcohol, and its heavy tech weighting makes it swing more.
SPUT: US stocks paired with a daily put-writing program that sells S&P 500 put options every day to collect premium income. The steady premium softens small drops and adds income, but a fast sell-off still hurts, and gains lag in strong rallies.
SPVM: One hundred stocks from the S&P 500 that rank well on being cheap and on recent price momentum, led by financials, energy and utilities. It's a value-and-momentum tilt on large companies, with little technology, so it can lag when tech leads.
SPWO: Companies outside the US that pass a faith-based screen, with technology over half of the fund and industrials, health care and consumer companies behind it. It's a foreign stock fund with a heavy tech tilt, and the screen leaves out sectors like banks.
SPXD: The S&P 500 reweighted so sectors are more balanced and no single giant dominates. Compared with a plain S&P 500 fund, it holds less of the biggest tech names and more of areas like health care and consumer staples.
SPXE: Large US companies across every major industry except one: energy is left out entirely, so there are no oil, gas or pipeline firms. It suits investors avoiding fossil fuel stocks without hand-picking, though it will lag whenever energy shares lead the market.
SPXN: The S&P 500 without its financial companies such as banks and insurers, held in index proportions. Technology dominates: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund, so it works as a US large-company fund that skips the financial sector.
SPXP: The 500 biggest US companies, plus an overlay of derivatives designed to add a little extra exposure on top of the index itself. It works like a core stock holding with a slight amplifier attached, so it edges ahead in rising markets and edges behind in falling ones.
SPXT: The S&P 500 without its technology companies, so it's mostly financials, communication, health care and consumer firms. It's for investors who already own plenty of tech and want the rest of the market, and it can trail when tech surges.
SPXV: The S&P 500 with the entire health care sector left out, so technology takes an even bigger share than usual. It suits investors who already hold health care elsewhere or want less of it, while keeping the rest of the big-company market intact.
SPY: America's largest companies in one fund, covering every major industry. Technology is the biggest slice at about 40%, followed by financials, health care and consumer companies, so it's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy.
SPYA: A US stock fund with a built-in hedge meant to soften losses when the market falls. It's aimed at investors who want stock exposure with a cushion, and the hedge likely means it trails the market in strong rallies.
SPYC: Mostly an S&P 500 index fund, with a small side of options bought to try to gain more when stocks fall sharply. The options are meant to add a cushion in bad markets, but they cost money, so in calm or rising markets it can trail a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPYD: The 80 highest-dividend-paying stocks in the S&P 500, with real estate the biggest slice, followed by consumer staples, financials and utilities. It's for dividend income, and it has little technology, so it can trail the broad market in growth-led rallies.
SPYG: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, where technology is more than half the fund and communication companies add about a seventh. It's meant for growth, but it's concentrated in a few industries, so it tends to fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
SPYH: The actual stocks of the S&P 500, paired with an options collar that buys downside protection and sells calls to pay for it and add income. The hedge trims both ways: smaller losses in falls, smaller gains in rallies, plus extra income along the way.
SPYI: Large US companies in the S&P 500, led by technology at about 40 percent, paired with an options strategy that sells some upside in exchange for monthly income. It's aimed at income, so it trails in strong rallies and still falls when stocks drop.
SPYM: Hundreds of the largest US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It is a core holding for US stock exposure, and since bigger companies count for more, a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
SPYT: Large US stocks, led by technology, paired with an options strategy that sells upside on the S&P 500 to generate regular income. It's meant for income from stock exposure, but gains are limited in strong rallies, and it still falls when the market drops.
SPYV: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, with technology at about a quarter, then financials, health care and industrials. It leans toward established, lower-priced companies, so it tends to hold up better than growth funds when tech stocks sell off but can lag in tech rallies.
SPYX: America's 500 largest companies with the fossil fuel producers removed, so technology is the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's a core US stock holding for people who want to skip coal, oil and gas reserve owners, so it differs slightly from the plain index.
SQBA: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 15 percent of losses, resetting the shield every quarter. The frequent resets keep protection close to current prices, paid for by capped gains in each quarterly period.
SQBR: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks built around a barrier set 20% below the market's starting level, resetting every quarter. If stocks end the quarter above that line, the fund aims to deliver a set gain; if they fall through it, losses arrive much like owning the market.
SQLT: Smaller US companies screened for quality: strong profits, steady earnings and clean balance sheets, spread across technology, industrials, health care and banks. It aims to keep the growth potential of small companies while skipping the shakiest ones, though small stocks still swing more than large ones.
SQLV: Hundreds of small US companies picked by a quantitative model looking for quality and value together: profitable firms at reasonable prices. The wide spread keeps any single company tiny, and the model trades often, so the lineup changes more than in most index funds.
SQMX: Options on the S&P 500 in a quarterly design that aims for the deepest loss cushion available each quarter, resetting four times a year. Shorter outcome periods mean the protection and the gain cap refresh often, suiting investors who do not want to commit to a full year.
SQS: Companies the managers see as high quality and growing, with technology the biggest slice at over two fifths, plus communication, consumer and financial companies. It's a growth leaning stock fund held in a limited number of names, so it can swing more than the broad market.
SRET: High-yielding real estate investment trusts around the world, all in property. It's built for large dividend income, but the high yields come with more risk, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
SRHQ: US mid-sized companies spread across technology, health care, industrials and consumer businesses, each making up roughly a fifth or less. It aims for growth at a fair price, picking firms with steady, moderate sales growth that don't look overpriced, so it tilts away from fast-growing but expensive stocks.
SRHR: Real estate investment trusts plus covered calls sold on those holdings, turning rent backed dividends and option premiums into a higher income stream. It gives up part of any REIT rally to pay that income, and it still falls when property stocks drop.
SRLN: Senior bank loans, which are floating-rate loans to companies with weaker credit ratings that get repaid before other debts. It's meant for income that adjusts upward when interest rates rise, so its price is steadier than regular bonds, but it can fall when the economy weakens and borrowers default.
SROI: Growth companies worldwide that also meet sustainability criteria, spanning technology, industry, finance and health care. It pairs a growth hunt with environmental and social screens, so some popular stocks are left out on principle.
SRVR: Companies that own the physical backbone of the internet: data centers, cell towers, and fiber, mostly real estate firms with some industrials and communication companies. It's a focused bet on digital infrastructure, so it swings more than a broad fund and reacts to interest rates.
SSCP: An actively managed fund of small companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. Its top holdings are a mix of aerospace, aluminum, food and firearms makers, each about 5% to 7%, so a few names matter a lot.
SSFI: A fund of bond ETFs that rotates among fixed income sectors using a smart sector model weighing factors like value and momentum. It is a flexible, nontraditional bond holding that shifts its mix as signals change, so it can look defensive or aggressive depending on the model's reading.
SSK: Solana, the fast blockchain network's token, held directly, with a staking feature that locks up part of the holding to help run the network and earn extra tokens. Staking adds a trickle of extra return on top of the price, but Solana itself remains highly volatile.
SSMG: Small and mid-sized US growth companies picked by Silvant's managers, spread across technology, industrials and health care. It hunts the next generation of big winners while they are still mid-sized, which means bigger swings than large-company growth funds.
SSPY: The same 500 companies as the S&P 500, but spread more evenly across sectors rather than weighted by size, with technology, consumer, health care and staples all close in size. It's a core stock holding that leans less on the biggest tech companies, so it can trail when they lead.
SSS: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in Solana, a fast blockchain network's token. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the Solana slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
SSUS: A fund of sector ETFs for the S&P 500, with technology the largest at over two fifths and financials next. It's meant to be a core US stock holding that shifts toward the stronger industries, and the manager's moves can cause it to lag the market.
SSXU: International stock funds weighted by a smart sector process that overweights and underweights countries and industries against a broad foreign benchmark. It is active allocation among funds rather than stock picking, so its edge depends on the country and sector calls landing right.
STAX: Short-term US municipal bonds, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, such as cities, states and hospitals, with no single bond above about 2.5%.
STBF: Short-term bonds actively traded across the quality spectrum, from Treasuries to below-investment-grade debt, all maturing soon. Short maturities keep its price calm when interest rates move, and active allocation lets the managers hunt for extra yield without taking long-term rate risk.
STBQ: Companies building stablecoin technology and infrastructure, mostly financial firms with a large technology slice, plus some digital asset funds. It is a focused bet on dollar-linked crypto going mainstream: it swings with both payment stocks and crypto sentiment.
STCE: Companies tied to the crypto industry, mostly financial firms like exchanges and payment businesses, along with technology companies. It's a focused bet on the crypto economy that doesn't hold any digital currency itself, so it tends to rise and fall with crypto sentiment.
STEN: It holds a big US stock fund and adds options targeting protection against roughly the first 10% of losses over a year starting each September, as the name says. In return, gains are capped, and the buffer only fully applies to those who hold the whole period.
STHH: One company, STMicroelectronics, the European chipmaker, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge against euro moves. It is a single-stock technology bet with currency swings removed, so the result follows the chip business alone, for better or worse.
STIP: Treasury bonds whose payments rise with inflation, limited to those maturing within five years. It's meant to protect purchasing power with little price swing, and because the bonds are short, it's far less sensitive to interest rate moves than longer inflation-protected funds.
STLR: Exposure to Stellar's XLM crypto token through regulated futures contracts, backed by cash and high-quality collateral. It offers a way to trade XLM's price in a brokerage account without holding the token, but futures-based pricing can drift from the spot price and crypto swings are large.
STNC: US companies that meet the manager's sustainability standards, spread across technology, health care, consumer and industrial firms in roughly equal measure. It is an actively managed core stock fund with a green screen, favoring established businesses rather than speculative clean-tech names.
STOT: Short-term bonds from the US government, mortgage-backed issuers and corporations, actively managed with room to pick any credit quality. It aims for steady income with less sensitivity to interest rates than longer bond funds, so its price moves less.
STOX: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about forty percent, followed by financials, health care and communication. It's a core stock holding where the manager actively shifts between stocks and other funds, so it can differ from the broad market.
STPZ: Treasury bonds with maturities of one to five years whose principal rises with inflation. It's meant to protect purchasing power with relatively modest price swings, though it still loses some value when real interest rates rise.
STRN: Twenty-five large US stocks picked by a trend-following model that favors shares in established uptrends, currently heavy in technology and energy. It is a concentrated, rules-driven growth holding that can shift its lineup as trends change, so it looks quite different from a plain large-cap index fund.
STXD: Large and mid-sized US growth companies that also have a record of paying and growing dividends, tracking a Strive index. It holds a mix of tech, financials, industrials and health care, with Eli Lilly, Broadcom, JPMorgan and Microsoft each around 4% to 6%.
STXE: Large and mid-sized companies across 24 emerging markets, leaving out China, with technology over half and financials about a fifth. It's meant for growth from developing economies, and its heavy tech tilt makes it swing more than US stocks.
STXF: The 500 largest US companies in one fund, covering every major industry, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy.
STXG: US large and mid-sized growth companies, with technology close to half, followed by communication and consumer companies. It's built for growth with a heavy tech tilt, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
STXK: US small-company stocks, following a Strive index of small caps. It is very widely spread, with every top holding around 0.5%, and technology, financials and industrials are the biggest areas.
STXT: A broad mix of bonds of different maturities, mostly US investment-grade debt, with a small slice of preferred shares. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
STXV: About 1,000 large US companies that look cheap compared with their size, such as banks, health care and energy firms, following a Strive value index. It is spread widely, with no single stock above about 3% of the fund.
STYL: Lifestyle brands: clothing, footwear, sports cars and premium labels that sell an image as much as a product, almost all consumer discretionary companies. It is a focused bet on brand power and consumer taste, so it does well when shoppers feel flush and suffers when they trade down.
SUB: Short-term bonds from state and local governments, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It's a low-risk home for cash you want to earn tax-friendly income on, and because the bonds mature soon, the price barely moves when rates change.
SUIS: This trust holds SUI, the token of the Sui blockchain, and stakes it to earn additional tokens as rewards. Like other single-coin funds, its price is simply the coin's price, with all the sharp rises and crashes that crypto brings.
SUPP: An actively managed fund of companies that help move and make goods around the world, such as chip makers and industrial firms, in the US and abroad. Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA, Carpenter Technology and Eaton are each about 6% to 8%.
SURE: US companies chosen by watching what corporate insiders do: stocks where executives are buying their own shares or the company is buying back stock get the nod. The idea is that insiders know their businesses best, making this a signal driven twist on stock picking.
SURI: An actively managed fund that puts its money into a small number of biotech, pharmaceutical and healthcare companies, plus some energy holdings. It is concentrated in a few names, and it also uses Treasury bills and other instruments alongside the stocks.
SUSA: Large US companies tilted toward stronger environmental, social and governance scores, with technology about 43%. It's a core holding for investors who care about ESG, built to stay close to the broad US market while leaving out or underweighting some companies.
SUSB: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies, maturing in one to five years, with a tilt toward firms that score better on environmental and social measures. It's meant for steady income with smaller price swings than longer bonds, though prices still drop when rates rise.
SUSC: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US companies, screened to favor those with better environmental, social and governance records. It's meant for steady interest income with less risk than stocks, though its price falls when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
SUSL: Large US companies chosen for stronger environmental, social and governance records, with technology at about two fifths of the fund. It's meant as a core stock holding for people who want to screen out some laggards, and it is heavier in tech than a typical broad fund.
SVAL: Small US companies that look cheap on measures like earnings and book value, with financials the biggest slice at about a fifth. Each stock gets roughly equal weight, so it's a value tilt that swings more than large company funds.
SVOL: Mostly short-term Treasuries as collateral, combined with a strategy that sells insurance against stock market volatility to earn income. It pays well when markets are calm but can lose heavily, and fast, when markets drop sharply.
SVTN: US Treasury bonds with between seven and ten years until they mature, the heart of the government's own medium-to-long-term debt. It pays a bit more than shorter Treasury funds and swings a bit more when rates move, a middle path between cash-like safety and long bond drama.
SWAN: Mostly US Treasury bonds, with a smaller part in long-term call options on the S&P 500 to capture stock gains. It's meant to protect capital while still joining some of the market's rise, so it usually trails stocks in strong rallies.
SWP: US dividend-paying companies that also show growth potential, led by technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's meant for income and growth in one fund as a core holding, and it may trail in rallies led by companies that pay no dividends.
SXQG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the manager sees as high quality and growing. It leans toward tech and health care: Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund.
SYFI: Mostly bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (often called junk bonds), limited to shorter maturities. It aims to pay higher income than safer bonds, and the short maturities mean it should react less to interest rate moves, though it can still fall when the economy sours and defaults rise.
SYLD: US mid-sized companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends and buybacks, spread across financials, consumer companies, energy and industrials. It's a value-style holding meant for steady returns, and it holds more cyclical businesses than the broad market.
SYSB: A rules-based mix of Treasuries, mortgage bonds, and investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds, shifted among them as conditions change. It's meant as a core bond holding with a bit more income, though the riskier corporate bonds can fall when the economy weakens.
SYZ: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen by Lazard using a systematic, rules-based process. It is very spread out, with no holding above 1%, which is much less top-heavy than most funds.
TABD: A professionally managed mix of US government, corporate and other bonds, with a small slice in cash. It aims for income plus some price gain as a core bond holding, and because managers choose bonds actively, results can differ from the broad bond market.
TACK: A rotating mix of US sector funds, with some gold and Treasuries, shifting toward whatever the manager sees as strongest. It's meant as an all-in-one holding that tries to dodge big drops, but frequent shifts mean it can miss rebounds.
TACN: A core portfolio of large companies in developed markets outside the US, actively managed, with banks the biggest slice at about a quarter. It is meant as the main international holding in a portfolio, spreading across Europe, Japan and peers with manager stock picking rather than an index.
TACU: Core US stocks picked actively, spanning technology, finance, health care and communications in proportions close to the broad market. It aims to beat a plain index fund through research, while staying diversified enough to serve as a main holding.
TAFI: Mostly short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to local governments, with a small amount of taxable bonds and cash. It aims for tax-friendly income with little price movement, though short bonds usually pay less than longer ones, and it's actively managed.
TAFL: A national mix of long-term municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, with interest that is mostly exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed with an eye on taxes, and holds many bonds, none above about 3%.
TAFM: Mostly municipal bonds issued by US states and cities, with interest that's generally exempt from federal income tax, plus some taxable bonds. It's for tax-aware income from medium-term bonds, mainly useful for people in higher tax brackets, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
TAGG: A mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that are mostly investment grade. A manager tries to beat the standard bond market using research on the bonds, and it works as a core income holding and cushion for stocks, though prices drop when rates rise.
TAGS: Futures contracts on four farm commodities, corn, wheat, soybeans and sugar, held through four sister funds in roughly equal parts. It gives broad exposure to crop and food prices in one fund, and futures-based returns can differ from spot commodity prices over time.
TAIL: Mostly US government bonds, plus put options that gain value when the stock market falls sharply. It's a hedge meant to cushion a stock-heavy portfolio in a crash, and the monthly cost of those options means it tends to lag in calm or rising markets.
TALV: Large US companies the managers see as priced below their worth, with financials about a fifth and technology, health care and industrials behind. It's a value stock holding, with active picking, that suits the stock part of a portfolio and may trail growth funds in tech-led rallies.
TAN: Companies in the solar power business, with technology firms making solar panels and equipment about 60 percent and utilities and power producers about a third. It's a focused bet on one clean energy industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and can drop hard when interest rates rise.
TAOZ: US companies the managers think are priced below their worth, led by technology and financials, then communication and consumer companies. It's a core stock holding with a value tilt, and the managers pick stocks themselves, so results can differ from a plain index.
TAPR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against a set amount of losses over a two-year period ending in April 2027. In exchange, it gives up some gains, and the protection only applies if you hold through the whole period.
TAX: US stocks above five billion dollars in size, run through Cambria's quantitative model with tax management built in from the start. It aims to keep more of its returns after tax by harvesting losses and minding holding periods, a twist most stock funds leave entirely to the investor.
TAXE: Investment-grade municipal bonds from US states and cities with medium maturities. It's meant for steady income that is typically free from federal income tax, suiting higher earners, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
TAXF: A varied mix of US municipal bonds, mostly investment-grade, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-aware income with medium maturities, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
TAXI: Investment-grade bonds from US states, cities and local agencies that mature in under 15 years, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-friendly steady income and a cushion for stocks, and its medium length means it falls less than long bonds when rates rise.
TAXM: Municipal and other tax-aware bonds picked mainly for Massachusetts residents, so the interest can dodge both federal and state income tax. It is a narrow, state-specific income fund, meant for Massachusetts taxpayers rather than as a general bond holding.
TAXS: Short-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, with most maturing within five years and interest generally free of federal income tax. It's for steady, lower-risk income for taxpayers in higher brackets, and short maturities keep its price from falling much when rates rise.
TAXT: Investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by US states and local governments, following an ICE index. The interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%.
TAXX: A mix of short-term municipal and taxable bonds chosen for good income after taxes. It's meant for investors in taxed accounts who want a calmer bond holding, and its short maturity means its price moves less when interest rates rise.
TBFC: A balanced mix of nearly half bonds and just over two fifths stocks around the world, with technology the biggest stock area. It's a conservative all-in-one holding, and managers shift between stocks and safer assets using rules, so the mix changes over time.
TBFG: A mix of stocks (about three quarters, led by technology and financials), some bonds and a bit of other assets spread around the world. It's an all-in-one growth portfolio that shifts its mix using its own rules, so the blend changes over time instead of staying fixed.
TBG: Mostly US stocks across health care, energy, financials and consumer staples, chosen because the managers think they can raise their dividends over time. It aims for growing income plus some price gains, and it leans toward established companies rather than fast-growing tech.
TBIL: Ultra-short US Treasury bills that mature in about three months, which makes it essentially a cash parking spot. It's meant for safety and income that follows short-term interest rates, with almost no price swings, though its income falls if rates drop.
TBJL: Uses options on a long-term US Treasury bond ETF to cushion part of its losses over a one-year period starting in July, while capping gains. The protection works only if the fund is held for the full period, and long-term bonds can swing a lot.
TBLL: Very short-term US Treasury bills that mature within a year, split between bonds and cash-like holdings. It's a place to park money safely while still earning interest, and since the bills mature so quickly, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
TBLU: Water companies worldwide: utilities that deliver drinking water, plus makers of pipes, pumps, meters and treatment equipment, with industrials about three fifths of the fund. It is a focused bet on the business of clean water, a steadier theme than most single industry funds.
TBX: A daily bet against intermediate Treasury bonds, designed to rise when seven to ten year Treasury prices fall and interest rates climb. It resets daily and is meant for short-term trades or hedging, not for holding through calm markets.
TCAF: Large US companies picked by a manager who looks for steady growth at reasonable prices, with technology over a third and health care about a sixth. It's a core growth holding, and because it's actively managed, it can behave quite differently from the broad market.
