TCAI: Companies that build and power the AI boom, with technology about half and industrials and utilities behind it, including makers of chips, data centers, networks and energy supply. It's a themed bet on AI infrastructure, so it swings more than the broad market.
TCAL: US stocks across health care, industrials, technology and financials, combined with covered calls, which sell away some upside in exchange for cash payments. It aims for regular income, but it trails in strong rallies and still falls when stocks drop.
TCAN: A fund built to hold Canton Coin, the token of the Canton Network, a blockchain used by financial institutions. Roughly half of the fund is the coin itself, and the rest is mostly cash-like holdings, so it is a concentrated bet on one crypto asset.
TCHI: Chinese technology in the broad sense: chip and computer makers, internet platforms, online retailers and battery firms all count. It captures how blurred the tech label is in China, and like all China funds it swings with policy and sentiment toward Beijing.
TCHP: Large, well-established US companies with strong growth, with technology over half and communication and consumer companies next. It's built for growth, so it leans much more on tech than the broad market and tends to rise and fall harder, with managers picking the stocks.
TCPB: A broad mix of mostly investment-grade US bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, with room for riskier bonds. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income, and its price tends to fall when interest rates rise.
TCV: Smaller US companies the manager thinks are priced below their worth, spread across technology, consumer businesses, industrials and health care. It's meant for investors wanting a value tilt in small companies, and it holds a limited number of stocks, so it can swing more than a broad small-company fund.
TDAQ: Large Nasdaq-100 stocks, about 60 percent technology, combined with a strategy of selling call options on a daily basis that gives up some upside for cash. It's built for income from tech, so it lags when tech rallies hard.
TDAX: A leveraged fund aiming for roughly 120% to 140% of the daily performance of an index tied to Nasdaq-listed stocks. It uses derivatives to get that extra exposure, so gains and losses are magnified and the results can drift over longer periods.
TDEC: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each December. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
TDEM: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies across Latin America, Asia, Europe, Africa and the Middle East, actively managed as conditions change. It pays higher interest than developed-market debt, with extra risk from weaker economies and political turmoil.
TDI: Stocks from companies outside the US, led by financials and technology, followed by industrials and energy. It's a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and the managers adjust holdings actively, so it can differ noticeably from a standard international index.
TDIV: Technology and telecom companies that pay dividends, with technology about 85% and communication about an eighth. It's for income plus tech exposure, and it leans toward established, cash-rich firms, so it can trail pure growth tech funds in strong rallies.
TDNA: An actively managed fund of biotechnology companies, the ones developing new treatments for disease. It is spread thinly across many names, with the biggest, argenx, only about 5% of the fund, and it is entirely health care.
TDOG: A single crypto asset, Dogecoin, the meme-born token, held directly by the trust. It is a pure price bet on one of the most sentiment-driven coins: there is no income and no diversification, and the price can swing wildly on social media mood.
TDOT: A fund that holds Polkadot (DOT), a cryptocurrency, directly and stakes it to earn extra rewards. Its price follows the price of DOT, so it is a bet on one cryptocurrency and can swing sharply.
TDSB: A cautious allocation across stocks, bonds, real estate and other asset classes, managed to keep its overall risk near a set target rather than chase returns. It is built to participate modestly in good times and protect in bad ones, suiting investors who prize a smoother path.
TDSC: A shifting mix of stock sector funds, bonds, real estate and gold, managed to keep losses in a bad stretch near its 10 percent drawdown target. It is a moderate, defense-minded allocation fund that steps toward safety when markets wobble, accepting smaller gains in strong rallies.
TDTF: US government bonds whose payments rise with inflation, kept to a medium length of about five years. It's meant to protect buying power while limiting how much the price moves, though it still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
TDTT: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, kept to about three years of average sensitivity to rates. It's meant to protect buying power while keeping price swings small, though it can still lose a bit when interest rates rise.
TDV: US technology companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least seven years, with a small amount in industrials and financials. It combines tech exposure with income, so it holds steadier, mature tech firms and usually trails in rallies led by fast-growing names.
TDVG: Large US companies with a record of paying and growing dividends, with technology the biggest slice and financials, health care and industrials next. It aims for steady growth plus rising income, so it's a core holding that may lag when fast growing stocks lead.
TDVI: Dividend-paying technology companies, mostly software and chip makers, with some communication firms, plus an options strategy that gives up some gains for extra income. It's meant for income from tech, and it trails in strong rallies while still falling when tech falls.
TEC: Companies building or riding major technology shifts, mostly software, chips and internet firms, with technology about three quarters of the fund. It is an actively managed bet on change, so it leans into growth names across industries and will swing more than a plain tech fund.
TECB: US technology companies working on areas like robotics, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud and fintech, plus some genomics firms. Tech is about 60% and health care about an eighth, so it's a growth theme bet that swings more than the broad market.
TECY: Weekly income from selling put options on a leveraged technology fund that triples its index's daily moves. It is an aggressive income trade on the tech sector: the triple leverage underneath makes payouts and losses both extreme, so it is built for short holding periods.
TEK: Technology companies from around the world, from giant chip and software makers to smaller growers, picked actively for fast, lasting growth. It goes beyond US tech, so it holds Asian chip giants too, and it swings with the global tech cycle.
TEKX: Companies accelerating transformative technology: crypto miners, data center builders, energy innovators and chip firms. It mixes the crypto economy with the AI buildout, so it is volatile and heavily influenced by bitcoin's mood.
TEKY: An actively managed fund of technology companies around the world that the manager sees as the next wave, such as chips and AI. It is tech heavy at about 79%, with SK Hynix, Alphabet and NVIDIA the biggest holdings.
TEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, in dollars and in local currencies, paying higher interest to compensate for political and currency risk. It is an income holding from the developing world, actively managed, that swings more than rich country bond funds.
TEMR: Emerging market stocks researched company by company, with Asian technology near half the fund and banks about a fifth. It is an actively managed developing markets holding from a large research-driven shop, leaning into the region's chip and internet champions while spreading across many other countries.
TEMX: Growth companies in emerging markets excluding China and Hong Kong, led by Taiwanese and Korean chip giants, with Indian finance and Latin American e-commerce behind. Skipping China sets it apart from standard emerging market funds and concentrates it in Asia's tech exporters.
TEND: Holds the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF and uses options to try to cushion a set amount of losses over a 12-month period, in exchange for limiting gains. The name points to a 10% buffer, and the protection only applies to people who hold through the full period.
TENJ: Options on large US stocks set each June for a twelve month outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The buffer is the design target for each period, and the terms restart every June for the next round.
TENM: Options on large US stocks set each March for a twelve month outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The buffer is the design target for each period, and the terms restart every March for the next round.
TEQI: Large US companies with a record of paying dividends that look underpriced, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It's meant as a core value holding that earns income, and it tends to trail growth funds when tech-heavy stocks lead the market.
TESL: A concentrated Tesla strategy: a large direct stake in Tesla's stock amplified with call options, while the rest sits in Treasury bills. It magnifies life as a Tesla shareholder, bigger gains in rallies and deeper pain in drops, all on one company.
TEST: Synthetic exposure to Tesla stock plus an options program targeting a 25 percent yearly payout rate. The distributions ride on Tesla's wild price swings, so the fund itself is extremely jumpy, and the option strategy limits gains when Tesla surges.
TETH: Direct exposure to ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, held as the fund's asset rather than through futures contracts. Ether's price swings hard with crypto sentiment and with activity on the network, so this is a simple but volatile way to hold it in a brokerage account.
TEXN: Companies headquartered in Texas, where energy is the biggest slice at about a third, with technology, industry and consumer firms behind. It is a single-state bet, so Texas's oil-driven economy and business climate drive the results.
TEXX: Texas-based companies, with energy firms making up about 70% of the fund and smaller stakes in industrial, consumer and utility businesses. It is a focused bet on one state's economy, so it rises and falls with Texas oil and gas more than a national fund would.
TFFI: Bond funds spanning short and longer company debt, preferred shares and emerging market bonds, moved around by a long-term trend-following program. The strategy rides bond trends up or down and can step aside into cash, so it behaves unlike a normal buy-and-hold bond fund.
TFGZ: A small collection of growth companies, led by technology at about forty percent, with communication and financial firms next. It's built for growth, and since it holds relatively few stocks, it can swing more than the broad market.
TFI: Long-term bonds from US state and local governments, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It suits investors in higher tax brackets who want steady tax-friendly income, though prices fall when interest rates rise, especially for long maturities.
TFJL: Options on a fund of long-term US Treasury bonds, built with a floor meant to stop losses past a set point over the year starting each July. It is a defensive way to hold interest-rate bets: cushioned against deep bond sell-offs, capped if bonds rally hard.
TFLO: Short-term US Treasury notes whose interest payments reset as rates change. It's a safe place to park cash, and since its income follows short-term rates up, its price barely drops when rates rise, though income falls when rates are cut.
TFLR: Mostly loans to companies with weaker credit ratings, where the interest rate resets as market rates change. It aims for higher income, and its price holds up better than ordinary bonds when rates rise, but it can fall if borrowers struggle to repay.
TFNS: Financial companies of every kind: banks, card networks, insurers, exchanges and investment firms. It is a focused bet on the finance industry, which tends to thrive when lending is healthy and suffer when credit problems spread.
TFPN: A managed futures fund that follows price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, going long on rising markets and short on falling ones. It's meant to diversify a stock portfolio, and it can do well in prolonged moves but struggle when markets keep reversing.
TGLB: Large companies across global developed markets, actively picked, with technology about a third and the rest spread across finance, media, industry and health care. It is a core worldwide stock holding run on manager research, including US giants alongside their European and Japanese peers.
TGLR: High quality large companies chosen for strong earnings and dividend growth plus an above-average dividend yield, spread across technology, banks and industry. It blends value discipline with growth in payouts, a new era take on classic dividend value investing.
TGRT: Large US companies a manager picks for strong growth, with technology at well over half and communication companies next. It's a growth fund and an actively managed one, so it's built to rise faster in good markets and fall harder in bad ones than the broad market.
TGRW: Large US companies with fast-growing sales and profits, with technology over half and communication companies next. It's built for long-term growth, and with so much in tech it tends to swing more than the broad market.
TGRZ: Chinese companies building large language models and AI foundation technology: the firms racing to match Western AI with their own models and cloud platforms. It is a single-country bet on the most contested corner of tech, so export controls and Chinese policy hit it directly.
THD: Thai companies, with industrials the biggest slice, then energy, financials and communication. It's a single-country bet for adding emerging-market exposure to a portfolio, and it swings more than the broad market, with extra risk from Thailand's economy, politics and its currency.
THEQ: Large US stocks picked through the manager's own research, held mainly through a house stock fund, with a derivatives hedge layered on top. The hedge reduces volatility and offers protection in downturns, aiming for stock exposure with smaller bumps along the way.
THIR: A rotating mix of US stock index funds, mostly large companies with technology about two fifths. It's built to give large US stock growth while trying to lower swings, by moving out of areas of the market that look weak, though those moves can miss rebounds.
THLV: A basket of US stock funds held in equal weights and selected by rules meant to keep volatility low, with the mix adjusted as conditions change. It aims for a smoother ride through the stock market, and the large cash stake it can hold will drag when markets climb steadily.
THMR: A tactical mix that shifts between stocks, bonds, gold, commodities and even crypto, using other funds and some individual shares. Its managers move money toward whatever looks safer or stronger, so it can sit partly in cash when markets look risky.
THMZ: Established large companies around the world, including emerging markets, chosen for their place in long running megatrends like technology change and health care demand. It is an actively managed global growth holding, spreading bets across industries so no single trend carries the whole fund.
THNQ: Companies that earn a big share of revenue from artificial intelligence, with technology about three quarters of the fund. It's a focused growth bet on the AI theme, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop sharply if tech stocks fall.
THNR: Companies worldwide that stand to gain from weight loss drugs and treatments: drug makers, drug distributors and related health care firms make up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on one booming corner of medicine, so it swings with drug news and competition.
THOR: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, including phone companies, banks, preferred shares and property trusts, plus other income-paying instruments. It builds income from many sources at once, favoring steady global payers over chasing the single highest yield.
THRO: US stocks chosen by an active manager who rotates among themes expected to grow faster than average, with technology close to half. It's a growth holding, and the themes change over time, so it can swing more than the broad market.
THRU: The infrastructure behind commodities: pipelines, storage terminals, ports and processing plants that move oil, gas, metals and grain from ground to market. It is a steadier way to own the raw materials economy than buying the commodities themselves, with income from fees for moving and storing them.
THRV: An actively managed fund that spreads money across other bond ETFs, closed-end funds and similar holdings to produce income. About 60% is in bonds, with a good share in short-term and high yield funds, so it is more a mix of funds than individual securities.
THTA: Short-term US Treasury bills with a set of options spreads layered on top to try to earn extra income. The bills are the core holding, while the options add income but also add risk compared with a plain Treasury fund.
THY: A tactical income fund that shifts among high yield bonds, investment grade bonds, municipals, Treasuries and cash, and can hedge or retreat entirely to cash when its managers judge risk too high. That freedom sets it apart: safety, not yield, takes over in stormy markets.
THYF: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, spread across financials, materials, health care and consumer firms. It pays higher interest than safer bonds, but those companies are more likely to miss payments, so it tends to fall alongside stocks in downturns.
THYM: Lower-rated municipal bonds paying higher tax-exempt interest, issued by cities, hospitals and projects with shakier finances. It aims for the highest tax-free income in the muni market, suiting high-bracket investors, and the weaker credits mean it falls more than quality muni funds when markets worry.
THYP: A single cryptocurrency, HYPE, the token of the Hyperliquid trading platform, with part of the holdings staked, meaning locked up to support the network in exchange for extra tokens. Staking adds yield to a pure price bet, though the token itself can swing violently.
TIER: Stocks from companies outside the US, picked by in-house analysts rather than an index, with financials and technology each making up about a quarter. It's a diversified way to add international exposure, and because people choose the holdings, results can differ from the overseas market as a whole.
TIH: A manager's picks of large US growth companies, with technology the biggest slice at over a third, then communication, health care and consumer businesses. It's a growth fund with only a modest number of holdings, so it can swing more than the broad market.
TIIV: Large companies outside the US, bought as ADRs and foreign shares, with banks the biggest slice at about a third, then industrial and technology firms. Managers hunt for stocks priced below what the business seems worth, so it plays the patient value role in an international stock holding.
TILC: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials at about 30 percent, then industrials, technology and health care. It's a way to diversify beyond US stocks for long-term growth, and currency moves can add to its ups and downs.
TILL: Agricultural commodity futures: corn, wheat, soybeans, livestock, sugar and other farm goods, traded actively rather than held to a fixed recipe. It packages farm price exposure without a K-1 tax form, and it swings with weather, harvests and food prices worldwide.
TILT: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, with technology about a third and financials about a sixth. It's a core holding that leans toward smaller and cheaper companies than the broad market, so it can lag when big growth stocks lead.
TIME: Large US growth companies, mostly technology, combined with a hedge position that bets against the Nasdaq-100. Carrying a built-in hedge is unusual for a core equity fund: it trims losses in tech-led sell-offs but drags when tech rallies.
TINS: Stocks from countries outside the US, picked by Templeton's managers using on-the-ground research into each company's prospects. It is an actively run international holding, so its country and industry mix shifts with where the managers see the best value.
TINY: Nanotechnology companies: firms working at the scale of atoms and molecules, from chip-making equipment and precision instruments to advanced materials. It is a niche science theme spread across technology, health care and materials, with many small, research-heavy names.
TIP: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, with maturities longer than one year. It's meant to protect buying power and diversify a portfolio, but its price still drops when interest rates rise faster than inflation.
TIPA: A ladder of inflation-protected Treasury bonds with maturities running up to 2030, designed to pay out income as the rungs come due. It is a spend-down style holding for money earmarked for around 2030, with inflation protection built into every bond.
TIPB: A fund of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, whose payments rise with inflation, laddered to mature around 2035. It pays out income regularly, and nearly all of it is US government debt.
TIPC: Inflation-linked government bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at 2045, meaning their values and payouts rise with inflation. It is designed for savers planning spending around that year, paying out distributions along the way rather than holding everything to one end date.
TIPD: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2055, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is built for decades-long income plans: the fixed end date sets the schedule, and the inflation link guards purchasing power across a working lifetime.
TIPE: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2031, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is an income planning tool with built-in inflation protection: the 2031 end date fixes the schedule, and the payouts rise with inflation instead of losing ground to it.
TIPF: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2036, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is a longer-horizon income planning tool: the inflation link protects purchasing power, and the fixed 2036 schedule makes the payout path predictable.
TIPG: A ladder of inflation-protected Treasury bonds arranged to mature in steps toward 2046, paying out distributions along the way. The ladder spreads interest rate risk across years instead of betting on one maturity, and the 2046 end date makes it a tool for a goal about twenty years out.
TIPH: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2056, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is built for very long income horizons: the decades-long schedule sets it apart, and the inflation link keeps payouts from losing purchasing power over time.
TIPX: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, US government bonds whose value rises with inflation, with maturities from one to ten years. It's meant to protect buying power and cushion a stock portfolio, though its price can still drop when real interest rates rise.
TIPZ: US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, following an ICE BofA index of them. Their principal rises with inflation, so the fund is a way to hold government bonds that adjust for rising prices, with holdings spread across many Treasury issues.
TISC: Hundreds of small companies outside the US, spread thinly across Europe, Japan and other developed markets, with industrial firms the biggest slice at about a quarter. It offers the small-company growth effect abroad, where less analyst coverage can mean more mispricing and more volatility.
TIZE: Securitized debt picked by TCW specialists: bonds backed by mortgages and other loan pools, many issued or guaranteed by US government agencies. It is an income holding built on housing and consumer credit, where loan-level analysis matters more than picking between famous corporate borrowers.
TJAN: Options on the largest US companies give this fund stock market exposure with a built-in shield: it is designed to protect against losses over its two-year outcome period, which runs to January 2027. In exchange, gains are capped, so it suits investors who want equity growth with the downside taken off.
TJUL: Large US stocks, mostly technology, held through options that protect against some losses over a two-year period ending July 2027. It's for investors seeking a cushion, but gains are capped and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
TJUN: Uses options tied to an emerging markets stock fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each June. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
TKNQ: Companies building tokenization technology: the platforms turning real-world assets like property and bonds into tradeable digital tokens, mostly financial firms. It is a focused bet on finance moving on-chain, mixing payment and exchange stocks with crypto funds, so sentiment swings it hard.
TKNS: A basket of crypto funds holding bitcoin, ethereum, solana and newer tokens, actively shifted between them by the manager rather than fixed in place. It gives one-ticker access to a spread of digital assets, but crypto prices swing violently, so the whole fund moves far more than a stock portfolio.
TKNZ: An actively managed basket of cryptocurrencies, spread across several digital assets rather than just bitcoin, run with the aim of beating a broad crypto index. It is a diversified-by-crypto-standards bet on the whole asset class, still far more volatile than any stock or bond fund.
TLA: A note-like bet on Tesla stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or climbs. If Tesla drops hard, the fund can fall steeply with it, and its gains come with a ceiling.
TLCE: Large US companies across every major industry, actively picked by Thrivent's managers rather than held in index order. It is meant to work as a core stock holding, and its results depend on the managers' picks beating the big-company market over time.
TLCI: A focused portfolio of roughly 25 to 40 large companies outside the US, hand-picked across industries like aerospace, hotels, drugmaking and chip equipment. With so few holdings, each pick matters, making it an active core international holding rather than a whole-market fund.
TLDR: A ladder of Treasury bills, the shortest-term US government debt, with maturities spread out over six months or less. It is a cash-like parking spot that pays a bit of interest, with safety and daily access as the point.
TLG: Large US growth companies picked by active managers, with technology close to three-fifths of the fund and big weights in chipmakers, software and internet platforms. It is a concentrated bet on fast growers, so it tends to outrun plain index funds in tech-led rallies and lag when growth falls from favor.
TLH: US Treasury bonds that mature in 10 to 20 years, backed by the federal government. It's a safe-credit cushion for stock portfolios in downturns, but its price drops noticeably when interest rates rise.
TLIE: Large US companies picked for income and value by a manager known for patient, concentrated stock picking, spread across technology, banks, industrials and health care. It favors profitable payers bought at reasonable prices, aiming for dividends plus steady growth rather than chasing hot stocks.
TLT: US Treasury bonds that won't be repaid for more than twenty years. It can jump when stocks fall and is used as a cushion, but it drops sharply when interest rates rise because the bonds are so long.
TLTD: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, tilted toward smaller and cheaper companies. It's a way to add international diversification, and the value tilt means it can trail when growth stocks lead.
TLTE: Companies in emerging markets, such as China, India and Taiwan, led by technology and financials with industrials and consumer businesses next. It's for adding developing-economy growth, and it tilts toward smaller and cheaper stocks than a standard emerging markets fund.
TLTI: Treasury bonds with more than 20 years to maturity, plus income from selling put options on the S&P 500. Long Treasuries already swing a lot when rates move, and the stock options add extra income along with extra risk in a stock sell-off.
TLTP: Long-term US Treasury bonds paired with weekly at-the-money call options sold against them to harvest premium income. Bond funds usually pay modest interest, so this design aims for a much higher income stream from the options, while the long Treasury holdings still swing hard when rates move.
TLTW: Long-term US Treasury bonds, with a call options strategy layered on top that gives up some price gains in exchange for extra monthly income. It's meant for income from long bonds, but it still drops when interest rates rise and trails if bond prices jump.
TLTX: US Treasury bonds, held directly and through a Treasury ladder fund, with call options sold on Treasury funds to add income on top of interest. The options boost payouts in calm markets, while rate rises still push bond prices down.
TMAR: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each March. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
TMAT: Global small and mid-sized companies tied to emerging themes like genomics and fintech, with technology the biggest slice at over half. The managers rotate between themes over time, so it's a growth-focused bet that swings more than the broad market.
TMB: A wide mix of bonds of any type, quality and length, chosen by active managers to earn income. It's built for higher income than a basic bond fund, but it can take on lower-rated bonds, so it carries more credit risk and its price drops when interest rates rise.
TMDV: Companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least 35 years, drawn from across the US market and led by everyday consumer brands, industrials and banks. That long record makes it a steady income holding, heavy on mature firms rather than fast growers.
TMED: Health care companies of every kind: drug makers, insurers, device firms, lab tool suppliers and distributors, picked actively by researchers who specialize in the field. A single-industry fund like this can outrun the market when medicine advances, and stumble when politics turns on drug prices.
TMFC: About 100 large US growth companies picked by the Motley Fool using its own rules, with technology nearly half and communication and financials next. It's built for growth, so it leans heavily on tech and tends to swing more than the broad market.
TMFE: About 100 large US companies picked by a Motley Fool index that scores how well each uses its money, and that the Motley Fool has recommended. Alphabet, Lam Research, Amazon and Apple are each around 5 or 6% of it.
TMFG: A hand-picked set of high-quality growing companies from the US and abroad, spread across industrials, financials, communication and technology. It's a growth fund for the stock part of a portfolio, and because it holds a focused list, it can behave differently from broad global stock indexes.
TMFM: Mid-sized US companies picked for quality and growth by the Motley Fool team, spread across technology, health care, industry and finance in a focused portfolio. It is an active growth fund whose results depend on a few dozen stock picks, so it can stray well away from index returns.
TMFS: Small US growth companies in a focused portfolio picked by an investor education company's team, spanning health care, industrials, technology and finance. Small caps picked for quality and held with conviction make it livelier than broad small cap funds, with bigger swings in both directions.
TMFX: Mid-sized and smaller US companies that Motley Fool analysts have recommended in their newsletters, spread across technology, health care and industry. It packages the Fool's next-wave picks after its best-known recommendations, so it is more speculative than its flagship fund.
TMGN: The Magnificent 10, a short list of ten mega-cap growth giants drawn mostly from technology and media, paired with an options program designed to pay daily income. It is a concentrated bet on the biggest names in the market, with the options overlay trading some upside for regular cash.
TMH: One company, Toyota, held through its US-listed depositary receipts with a built-in hedge that removes most of the yen-to-dollar exchange rate effect. It is a single-stock bet on the world's biggest carmaker with currency swings stripped out, so the result follows the car business alone.
TMID: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies chosen using the manager's in-house research. It is widely spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, with no holding above about 1.5%.
TMLP: Master limited partnerships that move, process and store oil and gas, held through swaps rather than directly to sidestep the tax headaches MLPs create for funds. These pipeline partnerships pay generous distributions, and their prices follow energy volumes and oil markets.
TMNL: Long-term municipal bonds issued by cities, states and agencies across the US, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds mature far in the future, the price moves more than shorter muni funds when interest rates change.
TMNS: Short-term municipal bonds paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax, actively managed for stability and income. It is a conservative tax-free holding for money with a near-term purpose, keeping maturities short so its price barely moves when interest rates change.
TMSF: Bonds from every sector that pays income: government debt, corporate bonds, mortgage securities and floating rate loans, with room to reach into emerging markets for extra yield. Managers shift the mix actively, making it a flexible income core that takes more credit risk than a plain index bond fund.
TMSL: Small and mid-sized US companies spread fairly evenly across technology, health care, industrials and financials. It's an actively managed growth holding for the middle of the market, and it swings more than large company funds.
TMVE: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaply priced, led by industrials and financials, with technology and consumer firms behind. It's a value-focused stock holding, and it has less technology than the broad market, so it can trail when growth stocks lead.
TMYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund holding Taiwan Semiconductor stock, the giant chipmaker, rather than on owning shares directly. It aims to pay out frequent distributions, but the leveraged link makes it swing hard, so it suits short holding periods rather than a set-and-forget core position.
TNGY: Nearly all energy companies, mostly oil, gas and pipeline businesses, with a small slice of utilities. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it swings more than the broad market and moves closely with oil and gas prices.
TNTW: US Treasury bonds with between ten and twenty years until they mature, a long stretch of the government's own debt. Bonds this long pay interest for many years and move a lot when rates change, so this is a bolder Treasury holding than the intermediate funds.
TNUK: Companies across the nuclear energy chain: uranium and fuel, plant builders and operators, and utilities running reactors, split among industrials, utilities and energy. It is a focused bet on a nuclear revival driven by AI power demand, swinging with uranium prices and politics.
TNXT: Companies leading in innovation across developed markets, from chip and software giants to medical pioneers, with technology near half the fund and health care about a quarter. It is a growth portfolio built around new technology and business models, so it swings more than the broad market.
TOAK: Short-dated options trades on US stocks, built as defined-risk spreads where the most a trade can lose is set when it is placed. It aims for steady positive returns with a cash-like holding period, and its options-only design sets it apart from ordinary short-term bond funds.
TOAO: A mix of stocks and bonds that an active manager shifts around, aiming to balance growth and stability in one fund. It's meant as an all-in-one moderate holding, and since the manager makes the calls, its results depend on those choices rather than a fixed recipe.
TOCT: Options on the S&P 500 structured for defined protection over a two-year period ending in October 2027, taking gains up to a cap while aiming to shield against losses. The two-year horizon is the trade-off for that level of protection.
TOGA: A concentrated group of global growth companies, led by technology, consumer businesses and communication, with at least a third based outside the US. It's a manager's high-conviction growth bet, so holding relatively few stocks means it can swing more than a broad global stock fund.
TOK: Large companies from developed countries around the world except Japan, with the US making up most of it. Technology is about a third, followed by financials, industrials and health care, so it works as a core global stock holding that leaves out Japanese companies.
TOLL: Companies that dominate their markets: monopolies and near monopolies with pricing power, measured by how concentrated their industries are, across technology, finance, industry and health care. The idea is that dominant firms defend profits better, making this a quality tilted bet on market leaders.
TOLZ: Owners and operators of infrastructure like utilities, pipelines and energy transport, plus some industrials and real estate. It's meant for steady income and an inflation-resistant slice of the economy, and it follows only pure-play infrastructure companies worldwide, so it sits apart from broad stock funds.
TOPC: The S&P 500 with every company capped at 3 percent of the fund, so the mega-sized tech giants count for far less than usual. The cap spreads influence across all 500 names, making it a more even-handed version of the classic big-company index.
TOPT: Only the 20 largest US companies, with technology over half, so the fund is far more concentrated than the full S&P 500. It's a core-style holding that gives big-company exposure, but when a few giants stumble, it falls harder.
TOPW: A basket of Roundhill's weekly-pay funds, each built on options around a single famous stock such as a chipmaker or a tech giant, gathered into one ticker. It aims for weekly distributions from many names at once, but every ingredient is a leveraged, single-stock strategy, so the swings stay large.
TORK: Companies that make actuators, the motors and motion parts that move machines, robots and vehicles, mainly industrials with some consumer names. It is a narrow robotics supply-chain bet: demand rides factory automation and electric vehicles, so it swings with manufacturing spending.
TOS: A flexible mix of US and international stocks of every size, with technology over half, plus some cash. A manager picks it for total return, so it works as a core holding with a strong tech tilt and fewer holdings than a broad fund.
TOT: An actively managed fund that mostly holds a broad US stock market ETF, so it behaves much like the overall US market. It is run to cut down on taxable payouts, and nearly all of it sits in that single underlying fund.
TOTL: An actively managed mix of bonds of all kinds, including government, mortgage-backed and corporate debt, with no limit on credit quality. It's a core bond holding that aims to beat the broad bond market, but the manager's choices mean it can differ a lot from it.
TOTR: A manager-picked mix of US government bonds, corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and other debt. It aims for steady income and total return as a core bond holding, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
TOUS: Companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials at about a quarter, with industrials, technology and health care behind. It's an actively managed way to add international diversification, so a manager's picks, not just the index, decide how it differs from the market.
TOV: Large US companies across the broad market, with technology at about two fifths, screened to match Jewish values. It's a core stock holding for values-minded investors, and its screens make it differ a little from the broad market.
TOXR: A fund that holds the digital currency XRP directly instead of stocks or bonds, so its value follows the coin's price. It's a speculative bet on one cryptocurrency, and it can swing wildly in a single day, far more than the stock market.
TPAY: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to pay regular managed distributions, using the index's 500 big US companies as the engine rather than holding the stocks. The payout schedule is the point of the design, so it behaves more like an income product than a growth fund, with gains capped by the options.
TPFC: Fifty large and mid-sized US companies chosen for strong free cash flow, drawn from an index that applies biblically responsible screens. Energy, health care and technology lead the mix, and the values screen sets it apart from ordinary cash flow funds.
TPFG: Fifty large and mid-sized growth companies picked for strong and rising free cash flow, drawn from a biblically screened universe. Technology and industrial firms dominate, and the Christian values screen sets it apart from typical growth funds.
TPFI: A core-plus bond portfolio of government, corporate and other debt, actively managed by a firm known for faith-based investing screens. It plays the steady income and ballast role, with the manager's values-based exclusions and active shifts across bond types setting it apart from a plain aggregate bond fund.
TPHD: Larger US companies that pay high dividends, led by utilities, industrials and energy, with financials next. It's meant for steady income, and it weights stocks by how calm they've been and follows a faith-based screen, so it leaves out some businesses.
TPIF: Companies from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, weighted by how calm their prices have been rather than by size. It screens out businesses that conflict with biblical values, so it's an international holding with a faith-based filter.
TPLC: US large and mid-sized companies spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care, weighted so calmer stocks count for more. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward steadier names, and it screens out companies that conflict with the manager's faith-based values.
TPLS: A core-plus bond portfolio: Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt at the center, with room for up to a quarter in lower-rated junk bonds for extra yield. The plus sleeve lifts income while adding credit risk to a mainly high-quality base.
TPRY: US stocks picked with a contrarian streak, favoring companies beaten down when markets throw a tantrum, led by technology at about half the fund. It pairs that bargain hunting with a strategy targeting 15 percent yearly payouts, a bold income goal.
TPSC: Small US companies spread across financials, industrials, technology and consumer businesses, with financials about a quarter. It's a core small-company holding that weights stocks by how calm they have been, and it follows a faith-based screen that leaves out some businesses.
TPUT: An options-based strategy that adjusts how much stock market exposure it takes, holding Treasury securities and cash-like assets as collateral and an income source while conditions are calm. It aims for capital growth with a disciplined, rules-driven options program, and it can sit largely in safe assets at times.
TPYP: Companies that own pipelines carrying oil and natural gas across North America, nearly all energy with a small slice of utilities. It's meant for income from steady fee-based businesses, and it's a focused bet on one industry, so it moves with energy markets and interest rates.
TPZ: Companies that generate and deliver electricity: pipeline and gas network owners, power producers and electric utilities, with energy about three-fifths and utilities about a third. It is a focused bet on the build-out of the power grid, and these businesses tend to pay steady dividends.
TQQY: An income strategy built on options over a triple-leveraged Nasdaq fund, turning that fund's huge daily swings into regular payouts. It is among the riskiest income designs: leverage resets daily and the options cap gains, so losses in a tech slide can be severe.
TRBF: A bond portfolio concentrated in mortgage related debt: home and commercial mortgage securities from government agencies and private issuers, plus mortgage loans. That concentration is its identity, aiming for mortgage market income with active management, and it lives and dies by housing and property credit.
TRFK: Companies behind data and digital infrastructure, almost all technology, with chip makers, networking and security firms leading. It's a focused bet on the tech build-out, so it swings more than the broad market and does best when tech spending is strong.
TRFM: Companies tied to AI and the transformer technology behind it, with technology about 57 percent and industrials nearly a quarter. It's a growth bet on a single theme, so it swings more than the broad market and can drop hard if AI enthusiasm fades.
TRIL: The world's trillion-dollar companies: the handful of giant firms, mostly US technology names, big enough to be worth over a trillion dollars each. Owning them in one fund is a concentrated bet on mega-cap dominance, so it swings with a short list of stocks rather than the broad market.
TRIO: Options on funds covering large US, small US and developed foreign stocks, set up to absorb some losses over a set period while limiting gains. It's meant as a cushion across a broad stock mix, and it trails in strong rallies.
TRND: A fund of other Pacer Trendpilot funds, split roughly evenly across US large caps, US mid caps, international stocks and US bonds. Each underlying fund uses a trend rule that can shift from stocks into Treasury bills when markets weaken, so the mix changes over time.
TROT: US Treasury bonds with a twist: the fund rotates between longer and shorter maturities to adjust how hard interest-rate moves hit it. It is an actively timed government bond holding: when the rotation is right it cushions rate rises, and when wrong it adds swings a plain Treasury fund avoids.
TRPA: The safest slice of collateralized loan obligations: AAA-rated bundles of corporate loans, where many company loans are pooled and this fund holds the tranche paid first. It is an income fund designed to pay more than Treasury bonds while taking the most protected seat in the loan pool.
TRSY: US Treasury debt maturing within a year, the closest thing to cash that still pays a little interest. Investors use it to park money safely for short periods, and its price barely budges when interest rates move, unlike longer-term bond funds.
TRTY: A mix of other funds spread across stocks, bonds, real assets and a large amount of cash and short-term holdings. It's an all-in-one portfolio meant to hold up across different economies, but it can trail the stock market in strong rallies.
TRUC: An actively managed fund of communication services companies, such as Alphabet, Meta and Netflix, a limited number of which dominate it. Alphabet and Meta alone make up around 40% of the fund.
TRUD: Companies that sell discretionary goods and experiences: online retail, carmakers, home improvement stores, restaurants and travel, essentially the full consumer discretionary sector in one holding. It is a focused bet on household spending, so it shines when consumers feel flush and sags when they pull back.
TRUF: Financial companies across the industry: banks, insurers, payment networks and asset managers, actively picked rather than held in index weights. It is a focused bet on the financial system, so it does well when lending and markets are healthy and falls hard in banking scares.
TRUH: Health care companies of every kind: drugmakers, insurers, hospital operators and medical device firms, actively picked across the whole sector. It is a focused bet on medical spending, which tends to hold up in recessions, though drug pricing politics can hit parts of it hard.
TRUI: Industrial companies across the sector: machinery makers, aerospace firms, electrical equipment builders and transport suppliers, actively picked rather than index-weighted. It is a focused bet on factories, construction and infrastructure spending, so it does best when the industrial economy is humming.
TRUM: Materials companies: chemical makers, miners and industrial gas producers, actively picked across the sector, with a small slice of consumer firms alongside. It is a focused bet on the raw ingredients of the economy, so it rises and falls with construction, manufacturing and commodity prices.
TRUN: Energy companies across the business: oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline operators, actively picked across the whole sector. It is a focused bet on fuel prices and energy demand, so it does well when oil is expensive and struggles when crude falls.
TRUO: Consumer staples companies: the makers and sellers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products that people buy in any economy. It is a defensive holding, actively picked across the sector, and it usually falls less in downturns but grows more slowly in booms.
TRUR: Real estate companies: landlords of apartments, offices, warehouses, shops and data centers, actively picked across the property sector. It is built for rent-based income and property exposure without buying buildings, and it tends to fall when interest rates rise because borrowing costs shape property values.
TRUT: Technology companies of all kinds, from software and chips to hardware and IT services, picked by active managers. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, and because it's all one industry, it swings more than the broad market, rising fast in good times and falling hard in bad ones.
TRUU: Utility companies: the regulated providers of electricity, gas and water, actively picked across the sector. Utilities are a classic defensive holding, paying steady dividends and usually moving less than the market, though they tend to lag when interest rates rise.
TRXS: A trust holding TRX, the token of the Tron blockchain network, that also stakes its holdings to earn extra tokens for helping run the network. It offers stock market access to a mid sized cryptocurrency whose price swings are sharp and sentiment driven.
TSCM: Mid-sized companies picked actively for quality growth, meaning strong businesses that can keep expanding, led by software and industrial firms. Mid-caps sit between small and large stocks, so this aims for faster growth than giants with less drama than small caps.
TSCV: Small US companies, with financials and industrials each about a fifth and consumer and technology firms behind. The managers hunt for cheap shares and keep a little cash, so it's a way to tilt toward smaller value stocks, which swing more than large companies.
TSCZ: Bonds backed by loans and property: home mortgages, commercial mortgages, asset backed securities and loan bundles, in both government backed and private forms. It hunts income in the securitized market with active management, offering a different flavor of bond risk than corporate or Treasury funds.
TSEC: Bonds backed by pools of loans, mainly mortgages and similar debts, with a bit of cash. It's meant for income that is higher than Treasuries, with managers choosing across types, though prices can fall when rates rise or when borrowers struggle to pay back loans.
TSEE: An actively managed fund of small US companies, defined as ones no bigger than the largest in the Russell 2000 index. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward health care, financials and industrials.
TSEL: Select US growth companies hand-picked by Sands Capital, with technology over half the fund, from chipmakers to specialty steel and power infrastructure firms. Sands holds a focused list of businesses it believes can compound earnings for years, accepting concentration as the price of conviction.
TSEP: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each September. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
TSES: US energy companies, including oil and gas producers and power-related firms, selected by an index built around American energy security. ExxonMobil and Chevron are each around 8% of the fund, and it also holds utilities and industrials.
TSIB: Income built around a single stock, Tesla, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on one famously volatile company: the income plan cannot tame Tesla's swings, it only harvests them.
TSIC: Famous American consumer brands: the food, drink, retail and lifestyle companies that define everyday American life, over half in consumer staples. It is a patriotic-themed core holding: the screen picks iconic names, which tilts it toward familiar household brands rather than the full market.
TSIE: Securitized bonds: pools of mortgages and other loans packaged into bonds that pay interest from the payments flowing in. It is an income fund built on loan pools rather than company or government debt, so its risks hinge on borrowers keeping up with their payments.
TSII: Exposure to Tesla shares paired with income-producing investments, aiming to combine growth in that one electric vehicle and energy company with regular cash payments. Everything depends on a single volatile stock, so it is a concentrated bet for committed Tesla watchers rather than a diversified holding.
TSLP: An options income strategy on a single stock, Tesla, using contracts on its shares while much of the fund sits in Treasury bills. It pays distributions from Tesla's famous volatility, with gains capped and full exposure to the stock's famous drops.
TSLW: An income strategy wrapped around one stock, Tesla, the electric car maker, using options and Treasury bills rather than simply holding shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and the trade-off is that everything rides on one famously volatile stock, with options capping some of its biggest jumps.
TSLY: A fund built around one stock, Tesla, using options so it earns income, with the rest kept in Treasury bills. It pays high income, but it gives up much of Tesla's big gains while still sharing the losses, so it can be very risky.
TSME: Small and mid-sized US companies, with industrials and technology each about a quarter, then consumer businesses and health care. It's a growth-oriented way to add smaller companies to a portfolio, and it tends to swing more than large-company funds.
TSMY: An options strategy built on one stock, Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's biggest contract chipmaker, selling call options against it to turn its price moves into monthly income. The trade-off is capped gains when the stock jumps, and income that rises and falls with market volatility.
TSNF: US-listed companies in areas like technology, health care and industrials that the Truth Social index considers part of America's next frontiers. It holds many stocks in small amounts, with none above about 1.5%, so it is spread out rather than top-heavy.
TSOL: A trust that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, directly and tracks its price. Its value moves with the price of SOL, which can swing sharply, and it holds no stocks or bonds.
TSPA: Large US companies in a mix built to resemble the S&P 500, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care next. It's a core holding, but the managers' research-driven picks mean it can lead or lag the plain index.
TSPX: A mix of mostly stocks, with technology the biggest slice at about 40%, plus some bonds and cash, chosen by active managers across small, medium and large companies. It's a flexible balanced fund that aims for growth with some cushion, so its mix can shift over time.
TSPY: Large US companies in the S&P 500, with technology near 40%, plus an options strategy that earns income from selling the right to buy those stocks. It aims for growth plus regular payouts, so it gives up some gains in strong rallies.
TSRS: Real estate investment trusts that earn most of their revenue in states that voted Republican in presidential elections, covering apartments, retail, offices and other property types. It is a politically themed property bet: the screen is about state politics, not property quality, so the mix is unusual.
TSSD: US-listed companies tied to national security: cybersecurity and software firms are about two thirds, with defense contractors and weapons makers making up the rest. It is a focused bet on defense and digital security spending, so it rises and falls with that one theme.
TSUI: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Sui, the token of the Sui blockchain network, with the holdings staked to earn extra tokens. It is a direct, concentrated bet on that one digital asset, so its price swings are extreme compared with stock or bond funds.
TSYW: Leveraged exposure to long-term US Treasury bonds through swaps on a Treasury bond fund, structured to pay distributions every week. It is a short-term trading tool rather than a buy-and-hold bond fund: leverage magnifies moves, and bond prices fall when interest rates rise.
TSYX: Leveraged daily exposure to an S&P 500 option income fund, aiming to amplify its daily move rather than match it one for one. The leverage resets every day, so it is a tool for very short holding periods and can drift badly in choppy markets.
TSYY: An income strategy built on options tied to Tesla shares, using contracts on a Tesla linked fund to collect option premiums that fund frequent payouts. It lives and dies with one very volatile stock, and its gains are capped, so it is an income play on Tesla rather than a way to own it.
TTEQ: Technology and tech-enabled companies, with technology nearly four fifths of the fund and communication next. It's a focused growth bet on the tech industry, and the managers choose the stocks, so it swings more than the broad market.
TTOP: The ten largest crypto assets globally: bitcoin, ether and the next biggest networks, reached through regulated instruments rather than direct holdings. It is the whole top of the crypto market in one fund: bitcoin dominates the weight, and the smaller coins add extra swing.
TTTT: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, known as TIPS, whose principal adjusts upward with inflation so payments keep their purchasing power. It is a defensive bond holding built for preserving buying power rather than maximizing income, and its price still moves when interest rates change.
TUA: Mostly Treasury futures and options, plus Treasury securities and cash, aimed at short-term US government bond exposure. It's a bond-market tool for managing interest rate risk, and the futures add leverage, so its price can swing more than plain short-term Treasuries.
TUG: A tactical growth fund that shifts between Nasdaq-style growth stocks, long-term Treasury bonds and cash-like bills as conditions change. The switching is the strategy: lean into growth when it works, hide in bonds or bills when it does not.
TUR: Turkish companies of all sizes, with industrials about 30% and financials, consumer staples and materials behind. It's a focused bet on a single emerging market, and it swings sharply with Turkey's economy, politics and its currency, which has been volatile.
TURF: Companies that dig up and produce raw materials: about half materials such as metals and chemicals, a third energy, and the rest farm and food resources. It's a way to add inflation-sensitive commodity exposure, and it leans on upstream producers rather than the manufacturers that use those resources.
TVAL: US stocks the manager sees as undervalued, led by technology and financials, with health care and consumer companies behind. It's a value-style core stock holding with a manager's judgment on top, and it can trail when growth stocks lead the market.
TWOX: An options design on large US companies that accelerates gains: returns aim to rise faster than the underlying stocks over each outcome period, up to a cap. It is an aggressive defined-window growth tool from iShares, where the amplification cuts both ways when the period ends in the red.
TXBC: The ten largest crypto assets excluding bitcoin: ether and the other big networks, reached through regulated instruments rather than direct coin holdings. It is the crypto market without its anchor: removing bitcoin makes it more volatile, since smaller coins swing harder in both directions.
TXCA: California municipal bonds of intermediate length, whose interest is generally free of federal and California income taxes. It holds many bonds from local issuers across the state, so it depends on California's credit health.
TXNY: New York municipal bonds of intermediate length, whose interest is generally free of federal, New York State and New York City income taxes. It holds many bonds from local issuers in the state, so it depends on New York's credit health.
TXS: Stocks of companies headquartered in Texas, from energy giants and airlines to health care and technology firms with Texas roots. It is a single-state bet: diversified across industries, but tied to Texas's economy, energy prices and business climate more than a national fund.
TXUE: Stocks of developed-market companies outside the US, led by industrials at about a quarter, then financials, technology and utilities. It's an actively managed way to add international diversification to a portfolio, with the manager choosing holdings rather than following an index.
TXUG: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US, led by technology at a bit over a third, with industrials behind. Thornburg's managers pick each stock for its growth prospects, so it is an actively run bet on foreign growers rather than an index copy.
TXXI: A blend of municipal bonds and taxable bonds of medium length, mixed to maximize what an investor keeps after taxes. At least half sits in tax-free municipals, with taxable bonds added when they pay better even after tax, a balancing act few funds attempt.
TYA: It uses futures on US Treasury bonds, with borrowed exposure, to behave like a portfolio of long-term government bonds. Long Treasuries pay steady income and often rise when stocks fall, but their prices drop sharply when interest rates climb.
TYLD: An actively managed bond fund that follows a model, shifting between bond types and ETFs depending on market signals. At the moment most of it sits in US Treasuries and cash, so it can look very different from a typical bond fund.
TYLG: Technology stocks from the S&P 500 with call options sold on only part of the position, leaving more room to grow than a full covered call fund. It splits the difference between income and growth in the tech sector.
TYYY: An income fund built around Tesla stock exposure, held mostly in cash and Treasury bills while options and other instruments provide the link to the shares. It aims to pay income frequently, but everything depends on one volatile stock, so it is a speculation tool rather than a steady holding.
UAE: Companies listed in the United Arab Emirates, led by banks and other financials at about 40%, then real estate, telecom and industrials. It's a focused bet on a single small country, so it swings more than a broad international fund and moves with Gulf region events.
UB: US Treasury bonds across maturities: the full range of the government's own debt, from shorter to longer dated issues, in one fund. It is a plain, low-risk core bond holding meant for interest income and safety, and its price still drifts down when interest rates rise.
UBEW: A weekly-reset strategy on Uber, the ride-hailing company, using swaps and shares to magnify its weekly moves a little while paying weekly distributions. The weekly reset makes it a trading tool, not a holding: in choppy weeks the magnification works against it.
UBIQ: Companies in the US e-commerce ecosystem: online retailers, marketplaces and the payment and delivery firms that online shopping runs on. It is a focused bet on shopping continuing to move online, so it leans consumer and technology heavy and swings with consumer spending.
UBND: A broad mix of bonds, mostly investment grade, from the US government, companies and mortgage lenders, with room for some riskier debt. It's meant as a core bond holding for income, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
UCBG: A mix of about nine tenths stocks and one tenth bonds, built to mimic the way a large university endowment invests. Technology is the biggest stock slice, and the goal is long-term growth with a bit of cushion from bonds, though it still falls in stock downturns.
UCON: A flexible bond fund that mixes government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, along with a small slice of preferred stock. It aims for steady income with limited sensitivity to interest rates, and the managers shift between bond types freely rather than following a fixed list.
UCRD: Mostly investment-grade corporate bonds, with room for a small amount of riskier ones. It's meant for more income than government bonds as a core bond holding, though it takes more credit risk, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
UDI: US companies that pay and grow dividends, chosen with environmental, social and governance screens applied, led by banks and health care. It aims for a high level of income today that can also grow, with the values screen shaping which payers qualify.
UDIV: US stocks across the whole market, weighted to pay a higher dividend than the broad market, with technology the biggest slice at over a third. It's a core holding for someone wanting more income, though it still looks a lot like the overall market.
UDN: A futures bet that the US dollar will fall against six major currencies, the euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc. It rises when the dollar weakens, so traders use it as a hedge or a short-term wager, and futures-based funds fit brief holding periods best.
UEVM: Companies in emerging markets such as China, India and Brazil, picked for being cheaply priced and having recent upward price momentum, with financials the biggest group at about 30%. It's a value tilted way to own developing economies, and it swings more than US stocks.
UFIV: Exclusively five-year US Treasury notes, a single point on the government yield curve in fund form. It is a building block for precise interest rate positioning: purer and simpler than broad bond funds, paying Treasury interest with moderate rate sensitivity and no corporate credit risk at all.
UFO: Companies that earn at least half their revenue from space, mostly industrials such as satellite and aerospace makers, plus technology and communications firms. It's a focused bet on one theme, so it swings more than the broad market.
UFOD: Aerospace, defense and technology companies the manager believes would benefit if governments disclose or exploit technology from unidentified anomalous phenomena. It is a speculative theme bet: industrials are over half the fund, and returns hinge on a disclosure story that may never arrive.
UFOX: Technology companies behind satellites, space launches and the networks that connect devices, with technology about three quarters and industrials about an eighth. It's a focused bet on a young, fast-changing theme, so it swings far more than the broad market.
UGA: Futures contracts on gasoline, so its price follows wholesale gasoline rather than any company. It's a short-term way to bet on fuel prices or hedge against them, and rolling contracts each month can make it drift from the price you see at the pump.
UITB: A diversified mix of US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds with medium-length maturities. A manager picks the bonds, aiming for steady income as a core holding that cushions stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
UIVM: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, led by financials and industrials, picked for being cheap and having recent price strength. It's a way to add international value stocks to a portfolio, and it can lag when growth companies lead the market.
ULTI: Options income strategies spread across a basket of mostly technology and other fast-moving US stocks, aiming to maximize regular payouts. The high income comes with capped gains on each position, and the speculative names underneath make it livelier than most income funds.
ULVM: Large US companies picked for being cheaply priced and having recent upward price momentum, with financials the biggest slice at over a quarter, then health care, industrials and technology. It works as a core stock holding with a value tilt, so it can lag when growth stocks lead.
UMI: Companies that run pipelines and storage for oil and natural gas, almost entirely in the energy sector. It's meant for high income from those businesses, which tend to pay generous payouts, but it's a focused bet that falls when energy prices or demand weaken.
UMMA: Stocks of companies outside the US that meet Islamic investing rules, with technology close to half and health care and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a way to hold international stocks that follow Shariah principles, so it screens out businesses like banks and alcohol.
UNG: Natural gas futures contracts, with the rest held in cash and short term holdings, so its price follows natural gas rather than energy company stocks. It's a short term trading tool: the price swings widely and tends to lose value over time when futures cost more than current prices.
UNHW: A weekly-reset strategy on UnitedHealth, the big US health insurer, aiming for about 1.2 times its weekly return plus weekly cash payouts. The weekly reset and slight leverage make it a short-term trading tool, far jumpier than simply holding the stock.
UNIY: A mix of US government, mortgage and corporate bonds, including some higher-risk ones, aiming for more income than a standard bond fund. It's a core bond holding that adds a little credit risk for extra yield, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
UNL: Natural gas futures spread evenly across the next twelve months of contracts, rather than betting on the nearest month alone. Spreading the contracts softens the cost of rolling futures, and the fund still rides gas prices, which swing hard with the weather.
UPGD: US mid-sized companies whose analyst ratings have recently improved, spread across industrials, consumer companies and technology. It's a momentum-style bet on upgrades, so the holdings change often and it can differ noticeably from the broad market.
UPGR: Companies building green infrastructure: renewable power producers, clean technology manufacturers and the industrial firms installing them, picked against sustainability criteria. Industrials are about half the fund, so it is a focused bet on the energy transition, and it can lag badly when clean energy falls out of favor.
UPSD: Large US companies plus options positioned to add extra upside when the market rises, rather than to protect against falls. It is a growth-leaning core holding with a kicker: the options can amplify good stretches, and they can also expire worthless in flat markets.
URA: Uranium miners and nuclear power businesses, with energy companies about 60% and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a focused bet on nuclear energy, so its price swings widely with uranium prices and energy policy, far more than the broad market.
URAN: Uranium miners and nuclear industry companies: fuel producers at about half, plus the utilities and industrial firms that run and build reactors. It is a focused bet on nuclear power's comeback, and the miners make it far more volatile than a utility fund despite the shared theme.
URNJ: Smaller companies that mine, explore for or produce uranium, the fuel for nuclear power plants, nearly all of them in energy. It's a narrow bet on the nuclear fuel industry, so it can swing sharply with uranium prices and shifting views on nuclear energy.
URNM: Companies that mine uranium or own physical uranium, the fuel for nuclear power. It's a focused bet on one commodity and the nuclear energy theme, so it can swing wildly with uranium prices and energy policy.
URTH: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries around the world, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and health care behind. It's a one-fund core holding for global stocks, though most of its money sits in US companies.
USAF: A multi-asset mix of property trusts, investment grade bonds, gold trusts and stocks from the US and abroad. It spreads money across assets that behave differently, aiming for balance rather than maximum growth, and gold gives it an inflation-sensitive streak.
USAI: US and Canadian energy infrastructure companies, all of them: pipeline, storage and gas processing businesses that charge fees to move oil and gas around. It is an income-oriented bet on energy plumbing rather than fuel prices, since these firms earn from volume, not from what a barrel costs.
USCA: Large US companies, with technology over two fifths, tilted toward firms with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans. It's a core stock holding with an environmental screen, so it looks much like the broad market but with fewer fossil fuel companies.
USCI: Futures contracts on a broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, with the fund's cash held in safe short-term assets. It's a hedge against rising prices and a way to diversify, but it swings with commodity prices and pays no interest or dividends.
USCL: Large US companies, with technology making up over two fifths and communication and health care next. It's a core stock holding that tilts toward firms with lower carbon emissions and better climate plans, so its mix differs a bit from the broad market.
USDU: Mostly cash and short-term bonds, paired with positions that gain when the US dollar rises against major world currencies. It's used as a hedge for investors worried about a stronger dollar, and it loses value when the dollar weakens.
USDX: Mostly short-term money market holdings, topped with an ultra-short-term options strategy meant to earn extra income. It aims for a bit more yield than cash, though the options can lose money and it's not as safe as a plain money market fund.
USE: An actively managed fund that trades oil, petroleum and natural gas futures, aiming to profit from the relationship between different contracts rather than simply betting on higher prices. Most of the money is held in Treasuries and cash as backing for the futures.
USEW: Large US companies, with each held in about equal amounts instead of by size, spread across technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a core stock holding that gives smaller giants more say than usual, so it behaves differently from funds dominated by a few big names.
USFE: US companies bought with First Eagle's value discipline, spread across health care, technology, media and materials. The managers hunt for solid businesses trading below their worth and hold patiently, aiming to grow money over years while avoiding big losses.
USFI: US bonds of many kinds, government, mortgage and corporate, actively shifted by Brandywine's managers as they hunt for value across the bond market. It is a core-style bond holding with an active hand on the mix, so it will not behave exactly like a plain index bond fund.
USFR: US Treasury bonds whose interest payments reset with short-term rates. It's a low-risk place to park cash for income, and because the rate adjusts, its price barely drops when rates rise, though income falls when rates fall.
USG: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to the price of gold through gold futures and warrants held in a subsidiary, and also aims to add income. The cash and futures positions shown are there to support the gold exposure, not a stock portfolio.
USHY: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, spread across many issuers. It's meant for higher income than safer bonds, but the companies are likelier to default, so it tends to fall alongside stocks in a downturn.
USIG: US corporate bonds from financially solid companies, rated investment grade, with nearly everything in bonds. It's meant for steady interest income with a bit more yield than Treasuries, though its price drops when interest rates rise, and it can lose value if companies' finances weaken.
USIN: US Treasury bonds with seven to ten years left before they mature, held in equal rungs across those years like a ladder. The ladder design spreads interest-rate risk, giving steady government income with moderate price swings when rates move.
USL: Crude oil futures spread evenly across the next twelve months of contracts, rather than betting everything on the nearest month's price. Spreading the contracts softens the cost of rolling futures each month, though it still moves with oil prices and is a trading tool, not a long term holding.
USLN: Floating rate bank loans made to below-investment-grade companies, drawn broadly from the US leveraged loan market. The interest resets with market rates, so the fund suits income seekers who worry about rising rates, though the borrowers' weaker credit means losses when defaults pick up.
USMC: The very largest US companies, with technology about 44% and financials, communication and health care behind it. It's a core holding focused on giants, so it moves with the overall US economy but leaves out smaller companies and leans heavily on tech.
USMD: US technology companies chosen for their importance to American innovation, security and industrial strength, with technology at about two-thirds and industrials making up most of the rest. It is an actively managed growth bet with a patriotic screen, so it leans into defense-adjacent and strategic tech rather than owning the whole sector.
USMF: Mid-sized US companies, with technology the largest slice at about a third, chosen using several traits at once such as value, quality and momentum. It's a rules-based core stock holding that leans toward stronger-looking companies than a plain mid-cap fund.
