USMV: Large US stocks picked and weighted to swing less than the overall market, with technology, health care and financials leading. It's built for a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
USNG: An actively managed fund of US companies tied to natural gas infrastructure, such as pipelines and power equipment. Around 80% is in energy stocks, with Williams, Kinder Morgan and Solaris Energy Infrastructure among the biggest, so it is a narrow bet on one industry.
USNZ: Large and mid-sized US companies, nearly half in technology, chosen to line up with climate goals by favoring those with lower carbon emissions. It can serve as a core stock holding for climate-minded investors, though it is heavier in tech than the broad market.
USO: Futures contracts on crude oil, held alongside cash and short-term bonds that back them. It's a short-term way to bet on oil prices, but it can drift away from the oil price over time because it must keep swapping expiring contracts for new ones.
USOI: A note from a bank that pays income tied to crude oil prices through a covered call strategy, meaning it sells away some of oil's upside in return for payments. It suits income seekers, but it's a bank-issued note, so it carries the bank's credit risk and can lose value when oil falls.
USOY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income by selling options tied to the United States Oil Fund, which tracks crude oil prices. Selling those options caps how much it can gain if oil rises, and most of its assets sit in Treasury bills as backing.
USPX: The whole US stock market weighted by company size, with technology about two fifths, then financials, communication and health care. It's built to be a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, though it's top-heavy in a few giant tech firms.
USRT: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, offices, shopping centers and storage and pass rental income to shareholders, excluding mortgage and infrastructure REITs. It's for income and real estate exposure, though it tends to fall when interest rates rise.
USSE: A concentrated group of large US companies chosen by a manager, with technology close to half, followed by financials, communication and industrials. It's a core-style stock holding aimed at growth, but fewer stocks and so much tech mean it can swing more than the market.
USSG: Large and mid-sized US companies screened for strong environmental, social and governance records, so some industries such as tobacco and weapons are left out, with technology close to 40%. It's a core stock holding with an ethical filter.
USSH: US Treasury bonds laddered across one to three year maturities, so some bonds are always near maturity and reinvesting at current rates. It is a conservative income holding for money needed soon, with minimal credit risk and modest price movement when interest rates shift.
USTB: Mostly short-term US bonds, with some cash and a bit of preferred stock. A manager picks mainly high-quality debt for steady income with modest price swings, which makes it a calmer cushion than longer-term bonds, though it can still dip when interest rates jump.
USVM: Small and mid-size US companies that look cheap and have recent price strength, led by financials, industrials and health care. It's a tilt for long-term growth that can swing more than the broad market, and it may lag when large companies lead.
USVN: A single US government bond: the newest seven-year Treasury note, replaced with a fresh one as new notes are issued. It gives precise exposure to medium-term interest rates, rising when rates fall and dropping when they rise, with the safety of government backing.
USXF: Large and mid-sized US companies with good environmental and social ratings, with fossil fuel companies removed. Technology is more than half of it, so it's a growth leaning core holding for values minded investors, and it moves with tech more than the broad market does.
UTEN: A single US Treasury note with about ten years left until it matures. It's a plain government-backed bond holding that pays steady interest, and its price drops when interest rates rise by more than a short-term Treasury fund's would.
UTES: Electric, gas and water utilities and similar companies, all in the utility sector. It's meant for dividend income and a steadier ride, since people pay these bills in any economy, but it's a one-sector bet whose prices tend to drop when interest rates rise.
UTHY: A single type of bond, US Treasuries that mature in about 30 years. It's a government-backed holding for income and a cushion when stocks drop, but its price swings a lot, since long-term bonds fall sharply when interest rates rise.
UTRE: A single Treasury note, the current 3-year US Treasury, followed through an ICE index. It holds basically one bond at a time and rolls to the new one, so it is a simple way to hold government debt with a few years' maturity.
UTWO: A single type of holding: the most recently issued 2-year US Treasury note. It's meant as a very safe place for money for a short while, earning steady interest, and because the maturity is short its price barely moves when interest rates change.
UTWY: US Treasury bonds with about 20 years left until maturity, held almost entirely in a small number of long government bonds. Because the bonds are so long, the price moves a lot when interest rates change, though credit risk is minimal.
UUP: Futures that rise when the US dollar gains against a basket of major currencies like the euro and yen, with the rest in cash and Treasury bills. It's a hedge or a bet on the dollar, so it tends to do well when the dollar strengthens and poorly when it weakens.
UUPP: Collateralized loan obligations, bundles of loans to companies, bought across their different risk layers rather than only the safest top slice. Reaching down the layers raises the income, and the managers choose how much risk to take as credit conditions change.
UX: Uranium exposure in two forms: derivatives tied to the price of uranium itself, plus shares of companies that mine it and trusts that hold it. It is a focused bet on nuclear fuel, an extremely jumpy market driven by energy politics and reactor demand.
UXAP: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to accelerate gains without an upside cap over a one-year period ending each April. It is built for strong bull markets, and it carries full exposure to losses when the market falls instead.
UXJA: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to try to deliver a multiple of the index's gains over a set one-year period that starts each January. It has no cap on those gains, but it also gives up some protection, so you can lose money if the market falls.
UXJL: Options built to amplify the US stock market's gains over a one-year period starting in July, with no fixed cap on the boosted upside. The amplification cuts both ways, so falls are not softly cushioned, making it an aggressive, short-horizon bet rather than a core holding.
UXOC: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to accelerate gains without an upside cap over a one-year period ending each October. It is built for strong bull markets, and it carries full exposure to losses when the market falls instead.
VABS: Investment-grade bonds backed by pooled loans and property: home mortgages, commercial property loans and asset-backed securities such as auto loan bundles, all actively picked. It aims for steady income with a different flavor of risk than ordinary corporate or government bonds.
VAIC: Autocallable notes tied to a basket of 500 large US stocks, using a conservative version of the structure that pays income and can end early. It is structured income with a cautious setting: returns depend on the notes' terms and the market staying above set levels, not on owning the stocks.
VAIE: Exposure to synthetic autocallable notes tied to large US stocks, instruments that pay regular income while stocks behave and can be called away early when they rise. The catch sits underneath: if the stocks fall past a set barrier, losses can arrive suddenly and run deep.
VALQ: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheap and high in quality, with technology the biggest slice at over a quarter, then health care, consumer and staples firms. It's a value-tilted core stock holding, and it may trail when expensive growth stocks lead.
VAMO: US stocks that are both cheap and trending upward, currently heavy in energy refiners and financial firms, with the ability to hedge the whole portfolio when trends break down. That hedge, which can leave it holding mostly cash, sets it apart from always-invested value funds.
VAVX: A single-cryptocurrency trust holding AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain network, valued daily against a published benchmark rate. It gives brokerage-account access to that one digital asset without a crypto wallet, and it swings as sharply as the token itself.
VAW: US materials companies such as chemical makers, miners and producers of construction materials and packaging. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it tends to rise and fall with the economy and commodity prices, and it has almost no tech or health care.
VB: Small US companies spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It is used to add growth potential beyond large companies, but small firms are shakier, so it swings more than the broad market and can lag when investors favor big, stable names.
VBCA: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2027, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCB: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2028, held almost entirely in investment-grade debt. It's meant for steady interest income with a known end date, so its price swings fade as 2028 nears, though it still falls when interest rates rise.
VBCC: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2029, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCD: Investment grade US corporate bonds that mature in 2030, held until the fund ends. It holds many bonds, with T-Mobile the biggest at about 1%, so it behaves more like one bond than a fund that keeps rolling.
VBCE: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2031, held like a single long dated company bond that pays interest along the way and returns principal at the end. It suits savers matching a future expense, and its price still moves with interest rates until the date nears.
VBCF: Bonds from large companies, banks, phone and tech firms among them, all chosen to come due around 2032, when the fund winds down. Knowing the end date lets investors line it up with a future spending goal, like a tuition or retirement bill.
VBCG: Corporate bonds from banks, drugmakers, technology firms and other big issuers that mature around 2033, when the fund itself is set to end. It works much like a single bond with a target end date: collect interest, then principal comes back as bonds mature.
VBCH: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature around 2034, tracking a Vanguard target maturity index. Because the bonds end near the same date, it behaves a bit like a single bond, with large banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America among the borrowers.
VBCI: Corporate bonds from big technology, banking and media issuers that mature around 2035, when the fund itself is set to end. It works much like a single bond with a target end date: collect interest, then principal comes back as bonds mature.
VBCJ: Corporate bonds maturing in 2036, in a Vanguard target maturity fund that will wind down as that year arrives. It works as a single rung for a known future goal, paying company bond interest while its sensitivity to interest rates steadily fades toward the end date.
VBIL: Very short US Treasury bills that mature within three months, backed by the federal government. It's a place to park cash for a short time while earning interest, and because the bills mature so fast, its price barely moves when rates change.
VBK: Small US companies expected to grow fast, led by technology at about 30 percent, with health care and industrials at roughly a fifth each. It's for long-term growth, but small companies swing more than large ones, so expect bigger ups and downs.
VBNB: A single crypto asset, BNB, the token of the BNB Chain network, held directly by the trust. It is a pure price bet on one coin: there is no diversification and no income, so it swings with BNB alone and can move violently.
VBND: A flexible mix of US bonds, including government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, managed actively. It's meant for income with some growth potential as a core bond holding, and because the managers choose bonds themselves, results can differ from a standard bond index.
VBR: Small US value stocks, meaning smaller companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials, industrials and consumer companies. It aims for higher long-run growth than large companies, but it swings more than the broad market and can lag for years.
VCEB: Investment-grade US corporate bonds, screened to favor companies with better environmental, social and governance records. It's meant for steady interest income with less risk than stocks, though bond prices drop when interest rates rise and it can slip when the economy weakens.
VCHY: High yield corporate bonds from hundreds of US borrowers, cruise lines, satellite firms, health care companies and more, each capped so no issuer dominates. It is a plain, broad junk bond holding built for income, with the usual warning that these borrowers default more often in recessions.
VCIT: Bonds from investment-grade US companies that mature in five to ten years. It is meant for more income than government bonds, and it suits the bond part of a portfolio, but it can lose value if interest rates rise or the economy weakens.
VCLN: Clean energy companies split fairly evenly between industrial manufacturers and utilities, with technology firms making up most of the rest. It covers the whole green power chain, from equipment makers to the utilities selling solar and wind electricity, and swings with energy policy.
VCLT: Investment-grade bonds from US corporations that mature in more than 10 years. It's meant for higher interest income than government bonds, but its price drops sharply when interest rates rise, and it can fall in a recession if companies struggle.
VCOB: Core US bonds actively managed: Treasuries, government mortgage bonds and corporate debt, chosen for a mix of interest income and price gains. Active management sets it apart from index bond funds, with managers shifting maturities and credit as they hunt for value.
VCR: Retailers, carmakers, restaurants, hotels, home builders and online shopping companies, all businesses that people buy more from when they feel flush. It's a focused bet on consumer spending, so it tends to do well in good economies and fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
VCRB: A broad mix of bonds, including US Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, of various lengths and credit quality. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, and an active manager can lean toward bonds that look attractive.
VCRM: Municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and local agencies, with interest free from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income and mostly appeals to people in higher tax brackets, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
VCSH: Investment-grade bonds from companies that mature in one to five years, spread across industrial, utility and financial borrowers. It aims for steady income with smaller price swings than longer bonds, though it pays a bit less than long-term corporate debt.
VDC: Companies that sell everyday necessities, such as food, drinks, household products and groceries, across the US. It's a focused bet on one industry, often used as a defensive holding because people keep buying these items in a downturn, though it can trail in strong rallies.
VDE: US oil, gas and fuel companies of all sizes, from producers to refiners and pipeline operators. It's a focused bet on the energy sector, so it rises and falls with oil prices and swings far more than the broad market.
VDG: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US: Europe, Japan, Canada, Australia and their peers, led by banks, technology and industrial firms screened for growth traits. It offers the growth half of foreign investing, complementing value funds abroad, with currency swings included.
VDI: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, spread across at least eight countries, with financial firms the biggest slice at over two fifths. It hunts income abroad, so currency swings add to the ups and downs foreign stocks already bring.
VDIG: Large US companies chosen by Wellington managers for their record and prospects of growing dividends, spread across technology, finance and health care. It is a core style stock holding aiming for income that rises over time plus steady growth, favoring established payers over the fastest growers.
VDV: Value companies in developed markets outside the US: the cheaper, slower growing names across Europe, Japan and peers, led by banks, industrials and energy. It offers the value half of foreign investing, often with higher dividends, and trails when growth stocks abroad are in fashion.
VEA: Companies in developed countries outside the US, such as in Europe and Japan, led by financials, industrials and technology. It is a way to add international stocks to a portfolio, and it leaves out emerging markets, so it is steadier than a fund that includes them.
VEEM: Emerging-market companies that stock analysts are most positive about, led by technology at close to half the fund. It tilts the usual emerging-market mix toward analyst favorites, adding their judgment to markets already known for sharp swings.
VEFA: Developed-market companies outside the US that stock analysts are most upbeat about, led by banks at a bit over a quarter. It tilts a standard international portfolio toward Wall Street's favorite names, so it leans on analyst opinion as its stock picker.
VEGA: A global mix of stock, bond and commodity funds with covered call options sold against the holdings, a strategy called buy-write. The option premiums add income and cushion small declines, at the cost of capping gains, making it a steadier, income-leaning way to hold world markets.
VEGI: Companies that supply the farming world, such as makers of equipment, fertilizer and seeds, plus food producers, spread across industrials, consumer staples and materials. It's a focused bet on agriculture, so its results depend on crop prices and farm demand, and it swings more than the broad market.
VEGN: Large US companies, with technology about two thirds of the fund, chosen because they avoid animal-based products and meet vegan-friendly rules. It's a growth-leaning stock holding with a values angle, and it has far more tech than the broad market, so it swings more.
VEGX: Large companies outside the United States screened to exclude animal exploitation: no meat, dairy, animal testing or other animal-derived businesses. It is a values-based foreign holding led by technology and industrials: the vegan screen removes whole industries, so it will not mirror a plain international fund.
VEM: Dividend-paying companies from emerging markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, picked by an active manager. It is top-heavy in tech, with Taiwan Semiconductor alone about 16% and Samsung and SK Hynix adding roughly another 16%.
VEMY: High yield bonds tied to emerging market countries, issued by governments and companies that pay extra interest to compensate for weaker credit. The yield is the draw, and the risks are real: currency swings, politics and defaults all hit harder here than in rich country bonds.
VETZ: Mostly mortgage-backed bonds guaranteed by US government agencies like Ginnie Mae, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It aims for steady income with high credit quality, and its twist is a tie to veterans' causes, though prices can still fall when interest rates rise.
VEU: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries, led by financials and technology with industrials next. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it holds no US companies, so it moves differently from American markets.
VEXC: Large and mid-sized companies in developing countries, leaving out China. Technology is the biggest slice at over two fifths, followed by financials, so it's a way to add emerging markets without China's heavy weight, and it swings more than US stock funds.
VFH: US financial companies of all sizes, including banks, insurers, asset managers and payment firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market and is sensitive to interest rates and the health of the economy.
VFLO: US mid-sized companies chosen for producing lots of spare cash after expenses, with technology, energy and health care the biggest groups. It's a value-style stock fund, and the tilt toward energy means it can behave differently from the broad market.
VFMF: US stocks screened for cheap prices, strong profits and recent momentum, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer companies. It's a core stock holding with a factor tilt, so it can behave differently from the market and trail when growth stocks lead.
VFMO: US stocks that have recently been rising fastest, spread across technology, industrials, health care and energy. It's meant for growth beyond the broad market, but the mix shifts as winners change, and momentum can reverse quickly when the market turns.
VFMV: US stocks picked because they tend to swing less than the market, with technology about 30% and health care, communication and consumer staples each near a tenth. It aims for a smoother ride, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
VFQY: Mid-sized US companies with strong profits and healthy finances, spread across technology, financials, industrials and consumer companies. It's meant as growth-minded core stock exposure, and because it picks quality traits it may trail the market when low-quality stocks rally.
VFVA: US stocks that look cheap compared with their fundamentals, led by financials at about a quarter, then health care, consumer companies and technology. It's a value-style holding for stock investors, and it can trail the market for long stretches when growth companies are the ones leading.
VGHY: Corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, often called junk bonds, chosen by an active manager. It's built for higher income than regular bonds, and it tends to fall along with stocks in downturns rather than cushioning them.
VGIT: US Treasury bonds that mature in three to ten years, backed by the federal government. It's meant as a cushion against stock market drops, with moderate price swings, though its price falls when interest rates rise.
VGK: Companies across Europe, led by financials and industrials, then health care. It adds European exposure to a US-heavy portfolio, and it has far less technology than US funds, while its results also depend on the euro and pound versus the dollar.
VGLT: US Treasury bonds that mature in more than ten years, all backed by the government. It's meant as a cushion when stocks fall, but its price swings a lot with interest rates, dropping sharply when they rise.
VGMS: Bonds from several parts of the bond market, such as corporate, government and higher-yielding debt, picked by an active manager. It aims to deliver steady income from many sources, though prices fall when interest rates rise and riskier bonds can slip in a downturn.
VGRO: Large US companies picked for above-average growth, with technology close to half the fund and media and internet firms behind. Silvant's managers hunt durable growers, so it leans into the market's strongest earners and swings more than a plain large-company fund.
VGSH: US Treasury bonds that come due in one to three years, backed by the federal government. It's a low-risk place for cash you may need soon, with small price swings, though it pays less than longer bonds.
VGSR: Real estate companies and real estate investment trusts around the world, all in the property sector. It's meant for income and diversification from property, with a screen for sustainability, and it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
VGT: US technology companies of all sizes, including software makers, chip companies and computer hardware. It is a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it leaves out most internet and social media companies, which are classed in other sectors.
VGTX: Technology companies plus options written on them, a combination built to turn the tech sector's movement into income as well as growth. The options trade some upside for payouts, so it behaves like a tech fund with the sharpest rallies trimmed, and tech's usual swings still apply.
VGVT: US government bonds and government-backed mortgage bonds of all maturities, actively managed by Vanguard's bond team. It aims to be a safe, steady core bond holding, with the managers shifting maturities as they judge where rates are heading.
VHT: US health care companies of all sizes, such as drugmakers, medical device makers, insurers and biotech firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, and it tends to hold up better than most in a downturn but can swing when drug pricing or regulation news hits.
VIDI: Stocks from outside the US, spread across industrials, financials, technology and consumer companies. It's meant as international diversification for a US-heavy portfolio, and it picks companies by a rules-based strategy aimed at value, so it leans toward cheaper stocks rather than just the biggest ones.
VIG: Large US companies with a record of raising their dividends year after year, spread across technology, financials, health care and industrials. It aims for steady growth with modest income, and it leaves out the highest yielders, so it pays less than dedicated income funds.
VIGI: Large companies outside the US that have a record of growing their dividends, led by financials, industrials, technology and health care. It's meant for steady growth with some income, and it leaves out the highest-yielding stocks, so it may pay less than other dividend funds.
VIOG: Smaller US companies with faster growth, spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials. It's meant for growth in the small-company part of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds and can trail when investors favor big, stable names.
VIOO: Smaller US companies, spread across financials, technology, industrials and consumer businesses, screened to include only those that are profitable. It's a way to add growth potential from small companies to a portfolio, and the profit screen means it leaves out unprofitable firms, though it still swings more than large-company funds.
VIOV: Small US companies that look cheap compared to their size, with financials the largest group, followed by consumer, technology and industrial companies. It's a value tilt for long-term growth, and small companies can swing more than large ones.
VIS: US industrial companies of all sizes, such as aerospace and defense firms, machinery makers, airlines and railroads. It's a focused bet on one industry tied to economic growth, so it tends to do well when the economy is strong and drop when it weakens.
VLU: US stocks of all sizes, weighted toward companies that look cheaper, with technology, financials and health care leading. It's a value-tilted core holding, and it can trail growth-driven markets since it holds fewer of the priciest stocks than the usual index.
VLUE: US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings, sales and assets, though technology still makes up nearly half. It's built as a value-leaning core holding, and it can trail growth stocks in strong rallies while holding up better when expensive stocks fall.
VMAX: Large US companies that look cheap for their earnings and assets, led by banks at about a third of the fund. It is a classic value holding: profitable, out-of-favor big names that can lag for stretches when growth stocks are fashionable.
VMBS: Bonds backed by pools of home loans, guaranteed by US government agencies such as Ginnie Mae, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It's meant for steady income with high credit quality, but homeowners paying off mortgages early when rates fall can cut the income, and prices drop when rates rise.
VMHY: High yield municipal bonds: below-investment-grade and unrated debt from cities, hospitals and projects paying the richest tax-exempt interest available. It is the aggressive end of tax-free income, and the weaker credits mean bigger falls than quality muni funds when investors worry about defaults.
VMSB: A mix of bonds from several parts of the bond market, such as corporate, government and higher-yielding debt, chosen by an active manager. It aims for a high level of income with some growth on the side, though bond prices fall when interest rates rise and riskier bonds can stumble in a downturn.
VMSD: Short-duration municipal bonds from states, counties and cities across the US, paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it is a cautious tax-free income holding, a step up in yield from a money market fund for taxed investors.
VNAM: Vietnamese companies across property, banking, industry and consumer goods, the whole young stock market of a fast-growing frontier economy. One giant conglomerate dominates the market's value, so the fund leans heavily on it, and frontier markets bring extra political and currency risk.
VNIE: An actively managed fund of companies outside the US, picked by Vontobel for quality and growth in at least three countries. Its biggest positions include Taiwan Semiconductor, Tokyo Electron and ASML, each around 6% to 7%, and it is mixed across technology, industrials and financials.
VNLA: A mix of short-term, mostly investment-grade bonds that mature soon, plus a bit of cash. It's meant to earn more than cash while staying steady, and since the bonds are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
VNM: Stocks of Vietnamese companies, with financials about a third, then real estate, consumer staples and industrials. It's a focused bet on a single small emerging economy, so it swings a lot and depends heavily on Vietnam's banks and property.
VNQ: Real estate companies, mostly trusts that own offices, apartments, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers. It adds property exposure and income to a portfolio, but it drops when interest rates rise.
VNQI: Real estate companies from outside the US, such as property owners and developers in Europe, Asia and elsewhere, almost all in real estate. It's a way to add global property income, and its value moves with interest rates and with foreign currencies against the dollar.
VNSE: A select, concentrated portfolio of mostly mid and large companies chosen by Vaughan Nelson's fundamental research, led by technology, with energy and industry behind. Few holdings means each pick matters, and the managers hold for years rather than trade.
VO: Mid-sized US companies, bigger than small firms but smaller than the giants, spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care. It offers more growth potential than large companies with less risk than small ones, and it has much less tech than a large-company fund.
VOE: Mid-sized US companies that look cheaply priced, spread across financials, energy, industrials and utilities. It leans to steady, older industries rather than tech, so it can do better when growth stocks stall but lag when they lead.
VOLT: Companies tied to electrification, mostly industrials such as electrical equipment, plus utilities, technology and energy firms. It's a themed growth bet on the shift to electric power, so it swings more than the broad market and has little in typical consumer stocks.
VONE: Nearly the whole US stock market's large companies in one fund, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care behind. It's a core holding that moves with the overall US economy, and includes more mid-sized names than a pure large-company fund.
VONG: Large US growth companies, with technology making up well over half and communication services about a sixth. It's built for growth investors who want big-company exposure, though with so much in tech it can swing more than the broad market.
VONV: Large US companies that look cheap relative to their earnings and assets, led by technology, financials and health care. It's a core value holding that can trail when fast-growing stocks drive the market and tends to hold up better when they falter.
VOO: Hundreds of the largest US companies, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care making up much of the rest. It is a simple core holding that moves with the big-company US market, and it is heavily weighted toward a handful of tech leaders.
VOOB: S&P 500 exposure with an options shield designed to protect more of the downside than a typical buffer, while keeping a share of the upside. It is a defensive core holding from a newer family of protection funds: the shield's exact terms, set by its options, decide how it behaves in a crash.
VOOG: The faster-growing half of the S&P 500, with technology making up over half the fund, followed by communication, financials and consumer companies. It's built for growth, so it tends to rise more in strong markets and fall harder in downturns than the full index.
VOOV: The cheaper-priced half of the S&P 500's large companies, with technology the biggest slice, then financials, health care and industrials. It's a value tilt on a core US holding, and it can lag when expensive growth stocks lead.
VOOY: Large US companies combined with options on large-cap stocks and indexes, built to turn part of the market's movement into income. It is an income-first equity holding: the options add regular payouts but limit how much it gains in strong rallies.
VOT: Mid-sized US companies expected to grow faster than average, led by technology and industrials, with consumer and health care firms behind. It's for long-term growth, and it swings more than a large company fund.
VOTE: US large companies in a mix resembling the S&P 500, with technology about 40% and financials, communication and health care behind it. It works as a core stock holding, and its manager votes shares on company issues to push for change, not just hold them.
VOX: Phone and cable companies, streaming services, social media and online search businesses, and media and entertainment firms, nearly all in the communication sector. It's a focused bet on one corner of the market, and a few giant internet companies dominate it, so it swings more than the broad market.
VOXP: Large US companies across every major industry, currently led by the giant technology and internet names that dominate the market. It works as a core-style stock holding, and because its top names are the market's biggest, it will move much like the broad US market itself.
VPC: Listed business development companies and closed-end funds that lend to private midsize businesses, giving ordinary investors a route into private credit. It is built for high income from those lenders' dividends, and it adds stock market trading swings on top of the underlying loan risks.
VPFF: US preferred shares and hybrid securities, mostly from banks, utilities and health care issuers, which pay fixed dividends like bonds but sit lower in line than debt. It is an actively managed income holding: payouts run higher than bonds, with more price risk if issuers wobble.
VPL: Companies from developed Pacific countries, mainly Japan, Australia, South Korea and Hong Kong, with technology at about 28% and financials a fifth. It's a way to add Asia-Pacific exposure to a portfolio, and it moves with those currencies and economies, not the US.
VPLS: A broad mix of bonds across US government, corporate, mortgage and some emerging market debt, all in US dollars. It's meant as a core bond holding for steady income and a cushion for stocks, with a bit of extra yield from riskier bonds, though prices drop when rates rise.
VPU: Electric, gas and water utility companies across the US, which sell essential services and tend to pay steady dividends. It's a focused bet on one industry, often used for income and stability, but its prices tend to drop when interest rates rise.
VPX: An actively managed US stock fund that shifts its mix of sectors depending on where it thinks we are in the economic cycle. About 20% sits in a broad US market fund, and the rest is in stocks such as Broadcom, NVIDIA and ExxonMobil.
VRAI: Income from real assets: oil and gas producers, property trusts, utilities and pipelines, mostly US-listed. It aims for dividends and inflation resilience from hard-asset businesses, and energy prices drive much of its movement.
VRIG: Investment-grade bonds whose interest payments reset as rates change, rather than staying fixed. It's meant as a low-risk place for income, and because payments adjust, its price barely drops when interest rates rise.
VRP: Preferred stocks and bonds from banks, insurers and utilities whose payouts adjust with interest rates. It's built for income, and because payouts float, its price holds up better than fixed-rate preferred funds when rates rise, but it can still drop in a credit scare.
VSDA: US companies with a record of raising their dividends, led by consumer staples at about a third and financials, industrials and health care next. It's meant for growing income and steadier holdings, though it can trail in fast tech rallies.
VSDB: High quality short-term bonds, a blend of corporate debt, Treasuries and mortgage- or asset-backed bonds. It's meant for steady income and low risk, and since maturities are short, its price moves far less than regular bond funds when interest rates change.
VSDM: Short-term bonds from US states, cities and agencies whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income with a steadier price, since short maturities mean it moves far less than longer municipal bonds when interest rates change.
VSGX: Large companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US, with financials and technology each over a quarter, screened to leave out companies that fall short on environmental and social standards. It's a way to diversify abroad while following those values.
VSHY: High yield corporate bonds with short maturities, so the higher interest of below-investment-grade debt comes with less sensitivity to interest rate moves. It is an income holding for investors who want junk bond yields but a somewhat steadier ride, though defaults remain the main risk in downturns.
VSLU: Large US companies chosen by a valuation formula that looks for cash-generating firms at fair prices, with technology around 40%. It's a core large-company holding with a value-minded twist, though it ends up heavy in tech like the broad market.
VSMV: US large companies selected using several measures to have lower swings than the market, with technology about 40 percent, then consumer staples and health care. It aims for a smoother ride in sell-offs, but it probably trails in strong rallies.
VSOL: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Solana, the token known as SOL, priced daily against a published benchmark rate. It lets investors hold that one digital asset in a brokerage account without a crypto wallet, and it swings as sharply as the underlying token does.
VSS: Small and mid-sized companies from developed and emerging countries outside the US, with industrials about a fifth and technology, materials and financials following. It's a way to add smaller international companies to a portfolio, and it can swing more than funds of big foreign firms.
VT: Stocks from companies all over the world, both developed and emerging countries, with technology about a third and financials, industrials and health care next. It is a whole-world core holding in one fund, with roughly six tenths of it in the US.
VTC: Investment-grade bonds issued by US companies across many industries, held through a handful of Vanguard bond funds. It's meant for steady interest income that is higher than Treasuries, and its price drops when interest rates rise or when companies' credit worsens.
VTEB: Bonds issued by states, cities and local agencies, with interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It's meant for steady, tax-free income in a regular taxable account, and its price drops when interest rates rise.
VTEC: Municipal bonds issued by California governments and agencies, mostly investment grade with medium maturities. It's for income that is generally free of federal and California income taxes, so it suits high earners in the state, but it depends on one state's finances.
VTEI: Investment-grade US municipal bonds with maturities of up to 20 years, whose interest is free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-efficient income for people in higher brackets, and it's a middle-ground choice whose price drops when interest rates rise.
VTEL: Investment-grade bonds from US states and cities that mature in more than ten years, with interest generally free of federal income tax. It's meant for tax-free income for people in higher tax brackets, and its price swings more than shorter bonds when interest rates change.
VTES: Short-term municipal bonds from state and local governments across the US, with a little cash, paying income that is generally free of federal tax. It's for a low-risk tax-friendly place to hold money, and because the bonds mature soon, its price moves very little.
VTG: Nearly the whole market of US Treasury bonds, from short to long maturities. It's a very safe holding for steady income and as a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
VTHR: Nearly the entire US stock market, from giants to small companies, with technology the largest slice at almost 40%. It's a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and it adds small companies that the S&P 500 leaves out.
VTI: Nearly every publicly traded US company, from giants to small firms, with technology around a third and financials and health care next. It works as a one-fund core holding for US stocks, and because it includes small companies it is slightly broader than an S&P 500 fund.
VTIP: US Treasury bonds that adjust their value with inflation and mature in under five years. It is meant to protect buying power while holding steady, and its price moves little, though its income falls when inflation cools.
VTP: US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, spread across short to long maturities. It's meant to protect buying power in a portfolio, and its price can still drop when interest rates rise, though it tends to hold up better when inflation picks up.
VTV: Large US value stocks, meaning companies priced cheaply relative to their size, led by financials and health care with technology and industrials next. It leans toward established, steadier businesses, and it has far less tech than the broad market, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
VTWG: Small US companies with faster expected growth, led by health care at about a third and technology at over a fifth. It's a growth bet on small companies, so it swings more than the broad market, and many of its holdings are biotech firms not yet profitable.
VTWO: Roughly 2,000 small US companies, with health care about a fifth, financials just under that, and technology and industrials making up much of the rest. It's a way to add growth potential to a portfolio, but small companies swing more than large ones and can fall harder in downturns.
VTWV: Small US companies priced cheaply compared to their earnings and assets, led by financials at about a quarter, then industrials, health care and real estate. It's a value tilt for diversifying beyond big names, and it tends to swing more than large company funds.
VUG: Large US growth companies, meaning firms expected to expand faster than average, with technology about 60 percent and communication and consumer companies next. It is built for long-term growth, but it is concentrated in tech and tends to fall harder than the broad market in downturns.
VUS: US companies that pay dividends, led by technology at about two fifths, with finance, health care and property firms behind. It aims for income plus growth from established payers, and its big tech weight makes it livelier than old-style dividend funds.
VUSE: Large US companies chosen by a rules-based score, with technology about 40 percent, then financials, health care and communication. It's a core stock holding with a tilt toward technology, so it can swing more than the broad market.
VUSG: Large and mid-sized US growth companies picked actively by Wellington, the firm behind Vanguard's oldest fund, with technology over half the portfolio. It aims to beat plain growth indexes through stock picking, so it can pull ahead or fall behind its benchmarks for stretches.
VUSV: Large US value stocks actively picked by Wellington Management, spread evenly across finance, technology, health care and industry. Vanguard pairs its low-key index heritage with active stock picking here, favoring companies priced below their worth, including some big tech names value funds usually skip.
VV: Large US companies making up the top share of the American market, with technology about 40 percent and financials, communication and health care next. It is a core holding for big-company US stocks, and a few tech leaders drive much of its movement.
VWO: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India and Taiwan, with technology about a third and financials next. It offers growth from developing economies, but it swings more than developed market funds, and it includes mainland Chinese shares that can be affected by government policy.
VWOB: Bonds issued by the governments of emerging market countries, mostly priced in US dollars. It's for extra income beyond US bonds, and it carries more risk than safe bonds, since these countries can have weaker finances and prices fall when worries rise.
VXF: Small and mid-sized US companies, everything except the S&P 500, led by technology and industrials with health care and financials next. It is a way to add smaller companies beyond a big-company fund, and it swings more than the broad market.
VXUS: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries, led by financials and technology with industrials next. It adds international diversification to a US-heavy portfolio, and it has no US companies at all, so it moves differently from American markets.
VYM: Large US companies that pay above-average dividends, led by financials, technology, health care and industrials. It is built for dividend income with moderate growth, and it leaves out real estate trusts, so it often trails in growth-led rallies.
VYMI: Large companies outside the US that pay above-average dividends, with financials about 44 percent, then energy, consumer staples and materials. It's meant for income and international diversification, and it leans heavily on banks, which makes it sensitive to the financial sector.
WABF: An actively managed bond fund holding a broad mix of US government, corporate and other debt of different maturities. It can also hold some lower-rated and credit-linked bonds, so the managers have room to depart from a standard bond index.
WAGN: A small group of companies the manager believes are strong, long-lasting businesses, with energy, technology, real estate and industrials leading. It's a concentrated stock holding, so it can look very different from the broad market.
WAMA: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent, that can shift into cash or safer holdings when the market trend turns weak. It aims to cut the damage from big drops, but it can miss part of a rebound if it moves out too late.
WAR: Companies selling technology to militaries: drones, satellites, cybersecurity, chips and aerospace systems, split between tech and defense industry names. It is a focused bet on defense spending in a dangerous world, and its smaller, specialized firms make it swing more than big defense funds.
WARP: Companies in the space business: rocket launchers, satellite builders and operators, and the services around them. It is a narrow bet on a young industry where a few firms take most of the weight, so expect sharp swings as launches and contracts make news.
WATS: Companies that build battery storage systems, from home backup units to grid-scale installations that store solar and wind power for later use. It is a focused bet on batteries becoming part of the power grid, so it rides the fortunes of renewable energy and electric vehicles.
WBEM: Companies in emerging markets, the faster-growing economies of Asia, Latin America and beyond, actively picked by William Blair's managers. Emerging stocks can grow quickly but swing hard on politics, currencies and commodity prices, so this is the adventurous end of a foreign stock allocation.
WBIE: Companies outside the US, actively picked by William Blair's managers for growth, across developed and other international markets. It gives a stock portfolio its foreign piece, chosen stock by stock, so currency moves and foreign market moods both shape its returns.
WBIF: US and foreign stocks of all sizes picked for value by WBI managers, with a large cash cushion of about 27 percent that shifts with their outlook. It is a tactical value holding aiming for growth with an eye on protection, so its results rest heavily on the managers' market calls.
WBIG: A tactical mix of US and foreign stocks of all sizes picked for value and dividend yield, plus bond funds and a large cash cushion that shifts with conditions. It aims for income with active risk control, moving defensive when its managers see trouble, so results hinge on their calls.
WBIL: US and foreign stocks of all sizes screened for quality and value, with the mix managed tactically by WBI managers who can turn cautious. It aims for growth with downside awareness, and because its positioning reflects the managers' market calls, results can differ sharply from plain index funds.
WBIY: US companies screened for high dividend yields and solid underlying value, spread across industries like telecom, food, tech hardware and banks. It is built for income first, so the payout is the point, and the stock picks lean toward cheaper, cash rich businesses rather than fast growers.
WCAP: An actively managed stock fund that can invest in companies of any size, in any sector and anywhere, and does not follow an index. It holds mostly large US names plus a few ETFs, with Microsoft and Alphabet about 6% each.
WCBR: Technology companies that make cybersecurity software and services, such as network protection and data security, from around the world. It's a focused bet on one corner of the tech industry, so it swings more than the broad market and depends on companies keeping up sales growth.
WCEO: An actively managed fund of US companies that are led by women CEOs, leaning toward smaller and mid-sized firms. Holdings are spread thinly across many industries, with no single stock above about 2.5%, so it is not dominated by a few names.
WCLD: Companies that sell software over the internet, such as subscription business tools, all classed as technology. It's a focused bet on cloud computing, so it swings far more than the broad market and drops when interest rates rise.
WCME: Companies in developing countries picked actively for quality growth, dominated by Asian chip makers plus banks and drug firms. WCM's concentrated, research-driven style means it looks quite different from a broad emerging markets index, for better or worse.
WCMG: Companies from around the world picked by WCM's managers, spread across health care, technology, media and banks. It is a core global holding built on careful stock selection, aiming for durable businesses rather than copying a world index.
WCMI: Companies outside the US, with technology, financials, industrials and health care making up most of it. Managers pick firms with strong competitive advantages, so it's a growth-focused way to own international stocks, though results can differ from the broad foreign market.
WCPB: A mix of US government, corporate and other bonds, with a little room for stocks and convertible bonds, picked by active managers. It's meant as a core bond holding that reaches for a bit more income, so it takes on somewhat more risk than a plain bond fund.
WDAF: Defense and aerospace companies in Asia, tracked through a WisdomTree index, with a big focus on India, South Korea and Japan. It is concentrated, with Hindustan Aeronautics, Bharat Electronics and Korea Aerospace each about 8%.
WDAI: The 300 largest companies from stock markets around the world, chosen with an AI-driven scoring approach, in one global growth portfolio. It is a broad core holding with a machine-made selection: the AI screen decides the leaders, but the fund still moves with world markets.
WDE: Securitized debt: bundles of commercial mortgages, car loans, equipment leases and similar loans packaged into bonds. It hunts for income in corners of the bond market beyond plain corporate and government debt, so it depends heavily on borrowers keeping up their payments.
WDEF: European defense and aerospace companies, such as BAE Systems, Thales, Rheinmetall and Safran, picked to follow a WisdomTree index. It is a narrow theme: the top four holdings are about 34% of the fund, and nearly all of it is industrials.
WDGF: Defense companies from around the world: weapons makers, military aircraft and ship builders, and the tech firms that support them, with industrials about 90 percent of the fund. It is a global bet on military budgets, moving with government spending and world tensions.
WDIG: Companies that mine rare earths and other strategic metals, plus futures tied to those metals used in magnets, batteries and defense gear. It is a focused bet on a small, strategic corner of mining, so it can be volatile and driven by government policy.
WDIV: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, led by financials, industrials, utilities and real estate. It's built for income from stocks, with a tilt toward steady, mature businesses, so it often lags in tech-driven rallies since it holds little of the fast-growing technology sector.
WDNA: Companies in the genetics and biology revolution: gene editing, DNA sequencing and new drug discovery firms make up nearly the whole fund. It is a bet on biology becoming a technology industry, so it swings on research breakthroughs and trial results.
WDRN: Companies building physical artificial intelligence: humanoid robots, drones, self-driving systems and the chips and parts inside them. It is an early-stage theme where many holdings are small and unprofitable, so expect sharp swings.
WDTE: An actively managed fund that holds S&P 500 exposure through options and pays out income every week. Selling options caps how much it gains when the market rises, so it trades upside for income and still holds downside risk.
WEAT: Wheat futures contracts, so it follows wheat prices instead of holding any companies. It's a focused bet on a single crop, and its price can swing wildly with weather and harvests, plus costs of rolling contracts forward can hurt returns.
WEED: An actively managed fund giving exposure to cannabis companies, including Curaleaf, using stocks and swaps, which are contracts that pay a stock's returns. The Treasury bills are collateral for the swaps, and the fund is concentrated in a small, volatile industry.
WEEI: Nothing but energy companies, and mostly the giants: the two biggest US oil majors alone are well over a third of the fund, with refiners, drillers and pipeline firms behind them. It is built for income from oil and gas, so it rises and falls with energy prices and dividends.
WEEK: Short-term US Treasury bills maturing within three months, held to pass along interest as weekly payouts. It's meant as a very low-risk place to park cash while earning income, and its payouts move up and down with short-term interest rates.
WEEL: Sector funds and selected stocks paired with an option wheel: selling cash backed puts to collect income, and if assigned, selling covered calls on the shares until they are called away. The wheel turns market swings into a stream of option premiums, capping gains in strong runs.
WELD: US companies that benefit from bringing manufacturing back home, with industrials making up over three quarters and technology most of the rest. It's an actively managed bet on that reshoring theme, so it's more concentrated and swings more than a broad US fund.
WEPN: Defense contractors and rare earth miners, two areas governments treat as strategic, with technology and industrial names split fairly evenly. Options are sold against the stocks to add income, which can soften drops a little but also limits gains in strong runs.
WGMI: Companies that mine Bitcoin or supply power for digital-asset operations, mostly technology and financial firms. It's a high-risk bet on the crypto economy, so it tends to swing wildly with Bitcoin's price and is no substitute for holding Bitcoin itself.
WIMA: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, with a rules-based twist: it adjusts how much it holds in stocks versus cash-like assets depending on recent market trends. Top holdings such as ASML, HSBC and Novartis are each only a few percent.
WINC: An actively managed fund of bonds from emerging market countries, such as developing economies in Latin America, Asia and Africa, chosen by William Blair's managers. These bonds usually pay more interest than US ones but carry higher risk, and the fund may use derivatives to get exposure.
WINN: A small set of large US companies a manager expects to keep growing for years, with technology at about half and communication, consumer and health care businesses making up much of the rest. It's built for growth, so it tends to swing harder than the broad market.
WIP: Inflation protected government bonds from countries outside the US, whose payouts rise when prices rise. It's a hedge against inflation with some foreign currency exposure, so it can swing with exchange rates and falls when interest rates rise.
WISE: Companies building generative artificial intelligence: chip designers, cloud platforms, software firms and the data infrastructure behind AI models. It is a focused bet on the generative AI wave specifically, so it is more concentrated than broad AI or technology funds and swings with that theme's hype cycle.
WLDR: A broad group of 150 to 250 companies from the US and other countries, led by technology at about 37 percent, then financials. It works as a global core holding, though it is tilted toward the US.
WLTG: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mainly US stock funds, and shifts between asset classes and sectors based on market trends. It is actively managed and aims for long-term growth rather than tracking one index.
WMSB: A multisector bond portfolio run by Weitz managers, free to roam across government, corporate, mortgage and other debt in search of value. It is a flexible core income holding from a value-minded shop, so its mix can look quite different from the standard bond index at any time.
WMTI: A fund built around Walmart stock that aims to pay income while keeping some exposure to Walmart's share price, using options and derivatives. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, so it follows a single company and does not match owning the stock.
WNDR: Travel and leisure companies: airlines, hotels, theme parks, cruise and booking platforms, and the card networks travelers pay with. It is a focused bet on people spending on trips and experiences, so it falls hard when households cut back or travel is disrupted.
WNTR: An options strategy that bets against MicroStrategy, the bitcoin holding software company, while selling options to generate monthly income from its wild price swings. It gains when that stock falls and loses when it jumps, so it is a hedge or speculation tool, not a steady income holding.
WOMN: Large and mid sized US companies rated highly for empowering women, through measures like women in leadership and fair pay and promotion practices, across technology, banks, health care and more. It keeps a broad market shape while tilting toward employers with strong records on gender equity.
WOOD: Companies that own forests and timberland or supply the wood, paper and packaging industry, with materials about 70% of the fund and the rest in consumer goods and real estate. It's a focused bet on timber, so it swings with building and paper demand and spreads across countries, including emerging ones.
WQTM: Companies working on quantum computing, mostly in technology, such as chip makers and computing hardware and software, with a few communication and industrial firms. It's a small, speculative bet on an early industry, so expect it to swing far more than the broad market.
WR: Mostly energy companies, plus defense contractors and security technology firms, picked for their role in US defense and energy security. Energy is almost two-thirds of the fund, so it is a focused bet on conflict and defense spending rather than a broad market holding, and it rises and falls with oil prices.
WRND: Large companies around the world that spend heavily on research and development, picked by an index that treats that spending as a sign of innovation. It is top-heavy with big tech, as Alphabet, NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 30% of it.
WRTH: An options income strategy guided by chart analysis, reading price patterns to decide where to sell contracts, with Treasury bills held as collateral. The chart-driven approach sets it apart from systematic covered call funds: trades follow a technician's view of the market's direction.
WSDB: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mostly US Treasuries and other government-backed debt. Because the bonds mature soon, its price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates change.
WSGE: An actively managed fund that gets worldwide stock exposure mostly by holding other ETFs, covering companies of all sizes in the US, developed markets and emerging markets. The top holding, a global equity factor ETF, is about 17% of it.
WSLS: US small companies held two ways at once: a long-only portfolio of small caps, plus a long-short overlay that bets on some and against others. The design aims to squeeze more return from small-company stock picking, and the short side can soften drops but adds its own risks.
WSMD: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, selected by Wasatch's research team with an eye on growth. It invests at least 80% in these stocks, so it tends to be more volatile than funds of big companies.
WSML: Small companies from developed markets around the world, thousands of them across every industry, in a single fund. Small stocks swing more than large ones and can outperform for long stretches, so this fills the small-company corner of a global portfolio that big-company funds miss.
WSPC: Companies in the space economy worldwide: launch providers, satellite operators and the firms supplying them, mostly industrials. It is an actively managed growth bet on orbit as a business, where the manager picks winners in an industry still short on profits and long on ambition.
WTAI: Global companies tied to artificial intelligence, with technology about 80 percent, including memory and chip makers, and some communication and industrial firms. It's a focused growth bet on AI, so it swings far more than the broad market.
WTAL: A long-short fund that bets on some global stocks rising and others falling, using swaps and other derivatives to run both sides at once. It aims to make money from the gap between winners and losers rather than from markets rising, so its results can look nothing like a stock fund's.
WTBN: A hand-picked set of five to twenty bond funds chosen by Bianco Research, spanning Treasuries of many maturities, corporate bonds and inflation-protected debt. The research-driven selection sets it apart from plain core bond funds, aiming for total return by shifting the mix as the outlook changes.
WTIB: Two commodity bets in one fund: crude oil and bitcoin, both reached through futures contracts and related products. It is a speculative diversifier pairing an old-school commodity with a digital one: both legs are volatile, and futures pricing can add its own drag.
WTIP: A model-driven inflation defense built mainly from inflation-protected Treasury bonds, with room for other inflation-sensitive assets alongside. It aims to hold its value when prices rise and inflation bites, serving as the protective corner of a portfolio rather than a growth engine.
WTLS: A long and short portfolio of US stocks, holding companies it favors while betting against others, combined with a straightforward long-only stock sleeve. It aims for stock-like returns with smaller swings, and it can trail badly when the market races upward.
WTMF: Mostly bonds and futures contracts that bet on rising or falling trends across currencies, commodities, stocks and interest rates. It's meant as a diversifier that tends not to move with stocks, though it can lose money when markets keep reversing.
WTMU: A broad mix of US municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, spread out over different years in a ladder, where bonds come due steadily. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 4% of the fund.
WTMY: Municipal bonds of many different maturities arranged in a ladder, chosen for high tax-free income. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the ladder spreads maturity risk, though the high income focus means some bonds are lower quality.
WTPI: A fund that sells put options on the S&P 500, collecting premiums as income, while holding short-term Treasuries as backing. It aims for monthly income with less ups and downs than stocks, but it can lose in sharp drops and trails in strong rallies.
WTRE: Real estate built for the new economy: data centers, cell towers, logistics warehouses and the landlords behind them, worldwide. It ties property income to digital demand rather than shops and offices, though it still moves with interest rates like other property funds.
WTV: US companies chosen because their prices look low compared with their earnings, spread across financials, technology, health care and consumer staples. It's a value holding for the middle of the market, and it can lag when fast-growing stocks drive returns.
WUGI: Companies building or benefiting from the 5G digital economy, heavily weighted to chip makers and the equipment behind fast networks. It is a theme bet on connected everything, from phones to factories, and its chip concentration makes it swing with the semiconductor cycle.
WWJD: Large companies outside the US, including some from developing countries, screened to meet faith-based values, with industrials, financials, materials and utilities leading. It adds international stocks to a portfolio, and the screen leaves out businesses that conflict with those values.
WZRD: An actively traded fund where the manager moves between individual stocks, index funds and options or futures as opportunities appear, so its mix can change fast. Right now it leans toward technology, but nothing about the portfolio is fixed, making it a bet on the trader's timing calls.
XA: Cybersecurity companies that build artificial intelligence into their defenses: firms guarding networks, identities and cloud data. Technology is the entire fund, making it a narrow bet on digital security spending that can swing with the threat headlines of the moment.
XAGG: A wide mix of bonds, including corporate, mortgage-backed, asset-backed, emerging market and convertible bonds, with financials and real estate the biggest groups. It's meant for higher income than a regular bond fund, in exchange for more risk of losses in downturns.
XAIW: Companies in the ecosystem around SpaceX and its AI ventures: launch and satellite suppliers, connectivity firms and the industrials and tech names in their orbit. It is a focused bet built around one private empire's supply chain, so it captures partners rather than the private companies themselves.
XAIX: Companies around the world tied to artificial intelligence and big data, with technology about 72% and communication, consumer firms making up much of the rest. It's a growth-focused theme bet, so it swings more than the broad market when AI enthusiasm shifts.
XAPR: Options linked to the S&P 500 give this fund a set outcome for a one year period starting each April: it cushions a moderate slice of losses and boosts gains up to a cap. It suits investors who want stock exposure with a softer landing, accepting limited upside in strong years.
XAR: Aerospace and defense companies, from aircraft and engine makers to defense contractors and space businesses, all in industrials and held in roughly equal amounts. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it depends on government defense spending and air travel demand, and swings more than the broad market.
XAUG: Options on a fund of the largest US companies shape an enhanced return over the year from August: gains get a boost up to a cap, with a moderate buffer against losses. It sits between plain buffer and growth funds, trading some protection for a faster start on the upside.
XB: Corporate bonds rated B, a single slice of the junk bond market below the stronger BB tier and above the riskiest CCC names. It pays higher interest than safer high yield funds in exchange for borrowers with shakier finances, so defaults are the ever-present trade-off.
XBAP: Options tied to the S&P 500, set up to deliver amplified gains up to a cap, while also absorbing some losses over a year starting each April. It aims for boosted growth with a cushion, but it gives up the biggest rallies.
XBB: Corporate bonds from US companies with credit ratings just below investment grade, the top tier of high yield. It aims for higher income than safer bonds, but it can fall in recessions when companies struggle to repay.
XBCI: Mostly cash and short-term holdings, with a layer of bitcoin exposure gained through other bitcoin funds and a small slice of stocks. It aims to pay high income from options-style strategies tied to bitcoin, so it swings with bitcoin's price and can lose value when bitcoin falls.
XBFR: Large US stocks held directly, paired with options that absorb about the first 10 percent of losses over each outcome period while keeping much of the upside. It is actively managed rather than set once a year, so the managers can adjust the hedge as markets move.
XBI: Almost entirely biotechnology companies, spread fairly evenly across large and small drug developers rather than weighted toward the giants. It's a focused bet on the biotech industry, and because many holdings are small firms waiting on trial results, it swings much more than the broad market.
XBIL: Short-term US Treasury bills that mature in about six months, so the whole fund is government debt. It's a place to park cash for modest interest with very little price swing, though income drifts down when interest rates fall.
XBJA: Options on large US stocks with a twist: gains are amplified up to a cap, while a buffer (the 9 in its name) absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each January. It is a leveraged-feeling but bounded bet for investors expecting a decent, not spectacular, year.
XBJL: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a one-year period starting in July, aiming to absorb a set amount of losses and to speed up gains up to a cap. Protection only applies if held for the full period.
XBOC: Uses options tied to a US large company index to absorb losses, with a 9% buffer, over a one year period that starts in October. In return, it is able to capture a boosted share of gains up to a cap, so it works best when held for the full period.
XBTY: An options income fund built around Bitcoin, using derivatives on a Bitcoin ETF rather than owning coins directly. It aims to pay high income by selling options, which limits how much it gains if Bitcoin rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing.
XC: Emerging market stocks, picked by an index that tries to reflect true emerging economies by leaving out state-owned companies. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3%, and financials are around a third.
XCCC: US dollar bonds from companies with the lowest credit ratings in the high-yield group, rated CCC. It pays higher income than safer bonds, but these companies are likelier to miss payments, so it can fall sharply in a weak economy.
XCEM: Stocks from emerging markets like India, Taiwan and Brazil, with technology just over half and financials about a sixth. It's a growth holding for adding developing economies to a portfolio, and it leaves out China entirely, which sets it apart from most funds in this space.
XCHG: Large US companies chosen by an active manager, with technology the biggest slice at about 37%, followed by financials, communication and industrials. It's a core stock holding that aims to beat the market, though the manager's picks can also lag it.
XCNY: A fund following an S&P index of emerging-market stocks outside China, in places like Taiwan and South Korea. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 20% of the fund, and technology is around 40%.
XCOR: A fund of funds that mostly holds other stock ETFs, tilting toward growth sectors like technology, and the manager rotates among them based on which look strongest. It's meant as an actively managed stock core, so its results depend on those choices rather than on the market alone.
XCSH: A very short-term fund that uses box spreads, paired options trades that work like a short loan, with an average life under 90 days. It is meant to behave like a cash-like holding that earns interest, with little price movement.
XDAT: Companies riding the flood of data: the firms storing, moving and processing the world's information, with technology about 70 percent and media firms behind. It is a growth bet on data use exploding, a theme powered by AI and cloud computing.
XDEC: US large company stocks, through options that enhance some gains and absorb a set amount of losses over a year, resetting each December. It's a cushioned way to own the market, though gains are capped and it needs the full year.
XDEF: European defense technology companies: weapons makers, space firms and cybersecurity specialists, with industrials over 90 percent of the fund. It is a focused bet on Europe rearming, moving with government military budgets and security worries.
XDIV: Large US stocks across every major industry, managed with a twist: it is designed to avoid collecting dividend payouts, shifting holdings around payment dates. That suits investors in taxable accounts who prefer no dividend income, though the maneuvering can make it trail a plain index fund slightly.
XDQQ: Gives about two times the gains of the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, up to a set limit over a three-month period. Losses are not cushioned, so it can fall as much as the index when prices drop.
XDSQ: Gives about two times the gains of the S&P 500 up to a set limit over a three-month period, using options on an S&P 500 fund. In exchange, losses are not cushioned, so it can lose as much as the market if prices fall.
XDTE: Exposure to the S&P 500, which is about 40% technology, combined with options that are sold each week to collect cash. It aims to pay regular income, but selling those options caps how much it gains in a strong rally while it still shares in most market drops.
XEMD: US-dollar bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, with medium lives of one to ten years. It's meant for higher income than developed-market bonds, but these countries are riskier, so prices can fall when investors get nervous or interest rates rise.
XEML: Leading companies from across Europe: the continent's biggest banks, drug makers, energy firms and manufacturers. It gives diversified European exposure in a single fund, though returns for US buyers also ride on the euro's moves between currencies.
XES: Nearly all companies that sell equipment and services to oil and gas drillers, such as rig operators and well-service firms. It's a focused bet on energy spending, and it rises and falls with oil drilling activity, so it swings more than the broad energy sector.
XEY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, rather than holding ether itself. It aims to pay weekly distributions, but ether is volatile and the leveraged options link magnifies every swing, so it is a trading tool.
XFEB: Options linked to the S&P 500 give this fund a set outcome for a one year period starting each February: it cushions a moderate slice of losses and boosts gains up to a cap. It suits investors who want stock exposure with a softer landing, accepting limited upside in strong years.
XFIV: US Treasury bonds that together have an average sensitivity to interest rates of about five years. It's a middle-of-the-road government bond holding for safety and income, and its price drops when interest rates rise, though less than long-term bonds.
XFLX: A flexible fund of bond funds, spreading money across other ETFs that hold government, corporate and mortgage bonds of varying maturities and quality. The manager shifts the blend as conditions change, aiming for income with managed risk rather than a fixed bond recipe.
XHB: US homebuilders and related companies like building materials and home improvement, with consumer discretionary about two thirds. It's a focused bet on housing, so it tends to fall when mortgage rates rise or the housing market cools, and it swings more than the broad market.
XHE: Companies that make medical devices and supplies, almost entirely in health care, from smaller firms to large ones held in similar amounts. It's a focused bet on one corner of health care, so it swings more than the broad market, and it has no drug makers.
XHLF: Short US Treasury bills and notes averaging about six months to maturity. It's a very low-risk place to park cash and earn interest, and because the maturities are so short, its price barely moves when interest rates change.
XHS: Almost entirely health care services: insurers, hospitals, clinics, labs and pharmacy benefit firms, rather than drug makers. It's a focused bet on how medical care is delivered and paid for, and it's equally weighted, so smaller companies matter more and it swings more than the broad market.
XIDE: Options on a fund of the largest US companies plus short-term Treasury securities combine two aims over the period from December: a buffer against a slice of stock losses and a stream of premium income.
