It is built for investors who want equity exposure with built-in cushioning and regular payouts.
XIDV: Dividend paying companies in developed markets outside the US, with the mix optimized to boost the dividend yield above a plain foreign index, led by banks and energy firms. It targets fatter payouts from abroad, accepting a tilt toward slower growing, cash heavy industries.
XIGV: One hundred big US technology companies with software deliberately left out, leaving chipmakers, hardware firms and other non-software tech. It is a more physical slice of the tech sector, so it leans on the chip cycle and device demand rather than on subscription software growth.
XIJN: Options on the S&P 500 set each June, combining a buffer against losses with an income feature that pays premiums along the way, over a one year outcome period. It mixes two defined outcome ideas, cushion plus income, and like its cousins it caps how much of a rally you keep.
XIMR: Options on a fund of the largest US companies plus short-term Treasury securities combine two aims over the period from March: a buffer against a slice of stock losses and a stream of premium income. It is built for investors who want equity exposure with built-in cushioning and regular payouts.
XISE: Options on the S&P 500 that combine a loss buffer with premium income, paying out option premiums as regular income over a year to September. It trades stock market thrills for a paycheck style return, with gains limited by design.
XITK: About 50 to 100 US-listed technology companies picked for being in innovative parts of the sector, held in roughly equal amounts. That makes it less top-heavy than most tech funds, with its top holdings each only around 3% to 5%.
XJAN: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to give a boosted share of gains up to a limit, while softening part of the losses over a one-year period starting in January. It holds options rather than stocks, so the outcome depends on when you buy.
XJH: US mid-sized companies, led by industrials, then technology, financials and health care, with firms in controversial businesses screened out. It's a core mid-size holding for people who want an ethical filter, so it differs a little from the standard mid-size fund.
XJR: Small US companies across financials, technology, industrials and consumer businesses, with firms involved in controversial activities screened out. It's a growth-oriented way to own small companies with an ethical filter, and small stocks tend to swing more than large ones, especially in downturns.
XJUL: Options on the S&P 500 that boost participation in moderate market gains up to a limit, while buffering part of a loss, over a year that resets each July. The enhanced upside is the twist on a standard buffer fund, paid for by the cap on bigger rallies.
XJUN: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that start each June. It aims to give more upside than a plain buffer fund while still cushioning a moderate drop, but the protection only works if you hold through the full one-year period.
XLB: The materials slice of the S&P 500: chemical makers, mining firms, and packaging and construction materials companies. It's a focused bet on one sector tied to economic cycles, so it swings more than the broad market, and it doesn't hold tech or banks.
XLBI: Holds the Materials Select Sector SPDR fund, which covers chemicals, metals, mining and packaging companies from the S&P 500, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. That options income is meant to boost payouts, but it limits how much the fund gains when materials stocks rally.
XLC: The communication services slice of the S&P 500: social media, search, streaming, telecom and media companies. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a couple of giant companies make up a big share of it.
XLCI: Communication services stocks from the S&P 500, meaning telecom carriers, media companies and internet platforms, paired with an options overlay that sells options to add income. It targets income from a growth-heavy sector, giving up some upside when these stocks run hard.
XLE: Entirely energy companies, mainly oil and gas producers, refiners and service firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it rises and falls largely with oil and gas prices.
XLEI: The energy slice of the S&P 500, such as oil and gas producers and refiners, combined with an options strategy that earns extra monthly income. It's meant for income from energy, but it gives up some gains when energy stocks surge.
XLEM: The energy slice of the S&P 500: oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline companies among America's biggest corporations. It is a focused bet on fuel prices and energy demand, steadier than small energy funds because it owns only the giants, but still hostage to oil.
XLF: Nearly all financial companies, covering banks, insurers, and investment and payments firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to be sensitive to interest rates and the health of the economy.
XLFI: A fund that holds the Financial Select Sector SPDR, the financial companies of the S&P 500, and adds options to produce extra income. Nearly all of it is financials, and the income comes in exchange for limiting some of the upside.
XLG: Just the 50 largest US companies, with technology about half the fund and communication, financials and consumer companies behind. It's a core-style holding with heavy mega-cap concentration, so it leans harder on a few giants than the broad market does.
XLI: Nearly all industrial companies, including aerospace and defense, machinery, airlines, railroads and construction firms. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and it tends to follow the strength of the economy.
XLII: Industrial companies from the S&P 500: airlines, defense contractors, machinery, railroads and logistics firms, paired with an options overlay that collects premium income. The options add regular payouts on top of a cyclical sector, in exchange for part of the upside.
XLK: The technology slice of the S&P 500: software makers, chip companies, and computer and networking hardware. It's a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and internet and social media companies are classed in other sectors, so they aren't in it.
XLKI: Technology stocks, the full sector from chipmakers to software giants, paired with an options program that collects premium income on top. It aims for sector returns plus extra income with a slightly smoother ride, giving up some upside when technology shares climb quickly.
XLKM: The technology slice of the S&P 500: software makers, chip companies and computer hardware firms drawn from America's biggest corporations. It is a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and some internet giants are classed in other sectors and sit outside it.
XLP: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: makers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products, plus grocery and discount retailers. It's a defensive holding since people keep buying these items in downturns, though it can trail in strong rallies.
XLPM: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: makers and sellers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products. It is a defensive sector holding that usually falls less in downturns and grows more slowly in booms, the steadier corner of a stock portfolio.
XLRE: Real estate companies only, such as owners of apartments, offices, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers, drawn from the S&P 500. It's a focused bet on property that pays solid dividends, and it tends to drop when interest rates rise.
XLRI: Real estate stocks from the S&P 500, mainly property owners and REITs, paired with an options overlay that sells options against them to generate extra income. It is an income-focused way to hold the property sector, trading some upside in strong rallies for regular option premium.
XLSI: Consumer staples companies from the S&P 500, the makers of food, drinks, household and personal products, paired with an options overlay that collects premium income. Staples are a defensive corner of the market, and the options add payouts in exchange for some upside.
XLSR: A fund of funds that shifts money among S&P 500 sector funds, favoring the sectors the manager expects to do best, now leaning toward technology at about 40%. It's a core stock holding with an active twist, so it can differ sharply from the plain S&P 500.
XLU: The utilities slice of the S&P 500: companies that supply electricity, gas and water. It's a focused sector holding known for steady dividends and steadier swings, but it's sensitive to interest rates and drops when rates rise.
XLUI: Utility companies, the power, gas and water providers known for steady dividends, paired with an options program that sells calls to add premium income. The result aims for dependable payouts from a usually calm sector, giving up some gains when utilities run.
XLV: Entirely health care companies, including drug makers, medical device firms, insurers and care providers. It's a focused bet on one sector, often viewed as steadier in downturns, though drug pricing news can move it sharply.
XLVI: Health care stocks, the full sector from drugmakers to insurers, paired with an options program that collects premium income on top. It aims for sector returns plus extra income with a slightly smoother ride, giving up some upside when health care shares climb quickly.
XLY: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, carmakers, restaurants and travel companies selling things people want but don't strictly need. It's a focused bet on one sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and a few giants dominate it.
XLYI: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, restaurants, car makers and travel companies, held through the sector's big fund with options sold for premium income. It lives and dies by consumer spending, with the premiums adding a payout on top.
XLYM: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, carmakers, restaurants, travel firms and online shopping giants. These companies sell things people want rather than need, so the fund does well when households feel confident and falls harder when spending tightens.
XMAG: The 500 largest US companies minus the seven biggest tech names, so technology is still the largest slice at about a quarter, followed by financials, health care and industrials. It's a core stock holding for people who want market exposure without those seven giants.
XMAR: Options on the S&P 500 set up to cushion part of the market's losses over a one-year period starting in March, while limiting how much gain you keep. It's for cautious investors, and it works best if held the whole period.
XMAY: Options on the S&P 500 set to enhance gains up to a cap while moderating losses over a one-year period ending each May. It softens the ride for cautious investors, trading away part of strong rallies for a cushion against moderate drops.
XME: Metals and mining companies such as steel, aluminum, copper and coal producers, with materials about 80% and energy about 14%. It's a focused bet on a cyclical corner of the market, so it swings more than the broad market and follows commodity prices.
XMHQ: US mid-sized companies chosen for high quality, meaning strong profits and sound finances, with industrials the biggest group at about 30% and technology, financials and health care behind it. It's a core mid-size holding that trades some breadth for sturdier businesses.
XMLV: Mid-sized US companies picked for the lowest price swings, heavy in financials, real estate and utilities, with little technology. It's meant to be a steadier way to own mid-size stocks, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but trails in strong rallies.
XMMO: Mid-sized US companies whose stock prices have been rising fastest lately, led by technology, industrials, health care and energy. It's a momentum bet on recent winners, and it can drop quickly when market leadership changes.
XMPT: Municipal bonds held indirectly by owning closed-end funds that invest in them, with a small portion in other holdings. It's for income that is generally exempt from federal income tax, and because it buys funds that use borrowing, it can swing more than ordinary municipal bond funds.
XMVM: Mid-sized US companies chosen for being cheaply priced and having recent price momentum, about 80 stocks. Financials are the biggest slice at over a third, then energy and consumer companies, so it's a value-style tilt and swings more than a broad market fund.
XNAV: A fund of other ETFs that leans aggressively into whichever stock sectors and growth funds are showing strength, so technology-heavy funds can dominate. It is a momentum style growth holding that shifts its mix over time, accepting concentrated bets and bigger swings in pursuit of stronger returns.
XNOV: Options on a fund of the largest US companies shape an enhanced return over the year from November: gains get a boost up to a cap, with a moderate buffer against losses. It sits between plain buffer and growth funds, trading some protection for a faster start on the upside.
XNTK: Large technology and tech-related companies, with about six sevenths in tech and small slices in communication and consumer firms. It's a concentrated growth bet on the tech sector, so it tends to rise and fall harder than the broad market.
XOCT: Options on the S&P 500 that enhance participation in moderate gains up to a cap, while cushioning part of a decline, over an outcome year resetting each October. The boost on medium-sized rallies is the draw, balanced by limited gains in the biggest years.
XOEF: The big US index with its hundred largest members removed, leaving the roughly four hundred other large companies in more even measure. Technology shrinks to about 22 percent, so it is a core holding for investors who find the usual index too concentrated in mega-cap giants.
XOEX: The big US companies of the S&P 100 with the twenty largest deliberately removed, leaving the next tier of blue chips across industries. Cutting out the giants makes it less top-heavy than a normal large-company fund, so it behaves like a mildly contrarian core holding.
XOMO: A single-stock income fund built on Exxon Mobil: it uses options to mimic owning the shares while selling covered calls for monthly income. The call selling caps how much it gains if the stock jumps, so it is an income play on one oil giant.
XONE: Short-term US Treasury bills and notes that average about one year until repayment, backed by the federal government. It's a place to park cash-like money for steady interest, and with such short maturities its price barely moves when interest rates change.
XOP: Oil and gas drillers and producers, almost all energy, with no big refiners or pipelines in the mix. It's a focused bet on energy prices, and since the companies are equal sized and many are small, it swings far more than the broad market.
XOVR: Growth-minded stocks led by technology, with communication companies and health care making up most of the rest. It also holds private companies through special investment vehicles, which makes it a more adventurous growth pick that can swing more than the broad market.
XPAY: Exposure to the S&P 500, with technology about 40 percent, through options, built to pay out a steady targeted monthly income. It's meant for investors who want regular payouts from large US stocks, but gains are capped and a high payout can eat into your principal.
XPH: US drug companies, covering both large pharmaceutical makers and smaller ones. It's a focused bet on one health care industry, so it swings more than the broad market, and its equal-style weighting gives smaller companies a bigger role than usual.
XPND: Technology companies in the wider sense: chip and software firms plus the payment networks and platforms whose businesses run on technology. Actively chosen rather than index-bound, it captures tech's reach into finance and media while swinging like a sector fund.
XQBT: The ten standout companies in quantum computing, from pure-play quantum firms to big tech names with quantum programs. It is a concentrated bet on an experimental technology: the science is exciting, revenues are small, and prices swing on headlines rather than earnings.
XQQI: Nasdaq-100 stocks, with technology about 60 percent, plus sold call options that turn some of the upside into high monthly income. It's built for income from a tech-heavy portfolio, but it trails the plain index in strong rallies and still falls with it in sell-offs.
XRLX: A conservative fund of funds, mixing core stock ETFs with a solid base of bond ETFs and adjusting the blend as conditions change. It aims for modest growth with limited drama, suiting cautious investors who want one holding that leans defensive by default.
XRMI: Large US stocks across every major industry, paired with an options collar that sells calls and buys protective puts on the same basket. The collar turns part of the market's upside into monthly income and softens drops, so it trails strong rallies but falls less in sell-offs.
XRP: Holds the XRP digital token directly, so it has no companies, bonds or income behind it. It's a focused bet on a single cryptocurrency, and its price can swing wildly in a day.
XRPC: Directly held XRP, a digital currency used for payments, kept with professional custodians rather than tracked through futures. It's a focused bet on one crypto asset, so it pays no income and its price can swing wildly in either direction.
XRPI: A single cryptocurrency, XRP, held through linked instruments rather than coins in a wallet, giving brokerage-account access to its price moves. It is a concentrated crypto bet that can swing violently in either direction, with none of the diversification a stock or bond fund provides.
XRPM: A fund giving exposure to the price of XRP, a cryptocurrency, while selling options on XRP ETFs to earn monthly income. The options cap some of the gains, and the fund holds a Canary XRP ETF and a short-term bond fund.
XRPR: Direct exposure to XRP, the token of a blockchain network built for fast cross-border payments, held rather than traded through futures. XRP's price is driven by crypto sentiment and by the legal and adoption news around its network, so it swings hard in both directions.
XRPZ: The XRP cryptocurrency, held directly rather than through companies that use it. It's a focused bet on one digital coin, not a diversified investment, and its price swings far more than stocks and can move sharply on news about regulation or the coin itself.
XRT: Retail businesses such as clothing, home goods and online sellers, with food and drug stores making up about a fifth. It's a focused bet on shoppers spending, equally weighted so smaller retailers count as much as big ones, and it swings more than the broad market.
XSD: Chip companies in the S&P Semiconductor index, which spreads money more evenly across large and small firms than most chip funds. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings far more than the broad market and rises and falls with chip demand.
XSEP: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, with an enhanced payoff design and a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September. It trades a cap on gains for partial protection plus a boost to modest returns.
XSHD: Around 60 small US companies with high dividend yields and lower price swings, chosen by an S&P index. Real estate makes up about 40% of it, and it holds names like Innovative Industrial, Kinetik and Easterly Government Properties.
XSHP: An income fund built around SpaceX stock and contracts tied to its price, with a portfolio of bonds behind them. It uses options to generate income, which limits how much of SpaceX's gains it can capture, so it is a bet on a single company.
XSHQ: Small US companies chosen for quality, such as steady profits and solid finances, led by financials and technology. It's a stock holding for the small end of the market that aims to avoid weaker businesses, though it still swings more than large company funds.
XSLV: Small US companies with the steadiest recent prices, tilted toward financials, real estate and utilities. It's meant to give a smoother ride within small companies, so it usually falls less in sell-offs but can trail when the market rallies hard.
XSMO: Small US companies chosen because their share prices have been climbing fastest lately, spread across technology, health care, financials and real estate. It's a growth-leaning way to own small companies, and momentum picks can reverse quickly, so it swings more than large-company funds.
XSOE: Emerging market stocks, with technology around two fifths and financials about a seventh. It's a growth holding for developing economies that screens out companies controlled by governments, which sets it apart from standard emerging market funds.
XSPC: Companies building the space economy and the AI that supports it: launch, satellites and orbital infrastructure, split between industrials and technology. It is a speculative growth bet on two hot themes at once, so it can swing hard when either theme cools.
XSPI: S&P 500 stocks, with technology about 40 percent, combined with sold call options that pay out high monthly income. It's built for income rather than growth, and the options give up some of the market's upside, so it trails in strong rallies.
XSVM: Small US companies that look cheap and have been rising lately, with financials such as banks making up almost half. It's a value-and-momentum play on smaller stocks, so it leans heavily on one industry and can swing more than the broad market.
XSVN: US Treasury bonds managed to keep an average sensitivity to interest rates of about seven years. It's meant as a medium-term, government-backed bond holding and a cushion for stocks, though its price drops when interest rates rise.
XSW: Software and online services companies, with technology making up roughly 90% and a small slice of financials. It's a focused bet on one fast-moving corner of tech, with companies of all sizes weighted fairly evenly, so it swings more than the broad market.
XT: Companies building new technologies such as AI, robotics, genomics and cloud computing, with technology 45% and health care 26%. It's a growth bet on innovation spread across several themes, so it swings more than the broad market.
XTAP: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to deliver accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each April. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, carrying full losses when the index falls.
XTEN: US Treasury notes and bonds picked so the fund's average sensitivity to interest rates matches that of a ten-year Treasury. It's a pure government bond holding for safety and income, and its price falls noticeably when interest rates rise.
XTJA: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to deliver accelerated gains, magnifying the index's rise up to a preset cap, over a one-year period starting each January. The flip side is full exposure to losses, so it suits short, confident bets on a rising market.
XTJL: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each July. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, with no cushion when the index falls.
XTL: Telecom-related US companies, with technology firms such as communications equipment makers at nearly 60% and traditional communication services around a third. It's a focused bet on one industry, so it swings more than the broad market and is not mainly phone company stocks.
XTN: Transportation companies such as airlines, trucking firms, railroads and shipping businesses, nearly all in industrials. It's a focused bet on the economy's movement of goods and people, so it tends to swing more than the broad market with business cycles and fuel costs.
XTOC: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each October. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, carrying full losses when the index falls.
XTR: The 500 big US companies of the S&P 500, plus protective put options that gain value when the market crashes. The puts cost a little performance in calm years, so it is stocks with built-in crash insurance for worried investors.
XTRE: US Treasury bonds averaging about three years until payback. It's meant as a safe, government-backed holding for income and stability, and sits in the middle ground, so its price falls when interest rates rise, but by less than long-term Treasury funds.
XTWO: US Treasury bonds with an average life of about two years. It suits investors wanting government-backed safety and a steady interest payment, and it moves little when interest rates change compared with longer bond funds, though its price still dips a bit when rates rise.
XTWY: US Treasury bonds with an average lifespan of about twenty years, including some zero-coupon types. It's a safe-haven holding that tends to rise when stocks fall, though its price drops sharply when interest rates rise because the bonds are so long.
XUDV: Large US companies with high dividend yields, chosen from a large-cap index and weighted to boost income. Holdings like UPS, Pfizer, Altria and Kraft Heinz are each about 5%, so it leans toward mature dividend payers.
XUSM: Companies outside the US whose share prices have been rising strongly, picked by momentum across the previous months and led by banks. Momentum funds ride winners and drop losers, which can work well in trends but whipsaws when markets reverse suddenly.
XUSP: Options on the S&P 500 designed to pay an accelerated return if stocks rise past a set point by the contracts' expiration date, with no cap on the boost. The flip side is downside that bites like a leveraged fund and an outcome that depends heavily on where stocks finish, making it a trading tool.
XV: Short-term government investments paired with an options spread strategy, built to pay monthly distributions at a target annual rate, the 15 in its name. The payout is the whole point, so it suits income seekers, though the distribution rate is a goal rather than a promise.
XVAD: AMD shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the chipmaker: the options trade some upside for payouts, and AMD's swings drive everything.
XVAP: Apple shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income on top of following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: Apple drives everything, and the options trade some of its upside for regular payouts.
XVAZ: Amazon shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: Amazon's retail and cloud fortunes drive everything, and the options swap some of that upside for regular payouts.
XVGL: Alphabet shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on Google's parent: the options harvest its steady climb for payouts, trading away some upside.
XVMS: Microsoft shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: the software giant drives the result, and the options swap some upside for steadier payouts.
XVMT: Meta Platforms shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the social media giant: payouts are the plan, but Meta's swings still drive the outcome.
XVNV: NVIDIA shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the AI chip leader: payouts are the goal, but NVIDIA's sharp swings still set the tone.
XVPT: Palantir shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on a famously volatile name: the options harvest its swings for payouts, but cannot smooth them away.
XVSP: Shares and options tied to a single private company, SpaceX, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its value. It is a rare way to hold the rocket company in a brokerage account: the income plan is clear, but valuing a private stock makes pricing less certain.
XVTS: Tesla stock held directly, combined with options designed to add a target stream of income on top of its price moves. It keeps real exposure to Tesla's rises, unlike pure options funds, but the income program trims the biggest gains.
XVV: Large US companies, with technology the biggest slice at nearly half, followed by financials and health care. It's a core stock holding that screens out firms with controversial businesses, so it can differ a bit from the plain S&P 500.
XWNG: The ten standout companies in the space industry, from launch and satellites to the technology supporting them, mostly industrials. It is a concentrated bet on orbit: only ten names carry the fund, so contract wins, launch failures and government budgets swing it hard.
XX: A defined-outcome bet that the S&P 500 reaches 10,000 by 2030, built with options that behave like one long call on the index. If the index gets there early it can pay off handsomely, but if 2030 arrives below the target the options can expire worthless, so it is an all-or-nothing wager.
XXQQ: The growth giants of the Nasdaq 100, minus a set of companies the manager excludes on principle, which is the redacted part of the name. What remains is still a tech-heavy growth portfolio, so it swings like one, with a values-based screen layered on top.
XXSP: America's 500 largest companies across every major industry, minus a set of companies the manager excludes on principle, the redacted part of the name. What remains still behaves like a core market holding, moving with the US economy, with a values-based screen layered on top.
XXV: Treasury interest plus an option spread strategy, combined to target steady distributions that the fund aims to pay out regularly. Most of the money sits in bonds, so the options do the extra work, and payouts can vary with market conditions rather than being guaranteed.
XXX: A fixed blend in one fund: about three-quarters in the 500 biggest US companies across every industry, and about a quarter in XRP, the token of a payments-focused blockchain network. The stock side behaves like a core holding, while the XRP slice adds sharp swings that can dominate the fund's moves.
XYLD: Large US stocks, about 40 percent technology, paired with an options strategy that sells away much of the upside in exchange for regular income. It aims to pay out steady cash, but it trails in strong rallies and still drops when the market falls.
XYLG: Holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on half of them, a covered call strategy, to collect extra income. That limits some upside when the market rallies, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up around 20% of it.
XYZY: An options strategy on a single company, Block, the payments firm behind Square and Cash App, using synthetic covered calls to produce income. Distributions can be high, but gains are capped and the fund rides one volatile fintech stock.
YALL: US stocks chosen to reflect a faith-and-America-first theme, with holdings spread across all eleven market sectors. It looks like a broad large-company fund, with Broadcom, NVIDIA and Tesla each making up around 7% of it, but its picks come from a custom method, not a standard index.
YBIT: An actively managed fund that gets indirect exposure to bitcoin through bitcoin ETPs and sells options on them to produce income. That options trade caps its gains if bitcoin jumps, and the fund mostly holds Treasury bills as backing.
YBST: A basket of GraniteShares YieldBoost funds, each selling options on a different leveraged single-stock product to pay weekly income. It spreads the income strategy across several stocks instead of one: the diversification helps, but every underlying layer still caps gains and adds leverage swings.
YBTC: Exposure to bitcoin through bitcoin ETFs, paired with a covered call strategy that sells away some upside in exchange for monthly income. It's built for income from bitcoin, but it trails in big bitcoin rallies and still falls when bitcoin drops.
YBTY: A fund of GraniteShares YieldBoost funds, each selling options on leveraged single-stock products to pay high weekly income. It is income squared: layers of options and leverage underneath, diversified across several underlying stocks but with every layer capping gains and adding its own swings.
YCLO: Collateralized loan obligations, bundles of corporate loans sliced into layers, with this fund buying the floating rate debt those vehicles issue. The payments adjust as interest rates move, and the layered structure pays more than plain loans while carrying more complexity and risk.
YDEC: Options on a fund of developed-market stocks outside North America, tilted toward financials, industrials and technology. It aims to absorb a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in December, but gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if held for the entire period.
YETH: Aims to pay monthly income using a covered call strategy tied to Ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, mostly through options rather than owning it directly. Selling those options caps how much it gains when Ether rises, and its cash is held mainly in Treasury bills.
YFFI: A yield-focused mix of corporate bonds, Treasury securities, asset-backed bonds and preferred shares, spread across many issuers. It is built to pay steady interest income as a core bond holding, with more credit risk than a Treasury-only fund carries.
YFYA: A fund of other ETFs, mostly ultrashort bond and income funds plus some preferred and high-yield bonds, aiming for steady income. It owns funds rather than individual securities, and a few of those holdings use options to boost income.
YGLD: Leveraged exposure to gold through futures, targeting up to about one and a half times the gold price move, with option selling on other markets to add income. The leverage magnifies gold's swings, so it is a punchier, more complex way to hold the metal.
YJUN: Large companies in developed markets outside North America, led by financials and industrials, held through options that cushion moderate losses over a one-year period starting in June. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it trails in strong rallies.
YLD: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, which pay more interest to make up for the extra risk, with a bit of cash on the side. It's for higher income than safer bonds, and it tends to fall with stocks in downturns because defaults rise.
YLDE: Dividend-paying large US companies spread across technology, financials, energy and communication, paired with call options sold on large-company indexes. The options add extra income, so it suits people seeking yield, but they cap gains, which means it trails in strong rallies.
YLDW: A mix of dividend-paying stocks and interest-bearing bonds, led by big technology, health care and bank names, built to pay income. It targets a calmer ride than a stock-only fund, accepting slower growth in exchange for regular payouts and smaller swings.
YLDY: Large US companies, led by technology, paired with an options program that sells index contracts to turn part of the market's movement into income. It aims for high regular payouts, and the options overlay means it keeps less of the gain in strong rallies.
YMAG: A fund that holds other income-focused funds tied to the Magnificent Seven tech giants, plus mostly cash and bonds. It's built to pay out high monthly income from options, but it gives up much of the upside if those stocks surge and can still fall hard when they drop.
YMAR: Options on a fund of developed-market stocks outside North America, tilted toward financials, industrials and technology. It aims to absorb a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in March, but gains are capped, and the protection only fully works if held to the end.
YMAX: A basket of other option income funds, each tied to a single well-known stock, mainly tech, with the rest in Treasuries and cash. It's built to pay high monthly income across many stocks, but it gives up most of the gains and can lose a lot in sell-offs.
YNOT: Almost entirely stocks, with technology a little over half and industrials, consumer companies and financials making up much of the rest. It's a growth bet on emerging technologies in the US and abroad, and since it's actively managed, a manager picks the holdings rather than following a fixed list.
YOKE: A mix of stocks and funds across US and international markets, with a manager shifting around based on market conditions. Industrials and technology are the biggest groups, so it's a core-style holding that can look quite different from the broad market.
YOLO: Companies that make most of their money from marijuana and hemp: cannabis growers, dispensary chains and related suppliers, picked actively. It is a pure bet on legal cannabis spreading, and the industry's legal and banking troubles make it one of the wildest stock funds around.
YQQQ: An income strategy built to move against the Nasdaq-100: options give indirect inverse exposure to that tech-heavy index while generating regular payments. It is a bearish, tactical trade rather than an investment, with gains from index falls limited by design and losses if the rally continues.
YRAM: Memory and storage chip companies, the firms making the parts that hold data in computers and AI servers, plus options sold on them for income. It pairs a hot, cyclical corner of tech with monthly payouts, though the option sales limit gains in big rallies.
YSAG: Physical silver, held as bullion rather than through mining stocks or futures. Its price follows the metal itself, so it is a direct bet on silver, which tends to swing harder than gold and plays both precious metal and industrial roles.
YSAU: Physical gold bars held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of gold. It holds no stocks or bonds, and the gold is delivered to and from large trading firms when shares are created or redeemed.
YSEP: Options tied to an international developed-markets stock fund (Europe, Australia and Asia), set up to absorb some losses over a year starting each September, with gains capped. It's meant as a cushion for foreign stock exposure, and it trails in strong rallies, so it works best held the full year.
YSPC: An income fund built on indirect exposure to SpaceX, the private rocket company, using a synthetic covered call strategy on instruments tied to its value. Because SpaceX does not trade publicly, the exposure is indirect and hard to value, making this a speculative oddity.
YSPY: Aims to pay high income by selling options on a 3x leveraged S&P 500 fund, so it keeps some exposure to the market but caps how much it can gain. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and it is complicated, with risk from leverage.
YUNG: Companies selling to older consumers: health and wellness, leisure, housing and services for retirees, led by health care and consumer names. It is an actively managed bet on aging demographics: the longevity theme is slow and steady, but the fund depends on one demographic story.
YXI: A short-term trading tool that rises when the 50 biggest Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong fall, resetting its bet every day. The daily reset makes it drift over longer stretches, so it is built for brief bearish bets, not holding.
YYY: A fund of closed-end funds, holding other funds that mostly own bonds and stocks and pay high income. It's built for income, and the underlying funds use borrowing, so it can drop sharply in sell-offs.
YYYM: Municipal bond closed-end funds, pooled through an index, which together hold tax-exempt bonds from cities and states across the country. It is a high-income holding: closed-end funds often use leverage and trade at discounts, so payouts run high but prices swing more than plain muni bonds.
ZALT: Large US stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that absorb the first 10 percent of market losses over each three month period. It's for cautious investors who want stock exposure with a cushion, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
ZAP: Utilities at about three-quarters, plus industrial companies, all tied to the electric grid, power generation and equipment that supports rising electricity demand. It's a themed bet on electrification, and because utilities are a big part, it is sensitive to interest rates and can drop when they rise.
ZAPR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each April. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only fully works if you hold from the start to the end.
ZAUG: Options built on a fund of 500 large US companies, led by technology, designed to protect against a set amount of losses for one year starting in August. Gains are capped as the price of that protection, and it only works fully if held for the entire year.
ZCBA: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2030: bonds sold at a discount that return their full face value at maturity, with no interest payments along the way. It is a precise savings target with sharp rate sensitivity: prices swing hard when rates move, then settle at maturity.
ZCBB: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2031: bonds bought at a discount that return full face value at maturity, paying no interest in between. It is a precise long-term savings target: the long wait makes prices very sensitive to interest rates, rising and falling sharply.
ZCBC: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2032: deep-discount bonds that grow to full face value at maturity without paying interest along the way. It is a set-and-forget savings target for a known year: prices swing a lot with rates in the meantime, then converge at maturity.
ZCBE: Zero-coupon Treasury securities that all pay out in 2033: bonds bought below face value that mature at full value, with no interest payments in between. It is the longest target in its family: the distant maturity makes its price the most rate-sensitive of the set.
ZCBF: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2034, bought at a discount and paying no interest along the way. It is built for a goal dated around 2034, and because nothing is paid until maturity, its price swings more than most bond funds when interest rates move.
ZCBG: Zero-coupon US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2035, bought at a discount and paying no interest along the way. It is built for a goal dated around 2035, and because nothing is paid until maturity, its price swings more than most bond funds when interest rates move.
ZCSH: Holds Zcash, a cryptocurrency built around private transactions, rather than stocks or bonds. It gives brokerage account access to that single digital coin as a speculative bet, and its price can swing wildly from day to day, with no earnings or interest behind it.
ZDEK: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each December. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZDIS: An actively managed fund of fast growing US companies that are still relatively early in their growth. It is fairly concentrated, with Tesla, NVIDIA, Credo, Axon and Shopify each making up around 6% to 9% of it, and technology is about half.
ZECP: Large US companies picked because their earnings held up well through past recessions, led by technology, financials, industrials and health care. It's a core-style stock holding aimed at steadier results, but it may trail in fast rallies led by riskier companies.
ZFEB: Options on the S&P 500 designed to shield you from a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in February, while limiting your gains. It's for cautious investors who plan to hold for the full period, since protection applies only then.
ZHDG: US stocks combined with options hedges and income-producing securities in a buy-and-hedge design meant to keep a portion of stock gains while cushioning declines. The hedging trades some upside for protection, so it aims for a steadier path than an unprotected stock fund through rough markets.
ZHOG: Bonds picked opportunistically across the market: government, corporate and mortgage debt, with managers free to shift maturities and quality as they hunt for value. It works as a flexible core income holding whose results depend on the managers' judgment calls about rates and credit.
ZIG: About thirty US stocks chosen as undervalued but fundamentally strong, mostly midsize companies in consumer, energy and industrial businesses. It follows a deep value approach built on cash flow and balance sheet strength, so it is a concentrated bet that cheap, sturdy companies eventually get recognized.
ZINC: An actively managed fund of US stocks that its adviser considers good at producing income, mostly dividend payers. It leans toward financials, utilities, consumer staples and energy, with Altria, JPMorgan Chase, NorthWestern Energy and Chevron each making up roughly 3% to 5%.
ZINN: Fast-growing US companies, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths, followed by industrials and consumer businesses. It's built for long-term growth through a managed, concentrated set of stocks, so it swings more than the broad market and can lag when growth stocks fall out of favor.
ZJAN: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each January. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZJUL: US large company stocks, with technology about 40 percent, held through options that start a new one-year period each July. It's meant for people who want market exposure with a safety net against losses, but gains are capped, so it trails in strong rallies.
ZJUN: Options on the S&P 500 designed to shield you from a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in June, while limiting your gains. It's for cautious investors who plan to hold for the full period, since protection applies only then.
ZMAR: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each March. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZMAY: A defined outcome fund that holds options on the S&P 500 over a one-year period starting in May, built to cushion a set amount of losses. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only applies to someone holding from the start of the period to its end.
ZNOV: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each November. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZOCT: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each October. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZROZ: Zero coupon US Treasury bonds that mature in about 25 years or more, which pay no interest until the end. They are very safe from default and can cushion a stock portfolio in a downturn, but prices swing sharply when interest rates move, especially upward.
ZSEP: Large US companies, led by technology, held through options that protect against a set amount of stock market losses over a one-year period starting in September. It's meant for cautious stock investors, but the protection is tied to that cycle and gains are limited.
ZTAX: Municipal bonds issued by states, cities and public projects across the US, paying interest that is designed to be free of federal and state income tax. It is built for investors in higher tax brackets who want steady, tax-free income.
ZTEN: Investment grade corporate bonds chosen to behave like a single ten-year bond, with maturities clustered around a decade. It is a building-block holding for targeting a specific stretch of the yield curve, giving company bond income with interest rate sensitivity similar to a ten-year Treasury.
ZTOP: High yield bonds from the 100 largest junk bond issuers, the biggest borrowers in the below-investment-grade market. Sticking to the largest issuers keeps it in more liquid bonds, though the credit risk of junk debt remains.
ZTRE: Bonds from solid, investment grade companies that all come due in about three years, so the lineup rolls over on a tight schedule. Short maturities like these mean smaller price swings when interest rates move, suiting cautious income investors.
ZTWO: Investment grade corporate bonds with roughly two years left until they mature. The short lifespan keeps price swings small when interest rates move, making it a steadier income holding than longer corporate bond funds.
ZVOL: A fund that harvests the volatility premium, mainly by selling VIX futures, which measure expected stock market swings, when they price in more fear than usually arrives. It can earn steadily in calm markets and lose quickly in a crash, so it is a specialist trading tool.
